chapters.title: Chapter 1: Phainon
chapters.html:
When Trianne popped up next to Phainon in the shipyard it very nearly caused an accident. To his credit, the reflex to swing wildly at the jump scare only made it about halfway to target before he managed to steady the heavy beam balanced on his shoulder. Smashing one of the messengers of Janus with a garboard plank wasn’t the kind of thing that could be fixed with a heartfelt apology and baked goods. But it might be enough for the dock worker that had been knocked into the shallow water next to the drydock.

Phainon winced when he saw the poor guy flailing about with a look of bewilderment.

“Hey, you alright?” he called out, already setting down the beam before it could do anymore damage.

The man nodded but Phainon dropped down anyway to take his hand and help him to his feet. Salt water poured into his boots, soaking his pants and creeping up to where his chlamys was tied around his waist. It was too hot a day to wear anything but his bracers from the waist up.

He firmly held the man’s arm until he got his footing in the shallow water, offering a reassuring (and apologetic) smile.

“It’s really nothing,” the dock worker insisted, and Phainon let go, making sure the man was able to climb to safety before he finally gave Trianne his attention.

“You really shouldn’t be surprising people like that, Trianne.” His voice was light, more playful than scolding.

“Maybe we did come up to too fast. We’ve been practicing our flying to be even faster!” she said with a happy bounce and her arms outstretched like wings from the dock above Phainon.

He waded up the gentle slope along the underside of the ship’s skeleton and she followed with light steps along the walkway beside him. It was starting to take shape, but it would be a long time before this masterpiece was seaworthy.

“Did you want to show me? Maybe ask for a race?”

“You’re fast, Snowy, but we are a lot faster! It wouldn’t be much of a race.”

A quick stomp on dry land only cleared away a little bit of the sea and Phainon took the time to lean his shoulder against the wall beside him so he could take each boot off in turn to dump the water back where it belonged.

“So, what is the hurry, Trianne?”

“Oh!” She bunny hopped in place and put both her hands on her hips. “We have a very important message!”

Phainon wringed salt water from his top and then shifted it back over his shoulder, pinning it in place with the fibula haphazardly. It didn’t matter much to him if things looked perfect as long as it was functional.

“Agy wants to see you today.”

It was like a shock through his system, surging along his spine and making him stand up straight with a newfound sense of directive. It only took one hand and a light leap to vault back up onto the walkway and then Phainon was hurrying to say goodbye to the shipyard’s master. Even if he was working on a volunteer basis, it was rude to leave without saying anything at all.

Okhema was a shining beacon on the hill. One of the biggest and most beautiful port cities in Amphoreus. It was built under the watchful gaze of Kephale and the Dawn Device that kept the Black Tide as a distant and forgettable threat. Beautiful buildings climbed up the hills and mountains and stretched along the bay around bustling docks and shipyards. Dozens of big ships anchored on the water, waiting for the tide to go out to sea.

Phainon treasured the climb from the shore to the Marmoreal Palace. Where most would take the passages to travel swiftly, the steep road was an opportunity to work his calves, build more endurance, and challenge himself to sprint at the steepest stretches. He was only partly serious about racing, but Trianne zoomed alongside him anyway, cheering him on as she flew by until it turned less into a competition and more into coaching, pushing him along faster and faster. He had to take a second at the top of the hill to put his hands on his knees and catch his breath.

Eager or not, Phainon didn’t dare meet with Aglaea in soggy clothes. He had stopped dripping sea water along the way but there was still a shipyard smell that clung to the fabric, the wonderful scent of hard work, good lumber, and tar. He didn’t think she’d mind that part as much as the lingering fishy salty smell from the extra dip in the ocean.

He had a room here at the palace for his things. It wasn’t extravagant but Phainon was cared for like the other Chrysos Heirs. Aglaea wasn’t a Queen or the Ruler of Okhema, but she carried a weight as the leader of the Heirs and the Flame Chase journey as well as Okhema’s Admiral, overseeing the city’s protection from seafaring threats. Under her guidance a fair number of coreflames had been recovered over the centuries and the people respected her and her dutiful protection of the city and their surrounding territories. As the keeper of Mnestia’s coreflame, her golden threads carried a beautiful and delicate power that kept the peace.

It was Aglaea that had found Phainon in the barracks, devoid of life, little more than a blade to be directed. She gave him new purpose, a better reason to fight, and he owed her everything for that alone.

“Tell Aglaea I’ll be there soon,” he requested of Trianne, who gave him a happy salute.

“You got it!” Her red hair flashed in the corner of his eye as she zipped away.

He pushed the door to his room open without ceremony, stripping as he went, leaving articles of clothing wherever they fell. One of his boots got kicked into his bookshelf, his chlamys ended up on the kline. He ripped open drawers looking for something clean and, more importantly, appropriate. Phainon had learned the hard way that Aglaea felt very strongly about colors and appearance. The dressmaker knew her trade and took offense when he didn’t at least try to understand the basics of color theory.

He pulled on pants and his high-collared v-neck tee, black, gold, and matching. The long white and gold coat went on over the top. Then his black boots, his bracers, the pauldron, his blue half cape over the shoulder… Phainon double checked himself in a mirror as he adjusted the straps over his chest. Heaven forbid the motifs and patterns didn’t match. Most of his clothing was sun themed, but there were some stragglers in there somewhere with different patterns.

It was his usual look, so the quick check was enough to settle any brief anxiety. Confidence restored, he hurried to Aglaea’s office.

“Aglaea!” Phainon called cheerfully from the doorway. He gave the frame a gentle tap with his knuckles for good measure. “You wanted to see me? Do you need some help?”

She was standing near the balcony, not far enough out to be seen by the public, but enough to bask in Kephale’s eternal daylight. She sparkled in the light where it caught on shiny silk fabric, cream under gold, dancing with the thread and the natural curls that bounced under her chin. The laurels in her short hair perched as delicately as her manicured nails and the fine straps of her heels. She always dressed like one of her models, perfection among mortals, as guarded and picturesque as a marble masterpiece, and equally as unmoving.

“Phainon,” she greeted without turning, rolling his name on her tongue with a natural and alluring grace.

He took the greeting as permission to approach, stepping deeper into her office workshop. Despite her best efforts, her workspace was naturally cluttered. It was an organized cluttered with hand written labels in cursive pinned to shelves, boxes, and collections of expensive thread and fabric. Her garmentmakers drifted in a neat line along the wall opposite her massive desk, piled high with papyrus scrolls, maps, and clay tablets pounded thin.

“Did something happen?” he asked, careful to keep the worry from his voice, even if he harbored it in his heart.

For as light as she seemed, there was a weight to her shoulders. When she turned and walked back to her desk it was with measured footsteps, as though she’d be crushed by that weight with a single misstep.

“Pirates,” she said simply as though that explained everything and it kind of did. The distant Black Tide was less of a threat than piracy. Displaced people, separated from their homes and driven to desperation frequently turned to the seas and her bounty. Okhema relied less on foreign trade these days but no small amount of their food and supplies to fuel the city’s wealth and comfort came in the bellies of big ships. “They have plagued Okhema as long as there has been a city, but my fleet needs a more skilled warrior at the helm.”

His smile faded with the seriousness of the situation.

“I would not ask anything of you had I any other way,” she said softly, and he jumped at the chance to correct her.

“You don’t need to,” he promised with a hand over his heart, “tell me what you need me to do, and I’ll see it through.”

She matched his gesture and looked at him with clouded eyes. “I’m giving you a ship.”

-

Phainon was good at most things but not all of it was natural talent. In his heart he was still the son of a farmer, most comfortable with two feet on solid ground or at most the loose of good, tilled soil. The sway of a ship took a lot of getting used to. He knew how they worked; he helped build them in his spare time and every soldier learned how to sail. He knew which ropes loosed the sails, when it was best to anchor, how to follow the tides, and anything he didn’t know he trusted to his crew.

And for now, that was enough.

Aglaea had given him a single task when his new crew disembarked: to hunt the most notorious of pirates. The Goldweaver was certain, whether by intuition or by gathered intelligence Phainon wasn’t sure, that most of their lost ships were the work of a single crew. A single very strong crew that left burning husks of ships in their wake and few if any survivors, so scarred by their encounters that they were rendered mute or unsound of mind. A crew that sailed under red and gold with blood painted on their hull. Rather than feed the beast, Aglaea wanted to send her best, and Phainon was unrivaled in Okhema.

It was a lot of pressure, but Phainon was eager to please and eager to prove himself, starting with his new command. He learned the name of every crewmate on day one, establishing a rapport with his new first mate.

Marcus was attentive and friendly, a skilled and seasoned sailor and warrior. Bolaris already had ideas brewing for how to upgrade the ship while he managed their supplies. Zeno had plotted several routes using the neighboring isles as waymarks. To name a few.

All of Phainon’s crew were the best of the best and he had taken a liking to the Speeding Sol from the moment he stepped onto her deck and very nearly got clotheslined by the rising main sail. Despite the risks involved with their mission, speed was just as important as firepower, so Phainon chose the smaller vessel. She still had a solid bronze battering ram on her bow and courage in her sails, but the smaller and more elite crew would be easier to care for and they could spend longer stretches at sea.

Phainon took his turn at the oars with the men on breezy days and helped them hold the sails on the windy ones. They shared their meals together and sparred on deck. He took watches in shifts, and he personally took responsibility for every failing, even when he was reassured that something was easily fixed and not worth fretting over.

It had taken them a week of sailing, pressing farther away from Okhema to find any sign of something sinister in the waters.

The wreckage of a merchant ship had drifted by on the currents and a close inspection of the waterlogged wood showed strain and tearing.

“What do you think?” Phainon asked Marcus.

The man was feeling the wood, pressing into it with his fingers. “It’s possible they ran aground and a reef tore the hull…”

“There aren’t any shoals or reefs near here,” Zeno insisted.

Phainon scratched his chin with the back of his pointer finger, an absentminded gesture as he contemplated. “We found enough of the ship but none of the cargo.”

“Unless they were shipping heavy ores, it’s unreasonable to assume we wouldn’t find ANY cargo,” Marcus agreed.

“Not unless it was liberated from the sea. The wreck can’t be more than a day old, let’s stay around these waters for a time and shout if you see canvas on the horizon.”

--

The empty seas had taunted them for another few days, until a tired crewman had spotted a distant fire, beyond the reach of the dawn device. They took to their oars and chased the light to the horizon, crossing the threshold into the dark just before the entry hour but by the time they caught up…

The wreckage was slowly sinking, bright in the dark where it still burned above the water. There was blood everywhere, but no bodies, no cargo.

Phainon carded a hand through his hair, the other was on the railing. His crew lined up alongside him to lean over the edge of the Sol for a better look at the mess on the surface of the sea. Very slowly he let his hand fall over his face, stressed, before clenching a tight fist to drop onto the rail with a frustrated growl.

The men nearest him turned in surprise but he was already reining in the outburst. “Get the hooks and small boats. Let’s see if they left anyone,” he ordered softly. And then he turned on his heel and stalked to the bow to climb into the small boat himself.

He remembered the wreck in pieces. Each snapshot tugging at memories lurking under a thin but carefully crafted surface. The fire was too familiar; wood burned the same color as wheat. Streaks of blood in the water and on the sails, crimson in the firelight still glowed the same as when it was spattered across stone. The familiar smell of burning flesh clung to the air.

Every image accompanied by another from his youth that Phainon saw regularly in his nightmares. Death, destruction, and fire haunted him, providing kindling, motivation, and a deep desire under his duty for revenge. That flame flickered again inside him, but it was easily set aside for the more immediate concern and desperate hope for survivors.

Ash dusted their shoulders as they rowed quietly through the mess, using long fishing hooks to move debris, searching for life or even bodies that could be recovered and given a proper burial. Phainon used one such hook to drag a length of sail closer until he could grab it with his hands and pull the scraps in, but there was nothing but tears.

“Captain,” Zeno said in a near whisper just over the crackle of the flames. He didn’t need to say anything more.

Phainon tsked and steeled his jaw, grinding his teeth with his lip curled back ever so slightly as righteous fury crawled inside him until he trembled with the tension. “We need to find them before they do this again.”

--

It had been a very long time since Phainon had been outside of the reach of the Dawn Device but there wasn’t any time to appreciate the natural passage of time. Aquila had been vanquished several centuries past and had resumed the opening of their eyes. Day and night cycles resumed outside of Okhema but there was little time to appreciate it.

Phainon remained focused on the task at hand. Zeno was using stars and maps to chart their progress and there was undeniable energy in the crew. Even if there was no way to prove it, they were certain that they were catching up. There were little signs from birds to discarded ship waste, to yet more destruction. And through it all, Phainon remained driven but cheerful, checking on each of his men in turn at every junction in a gesture of responsible love.

“You should take some time for yourself,” Marcus told him in a whisper. He settled on the crate beside Phainon and offered him a waterskin.

“I do, I promise,” he whispered back with a muted chuckle. The waterskin nearly slipped from his hands when he reached for it. The ocean spray made it slick. Despite the choppy waters, most of the crew was sound asleep under the blanket of stars.

“I can take this watch. You should sleep.”

Phainon shook his head and his bangs swayed and bounced. “I couldn’t if I tried.”

“Still haven’t quite found your sea legs, Captain?”

“I’m sure they’re just around the corner,” he laughed, miming a curve with his hands as he did so. He took a long drink, tilting his head back and leaving it back even as the waterskin settled in his lap.

“I did miss the stars,” he admitted, and Marcus took a second to follow his gaze.

“Are you very familiar with them, Captain?”

“Marcus, you can stop with the Captain now.”

“…of course, Lord Phainon.”

Maybe it was a lost cause. Baby steps.

“Not very familiar,” he said instead, “but when I was a kid, my friend and I would watch the thief star just after curtain-fall hour and count the rest as they appeared in the sky.” Phainon had noted the thief star earlier that night. It had been a long time since he had seen it glow red. Perhaps it saved that color for the lands beyond Kephale. “And what of you, Lord Marcus.”

“I was born and raised in Okhema. This is my first time seeing the night sky.”

“And what think you of it?”

“It seems cold.”

Phainon mulled that over for a second, watching the sky and waiting for it to agree but then the wind carried the softest sound, and he was very suddenly on his feet striding towards the rail, staring straight ahead into the dark and waiting with a hand on one of the lines for balance.

“Lord-“

“Shh.” Phainon held out a hand towards Marcus without looking at him until he was silent and then he let the arm fall at glacial speed. As though the creak of his clothing would be too loud.

For a moment there was only the slap of choppy waves against the side of the Sol, the creak of the masts, the soft snores of his crew… and then the breeze tickled his ears and nose again with the faint sound of steel on steel, battle cries, and the smell of burning.

He turned his head like whip in the direction of the wind, squinting in the dark until the waves lifted them high enough to see the glow on the horizon.

“Found you,” he muttered to himself and then louder, “Marcus! Wake up the crew, to oars and arms!”

Marcus jumped and hurried to obey as Phainon hurried to the tiller. It was held in place with a rope when they were safe to drift. He kicked the heavy rope free and pushed his whole body against the beam. The ship groaned but began to turn as the crew started to rouse full of confused shouts and hurried scrambling.

The first mate was shouting orders; the oars were biting into the water. There was a rush of wind that grabbed at Phainon’s cape as the sail raised in a hurry and scooped the ocean breeze to lurch them forwards towards destiny.

The sounds got louder, the fire brighter and bigger as they raced and Phainon started praying, deep in his heart, that they would get there in time. It didn’t take them long to catch up enough to see the second ship, her red sails unfurled, ready to flee. She was a massive thing crowned in gold with a massive lion’s head carved into her bow. He could see ropes and men pulling supplies from the burning ship as they approached. There were shouts and the pirates turned to flee.

“To port!” Marcus shouted, “we must pursue!”

“No!” Phainon shouted over him and there was a pause in the rowers, as they waited. As much as Phainon wanted to give chase… “The burning ship, there’s still time to check for survivors.”

The sails were on fire, but the hull didn’t seem to have been broken. It floated aimlessly. “Ram the side at an angle,” he ordered.

Phainon gave the tiller to Zeno and was already hurrying to the bow in a zig zag, stepping around crewmates and grabbing onto the lines where he could until he was standing on the railing, waiting as the ship approached.

Too fast!

The Sol slammed into the burning merchant ship. Glancing enough to not tear the hull but hard enough for the bronze to grab onto her. Phainon leaped at the last second and for a long heartbeat he was airborne above the water.

He hit the deck hard. His knees buckled and the warrior rolled with the momentum until his side slammed into the base of the mast. Burning fabric was raining from above, filling his lungs with smoke and ash. There was no one on deck, not a single sign of life. A permeating sense of dread filled his chest as Phainon lurched to his feet with the roll of the ship. He could hear shouting from the Sol but couldn’t make out the words. As he looked back the main sail came undone and slammed onto the deck, cutting him off in a shower of burning splinters.

The fire licked at his boots and clothes as Phainon stumbled away with an arm held over his face to protect his eyes from the flickering embers.

“Lord Phainon!” Marcus shouted.

“I’m fine! Don’t let the fire spread to the Sol! I’m going to go look below!”

Phainon didn’t wait for a response before he was running and stumbling towards the stern, looking for stairs in the dark. It only took a moment. There was a lantern hanging beside the doorway, trying its best to be bright in the face of the raging fire beside it. He ripped the thing off the wall and half ran; half fell down the stairs into the belly of the ship.

“Is there anyone here!” he shouted, running the length of the hold, scanning the shadows for movement. All of the hammocks were empty, piles of intermittent dust kicked up as he ran through them and Phainon had to take a second to cough and clear his lungs before he could shout again. “Anyone!”

The ship creaked ominously. Water sloshed from below and when he looked down, Phainon saw water start to pool around his feet, leeching between the floorboards from the floor below, slowly filling the belly of the dying ship. The roar of the fire above was so loud, he worried that he wouldn’t be able to hear the survivors, but there weren’t even bodies.

Had they already been thrown overboard? Were they kidnapped? Phainon snarled and punched one of the columns. He let the pirates go and any survivors could be onboard, kept as cargo, prisoners!

He turned to run back to the stairs and then the whole world tilted at an impossible angle and Phainon was thrown sideways into a hammock. It softened the initial blow and then dumped him into empty space where time stilled for a breath and then he hit the side of the ship and flopped onto a puddle. The ripping of the hull was loud enough to make the fire seem distant as a second ship slammed into the side of the sinking vessel.

For a mercy, the impact settled, and the ship didn’t capsize. It slammed back down, upright, and Phainon was jostled, the water that had pooled with the tilt raced back across the floor, dragging him along until he managed to grab another hammock and drag himself back to standing with a shake of his head. Salt and smoke stung his eyes and stiffened his joints. The ceiling above groaned and he could see the glow of fire above the flimsy flicker of his noble lantern.

But above it all, Phainon could hear the distant and unmistakable sounds of battle. His men were screaming, battle horns cried, steel met steel amid the snarls of war beasts; metallic and awful screeches that tore through Phainon’s soul with a shiver, a familiar and horrible sound he couldn’t quite place. The water beneath him bubbled, ankle deep now, the timer was ticking like sand in an hourglass and above him, his people, his friends were dying at the hands of murderers.

With an angry shout, Phainon scrambled towards the stairs, the lantern left behind to roll into the inky water where its meager flame was swallowed without mercy.

He was nearly there when the ceiling gave way and the main deck collapsed above him. Phainon recoiled from the burning mast and the shower of dust and embers. The burning sail billowed around movement in the smoke and when the ocean wind finally pushed that curtain aside, Phainon’s eyes met that of another warrior.

He was fury and battle incarnate, a lion of a man, all muscle and power, with a thick mane of blonde hair that hung past his shoulders. The fire glinted off his golden gauntlets, embers and burning flesh clinging to the sharpness of his claws. Blood glinted where it splashed across his armored legs and disappeared in the crimson and black of his robes and the tattoos that danced on his exposed chest.

Blue flashed as Phainon drew his sword, fury rising in his chest when the pirate stood and flicked blackened flesh from his fingers. He snarled and surged forward but Phainon’s first step was cut short as the ship lurched again with a tearing scream.

He hit the water and all sound stopped entirely.

It couldn’t have been more than a minute that Phainon had been under the water. At least that’s what he told himself. He distantly remembered feeling a rough hand on his collar, sharp tugs at his feet, an orange glow in the water, but then he was heaving and sputtering with his cheek pressed against waterlogged lumber.

He felt so heavy blinking away the salt as he tried to push himself up on the makeshift raft. Phainon shook his head rapidly to cast away some of the sea, to keep it from dripping further into his eyes as he searched for something familiar.

The Sol was on fire, sinking into the depths of the ocean just as the creeping light of dawn started to color the sky behind her. Phainon felt his heart go with it and as he scanned for more life, searched for any struggling in the water, any sign of his crew, that feeling sank deeper and deeper.

“No!” he shouted to no one and then the sea shifted behind him.

Phainon clung to the wood with white knuckles, careful to keep his balance, to not submit to the ocean, as he glared over his shoulder. The massive hull of the pirate ship crept up alongside him and someone dove into the water next to him. He instinctively kicked at the person, but a strong arm grabbed his leg and pulled him into the water, embracing him from behind and looping a rope around his chest. Phainon felt the squeeze as it tightened under his arms and for a moment that was all he could feel. The arm had let him go and he was drifting deep, watching his ship join the other in a slow-motion fall into the black.

Failure crept up his bones.

Not again.

The rope tugged. Water ripped by with the rest of the weight on his shoulders.

And then he was breathing again, up and up until he felt the smooth wood of a well-crafted deck against his back while that glorious light of dawn glittered on the red and gold sails above.

chapters.title: Chapter 2: Chryseus Leo
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Phainon and Mydei meet

Chapter Notes

I've literally already ruined the pacing of my outline. This will be so much longer than 19 chapters I can tell. Why am I like this?

Mydei’s bare feet hit the deck with a soggy splash less than a minute before the body they pulled out of the water landed behind him with a squelching thud. He unwrapped the heavy rope from around his arm and waist and tossed it to the side, giving his men a grateful nod in the process. The water weight was pulling his pants low on his hips, but he at least had the common sense to take everything else off before he dove back into the water.

He walked away from where the others were starting to crowd, up the steps to the upper deck where his armor and the rest of his clothes were laid across a crate, still damp from when the capsizing ship had thrown him into the sea with the other guy. With the sun rising it wouldn’t be too long he hoped with a sigh.

“Prince,” an old man said to get his attention.

Mydei ran a hand through his bangs to brush them away from his eyes, the seawater dripping down his arms and chest as he squeezed the silken strands and turned to face his teacher. Krateros was offering him dry boots. Simple, but his size, and he gratefully took them with both hands to set them on the crate while he wrung the worst of the ocean from his pants.

“Is he alive?” Krateros asked, peering over the railing at the crowd.

“Alive enough to nearly kick me.”

“Give him space!” Perdikkas shouted, no more than a voice in the pit of curious people. The men weren’t listening.

From the upper deck it was easy enough to see them crowd the puddle near the railing, curiosity getting the better of them. They rarely took survivors onboard. There were rarely any survivors to bring aboard.

“I said give him space!” he heard Perdikkas shout once more and then there was a flash of blue light, and everyone was scattering with shouts and hurried gasps.

Mydei’s eyes narrowed as he pulled on the boots, watching the pack scramble to lower their spears and point their swords at the most beautiful and simultaneously pathetic looking person he had ever seen.

“Alive enough to think he can fight.”

“If he is a danger,” Krateros was saying, “we should kill him and give him to the ocean. It won’t do to have a rabid dog on board.”

Soaked to the bone and holding a great sword taller than he was, the warrior swung in wide, clumsy arcs, a demand for space more than a declaration of war. He stumbled to the railing, sword held out in response to the spears pointed his way while he coughed and heaved water from his lungs. Snow-white hair clung to his forehead and neck, plastered on his head with the water weight aside from two stubborn bits on the very top his head that stood upright. It dripped into his wild eyes that darted back and forth over his men who had expertly cornered him against the rail, an unmoving cage.

He was acting like a startled, injured animal. In a way, he was. He was displaced from his ship, removed from his people, and had just suffered through a traumatic encounter. Even bogged down by heavy clothes, the man had a solid stance and was potentially very dangerous.

“Hey, it’s okay!” Perdikkas was saying, one hand outstretched, the other resting on the hilt of his sword as he tried to approach.

Mydei started running the moment the second boot was on.

The warrior’s attention had latched onto Perdikkas and in a fraction of second he had turned from confused to enraged, lashing out with his sword in an expert, if somewhat slow strike.

In the middle of its horizontal arc, Mydei landed on the flat of the blade with both boots. He had run along the rail and leaped, forcing the tip of the weapon into the deck and the warrior to stumble as the unexpected weight ripped him forward. The sword clattered uselessly across the polished wood and half a dozen men rushed to contain him.

Mydei rolled as he fell, and his men hurried to catch him and help him to his feet. Perdikkas steadied him with a firm grip on his arm, and they waited for the whole five seconds that it took for his soldiers to pile the guy and wrestle him to his knees, both arms pulled out to the sides. Still, he struggled and Mydei had to admire his strength. It was taking four men to hold him down.

“Perdikkas!” Leonnius shoved through the masses to their sides. “Are you alright?”

“Yeah, Mydei stopped him.”

“How did you-?” he started to say but stopped when Mydei tilted his chin.

“Cornered hounds bite,” the Prince said and then he was walking towards the man.

“You have a funny way of thanking the people who saved your life,” he scolded as he stalked forward, snatching a spear from one of his men as he went. The brightest blue eyes glared at him, lip curled back.

“Where are the others?” he spat, voice rough, no doubt the salt from the sea had ravaged his throat.

Mydei tilted his head. “What others?”

“Your other captives, pirate!”

What was he talking about? Mydei drummed his fingers on the spear and firmly told him. “We have no captives.”

The struggle slowly came to a stop, and the warrior visibly slumped. Mydei could see his emotions cycle in his expressions: surprise, skepticism, and finally grief when he studied Mydei’s face and seemed to find the truth there. He also saw the exact moment that the man steeled himself, tucking away those emotions and hiding them behind a mask of defiance with gritted teeth and a sharp gaze.

“You killed them…” the survivor growled.

“Yes, we did. We had to.”

He turned his face to the side, glaring at Mydei’s men as he started to pull again, fighting to get free.

Up close and straining it was easier to appreciate him. In the hold of the broken ship, it had been hard to really see the man, but he had a pleasing outline and a solid build. His clothes were very fine but there were calluses on his hands from working ropes and swinging swords.

“Look at me, Okheman,” Mydei instructed but the man refused.

The Prince tapped the butt of the spear against the deck with a commanding thud, spun it in a circle and then slid his hand up the shaft to steady the point under the man’s chin, forcing that delicate face and sharp jawline to tilt back until their eyes met again.

There was hatred there, yes, but there was also grief, and Mydei got the feeling this pathetic, wet dog had been misinformed.

“What’s your name?” he asked.

White-hair refused to respond, his lips pressed into a tight, thin line. Mydei pressed with the spear, forcing his head to the side as his eyes flicked down.

“Did anyone check his collar for tags?” Mydei called out to the crew with slightest curl of a smile.

“I am no one’s dog!” the man snapped and Mydei pulled the spear back to crouch low in front of him instead, their noses nearly touched. He could see the way the man’s breath hitched, held tight while those sapphire eyes briefly dropped to study Mydei’s still bare chest and arms. They roamed around the gold ring around his bicep, the tightness of his still wet pants against his thighs and counted his tattoos before darting back to meet Mydei’s own judging gaze.

“Are you not?” Mydei asked as he reached for the man’s collar.

He recoiled, pressing back as far as his captors would allow, and Mydei paused until he stilled again. Bare fingertips traced along the leather collar on the man’s neck, over the sun marking beneath it, deceptively gentle, feeling along his fluttering, too fast pulse, until he found what he was looking for. The thread was barely thicker than hair when Mydei pulled it from the collar and held it between them so it could shimmer in the light of the spreading dawn like spun gold.

He must not have known. There was surprise in that blue-eyed stare when he saw it and utter bewilderment when Mydei snapped it in two, the length of it dissolving into dust.

Mydei reached out again to press his fingers into a cut across the man’s cheekbone. It was a scrape, undoubtedly caused by the chaos on the merchant ship and cleaned by the sea. No doubt it would sting later when the adrenaline faded, and this man had a chance to set aside his rage and take stock of his situation. He pressed hard enough to make it bleed again until the gold streaked across his fingertips.

“This is why you survived, Okheman,” Mydei told him. He showed the man the golden blood on the pads of his fingers. “Not because we chose to spare you, but because the Black Tide couldn’t take you.”

Mydei watched the recognition settle in his face and filed away every minute reaction.

“The Black Tide?” he repeated aloud, as though he didn’t quite hear him the first time and Mydei saw the fight drain from his shoulders with a shaky, long-held breath.

He looked up at the men holding him and gave them a reassuring nod. They let go and the man fell forward onto Mydei’s arm. He held him steadily for a second by the chest and then slowly pushed him back to sit on his own heels when it was clear he wouldn’t fall over without help.

They sat there for a moment, the Okheman processing what he had heard with his head down and his arms at his side and then he started to laugh. It was a rolling, wheezing sound, the hint of something melodic buried under a layer of weariness.

“Do you really expect me to believe the word of a murderer?” he asked when he finally calmed.

“Were you not there?”

The Ohkeman’s brow furrowed, and his frown deepened, straining to recall. Mydei stood up straight and waited, looking down at the man who seemed to still be struggling with his memory.

One breath.

Two.

“Hephastion,” the Prince said softly, and it took all of two seconds for the First Mate to take charge.

“Nothing left to see, let’s get underway!” he ordered, and the men dispersed, returning to their duties.

“Perdikkas is going to get you dry clothes,” Mydei told their guest firmly, “If you attack him again, I will snap your neck and feed you to the sea, Nameless Hero.”

“Phainon,” he mumbled and for a second Mydei almost didn’t hear him, “my name is Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

“Welcome aboard the Chryseus Leo, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

-

“The Deliverer of Okhema?” Hephastion asked.

Ptolemy nodded. He had a scroll open on his lap. Tomes were hard to keep at sea, and the older ones were starting to fray along the edges, but it didn’t stop their resident record keeper from doing his very best to maintain a collection worthy of the Crown Prince of Kremnos and his own curiosities. The book worm had managed to assemble a wide variety between the pieces he had taken from Castrum Kremnos, the books smuggled from the library at Garbaniphoro, and the mass of writings plucked from ships they had conquered at sea.

The scroll on his lap was one such piece, liberated from the private collection of a Captain of the Goldweaver’s Navy. It seemed the hero that Mydei had plucked from the sea had the accolades to be worthy of song and poetry.

“…that guy? Are you certain?”

“Do you know any other Chrysos Heirs with blue eyes, white hair, and a golden sun on their neck?” Perdikkas asked.

“The thread proves it,” Ptolemy reminded them.

Mydei lay on his bed while they talked. His room was small, but private. It served as his Captain’s Office, full of maps, charting equipment, records, odds and ends, and personal supplies. His friends had piled in while he had finished changing and insisted on discussion while he tried to nap after another long night.

“I would have thought the Goldweaver’s golden hero would’ve been smarter. Sending himself and his men onto a corroded ship?” Hephastion wondered aloud.

“Arrogant.”

“Ignorance,” Mydei corrected. He could hear them twist in their chairs to look at him, but he kept watching the ceiling, looking past it as the hammock swayed with the ship. “It was on his face.”

“Why would the Goldweaver send the Deliverer away from Okhema without telling him about the Black Tide?” Ptolemy tried instead.

“Maybe she doesn’t know,” Leonnius finally chimed in.

Perdikkas shook his head. “She knows everything.”

“Even beyond the reach of the Dawn Device?” Ptolemy questioned.

Mydei sighed and sat up, effectively silencing the room. They watched him walk across the room to get his gauntlets from the desk and slide them on one by one. He flexed his hands and tightened the straps and then excused himself without saying another word.

Behind him the room continued to chatter, speculating wildly even when he closed the door and stepped out into the sunlight.

“Are you also here to waste my time with pointless speculations?” Mydei asked with crossed arms, “or perhaps you want to force my hand instead?”

Krateros shook his head. He was leaning beside the door. There was no need to keep guard, so he was likely there to eavesdrop and be readily available if he was called.

“It was your mother’s wish that I teach you, not make decisions on your behalf but if you would hear my advice, I would give it.”

Mydei twisted just enough to look over his shoulder at the old Kremnoan. “I would.”

“The Okheman is trouble. No good can come from having him on board.”

“Ptolemy claims he’s the Goldweaver’s Deliverer. They believe him to be a Chrysos Heir without equal. Surely, such a warrior is strong enough for my ship.”

“He is at most a prisoner of war, a prized agent of our ancient enemy. Mydeimos, you are not his Captain, not his King,” Krateros insisted.

“I am no one’s King,” Mydei growled and then he stomped away.

-

The boots and exomis Phainon had been given were rough but dry, which for now was a blessing while he waited in the dark. Perdikkas, who seemed to be the ship’s medic, had been kind and gentle helping him get free of his familiar clothing without destroying them. He hadn’t said much, and Phainon hadn’t asked much at the time, still reeling. When he was clothed and dry, the man had left him in a cell in the belly of the ship to be alone with his feelings.

The brig was cold and replete with shadow; one row of half a dozen cells made of steel bars and lit by dull, intermittent lanterns. Some daylight filtered in from above through the checker patterned grate in the ceiling, but the light had two floors to get through and there was something partially covering the grate on the top deck.

Phainon had hoped that the pirate was lying about the others, that there would be familiar faces in the dark, but while the cells were full to bursting, it was with treasures and supplies, not people. Even the cell Phainon was locked inside was nearly packed tight with spare rope and treasures taken from other ships. There almost wasn’t any room for him and his guilt.

He sat on one of the crates with his knees pulled up and his back to the bars. If he listened, he could hear the crew moving above him, the steady beat of a drum as they rowed farther from home.

Phainon wanted to be angry, he wanted to be sad, but truthfully, he was mostly confused.

The Black Tide was a distant, familiar threat. When he was very young, Phainon saw his small isle of Aedes Elysiae swallowed by the Black Tide, a literal surge of putrid corruption that ate at the wheat and flesh, warping his friends and family into monsters that crumbled into dust when his shaky hands drove a sword through their tortured bodies. At the time he didn’t know why he had been spared, and the grief had crushed him, turning him into a shell of himself that longed for vengeance against an impossible enemy.

Aglaea had given him answers but not closure, the motivation to always press on but with the weight of them on his back.

They were not buried memories that he had tried to forget, he kept them close, but a part of him must’ve still been afraid enough to overlook the signs as the Sol had sailed. There was the dust in the hold of the merchant ship, the horrible feeling in his chest when they couldn’t find any corpses, the familiar sounds of newborn black tide monsters screeching for relief, and the realization that the corruption had probably doomed the Sol the moment she rammed into her side.

He had made excuses in the moment without realizing it, assigning the carnage to pirates and feeling validated when he recognized them as Kremnoan. Their reputation as warmongers made it easy to assume and he felt terrible for that condemnation when evidence proved otherwise. Marcus, Zeno, Bolaris, and all the others. He’d have to carry them now too.

Phainon hadn’t seen evidence of the Black Tide this close to Okhema since Aglaea had sent him to Janusopolis to escort refugees. The monsters there had strayed from the Tide, still dangerous, but bearing no risk of corruption. In the couple years since, the Council had stopped worrying over the absent threat, focused instead on the keeping of Okhema’s wealth and Aglaea had returned to focusing on the Flame Chase Journey.

He ran a hand along his bare throat. That man, the Captain of this ship… the heat from his fingertips still lingered where he had touched Phainon with unexpected gentleness, as though he was supremely aware of the roughness of his skin and was afraid to hurt him. The shock of it had sent shivers down his spine and a warmth in his belly that had Phainon questioning his mission entirely.

He hadn’t known that Aglaea had left one of her threads on his person, but he wasn’t surprised in retrospect. The way it had been so easily plucked and destroyed explained their missing intelligence. How else could Aglaea have not known that the ship roaming the seas, taking their goods was Kremnoan? How else could they not know how far the Black Tide now reached? If this ship was the one hunting the Black Tide across the water, and they were destroying Aglaea’s threads and network along the way, there was no chance she would know these very critical pieces of information.

He needed to return to Okhema, but there was little hope of that now. Eurypon’s Navy was the stuff of legends and had regularly clashed with Okhema in the past. Before the Black Tide they had battled over territories giving rise to heroic feats that were painted in mosaic on temple walls. Eurypon had been quiet for a time, but that bad blood surely lingered still.

Phainon tilted his head back to bang against the bars and took a deep breath before a tiny movement caught his eye. He turned to see the biggest red eyes just a little too close.

On reflex he yelped and fell off the crate in a surprised leap and crashed into the bars in the small space.

The chimera watched him with calm amusement where he lay on the crate next to Phainon’s and while the man flailed for balance, it calmly picked itself up and hopped into the warm spot that was left behind to settle back down to watch the new toy.

It was such an unexpected crewmate that he took an extra few seconds to process that the little thing was here in his cell with him and then Phainon just had a dozen questions rapidly bouncing around his brain. It took a wide chimera yawn to shove them all aside and replace with them an overpowering need to pet and fawn over the perfect little guy.

“Hey,” Phainon crooned as he reached out, “what’s your name?”

The chimera was white on the bottom and orange on top, nearly red in the dim light of the hold. His ruff was dark brown with big tufty cheeks in soft cream. Phainon scratched the top of his head gently, tracing a triangle between both ears and the soft spot in the middle of his brow.

Pleased with Phainon’s offering, the chimera very slowly closed his eyes and rolled onto his side to stretch his paws, all four adorned with orange socks and pink toe beans and for a happy minute there was peace. And then Phainon tried to rub the chimera’s belly and then there were claws and teeth in his hand and they were back to a tentative standoff.

“I’m sorry!” Phainon apologized with his hands held up in a peaceful gesture and the chimera looked him up and down, contemplating forgiveness. “I won’t pet your belly again, promise.”

His tail swished back and forth, the tip of it curling ever so slightly on each pass, the chimera slowly relaxing again…

And then the door opened.

Phainon got to his feet and turned to face his captor with a guarded expression. The Captain was dressed the same way as he had been when first they met in the brief moment on the merchant ship, long flowing red robes, half his chest exposed, and armored legs. His arms were crossed, sharp claws tapping lightly on his arm as bright gold eyes studied Phainon in the limited light.

He felt like a caged animal, waiting for the predator to come along to consume him. This was a lion, content in his den, and Phainon was the defiant Oryx who wasn’t going down without a fight.

The chimera stretched once more, peeped in greeting, and then jumped from the crate to pad up to the bars. It took the animal a moment to squeeze between them and when its face got stuck for a few long seconds, Phainon very nearly dropped to his knees to help it. But it managed with a long purr, bug eyes, and pawing at the air until it sprang free with a pop! He shook himself off as though that wasn’t the greatest prison break of all time and trotted up to the pirate to rub against his legs and paw at his knees.

The Captain uncrossed his arms and very slowly dropped to one knee so he could scratch the chimera’s back and sides. Once more, the fuzzy menace flopped over with a happy coo.

“W-Wait-!” Phainon cautioned when the pirate went to scratch and pet the animal’s belly, but he was undeterred and to Phainon’s surprise the warning was misplaced. The chimera happily accepted the belly scratches to become a satisfied and comfortable puddle on the floor.

“He bit you.” It wasn’t a question and there was no concern in the deep voice that rumbled in his chest.

Phainon instinctively reached to rub at the little bites and scratches on his hand. Gold smudged across the raised injuries. “…yeah.”

“Only those that Fig Stew deems worthy may pet his belly.”

So, the chimera’s name was Fig Stew. Cute. “And a pirate like you is worthy?”

The scratching stopped and the man stood up straight again. “More worthy than you, Deliverer.”

Phainon tsked and looked down at his hand, rubbing a little more firmly as though that would erase the sting of rejection. “He just hasn’t given me a chance to prove myself yet.”

“And you think you will get that chance?”

“Yes,” Phainon said, assuredly.

The pirate tilted his head, the barest curl of a smile there, but it might have been a trick of the light. “My men are upstairs debating what to do with you, trying to determine your purpose in these waters.”

“And?”

“And I don’t waste time with speculation. Why were you on that merchant ship?”

“I was looking for survivors.”

“The ship was on fire,” he reminded his prisoner, “surely the chance of survivors was not worth the risk of your own life.”

“It’s always worth the risk,” Phainon fired back. There was a pause as those words hung in the air between them. “And I think you agree with me.”

A scoff. “What makes you think that?”

“Because you came back for me, a stranger.”

Another long pause, heavy with accusation. Neither man faltered, keeping their expressions schooled, unwilling to give the other any advantage as though this conversation was something to be won.

“Did you know that the Black Tide has infested these waters?” the Captain finally asked.

“…no,” Phainon admitted.

The pirate reached up to pinch the bridge of his nose and Phainon was impressed and amused that the action was so practiced he didn’t accidentally poke an eye out with those long claws.

“Why were you sailing here if not to fight the Black Tide? Is that not the Deliverer of Okhema’s duty?”

Phainon didn’t really want to be called that. If their situations were different, maybe he would’ve requested otherwise, but right now it didn’t seem wise to make demands of his host. “We were hunting you,” he admitted somewhat softly, expecting retribution, but it didn’t come.

Instead, the man was chuckling, “and how did that go for you?”

A lost ship, a lost crew, and now Phainon was in the lion’s belly. He didn’t answer.

“So, the Goldweaver doesn’t know as much as the bards would have the people believe,” the pirate went on, “destroying her threads works after all.”

“And maybe my crew would still be alive.”

“They died fighting the corruption and then in battle with my men, in service to their Captain, believing they were heroes rendering aid. Is this not an honorable death?” It was said so plainly, as though the words should make Phainon completely forget them, move on in a moment. Kremnoan philosophy at its finest.

“I should expect such cruelty from one of Eurypon’s Captains,” Phainon said instead with a slight shake of his head and for the first time, the pirate seemed uncomfortable. He looked away, studying the floor at Phainon’s feet while he shifted his weight.

“Mourn them as you see fit, but there is no room for sulking on my ship.”

“What does it matter to you what I do in my cell?”

“Does my hold seem a dungeon to you?” he asked, looking up again. “You are the first to be behind bars since this vessel was liberated from Castrum Kremnos.”

Liberated? Phainon tilted his head at that implication. Weren’t they part of the Kremnoan Navy? He was tempted to pry, that tenacity making him itch like a dog eyeing a bone and trying to muster the willpower to resist, choosing instead to say with a playful tone, “Aw, I’m so honored to be your first, Captain.”

The man tensed and went wide-eyed for only a second and then found his composure again.

“I meant it when I told you before, there are no captives on my ship. You are here because your reputation proceeded you and I had to be sure you were no danger to my people.”

“And what do you think now?”

The pirate shrugged. “That you are no match for me and therefore not a danger that cannot be handled.”

Phainon twitched. “You could certainly try to handle me, pirate.”

Another scoff and a dismissive wave of his hand. “Perhaps you should stay in there then, until your hungry belly shakes the ship and my men decide to throw you to the sea so they can sleep without the growling.”

He shuffled behind the bars, grabbing them with both hands and leaning forward to give voice to the question left in the stagnant air. “Or?”

“Or you earn your meals and passage with work, until I decide what to do with you.”

Phainon mulled that over. These were still pirates. Not just pirates, they were Kremnoan, enemies of Okhema, followers of Strife. The damage that led the Sol to them may have been the Black Tide, but Phainon had seen ships ravaged by conflicts between men as well. There was blood on their hands but… there was blood on his hands too and his options were slim.

Phainon held a hand out through the bars, reaching for the pirate. “I’ll earn my keep for now,” he agreed. The man walked slowly up to the bars to take his hand, meeting his squeeze to shake, but Phainon held on, trying to crush the man’s hand as he pulled him in a little closer, until their foreheads nearly touched through the bars. He was breathtaking up close.

“But I won’t participate in piracy,” he growled, drawing the line. “Do we have a deal, Captain…?”

That little smirk was back in the corner of the pirate’s lips; the dim light made the red in his eyes glitter like wine spilled in blood. The hand holding his crushed back with equal force, measured carefully to match.

“Mydei,” he said and Phainon’s eyes flicked briefly to his lips when he did, “Captain Mydeimos. We have a deal, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

They let go and Mydei backed up out of reach before turning away. “I will send Hephastion with the key to release you. He will give you instructions.”

“This is just until I can return to Okhema!” Phainon called after him and Mydei paused at the door to look over his shoulder with a mischievous look in his eye.

“As you say, Deliverer.”

Chapter End Notes

Here's hoping I didn't lay it on too thick from the start. I want them to click but also grow into the flirting!

chapters.title: Chapter 3: Gestures of Love and Respect
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

There are a lot of different kinds of love and lots of ways to express it.

“A dog,” Mydei repeated, stating it as a matter of fact.

He was sitting on the railing of the upper deck, one leg up beside him so he could rest his elbow on his knee and his chin in his palm. The ocean churned against the side of the ship, waving at him on his precarious perch, threatening to knock him loose, but he paid no mind. His amber eyes glittered in the sunlight, boring a hole into the back of Phainon’s head while he watched the man.

“Yep,” Leonnius agreed from the floor beside him. He held a shield up to better catch the light and tsked to himself when he found another dirty spot. Squeak, squeak, squeak, sang the rag as he rubbed the metal with newfound determination.

Even from here, Mydei could see Phainon’s lips moving, chattering away at his partner on the lines. He was smiling but he had been from the moment Hephaestion had released him with a to do list of daily tasks. Not once had Mydei felt like it was completely and truly genuine, nor did he expect it to be. Somehow the smile never quite reached his eyes. It strained under a weight that only Phainon could feel, but despite the trauma of the early morning he was smiling, making the most of his situation and stepping forward rather than wallowing in his grief. For now at least, that vengeful fire from earlier was contained, no longer pointing at Mydei and his crew.

They returned his clothes to him when they had finally dried but like most of the men, he had opted on the nice day to forego his top, wearing only that ridiculous collar and his bracers. Sweat glittered on his back, running the length of his spine as he worked the ropes. The man was very fit, exceptionally beautiful, with a few faded scars between his back and chest.

Less than a day, and the Deliverer had ingrained himself with the crew as though he belonged, either oblivious to the wary tension or choosing to ignore it. His natural charisma made him instantly likeable, and the crew weren’t entirely sure how to handle it. They couldn’t tell if he was a lost puppy begging for a home, or a fox smiling at hens. Even with that leash cut, there was no doubt, Phainon would report to his mistress as soon as he was able.

“A dog digging holes looking for bones,” Hephaestion agreed from the little table beside the tiller. He absentmindedly fiddled with a compass. “He’s been asking questions. How does a man talk so much but say so little?”

“He may not be Okheman by birth, but the Goldweaver has taught him to be one of them, duplicitous and silver-tongued,” Leonnius theorized but Mydei wasn’t so sure that was all it was. Phainon harbored secrets and had a quick wit, that much was obvious, but he was also honest when they spoke. When Mydei had faced him in the hold, even through bars, Phainon hadn’t lied to him. He really believed, watching the man now, that this was genuine curiosity and not malicious intent.

“Do you know if the men have told him anything?” Mydei asked.

Hephaestion shrugged. “If they have, I wouldn’t know. Only half of them even speak his language. All that matters to them is that he works hard, knows how to sail, and isn’t sharpening his sword behind their backs.”

It wouldn’t make a difference if they had answered his questions. Innocent or not, Mydei was realizing with each passing minute that he had lied to Phainon and to himself. Krateros had been right, as long as they were at odds with Okhema, Phainon was a prisoner of war. He could not be allowed to return to report their strength and numbers. If he already knew that much through observation, it didn’t matter if he knew more.

“If he asks,” Mydei told them, “you may answer at your own discretion.”

The squeaking stopped. “Are you sure, Mydeimos?”

“And what if he tells the Goldweaver?” Hephaestion asked.

A harp behind them twanged twice. Peucesta, who had been listening the whole time in his calm silence, broke it to ask, “You aren’t letting him go, are you, my Prince?”

“We don’t keep prisoners,” the first mate reminded them, “we agreed we wouldn’t when we took this ship.”

“No, we let him out of that awful little cell,” Leonnius pointed out, “so he’s not a prisoner…?”

“What else do you call a guest that isn’t allowed to leave?” Hephaestion huffed.

“Captive, hostage, convict,” Peucesta answered unhelpfully, with a lovely pluck of the harp at every word.

“He is most certainly not crew,” reminded Hephaestion and Mydei resisted the urge to sigh.

The corner of Mydei’s lip twitched with suspicion as he watched Phainon stumble when the ship swayed with a particularly strong gust of wind. The ship settled but Phainon overcorrected the recovery and collided with Ulixes, their drillmaster, who shoved him back. Hostility singed the air, but Mydei stayed seated and immediately held his hand out to stop Hephaestion from interfering when he saw his friend shift in the corner of his eye.

Phainon held both of his hands up, slowly backing away from the offended warrior. For a moment it seemed like peace would be maintained but another unexpected bump on the ocean sent those raised hands right onto Ulixes’ chest. Phainon’s lips moved, he smiled, and then he was punched in the face.

The brawl broke out immediately after. Rather than roll over and take it, Phainon had stumbled with the hit and come right back to grab the Kremnoan around the middle, shoving him against the mast with a thud that Mydei felt in his bones from across the ship. He watched with guarded amusement, hand still outstretched even though Hephaestion was ignoring the unspoken command to walk to the rail to see what was going on.

A handful of the others on deck hurried to tie the lines, yelling and straining to hold the sail without the pair of squabblers helping them. Someone had to dive onto Phainon’s abandoned rope to secure it to the railing before it became a hazard. A couple others were trying to get a hand on Phainon himself, to pull them apart, but a firm kick kept the boldest of them away while Ulixes kept trying to pry him off between punches and shouts.

“Captain-“

“No, let them finish.” If there was any real risk, Mydei would personally intervene.

The fight only lasted another minute. Another few good blows each and then Phainon was dislodged by a knee to his chest, and he was stumbling back. A few of the others caught him by the shoulders but made no move to restrain him, just gave him a little nudge. The two of them panted, words were exchanged, and then Phainon shook his head, just a little shake with a smile.

Mydei watched them clasp arms, having found some mutual understanding in their altercation. Ulixes let go first and immediately returned to work, but Phainon stood still for a moment, processing what had happened with a nervous shuffle. He looked around while he rubbed his wrist, it must’ve twisted in the fight, and eventually noticed Mydei watching him. His eyes widened in shock. He must have been expecting some sort of punishment for causing trouble.

Would Phainon fight back if Mydei demanded retribution? Would he take responsibility and endure any punishment?

Mydei lazily let Phainon stew in his worries as they watched each other like a cat and a mouse, caught in their own suspended snapshot of time until Mydei showed mercy and looked away.

Out of the corner of his eye, he saw Phainon’s shoulders drop as he started breathing again and then hurried to help with the sails once more, all awkward apologies, a bowed head, and awkward scratches at the back of his neck.

“He’s been on the ship for a day, and he is already solving disputes like a Kremnoan,” Hephaestion noted blandly, but Mydei could hear the compliment buried under his tone.

Hephaestion was one of Mydei’s oldest friends and arguably the person he trusted the most. If he had not agreed to be Mydei’s first mate, the Prince may not have taken on the role of Captain at all. Mydei had no desire to lead but had fallen into the responsibility at a young age when his core friend group had found him on the shore of the Sea of Souls as a child and raised him on the sea, always sailing from one isle to the next in search of conquest and glory in the tradition of his heritage. Always treating him as the Crown Prince he was, the future King they wanted him to be.

At least that’s how it started.

They kept sailing, kept searching for glory in combat, stealing what they needed and selling the rest, but Mydei wasn’t sure he wanted to do that forever. He didn’t want to be like his father. He didn’t want to be King. He just wanted to protect his family.

How hard could that be?

His thoughts drifted back to the Black Tide, that ever-present threat, creeping in the depths.

“Phainon sleeps in the cell at night,” Mydei decided, “for his protection as well as ours.”

Leonnius held the shield up to the light again. “You think the men will try to slit his throat while he sleeps?”

“Until I make a decision about him, I don’t want to find out.” The Crown Prince finally got down from the rail. He had his own chores to do after all. Without another word he walked away, all focus and business.

A lovely refrain drifted from the harp as Peucesta kept playing.

“Yeah,” Hephaestion sighed with a smile. He rolled his head to stretch his neck, long hair spilling over his shoulders. “It’s been a while since our beloved Prince has shown so much interest in someone.”

“Yep,” Leonnius agreed.

“I suppose we should take the time to introduce ourselves.”

The music swapped to a major key in agreement.

-

Phainon had fully expected to get in trouble when he realized the Captain had seen them, especially after he had puzzled out who the man really was. Surely, the heir to Castrum Kremnos would favor a bloody punishment for such an outburst on his ship.

History was a hobby of Phainon’s. If he wasn’t building ships or training, he was reading or digging through local shops for antiques. Castrum Kremnos was a dream destination for those that wanted to train to fight. Before the fall of Aedes Elysiae it was something Phainon had talked about with his parents and friends and even started making a travel plan before his whole world collapsed, dragging his dreams into the depths with icy claws.

When he heard the name, Mydeimos, Phainon thought it seemed familiar and the barest of digging and one man’s slip up confirmed it. Crown Prince Mydeimos the Undying wasn’t just a Captain in Eurypon’s Navy, he was the King’s only child. There had been rumors that he had lived in self-imposed exile with other Kremnoans, that the famous Kremnoan Detachment followed their immortal Prince into glorious battle.

The Chryseus Leo and her crew were that same Kremnoan Detachment.

Knowing as much it was hard not to feel the slightest trepidation when he saw the Prince descend from the upper deck but the intimidating man didn’t continue towards Phainon and went below deck instead. He watched those broad shoulders and strong back disappear into the dark of the stairs and then let out his held breath to look around.

Most of the crew had decided to ignore him, moving through their tasks and loudly chatting in Kremnoan, correctly assuming that Phainon couldn’t understand them. He thought about trying to chat with them again, as he had throughout the morning, but it hadn’t worked then and it wasn’t likely to work now. Mid-afternoon and sailing on favorable wind, there wasn’t much left for him to do now that the ropes were secured, and his assigned tasks had already been completed. Left to his own devices, Phainon chose to be proactive, wandering and looking the ship over with an experienced eye. She was a remarkable masterpiece, a feat of engineering made by the master smiths and craftsmen of Kremnos.

She was built for luxurious war, massive, long, with three masts and that gorgeous roaring lion figurehead carved from red crystal for a ram. The detailing etched into the railings, doorways, the mast, and the aplustre told tales of Strife, images of war, and murals of victory. They were marred in places, and it was obvious where damage had been repaired with new wood, leaving stories unfinished or in pieces, changing their meanings in the process.

Phainon gave the crew space as he wandered and traced those carvings with his fingers, appreciating them from his own world, giving every relief the attention it deserved as though he was appraising a rare gem back home. It was behind the tiller, near the aplustre that he found a scene that surprised him into stopping his wandering entirely. In loving detail was pictured a feast between two Titans. Nikador’s spear was raised in salute to Kephale, who gifted to Strife the Dawn. They were depicted as equals, as friends. It was the last thing Phainon would have expected to see carved into a warship by a hopeful hand.

“Oh, sing to me muse, of those halcyon days when Titans spoke of peace.” Phainon nearly jumped out of his skin. His eyes shot up and his head twisted like a whip to look at Hephaestion. “Or so Peucesta would sing.”

The first mate smiled and tilted his head, the same gesture as when he had turned the wrought iron key and let Phainon loose that morning. They had exchanged names then. He was all lean muscle and sinew, not the kind of figure Phainon would have expected from a Kremnoan warrior at a glance. He kept his hair long, very long, long and straight enough that when he pulled his locks over his shoulders it reached his waist. Sharp eyes full of experience glittered with cautious optimism and Phainon felt the connection there, seeing this interaction as the olive branch that it was.

He turned back to where his fingers were still resting on the sun behind Kephale. “They’re beautiful.”

“They’re worn and faded,” lamented the Kremnoan.

“And they’re more beautiful for it,” Phainon countered fondly, “I noticed many of these stories are incomplete, how old is the ship?”

For a careful second Hephaestion hesitated, but he answered clearly, “She was finished nearly twenty-five years ago, to be the flagship of King Eurypon’s royal navy. He commanded her for a few years during his campaigns in the North and maintained her glory when she was damaged, but there are none among us that can repair the carvings.”

That was a shame. Phainon moved the tip of his pointer finger along the back of a carved image of a lion. It was mid roar and bathing in golden sunlight. “I’m surprised King Eurypon does not command her himself still,” he mused, testing the waters. This was the first time someone had been so forthcoming when he had made inquiries, and he was very curious. The last time Okhema had seen an organized Kremnoan attack was more than five years ago. “The Captain suggested the ship had been stolen?”

Hephaestion smiled. “In a way it was.”

“In a way?” Phainon asked.

Hephaestion nodded and said, “That King… didn’t need it anymore.” There was an edge to the man’s voice, an underlying disdain when he referred to Eurypon.

“You harbor no love for your King,” he observed.

“I have nothing but love for my King,” Hephaestion corrected, “even if he has yet to pick the crown up from the ground.”

Phainon turned again to look at Hephaestion, letting his hand fall from the aplustre to his side. The man was watching Phainon with the same intensity that he had seen in Mydeimos’ gaze earlier, searching for a reaction, judging Phainon’s knowledge just as fervently as he was giving it. Not that there was much to find and Hephaestion knew it. The comment was lost on Phainon who puzzled over the man’s careful word choice.

“If you’re done admiring the décor,” Hephaestion continued, closing off any further discussion, “I do have a task for you.”

He gave the carvings one more lingering look and touch, rolled his shoulders and gestured politely to the first mate. “However, I may be of service.”

Pleased, he gestured for Phainon to follow and led the way towards the bow. The raised deck there had another set of stairs leading below. A shortcut to where the crew slept and kept their things. It was also host to some of their more readily accessible supplies and armory.

Hephaestion led Phainon to one such storage closet full of odds and ends generally used for patchwork repairs. The sort of things that seemed like junk until they were miraculously needed for weirdly specific reasons. Phainon’s father used to keep a small basket for such things under the kitchen washbasin, insisting that none of it could be thrown away or repurposed ‘just in case.’ On a ship, space was a resource to be managed like any other, so it was important to only keep things that would be necessary and to budget the use of those supplies wisely. From what Phainon could tell of the organized mess, they had prepared for many months at sea and restocking had come from inconsistent sources, taking supplies from ships they had conquered, or, as Phainon now knew, ships that had already been lost to the Black Tide. Anything that was free of corrosion was fair game on the high seas.

Hephaestion handed Phainon a wooden bucket and started throwing things in there. He recognized all the items immediately. Scrap pieces of wood, a ceramic jar of pitch, a brush… these were all tools for patch repairs.

“Is this for the deck?” Phainon asked and the first mate stopped what he doing to look at him quizzically.

“Yeah, there are some small holes in the deck from this morning.” A pause. “Are you familiar with patching holes?”

“I help the ship builders in Okhema when I can. May I?” he asked and Hephaestion stepped out of the closet so that Phainon could step inside.

The longer Phainon studied the haphazard shelfing, awkward cases, jostled containers, clay jars, and loose trash the more a pattern started to emerge. At one point the closet had been organized. Rough seas shook everything together, but the collection of miscellany was trying to adhere to materials of like purposes. Plenty of oils, lots of tar… He unsealed a couple of amphorae and twisted them in turn towards the light until he found a wide-necked jar full of old beeswax.

“This is going to hold up better to the weather than the pitch for small scrapes on the deck,” he offered, holding the jar out to Hephaestion. The man balanced the ceramic precariously in the bucket and offered his hand to Phainon to help him to his feet. Despite his lean appearance, the Kremnoan had an iron grip and tugged Phainon to standing with ease.

“It’ll look better too. How big are the holes?”

Hephaestion moved the bucket under one arm and gestured with his hand to demonstrate a circle with his finger and thumb. “Not big, more scratches than anything. The worst of them may be buffed out by sharkskin.” He pointed to another jar. This one was at least labeled with what looked like a child’s drawing of a shark.

Phainon leaned over a pile of discarded lumber scraps to grab it. Strips of shark hide were neatly placed inside, some already worn. “This is high quality,” he praised as he ran his thumb over the rough hide.

“Leonnius caught and tanned them himself.”

With an impressed hum, Phainon added a few sheets of the skin to the bucket in Hephaestion’s hands and then took the supplies from him. He crouched on the ground and started sorting through the stock. They wouldn’t need the whole jar of wax. Phainon pointed into the closet again.

“Will you hand me that small adz?”

The tool was hanging on the wall by a string and a stubborn hook. It wasn’t very sharp, old and worn as it was, but the curved, wide, flat blade was exactly what he needed. For a brief but heavy pause, the First Mate hesitated to hand it over. The tool could easily be used as a weapon and Phainon was reminded how tenuous their partnership was for the day. They were enemies yesterday, it was only Kremnoan confidence and Phainon’s agreement with the Captain that kept him from being thrown right back into the brig.

“Oil lamp?”

Again, Hephaestion provided. The lamp and flint were added to the bucket while Phainon used the short end of the adz to scoop a generous amount of wax from the amphorae. He counted his supplies in turn and then finally stood with the tools of his trade.

“Did you want to supervise?” he cheerfully invited.

“Do you think I need to?”

“I wouldn’t mind the company.” But he didn’t have any expectations.

Hephaestion reached into the bucket in response and pulled out a piece of shark skin. “I’ll even help.”

The deck was well cared for as it was. Despite its age the Chryseus Leo was maintained as though it was waiting for a royal maiden voyage, the only nicks and problems in the deck were caused by the scuffle that morning. The biggest of which was caused by Phainon’s blade when the Prince had deflected the swing meant for Perdikkas and the heavy weapon had gouged into the wood.

Phainon squatted beside the spot and ran his hand over the sharp, raised edges caused by the splinters removed from their natural grain.

“A blade as heavy as yours, I’m grateful it only bit the deck and not my friend,” Hephaestion said over his shoulder but the nip of guilt in Phainon’s chest burned away as quickly as it appeared.

“I am too.” He meant it.

Phainon got to work using the adz to gently scrape away the bigger splinters and round out the cavity; shark skin smoothed the edges. There was peace in hard work, something so satisfying in being a part of the process of repair.

Hephaestion was only a spear’s length away, rubbing at much smaller wounds with the skin. Those nips in the ship were from enemy arrows that had embedded in the wood. Phainon recognized the marks from past experiences. Most crews and Captains would overlook those common scars as natural wear and tear, but the first mate was taking extraordinary care to make those tiny rough spots smooth, leaving the markings faded but not erasing them entirely. He worked in slow circles, carefully running his free hand over every spot to check that it was exactly the right texture before he moved on to the next one.

Phainon slowed his own work as he watched to appreciate the meticulous attention.

“You love this ship,” he observed aloud in a soft voice.

And Hephaestion stopped to look up at him with surprise that melted into a genuine smile. “What sailor doesn’t love their home?” The first mate went right back to work, humming to himself in the lighter mood carried by such a lovely sentiment.

When Phainon filled the empty space he had carved with wood chips and heated the wax with the lamp to pour between the cracks, it was with extra care. When he used the flat of the adz’s heated blade to burn the wax in place, smoke curling briefly in the air until a damp rag soothed the aching lumber, it was with respectful concentration. And as he sanded down the wax to make it even, running his hand over his work just as Hephaestion had done, it was with love. Not because Phainon loved this ship himself, but because Hephaestion had convinced him with his actions that the vessel deserved nothing less.

-

By the time they were done the sun was dipping low. That was yet another thing to get used to this far from the Dawn Device. Phainon liked the colors of the sky during parting hour, even if they felt a little colder now after a trying day of loss and discovery.

Hephaestion had left him to check on dinner midway through their work and Phainon had been left alone for the most part to clean up. As alone as one could be with a crew of Kremnoans frequently glancing his way and bumping his back while he sorted his supplies in a desperate attempt to tame the chaos of the closet. The endeavor already felt a lost cause before the smell of grilled fish wafted by on the breeze and his angry stomach decided that was a more worthy pursuit.

The galley below decks had long tables and benches but there wasn’t enough space for the entire crew to eat at once. Many of the men were fine with the arrangement and took their food to their private spaces in the crew’s living quarters, others made makeshift tables and chairs of crates and barrels to eat on the deck. Some took their food and ate as they worked, making up for any lost time that may have been wiled away throughout the day.

When Phainon wandered down the stairs to the galley below in search of the source of that wonderful smell, the happy chatter quieted. The elephant in the room had blue eyes and white hair and he nearly wilted under those piercing stares but Phainon returned them with a soft smile and a playful wave. A few of the crew laughed and returned to their conversations, chatting in Kremnoan while they waited.

The food was already prepared and waiting in baskets and half covered by cloth to keep it warm but no one made a move to take some. Standing beside the lineup with his head bowed, eyes closed, and his arms crossed was the Captain. He leaned against the countertop, keeping the line from advancing, infinitely patient and stoic, “What are we waiting for?” Phainon asked a man next to him, but he only got a confused expression in response. More people shoved into the galley and took seats or found places to stand. Someone had already uncorked a barrel of wine and many were choosing to indulge there while they waited.
