Phainon’s belly rumbled and his mouth watered. He still wasn’t sure if he’d be allowed to eat yet and he certainly wasn’t going to find out if no one was eating at all. The temptation to make a scene, to ask, was beginning to outweigh his curiosity until something bumped into his shin.

Fig Stew put both of his front paws on the top of Phainon’s boot, looked right up at him, and then rubbed those tufty cheeks against the leather. He blessed the man with a rub from both sides of his perfect, round face before moving to the next man in line, rubbing against everyone in turn and ending with the Prince. The chimera sat in front of the man, mewled, and then waited with his tail swishing back and forth.

Mydei and Fig Stew watched each other for a respectful moment and then the Captain reached into one of the baskets and pulled out a single pita pocket stuffed full of cooked fish. He offered it to the chimera, who took it happily in his mouth, waited for head pats, and then happily bounded out of the galley with his meal.

Only then did the Captain move from his place and the men descended on the meal with disciplined eagerness. Those close to the front of the line took their food straight from the baskets on the countertops, while the Prince brought one basket to the tables and then took another to the back of the line, serving those there himself. Every hand that took food muttered phrases in Kremnoan, giving thanks to Mydei directly, who muttered back to them in their native tongue.

There was no shoving, no jostling, no one took more than their share on a first pass, and Phainon was impressed. He also was hesitant. For as disorganized as it appeared, there was a definite system and he wasn’t sure where he fit, much less that persistent fear that he wouldn’t be allowed to eat at all.

“Did you not want any, Deliverer?” Mydei asked and Phainon only just realized that the man had come up beside him with a nearly empty basket. The Captain held it out to him, watching with that steady gaze as though he would pounce the moment Phainon failed this test.

“Is this you telling me that I earned it?”

“If you don’t want any…” the Kremnoan growled and started to turn away, but Phainon hurriedly caught the edge of the basket to stop him.

“No, I do! I thought maybe you would be upset with me for earlier.”

“Hephaestion said you worked hard today and Chryseus Leo is happy,” Mydeimos explained, somewhat dismissive, “if you believe your fight with Ulixes should be punished further than the bruises he already gave you, then go and ask him to hit you again, but do it on your own time and with a full stomach.”

Phainon didn’t really want to get hit again. “…thank you.” He reached in and took one of the pockets and was determined to leave it at that, but Mydei sighed and pushed a second one into his hands.

“I said a full stomach,” he grumbled. The Prince muttered something to himself in Kremnoan looked Phainon up and down with a furrowed brow and narrowed eyes. He gave Phainon a third pocket with more mumbled Kremnoan musings and wandered off to feed more of his men.

Phainon waited in shock with his hands full, too tired to really process the interaction. He stayed standing there, doe-eyed and lost, until Hephaestion waved him over to one of the tables to sit and sip at pomegranate wine.

There were others there, one of them, the man he had fought with earlier, raised his wine in a gesture of respect and Phainon returned it with a half-smile and a bow of his head. But the weight of the day was heavy and though he still smiled, Phainon ate in silence while the others talked around him in a language he couldn’t understand. They gave him space to enjoy his meal near others, not really one of them, but not entirely alone anymore either.

The fish was moist and delicious, well-seasoned and mixed with herbs and vegetables. The bread was soft and warm. It was exactly the comfort that Phainon needed after a long day, so much so that he didn’t complain when he was escorted back to that cage in the dark. He still felt warm when Hephaestion reassured him with apologies and gave him a mat to sleep on and a heavy blanket to use. He was warm when they bade each other good night; when the locked clicked. And that comfort stayed with Phainon in the dark until the mercy of night wrapped him up tight in sleep.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Shared Stories
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Yay bonding!

It only took Phainon a couple days to find a rhythm. There was a routine on the ship and now that he was finding it, things were clicking a little bit better, a little bit faster. Hephaeston would unlock his cell in the mornings, he would get whatever quick breakfast was available in the galley and then join the men for morning drills.

The Drillmaster, Ulixes, was the man that Phainon had scuffled with on his first day. Apparently, fighting between the men wasn’t a rare occurrence and the Captain only involved himself in those disputes if the violence escalated beyond problem solving and encroached into genuine rage. It made sense when Phainon realized it. These were warriors from a warring culture, it was only natural that they would get twitchy between fights and need an outlet. Sometimes all two men really needed was to beat the shit out of each other and then laugh about it later.

After morning drills were daily chores. Phainon was the bottom of the rung on this ship, so his tasks were important but demeaning. Tasks like dumping the overnight bedpans, swabbing both high traffic decks, laundry, washing dishes, and working the lines and oars when called upon. Fortunately, the rowing wasn’t something he had to do yet. The Chryseus Leo was plenty fast if there was wind and there was no shortage of that.

As long as his list of chores was, Phainon was a hard worker and buckling down and knocking those tasks out quickly left him with more free time to explore the ship, nap, talk to the others, and just appreciate the ocean and the crew.

Phainon had always loved people. Only about half of the detachment understood him when he spoke and fewer than half could respond, but Phainon made every effort to not let that language barrier deter him and made use of universal hand signs and gestures to try and bond indiscriminately. Most everyone was receptive to his friendly teasing albeit from arm’s length. Aside from Hephaeston, most of the crew remained guarded, but there were two people on the ship that seemed to have a real problem with him, a seasoned veteran named Krateros and the Captain, Mydeimos.

While the Captain was dismissive and short, he was at least willing to speak with Phainon whenever Phainon approached to ask simple questions, but Krateros wouldn’t even look at him. It made sense, there was bad blood between their city-states. There had been years of a tenuous silence between leadership, but their conflict spanned centuries, all the way back to the Titans. Anywhere Kremnoans and Okhemans met there was conflict. That hostility was what made Phainon realize that the cell wasn’t because they were afraid of him, but worried for him.

Another mixed message from the Captain to let simmer on the back burner of Phainon’s inner thoughts.

In any case, Phainon wanted to make the most of his free time with his chores completed and with nothing urgent to do, he wandered to the ship’s library.

That had been a happy discovery in his exploring. What had once been a massive and lavish Captain’s quarters had been divided into a few different rooms. Mydei still had his own private space, but they had filled the largest storage space with books, scrolls, and tablets that the Kremnoans had collected. It was small compared to a real library of course, but easily the largest collection he had personally seen on the sea.

Phainon let himself into the unlocked room with a soft click of the latch and poked his head in first to be sure he wasn’t intruding on anyone. Almost immediately he was spotted.

“Perfect timing,” a confident voice called from across the room. Against the far wall, more than half buried under a partially collapsed shelf and a massive collection of clay tablets and books was a man with short hair and a shrewd expression. Despite being very trapped he was holding a book open with his only free hand. “If you’re not busy.”

Phainon’s eyes widened in the same breath that he was hurrying across the room to assess the situation. “Oh Titans, are you alright??”

The Kremnoan smiled with just the corners of his mouth, amused. He set the book down, holding it open with his arm so he could slowly reach for a scrap of paper to put between the pages of his book so he could close it without losing his place.

“’A man who has been through bitter experiences and travelled far enjoys even his sufferings after a time,’” he recited in the clear monotone of someone quoting a favorite passage from a book.

“…so you want me to leave you here?” Phainon asked, pointing at the pile.

“Of course not!”

The man had twisted at an angle and once trapped had almost no leverage to free himself. What books he could move one-handed had already been set aside, or in some cases tossed. Phainon managed to free his other arm where it had been pinned by a scroll jammed between the wall and a heavy tablet and then he was able to help, systematically moving treasured tomes and bound leather to reveal the crux of the problem.

“Ah wait,” the Kremnoan said when Phainon reached for the stone tablet. “That’s a load bearing record.” He pointed at where the tablet and the bookshelf met, for now it was preventing an even greater disaster as the haphazard shelf threatened to dump the other half of its charges onto the pinned man.

Phainon backed up to reassess the situation. There was still urgency churning deep in his belly, but the trapped man seemed unbothered, waiting patiently and calmly.

“Any ideas?” Phainon asked when he saw the man watching him.

“I haven’t the angle nor the means to see all the pieces. I fear I am entirely at your mercy, Deliverer,” he said with a small chuckle, laughing at his own joke under his breath.

Phainon bowed his head and shook it back and forth twice. “Should I fail, and you be crushed under these words, who will I mourn?” he asked, equally playful, channeling his inner poet in response to this book worms own eloquent musings.

The man laughed a proper laugh, a breathy sound louder than a true librarian or scholar of the Grove but softer than a soldier’s echoing boom in the barracks. “I am Ptolemy. I suppose it wasn’t fair of me to not offer that when I already knew who you were.”

“I guess I have caused a few ripples, enough to be known,” Phainon apologized. He started delicately removing books from the teetering shelf. They were held in place by a thin metal rod. The restraint was enough to keep them from dislodging when the ship tilted and twisted with the waves, but not enough to hold their weight at this angle. The nail holding the rod was wiggling loose. It wouldn’t hold if Phainon simply pushed the shelf upright without easing some of the weight.

“You have,” Ptolemy admitted, “but it’s a pleasure all the same. It has been some time since the ship has felt so alive.”

“Bold words from someone who may perish under these stories.”

“You seem studied.” The casual brushing off impending death must be a Kremnoan thing.

“I graduated from the Grove of Epiphany,” Phainon confirmed and then added proudly, “five-time debate champion.” He set the books on a neat pile as he removed them and then paced around the mess on the floor, to see how to best get at the books on the next shelf. There was plenty of light from the line of windows but not a lot of space between shelves to work with. It wouldn’t do to knock another one loose.

“A silver-tongue indeed.”

“I don’t know that I am all that.”

“You may even have the wit to compete with Mydeimos.”

Phainon paused. It was only for a moment, but he could feel Ptolemy’s eyes on him all the same. “Well, you don’t have to worry about that. The Captain barely seems willing to interact with me at all.”

Ptolemy tsked and mumbled under his breath in Kremnoan.

“Ah! Did I twist your leg?”

“No, no, I’m bemoaning our Prince.”

The tomes on the lower shelves were considerably thicker and at the awkward angle for retrieval Phainon found himself struggling not to drop the heavy books on Ptolemy. He held perfectly still holding one such book, waiting for the sway of the ship before stumbling backwards to set the book down on the floor with the others.

“…I’m not sure I understand the Captain,” Phainon admitted. He gave the shelf an experimental shove. It budged but barely and that struggling nail kept trying to make an escape. “I expected him to be more like his father.”

“’Few sons are like their fathers--most are worse, few better,’” Ptolemy quoted.

“And which is he?”

Ptolemy shifted his weight, testing his legs with a wince. They were still trapped. “If you are well-read, than you have heard of Eurypon, the mad king of Castrum Kremnos. Do you think a man worse than he would have pulled you from the sea?”

Phainon tentatively reached a leg over the pile, effectively straddling Ptolemy to widen his stance for better balance. It was the only way he had a chance of moving the stone tablets from the middle shelf without stepping on something breakable.

“Is that why the Prince exiled himself?” Phainon asked. He was interested in the story of course, but his attention was admittedly divided. He put one hand on the wall to brace himself while he delicately started pulling the thickest of the stone slabs off the threatening bookcase.

“Is that what the bards of Okhema sing?” Ptolemy scoffed, but for the first time the man’s words seemed to catch in his throat as he hesitated. “It is not my story to tell… but perhaps it’s best you know, if you are to walk the same ship as he does, for however long.”

“I wouldn’t want to put you in troubling situation…”

The stone slab slipped from his fingers and slammed into the floor next to Ptolemy’s leg with a sickening crunch and they both froze, wide-eyed, holding their breath.

“…Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, I already am.”

“I am so-“

“Please do not apologize for what, thankfully, did not happen.”

Phainon bent a knee and kicked to return to one side of the pile, flapping his arms to balance as he did so. That heavy slab wasn’t moving for awhile but it wasn’t on the shelf anymore. He gave it another shove and this time the shelf rocked more agreeably.

“I’ll not give you details, lest he not want you to know them, but there is enough that is common knowledge to tell. The Prince was not raised in Castrum Kremnos by King Eurypon’s hand.”

“I know he left in his youth…”

“Eurypon threw Mydei into the sea of souls when he was newly born to appease Nikador,” Ptolemy explained, “the tale is famous in Castrum Kremnos. I am surprised it has not made its way to Okhema.”

Phainon stood still for a moment to process his shock. It was hard to imagine a father’s cruelty when Phainon’s own family had been loving and wonderful. To grow up with no one… More than that, such an origin explained the Undying title. Older soldiers who had scuffled with Kremnoans talked about their strength and conditioning. When they spoke of Mydei who couldn’t be killed at all, Phainon had assumed those were embellishments, but perhaps he really was immortal, if he survived the sea of souls as an infant.

“My professor used to complain about war,” he said softly, “not because he abhorred violence but because animosity could prevent the exchange of information and he believed all knowledge should be shared.”

He bent down to clear more of the books and scrolls that were across Ptolemy’s lap. His smile had faded and the Kremnoan took notice, both of his solemnity and of his unwillingness to directly address this new tidbit about the Prince.

“Mydei is not without family,” Ptolemy told him firmly, even reaching out to put his hand on Phainon’s arm to stop him from working for a moment. Their eyes met and Phainon could see in those harsh eyes that this was immensely important to the man. His gaze glittered with desperate need to make Phainon understand, regardless of any prejudices.

He squeezed Phainon’s arm once, then let go and resumed digging. It was easier now that they had cleared the heavy scrolls from Ptolemy’s belly. Now that he could sit up, it was easier for him to be proactive in his own rescue.

“I was very young when I chose to leave Castrum Kremnos,” he started to say and Phainon twisted in place to better face him as they worked. “Training begins for Kremnoans from the moment our little hands are strong enough to hold a spear, by the time myself, Hephastion, and Leonnius realized we did not want to serve a corrupted King we were not yet men.” His expression grew distant, no longer sitting on the floor of a ship but back in his homeland, reliving difficult memories. “It is a long story, one that need not be recited in its entirety, what matters is that there were no small number of us that latched onto a rumor carried by wayward fishermen of a child that saved them from monsters in the sea, a child with red markings and an animal ferocity, blessed by the titans.

“We scoured the waters and found Mydei to raise him ourselves while we showed him the freedom of the open ocean. We are his family and we would follow our King without question because we know him to be an honorable man of the highest quality.”

Phainon grunted as he moved a scroll to get at the last heavy tome trapping Ptolemy’s thighs. He stayed quiet, letting the story roll over his understanding of the man.

“Have I said too much? Perhaps not enough?”

“Ah, no, Ptolemy,” he mumbled. Phainon stood again to push at the bookshelf. It was still holding onto the Kremnoan’s ankles and would need to be moved if the man was to be free once more. “I am simply appreciating what you told me.”

“The bards sing of you too, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,” Ptolemy explained, “like Mydei, I assume your story has more layers than what is written in poetry.”

Phainon chuckled sadly. “I wish they wouldn’t hold me in such light.”

“Are they not your deeds?”

“They are wildly embellished.”

“Even those of the Nameless Hero who wandered from a burning village?” Phainon’s mood darkened, and Ptolemy looked away. “I overstepped.”

The silence stretched between them as they removed the last of the books and Phainon tried to puzzle out the best way to move the shelf without hurting Ptolemy’s foot.

“The bards make it sound like I’m something special,” Phainon finally said in a quiet voice, “but the truth is I’m just the son of a farmer who played hero with a wooden sword. A boy that lost everything, could do nothing, and became nothing. I don’t know why Aglaea picked me, when I was covered in dust and salt, just a shell of a man.”

Ptolemy mulled that over and then quoted with sincerity, “’Is he not sacred, even to the gods, the wandering man who comes in weariness?’ I am glad that fate has crossed our paths Phainon of Aedes Elysiae and not just because you are about to free me from the result of my hubris.”

Phainon smiled again. “Then I will not disappoint.”

He pressed his shoulder to the heavy shelf, braced himself, and pushed. The shelf teetered unhappily and then groaned its way back to standing. Ptolemy hurried to pull his foot free and scooted backwards to safety.

“These bars will need to be replaced,” Phainon muttered.

“Phainon,” Ptolemy said as he slowly got to his feet, leaning heavily on the wall for support, “it was not my intention to cause you distress…”

But Phainon was already smiling again, feelings buried back where they belonged in the depths of his heart. He could see the skepticism on Ptolemy’s face and did his best to convey reassurance in response. “All is well, Ptolemy. I’m just glad I could help, and especially glad for the insight. It seems my professor was right; knowledge should be shared freely.”

“I can’t promise that I will answer all your questions,” Ptolemy admitted, “but that is more a matter of timing than an unwillingness.”

“I do appreciate it. How are your legs?”

Ptolemy tested his injured foot and tsked. “Nothing compared to how my arms will feel after reorganizing this mess.”

“May I help?” Phainon asked.

“I would be grateful for it.”

Ptolemy was less forthcoming when he started sorting. His concentration was focused on ensuring everything was put back exactly where he wanted it and it was good thing he knew because this library was not organized in any way that Phainon understood. To make matters worse, half of the collection was in Kremnoan and he had to pause to compare the letters, relying on symbol recognition more than actual understanding of what they said.

“Where did you get all these?” he asked.

“We liberated nearly all of it from other ships, a couple libraries.”

“That is the second time I have heard someone on this ship use that word to justify stealing,” Phainon grumbled.

“It’s not stealing,” Ptolemy insisted, indignant. Even punctuating the statement by smacking Phainon lightly on the head with one of the books, making him blink in surprise.

He may have loved his books and stories, but Ptolemy was still a Kremnoan warrior. All of them readily expressed themselves with physical gestures and disregarded personal space when they were comfortable, from the way Mydeimos had shamelessly reached for his neck to snap Aglaea’s thread on day one, to the way Ulixes had punched him for a too friendly comment, and now as a playful gesture with Ptolemy. It made him laugh.

Ptolemy gave him a funny look with pursed lips and one raised eyebrow before he smacked Phainon again with the book. He put it away on the shelf with a mumbled Kremnoan curse.

“I’ve also heard that word a lot too,” he chuckled. Phainon handed Ptolemy a scroll to put away.

“Good. It is an unflattering insult.”

“I suppose I may deserve it.”

“You sound so happy about that…”

The chuckles faded into giggles. “I don’t mean to be. …would you teach me?”

Ptolemy paused with a clay tablet in hand. Maybe Phainon shouldn’t have handed the man something so heavy to be weaponized if that question was inappropriate to ask but Ptolemy seemed to have forgotten he was holding it when he tilted his head.

“Teach you what?”

Phainon pointed to the clay and the lettering there. “Teach me Kremnoan.”

He tsked as he put the tablet back on the shelf, the bottom shelf this time, and pushed it into place with his uninjured foot.

“Why?”

“Why not? For one, I’d like to know when people are calling me rude things,” Phainon explained, “but I also would like to be able to understand the crew. Understand and be understood.”

“…you are a fascinating person, Deliverer of Okhema,” Ptolemy deadpanned, “that is a lofty goal for someone that expects to return home before long.”

Phainon shrugged. “I have seen the ships supplies. I know the crew was not expecting to dock at any port for at least a few more weeks. Surely that is enough time to at least learn Kremnoan curses.”

Ptolemy gave Phainon a sad look, one that left Phainon confused and a little worried. Was the language that hard to learn that it warranted such pity?

“I will teach you, but it may take some time and if you aren’t giving it your all-“

“I will,” Phainon promised.

They were getting to the end of the pile and the incident in the library was a thing of the past, a secret between them that made Phainon happy to have shared in the moment.

“I assume you originally came here for something to read,” Ptolemy said. He brushed dust off his chiton and stepped over to another shelf, scanning the spines and occasionally pulling out a scroll to check its contents.

“Ah, I did,” Phainon admitted. “I wasn’t sure what you had in your collection and was curious. I guess I didn’t really consider that most of it would be in Kremnoan.” He brushed his hands over the shelf, noting with relief that at least some of it was in familiar tongues. They must’ve ‘liberated’ those stories and records from Okheman ships they had taken over. The reminder left a sour taste in Phainon’s mouth. They were still pirates. They were still enemies. When he returned to Okhema, it would be with important information to report, and then he would back to hunting them again as was his duty…

“If you’re earnest about learning Kremnoan,” Ptolemy was saying. He had wandered to the far side of the library while Phainon was browsing. “You can start here.”

Phainon would’ve willingly gone to him, but Ptolemy met him in the middle next to a small desk. He set two little books of near equal shape and size on its surface, extra mindful to not knock over the open inkwell and pen there.

“This is one of Mydei’s favorite stories.”

“Oh, it’s fiction?” Phainon asked.

“Yes, is that a problem?”

“It’s not what I usually read…” he cut himself off at the look on Ptolemy’s face and held a hand up apologetically, “I’m sure it’s an excellent tale.”

“What’s important is that we have two copies, one in Kremnoan…”

“And one in Okheman Common,” Phainon finished when he recognized the language scribbled on the spine. He picked up one of the books and flipped through it. The one in Kremnoan was older, more frayed, more loved. There were notes in the margins, scribbled quickly and barely legible. They might’ve been doodles if the scribbling wasn’t so frequent and so unrecognizable as anything resembling a picture.

“You can compare them to start building associations,” Ptolemy explained, “it won’t help you speak it or even understand it until I can teach you how to vocalize the words, but it’s a start so you can familiarize yourself with our letters.”

“Can we not start learning how to speak it now?” Phainon tried.

Ptolemy stared at him and then grumbled to himself in Kremnoan with a long-suffering sigh. “You must’ve been popular with your professor.”

Phainon laughed again, “I thought I’d ask, but I understand. Thank you for the start, Ptolemy.”

Ptolemy huffed and sat at the desk. He picked up the pen and tapped it on a scrap of paper. Little flecks of dried ink scattered in all directions. “I’ll try to prepare a teaching plan and we can practice at dinner, perhaps before bed. You don’t have any night shifts, do you?”

“Ah, no, I’m not sure they’ll let me,” he admitted sheepishly.

“That’s alright. I have my own duties on the ship too, but when I’m available I can come find you.”

“I appreciate that.”

Phainon scooped up the second book. They weren’t very big. Not quite pocket-sized but each book fit comfortably in his hand. He held them reverently. Not only were these entrusted to him with love, but they were a bridge to communication, and while this was a distant and unlikely dream, a better chance for a peaceful resolution between Kremnos and Okhema.

“Ptolemy,” Phainon asked now that it was on his mind, “if Mydeimos isn’t like his father, is better than him, do you think he’d be open to peace with Okhema?”

Ptolemy looked up at him thoughtfully, then down at the pen to fiddle with it with both hands. “Is there not already?”

“What do you mean?”

“Phainon, when was the last time Okhema and Kremnos clashed?” Ptolemy held up a hand to stop him from speaking just yet. “I don’t mean between isolated parties such as ours whom Okhema have labeled pirates, I mean a true act of aggression, of war.”

Phainon thought about that. “Six years ago,” he said, “the clash outside Ladon.”

Ptolemy studied him with a goading expression, waiting for him to think things through.

“King Eurypon doesn’t see Okhema as a priority anymore,” Phainon thought aloud, “Okhema hasn’t instigated any engagements in a long time to focus instead on our trade partners but why wouldn’t Eurypon still try to attack?” He held a hand to his chin and studied the floor intently while he thought. “Something else has his attention, something more important, or…” Something clicked. Phainon looked up at Ptolemy. “King Eurypon is dead.”

“As of five years ago, yes,” Ptolemy confirmed.

“This is-“ Phainon stumbled, “then Mydeimos is-“

“He should be, yes. The Kremnoan rite of succession dictates that the man or woman who kills the King be crowned in royal blood and take his place,” Ptolemy explained.

More clicking. “Mydeimos killed his father,” Phainon breathed.

Ptolemy nodded. “He exacted revenge on King Eurypon for himself and his mother who died at Eurypon’s hands the day Mydei was thrown into the sea. Then he rejected the crown, claimed this ship, and those of us that wanted to follow him left Castrum Kremnos.”

“We haven’t clashed with Castrum Kremnos in five years because-“

“There is no Castrum Kremnos with which to clash,” Ptolemy confirmed, “at least not as it was in the past. It still exists, the city is… lost, for now, but her people are still proud and there are a great many of us that still wait for our Prince to embrace his destiny and lead us home.”

Phainon felt like his head was spinning. “How does Okhema not know of this?”

Ptolemy shrugged. “Perhaps they simply do not care as long as there are no red sails on their horizon.”

There was a flicker of truth there. Many people in Okhema didn’t bother to study history, what mattered was that they were safe to focus on the next day, on enjoying the wealth that flowed from the harbor and from Kephale. What did it matter if their ancient rivalry simply faded away into the background? Especially with the Black Tide, the rise of piracy, and other allies to bicker with, something that seemed open and shut didn’t require answers.

That didn’t sit right with Phainon but the knot in his stomach would need to time to unravel the complexities of this new information. He felt like it should change everything, but realistically, to Okhema, it was unlikely to change anything.

“Speaking of history,” Ptolemy interrupted his thoughts, “I really should get back to work.” He pointed with his pen at the papers.

“And I should get to studying,” Phainon agreed. He held the books up with a smile, already tucking away that turmoil.

He started walking to the door reaching for the latch.

“Deliverer… Phainon,” Ptolemy called.

Phainon paused with his hand on the metal and turned to look at the Kremnoan over his shoulder with a questioning tilt of his head.

“’For a friend with an understanding heart is worth no less than a brother,’” he quoted, fiddling with the pen again, “Thank you for swapping stories with me.”

“It was my honor.”

-

Mydei’s claws glanced across Hephaestion’s small shield with a grating screech offensive enough to wake Fig Stew from his afternoon nap to glare daggers at the pair from his sunny spot on a crate. The spear that lashed out from beneath it kissed the Captain’s belt at the hip but he danced away before it could bite flesh.

Hephaestion grinned and pressed his advantage. He was light on his feet, not as fast as Leonnius, but agile enough to keep pace with Mydei and fierce enough to have earned his place by his Prince’s side. His spear swung in from the side, the blade of it whistling all the way up until it was stopped by shining gauntlets.

Mydei twisted his arm to grab the weapon and pulled Hephaestion in close, but that shield blocked his claws again when they reached for his first mate’s face.

“Have you decided then?” Krateros asked again from the side, continuing their conversation about Phainon. He was leaning against a barrel next to Fig Stew’s crate, arms crossed and one leg folded over the other at the ankle. The old teacher was only half paying attention to the spar as they danced across the upper deck.

“No,” Mydei said firmly and then dodged under another strike.

“The longer you delay the worse the outcome,” the teacher scowled, “this is the time for swift and decisive action.”

Mydei growled angrily and lashed out at Hephaestion with a kick right in the middle of that damned shield. The force of the blow drove the first mate back and bought them both time to take a breath.

“And what would you have me do, teacher? Snap his neck as a reward for his loyal service these past few days?”

“Yes,” Krateros returned, “do not call him loyal. You are already confusing his self-preservation for loyalty. He is playing you, Prince.”

Mydei cracked his knuckles by pressing his fist into his palm and repeating the action on the other side.

“For what it’s worth,” Hephaestion said, “I like Phainon. He offered respect to Chryseus Leo without demand and treats the crew as equals without judgement.”

That did matter to Mydei. He was more inclined to believe Krateros if Phainon simply went through the motions, following instruction and nothing more. But every time Mydei turned to watch the man, Phainon was doing something helpful unasked. He never tried to draw attention to his actions either, he simply did them because he could. Phainon genuinely wanted to help and he gave his all in everything he did.

“He is a manipulative, duplicitous Okheman,” Krateros reiterated, “there is nothing he does or says that can be trusted."

“Except he is not,” Mydei reminded, “he is from Aedes Elysiae.”

“An isle that no longer exists, Mydeimos. He serves the Goldweaver and has for long enough to have a reputation, to be called their Deliverer. From whom do think they believe him to deliver them from?”

“We have no conflict with Okhema.”

“Only the King may declare as such,” Krateros huffed. It was an obvious jab and Mydei very nearly took the bait, but Hephaestion saved him from that mistake by throwing his spear. The metal head glinted in sunlight, and he was easily able to dodge when he saw the light flash in the corner of his eye.

Hephaestion was already rushing in with his shield, keeping low to chase Mydei from the same side as his spear sticking into the deck.

The shield met Mydei’s gauntlets, and he threw Hephaestion back.

“Castrum Kremnos no longer exists, there can be no conflict with Okhema,” he growled instead, stomping his foot for emphasis.

“Have you forgotten our people still waiting in settlements beside the sea? Or your crew here on this ship? Are they not the spirit of Castrum Kremnos and Nikador's chosen?” Krateros paused but only for a second. He met Mydei’s glare with a steady gaze. “And do you believe Okhema feels the same? A pretty face and you already forgot that he was sent here to hunt us, to hunt you.”

Mydei scoffed and pulled the spear from the deck. He expertly spun it around his body until it settled across his shoulders with his wrists draped across the shaft.

“How long will you harbor this resentment, teacher?” he said with a softness to the edges, a genuine sadness.

“If you will not see him as the enemy he is, then I will deal with the Goldweaver’s spy myself,” Krateros threatened.

Mydei felt the twist in his heart, a burning anger as his hunch was validated. He was right to leave Phainon in the brig for his own protection. Krateros wasn’t the only old guard on the ship who ached for revenge against Okheman’s Navy for long past grievances. They would treat Phainon as a proxy for all of Okhema’s armies if Mydei let them.

It felt hypocritical to reject their desire for revenge when it was Mydei himself who ripped the heart from his father’s chest. That had been about vengeance too, no matter what he told himself, but Phainon had yet to hurt anyone, had yet to prove himself an enemy.

Mydei saw Phainon and saw hope for a future that he had yet to consider for his people.

“This is my order to you Krateros, you will leave him be,” Mydei growled, “the Deliverer is mine to do with as I see fit and I take full responsibility for his actions, even those he has yet to take. If he becomes a danger to our people, as you are so convinced he will be, then I will hang him from the mast myself.”

Chapter End Notes

10 points to anyone who can figure out what Ptolemy is quoting

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Fishing with the Competition
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

I wonder whose turn it is to bond with Phainon this time

I'm trying to update every other day or so while I still have steam. I really wanted to write this chapter yesterday but I ended up too busy. :')

All was fire and smoke. It burned Phainon’s lungs, melted his flesh while he screamed. The agony that started in his toes spread until it consumed him entirely, and when he was certain this was the end of him, a blackness swallowed him up. The fire was replaced by ice but still his lungs burned. Every breath was devoid of air as water rushed inside him on every inhale.

He was about to drown and then Phainon was very suddenly awake, choking and gasping. He sat upright and tried to summon his sword, but it didn’t come, still locked up tight from when it was confiscated on day one.

Those wide blue eyes darted around in the dark, from his empty hand to the steel bars, and finally to Leonnius. The Kremnoan was crouched down on one knee with a hand through the bar, hovering over the spot that Phainon’s foot had occupied prior to waking. They watched each other while Phainon caught his breath and his eyes adjusted to the light.

It was so early in the morning that nothing but black trickled in from above, the only light was from the extra lantern on the floor where Leonnius had put it.

“Oh good, you’re awake,” he said softly, like he hadn’t just woken Phainon up himself.

“Wha?” Phainon managed. His heart was still racing. Short hair, a playful smile, and scars under his right eye and over his nose made for a memorable face. He had met Leonnius before, but it had been a brief interaction at dinner and under the influence of a rough night of sleep Phainon struggled to remember his name. “Leonnius?”

“I got the key from Hephaestion last night.” Leonnius held the cast iron key up on its ring.

“…It’s the middle of the night, go back to bed,” Phainon whined.

“We’ve got stuff to do.”

“We?”

“Ptolemy said that you’re nice to a fault so you can’t so no,” Leonnius said as he stood up straight to unlock the door. It swung open with a soft squeak, but Phainon was already covering up with his blanket again, hiding his whole head under the covers.

“No,” he huffed, in defiance of Ptolemy.

Leonnius leaned against the bars and sighed dramatically, “Cold, but that’s fine, this is a pretty big chore, you probably couldn’t do it anyway.”

Phainon twitched.

“I’ll just have to ask Hephaestion or maybe even Mydeimos to give me a hand.”

Another twitch and Phainon sat up with a groan. He roughly reached for his boots and yanked them on. Leonnius handed him his shirt and helped him stand.

“You’re gonna want your bracers too.”

“What are we doing?” Phainon grumbled. He slipped his shirt on over his head but left his coat and cape behind.

“It’s cloudy, early, and chilly, which is the best time for fishing,” Leonnius explained. He was helping Phainon with the armguards, way too chipper for the early hour as he strapped them down and then fixed the high collar of Phainon’s v-neck for him.

Oh, well, that explained being awake so long before entry hour. Fishing was easiest right at dawn.

Leonnius recovered the lamp from the floor when he was sure Phainon was awake enough to stand on his own, which was generous considering the way he swayed with the ship. Phainon was still working on his sea legs, this tired it was a tall order asking him to walk in a straight line, but he at least managed to keep up and every step came with more lucidity. Until he slammed into Leonnius’ back on the stairs. The Kremnoan had paused briefly when they turned the corner and saw who was waiting for them at the top.

Fig Stew’s eyes reflected the lamp, glimmering in the dark and framed by dim lamplight. His tail stood straight up, vibrating for a few seconds.

“What’s he doing?” Phainon asked.

“Being impatient.”

Leonnius sighed and walked up to Fig Stew who happily led them both to the upper deck where a tired helmsman waved at them from the tiller. The sails were rolled up tight, but the ship still drifted on currents. The tiller had to be watched at every hour. Both newcomers gave him an acknowledging nod and then set up back by the aplustre.

“Okay so,” Leonnius started, “see this?” He kicked at a big, long storage box built along the side railing. “There’s one on the other side too.”

Phainon gave the side a kick and was rewarded with a hollow sounding thud. He hadn’t realized these were containers. They looked more like benches or wide steps running along each side not quite the full length of the upper deck.

Leonnius leaned down and felt along the shallow lip, searching for the stiff hooks to undo it. “The latches stick a little sometimes.” The same hooks that kept the storage space closed also hooked to the railing to hold the lid open. Leonnius walked the length of one side, opening each section in turn and securing the lid in place. Piled high inside was a collection of fishing equipment, everything from massive, weighted nets to harpoons to long pole fishing hooks, buckets, rope, and so on.

“The same stuff is on the other side,” the Kremnoan was explaining, “have you ever fished with nets before?”

“No,” Phainon said, “most of my fishing experience was your standard rod fishing from a dock back home.”

“Well, this is nothing like that. You sure you’ll be up for it?”

“Of course,” Phainon insisted with determined expression.

“Great, cause trawling is pretty easy, and we can make a game of it.”

Phainon was already interested.

Leonnius pulled out the net and started dumping it onto the deck. It was peculiarly shaped, conical with a wide mouth. One edge was lined with corks; the other was lined with bronze weights. Where they met at either end was a wooden plate fitted with bronze and attached to ropes. Phainon hurried to grab a handful of it, pulling it out to stretch across the deck and make more space for the rest.

“You’ve probably seen it done with two boats or two people on a shoreline,” Leonnius was explaining, “but it’s really easy off the back of one boat and we’re going the right speed for it. All we do is throw the net over, wait for a bit, and then pull it back up full of fish.”

“…that’s it?”

“That’s it.” Leonnius started to point to parts of the net. “This line of corks helps this edge float, while this longer loop is weighted to sink, so it opens up like a mouth under the water.” He pointed to where the net narrowed and became more fine with a tighter weave. “The fish get funneled back into the tighter part of the net where they get tangled up and trapped.”

Phainon picked up one of the attached planks. “What’s this for?”

“They’re like wings. They catch the water as it moves past them and spread apart, pulling the net open from side to side under the water. Without them the net would just pinch closed.”

Phainon followed the ropes from the planks to where they met, tying together into one rope that they would presumably use to pull the net up to the deck. “It’s like flying a kite.”

Leonnius beamed. “Yeah, underwater and full of fish, but yeah, it’s kind of like a kite.”

Fig Stew mewled from the crate and stomped a paw, demanding they both look at him before Leonnius patted Phainon’s arm. “The taskmaster has spoken. Do you think you can finish getting this net set up while I get the other one?”

“Yeah,” Phainon reassured him, now that he had a basic understanding of how this was going to work it didn’t seem too hard to get set up.

Leonnius patted him on the shoulder and then went to the starboard side to start pulling out the netting. Now that Phainon was pulling the net apart to check for tangles or detached corks and weights it was easier to tell how big it was. What seemed irrationally massive before was really a second layer. The inside of the conical part of the net was doubled up to make it sturdier and to more effectively trap thrashing fins. Spread out, each net was small enough to be cast at the same time as the other without tangling due to the width of the ship itself. He unwound the long ropes, making sure that when they went over the railing, they couldn’t tangle themselves. Lining the rope up without overlapping so that it moved back and forth in a line was safer than leaving it in a coil.

“Toss me that line,” Leonnius called while pointing to the single end rope. Phainon swung it a few times and then tossed it over. The Kremnoan tossed it over his shoulder along with his own and then jogged over to the shrouds. Of everyone that Phainon had met on the ship, Leonnius was hands down the most sure-footed. They hadn’t worked the lines side by side yet, but Phainon had seen Leonnius running the deck and racing up the shrouds to fix snagged ropes. Not once had he seen the man stumble. Even now as he carried the two heavy ropes across the yard, he was walking as though it were a sunny day on a stone road.

Leonnius straddled the yard beneath him for balance while he looped the ropes through pulleys on their respective sides of the aftermast. Then he tossed them both down to Phainon who properly split them up on their matching sides of the tiller. He started pulling his rope through the pulley, leaving himself a generous amount to eventually throw overboard with the net.

“Loop it through that pulley too,” Leonnius ordered. The man was as fast as he was sure-footed, already next to Phainon in a flash and pointing to where the aftermast met the upper deck. There were other smaller pulleys there. This one only had one groove, so it would need to be kept taut to avoid slipping. Phainon had made that mistake once. Never again. Once more, Leonnius matched him on the other side.

“Are you a gambling man, Phainon?” Leonnius called to him as he tied the end of the loose rope to a tie off near the railing.

“Depends,” Phainon answered with a grunt as he looped the rope one extra time for good measure.

“If you pull up more fish than I do,” Leonnius started to say as he gathered up his net, “I’ll give you a tip on how to win favor with Fig Stew.”

Phainon smiled, “and if you win?”

“You take my shift polishing shields in the armory.”

With how stingy that chimera’s heart was, that felt like a steal.

“Leonnius, you have yourself a deal,” Phainon said. And then they both shoved their nets into the ocean just as pink started to color the clouds. The ropes whirred and the pulleys spun as the organized coils disappeared over the railing. Phainon bounced away before the rope could snap taut with a twang. The knot held even when the pulleys groaned. The sea splashed around the ropes that dragged in the water and Phainon worried just a little bit as he peered over the railing into the inky black that he had missed a step and his net hadn’t properly opened.

Leonnius had confidently stepped away from his railing and taken up a spot next to Fig Stew to wait. The chimera was pacing along the top of the crate in even prancing circles.

“How long do we have to wait?” Phainon asked as he wandered over too. The impatience was contagious.

“How ever long you think you should,” Leonnius said with a smile.

The spirit of competition stirred in Phainon a bit. “I could just leave my net in all day.”

“And risk the line breaking? If you can’t pull the net up at all, then you’ll have to concede,” Leonnius said in a sing song voice and Phainon’s brows furrowed in thought.

The net had seemed sturdy, but the man was right, the net wouldn’t hold up if he scooped up something particularly big or strong and whatever he did get would need to be hauled up at all. The pulleys would offset most of the weight, but there was still the issue of pulling against the forward momentum of the ship and Phainon would still have to gauge what he could personally lift.

He reached out to offer his hand to Fig Stew who at least paused to consider it. The chimera sniffed Phainon’s fingers, gave him a little lick, and then mewled his disappointment and kept pacing.

“Is he feeling okay?” Phainon worried aloud.

“He’s waiting for his fish.” When Phainon tilted his head in an obvious question, Leonnius added, “any time we fish, Fig Stew gets first pick of the haul.”

“He’s really spoiled, huh?” he laughed.

“Oh, absolutely,” Leonnius agreed. He reached out to scratch Fig Stew’s sides and the chimera relented, rolling over to accept belly rubs from the Kremnoan.

Phainon thought he was being sneaky adding his hand to that soft belly fluff while Leonnius was keeping the critter distracted but not a second after the pads of his fingertips touched fur there were teeth in the meat of his thumb.

“Ow!” He recoiled and cradled his injured hand with a pout. Was Fig Stew smiling at him?

“Damn, still not worthy huh?”

“I thought the Captain made that up…”

Leonnius smiled sympathetically and turned his own hand over. There were two little scars across his palm, two thin lines. “I think everyone on the ship except Mydei have matching scars.”

Fig Stew resumed his eager, excited pacing with his tail straight up and vibrating the whole time.

Phainon very tentatively sat back down. “Does he belong to the Prince then?”

“I don’t think Fig Stew really belongs to anybody,” Leonnius admitted, “I know he favors the Prince but there’s history there.”

That was one of Phainon’s favorite words, history. “Is it the kind of history you could share with an Okheman?” He batted his eyelids for good measure.

“What do you think, Fig Stew? Do we tell the evil Okheman about you?” Leonnius asked as he leaned on the crate.

Fig Stew gave Leonnius an affectionate headbutt and then turned around to bless him with his butt in what seemed to be chimera approval.

“Fig Stew lived in the palace of Castrum Kremnos,” Leonnius said as he scratched that fluffy face, “and slept at the feet of Queen Gorgo.”

Phainon’s jaw dropped just a little bit. He recovered quickly enough not to be embarrassing. He knew that chimeras could live a very long time, but he didn’t know the ages of the chimeras that lived around Okhema. Meeting one that was older and from such a prestigious background felt special, perhaps a little humbling.

“A royal Kremnoan,” Phainon praised, “no wonder he’s so elegant and handsome.”

Fig Stew trotted across the crate to Phainon’s side and sat down with his chest puffed out, his head tilted back, and his eyes closed to bask in the praise.

“Surely, he is the fluffiest of all Chimeras.”

“A King among them, even,” Leonnius agreed, “Nikador envies his spirit.”

“I can see why, look at those perfect ears and mane. Even the hundred thieves of Dolos couldn’t hope to steal enough treasures to be worthy of him.”

The purrs were making the crate shake and Phainon had to put a hand on it to steady it.

“Supposedly, Fig Stew was there when the Prince was born,” Leonnius said, “instant friends. When we joined the detachment, Fig Stew was already there with Krateros, and when we were getting close to finding Mydei, he was the one that leaped into the water to lead us to him. Oh, when he was a baby Mydei was-“

Phainon politely held a hand up, “ah, Ptolemy told me.”

“Oh, good, he’s a way better storyteller.” Leonnius scratched the base of Fig Stew’s tail and the chimera leaned happily into the scratches. “To Mydei, Fig Stew is what’s left of his mother, a way to be closer to her even though he barely got to know her. Well, he and Krateros’ stories.”

“Krateros is the old guy with the bad eye, right?” Phainon asked.

“Yeah. You… actually might not want to get to know him,” Leonnius admitted.

It was a puzzling piece of advice that made Phainon want to know the guy even more. “Why?”

“Krateros is old guard, like leader of the Godshield Brigade elite kind of old guard. He’s not a bad guy, he’s just very traditional and has a lot of combat experience.”

“Sounds like the best kind of guy to learn from.”

“Phainon,” Leonnius said with a shake of his head, “combat experience against Okhema.”

“Oh.”

“Yeah. There are actually a lot of people on the ship that aren’t really sure about you. There’s a lot of really bad blood here that comes from personal experience. You’re really friendly but maybe be a little more careful?”

It was unexpected advice. Phainon rarely met anyone that wasn’t receptive to his charms. Even the Council of Elders and his prickly professor had been swayed over time, but those were neutral parties, and Phainon was once again reminded of the animosity between Okhema and Castrum Kremnos. An animosity that made no sense to him anymore after his talk with Ptolemy.

“Are you one of those people, Leonnius?”

The man chuckled, “if I was, Hephaestion would never have given me the key to your cell. Honestly, what I’ve seen of you so far, I think you’re great.”

Phainon blushed and shyly reached up to scratch the back of his neck. “I don’t know about that.”

“Then prove me right.”

Leonnius got up and dashed over to his rope to give it a tug. “I don’t know about you, but I’m getting close.”

Phainon very suddenly remembered the competition and hurried to check his rope as well. The tight line was rough under his fingers when he gave it an experimental tug. With one hand it gave a little, but it was difficult to pull it very much. With two hands the rope started to lift with minimal effort. He could wait… it looked like Leonnius was debating as well. When Phainon peeked over, he saw Leonnius watching him with a small smirk.

It was urgent mewling that broke them out of their standoff. Even if they weren’t ready, Fig Stew certainly was, which led to another internal debate. If Phainon pulled his net up first, he’d win favor with Fig Stew, but if he waited, he’d win his competition with Leonnius.

A splashing sound snapped him out of his thoughts. Leonnius was pulling his net up, those strong legs putting in the work as he walked backwards. The pulley creaked and squeaked as the net slowly but steadily lifted.

Phainon hurried to his own rope. In just the minute of deliberating it already felt heavier. They must’ve been sailing through a school. He wrapped the rope around his arm for leverage, very suddenly grateful for the advice to bring his armguards. The rough rope settled on the leather and spared his arms the chaffing as he pulled. The pulley stuttered for a second and then started to move. Phainon dug his heels in and held tight with both arms, feeling the tug of war as he fought the ocean and the fish to haul the net one inch at a time.

It was so much harder than he thought to pull those fish up. It would’ve been impossible without the pully system. The ship shifted in the water, and the swaying nearly knocked him over. Phainon’s shoulder slammed into the railing, and he lost a bit of ground, but he got it all back with a determined growl and capitalized on the momentum to rip the top part of the net out of the water. The splashing of the struggling fish was a welcome sign of progress singing to his ears.

Leonnius was in a similar state, struggling with a wild grin that made Phainon realize the Kremnoan was approaching this the same way he would battle, with excited determination and tenacity. This was a demonstration of willpower and physical prowess as much as it was a task to be completed.

He didn’t know exactly how long he struggled with the rope but by the time he managed to pull that net all the way out of the water, the clouds above were a lighter gray with the morning light hidden behind them and the crew starting to wake.

Phainon could see Leonnius out of the corner of his eye also struggling to get his net that last bit over the edge and then back up arrived. Right as Phainon slipped and almost lost the net entirely, another hand was on the rope.

Mydei had hurried to grab the rope just ahead of Phainon and was pulling with unfathomable strength. The muscles in his back were tense and defined, the flex of his biceps more than a little distracting as he pulled on the line. Ptolemy too was rushing to get a hand on the rough rope, coming in behind Phainon to grab the slack there, and the three of them easily pulled the fish up the rest of the way.

The net sloshed over the railing and hung from the pulley just over the deck, up close to the aftermast. The fish were still wiggling in the net, struggling against their bonds as they gasped. As soon as the knot at the split in the rope stuck on the pulley and the net ceased to move farther, both Ptolemy and Mydei let go.

Phainon didn’t realize that was the actual proper thing to do and most definitely did not do the same.

The net dropped to the deck, ripping Phainon forward. He slammed right into Mydei’s back and the both of them were thrown under the mass of fish with a surprised shout and panicked scuffling.

Individually the fish and other collected odds and ends were not particularly heavy, the entire mass of them coming down were. Phainon immediately went down under them alongside the Captain where they both flailed for purchase. Someone thought fast and loosened the top of the net so the fish could spill across the top deck alleviating the weight and leaving the two of them waist deep in sea life.

“HKS!” Mydei snarled, “why didn’t you let go??” He rolled over and sat up with seaweed in his hair and unhappy anchovies bouncing around in his lap. A handful of sardines were tangled in the loose fabric of his chiton and stuck in the metal of his pauldron.

Phainon’s head was spinning. He was trapped on his belly, only the white of his hair sticking out of the sea of scales and fins. A swordfish was bouncing on his back, knocking the wind out of him with every landing until Mydei kicked it off with a heavy boot and then physically pulled Phainon up by the back of his shirt. Ptolemy was trying so hard not to laugh.

Across the deck, Hephaestion and Perdikkas had helped Leonnius lower his net without any casualties and all three of them were laughing so hard that Leonnius was having a hard time staying upright. They wandered over to where Mydei was physically shaking Phainon up and down, whether in punishment or to get the fish out of his clothing it was hard to tell. Probably a bit of both.

“Phainon,” Leonnius was wheezing, “why didn’t you let go?”

“I didn’t know I was supposed to!”

And then everyone except Mydei and Phainon were laughing again.

Mydei let him go with an annoyed grumble and tried to wade to relative safety. He still nearly twisted his ankle slipping on a bream as he plowed through the mess of flopping fish.

“Leonnius,” Hephaestion tried to say around a chuckle. He was holding it together better than most of them. “Did you not tell Phainon on purpose?”

“I swear, I really thought he knew!”

Phainon smiled and shook his head. He started stumbling out of the pile towards Leonnius, dropping to one knee briefly on the way. Phainon played it off like he fell, with one hand extended for balance, but the other scooped up a handful of sardines.

“Really I should have!” he laughed, “it’s a silly thing that I didn’t realize!”

He dashed at Leonnius and playfully shoved the fish inside his exomis, making the man jump and squeal in a manner that had everyone roaring with laughter again. Even Mydei was smiling with his arms crossed and his head slightly bowed.

“Now we’re even,” Phainon laughed.

“Not quite,” Leonnius said with a grin. He pulled the last of the sardines out of his clothing and tossed it back on the pile, then he gestured with his thumb over his shoulder to his net. It was keeping the fish contained even as it spread across the deck in a blob. “I pulled more in than you did.”

Phainon’s face fell.

“Did you bet on this?” Perdikkas asked.

“We certainly did,” Leonnius declared proudly, “have fun polishing shields, Phainon.”

Phainon tsked. “How can you possibly tell with my fish scattered across the deck?”

“What were the terms of your agreement?” Mydei asked from the railing.

“Whoever pulled up the most fish wins,” Leonnius told him.

Mydei kicked a fish out of the way to walk to the center of the deck so he could assess both piles. “Your nets are fairly even, not accounting for the sizes of each fish, I’d say you each pulled up the same weight.”

As if on cue, Fig Stew made his grand entrance. He jumped from his crate, ran up to Mydei to tackle the Captain’s legs affectionately, and then bounded through Phainon’s pile of fish. The happy chimera walked away with at least seven sardines crammed into his mouth.

“…Leonnius wins,” Mydei announced.

Phainon wanted to protest, surely counting the fish after Fig Stew had stolen his cut wasn’t fair! But the others were already laughing and Leonnius was offering his hand to shake.

“You put up a worthy fight,” he praised, “and it is an honor to be the one to have appeased Fig Stew.”

Phainon huffed a happy little huff and grasped Leonnius’ arm. “As did you. I’d like a rematch.”

“Anytime, Okheman.”

“You know you still have to gut and sort the fish,” Hephaestion offered.

“That’s true. Are you any good with a filet knife, Phainon?”

“Oh, I have some experience,” he said. They were still shaking hands and smiling at each other, gripping the other’s arm a little tighter and a little tighter the longer they held on.

“Whatever gets these fish cleaned up the fastest,” Mydei grumbled, “it would be nice to walk across my deck again.”

“Then let us help,” Perdikkas offered, “would you two be amenable to partners for your competition?”

Phainon considered that for a moment. “I don’t mind, as long as the teams are fair.”

“’Many hands make light work,’” Ptolemy said in the monotone recital voice he used for quotes.

“Then I will be on Phainon’s side,” Hephaestion offered and Leonnius whistled.

“What did we just say about fairness?” he complained.

“I suppose the only way to balance these teams would be if His Highness would help Leonnius,” Perdikkas mused out loud. Everyone turned to look at Mydei.

“Do you really think so little of yourself Perdikkas, to assume you are no match for this Deliverer?” he said with a dismissive wave of his hand.

Phainon’s eyes glittered playfully, and he shrugged, “It’s alright if the Captain doesn’t want to risk losing to an Okheman. Does His Highness even know how to clean a fish?”

Every other Kremnoan on deck hummed a soft ‘ohhhh’ under their breath as they looked between Mydei and Phainon. Phainon who was standing confidently with a teasing, cheeky grin, knowing full well that he was poking the beast and Mydei who had barely reacted aside from tightening his own grip on his crossed arms.

Mydei mumbled something under his breath in Kremnoan and Ptolemy, who was next to him, snickered. “If you need me to personally humble you, Deliverer, then so be it.”

The four of them waited near their piles of seafood, until Ptolemy and Perdikkas could secure a few empty barrels, a couple buckets, and a small table. By then, word had gotten around and the rest of the crew were procrastinating their duties to sneak peeks at the competition. Some of them were watching from the shrouds, others were sneaking around to watch from the aplustre, but everyone was excited. Even Fig Stew wandered back after finishing his treat.

Perdikkas stood in front of the four men. “The middle barrel is for sardines, anchovies, and the other small fish. Each team has a barrel for cleaned breams, swordfish, and any other big fish. That’s gutting, scaling, the works. The buckets are for the discarded parts. The team that completely sorts and preserves their pile first wins.”

“What if we fill the barrel before we finish the pile?” Phainon asked.

“We don’t have the space to save all of it,” Leonnius admitted, “anything that doesn’t fit in the barrels we’ll toss over the side.”

“Any other questions?” Perdikkas asked.

“Are there any stakes in this competition?” Mydei inquired, “or is this only for bragging rights?”

“Does the Captain need anything more than that?” Phainon teased.

The Prince twitched and turned his head to look at him. “Are you afraid of what I may ask for when you lose?”

“It didn’t even cross my mind that we would lose,” he returned, locking eyes.

“Funny, I assumed you were already used to it.”

Hephaestion coughed to stop them. “Perhaps we should get started?”

“Leonnius,” Mydei said without breaking eye contact, and the runner stepped right up, “I will do all the gutting and scaling. I’m trusting you to sort the fish.”

Leonnius saluted.

“Hephaestion,” Phainon called while he kept eying Mydei with a playful smirk, “we’ll do the same. I’ll clean the fish.”

Ptolemy set two filet knives on the table, cleared his throat, and said, “My triumph always be yours… Begin!”

They were off in a flash. Phainon immediately snatched a big fish from the pile before he went to the table to scoop up the knife. He cut off the fins in clean swipes, then one clean slit down its belly and he was pulling the guts free. If he wasn’t so focused on winning it might have been gross. He hadn’t done this since he was a boy when his father taught him how to clean and cook his catches from the dock.

Across from him, Mydei had already trimmed his first fish and was almost done scaling it. Phainon looked up in confusion when he saw that Mydei had skipped slitting its belly. He was about to flag a judge when he saw the man expertly cut the fish along the gill… and pull out all the insides in one go. The fish was tossed into Mydei’s barrel, and Leonnius, as fast as he was, already had the next one in front of him.

He may have underestimated Mydeimos.

The next hour was a flurry of scales, fish guts, and runners. Leonnius was easily the fastest man on the ship, but Hephaestion made up for the lack of speed with efficient tenacity. Mydei and Phainon always had their next fish lined up and ready, with no down time.

“You’re better with a knife than I thought,” Phainon complimented while they worked.

“You’re not so bad yourself. A month of working in the galley and you might compare to me,” Mydei teased, smirking while his eyes glittered. He tossed another fish into his barrel.

Phainon wanted to be mad, but the banter didn’t make him angry so much as light a fire in his blood. There was something so invigorating about the competition. Competing with Leonnius had been fun but there was an energy that Mydeimos brought to the table that was so different. The playfulness was elevated into something so much fiercer and wild. More than anything else Phainon wanted to win, and he could see that Mydei did too.

The Captain was meeting Phainon’s eagerness with his own at every step until they were pushing themselves faster and faster. Twice he had to slow down when he almost cut himself, and once he had to redo a fish because he forgot to scale the other side. And every time, Mydei would smirk with glee like a warrior that had found the chink in an enemy’s armor on the battlefield. But for every mistake Phainon made, so did Mydei. That confidence led to tiny errors that needed to be fixed. Not every kind of fish could be gutted through the gills, not every fish cleaned easily, and while Mydei had the advantage in experience, Phainon matched him in fighting spirit and willpower.

It was the second quint of the action hour, clouds still covered the sky, a pale gray, plenty of light to see the last fish drop in each barrel just as both Mydei and Phainon declared simultaneously, “Done!”

Spectators cheered but both Mydei and Phainon were staring at Ptolemy and Perdikkas who leaned in close to whisper to each other. Hephaestion and Leonnius pressed in close with their respective teammates. As close as the race had been, this fell to the judges to decide.

“After discussing it amongst ourselves,” Ptolemy started.

“We decided to call in an expert to determine the winner,” Perdikkas finished. He waved his hand down at Fig Stew who happily hopped up onto the table to be more easily seen.

The chimera calmly strode across the table, head held high, steps regal, to peer into both barrels. He fished around with his paws and pulled a fish out of Mydei’s barrel. The men started to cheer and Mydei crossed his arms, staring Phainon down with a smug look until Fig Stew went to Phainon’s barrel and the smirk dropped. The cheering turned into confused mumbles before silence descended on everyone like a held breath.

More pawing.

Fig Stew pulled a fish out of Phainon’s barrel and put it on top of the one he had grabbed from Mydei’s. Both fish were the same size as the chimera. He struggled to hold both of them in his mouth at the same time, needing to hold them by what was left of their tails. He waddled with them both, stance wide to straddle his prize as the fish dragged between his legs. Everyone watched him go in stunned silence as he dropped the fish off the table, grabbed them again, and resumed his dignified waddle through the sea of spectators until he was out of sight.

Mydei and Phainon watched him go with loosened jaws and dumbfounded expressions.

“I guess that means it’s a tie,” Hephaestion laughed, and the silence broke into cheers.

- The only hint that Mydei was annoyed by the outcome was his insistent order that everyone finish cleaning up. Not even he could question Fig Stew’s ruling. He had grumbled about the fish smell and then disappeared to do his own chores, whatever those may have been, while Phainon and Leonnius got to work packing the nets away. There was a special way to do it, Leonnius had insisted, to ensure that they would be easy to use the next time they needed to fish.

Hephaestion and Ptolemy handled the barrels with a couple others on the crew. The fish would be preserved in oil or salt at the discretion of the head cook, who would inevitably be the one to serve it to them eventually.

With things put away, Phainon followed Leonnius and the others below decks to follow Mydei’s second and most important order. Fresh water was limited on the ship, but Mydei had expressly ordered that anyone who had participated in the morning escapade bathe, and not a single person argued with the demand. No matter how tired they were, all of them were eager to wipe themselves clean.

A communal bathing area was easy to set up in the crew’s living quarters with a changing area and a place to dump their dirty clothes until someone (probably Phainon) could get around to washing them. Phainon helped them fill several washbasins while Leonnius passed out sponges and towels.

It wasn’t the same as a bath at the Marmoreal Palace, but the water was warm from sitting in the barrels and it felt good running down his arms, his chest, and back. The sponge was soft and gentle; they even had sweet smelling soap and oil. Phainon didn’t even mind sharing the space with his new friends.

“I am so glad that I woke you up this morning, Phainon,” Leonnius said cheerfully.

“You know what, Leonnius,” Phainon said with a smile, “so am I.”

Even if it did mean the rest of his day would be spent polishing shields.

Chapter End Notes

I realized I've been using a lot of technical terms and not everyone wants to google things in the middle of reading, so I put some terms in here just in case!

Exomis – tunic that leaves one shoulder exposed Aplustre – The curved part of the back of a Greek trireme Bow – Front of a ship Stern – Back of a ship Aftermast/Aftmast – The third mast from the bow Yard – the part of the mast that the sails are hung from, the beam that runs perpendicular to the mast

chapters.title: Chapter 6: Storms
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Updating the tags with this chapter New tags: PTSD, Minor Injuries

Overcast skies that lured fish closer to hungry nets were also an opportunity to restock on fresh water. So Phainon wasn’t even kind of surprised to see the crew tightening the ropes that held empty and half full water barrels against the railing to catch the expected drizzle. They were sealing up the belly of the ship as best they could too, covering the cargo hatch so the water couldn’t get below and clearing out the scuppers to improve drainage.

Under the protection of the Dawn Device and the eternal day, storms and rain were a light affair in Okhema, welcome moisture for the plants along the coast but rarely anything of concern. In these farther seas, where night still shared the sky with the sun, it was harder to tell if this was a blessed raid, or the prelude to a harsher melody.

The seas themselves were choppy but not alarmingly so and the sails were already furled when Phainon finished polishing that last shield, handed it to the ship’s Armorer to lock up in the Armory, and headed sleepily to bed. He had underestimated the sheer number of shields to polish and had to eat while he worked. Leonnius had at least brought him one of the grilled fish cooked on a stick to perfection and Ptolemy had sat with him to start working on Kremnoan phrases. Phainon could very proudly now say, “hello, my name is Phainon” with a very heavy accent.

It was dark when he flopped on his bed and Hephaestion locked him in. Someone had cleaned his fishy clothing and left them on a crate nearby, but he was too tired to change out of his borrowed exomis and instead spread out on his mat facedown like a starfish.

This had been one of those days that had Phainon questioning his mission. Despite the chaos of everything, a couple very key things stuck in the forefront of his mind.

The first was what Leonnius had said about being too friendly. As much as Phainon understood why he had been given that advice, it still hurt to hear. But maybe he needed the wake-up call. It was easy to forget that he was a fleeting person on this ship. Hell, Phainon was literally sitting in a cage in the brig because there were people that didn’t trust him.

And they were right not to.

When they eventually made it to a port and Phainon left the ship, he’d return to Okhema with way more information than he had expected to have. Even if he wanted to protect the Kremnoan Detachment, Aglaea’s threads would read his lies and know if he held back. Even if she could be swayed to understand, the Council would not. What Phainon saw as proof of peace, they would see as an opportunity.

For all he knew, they did know that Eurypon had been killed and were waiting for news about the state of Castrum Kremnos. Aglaea’s fleet had been growing, maybe they were waiting for exactly the information Phainon would bring to them, that the Kremnoans were King-less, waiting on a young man that didn’t seem interested in continuing their conflict. Would the Council of Elders seek them out? Destroy them once and for all while Mydei’s people were scattered?

Aglaea had a vested interest too. She was still seeking coreflames. The prophecy that fueled her Flame-Chase Journey said that they were the key to the Black Tide. The only chance of long-term prosperity included retrieving the Coreflame of Strife, the last known whereabouts of which was Castrum Kremnos, supposedly in the care of Kremnoan priests. What better time to invade than when the city was leaderless?

The second thing that lingered in the forefront of Phainon’s mind was admittedly less noble and more self-indulgent. The sheer relief and joy that he had felt when he thought that fishing net was going to win and Mydeimos’ jumped on the line to help him.

Phainon felt his cheeks grow warm as he thought about Mydei’s back and arms and the definition of his muscles and the strength of his spirit as they pulled together. There was something charming about how well they worked together, how easily they fell into that rhythm even when they stood on opposing sides, and Phainon really wanted to spend more time with him.

Mydei’s friends were quick to share things about him, they had an eagerness for Phainon to understand their best friend, and the more he learned and the more he stood in the Prince’s presence the more he wanted to. It was a budding curiosity, Phainon told himself, nothing more. A chance for peace between their nations. Others were certain he would become King someday, surely it was Phainon’s duty to get to know the Crown Prince as a proper Ambassador, before they went their separate ways.

It was a happy bonus that the man was easy on the eyes.

-

Creaking lumber and battle instincts saved Phainon’s life. The ship listed violently to one side and the crates in his cell shifted as he jolted awake and sprang to his feet just as the supplies slammed against the bars, taking his sleeping mat with them.

It took him a very long second to process what was happening. Phainon hadn’t remembered falling asleep and now he was very awake and very concerned.

The ship lurched the other direction and the crates slid again, this time taking him along too. His fingertips brushed the bars, but he fell down the slope of the tilting ship before he could grab them and landed painfully against the edge of a box. Both of his boots followed, slamming into his stomach and face. The hanging lanterns were fighting for their lives. One of them broke free when the ship lurched back again. It crashed against the wall and sputtered out in the couple inches of water that was soaking the floor. Rainwater streamed from above, leaking through the cover over the grate.

Phainon hurried to pull his boots on and scrambled in the dark for his shirt and pants. He had been too tired to take off his bracers, which was a boon, when a barrel in his cell nearly rolled over him and he had to support its weight with his arms before he could wiggle free. Thunder shook the whole ship and Phainon felt his blood run cold. The ship shifted violently again, and he slammed into the bars of his cage. If the ship went down and he was trapped in here…

He waited until the ship was level for a few seconds and then tried to kick at the door to break the lock. Another lurch and he stumbled. Then tried again, then again, every kick the door clanged but held firm.

“Hephaestion!” Phainon yelled but there was predictably no response. It was almost impossible to hear anything over the sound of crashing waves, thunder, and rain. The roar of the sea was a battle cry against the Chryseus Leo, swallowing his pleas.

“Leonnius!” he tried. “Anybody!”

A box broke into splinters next to him when it crashed against the steel bars. He raised an arm to protect his eyes and fought to stay upright, so he could again slam his boot helplessly against the door of his prison, hard enough to feel the vibrations all the way up his spine.

“Mydeimos!” he yelled, desperate and praying.

A yowl responded. Clinging to the bottom most stair was Fig Stew. All his little claws were dug deep into the wood, holding tightly as those red eyes darted between Phainon and the floor covering puddle.

His heart and face fell seeing the chimera in distress. Phainon tried to kick the door again and snarled angrily when it didn’t give. He held tightly to the bars.

“You need to find somewhere safe, Fig!” he yelled, but the chimera was still trying to brave that final step. A peal of thunder rolled through them and Phainon worried it would startle him but the animal seemed to find courage in the sound. Unbothered by the crack and roll that hurt Phainon’s ears, Fig Stew was infinitely more upset with the rocking of the ship.

He waited until the ship leveled out and then dashed into the puddle, plowing through the water towards Phainon. Halfway between the bars and the stairs, the ship stuttered and tilted again, and Fig Stew traveled the rest of the way through the air.

The chimera popped right between the bars and into Phainon’s arms as the man hurried to catch the little guy. Phainon cradled the chimera to his chest, holding tightly and stroking his fur.

“It’s okay,” he muttered reassuringly, making a soothing shhh sound as he did. “I’ve got you, you’re okay.”

But Fig Stew was on a mission, and he wiggled his way loose enough of Phainon’s tight grip to slap him across the face without claws to make the man let go.
