He jumped from Phainon’s arms to the top of one of those sliding boxes and wiggled his tail back and forth to make the key jingle on its ring.

“You might have saved my life,” Phainon said with a sigh of relief. He nearly dove on the key as Fig Stew set it down and held on tight with the rocking of the ship to fumble through his freedom. Reaching around to feel for the keyhole was genuinely difficult to do while also dodging debris but he managed and Phainon left it in the lock while he raced out of the cell towards the stairs.

He turned back at the entrance to the stair well to wait for Fig Stew, but the chimera must’ve known something he didn’t. The animal mewled at him and then disappeared deeper into the hold, running for a safe spot.

The ship rumbled again and Phainon stumbled to the upper decks. Before he stepped out into the hurricane winds, he could hear shouting and yelling. There were people out on deck, even as the ship tilted at extreme angles, they were pointing and shouting, trying to communicate over the wind and rain, using the dim light of morning cloud cover and the lightning to see what they were doing.

A series of flashes ripped across the sky and Phainon saw red sails fluttering haphazardly in the wind. The storm must’ve knocked them free. Left unfurled, they could tear and be lost, or worse, capsize the ship. Loose and broken lines whipped in the wind. Phainon could see others trying to catch them, to tie them down or use them to close the sails. There were some people in the shrouds, fighting with the heavy canvas.

He ran out on deck, stumbling the whole way to grab a rope that was flailing nearby with both hands. It very nearly ripped him off his feet and Phainon reached with his boot to hold onto the railing with his foot for leverage. A shout ripped from his throat when the rope slipped in his hands, tearing the flesh there, still he held on while his body strained. The tiniest lull in the wind bought him reprieve enough to pull the rope down enough to loop it around one of the tie off spots along the railing.

The ship slammed into a tall wave and tilted just as Phainon was getting back to his feet. He slammed into the railing beside him, and looped his arms around the rail, holding tightly as the tilt threatened to spill him over the side. The water below was black and full of malice. He stared at it wide-eyed as primal fear washed over him with the rain. It felt like the ocean was reaching for him, desiring him. A horrible voice ripped through the back of his mind, speaking in layers, the language of the Titans. He couldn’t understand the words, but the intent squirmed under his skin to settle inside his bones with familiar terror.

Very suddenly, Phainon was no longer on a ship. He could still feel the rain, but the horrible memories of his burning village were all encompassing. The black of the ocean smelled like smoke and the creaking of the ship was replaced with the screaming of his parents and crackling of a hungry fire. He hyperventilated at the rail, desperate to find himself.

A rough hand on his shoulder pulled him back to waking. Leonnius was looking at him with wide eyes, shouting something he couldn’t hear. The man tossed a noose over Phainon’s head and the chill in his bones was back, but Leonnius wiggled it over his shoulders and tightened it around his waist instead.

Phainon gave the lifeline a tug. He was tied to the mast now, a safety net in case the ocean reached for him again.

Leonnius shouted again but thunder cut him off. He slapped Phainon’s cheek hard enough to clear whatever fog the Kremnoan had seen there and Phainon bounced back to the present. Above them one of the sails started to tear and Leonnius was off in a flash, scrambling up the shrouds and leaving Phainon to find another way to help.

He squinted in the rain, trying to make sense of the movement as he hiked up the deck against the wind. For a second, Phainon thought he saw gold glitter in the flashing lightning and he ran towards it.

Mydei was holding two different lines, one in each hand. His feet were sliding on the deck as he struggled to hold them while men worked from the shrouds. Phainon paused when the deck tilted and then ran when it tilted back, taking advantage of the temporary downhill to dive on one of those lines.

Mydei’s amber eyes locked onto his for a second. The Captain didn’t bother trying to yell at him as Leonnius had. He happily let go of the line that Phainon had grabbed and turned to focus on his own. Phainon wrapped the rope around his arm for the better grip, supporting the worst of the biting, water-logged lines over the hard leather of his bracers just as he had when fishing. This was notably harder than that had been.

Side by side with Mydei, Phainon had a better understanding of what was happening. The torn topsail needed to come down to the deck. The sail couldn’t be furled the way it was ripped. Blinking through the rain he could see others on the yard trying to untangle the ropes so it could be safely lowered to the deck and secured. He and Mydei were holding the sail mostly closed which explained how damn hard it was when the wind was working against them.

A gust of wind pulled Phainon off balance and the rope pulled him forward but a strong arm around his waist held him steady until he found his footing again. Mydei was still holding the bulk of the weight on his line with one arm, using the other to steady them both.

Phainon studied the way he was standing and tried to copy it, widening his stance and digging in his heels. It helped until the ship listed again and Phainon’s foot slipped, but Mydei once more grabbed him, holding him by the arm until he found his footing.

It was easy to understand in those little touches exactly what to do and Mydei was so in sync with Phainon’s sways that the moment he felt those gauntlets on his arm, Phainon was able to correct, to hold his stance, listening without his ears as his confidence grew and that crushing fear morphed into a distant worry. Standing next to Mydei, Phainon felt like they were at war, standing together under one banner against an impossible enemy, with no hope of winning, and not a single shred of hesitation between them. The odds didn’t matter as long as they had breath and strength to hold on tight.

They held like that until the sail was gathered. Phainon could feel the pressure on the line ease but then it was unexpectedly gone entirely. He turned to look at Mydei with confusion when he heard the shout.

Phainon reacted first. He tackled Mydei, pressing his shoulder into the man’s muscular chest and sending them both to the deck. The top sail crashed into the spot that Mydei had been standing, tearing through the railings on both sides of the ship. Phainon felt pain lance through his leg and held still where he lay across Mydei’s chest.

Mydei’s gauntlets grabbed at his shirt and shoulders, Phainon thought he could hear yelling but the only thing he could process was the sudden warmth below his knee.

-

When Phainon had come crashing out of the gloom, the first thing Mydei felt was relief. It was the kind of feeling that he would’ve liked to contemplate further if the urgency of the situation hadn’t taken priority. He was genuinely happy to see the man had somehow freed himself, was in awe of how he had braved the elements to help, and was deeply honored to stand next to him as he struggled.

Phainon was utterly hopeless on a ship tossed by rough seas. Mydei had seen the way he stumbled every damn day on this ship when the slightest breeze made the vessel wiggle. No sea legs to speak of, but despite that Phainon was here, beside him, holding tightly to a rope and doing his absolute best.

There was no need to communicate with words, every time Mydei reached for Phainon to steady him, the man responded perfectly to the touch and corrected himself. He saw those brilliant blue eyes taking in his own stance, mimicking him, striving to learn to be better, to meet Mydei on equal ground.

Their backgrounds, their statuses, nothing mattered to the storm aside from their matching indomitable wills. And for a heartbeat in that freezing rain, Mydei smiled at the thrill of the fight, the joy of standing shoulder to shoulder with someone of merit, and the poeticism of fighting against nature.

And then the rope went slack and in the second it took Mydei to realize what was happening, Phainon had slammed into him, sending them both across the deck. The wind was knocked out of him as his back hit the polished wood and again when Phainon landed across his body with his shoulder in Mydei’s belly.

He lay there with the rain beating on his face for one held breath and then tried to sit up, but Phainon was still laying on him. His white hair was sticking to Mydei’s chest with the rain, and he was barely moving.

Propped up on his elbows, Mydei could see the deck in splinters. If Phainon hadn’t have knocked him away… Mydei tsked. He was immortal. Crushed by the sail would certainly have been an unpleasant way to go but he would’ve woken up, complained to Perdikkas about the ache, and gone on with his day.

For Phainon to throw himself in harm’s way to save him, either he didn’t know, or he was acting on instinct. This wannabe hero really threw himself into danger for someone he should see as an enemy, as his captor.

“Deliverer,” Mydei shouted but it was swallowed in the din. He grabbed at Phainon’s shoulders and tried to shake him, but the man didn’t spring to his feet as he had hoped. Lightning flashed and Mydei’s eyes caught on gold running across the deck. Another flash and he could see the jagged piece of wood sticking out of Phainon’s pant leg near the meat below his knee. It was too dark and the rain too heavy to see how bad it was.

He tsked and then the ship started tilting again. The dislodged sail groaned and slid but it didn’t roll. For better or worse it had trapped itself in the railing when it broke through it on impact. Tangled as it was, they were unlikely to lose it over the side either.

Mydei wrapped an arm around Phainon, reaching across his back to hold on to his side under his arm, the other grabbed a handful of his shirt while the ship threatened to throw them to the sea. He could feel the man’s heartbeat racing under his fingers, feel him gasp as they slid a few feet until Mydei was able to get his heel pressed against something solid.

“Take a breath,” he ordered, not convinced Phainon could hear him. The man reached up and grabbed onto the fabric of Mydei’s chiton near his hips, holding on tightly. It was a good sign that he was conscious and coming back to himself.

Leonnius dropped onto the deck beside them, kneeling. He had been in the shrouds helping to drop the sail not a second prior.

“Are you okay?!” he yelled, only a few inches from Mydei’s ear and Mydei still barely heard him over the rolling peal of thunder.

“He’s hurt,” Mydei shouted back. He pointed to Phainon’s leg. Leonnius waited for the ship to list again and then crept on his hands and knees to Phainon’s injury.

Mydei tightened his grip on Phainon when he saw Leonnius reaching and he was glad he did cause the man tried to buck and recoil when Leonnius pressed on it. He tensed and quivered under Mydei’s grip, fists tight where he was holding onto Mydei’s clothes, as Leonnius ripped the plank free.

Phainon cried out and panted, curling his good leg up as he tried to relax while Leonnius tore the base of his own exomis to tightly bind the wound.

“It’s not nearly as bad at it looks,” Leonnius reported as he crept back up to Mydei, screaming in the rain. “Perdikkas will need to stitch it up for sure, but it went clean through the meat. It’ll hurt but he can probably still walk on it without making it worse.”

Mydei nodded and yelled, “Go help the others with that last sail.”

“May victory be ours, Mydeimos,” Leonnius yelled and then he was gone, running off in the rain.

Mydei took a deep breath, let the ship rock, and then he pulled Phainon further up his body so he could be close enough to yell at him.

“Listen to me, Deliverer,” he shouted, and he saw Phainon’s eyes move, “your injury is such that it would only stop a weak man.” Those blue eyes narrowed. “Are you a weak man?”

Phainon grunted and started shakily pushing himself up. The ship lunged to one side and Phainon crashed back into Mydei, chest to chest, but Mydei used it to get a better grip on him, wrapping one arm around his back again and using the other to pull them both up. He kept his hold on Phainon tight until the man was pushing Mydei off and holding himself upright without help. Even so, Mydei reached out to grab his forearm so he could lean in to yell again.

“If you would be a hindrance to my crew, crawl below decks now, but if you can yet stand, come help me.”

Phainon squeezed back. He looked a little pale but that could’ve been the dim light and the blue of lightning. Mydei trusted Phainon to know his own limits. He reached for Phainon’s waist to test that the lifeline was tight and then they were hurrying across the deck.

The last sail that needed to come down was the foresail on the foremast. It was the sail closest to the deck, and it wasn’t torn yet. They just needed to tie it closed and then everyone could get to safety below decks to ride out the rest of the storm. There were already men aloft and Mydei spotted Hephaestion and Krateros already on lines. He turned and grabbed Phainon’s arm, pointing him towards Hephaestion before Mydei hurried to help Krateros.

Phainon already had a hard time walking across the deck, the limp wasn’t doing him any favors, but Mydei saw him nearly throw himself on the rope, take it in both arms and start pulling with just as much ferocity as he had before.

Very slowly, the sail furled, Mydei’s body was barely starting to ache as the cold pelted his mostly bare chest. No doubt there were scratches on his back from when Phainon had tackled him too. He was ready to be below decks with the others, so as soon as the last sail was secured, Mydei began herding people to cover. He was unwilling to go down himself until every man was safe.

Unsurprisingly, Phainon and Hephaestion were lagging behind. Despite the injury, Phainon was helping his first mate double check the ties, both the ones for the sails and the lines holding the tiller. Mydei hurried to do the same and when all three men were satisfied, they stumbled towards the stairs at the bow.

Hephaestion ducked into safety and shed his lifeline as Mydei turned to wait for Phainon. He undid the knot of the rope around his waist as he waited, tossing the lifeline to the side. They would just be an unnecessary hassle below decks with the limited length of rope tangling on everything.

Lightning cracked again and the sea was illuminated; a massive wave was rolling their way. Mydei gestured for Phainon to hurry and held tightly to the doorway himself, but the warning came too late. The wave picked up the stern and the ship tilted again with a sharp jolt. Mydei watched Phainon’s injured leg give and he was thrown to the side. He hit the railing with a crunch and then his scrambling body went overboard.

With an urgent shout Mydei was hurrying to grab onto Phainon’s lifeline, a lifeline that should’ve already gone taut, but the loose end was whipping by, racing out to sea with the man. He would have surely been lost if Mydei hadn’t started running when he did. The Kremnoan dove on the end of the rope and pulled with desperation, holding on with his claws to the mere foot of remaining cord. He snarled and put his foot against the railing for leverage and yelled at the sky when the ship again tilted, nearly ripping him overboard too. Maybe he had taken his own lifeline off a little prematurely.

Someone slammed into Mydei’s back and wrapped their arms around his waist, helping him pull, then another until they finally made progress and a soaking wet Phainon was reachable from the rail.

Hephaestion and Mydei each grabbed onto him and pulled him over to drop him on the deck and Perdikkas slid to his knees to press on his chest with firm pumps until Phainon was coughing and vomiting seawater.

Perdikkas helped him sit up when the ship tilted in their favor, grabbing one of the man’s arms to throw over his shoulder. Mydei hurried to grab the other one and they half carried, half dragged Phainon below decks.

It was a tight squeeze, loud with people talking and shouting. Most of the crew were in a line with buckets, passing water from the hold up the stairs to dump on the main deck where it could drain through the scuppers. They weren’t at any risk of sinking due to water getting below decks, but they didn’t want the water to get above a certain threshold, lest it ruin their food supply.

Mydei shoved past most of them, following Perdikkas to the other end of the ship, to the warmth and dry of the infirmary with Phainon in tow. He kicked the door open and then dropped him onto the bed there with a gentle roll. He was still dazed, pale, and coughing, barely conscious.

“What the hell is happening out there?” Hephaestion said, “this storm came out of nowhere.”

Mydei shook his head. “No, it’s…”

“Hephaestion,” Perdikkas said, cutting them off with other priorities, “help me get him out of his wet clothes, I need to see how bad that leg is.”

They got to work while Mydei ran a hand anxiously through his hair. It hadn’t really clicked until now how terrifying that was. He shouldn’t have run back into the rain without his own lifeline attached, they could’ve both been lost at sea. Hephaestion and Perdikkas too had not been secured when they rushed to help. One more bad wave and the three of them assuredly would have drowned and Mydei would’ve lost more than a few lives waiting to be found and fished out again.

He took a shuddering breath and a step backwards to give the doctor some space and just about rolled his ankle stepping on Phainon’s lifeline. It was still attached to his waist, the rope trailing behind him like a tail.

He let his arm fall to his side as he followed the rope with his eyes to the unattached end. Amber smoldered in the lantern light, thunder rolled above them, but Mydei’s entire focus was on that splayed end of rope. He dropped to one knee to pick up the end, running his thumb over the even fibers. His whole body started to shake with barely restrained rage.

The rope had been cut.

Someone had tried to kill Phainon.

-

Perdikkas really wanted to tell Mydei to leave. Mydei could see it all over his face as he stood in the infirmary waiting patiently for Phainon to wake.

“Your Highness,” Perdikkas finally said with stress in his voice, “I gave him poppy in his water, he’s not going to wake for awhile.”

Mydei tapped his fingers on his arm and stayed put anyway.

“I’ll make sure he eats what you brought.”

Still no movement.

“Are you worried someone is going to try and kill him while he’s in here?”

Mydei’s grip on his arms tightened.

“Ah ha,” Perdikkas sighed and dumped the supplies he had been trying to sort back into the helpless pile on the floor. The storm had shaken everything up so badly that everyone was going to be on clean up and repair duty for a while. Poor Ptolemy hadn’t stopped sobbing in the library doorway since the storm had stopped around the Lucid Hour. Which was saying something as the light of the thief star had just barely passed by overhead not even a quint past. Mydei had brought food for both Perdikkas and Phainon and was notably upset that Phainon was still sleeping.

“How bad was his leg?”

“Not bad,” Perdikkas walked over to where Phainon was covered to pull back the blanket and lift the bandages. It was stitched up tight in two places. “The fragment went through but close enough to the edge of his leg that it barely went through the muscle. It bled a lot, but it will heal quickly and with few issues.” He covered the leg again and gave Phainon’s chest a gentle pat. The man was snoring lightly with a stupid smile on his face as he slept.

“Mydei, do you know who cut his lifeline?” Perdikkas asked softly.

“No, I don’t.” Mydei’s brow furrowed ever so slightly as he watched Phainon sleep. “And I will probably never know. It would be a fool’s errand to hunt for the culprit on behalf of a prisoner. The distrust would upset the veterans on the crew.”

“What are you going to do?”

“…I don’t know,” Mydei admitted, “For now, he no longer sleeps in the brig. He will sleep in my quarters.”

Perdikkas raised one eyebrow and Mydei looked away, perhaps a little shy about the suggestion no matter how confidently he ordered it.

“I told Krateros that I would take responsibility for him. It makes sense that I keep him close! This way I will be able to monitor his actions and if necessary, protect him.”

“You don’t need to explain yourself, Mydei. I think it’s a great idea.”

Chapter End Notes

New term:

Scuppers – drain holes along the deck so water won’t pool around the railings

chapters.title: Chapter 7: The Strength and Kindness of Strife
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Everybody needs healing after that storm.

New tags: Medicinal Drug Use

Chapter Notes

I’m glad we’re all in agreement that Fig Stew is the best and yes, he’s in this chapter too.

My husband sails and he came through to correct my terminology and I had to sit there like, man idek what these words mean, I’m not doing that to my readers too. Turns out sailors really have whole other languages on the water so if there are sailors reading this, I know I'm mixing it up a bit, bear with me. The coherency of the story takes priority over naval term accuracy.

Thanks to the poppy that Perdikkas had given him for the pain, Phainon had slept heavily for a full day and a half, only rousing to half consciousness for water and bathroom breaks at the urging of his doctor, who never once left him unattended. They even barred the infirmary door at night to lock it as a precaution.

When Phainon was finally, properly awake, Perdikkas sent Leonnius to fetch Mydei.

“Well, you wanted me to tell you when he woke,” Perdikkas said with a grin.

Mydei stood in the doorway of the infirmary with his brows pinched together and a meal in hand. He couldn’t decide if he needed to be worried or if he wanted to laugh.

Phainon was sitting up lopsided in bed, leaning heavily against the wall with one leg over the side of his bed and the other stretched out on top of the blankets like he was trying to claim as much space as possible. He had the dumbest grin on his face, glassy eyes, and was babbling like a child at Fig Stew. The chimera was bouncing back and forth in Phainon’s lap, climbing all over those strong, bare thighs while Phainon giggled when it tickled. Aside from his undergarments and an assortment of bandages across his chest, legs, and hands, the man wasn’t wearing anything at all.

He absolutely did not mind, as high as he was, and it gave Perdikkas better access to the awful bruises on his side.

“I thought you only gave him poppy the once…”

“I did,” Perdikkas insisted, “I didn’t think I gave him very much but it’s taking a long time to wear off.”

Phainon spotted Mydei and beamed like the sun, that dazzling smile so bright despite the late afternoon light trying to get in through the dusty windows.

“Captain!” he slurred, “come here! I have to tell you something important!”

Perdikkas raised a hand to cover his mouth to hide his smile and Mydei flashed him a suspicious look.

“Do you know of what he speaks?”

“I really don’t, Mydei. It has been an adventurous quint to say the least.”

Mydei set the bowl of sweet porridge down on the desk and cautiously walked over to Phainon’s side, pulling over Perdikkas’ stool as he went so he could sit down next to him.

“You should be resting, Deliverer,” he ordered, “sleep off the fog.”

“Mydei, Mydei,” Phainon babbled and Mydei had to fight to keep the smile off his face when he heard that adorable voice saying his name. “This is important.”

“If I listen, will you swear to me that you will eat and then sleep?”

“I swear… swur… sweer.” Phainon rolled his head heavily while he played with that word and smacked his lips.

Mydei had poppy sometimes when he was recovering from death, only a little, enough to dull the pain but not enough to completely take his senses and wits. He didn’t like the way it made his body feel heavy and his tongue feel fuzzy, so he sympathized with Phainon. Of course, this out of it, Phainon might not have cared about the unpleasant side effects.

The man was staring intently into empty space, his eyes darting about to chase a fly that wasn’t there. Mydei sighed and reached out to take his face in both hands, cradling his cheeks and jaw, grounding him with his thumbs pressed to the soft skin in front of Phainon’s ears.

“Deliverer, focus!”

Those glittering blue eyes, even glassy and cloudy, were so beautiful looking at him like he was the only thing in the world that mattered. This close Mydei could see the gold flecks scattered in the cerulean. Phainon smiled despite his squished cheeks and when Mydei tried to pull back, Phainon held him loosely by his wrists, leaned forward, and chased his touch with his lips and cheek.

“…is this focusing?” Mydei asked firmly.

“Yes.”

Perdikkas was trying so hard not to laugh behind Mydei. His little snorts and nasally squeaks were still escaping and Mydei finally had to look over his shoulder to give him a pointed glare.

“I’m sorry, it’s just,” Perdikkas started to say but he had to stop to suppress a giggle.

Mydei sighed and turned back to Phainon who was rubbing his cheek against Mydei’s hand, and he kept doing it until Mydei used his thumb to firmly press along his cheekbone under his eye to soothe him.

“You’re really strong,” Phainon mumbled, “I saaaw you in the rain, being really strong.”

“Is that what you needed to tell me?”

“No… Do you have tattoos on your legs too?”

Mydei sighed and very gently guided Phainon back against the wall so he could have his hand back.

“Did we not have a deal? Should I leave?”

Phainon pouted and Mydei felt his heart turn over. Something about a sad Phainon just didn’t settle well in his belly, but he crossed his arms and held his ground.

“Oh, yeah, okay, listen,” he slurred as he fumbled around in his lap. Phainon grabbed Fig Stew under his little arms and held the chimera up so Mydei could see. In the most serious voice he could muster, he said, “he looks just like you.”

Fig Stew blinked at Mydei with a smug expression.

“…truly, it is as though I am peering into a mirror,” Mydei grumbled with a deadpan tone.

“Right??” Phainon breathed. He set Fig Stew down in front of him and reached with both hands for Mydei, gently grabbing his face with both of his hands to squeeze the Prince’s cheeks. “You have prettier eyes though, don’t tell Fig, he might be upset.”

The heat rushed to Mydei’s cheeks and the tips of his ears at the praise. He very gently took hold of Phainon’s wrists to pull his hands away and flashed Fig Stew a look. The chimera seemed very okay with Mydei having prettier eyes and was watching his Kremnoan best friend with half-lidded eyes and that same knowing smug smile from before, like he had figured out a secret.

“I won’t tell him,” Mydei promised, “now do as I ordered of you, Deliverer. Perdikkas will help you eat and then you will sleep. Do you understand?”

“Okay,” he agreed and leaned back again. His head hit the wall with a hollow thunk like he was already jumping ahead to the sleep part. It was as good a time as any to make his escape and Mydei stood up to leave before he could be grabbed again.

“He’s insufferable,” Mydei grumbled to Perdikkas.

“You are so much worse when you’re sick.”

The Prince pouted and Perdikkas playfully slapped his arm at the shoulder. “I’ll have him sobered up and back to work in three entry hours. Nothing strenuous mind.”

“There is work aplenty,” Mydei sighed, “I have no shortage of tasks he could handle.”

They both looked over at Phainon when he started mewling. He and Fig Stew were having a conversation with meows, growls, and the grumbling squeaks of chimera speak.

“…three entry hours. No earlier than that.”

“Of course,” Perdikkas agreed.

Mydei turned to leave, halfway out the door when he heard Perdikkas call to him again and turned to look at his friend over his shoulder.

“You have to admit, Phainon is cute.”

He slammed the door.

-

By entry hour the next morning, Phainon was clear-headed and properly dressed in his exomis. He only vaguely remembered the prior day when Perdikkas asked him about it. He knew the Prince had to come to check on him and had a vague recollection of being held but it was hard to tell if that last part was a memory or a fading dream. In any case, Phainon was ready to be out of bed and frustrated that Perdikkas wouldn’t let him return to his duties right away. He knew that working out would be out of the question but after the storm there were lots of things to do, surely there was something.

“I’ve already wasted a whole day,” he insisted.

“Phainon, your leg is healing well but if I let you get back to work too fast, you’ll tear the stitches and waste my hard work.”

Phainon pouted. “I’ll be careful…”

“If you’re that bored, then help me in here for now.”

Even after a day of sorting and cleaning, Perdikkas only had half the infirmary put back together. Everything had been hastily stuffed into boxes to recover floor space but now nothing was organized, and it was taking him forever to find things he needed without dumping it all out onto the floor again.

The doctor was already going through a box on his table, pulling out jars and herbs that didn’t belong and setting them aside. Phainon rocked in bed to get to a stand and limped over to look at what he was doing.

“If you want to take this box,” Perdikkas was saying, “anything that’s in a jar needs to come out and be put into this case.” He pointed to a small chest on the table. “And anything that’s in a packet needs to be piled up for me to sort. Bandages go in that box and if it was damaged, put it in this crate.” He kicked the crate on the floor with his foot.

Phainon listened to the instructions intently, delighted to be able to help. He took Perdikkas’ spot at the table and started rifling through the box. He was a little surprised to see that the war ship had a vast collection of state-of-the-art medical equipment, bandages, herbs for poultices, oils, salts, and so on.

“Perdikkas,” Phainon started, “I thought Kremnoans wanted to die in battle.”

“There is glory in dying in combat, yes.”

Perdikkas grunted as he lifted another big box onto the table next to Phainon’s. He took up a spot next to him to sort through those supplies.

“Why all this stuff then?”

“What do you mean?”

“All of these supplies are for preserving life, staving off death. Why keep so much if it’s contrary to your creed?”

“’Valorous death before glorious return,’” Perdikkas quoted, “it’s true, that is the Kremnoan way. Scars and wounds are symbols of honor and courage, to die on the battlefield is to send our souls and those of our respected enemies to fuel Nikador’s blade, the ultimate sacrifice to serve alongside our Titan even in death.” He tossed a roll of bandages over his shoulder into the correct container with one hand and set a jar of something that smelled strongly of flowers into the chest. “But if it was as simple as throwing our lives away, we wouldn’t train, we wouldn’t condition ourselves, nor learn how to efficiently draw blood from others just as we’re willing to spill our own. Sacrifice isn’t as simple as throwing yourself on the sword in ritual. It’s fighting and dying with purpose, and one can’t find and fall in love with a reason to die, if they don’t first find and fall in love with a reason to live.”

Phainon thought about that for a second and then asked, “have you found a reason to die, Perdikkas?”

“Of course,” he said, cheerfully, “my reason to fight, my willingness to die, is my vow to serve my Prince. He would be furious to hear me say it, but I would gladly throw my life away in service to his ambitions.”

“Isn’t that rude of him?” Phainon asked, “for Mydei to be mad at you for your choice?”

Phainon pulled out pieces of a broken jar and gently put them and the spilled contents into the crate at his feet. The little round balls smelled funny and were greasy as he gathered them up alongside the shards of clay.

“Maybe a little bit, but he has his reasons. Mydei is uniquely blessed by the Titans. He thinks it’s ridiculous that people would throw away their lives if they don’t need to, to fulfill a sense of duty to a crown he won’t pick up.”

Phainon set a few packets of dried herbs on the pile that Perdikkas had started and dug around in the box for more. It felt more efficient to search for specific categories of supplies rather than pull things out at random.

“Ptolemy told me that he shared Mydei’s story with you,” the doctor continued, “so you know he spent his youth in the Sea of Souls while his father was fighting his campaigns. Mydei saw all those lives that were lost, he still appreciates their sacrifices, but I don’t think he likes it. I have never heard him say the creed, even before going into battle. I think he would rather his people live and find happiness than seek noble ends to satisfy our god’s recent bloodlust.

“But more than that I think Mydei is the purest embodiment of Strife, not as a war machine that marches endlessly hoarding souls, but Strife as it was in days long past, that followed the five tenets of Nikador. He wants to shield the people he loves, to pursue glory not through conquest but through protection, for Strife to be a motivator for growth and inspiration.”

That was not the picture of Kremnoan royalty that had been painted for Phainon in Okhema. The Council taught the people that Kremnoans were bloodthirsty and violent simply because they enjoyed it, because Nikador demanded it. He had been told that Strife was the antithesis of peace and that was why a nation of soldiers could never find happiness, why they marched into battle on the orders of their King and god with no fear of death.

“Five tenets?” he asked.

“The five parts of Nikador that together create Strife,” Perdikkas explained. His voice was a little strained as he tried to peel some leaves apart. A jar of oil had spilled on them, and they were drying stuck together. He gave up after a few tries and dumped them in the ‘damaged’ crate.

“Kremnoans uphold all five as virtues to embody: courage, honor, tenacity, sacrifice, and reason. Although, Eurypon seemed to have given up on those towards the end of his life,” grumbled Perdikkas.

“If honor is so important, why did you guys become pirates?” Phainon asked.

“What other choice was left for us? Okhema considers us pirates,” Perdikkas grumbled, “only because we’re breaking their laws, even though we aren’t citizens.”

“But you do steal from ships and fight against other nation’s navies?”

Perdikkas shifted his weight from side to side. “Yes, even if Mydeimos is not like his father, hungry for conquest, we’re still Kremnoan. Our hearts still sing for battle, we still need to get supplies to take care of ourselves and our people, but there is honor in how we choose to emulate Strife.”

“Honor-” Phainon mumbled.

“Yes, Phainon. Honor. We don’t attack and slaughter indiscriminately. When Mydei, Hephaestion, and Krateros choose our targets we are very careful to avoid collateral damage. Eurypon would raze whole cities to the ground, Nikador famously destroyed whole civilizations, we only target hostile military installations, other war ships, and mostly, the Black Tide.” He fixed the pile of paper packets on the table so they wouldn’t fall off. Each one of them was at least labeled. Phainon couldn’t read the Kremnoan just yet, but he could recognize the individual letters. “And Mydei is very careful to lead the way at every step so he can protect us and show mercy where need be. This lifestyle suits us.”

“The history we have in Okhema about Castrum Kremnos focuses mostly on Eurypon and Nikador as insatiable, they paint you all as less than men, bloodthirsty to a fault,” Phainon said.

“I’m not surprised, Eurypon may not have started that way, but he became it,” Perdikkas lamented, “it was before my time, but something changed when Eurypon came back from his campaign in the North. He started getting wild, becoming the mad king, even throwing his son away to appease an equally mad Titan on the hearsay of a soothsayer.”

“Are the stories about Mydei true?”

“Which ones?”

“The ones about him being immortal.”

“Oh, those are true.”

Phainon paused and flashed Perdikkas a skeptical look, his hands full of bandages. There were weirder things in Amphoreus but it still felt like a stretch, even with golden blood.

“They are. I have held my Prince’s body, marred beyond hope of repair, and watched it stitch back together as flawless as the day he was born. It’s unpleasant for him, but he cannot die.”

“…so when I pushed him out of the way of that falling sail.”

“He was upset with you, yes,” Perdikkas laughed, “he doesn’t like when people risk their lives for his, because he sees his own life as cheap compared to those of his people.”

Phainon pouted. “Does it hurt him? Does he feel it when he dies?”

“Yes.”

“Then I’d do it again,” Phainon said firmly with a soft smile, “immortal or not.”

Perdikkas puzzled over Phainon for a long moment, playing with a cracked jar of salts as he did so. “Phainon, when you jumped to save him, did you forget that he’s your enemy? I just told you as much.”

He looked down, white hair hiding his eyes, as he whispered, “Why do we have to be?”

Perdikkas didn’t really know how to respond to that, Phainon could see it on his face and maybe it was just a childish dream, but Phainon wanted to believe that they could be allies. When he returned to Okhema, he’d make them see that there didn’t need to be bad blood between them, that the Kremnoans would make incredible partners against shared enemies.

He still remembered that feeling in the rain, standing shoulder to shoulder with Mydei, the way it felt to stand as comrades. It made his spirit soar to think of that moment. He wondered if Mydei had felt it too.

They chattered about lighter topics after that. Any discussion of politics was chased away by questions about their supplies. Phainon’s curiosity had gotten the better of him while they were sorting medicines and Perdikkas happily told him about some of them. He taught Phainon about doses, what medicines could heal or harm, poisons that could cure illness when mixed correctly, and ways to care for injuries. Phainon even shared what he had learned from the grove regarding alchemical mixtures until they were exchanging knowledge in equal spades.

They talked until they finished repairing the infirmary and Leonnius visited with dinner and Phainon’s repaired clothing, neat little stitches fixed the tear in the leg. The crew had managed to keep most of their supplies safe from the rain, but a lot of the fresh products were wearing thin. The chef had managed to make the most of what they had, and dinner was a hearty stew and paximathia, a dried, hard bread.

All three of them let the bread soak up the stew to soften it while they talked. None of the sails had been lost but several needed to be fixed, the railing would need major repairs in places, but the biggest casualty was Ptolemy’s library which was taking four people to put back together. Leonnius reassured the two of them that the repairs were coming along nicely, but Mydei had made the decision to change their course. When Phainon asked where they were headed, he was met with a shrug in response and Perdikkas mumbled something about trusting the Captain and needing to get to bed.

Even though Phainon felt fine, Perdikkas insisted he spend another night in the infirmary and locked them both in when the sun set outside. Even though this was just another cell, Phainon was grateful to be away from the steel bars and Perdikkas’ soft breathing was a better soundtrack than the creak of the ship alone.

He studied the long shadows in the infirmary from his narrow bed, both hands folded over his chest. Every rock of the ship pressed one of his shoulders against either the wall or the little rail attached to the side to keep him from rolling onto the floor. Phainon’s leg and bruised chest ached but it was manageable and grounding, the subtle pain was a reminder that he was alive, and he almost wasn’t. Mydei had saved him twice now to his once. Not that it was a competition of course.

He remembered hitting the water, the way the waves muted the thunder above until all he could hear was the rumble of the deep. Before the ice filled his lungs and he was pulled back on board, Phainon remembered the voice of the Titan again, a malice wrapped in sweet melody, coaxing him to sink deeper into an endless abyss. He remembered even as he sank towards the depths the memory of fire licking his skin and the screech of monsters.

Deep in the core of that unnatural storm, the Black Tide beckoned.

-

If Mydei thought Phainon was insufferable before then there was no word to describe him now. Eager to please and with no sense of personal self-preservation, Phainon took every opportunity to escape the infirmary to be of use.

It had started early that morning when Perdikkas woke to find the wooden bar they used to lock the door tucked into Phainon’s blankets and had to go find his patient who was helping pull the patched sail back up into place. The doctor literally dragged Phainon back to bed by the collar.

The second time, Phainon had slipped out when Perdikkas went to fetch them both water after his thirsty patient had drained their waterskins in the infirmary. He found Phainon helping move the now full water barrels below decks and dragged him back to bed by the ear.

The third time, Perdikkas had to check on another member on the crew who had twisted his ankle. When he got back, of course Phainon had left. That time Mydei found him helping carry spare lumber to replace the damaged railing. Phainon insisted that he was fine, nearly convincing Mydei he was okay to work, until a red-faced Perdikkas started yelling and swearing at him from across the deck in Kremnoan and then Mydei was throwing Phainon over his shoulder to drag him back to the infirmary himself.

That’s when it turned into a game. Leonnius, Ptolemy, and Hephaestion started taking turns helping Phainon escape, creating opportunities for him by distracting Perdikkas, and helping to smuggle him to help with tasks and betting on how long they could keep the doctor and captain from finding him. It was easy on paper and much harder in practice once Mydei started to catch on and went on the offensive. The Captain was a motivated bloodhound on the hunt and their only advantage was in numbers.

Phainon understood that he didn’t want to be caught, but he was none the wiser when it came to the betting. He was just happy that so many of his friends had things for him to do, even when they hurried him from one job to the next sometimes without finishing the task he had just been working on. The longest he spent on a single job was when Leonnius managed to get him up into the shrouds to reorganize the lines for the repaired sail, but then Mydei had shouted from the other end of the ship and Leonnius kicked him off the yard and into Hephaestion’s arms on deck to be hurried off to his next job securing barrels and crates around the hold.

They were trying to hide Phainon under a hat, crossing the deck while he hunched to get him to the navigation room to organize maps, when Mydei finally slid in front of them with an annoyed expression. Immediately the three Kremnoans hid Phainon behind them.

“Heeey, Mydei,” Leonnius started.

“Don’t start,” he growled.

“Start what?” Hephaestion said coolly and Mydei rolled his fingers so the gauntlets would clack threateningly.

“That damn dog is supposed to be resting.”

“I’m not a dog!” Phainon called over their shoulders and all three of them immediately put their hands on his hat to pull it down to cover his face.

“Certainly a dog would be more obedient!”

“’Each man delights in the work that suits him best,’” Ptolemy quoted.

Hephaestion agreed, “yeah, Mydeimos, he just wants to help.”

“My leg doesn’t even hurt anymore!” Phainon insisted.

Mydei crossed his arms and zeroed in on those bright blue eyes peeking over the first mate’s shoulder. “Are you lying to me?”

“Surely, I’ve earned some trust after saving your life.”

Mydei’s eye twitched. “Bold words coming from the mouth that I have had to pull out of the ocean twice.”

“What if we give him easy jobs?” Leonnius offered, “nothing that would hurt his leg.”

“Perdikkas explicitly said three entry hours, not two,” Mydei insisted with an annoyed growl.

“I’ll take him,” said a soft but clear voice. All five of the men turned to look at Peucesta standing beside them with his lyre under his arm. “I’ve been watching,” he explained, “if he must work to not be a nuisance, then he can help me.”

Mydei turned back to look at Phainon with a pointed stare that Phainon immediately countered with a brilliant smile. “Fine. You’ll help Peucesta and then return to Perdikkas.” He held up a hand to silence any protests. “This is the only compromise you will get. The alternative is I tie all four of you to the mast until dinner.”

Leonnius, Hephaestion, and Ptolemy all agreed immediately and without protest, leaving Phainon with no choice but to accept his new fate as they scattered with the breeze… whatever that fate was.

Peucesta was a thoughtful looking man with elegant long hair that reached just past his shoulders. He didn’t have the same bookish sharpness that Ptolemy had but they shared some softness in the cheeks. Like all Kremnoans he was in shape, a warrior, but the calluses on his hands were more towards the tips of his fingers rather than on his palms.

They hadn’t met properly but Phainon had heard him playing his lyre at mealtimes and in the mornings. His role on the ship was guarding morale and their spirits more than their bodies.

“Um,” Phainon asked as he followed the man towards the bow, “Peucesta right? What are we doing? Do I need to get any tools?”

“No,” Peucesta said assuredly, and then it was awkward silence until they got to the very front of the ship.

Nestled behind the crystal lion head ram was an old sculpture of a lion’s face. Phainon had been up here before when he had been exploring and had been reminded of Verax Leo at the Marmoreal Palace, but this one was much, much older, a lot bigger, and more stylistic, cast in some sort of bronze rather than stone. While it had the same jaws and a similar ruff, this one had a glorious pair of horns that curved over its brow and met on its muzzle in a V-shape to frame its face. The carved tufts of its cheeks were full and regal, matching the strong and pointed jaw. It was mounted on a massive circular plate that was installed against the back of the ram so the lion could face inwards with its own private horseshoe shaped deck just a few steps lower than the forecastle deck.

This spot was quiet, reverent, not so isolated that Phainon felt alone, but set apart in a way that that the hustle and bustle of the ship felt distant.

Peucesta gently put his hand on the lion’s nose.

“I know you went overboard during the storm,” he said, “so you must have heard it too.”

Phainon felt his blood go cold. He swallowed slowly but the lump in his throat held firm. “Heard what?”

“The language of the Titans and the Black Tide. It’s easier to hear in the water.”

“…if you don’t have anything for me to do-“

Peucesta tossed him a sponge and Phainon fumbled to catch it. Water splashed against his chest and got his clothes wet. He blinked at it in surprise as the man sat down next to the lion head to play.

“We are here to clean and sing to the great lion.”

“…we’re doing what?”

“I know from Hephaestion that you respect the ship and take great care to show him that love when you help with repairs. That includes the ship’s spirit, especially after encounters with the Black Tide.” He started to pluck at the strings.

Phainon mulled that over for a second while he studied the silent lion. If the ship’s figurehead was a living simulacrum like Verax Leo, then it would make a lot more sense why they treasured the ship like a living thing. This was a symbiotic relationship and sponging clean a statue wouldn’t be too exertive.

He wrung out the sponge and stepped up to the bronze to put his hand on the lion’s nose. It was warm, not the same as stone warmed in sunlight, more like it had a buzz to it that Phainon felt through his fingertips all the way down his arm, just the tiniest prickle of recognition.

“There are statues in Okhema that look a little like this one,” Phainon said reverently, “albeit more like lions and much smaller.”

“Verax Leo?”

“Yeah, they talk a lot.”

“Chryseus Leo does not speak except on the rarest of occasions.” Peucesta sounded very sad as he said it, the melody on the lyre turned to a minor key. “He is old and tired.”

Oh, the ship was named for him.

“Oh, muse,” Peucesta said clearly, melodically in time with his strumming, “speak through me of the lion of Tretos, whose roar shattered shields and whose claws were as spears. That most grand of beasts, with fur of gold and flame, the lord of the plains, Chryseus Leo, who one day met his fate. For many years he lay siege to the city, consuming of them their offered herds, lest he come for them in their beds.

‘Behold the great lion,’ they cried, ‘from whom we will never be free, for none dare contend with the Titan’s blessed beast.’”

Phainon listened, doing his best to use broad, slow, quiet strokes to wipe the salt and grime from the golden lion. He didn’t want the sounds to interrupt the music.

“Then came fate, when the city could bear the beast no longer. He was clad in red and gold, a leader of legions on their eternal march for glory. Gorgo was his name, and when he heard tale of the lion he was moved to action. When thus they met it was without steel, for so inspired was Gorgo by the lion’s might he cast aside his spear. And when Leo roared his final breath in that great battle, it shook the city for a hundred years.”

“I think I’ve actually heard this story,” Phainon admitted, quietly but with thinly veiled excitement.

Peucesta stopped playing. “You have?”

“When I was young, I dreamed of traveling to Castrum Kremnos, to learn how to fight. I read whatever I could about its history, what little there was. King Gorgo, the founder of Castrum Kremnos, was known as the Lion-Slayer King for his feat. Supposedly, Nikador flung the head so hard it stuck to the fortress wall. Was this lion head modeled after the original then?”

Peucesta shook his head. “This is Chryseus Leo, the lion of Tretos. There was always only one.”

Suddenly Phainon felt a lot more humbled by this task. He paused before reverently continuing his work.

He swallowed around that nervous lump in his throat again. “How did he end up here?”

Peucesta started to play again, but he didn’t sing the story like before. “Chryseus Leo was given as a gift many Kings ago to a monarch of the northern kingdoms. When King Eurypon invaded, the lion was recovered, the only treasure that had not been corrupted by the Black Tide. Eurypon believed that the lion harbored special power that kept it clean of corruption, and instead of returning him to the fortress wall, had this ship built around him. The lion and the ship are synonymous now. He feels it as an extension of himself and as we care for him, he extends his protection to us.”

“… you asked me about the voice I heard in the water,” Phainon realized, “Peucesta, was King Eurypon right about the lion?”

He smiled and the music changed to a major key. “He was. This ship is not immune to the Black Tide, but it is highly resistant. Not even Chryseus Leo knows why he was spared the corruption, but it gives us a fighting chance against the deep that so desperately tries to reach for us. That storm was not natural, if it had not been for the lion, we may not have survived.” Peucesta leaned against the lion from where he was sitting, still playing, but offering physical contact with his shoulder as well.

“A few years ago, in a battle with the Black Tide, I nearly turned when I went overboard. The black had reached for me, and I heard it speak, beckoning in a sweet voice and enchanting melody. The others pulled me from the water and left me to rest here in front of the lion and we talked of Strife, of the future we wanted to see. Because of him I did not turn, my brothers did not need to slay me in my madness, and I have honored the lion with song ever since.”

This was the most Phainon had ever heard Peucesta speak. He respectfully held his silence and listened to those delicate notes while he polished the lion’s teeth until the man was done speaking. “Why share this with me?”

“The others speak of you fondly, and I thought it was important that you know. It seemed a good time since we now share that brush with death and that song that lingers still.”

Peucesta was right about that. The Black Tide was a haunting memory, both from his past and now the singing from the storm. It was sticky and staining like ink on the soul, crawling under his skin.

“Caring for Chryseus Leo,” Peucesta was saying, “even though he is mostly silent now, is a way to thank him for his protection, for his diligent duty to Strife. Golden blood would’ve spared you and Mydei, but that storm would’ve claimed the rest of us. Fixing what was broken is important and this may seem like a boring task, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, sitting and singing to the ship, but it is equally as valuable to him.”

Phainon ghosted his fingers over the lion’s cheeks, tracing the worn carvings. The bronze shimmered golden in the sunlight, warming his soul, shining light onto those stains. Now that he was holding still, listening only to the pluck of those strings and concentrating on the lion, it felt like there was a soft heartbeat there. Imagined, he reasoned but special all the same.

“I only know reverent harvest songs and noisy drinking songs,” Phainon admitted, “I’m not sure a lion of such renown would take interest in those.” He set the sponge down in the bucket to float on the surface of the water and sat down on the deck in front of Peucesta. It hurt to cross his legs, so he only folded the one, pulling his knee up to his chest so his injured leg could stay extended.

“I don’t think he would mind.”

“Then I will trade you,” Phainon offered, “show me how to play the lyre as you do, and I’ll teach you a few songs.”

Peucesta smiled gently. “I think he would love that.”

They didn’t move from the bow until the thief star crossed the sky and Perdikkas came for his patient and even then, Phainon whined and begged for more time. He really felt like he was getting the hang of strumming the strings and was eager to practice further. But Peucesta gently took the lyre from him, patted him on the shoulder, and told him that the rest would be best for both Phainon’s fingers and both their ears.

Pouty, but pliant, Perdikkas led him by the sleeve back to the infirmary.

Behind them, the lion purred.

Chapter End Notes

This chapter is 1000 words over my target word count per chapter because I couldn't bring myself to cut medically high Phainon. It was just too funny.

Chapter Notes

Soooo, my original outline had the contents of this chapter as the end of chapter 3. So, uh, there are going to be way more than 19 chapters unless I make them longer and post less frequently. Do readers prefer these shorter chapters (~5k-6k words) updated as I finish them every 1-2 days, or weekly updates where chapters are potentially longer? I'm pretty happy with lots of short chapters but I know that can be intimidating.

Also, I see and love you repeat commenters. The only way you guys could sustain me more, would be if I printed out your kind words and ate them.

As promised, Perdikkas let Phainon go after he ate breakfast the third entry hour after the storm. The doctor had applauded Phainon for his quick healing, mumbling about Chrysos Heirs before he kicked him out of the infirmary under the condition he still take it easy for at least a few days. No working the lines, no combat drills or training, and no fishing. No exceptions.

Phainon had happily promised to adhere to Perdikkas’ rules and tried very hard to say so in Kremnoan to show he was serious. With all that extra time he had been reading his two books and felt like he was picking up the right words.

At least he felt that way until Perdikkas had very politely told him to keep practicing and to never say those words with that accent, in that order again. He refused to elaborate further.

As eager as Phainon was to utilize his freedom productively, he also needed to get his bearings. Now that he was headed back to his cell, he felt like it was worth checking on what was left of his outfit that he hadn’t worn during the storm. With all the supplies being properly packed and inventoried, he was worried that his things had been misplaced.

Using the daylight filtering in from above and a lantern he took from the wall, Phainon dug around in his cell with increasing disappointment. None of his clothes, his greaves, not even his blanket was there anymore. Theft on a ship was almost unheard of, getting away with it was borderline impossible with the tight quarters so it was more likely that his things had been confused with spoils of war when supplies were being shuffled. Worst case scenario, one of the old guard had thrown his clothes away out of spite, tossing them overboard. Phainon didn’t want to think about how upset Aglaea would be if that was the case.

Still hopeful, Phainon went upstairs to the crew’s living quarters to find someone who might know. He was halfway across the deck when he spotted Hephaestion and waved to the first mate who gave him a quizzical head tilt in response.

“Perdikkas set you loose?”

“Haha, yeah,” Phainon smiled and scratched the back of his neck, “Hephaestion, do you know what happened to the rest of my clothes?” He gestured to what he was wearing. Phainon had his repaired pants, boots, and his high-collared, v-neck but his coat, cape, and armor were gone.

“Oh yeah-“

“I have them.”

Phainon turned to look over his shoulder at Mydei. The Captain had said it so casually.

“…on purpose?” Phainon asked, more suspicious than surprised.

“Yes. I put them in my room where I expect you to sleep at night going forward.”

The silence stretched long enough that Hephaestion shuffled uncomfortably away, mumbling an excuse about being called.

“Is there a problem?” Mydei prodded when Phainon seemed to have completely short-circuited.

“I must have misheard you,” Phainon laughed as he snapped out of his stunned trance, “for a second I thought you said you wanted me to sleep in your room.”

“That is what I said.” Mydei turned and started walking towards the stern where his room was. The doors to his space, the library, the navigation room, and more were next to the stairs to the top deck.

Phainon followed him closely, struggling to find his words. He could feel his cheeks burning. “…why?”

“Would you rather sleep behind bars?” Mydei asked as he held the door open for Phainon.

“I might!”

Mydei scowled. Phainon couldn’t see it through the back of Mydei’s head, but he could almost hear it and could feel it as they stalked down the hallway.

“That’s absurd. The hold is dark and miserable and it’s a hassle for Hephaestion to unlock your door every morning.”

Mydei stomped into his room with Phainon on his heels. The other person in the room looked up, starting to address the Captain, but Krateros held his tongue and frowned when he saw the other man. The old soldier gave Phainon pause too. Mydei was the only one that seemed unaffected by the sudden chill in the room, if he noticed it at all.

“Your things are here,” he was saying, crossing to the far wall where an ornate dresser was built into the space between windows. The drawers were held closed by twisting latches so as not to spill their contents in rough waters. He twisted the latch on the third drawer up from the floor and pulled it open so Phainon could see but Phainon was still waiting by the door.

He felt very uncomfortable, like he was intruding. Even though Mydei had been welcoming, Krateros’ obvious disapproval was suffocating.

The room was spacious, but not as big as it used to be. The furnishings built along the walls felt lopsided, only occupying the original three walls while the one that divided the room from the others felt much newer. Any furniture or trappings along that wall had been added and nailed into place rather than elegantly blended into the original construction under and around a line of thick paned windows. There was a place for a large bed but there was no mattress, instead, there was a hammock hung over the space and the surface was instead used for storage like the cluttered top of a desk. Books, stationary, maps, collected goods, and so on were littered about. In one corner was a small pile of weapons, a spear, an unstrung bow, several quivers of arrows, a shield, and Phainon’s greatsword.

Krateros stood over a long table in the middle of the room. There were chairs and stools scattered around along the walls, by Mydei’s mini arsenal, everywhere except beside the table. Phainon could see a massive map spread out across the surface. Heavy books and boxes of carved ships held it open at the corners. Figurines were meticulously placed across its surface. Krateros had his hand on one of them, but he left it where it was and slowly pulled his hand back when he saw Phainon.

“You may as well, reclaim that while you’re here,” Mydei was saying. He pointed with his gauntleted hand at Phainon’s sword.

When Phainon took a step towards it, Krateros straightened and crossed his arms. “Are you sure that’s wise, Prince Mydeimos?”

“I see no reason why he should not have it.”

“See no reason?” Krateros hissed. His fists clenched at his sides.

“It’s fine,” Phainon said. He put both of his hands up. “I don’t need it right now. Leave it where it is.”

“It should be locked in the armory,” Krateros insisted.

“Take the compromise, teacher,” Mydei ordered with a sigh, “the sword stays where it is. I would rather Phainon know where he can reclaim it and be able to wield it should the need arise.”

“And would he raise his sword in defense of your crew?”

“I believe he would.”

Phainon shuffled uncomfortably. Conflict like this bothered him. Leonnius’ warning about Krateros rang in his ears. This was Mydei’s oldest confidant, perhaps even a father figure, who had helped raise him after Mydei had been pulled from the Sea of Souls. Maybe this was a discussion he was best left out of. Stay quiet, keep to himself, better not to interject.

“I would,” Phainon said firmly, “if I could.”

The old man turned on him. “There is nothing you can say Okheman that would convince me that what you say is true.”

Mydei stepped forward but Phainon cut him off, stepping up to the table to look Krateros in the eye when he responded, “Then I will say no more to you. I’ll just have to show you … should the occasion arise.”

Krateros glared at him and for a heartbeat they watched each other until Mydei laughed, it was one laugh, almost a bark, short like a punctuation.

“What more can you ask for, Krateros,” the Prince said, “Deliverer, do you have need of any of your things?”

Phainon shook his head. “Not right now.”

“Then wait outside for me.”

Krateros never stopped glaring at Phainon. That one good eye was boring a hole through the back of his head the entire way from that table back to the door and Phainon even worried the old man could see through the door the way that weight lingered even when the latch clicked. He went down the hallway and waited on deck, leaning against the wall beside the door, using the stairs as shade from the morning sun.

It was shaping up to be a beautiful day. The sails were already unfurled, catching the wind, pulling them along. Driving them farther away from Okhema.

Phainon had seen the map when he was leaving. He had heard that after the storm, Mydei had ordered a change of course, and without knowing their route prior it was hard to tell how much that had changed, but now Phainon knew for sure; the Chryseus Leo was heading away from Okhema, away from any of his city-state’s allies. Even worse, it looked like they were traveling along the estimated line between free waters and the Black Tide, heading towards a distant isle that Phainon didn’t recognize. A home port perhaps? But why would they make berth so close to the reach of the Black Tide? Was Chryseus Leo’s protective nature strong enough to protect them even in harbor?

More importantly, was there any way for him to return home from there? And did he even want that anymore?

- Krateros at least waited until the door closed to express his displeasure. “You should not be wasting your time with him. Kill him before we get to the settlement.”

Mydei sighed and stepped up to the map. He picked up the little carving of a lion, the Chryseus Leo, and moved it to a collection of isles. The Black Tide was infringing on their safe haven, it wasn’t moving as quickly as it had been five years ago, but it still marched steadily to eat the seas and islands.

“I told you already, teacher,” Mydei huffed, “I won’t unless he forces my hand.” He put both his hands on the side of the table, holding tightly to ground himself as the bubble of anger kindled in his belly. “But someone has already tried to take this needless task upon themselves.” Next to him he felt Krateros shift in place. Mydei turned just enough to glare at him with one eye. “You wouldn’t happen to know anything about that, would you, Krateros?”

The old warrior was a stone wall, giving nothing away. “I don’t, if any of my men had tried to take his life they would not have failed.”

They stood in tense silence until Mydei relented. Prince or not, he still respected Krateros’ authority and experience.

“We will finish the repairs at the Kremnoan Settlement, rest, and then resume our patrol,” Mydei ordered, “any other ships caught in that storm will have turned.”

Krateros nodded and turned back to the map. He pointed and ran his finger along the black line they had drawn on it. “If we are quick, we may be able to prevent the Black Tide’s territory from expanding further.”

“The men are tired. We will lose too many if we don’t let them rest.”

“Any longer than a day is too long of a delay.”

“A day then,” Mydei agreed, “let them properly bathe, see their families.”

“And what will you do with the Okheman? He will try to flee the moment his feet touch the shore.”

Mydei tapped his fingers on the desk. Phainon stood here and insisted he would fight for the ship if pressed, but he also refused to engage in piracy. He had a sense of duty that meant nothing when they were at sea but how would Phainon act given the choice between this crew and returning to Okhema.

“He cannot be allowed to see where your people have settled,” Krateros insisted, “he will tell the Goldweaver and they will seek us out to destroy us, until every Kremnoan is buried. You must end him before we make berth.”

It pained Mydei to consider, but Krateros was right. Phainon was not one of them.

“I know,” he admitted in a growl, “I will deal with Phainon personally, when the time comes.”

-

When Mydei left his room and spotted Phainon leaning against the door, he was surprised to see how puzzled the man looked. Those blue eyes were staring so intensely at the deck that he had stopped blinking. His brow was pinched tight in concentration; his normally jovial expression contorted into a tight frown. It was cute, if a little strange watching him think that hard.

“Something on your mind?” Mydei asked and Phainon had blinked himself back into his usual animated self, smiling wide enough to reach his eyes at last.

“Ah, no, nothing important.”

He was a bad liar, but Mydei let it go.

“Come,” he ordered, “you will be helping in the galley today.”

Phainon perked up immediately. “That sounds like fun.”

“It is very hard work,” cautioned Mydei.

“Aw, are you worried about me?”

“I am worried for my crew eating a subpar meal because you were unable to handle the task assigned to you.”

“How hard can it be?”

Mydei smiled to himself as he led the way down to the galley.

The kitchen was past the eating area, behind the long countertop that separated the spaces. It was an expansive kitchen built with royalty in mind. When Mydei and his detachment had fled Castrum Kremnos after killing the King, the galley was one of many reasons why they had stolen this ship. It had three stone and clay ovens, plenty of counter space, lots of light, storage for all their cooking equipment, several washbasins, two open cookfires with massive hung pots, lined with stone to protect the ship, and so much more. It was a dream come true.

Phainon whistled behind him.

“There are usually three people that work the galley,” Mydei explained as he walked over to a cubby to take off his gauntlets. “I have given two of them the day off to rest and handle personal tasks.” He put them in the cubby and then undid his pauldron so he could gather up the loose fabric of his chiton. “You will have to work hard to make up for the both of them. Will that be too much for you, Deliverer?”

Phainon scoffed behind him. “I can handle it.”

Mydei could hear the hesitation in his voice and feel eyes on his bare back. He folded up his chiton reverently, down to just his pants and tall, armored boots, and traded them in the cubby for a worn, loved apron that he slid over his head. Mydei ran his hands through his hair, giving it a toss so the apron strap could settle comfortably on the back of his neck and shoulders. The little bronze buckle clinked against the clasp of the braid over his shoulder.

“Wait…” Phainon mumbled, “Are you helping in the kitchen today too?”

Mydei grabbed a spare apron and tossed it to him, the folded fabric slammed into Phainon’s chest, and he very nearly smiled at the way the Deliverer fumbled to catch it.

“It’s my kitchen,” Mydei explained as he tied the apron closed behind his back with practiced precision. “Of course I will be working here today, as I do every day.”

Phainon’s expression was priceless. That wide-eyed confusion and awe made Mydei’s heart flutter.

“You’re… the cook?”

Oh, he was so cute trying to put the pieces together. “I am the Chef, yes. Do you need help with your apron?”

Phainon startled and scrambled to get the apron on. “No, I don’t.”

“Good, then put your bracers in a basket,” he ordered, pointing over his shoulder, “and wash up, we have a lot to do today.”

Mydei was determined to give Phainon the benefit of the doubt about a lot of things. Even with Krateros’ warnings at the back of his mind, even with the weight of being from two distant worlds hovering over him like a blade waiting to fall, even knowing that something would need to be done about him at some point…

It was his friends holding that blade away, keeping it from falling. As Mydei watched Phainon tuck his armguards away, fumble with his apron, and wash his hands, he could hear the excited chatter of his friends from the last week. How excited they were to tell him about Phainon, how much they liked him, how much they wanted to trust him, and oh Mydei wanted so badly to trust him too.

“Aedes Elysiae,” Mydei said and Phainon’s head jerked up and looked over at him with those stunning, thoughtful eyes. The light glittered on the tattoo etched into his neck under that collar when he tilted his head. “It was a farming isle, known for it’s wheat was it not?”

“Yes, it was.” Phainon’s voice was small and Mydei worried briefly that he overstepped.

He cleared his throat. “Then you know how to process wheat, to turn it to flour?”

“It has been a long time,” Phainon admitted, “but I know how to work a millstone yes.”

“The moisture from the storm ruined my flour,” Mydei explained. He gestured for Phainon to follow him through the kitchen to the millstone.

The contraption was attached to a table in their big, walk-in pantry surrounded by barrels stacked along the walls and labeled in Kremnoan. The millstone itself was a rectangular shape, almost square, with a deep v-shaped basin. A rod was attached to a pole on one end of the basin, stretching across the mill long ways to extend well past the length of the basin. It served as a handle, with the operator pushing and pulling the rod back and forth. Every pass dragged a heavy stone affixed to the rod along the inside of the basin to grind the wheat into flour. For a ship this size the mill was large, perhaps not as big as the millhouses Mydei had seen in his travels, but too large for a domestic, single-family’s use.

Phainon confidently stepped up to it, checking the joint with a practiced eye. He gave the lever an experimental pull to test the weight and Mydei felt his cheeks warm at the sight of those biceps flexing.

“It’s bigger than the one I used at home,” Phainon admitted.

“We Kremnoans have hefty appetites,” Mydei explained, “and we don’t really do small.”

Phainon snorted and flashed Mydei a sly smile. “Is that so, Prince Mydeimos?”

“HKS, think before you speak,” he scolded and looked away, “can you handle it?”

Phainon chuckled, “It’s not too big for me.”

Mydei walked over to a barrel and opened the lid. He ran a hand through the grain there, checking it. “This is the barrel to be turned to flour.”

Phainon stood next to him, in the close space they were nearly touching. “Zea.”

“You know your wheat.”

“Son of a farmer.”

Mydei swallowed and stepped back. “There is a sieve on the wall, to filter out the sprouted wheat. We will grind it separately.”

“Why?”

Mydei looked over at Phainon and was surprised to see genuine curiosity there. With how cheeky Phainon was on a good day, Mydei half expected a question like that to be a gesture of defiance, trying to annoy him. But the slight tilt of his head and clear eyes were genuine.

“Germinated wheat tastes different when it has been ground into flour,” Mydei explained, “I would prefer such flour be used to make cakes mixed with honey rather than paximathia or pita.”

Phainon nodded slowly and then reached for the sieve. “I better get started,” he said playfully, “I have a lot to do. You’re welcome to watch me if you’d like, Mydei, but I’m going to have to ask you to stay out of the way.”

Mydei bristled at his nickname, especially with how sparkly Phainon said it, but he huffed and gave the man the room all the same.

It wasn’t like there was a shortage of tasks to do. It wasn’t even Action Hour yet but cooking good meals for his men always took the better part of the day. Krateros had once scolded him for it, emphasizing that his role as Captain and Prince needed to come first but Hephaestion was more than capable of handling disputes and Mydei liked how cooking made him feel. It was hard work, in a hot kitchen, a battle in its own way, but very little was as satisfying as creating a wonderful meal.

He left Phainon in the pantry and returned to the galley to start assessing what he could make. His original plan for the day was to use the rest of those cabbages that had started to wilt but the storm had hastened their demise and there weren’t enough good leaves left to wrap any hearty filling.

The lentils were still good and thanks to Leonnius and Phainon there was plenty of fish. Fish and lentil stew then, with pomegranate on top.

Mydei rolled one of the big water barrels they kept in the kitchen over to the massive pot and started filling it with a separate bucket. He was strong, but he wasn’t that strong. No sense risking injury on a shortcut by lifting the whole water barrel.

When it was about half full, he covered the pot with a lid. It would be a while yet until it was time to start the fires. He still prepared the wood, lining them on top of old coals. Mydei filled the ovens and the stove as well. He still wanted to make bread today so the loaves could properly dry for storage.

Mydei started pulling out ingredients next, moving efficiently and with purpose through the kitchen and setting things out on the biggest countertop. Olive oil, salt, pepper, garlic, onions, and a whole lot of pomegranates. He scowled at the onions and garlic. They were in better shape than some of their food, but he wouldn’t be able to use all of them this time.

The pomegranates were easy but time consuming. Mydei spun the knife in his hand and expertly cut into each fruit, five cuts around the calyx to pull off the tops and then it was easy to pull them apart into sections from there. He used the back of a wooden spoon to smack the rinds to dislodge the seeds, letting them fall into a big bowl of water. The membrane would float to the top, saving him the trouble of having to pick the fibrous and tasteless part out by hand.

Although, it would be funny to make Phainon do that.

He tossed the spent rind away into a scraps bucket and peeked his head into the pantry. Phainon was still grinding away with the millstone. He had found a comfortable stance and every push and pull was careful and calculated, not a single wasted effort.

He didn’t say anything and Phainon hadn’t seen him so Mydei ducked back out. He thought there would be more chatter than this. The others made it seem like Phainon was endlessly nosy, verbose, and easy to converse with, but instead they had settled into a quiet and comfortable rhythm.

He set the pomegranate aside and went to one of the cabinets to find his jar of foamy wine yeast. It had a distinct smell so as he opened each lid it was only for a few seconds at a time until he found what he was looking for and set it out on another countertop. From the same collection of clay jars he pulled out a wide brimmed amphorae full of honey and on a second thought grabbed a basket of dried figs.

Candies and sweet things were some of his favorite things to make but it was hard on a ship with limited resources. Candied figs and dates lasted a long time when he made them right. Mydei set them out to snack on them while they worked. He cut up the onions, minced the garlic, dug out what was left of his dried thyme, cleaned the pomegranate seeds and then he went to start warming up the oven and stove tops.

Mydei clicked the flint over the kindling, got the fire started, and then paused. With a long-suffering sigh, he opened the oven door and pulled a sleepy Fig Stew out by the tail.

“One day, I will forget to check, and the crew will enjoy roasted chimera.”

Fig Stew was immensely unbothered by the prospect of being consumed and far more annoyed with having lost his warm spot to sleep. He yawned and batted at Mydei’s hand until Mydei set him on the counter to stretch and find another warm spot up against the warming oven to fall back asleep.

“Are you still alive in there, Deliverer?” Mydei called. He scooped out the yeast and added a generous amount to some water and added honey.

“Did you need this flour now?” Phainon called.

“May as well bring me what you have.”

Phainon had found a handful of empty flour sacks and was systematically filling them. He brought a full, heavy bag out to Mydei slung over his shoulder.

His bare shoulder.
