Mydei did a double take when Phainon set the bag down next to the countertop. He had taken his apron and shirt off to work. A light sheen of sweat glittered where dust hadn’t already clung to his skin.

“Will this be enough?” Phainon asked and Mydei had to tear his gaze away from those flexing muscles.

“…it will do for now.”

“Do you need me to grind more?”

Mydei really wanted to say yes but truthfully this was plenty. “You got through about a quarter of the barrel?”

“A little less?”

He nodded. Wheat almost doubled in bulk when it was ground to flour. “…put your shirt and apron back on and come help me make the dough.”

Phainon smiled and nodded, hurrying back to the pantry. “Should I have been grinding down the germinated wheat? Are we making cakes?” he called from there. It was muffled a little while he tugged on his shirt.

“No, we’re making pita,” Mydei told him.

The chef was already scooping up the freshly ground flour to add to the big bowl of bubbly yeast. Phainon knew his trade. The flour was exceptionally fine and excellent quality despite the relatively short amount of time he had spent grinding the wheat. He set it aside.

Phainon struggled to finish pulling his shirt down past his abs as he stumbled out of the pantry. Still no sea legs.

Mydei pointed at him with a spoon. “I would have expected Okhema’s Deliverer to have a firmer grasp of his stance on the sea.”

Phainon shyly looked away. “I thought we already established I’m the son of a farmer. I didn’t start sailing until after Aglaea took me in. I was already a young adult by then.”

That explained a lot.

“Come,” Mydei ordered. He set Phainon up at the countertop and pulled over the yeast to add the rest of the flour. They rolled out the massive ball of dough together, sprinkling more flour onto the countertop as needed to keep it from sticking.

“Do you know how to knead?”

“Have a little more faith in me,” Phainon protested lightly.

Mydei huffed and took half the dough himself. Next to him Phainon copied his actions, moving a little faster than Mydei who narrowed his eyes in suspicion and met his pace, until they were pushing each other faster and faster.

Flour was getting everywhere. It stuck to their hands and arms. Phainon let his dough hit the countertop hard enough to send flour across the kitchen and up onto their faces. He had flour across his cheeks and nose and Mydei was sure he matched.

“At least you aren’t totally hopeless,” Mydei praised when they started separating the dough, mess aside. It wasn’t lost on him that Phainon had somehow turned this into a race and he wasn’t about to let this novice beat him.

“I learned how to work dough so I could trade work for rest. Bakers tend to need the extra hands.”

“You traveled a lot.”

“I wandered for a long time after Aedes Elysiae…” he trailed off, but his hands kept pace, “I wandered for a long time. Took work where I could find it.”

Mydei thought about that for a second as he tossed another disc of dough to his pile. “Were you there when the Black Tide destroyed your home?”

“…yeah,” Phainon grumbled and Mydei felt a little guilty for bringing it up, “you fight the Black Tide a lot, you know what it’s like.”

Phainon reached over Mydei to get more flour to sprinkle on his side.

“But I wasn’t there when it took my home,” Mydei admitted. You have to give trust to get trust. He started to rub his readied dough with olive oil.

“…Castrum Kremnos is…?” Phainon asked and Mydei remembered his friends telling him that Phainon knew less than they had realized. He must not have known that the city had fallen.

“Yes.”

They both started tossing the dough into the oven. One of Phainon’s hit one of Mydei’s and pushed it out of the perfect cooking spot. He flashed Phainon a glare and was met with a cheeky smile, so Mydei made sure to aim his dough at Phainon’s, back and forth knocking the soon to be yummy bread into haphazard cooking places.

With the pita bread baking, Mydei moved them both over to fileting fish. They had a lot to get through. Already scaled from their fishing escapade it was just a matter of deboning and getting the fish into neat slices.

“Were you there?” Phainon asked.

“Hm?”

“When the Black Tide destroyed Castrum Kremnos.”

“No,” Mydei said simply, “we had left before that happened.” But not everyone had made it out. Mydei wasn’t sure how he felt about it. Had he been there, could he have saved more of the citizenry? Would it have mattered?

“Are you sad?” Phainon asked and Mydei was genuinely surprised by the question.

“Why would I be sad about that?”

“I’m not sure,” he admitted as he threw more bones into the waste bucket, “you just seem sad.”

“HKS, that’s ridiculous, focus on your fish, or I’ll beat you in this race too.”

Phainon dialed in fast at that comment. He still lost and Mydei smiled triumphantly as he set his knife down and went to get the lentils.

“Where did you learn to cook?” Phainon asked as Mydei started the fire in the pot and added the lentils to the warming water.

“Self-taught.”

“That’s amazing, Mydeimos,” Phainon praised and Mydei could hear how genuine he was. It made his heart sing.

He made Phainon turn the bread with a long wooden paddle while he seared the fish in a pan on the stovetop with oil, garlic, salt, and pepper. He added the filets, thyme and the chopped onions to the pot with the lentils and then covered it all to soak and cook.

“The bowls are stacked in the closet by the pantry, but it will be a bit yet,” Mydei told Phainon, but the Okheman took the initiative to fetch them while they waited.

“Deliverer,” Mydei started, to get his attention and Phainon turned to look at him, pausing with a stack of bowls in hand.

“Yes?”

Mydei hesitated. For someone that hated speculation, that hated wasting time, it was hard to get to the root of what he wanted to ask.

“If you return to Okhema,” Mydei finally managed, keeping his voice cool and level despite his racing heart, “what would you do?”

“If?” Phainon repeated. His demeanor was changing, hardening. He set the bowls down heavily on the countertop. “What do you mean if?”

Mydei felt his façade slip, eyes widening at his own mistake for a second before he gathered himself once more. “Answer the question, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

He could see the emotions cycle behind Phainon’s eyes, everything from pain and betrayal to resolute anger. It was taking him some time to process the implication.

“Answer me,” Mydei repeated, a little more gently this time.

Please, he begged inside his head, please don’t make this harder than it needs to be.

“What do you want me to say?” Phainon hissed, “that I’ll go home and retire, keep everything a secr-“ It was like everything was hitting Phainon at once. His eyes went wide, and he shook his head while raising a hand to his mouth. “You were never going to let me go, were you?”

Mydei’s eyes darted to the side involuntarily and Phainon must’ve seen it. The man put his hand on his face, slowly running his fingers through his hair as he cursed under his breath.

“Everyone answering my questions, telling me about the ship, about you… There’s no way you can let me go back to Aglaea,” he growled, voice suddenly strained.

“Deliverer-“ “Don’t call me that!” Phainon’s vitriol caught Mydei off guard and he was suddenly very aware of how naked he felt without his gauntlets.

“How the hell could I be so stupid? What the fuck happened to not keeping captives, Captain.”

Mydei frowned but stayed quiet. There was nothing he could say that wouldn’t upset Phainon further.

“Am I an ailing pet then?” Phainon growled. His eyes were wild and full of anger and hurt. “All of this kindness and camaraderie, was to put me at ease before you kill me in my sleep?”

Mydei met his anger with his own now. “Absolutely not. If I wanted you dead you would be.”

“Then what I am I? A pet? A slave?” Phainon demanded with his voice raised and Mydei sneered at those horrible words.

“You are neither of those things, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,” Mydei insisted, but he couldn’t answer the first question. He didn’t know. He knew what he wanted but it didn’t feel right to propose that now.

“Kephale, how was I this stupid?!”

“The hell is going on down here?” Leonnius asked as he hurried through the galley to peer into the kitchen.

“Nothing,” Mydei insisted firmly.

Phainon was standing still with his head bowed, shaking. Without another word and with stiff movements, he started setting out bowls and checking the bread.

“Go back to work Leonnius,” Mydei ordered softly and then he did the same, preparing food in uncomfortable silence.

Every time Mydei looked over at Phainon, the man had his head down and his back turned, refusing to look his way.

Worlds apart as they had been from the beginning.

Worlds apart as it felt like they may always be.

chapters.title: Chapter 9: Knowing the Enemy
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

No new tags.

Mydei and Phainon have some things to work out

Chapter Notes

I have been excited for this chapter for so long. I wrote the first half last night crazy late and woke up early to finish it cause I was too excited to share it.

All the sweet comments about how wholesome the fic is and I'm hiding behind the door with the angst bat like, haha yeah, so wholesome :)

If you return to Okhema, Mydei had said. IF. Not when. IF.

Getting kicked by a dromas would have had the same effect the way the air had been punched from his chest. Phainon’s entire fragile world had collapsed in that moment. Any hope he had for peace between their nations, shattered by the clarity that came from a two-lettered word.

If.

There was nothing that could immediately be done, reeling as he was, so Phainon had turned back to his assigned task, chores that now came with a rancid edge to them. Leonnius’ voice had been like cold water on a wildfire, a moment to breathe, but not nearly enough.

As he retrieved finished pita from the oven and set them aside on the countertop to cool, he couldn’t look at Mydeimos. As he lined bowls out, waiting to be filled with stew, he couldn’t look at Mydeimos. As he got started on washing dishes, he would not look up at the Captain.

Phainon felt like an idiot. From day one, Mydei had insisted they didn’t keep prisoners but still locked him in a cage to sleep. Like a fool, he had assumed it was for his own protection.

There was the pity in Ptolemy’s eyes when Phainon had mentioned trying to learn Kremnoan in only a few weeks. Phainon had thought that maybe it was because the language was hard to learn, now he understood, it was because Ptolemy knew the truth and couldn’t tell him that he would never see his home again.

Leonnius’ warning about not bonding with older crewmates because they hated Okhemans, Perdikkas reminding him that they were enemies. Earlier that very day, Krateros insisting that Phainon not be allowed to have his sword.

Phainon really stood there and told that old man to his face that he would willingly raise that sword to protect his new friends, that he would prove it given the opportunity…

How fucking stupid was he?

From the beginning it was a constant string of reminders that he was not one of them. He was a prisoner of war. They could not send him back to Okhema. Phainon knew as much. He had even worried himself how the Council would act. He knew that Aglaea would see through any deception and order him to continue his task hunting pirates, especially if she now knew that he had been in the enemy’s clutches. He had theorized himself that the Council of Elders would take all the things he had learned and exploit them, possibly try to finish the war between them.

If their roles had been reversed, if it was Aglaea who had been the Captain finding an enemy in a sinking wreckage, she would never have pulled Mydei from the sea in the first place. The strategic thing to do would’ve been to kill him as soon as they realized who he served.

Phainon put cooled pita bread in the serving basket, everything he did felt stiff and labored. Every movement weighed down with the sting of betrayal, of realizing that these people he had come to see as friends, who he had been proud to stand beside in the storm, had been leading him on, seeing him as a toy, a temporary plaything.

A plaything that they had welcomed. Now that Phainon knew Mydei was the cook he realized the comfort food that got him through that first night had been made by him. Mydei had pulled him out of the ocean twice now. The first could’ve been nothing more than an opportunistic gesture before the Prince knew who he was, but saving Phainon from the storm was another thing entirely. He could’ve let Phainon drown, saved himself the headache of keeping him around, but instead he had pulled Phainon to safety and personally seen to his well-being while he recovered.

He had let Phainon get close to his friends, his family, to learn about their history, their way of life, their religion …and sealed his fate in the process.

He could never go home again.

Would that be so bad? He wondered briefly to himself as he passed the bowls stiffly to Mydei to fill with lentils and fish.

Yes. It would be.

Phainon had a family back home. The other Chrysos Heirs needed him, loved him. Even now they probably mourn him, assuming he was lost at sea. How horrible did Aglaea feel, believing she had sent him to his death? What about the triplets or Castorice? Phainon had a purpose there, he had a home there. A history of standing shoulder to shoulder with purpose that lasted longer than a week. He couldn’t accept that those things were just gone without his choice, without a goodbye, because a Kremnoan Prince plucked him from the water and decided to keep him!

He fumed while he set the filled bowls on the countertop and sprinkled the pomegranate seeds on top, waiting as men started to file in. He seethed when he brought small barrels of wine to the galley tables so they could start drinking. He glared bitterly at Ptolemy who greeted him warmly with the Kremnoan greeting they were practicing and felt nothing when the librarian lowered his wave with a confused expression.

He ignored them when Hephaestion and Perdikkas started to mumble in hushed and worried tones, sending glances his way. He studied the floor when Fig Stew was given his offering of food and the men began to eat, refusing to take the bowl offered him by Peucesta. When Leonnius tried to speak to him, Phainon physically pushed him aside, shouldering his way through the kitchen to discard his apron and fetch his bracers from the cubby. When Mydei reached for him, Phainon smacked his hand away and fled, hurrying out of the galley and up to the deck for fresh air.

Even when the gentle sway of the ship threatened to take his feet out from under him, Phainon ran. He ran across the deck and upstairs, bursting into Mydei’s empty room. He stomped up to take his greatsword, that familiar weight heavy with responsibility.

Chartonus had sold him this sword with the promise of another down the line when he had earned it. Phainon hadn’t been able to afford to commission a better one back then. He still barely had any coin to his name. They had talked about him working off the debt, but he never found time. He might never get the chance now.

He saw his own twisted, outraged face looking back at him in the reflection of the blade. Phainon’s eyes glittered with grief as much as anger. The fury was easy. It was the sorrow that was hard, that wanted him to slow down for even a moment so it could latch onto him and drag him away to drown him. The fury was what pushed away the soft memories of trying to stumble through a lyre lesson, of standing shoulder to shoulder with Mydei in the rain, of reading a book in two languages, of Fig Stew biting his hand. Fury was what buried the memories of a gentle hand binding his leg, of the smell of burning wax on the deck, of a rope burning his hands while fish tossed in a full net.

Grief was what made him fall to his knees with that sword in his hands, to just feel the weight of it for a moment, only a moment to mourn something that didn’t feel real anymore.

And duty was what made him stand back up again. He owed it to Aglaea to get himself home, no matter the cost.

Phainon knew from his time on the Chryseus Leo that Mydeimos the Undying was a man of honor. While his trust in the words of the Kremnoans had been damaged, he had at least seen enough of the man’s actions to believe that much to be true.

Sword in hand, Phainon strode out into the evening. He could still smell the food from below, hear the voices of the men as they gathered below in the galley. Above him the thief star glittered red across the sky, heralding the end of the day while the sun settled on the horizon in orange and purple hues.

He thought through his plan with every step back to the galley, sword held loosely in his hands as crew scattered before him, shouting, a couple followed him warily, looking for a chance to stop whatever he may be planning. Treating him openly as the wild dog they thought he was, finally showing him how they really felt. But any time one of them moved in close he glared at them with such poison they stepped away.

Phainon saw a couple of them turn to run to the armory, putting him on a clock, but this wouldn’t take long.

“Mydeimos,” he called from the bottom of the stairs to the galley. The whole crew had stilled, eyeing his sword, judging the threat. With a heavy heart he saw Hephaestion resting a hand on the sword at his side.

Mydei gently set the basket down and turned to face him with his same guarded expression.

“I challenge you. Fight me,” Phainon said loudly, firmly, “for my freedom and my life.”

-

When Phainon had run from the galley, Mydei hadn’t had the time to pursue. Feeding his men was his top priority, but Phainon was a close second. He had wanted to breach the topic with tact, something that Mydei rarely cared for but had hoped the Okheman would appreciate but not only had things blown up in his face, they escalated out of control.

Phainon was standing in the galley, armed, angry, and out for blood. Mydei chanced a glance at Krateros. The old man was watching Phainon but there was a smugness about him, an air of ‘I told you so’ that hurt Mydei’s heart. His promise to Krateros bounced around in his head and Mydei was trying to decide if Phainon’s current actions needed to be answered with a noose. What excuse could he give to spare Phainon’s life for this?

“If I had known the heat of the galley would muddle what brains you had, I’d have sent you to work somewhere else,” Mydei said with a tilt of his head and softness in his voice to ease the tension. It didn’t work.

The men muttered uneasily. Mydei could hear shouting on deck.

“Do you accept?” Phainon growled.

He glanced over at Hephaestion. His first mate was stone-faced, focused. The switch had flipped, and the man was in combat mode. If Mydei didn’t do something soon…

At the top of the stairs, several of the crew had caught up, properly armed. Mydei could see their spears pointed at Phainon’s back, hear the creak of a heavy war bow drawn tight. They would kill him if he didn’t put his sword down.

At first it seemed to Mydei to be the desperate pleas of a cornered man, no more an animal than when they had pulled him aboard, but Phainon had proved himself to be more level-headed than that. He had controlled himself when his men had all died, been willing to set aside his feelings when they shook hands, made every effort to keep the peace, even between Kremnoans.

It clicked when Mydei was studying the way Phainon held himself, driven, angry, but composed. The sword rested lightly in his hand, not held tightly the way someone completely out of control would have grasped it. His stance was professional, measured, the mark of an expert swordsman, still and poised. Mydei could see the way his eyes systematically darted around the room that he was marking potential threats, ready to retaliate if any of them made a move but he stayed relaxed at ready.

Phainon was giving them both an out.

It was clever really and Mydei felt a rush of relief when he realized it. If Phainon won, then on his own honor as the Crown Prince, Mydei would have to let him go, consequences be damned. Krateros couldn’t do anything, none of them could. Any attempts on Phainon’s life would belittle the word of their Prince and Captain. Strife would never allow them to infringe on their honor in such a way. Phainon would’ve won his freedom and absolved Mydei of any responsibility.

“You do realize that by your own demand, if I win, your life and freedom will belong to me?” Mydei asked.

“You won’t win.” Resolute courage hung so heavily in the air that Mydei almost believed him.

Mydei smiled, a one-sided smirk. “Alright, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,” he said, “I accept. We will fight to first blood. If you win, I will honor your right to freedom and release you at a port of your choosing. Not my crew, nor I, will harm you from the moment of your victory until you have left Chryseus Leo in your wake.” He crossed his arms. “But if I win, you will abandon any notion of returning to Okhema and join my crew, not as a slave, but as a man in chosen self-exile.”

Phainon’s grip tightened on his sword, only for a moment, flexing. Every passing second, Phainon felt colder, more distant, a sharp contrast to the fire in his eyes. He was trying to close himself off. “I accept.”

The reaction from the crew was mixed. Mydei recognized the voices of older men shouting for him to reject the proposal, others were shouting words of encouragement, already caught up in the excitement of a fight, but most of them were just confused. They mumbled to themselves in harsh whispers, trying to understand what must have felt a dramatic change considering Phainon’s good nature until this moment.

Hephastion relaxed but only enough to let go of the hilt of his sword. He still carried a tension in his shoulders as he stepped around the bench he had been sitting at and moved carefully to Phainon’s side, gesturing without touching him to guide the man towards the deck.

“Mydeimos,” Krateros growled as he stepped up to Mydei’s side, “make the duel to the death, don’t run the risk of an angry Okheman on the crew.”

“That is hardly fair, Krateros,” Mydei sighed, “and I trust Phainon to honor his word, just as I will honor mine.”

“And what makes you think he will not harbor a grudge when he loses? When he’s forced to stay on a ship, he has no love of?”

“Are you so willingly blind, Krateros?” Mydei turned and went into the galley with Krateros on his heels. He took off his apron and folded it reverently, tucking it away in exchange for his chiton and pauldron. “He is torn and hurt. I heard it in his voice earlier and it’s plain on his face. This duel absolves him of guilt. He doesn’t know what he wants, so he’s letting fate decide and resolved himself to honor the outcome.”

“Then he is a fool.”

Mydei didn’t have the heart to tell Krateros that he was doing the same thing. The same difficult decision Mydei had been wrestling with was out of his hands now. As he pulled on his gauntlets and stretched his fingers, Mydei considered that Phainon was in the same position.

That puppy was too pure and innocent for his own good. It wasn’t a scheme falling in love with this ship and her people. It wasn’t manipulative acting that Mydei heard in Phainon’s voice as he cursed himself. There was a very real chance that Phainon was also torn between wanting his homeland, a sentiment that Mydei understood, and wanting to maintain these new bonds that he had formed. As betrayed as Phainon may have felt, that betrayal could only exist if those friendships had value to him.

They were equally trapped by the circumstances of their positions, their origins.

There was something freeing about the idea of solving it with brute force.

Mydei straightened himself, checked his jewelry with light touches, and double checked his pauldron and armor. He didn’t know what kind of a fighter Phainon was, but if the bard’s tales were true, then this would be as exciting as it was freeing.

He walked out of the galley with Krateros on his heels.

The crew had followed Phainon to the deck, creating a large circle. Hephaestion was standing next to him with a hand hovering over Phainon’s sword hand, not touching him, just making him wait, ready to catch him in case the man attacked before Mydei was ready. It felt entirely unnecessary to Mydei. Phainon was eerily calm, waiting patiently.

“Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,” Mydei called as he stood across the deck from him. He stretched his arms over his head and rolled his fingers. “I am obliged to offer you a chance to reconsider.”

“I will not.”

No banter. It hurt more than it should.

“Hephaestion, clear the deck.”

Reluctantly, the first mate stepped away from Phainon and started shouting at the men, making them retreat to higher decks to give the two warriors space. Mydei could see the glint of spears and shields mixed among his people. They didn’t trust Phainon. Should he let the Okheman win to appease his crew?

“Peucesta, give us a count of three.”

Clear notes sounded across the deck. Mydei saw Phainon adjust his stance, pointing his sword at Mydei. That damn thing was heavy and he was holding it so casually with the one arm fully extended. That alone was an impressive demonstration of strength.

A note. That was one.

Another. Two.

On the last chord, Phainon lunged. He was incredibly fast, closing the distance between them in three reaching steps, that sword building momentum as he swung.

Mydei responded by clawing the air in an uppercut. His tattoos flashed faintly in the dim light of dusk and crystal sprouted from the deck, sharp and reaching, cresting like a wave about to break on top of him. An opening attack like that, Mydei had timed it to not only block but to stab at Phainon, reaching for gold, but for once those horrible sea legs worked in Phainon’s favor and Mydei missed.

Crystal broke as the blade of the sword crashed against it, the bright red dissolving as Mydei dispelled it so he could reach for a surprised Phainon with his fist. The swordmaster recovered quickly and when Mydei pressed in close, Phainon twisted the blade in his grip so he could pull it in close to his body to intercept those gauntlets with the wide blade.

The grating sound of metal on metal made Mydei smile. Not very many people could keep up with Mydei, even on his bad days. They had only clashed twice and Mydei was already feeling the excitement in his blood, the rush of adrenaline that came from recognizing a worthy opponent.

Phainon shouted and spun, his foot came up but Mydei blocked it with his arm. He twisted to grab the leg but before he could scrape along the flesh to seal his victory, the sword spun around dragging in a wide arc parallel with the deck enroute to disembowel and Mydei had to retreat.

Phainon let the arc finish and then stumbled to recover his stance. On stable footing, the man was probably a monster. Mydei used the shifting ship to budget his stamina, letting the subtle rock work for him rather than against, so when he surged forward again, he expected it to be game over, but Phainon was able to counter his claws.

Back and forth they traded blows with several close calls, but even with the uphill tilt, Phainon showed no signs of exhaustion and Mydei was feeling a little humbled. He was so impressed with Phainon’s bladework as they chased each other across the deck that Mydei again considered letting him win. Let the man earn his freedom, and then he had to duck as that blade cut so close to his face he could’ve kissed it, and he knew more than anything he could never allow that. Not because of the stakes, not because he really wanted Phainon to stay, but because Phainon deserved Mydei’s best.

Mydei had a better grasp of naval combat. He used the railings, the lines, and the shrouds to his benefit, enjoying the verticality of their arena and the home field advantage, while Phainon had a better understanding of controlling his immediate space. The more Mydei tried to use his crystals, the faster Phainon learned the tells until it ceased to be a viable strategy entirely.

The only advantage Mydei had at all was Phainon’s inexperience fighting on an unstable surface and the longer they dueled, the faster he learned how to compensate for his own weakness.

The sword came down towards Mydei’s head and he reached up to grab it, pinching it tightly between both hands. Phainon was taller and Mydei was feeling that now as the man bared down on him, both hands on the hilt of his sword, leaning his weight behind the clash. Briefly Mydei considered letting the sword meet his shoulder, take the hit so he could land one of his own but then he remembered the win condition was first blood, and he lamented. How much better of a fight could this be if they were both allowed some recklessness?

The sword inched closer, Mydei’s arms shook from the angle. He chanced a glance at Phainon’s face and saw the glimmer of a smile that matched his own. Phainon was enjoying himself too. Under that resolve and desperation, the weight of high stakes, Phainon was having a good time.

“I understand now,” Mydei crooned, “there is no one in Okhema that can challenge you.”

Phainon’s eyes narrowed but he didn’t deny it.

This ship started to sway, Mydei felt the change in Phainon’s leverage. He let go of the sword and dropped to the deck. The blade slammed into the railing behind him and Mydei was able to land a kick to Phainon’s belly with both legs while he braced himself against the deck with his shoulder.

The Okheman went flying across the deck, slamming into the opposite railing with a crunch. He coughed and stumbled with the force of the blow but no blood. Phainon wiped some spit from his lips with the back of his hand.

Mydei used the sword lodged in the railing to pull himself up, appreciating the craftsmanship of the handle as he rose. It wasn’t the best sword Mydei had seen but whomever had made this weapon had cared even for their cheaper creations. He wrenched the weapon free with one hand and tossed it across the deck. It skittered and bounced until Phainon stopped the slide with his boot, but he didn’t bend down to pick it up right away.

Phainon was still watching him, waiting for the trap but Mydei held his hands out to the sides to show him he was waiting.

“If I am going to win, it will be because I am the better fighter,” Mydei promised.

“If you win,” Phainon repeated, jabbing at the unasked question there, the possibility that either of them could take this victory.

“If I win.” It was as good of an acknowledgement of Phainon’s skill as he was going to get right now.

Phainon tucked the toe of his boot under the blade right in front of the hilt and kicked it up to his hand, where he expertly swung it in a circle before he took his stance again. They watched each other carefully. Sweat dripped down Mydei’s chest and back. He could see it beading on Phainon’s brow.

The sun was setting; the lamps were being lit around the deck around them. Phainon waited for the glint of firelight to make Mydei blink and then he was leaping across the deck again.

Mydei’s crystals reached for him, compensating for his inevitable stumble, but Phainon was sure-footed this time and the tip of the blade nearly caught his chest. If he hadn’t have stepped backwards…

Phainon’s assault was flawless and Mydei found himself retreating. He hit the railing and threw up more crystals in defense, using them to dive around Phainon so he had more space to maneuver, but the man was relentless, swooping in low and cleaving at unexpected angles. Mydei was still able to meet him at every clash, still kept his blade from licking his skin, but the advantage that Mydei had a moment ago was just gone.

He waited for the sway of the ship, waited for it like a cue to turn the tides but it didn’t come and Phainon’s fist collided with Mydei’s chest, too close to the base of his neck for comfort. Mydei could see Phainon’s eyes glitter when he huffed, still smiling. The man had aimed for Mydei’s throat and missed but he was already moving on, thinking ahead with glittering eyes and an excited smirk, and if it wasn’t one of the most attractive things Mydei had seen in a long time.

Phainon fit in with Mydei’s crew so much more than he had realized. He belonged here, Mydei was so sure of that. He didn’t want this synergy to ever end.

With renewed resolve, Mydei roared and leaped back into the fray, finally putting Phainon on the back foot. The whole world fell away from them. The cheers and jeers of the crowd were a distant rumble. All that mattered was the flow of the fight and the stupid grins on both their faces.

Again, they clashed, sword and gauntlets ringing against each other.

“We should have done this earlier,” Phainon told him while they were in close. He sounded a little sad and for a second Mydei wondered if he meant sparring or meant dueling for his freedom.

“When we started, I didn’t care which of us won,” Mydei admitted, “but the longer we fight the more I need to.”

Phainon’s eyes widened and Mydei won the clash, pushing him back. He took a step towards Phainon but paused, waiting for the ship to sway so he could rush with Phainon’s stumble, but it didn’t come.

Mydei’s smile faded, his brows furrowed, suddenly very serious, snapping out of his battle haze to look up at the sails. Phainon must’ve noticed something too. He tilted his head, puzzled.

The sheets above hung limp and heavy. No wind.

Around them the crew was uneasy. Krateros barked orders in Kremnoan, calling them to arms and many of them swarmed below, heading to the armory.

Phainon raised his sword again, but Mydei had abandoned the fight entirely. He raced to the railing and looked over the side. The ship wasn’t moving at all. The water beneath them was still a dark blue, a good sign, but it was churning in a circle like an eddy.

An eddy on the ocean.

Mydei turned to face Phainon again. The man looked frustrated, coiled, ready to pounce, to finish this fight.

“Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,” Mydei called, “I’m sorry, but we cannot finish this fight.”

Phainon frowned. “Then you concede?”

“I do not.”

“Then fight me!” he growled but the words fizzled when the sounds carried across the water, tearing screeches ripped through the darkness and then the whole ship lurched when another vessel collided with them.

-

Phainon had been torn the entire fight. He was torn when he proposed the fight, it was why he had proposed the fight to begin with. Faced with an impossible decision this just seemed the easier way to solve the problem. He had every intention of honoring the outcome of their clash. But the longer they fought, the more his blood cheered with every movement, the more Phainon started to beg and plead with the Titans that he could somehow have both.

Why couldn’t this be the end of it? Why couldn’t this clash be the end of the Okheman/Kremnoan conflict? Of course the answer was more complicated, but it angered Phainon to no end that it had to be.

He loved this. He loved the way Mydei fought. That same synergy they had fighting the storm surged and flowed in the combat against one another. He loved that Mydei didn’t hold back, that he respected Phainon enough to want to win. The longer they danced around each other the more obvious it was how much of a compliment they were giving to the other to fight fairly and with their whole hearts. They both wanted to win, not because of the high stakes, but purely for the joy of victory against an incredible opponent.

Every gasp, every clash, every drop of sweat made Phainon want.

And that duty and desire fought inside him more bitterly and tumultuous than the fight happening before his eyes.

He was so angry when Mydei stopped, when the fight came to an anti-climatic end.

“Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,” Mydei called with genuine disappointment and urgency in his voice, “I’m sorry, but we cannot finish this fight.”

“Then you concede?”

“I do not.”

“Then fight me!” Phainon snarled, but then he felt it too. The weight on the air, the foul smell of bloody ashes and cooking flesh, and then the sounds curled in the shell of Phainon’s ear. The ripping screeches of Black Tide monsters.

The ship lurched and Phainon stabbed his blade into the deck to keep his balance. He dropped to one knee as he fell, leaning heavily against his weapon. The crew was springing into action. Monsters were spilling onto the deck. One of them raced at him, but Mydei’s fist crushed its head, and it crumpled into dust. The Kremnoan looked down at him with sharp but worried eyes. They darted towards the Black Tide, then back to Phainon, taunting him with guarded curiosity.

“Did you mean it?” Mydei asked him, “this morning. Did you mean it?”

‘And would he raise his sword in defense of your crew?’

‘I would, if I could. …I’ll just have to show you…should the occasion arise.’

Phainon saw a massive Black Tide monster lunge at the pair of them. Arrows from across the deck slammed into its side but it was undaunted, lumbering with a metallic roar, claws reaching for the Prince. Mydei turned to catch it, but Phainon was faster. His sword ran through the beast’s chest, and it collapsed in a gurgling mess at the Prince’s feet.

“Yes,” Phainon breathed and raised his sword, pointing it at the Black Tide as he twisted his stance, taking a step backwards to be in line with Mydei, his back turned towards the Kremnoan. The Prince grinned wider than before and cracked his knuckles. He too adjusted his stance, turning his back towards Phainon as well in a returned gesture of trust, eyes trained on the invaders, ready and excited to fight.

Okheman, Kremnoan, it didn’t matter anymore.

It was time to remember who the real enemy was.

Chapter End Notes

I can't even tell you guys how happy the comments make me. I wiggle in my chair every time I see them in my inbox.

chapters.title: Chapter 10: Trust Earned With Blood
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

They have some stuff to work out but priorities priorities

Chapter Notes

Thank you all again for your comments. I write for myself first but the excitement and energy to write quickly is 100% fueled by you guys and how badly I want to share what I have planned :3c

Already warmed up from their original conflict, Phainon moved seamlessly into combat with the Black Tide. The ship that had rammed the Chryseus Leo had slammed into her at an angle, leaving them all shaken but not at any risk of sinking. The hull was too thick, too solid to be taken down so easily even by another war vessel. It was only enough contact to keep the ships together in the still water while monsters poured over the railing.

The Kremnoan Detachment was quick to respond, professionally engaging the monsters on deck with their shields and spears. Heavy bows twanged in time with Krateros’ shouted orders, firing at enemies as they made the crossing. Several Kremnoans, protected by their archers, retrieved wide planks, creating bridges to ease the monster’s crossing, luring them onto the Chryseus Leo.

They didn’t know yet if the ship was infected, if crossing would turn the crew. The ship protected them on home turf, but until they were sure, it wasn’t safe to cross themselves. Better to lure the monsters to their deaths than succumb to bloodlust and race into the Black Tide’s trap.

Phainon’s sword gleamed in the orange glow of monster parts and those pinpricks of lantern flames that tried to stave off the darkness of night in a battle of their own. The sun’s last rays disappeared as he cleaved a monster in two and slid under another. Mydei’s crystals destroyed that one, protecting Phainon’s back as he surged to the next.

There was no time to entertain his fears, no time to listen to the terror in his memories, no time to heed the whispers of the Titan in the back of his mind. Every time Phainon started to struggle with the inherent fear of fighting the Tide, that impossible enemy that only knew how to consume, he would see the flash of red in the corner of his eye.

Against all reason, Mydei gave him courage.

While the others played defense, Phainon and Mydei were tenacity incarnate, two harbingers of Strife, tearing through the swarm back-to-back, meeting each other swing for swing, counting under their breath as though they had shared the battlefield their entire lives. A dance that they had created, a song that only they could harmonize. They were keenly aware of the other at all times, could sense when the other needed help, and when they needed to move on. When Phainon pressed a monster, Mydei dashed to the next, leap frogging to efficiently dispatch enemies until the spill onto the deck ceased to be enough to sate the lust for battle.

Mydei pinched Phainon’s arm, just enough to get his attention and then wordlessly sprinted across the deck to jump to the other ship. If it had been anyone else, Phainon might’ve hesitated. He might have sat back and thought about the risk, may have reasoned it out properly and realized that only Chrysos Heirs could safely resist corruption, that it made sense for them to be the Vanguard. He may have still considered the sizes and strengths of the monsters waiting on that other deck, one of which lunged at Mydei the second the man’s boots touched lumber.

But Phainon didn’t take the chance to second guess himself. Mydei lit a fire in Phainon that no one else had before. His sword ripped through the neck of the monster as he crossed the gap on Mydei’s heels. Crystal covered his weakness. His sword watched Mydei’s back.

They fought until the deck was nearly cleared and then Mydei was shouting for Phainon from the stairs to the hold.

He paused then, as Mydei disappeared below decks to search for monsters there in the dark. Phainon was surrounded by dust. Monsters still screeched and raged against the Kremnoans on the Chryseus Leo, feeling far away now that he had a single moment to himself, to appreciate the lingering ache starting to creep in his muscles. Adrenaline still screamed along his veins, craving this battle, enjoying it deep in his gut, feeding his long-buried desire for revenge against the monsters that destroyed his beloved home and threatened his new one. The problems of a few quints ago seemed so pointless now in the face of their shared extinction.

“Phainon!” he heard Leonnius shout, and his head jerked up to see the man pointing from the shrouds of the Chryseus Leo. Phainon wasn’t sure how to tell if it was safe or not for them to come aboard, he wanted to yell back, but Leonnius pointed again to the stairs.

Someone needed to watch Mydei’s back. Phainon took off running again. He nearly leaped down the stairs, skipping four or five with every step.

There was almost no light in the belly of the war ship, just the fading glow of monsters as they dissolved, ripped apart by claws. Down here the sounds of battle were muted. He crept along slowly, listening for movement in the stillness.

“Deliverer.”

Phainon nearly jumped out of his skin when the gauntlet came down on his shoulder.

“Mydeimos!” he yelped back, “I could’ve hurt you!”

Even now the sword shook in Phainon’s hands, resisting the instinct to swipe.

A faint red glow filled the space as Mydei summoned crystal to his palm. His tattoos pulsed with light that flowed to his hand, circling brightly as he kept the tool suspended.

“This is not a merchant vessel,” he mumbled as he walked through the space, noting supplies.

Phainon dispelled his sword for now in a glimmer of blue light. He gestured to a flag on the wall with his chin. “Okheman Navy…” he mumbled and that horrible pit in his gut returned.

“They must have been caught in the storm and turned,” Mydei mused. He was already digging through boxes one-handed, the other still holding their light.

Searching for me? Phainon worried with horrible dread.

Mydei was searching more deliberately now, digging through chests and speed walking through the hold until he found what he was looking for. His claws pulled a golden thread from the edge of a barrel, one of Aglaea’s. Before Phainon could stop him, Mydei crushed it and the broken thread dissolved.

“There are good weapons here,” Mydei reported, “and the ship is not infected. The water in the barrels is clean, it must have drifted away from its master’s reach for now.” He wandered back over to Phainon, who was standing still, staving off the guilt that was budding in his gut. “Deliverer, go back to the Leo and tell the others that it is safe to loot the ship.”

That snapped Phainon out of his trance, back to reality. “What?”

“When you return, help me mark what supplies are worth keeping.”

That’s right. Mydei was still a pirate.

Any joy and excitement that had come from teaming up against the Black Tide shattered like glass. They had literally been fighting for Phainon’s freedom a quint ago. The feelings of betrayal surged back up again with the bile in the back of his throat. He tried to swallow it back down, but everything stuck.

“You want me to steal from my own people?” he asked in a low whisper.

Mydei’s brow furrowed, and he shuffled uncomfortably in place, as though it just occurred to him what he had asked of Phainon.

He opened his mouth to respond, a command, Phainon assumed but it never came. A vicious squeal ripped through the dark. There was a flash of orange and then a blade erupted from Mydei’s belly.

The moment passed in an extended blink. The kind of moment that felt longer than it was, that lasted less than a second to everyone who wasn’t trapped in that bubble of time. The annoyed shock on Mydei’s face, the twist of the blade attached to the monster’s arm, the way golden blood spattered across Phainon’s chest and legs.

Phainon’s sword was summoned and cleaving the monster in half from the head down before he really had time to process the weight of what happened. It screamed and collapsed in orange embers, gleaming in the dark, as the blade ripped free with a sickening squelch.

The light went out as Mydei stumbled forward, colliding with Phainon’s chest. He hurried to wrap his arms around the man and felt the warmth of precious blood spilling across his belly where he slumped.

“Mydei!” he shouted.

“Try not to sound so upset,” Mydei scolded, “we are enemies are we not?” The Kremnoan laughed a little bit at his attempt at a joke but he still sounded like he was in pain. “I have suffered worse.”

Again, Phainon dispelled his sword so he could use both hands to hold him up. He knew, he knew that the Prince was immortal but experience in combat still screamed that Death was fast approaching. He could feel where the sword had entered at Mydei’s side, slick and hot.

“You’re shaking,” Mydei noted in the dark, “you better not be crying. How shameful, Deliverer, stressing over someone who cannot die.”

Phainon felt him shift and then strong arms were pushing him off, towards the dim glow of the stairs.

“Let me help you,” he insisted but Mydei shoved him again.

“We still have work to do and my people are still fighting. I am behind you, go tell them it is safe to cross and that we have supplies to load.”

Phainon shuffled uncomfortably in the black.

“I’ll not make you help,” Mydei promised, softer this time, “I promised you I would honor your desire to not engage in piracy.”

“Let me help you back to the Leo-“

Mydei hissed, “this is nothing, Deliverer, stop wasting both our time with misplaced sympathy.” The light returned to Mydei’s hand. The shine of golden blood was everywhere but he was at least still standing, hunched but upright. “Until our duel meets an appropriate end our original agreement is still binding. If you really want to help, then do as I say!”

He stumbled after Phainon enough to shove him again and then Phainon relented.

Phainon ran up the stairs as fast as he had stumbled down them the first time, hurrying up to the deck where the only shouts were the calls of the Kremnoans, still waiting for word from their Prince. There were no monsters left, all of them dead, the crew waiting patiently.

More shouts when they saw him. A ripple of unease that Phainon disregarded in favor of finding his footing. The swaying ship made Phainon stumble, but he hurried to one of their bridges and scurried over to the Chryseus Leo where Hephaestion caught him and held his arms tight to steady him.

“The ship is safe,” Phainon reported, “Mydei is-“ He trailed off when he saw how the others were looking at him. He followed their eyes to where he was covered in blood.

“Perdikkas!” Hephaestion shouted. Others were crowding, getting in close to see what was happening.

The doctor shoved through and pressed a hand to Phainon’s chest and belly, demanding, “where are you hurt?”

“It’s not mine,” he hurried to say. The moment the words were out of his mouth, he regretted them.

The legion pulled him away from Perdikkas, rough and experienced hands were forcing him to his knees, pulling his hands behind his back, shouting in Kremnoan. He heard Krateros’ voice among them. Hephaestion was yelling, speaking so rapidly that he couldn’t even try to understand them.

“Mydei is still over there!” Phainon shouted but he was drowned out. The shafts of spears were crossed in front of him, someone had a firm grip on his hair, holding his head down so all he could see was the deck and Mydei’s blood soaking through his clothing. He felt sticky and uncomfortable. His muscles ached from fighting, from being held so tightly. Tiny, unshed tears pricked at the corners of his eyes, finally spilling over at the feeling of helplessness on top of everything else.

“Someone needs to go get him! He told me to send people over!” he shouted desperately but no one was listening.

-

Mydei felt embarrassed more than anything else. He stood still in the dark, wincing when he tried to move, mumbling ‘ow’ every time he shifted. The pain was whatever, compared to dying a stab wound was nothing, even if it did go through.

He actually let that puppy distract him. It had been a very long time since a monster had managed to slip under his radar like that.

He gently pressed on the exit wound and followed its path to his side where the blade had entered. Golden blood would save him from turning at least. The injury was already starting to knit back together from the inside out like always. It wouldn’t even scar when it was done healing. For now it was just annoying, but not half as annoying as Phainon’s worried shouts.

It was probably jarring for Phainon to see that, but he’d have to get over it if he was going to be around for a long time …he hoped Phainon would be around for a long time. That seemed less likely after how Phainon had reacted earlier in the galley. They would need to finish their fight to settle that daunting loose end.

Mydei pouted to himself thinking about how incredible it was to fight alongside Phainon. The flow of that engagement had been electric, even before the Black Tide and fighting side by side had felt better than clashing against each other. He really hoped they could do it again.

He pressed a hand to his side and stumbled towards the stairs. If Perdikkas could get this wrapped up fast enough, Mydei could help move supplies. He was surprised his men weren’t already over here helping, they were usually on standby and Phainon had run out of here so fast he might’ve been flying. There was no reason it should be taking this long to wrap up such a straightforward skirmish.

The fresh air on deck was still heavy with strife, not only were his men still on the Chryseus Leo, they were arguing and yelling at each other. Mydei frowned and stomped over to the bridge to cross to his own ship where he stayed on the railing, holding the lines for balance.

Hephaestion and Krateros were yelling at each other. He could see the old man standing over Phainon with his sword drawn and held at his side.

The Okheman was pinned down on his knees, held still by men of the old guard. They had crossed their spears in front of him and forced his neck over the spot where the shafts joined by his hair. Even from there Mydei could see him shaking, with fear or frustration he couldn’t tell.

Hephaestion, Leonnius, Ptolemy, and Perdikkas were trying to get to him, demanding Krateros release the man while the old teacher insisted it was for everyone’s safety.

“What the hell is going on over here?” he snarled in Kremnoan, and the crew silenced immediately, turning to look at Mydei.

Perdikkas moved first, instantly stepping towards the Prince and reaching into his pack at his side, presumably for bandages, Mydei didn’t give him the chance. He held a hand out to stop him and dropped onto the deck, priorities had changed. His crew parted for him and he stalked towards where they had Phainon. Blood squelched in his footsteps, leaving shiny spots on the deck.

“Krateros,” Mydei hissed, “what is the meaning of this?”

“This treacherous Okheman snake returns to us covered in your blood after demanding a duel with you and you question my actions?” Krateros asked. The teacher was fuming, shaking with anger Mydei hadn’t seen in many years. “I knew he could not be trusted to honor his word.”

“Phainon wouldn’t do that,” Hephaestion hissed, “he is truer to Strife than you are Krateros! Where is your honor and reason?”

“How dare you speak to me of honor and reason when you have also been enchanted by this siren in our midst!?”

Mydei watched Phainon who was holding still, defeated. They were arguing in a language he couldn’t understand. Was he afraid? Was he angry?

“’The sort of words a man says is the sort he hears in return,’” Ptolemy quoted from behind Hephaestion, “Phainon has done nothing wrong! You are making him the image of your own fears!”

“Then how do you explain our Prince’s blood?” Krateros countered.

“He saved me from a Black Tide creature,” Mydei said bluntly.

“You expect me to believe that a Black Tide creature could injure you so deeply?” Krateros raised the sword, pointing with it at Mydei’s injury before swinging it close to Phainon’s bowed head. Phainon flinched when the steel flashed close and Mydei tensed.

Mydei sighed and crossed his arms, fighting to stay level-headed, “Now you doubt my word, teacher?”

Krateros hesitated then, so did his men.

“Are you so determined to hate this Okheman that you would doubt me? When he has proven your words of this morning wrong?”

“I know you have a soft spot for this beast,” Krateros growled.

“And would you have killed him before I gave the order? Did I not tell you that I would tighten the noose around his neck myself if I deemed him a threat?”

Krateros wilted under Mydei’s growl. “You misunderstand, Prince,” he insisted, “it was only right that we hold him until we knew what happened.”

“And now that I have told you the truth, what will you do Krateros? Our fight is not yet concluded, I have a vow to him, would you shame me?”

They waited in silence while Krateros and Mydei glared at each other.

“Now, Krateros,” Mydei demanded, “there is yet a ship we must deal with before the winds and ocean resume their natural course.”

Krateros tsked and sheathed his sword. His men let go of Phainon who collapsed onto his hands and knees. Mydei had to resist the urge to drop beside him, to pull Phainon into his arms and make sure he was okay.

It was Leonnius that hurried to do what Mydei could not, rushing to Phainon’s side to help him sit back on his heels, to whisper softly to him with reassurances. Still Phainon held still with his hands resting in loose fists on his thighs and his head hung low. No doubt he was trying to make sense of what was happening, lost in his own thoughts. They would have to clear things up later.

“Hephaestion,” Mydei said softly, and the first mate was hurrying to bark orders, sending men across to the Okheman war ship.

“Perdikkas,” he called next, and the doctor stepped up with bandages. Again, Mydei waved him off and asked for a report instead. He never stopped looking at Phainon as the doctor gave him the catalog of injuries. No one had died; injuries were minor aside from his own.

“We should get him somewhere safer,” Leonnius insisted. He had an arm around Phainon’s back. “He doesn’t look good.”

Mydei shook his head. There was a discussion that needed to happen. Krateros’ concerns needed to be addressed before they could be allowed to fester further than they already had.

“Deliverer,” Mydei called, changing his tongue to speak in a way he could understand.

Phainon tilted his head back to look at him. His eyes were dull, tired, overwhelmed but his face was guarded, carefully neutral, already gathering himself.

“Are you well enough to stay here on your knees for a time?” he asked, trying to be gentle despite the gravel in his voice.

Phainon nodded and bowed his head again.

Perdikkas grabbed Mydei’s shoulder and turned him so he could hiss low. “What are you doing?”

“Krateros holds the ear and hearts of half the crew,” Mydei explained, “I must make peace with him.”

The grip on Mydei’s shoulder tightened. “You cannot kill, Phainon.”

“I gave my word,” Mydei reassured him, “I will not kill him unless he gives me reason to need to.”

Perdikkas’ eyes darkened. “The way he confronted you in the galley-“

“Is not enough. Perdikkas, please, have faith in me.”

“…I do, Mydeimos,” Perdikkas insisted, “but please remember when you pass judgement, that Phainon isn’t just yours to do with as you please anymore. He’s one of us now too.”

Mydei’s eyes darted to Perdikkas but otherwise he didn’t react. He lazily watched the crew bringing supplies over, he noted the way Peucesta and Hephaestion kept glancing his way with worried expressions. The whole crew was uneasy, uncomfortable with the situation, with the way their Prince and a respected General had clashed.

He waited until they had rolled the goods to the hold and set the sails of the Okheman vessel alight with fire. Mydei waited until the ship began to sway, free of the Black Tide’s eddy. The sails caught the wind as they kicked up again to gently pull the ship along on their lazy glide as though they had never ceased. The crew lingered on deck, curiosity keeping them close.

“Krateros,” Mydei called, loud enough to command all their attention.

The old man shouldered through the crowd to stand where his Prince could see him.

“I would hear your thoughts.”

Krateros was already a hardened man with a permanent scowl. A man of action, a man that Mydei knew to be reasonable and good. But he was also stubborn and heavy with grudges and experience that narrowed his vision.

He was confident when he spoke, keeping his voice loud enough to be heard, and keeping to Kremnoan so that everyone would understand. Everyone except Phainon.

“The Okheman is a problem,” he said simply, “he cannot be trusted. I stand by my order to arrest him when he returned without you.”

“You assumed me dead?” Mydei asked.

“No. Of course we know that you cannot die, Mydeimos, but I could not allow him to roam free while evidence suggested he attacked you. Not on the heels of an important duel with stakes of such value. How could I be sure that he would not raise his blade to any of the crew after behaving so dishonorably?”

That was a reasonable concern from a paranoid parent figure.

“Bullshit,” someone coughed from the side and Mydei turned.

“Do you have something to say, Hephaestion?”

“I do.”

“Speak.”

“Krateros is so buried in the past he refuses to acknowledge the proof of Phainon’s actions.” Hephaestion turned to the crew, appealing to them directly. “Has he done anything to suggest that Krateros is right to be suspicious? That he is a spy sent by the Goldweaver? He has only served and now protected this crew and our Prince.”

“My caution is not blindness,” Krateros insisted, “you are too young to remember, Hephaestion, what the Okhemans did to your elders when we clashed in the waters outside of Styxia.” Some of the older crew, people that had served Kremnos for decades, were nodding, shuffling at the memories. “You don’t remember how much blood was spilled because of their spies when they came for us on home soil, or the way they infiltrated our ranks at the isles of Sabany. Trust is a luxury you enjoy paid for with Kremnoan blood.”

“You would pin the sins of a nation on the shoulders of one man!”

“They call him Deliverer. From whom do you believe they want to be delivered from?”

Hephaestion growled. Tensions were high. Mydei could see his first mate and best friend fiddling with the hilt of his sword. Normally, he would welcome a fight, let them clash to resolve their feelings but Mydei knew it would escalate too far and there had been enough blood spilled for one night.

Krateros noticed too. He also reached for the sword at his side, drawing it and holding it to the side so it could catch the light. Others responded in kind until steel flashed in every hand. The deck was divided. Mydei saw Phainon shift in the corner of his eye, still on his knees but with his head raised, watching with a sour expression.

“I will not lose sleep over one more dead Okheman,” Krateros huffed.

“You will not harm him without spilling Kremnoan blood first,” Hephaestion snarled, and a few others shouted their agreement.

Mydei stepped forward so he was between them, gore from his own belly still prominently on display. Blood still dripped to the deck, spilling down his sides in rivulets. He wanted them to see it.

“I tire of bloodshed,” he admitted tiredly, arms crossed.

Mydei continued with a firmer voice, channeling the authority he despised to appeal to the traditionalists on the crew, “Krateros, I understand your fears. I know they are born of experience and grief. Hephaestion, I agree that Phainon has done nothing yet to prove himself a threat. His challenge to me was a gesture of respect and it is still binding. Our battle is not yet concluded and until it is, Phainon is not to be harmed, lest you who are my people bring shame upon me in the eyes of our Titan.”

The crew murmured but most of them lowered their weapons. Krateros was not one of them. Mydei could see fear and worry in his eyes. Not good enough. That was fine, Mydei had more to say.

“When I ripped out the old King’s heart it was with the promise of a new beginning for our people,” he huffed, “there is no beginning in nursing this hatred of Okhema, only chains that keep us bound to a bloody past with no absolution! Even now we bicker at each other’s throats, divided over an enemy that has not mattered since Eurypon’s head rolled. If a single man can tear us so completely, what hope have we against the Black Tide?”

Mydei looked over his shoulder at Phainon, at his expression. The Okheman's brow was creased with confusion, he still didn’t understand.

“Do we not all bleed?” Mydei asked while he looked at the warrior, “do we not all want freedom from the encroaching Tide?”

Phainon tilted his head, it was subtle, but it was there. Even if he didn’t understand Mydei’s words, the sentiment was getting through.

“This obsession stops right now,” Mydei growled as he turned back to Krateros, “we move forward as a united Kremnos right now. And if you are not ready to accept that Krateros, then at least continue to uphold our traditions of Strife. Until such time as our duel concludes, Phainon is to this ship as he has been. He will earn his keep with his work, share our meals, and be left to his own peace.”

Krateros slowly lowered his sword to sheathe it. He sighed and shook his head but he still respected Mydei. “For your sake and for my oath to your mother,” he said, “I will honor your wishes.”

Satisfied, Mydei nodded. “Then let us see to our wounded and rest.”

The crew started to scatter until only Mydei, Phainon, and his five closest friends were left, only then did Hephaestion sheathe his own sword. There was still a feral glint to his eyes.

“You should have killed me,” Phainon told them. Firm, cold, and resolute.

Peucesta slapped him across the back of the head beating at least three others who had raised their hands to do so. He startled and looked up at them with surprise coloring the edges of his fury.

“What do you think all of that was about?” Perdikkas scolded. The doctor was still trying to get close to Mydei with some sort of medicinal cream in his hands.

“We care about you, HKS,” Leonnius growled. He put an arm around Phainon’s neck and pulled him in tight to ruffle his hair, a playful salute, but Phainon pushed him away and scrambled backwards to his feet.

“Just stop,” he insisted, “stop pretending.”

“Pretending?” Hephaestion snarled, with such venom that even Mydei leaned away with wide eyes. “Is that what all of this is about? Your caustic mood today, challenging the Captain for your freedom? Because you think we’re all messing with you?”

Phainon blinked away his surprise. All his fire was draining away under the assault.

“You are no different than Krateros!” the first mate panted. Peucesta put a hand on his shoulder to calm his friend down and Hephaestion took the hint, shrugging him off to pace in a tight circle instead.

“Phainon,” Leonnius started, but he hesitated searching for the words, and Ptolemy stepped up instead.

“You have earned the truth,” he admitted, “but not right now. It’s late, everyone is tired. Exhaustion and battle high make for short tempers and this is a discussion that should be had with clear minds and open hearts. For all our sakes, please set aside your anger with us for tomorrow and we will do the same.”

Phainon thought that over and then nodded, just a tiny back and forth tilt of his head.

“Good. Tomorrow we will speak with you of what just happened too,” Ptolemy promised, “I imagine you are confused. For now, know that we here are on your side, no matter what happens in the future, you have earned that much from us.” He looked to the others for approval and every one of them nodded in agreement.

Mydei held a hand out, gesturing towards the upper deck. “Leonnius, will you take him to my room? Help him set up his hammock and get him a wash basin.”

“Yeah, of course.”

Leonnius gently took Phainon by the wrist and led him away.

They watched in silence until he was gone and then the collective sigh settled on them all at once.

“I can’t believe you were jumped by a Black Tide monster,” Hephaestion teased and Mydei twitched irritably. “Were you distracted by something else? Maybe someone else?”

Mydei punched at him, but Hephaestion dropped under the fist, chuckling.

“Damn it, stop moving,” Perdikkas scolded, “I should really look at this after you bathe.”

“It will be healed before I could wet the sponge. Leave me be!” he grumbled.

“Will Krateros honor his vow?” Peucesta said solemnly from the railing and the air of joviality was gone again.

Mydei frowned but nodded. “They will not be friends, nor do they need to be, but Krateros is still a devotee of Nikador. He will not harm Phainon until we finish our fight.”

“He wouldn’t have killed Phainon on the deck either,” Perdikkas reminded them, “not until you returned. I know it was tense earlier, but we should give Krateros credit. Just as Phainon has earned our trust, he has long since done so.”

“Everything he does is for love,” Peucesta mused aloud, “love of his people and King.”

Mydei scowled at the word King.

“Phainon isn’t his people,” Hephaestion reminded with a spit in his tone.

“Then we’ll have to change that,” Mydei said firmly and then he walked away before they could tease him again.

-

Leonnius was gentle with him, which Phainon appreciated. It was soothing, if confusing. He expected them to be rough. Maybe it would be easier if they were, but there was nothing but kindness in Leonnius’ callused hands helping him remove his bloody clothes.

The Kremnoan gently took Phainon’s hand and turned it over to press the sponge into it and that’s when he realized how tired he really was that even his body was struggling to respond to basic expectations. All the adrenaline had fled, taking with it the thrill of camaraderie and the simplicity of battle, leaving Phainon feeling empty and confused, trapped in the emotions that had been pushed aside in favor of something easier to understand.

It had hurt watching them fight. Even if he didn’t speak the language, Phainon knew they were fighting about him, about what he represented. He had not been able to defend himself, stuck hiding behind Mydei and the others.

Phainon squeezed the excess water from the sponge into the basin, watching the water turn yellow already from the blood on his hands. It shimmered in the dim light and very suddenly, Phainon was aware of the filth, how deeply, deeply uncomfortable he was with Mydei’s blood smeared across his arms and chest.

In a frantic fit he plunged both of his hands into the water to scrub them with his nails, scraping them clean until the skin was raw and red. He dragged the sponge over his body with more force than he needed as though he could rub away the ringing in his ears and those gnawing doubts alongside the blood. When that wasn’t enough, he thrust his face into the water with half a mind to drown himself but rose with a start when his lungs screamed for air, leaving him gasping while bloody water streamed and dripped from his hair.

He watched his own reflection as it tried to clear but every time Phainon’s eyes were almost able to glare back at him, water dripped and the ripples scattered his image into pieces. A more accurate reflection of how he felt than how he looked.

Phainon slowly sank down to his knees and rolled to sit on the floor with his back against the cupboard. At some point in his bathing Leonnius had left him alone.

At first Phainon was upset that he had been abandoned but the more he thought about it the more he was grateful for the solitude, and the more he appreciated the offered trust. They trusted him to be alone. The same way they promised to protect him, looking at him with such genuine faces that Phainon wasn’t sure how else to describe it other than as love.

He sat there zoning out until he was too cold in just his undergarments. Shakily, Phainon got to his feet and went to his own drawer to fetch his exomis. He ran his fingers over the royal blue of his cape, folded nicely inside. Briefly he considered wearing his coat, even without his undershirt, just for the comfort of something familiar, to hide how naked he felt, but the gold lining shimmered and he was again reminded of blood dripping on the deck while Mydei had pleaded in defense of him.

He left it, settling for the simple clothing.

“Deliverer,” a soft voice said behind him as he closed the clasp over his shoulder to pin the fabric in place.

Mydei had bathed elsewhere. He was clean and wearing nearly the same thing Phainon was, simple attire for tired men. In his hand was a plate with a small cup and a fork balanced around something warm and probably very tasty.

The Prince cleared his throat and set the plate down on the table. The map had been rolled up, tucked away somewhere unimportant.

“You didn’t eat,” he noted, “before we fought. I could barely concentrate on the fight with your stomach growling louder than the Tide.” The attempt at teasing was comforting.

Phainon stepped forward on shaky legs. He reached for the plate and pulled it closer with two fingers. “Did you make this special for me?”

Mydei blushed, the faintest color in his cheeks, maybe even a trick of the light.

“If I am going to defeat you in combat, it will be when you are at your best,” he said with a dismissive wave of his hand, “I won’t have you blaming weakness from malnutrition when you lose and join my crew.”

Phainon managed a small smile and would’ve bantered further, but Mydei had already turned away. Their hammocks were on opposite sides of the room and the Prince was already settling into his.

The food was perfect. A soft filet, warm bread, a sauce with a savory sweet flavor that Phainon couldn’t quite place. Pomegranate wine that made the tension turn drowsy.

He settled into his hammock full and warm, contemplating kindness. The faces of his worried friends, for undeniably he could call them friends, as they pledged to speak with him, pledged to protect him. The way Mydei literally bled for him.

Phainon wasn’t sure he deserved it if he really thought about what would happen if he won the duel and returned to Okhema, to the family he had made there. In a lot of ways, he agreed with the men who seemed ready to take his life. Even if he didn’t know their words, it wasn’t hard to piece together a hypothesis from what he already knew. They still saw him as their enemy, he still was… wasn’t he?

But as he fell asleep, the most important thing Phainon remembered, was fighting back-to-back against the one thing that didn’t care about the flag they sailed beneath.

And he laughed aloud to himself in tired gasps when he realized that was the answer to all of their problems.

Chapter End Notes

I have some work obligations coming up that I expect will eat my writing time for a few days. If you guys want any updates on delays on chapters you can follow me on Twitter. My name is the same there as it is here. Otherwise I should go back to regular updates by the end of the week.

chapters.title: Chapter 11: Clearing the Air
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Oh thank goodness, Fig Stew is back

Chapter Notes

This might be the last update for a few days so I spared you all the cliffhanger

The hammock had seemed like a silly choice when Phainon had first seen them in the crew’s living quarters but settled deep in the pocket and overcome with exhaustion, he slept better that night than any night prior on the Chryseus Leo. The rock of the ship was almost entirely negated by the natural sway of the hammock, and it was much easier to enjoy his rest when he wasn’t rolling into crates or steel bars.

That weighing exhaustion is what kept him falling back to sleep even when things started to move around him. He dimly remembered the moment when Mydei woke up and had come to check on him. Phainon remembered soft hands on his forehead, brushing hair out of his eyes, checking his pulse with a gentle press of fingers under his choker. He remembered soft murmurs when Mydei turned away to address whoever had come into his room before they both had stepped outside, leaving him to drift away again, quietly mourning the loss of the prince’s presence.

He vaguely recalled several voices, reviewing the map spread again across that big table. Mydei’s voice low and deep as he talked to Krateros and Hephaestion in whispers so as not to disturb him. He could pick out a couple words in Kremnoan, words that he recognized from his limited study time. The most important of which was ‘home.’

When he finally came around to full wakefulness, it was to the chime of soft laughter. There were a number of people in the room with him, talking in whispers and pouring juice. He held still to listen, and recognized their voices, even if he didn’t know what they were saying.

Phainon rolled to his side so he could blink at them, bleary in the bright light shining through the windows. It was well past Entry Hour.

“’My poor unhappy man, why do you lie awake in this way?’” Ptolemy quoted with words that Phainon could understand and very suddenly the rest of them knew who he was talking to and turned to flash comforting expressions. He smiled at Phainon from where he was leaning on the table and raised a glass to him.

“What time is it?” Phainon managed.

“A few quints past the Lucid Hour,” answered Perdikkas. He was tightening the bandages around Mydei’s belly while the prince sat patiently on a stool. “You must have been very tired.”

“If you’re hungry, we brought you food.” Hephaestion gestured to a plate of purple and green grapes, soft cheese, olive oil, and hard bread.

Phainon blinked at them. His head felt fuzzy and his body felt heavy, too comfortable. He rolled again to try and get up, but his leg caught in the fabric of the hammock and he didn’t get up so much as fall out in an awkward flail of limbs that dumped him on the floor to the tune of intermittent chuckling.

He pouted at them from the floor until Perdikkas abandoned Mydei to offer a hand.

“Sorry, sorry,” he said around his own giggles, “we don’t mean to make fun.”

“I do!” Leonnius called and a few of them laughed again. Even Mydei was smiling warmly.

“Were you all just, waiting for me to wake up?” Phainon asked as he rubbed his head. Things still felt a little awkward for him, despite how things had shaken out late the prior night. He didn’t feel quite as emotionally charged anymore now that he was rested, but sleep didn’t make the problems go away.

“They are here to annoy me, as usual,” Mydei grumbled, feigning annoyance despite the smile still curling the corners of his lips.

“And wait for you to wake,” Hephaestion confirmed, “if you’re ready to talk, we can get started while you eat.”

“Let the man be awake for more than a minute, Hephaestion,” Leonnius sighed. He reached for one of the two amphorae on the table to top himself off, but Hephaestion leaned over to snatch his cup from him.

“Go be useful and fetch Peucesta.”

Leonnius whined and sighed but he did get to his feet.

“Leonnius,” Mydei called, “fetch Krateros too.”

The mood in the room instantly soured but no one argued with him. Phainon felt in his bones how badly Hephaestion especially didn’t like that idea. Leonnius looked like he might argue for a second but then he turned and left.

“Maybe I should escape back to bed,” Phainon wondered aloud, trying to sound playful, eager to lighten the mood again.

It must’ve worked because Ptolemy laughed a single bark and whipped out another quote, “’Sleep, delicious and profound, the very counterfeit of death.’”

Even if Phainon wanted to, the moment he turned back to his hammock it was already occupied. Fig Stew had happily jumped in and was settling down, cutting off any hope of escape with a relaxed sigh and happy chirp. His belly was up and inviting but Phainon had learned his lesson the first two times.

Hephaestion kicked a stool his direction. “Come sit. Eat.”

Phainon obeyed. Food did sound good; good enough that he didn’t question where they got the fresher food. He was pretty sure he knew already. Okhema produced the best cheeses. The grapes were round and full with a satisfying and flavorful pop when he bit down through the skin. The oil was smooth on the crisp bread and paired nicely with the mild cheese.

Perdikkas tapped Mydei’s bandages one last time, finally content with his work, and sat next to Phainon at the table.

“So, um,” Phainon started. He put one of the pieces of bread in the oil so it could start to soften. “How does the whole immortality thing work with injuries?”

“They just heal fast,” Mydei offered with a shrug and then it was quiet again while the Prince reached for his chlamys from his stool to dress himself more appropriately.

Phainon felt the heat rise in his cheeks as he chanced glances Mydei’s way. Without his gauntlets he could see just how far those tattoos reached down his arms.

“So, you usually fight bare-handed?”

“Is that really what you want to talk about?” One of Mydei’s eyebrows went up.

Phainon shrugged. “Just curious. Didn’t realize it was a secret.”

“I can use weapons. I just prefer not to.”

More silence.

The Kremnoans all looked between themselves before Hephaestion sighed, “Please don’t let it be this awkward the entire time…”
