The door opened a second later and Leonnius returned to his seat, snatching his cup from Hephaestion as he did so. He leaned back in his chair until the back tapped against the wall and rested the cup on his chest between sips.

Peucesta, newly arrived, headed straight for the back of the room. He sat himself down on the top of one of Mydei’s dressers, against the window. He immediately started to play, just a soft soundtrack, the kind of thing that fades into the background and is easily forgotten until it stops and leaves behind a hollow feeling that something is missing.

It was Krateros that altered the mood the most with his presence. He glanced at the others there and then found a spot against an empty wall to lean, crossing his arms and bowing his head, eyes closed to listen.

“It is indeed going to be this awkward the entire time,” Ptolemy mumbled into his cup.

Hephaestion flashed Mydei a look, jaw locked, annoyed, but Mydei kept his cool.

“Krateros,” the Prince greeted, and the man looked up at him, “I don’t want your unsolicited input during this discussion.”

“Then why am here?”

“Because I want you to listen and council me when I ask it of you. You are still my teacher, I still value your advice, even if I decide not to follow it.”

The others didn’t seem nearly as welcoming towards the old veteran and Phainon was just trying not to draw attention to himself. It didn’t work. Krateros looked from Mydei to Phainon, watching him closely before he bowed his head again.

“I understand,” he said carefully. The respect that Mydei showed him was placating. Even if Krateros wasn’t invited to participate this was still an olive branch, and when Krateros closed his eyes and did his best to become one with the background, the edge in the room softened.

The silence lingered, no one knew where to start, so Mydei took the lead as he usually did.

“Deliverer- Phainon,” he said. Phainon looked up from his food.

“As promised, we owe you the truth.” He drummed his fingers on his leg. “Perhaps it is best if we start at the beginning. I did not lie to you when I told you this ship does not take prisoners. It was something we agreed to in our self-exile when we took the Chryseus Leo from Castrum Kremnos.”

Leonnius was nodding profusely. Hephaestion ran his finger along the edge of his cup.

“When I pulled you from the water the morning we met, it was not because I intended to put you in a difficult situation,” Mydei insisted, “we were simply surprised that were any survivors at all.”

Phainon swallowed. “Because of the Black Tide.”

Perdikkas spoke next, raising a hand in apology when he cut Mydei off. “We aren’t monsters. Any time we attack a ship, Black Tide or otherwise we look for innocent people to protect them. We’ve carried refugees before, freed would be slaves, but when the Black Tide is involved, there are never survivors… until Mydei saw you in the hold of that merchant ship.”

“Ptolemy looked you up,” Hephaestion picked up the story and Ptolemy nodded along, “we knew from how you were dressed and your sun mark that you had to be from Okhema and it wasn’t hard to piece together from there. Your notoriety made you dangerous, especially when you lashed out at Perdikkas, and with the crew’s …history, we figured the safest thing to do would be to kill you, as another casualty of war.”

“So why didn’t you?” Phainon asked. His appetite was gone. He just pushed grapes around his plate.

“It didn’t feel right,” Mydei said matter-of-factly, “we had just saved you from a mutual enemy. The way you talked with me on the deck and below, it was plain that you had come for us uninformed. You were as much a victim as the rest of your crew, regardless of our nations’ conflict.”

“And the rest of your crew was okay with that?” Phainon asked, suspicious. He looked over at Krateros, but the man didn’t react.

“I had promised Krateros that if you became a danger, I would kill you myself,” Mydei said simply.

Phainon drew in a breath and held it. That made a lot of sense.

“Even last night, when Krateros arrested you, your life wasn’t in danger,” Perdikkas told him, “because of Mydei’s vow to him, he would’ve left that judgement to the prince.”

“He even said so last night. You couldn’t understand the discussion,” Ptolemy acknowledged, “but he did.”

Ptolemy recounted the argument from the prior night, how Krateros and the old crew saw Phainon as a threat from Okhema, a spy, that arresting him until they got the whole story was the right thing to do when Phainon had returned alone. Then he shared what Mydei had said about how those grudges should not be directed to someone who had yet to do anything worthy of that hatred. That Mydei refused to continue the conflict with Okhema at all, that their war ended with Eurypon and they needed to move forward together.

All the feelings of being helpless came back and Phainon felt that lump in his throat. So that’s what they had been yelling about. As he had suspected, Mydei and the others had been his advocate, arguing for his innocence despite his allegiance.

“The Kremnoan Okheman conflict still lingers, especially for the older crew,” Mydei admitted, “but nothing has come of it since the King’s death. I was short-sighted and that first morning, I struck a deal with you as I have prior passengers.”

Phainon pulled his hands into his lap and looked down. “When you let me work the ship, all that bonding- “

Hephaestion kicked his stool from under the table, almost hard enough to knock him over and Phainon scrambled to grab the table for balance. “It was real, HKS.”

“When I realized the complexity of the situation left us with no choice but to feed you to the sea or hold you hostage, I told them they could answer your questions,” Mydei confirmed, “it was never my intention to lie to you about your status on the ship. By the time I realized I had, that I had lied even to myself, it was too late to change anything. You had barely begun on the ship and were already solving problems as a Kremnoan would, working hard, eager to please and obnoxiously curious. Even if you were a captive by circumstance, I saw no reason to make you suffer, and there was no need to keep our history and companionship from you when you were already trapped here. Not until I had another solution.”

That explained a lot. The hesitation in their voices before they told him stories, the pitying glances when he mentioned going home. They did know the situation but wanted to protect him from the truth for a time.

“The truth is,” Hephaestion told Phainon, “only half the crew consider you an enemy. Even locking you up at night, it wasn’t because we thought you were dangerous, it’s because we were worried someone on the crew might try to harm you. Even moving you here to the Captain’s room was so someone could be ready to protect you.”

“Not that it helped,” Leonnius grumbled.

Phainon tilted his head in confusion at Leonnius’ comment.

“During the storm,” Perdikkas said, taking a turn to speak, “someone cut your lifeline in the hope the storm would take care of you.”

The pieces were coming together. Phainon’s brow pinched deep in thought. “You were barring the infirmary door at night because you thought they might try to finish the job.”

Perdikkas nodded.

“We still don’t know who did it,” Ptolemy admitted.

“It doesn’t matter,” Mydei huffed, “the crew won’t harm you now, not while our battle is unfinished. To do so would dishonor the vow we made to honor the outcome.”

“But why go through all that effort to protect me? Wouldn’t my death have solved your problem?” Phainon asked. It wasn’t coming from a desire to die, when he asked it was with a genuine curiosity, a want to understand why a culture that treated death so casually would shy away from it, especially given it was the easy solution.

Mydei’s eyes were wide and thoughtful, he looked at Phainon like he had an answer stuck in his throat. Color rushed to the prince’s cheeks and he looked away. A gesture that left Phainon even more confused.

“You were innocent, but mostly because we like you,” Peucesta said from his corner, “because the more we got to know you, the more you got to know us, the more we wanted you to be one of us.”

Phainon huffed, feeling a little angry and once again torn. “That wasn’t your decision to make.”

All the Kremnoans looked down and away, ashamed.

“The situation was complicated,” Perdikkas tried.

“I get that but that doesn’t make it okay,” Phainon was saying, “you all made me believe that I would get to go home. Can you imagine how it felt to feel like one of you, to be happy here and then learn that it was covering a lie? That I didn’t have a choice? That you were all keeping things from me about my fate?

“Ptolemy you told me that you read those ridiculous songs the bards wrote about me, you knew that I was important to Okhema, to Aglaea. Even if my family-“ he stumbled a little, “even if the family I was born to is gone, I have friends and a new family at home. Did any of you even consider that?”

There was a shameful silence. Peucesta stopped playing. Perdikkas fiddled with the leftover bandages as though the answer was written on the cloth.

It was Mydei who broke the silence with the softest glimmer of hope in his whisper, “… you’re happy here?”

Phainon sighed and ran a hand through his hair, combing the white with his fingers until he looked as disheveled as he felt. “I was.”

The music started again, this time in a minor key, sad.

“But I owe you all some truth too.” Phainon pushed the plate away and leaned back on his stool. “I’m still angry and hurt because of how you lied to me, not because I was being held captive. I understood why you had to do that and if our situations were reversed, I would have done the same.”

They were all quiet while he talked, letting him gather his thoughts. Mydei loosely crossed his arms and tilted his head. The sunlight glittered on his earring. It was distracting so Phainon studied the table instead.

“I don’t like it, but the truth is, your fears were not unfounded. If I return to Okhema, I will have to tell them everything. Not because I want to, but because I wouldn’t have a choice. Even though I don’t agree with what you are doing, the piracy, the stealing, I don’t think you guys are evil like I was led to believe.” He clenched his fists on his thighs.

“But it wouldn’t matter how I felt, what I think, or what I’d try to keep to myself. Aglaea’s golden threads would keep me from lying or withholding anything I’ve learned, even if I could convince her to show mercy, I don’t know if I’d be able to convince the Council of Elders that Castrum Kremnos is no longer a militant threat. I’m not even sure they know about King Eurypon’s death, if they did… Krateros and your crew aren’t the only ones who believe this war between us is ongoing. I’m not sure what they would do if they knew about you and your people. They might even take up the banner of war in full force again, to try and end it on their terms.

“I’m not sure I could do it. It wouldn’t feel right, duty or not.”

Phainon looked up at Mydei specifically this time.

“When I realized in the galley that you also had an impossible decision to make like mine, I thought maybe the duel would be the best way for us both to put the decision in fate’s hands. Even if it was a coward’s idea, it felt like the best way for us to come to a resolution that we could both live with.”

Mydei nodded. “I suspected as much.”

The room was quiet as everyone mulled over the situation.

“So now what?” Perdikkas asked, breaking the silence with a soft voice. He was still fiddling with the bandages, wrapping his own fingers and then unwrapping them over and over.

“Easy,” chimed Leonnius, he finished his juice and then leaned forward to reach for more, but Ptolemy swiftly pulled the pitcher out of his reach until he finished speaking. “Phainon joins the crew.”

Phainon almost fell out of his chair. For a second, Mydei looked like he was going to agree but he retreated when Phainon cut in. “I can’t.”

“Why not?” Leonnius and Ptolemy asked at the same time. They smiled at each other when they realized they were on the same page.

“I’m not a pirate,” Phainon insisted, “I can’t-I can’t do the things you guys do. I’m sorry, I just can’t break the law like that. I still have a family and a purpose in Okhema. Aglaea saved my life, she finished raising me, I owe her a debt I’ll never be able to repay, a debt that I sealed with my oath to support the flame-chase journey. And that’s to say nothing of the other Chrysos Heirs that rely on me.” He moved one hand to his chest to rest over his heart.

Hephaestion sighed and reached for the amphorae. He handed it over to Leonnius who went to pour only to realize the pitcher was empty with a scowling frown.

“We’re back at the beginning of the problem,” the first mate lamented, ignoring the rude hand gesture from his thirsty friend, “you can’t join the crew because it conflicts with your oath, but we can’t let you go because, per your own admission, Okhema will use the things we told you to hunt us down and finish the war.”

“The war that really ended five years ago,” Leonnius reminded.

“That Okhema doesn’t realize because they don’t know Eurypon is dead,” Perdikkas sighed.

“Or they do know,” Ptolemy mused, “and are not telling their people because they don’t want the war to end.”

The whole room sighed.

“I don’t want to agree with Krateros,” Perdikkas grumbled, “but he might be right.”

In the corner, Krateros didn’t react. He didn’t smile or frown, just waited patiently, listening, as still as a statue.

“Not about the killing you part,” Perdikkas clarified with a slight wave towards Phainon, “about the treating you like a prisoner of war part.”

“’No man or woman born, coward or brave, can shun his destiny,’” Ptolemy quoted. He very sadly pushed a loose grape with a finger until it rolled off the table. “Okhema and Kremnos are doomed to hate until one of us is destroyed.”

Phainon saw Mydei out of the corner of his eye tense up tight. His relaxed expression had turned stressed, with a deep frown and his fingers pressing deep into his arms where he held them. His brow was pinched in thought, but he didn’t share what he was thinking. He looked so much more human like that. It made Phainon’s stomach flip, and his chest feel warm. That distressed face more than anything made Phainon want to fix everything so Mydei wouldn’t have to look like that ever again.

“Let’s just change our destiny,” Phainon offered. The room turned to look at him, puzzled.

“The answer has been in front of us the whole time,” he continued and stood up to emphasize what he was saying. “Ever since I got here, even last night, it’s been Kremnos against Okhema with no hope of resolution between our nations, but we already felt and lived the answer.”

The image of Nikador and Kephale united, carved in wood, sprang to Phainon’s mind.

Mydei looked up at Phainon. “The Black Tide.”

Hephaestion smiled, just a little twitch in the corner of his mouth, when Phainon pointed at Mydei. “You said as much yourself on the deck last night, your Highness.”

“Yeah but uniting two halves of a disagreement between people of the same culture and background is very different from uniting two entirely different peoples,” Leonnius pointed out. He was back to leaning in his chair, trying to get the last few drops of juice from his cup.

“That’s where I come in,” Phainon said with a reassuring smile, “when Aglaea and Tribbios started calling me the Deliverer, encouraging others to do the same, I was embarrassed. It didn’t feel like she gave such an auspicious title to the right person.” He put his hand back on the table but stayed standing, leaning his weight onto both his hands. “But maybe I can use this title she gave me, convince the people that our war with Castrum Kremnos is in the past and that the Black Tide should be our priority. They’ll listen to me.”

Ptolemy wrinkled his face as he worked through a few different expressions. His bookworm persona didn’t take it well and every contortion looked extra sharp and exaggerated. “Did you not say that your Council of Elders couldn’t be convinced?”

Phainon deflated. He hung his head and slumped down onto the stool again. “Yeah…”

“Phainon, does Okhema have to contend with the Black Tide at all?” Hephaestion asked. The question made Phainon tilt his head.

“When we talked in the brig,” Mydei started to say, “you were unaware of how far the Tide had spread.”

Phainon groaned as he realized the futility of his idea. Of course, the Council would reject the idea of setting aside an eons long war in favor of an Alliance to fight an enemy that they had all but forgotten about. They would consider it a problem for distant lands, not something to trouble the populace, especially with Kephale’s Dawn Device to protect them.

“There’s no reason for Okhema to join forces with us to fight something that isn’t a threat to them,” Perdikkas pointed out, giving voice to Phainon’s thoughts.

“They will have to confront it eventually,” Mydei reminded the room, and everyone looked over at him. He was back to his composed, stoic expression complete with nonchalant hand gestures.

“Not with Kephale’s Dawn Device,” Ptolemy argued.

The Prince shook his head. “Is it not the Goldweaver’s life ambition to gather the twelve coreflames of the Titans?” Everyone brightened at once. “The Deliverer even said that his oath is to her flame-chase journey. Is that not what the journey entails?”

“Yeah, but what does that have to do with the Black Tide?” Phainon asked before he remembered a few things. They all let him work through it when they saw the realization on his face.

“I don’t know how many coreflames Aglaea has already,” Hephaestion said as he knocked his empty cup over on the table with a deliberate push, “but there’s at least one that we know of that she doesn’t have.”

“The coreflame of Strife,” Peucesta mumbled, distracted. The song changed to something more ominous and faster paced.

“You know where it is?” Phainon asked.

“In the heart of Nikador,” Mydei said with a dark tone, “buried in Castrum Kremnos where we trapped him, deep in the Black Tide.”

-

Mydei watched Phainon’s face fall into a quiet but determined expression. It wasn’t the news he wanted but it was something and rather than slip into despair as he thought Phainon might, he seemed to be crunching numbers in his head. It was the exact crinkle of the eyebrows that Ptolemy had when he was calculating their earnings and expenses report every time they docked to trade.

“I could convince them,” Phainon said, confident, “Aglaea would take my side if I told them about the coreflame.”

“That might solve the whole Okhema Kremnos issue, but doesn’t that sign us up for something worse?” Leonnius pointed out.

“If we sell a truce on the promise of the coreflame of Strife…” Perdikkas mumbled, “we’d be expected to help retrieve it.”

The whole room grimaced. Mydei looked between each of them in turn. They were trying too hard to complicate a solution by creating another problem.

“Krateros,” Mydei invited, when he saw the old man watching them, a deviation from his prior position, “do you have any council that may benefit the room?”

“The Black Tide need not be a unifier,” Krateros said firmly, “if there is ever to be a truce between Kremnos and Okhema, only the King of Castrum Kremnos can broker such peace.”

Peucesta missed a note on the lyre, an ugly sound that was quickly glossed over when the melody resumed. Perdikkas also flinched, but the others held their silence, careful not to react. Mydei could see Phainon looking at him expectantly, confused but unsure if he should speak.

“Castrum Kremnos has no King,” Mydei said firmly, shutting that down.

“Then abandon any hope of change,” Krateros said, equally firm as he bowed his head again.

Fig Stew gave the room a sad awoo from Phainon’s hammock. His front paws were on the edge of the fabric so he could watch them with those big eyes, oblivious to how the tilting bed was about to dump the chimera in a replay of what had happened to Phainon.

“So, we’re back to the Black Tide?” Leonnius asked with a groan.

“Until we think of something else,” Hephaestion confirmed.

“I think we need more time,” Ptolemy offered, “we don’t need to solve everything right now.”

“That’s right,” chimed in Perdikkas. He crumpled up the bandages in his hand and stuffed them into the folds of his exomis. “We did what we intended to. Cleared the air, told Phainon the truth and got the truth, unless there’s something you forgot?”

They looked at Phainon whose eyes tilted towards the ceiling. He held a finger to his chin to think and fuck it was adorable. Mydei moved his hands to his thighs to dig his fingers in to keep his legs from bouncing.

“Not that I can think of,” he said, “but… nothing has changed yet, has it?”

“No,” Mydei confirmed, “you are still a prisoner of war, pending our fight’s conclusion.”

“Should we take care of that today?” Phainon asked.

Mydei shook his head. “My injury is nearly healed, but I will still need the rest. If we are to fight, I want us both at our best.”

He didn’t need to remind anyone that the pending rematch was also protecting Phainon’s life, buying them time until they could think of an acceptable alternative. The duel freed them of and social responsibility and guilt but it wouldn’t prevent the consequences that would come with either victor.

“For now, we act as we have been,” the first mate supplied, “Phainon still works the ship, we still watch his back. Until he leaves this ship, he’s one of us. Agreed?”

“Agreed,” the other four Kremnoans said.

Mydei saw Hephaestion’s eyes dart towards Krateros when they said it, but the old man was still and silent, waiting to be dismissed as though he were napping on guard duty.

“Agreed,” Mydei added after them.

Much softer and with awe, Phainon brought up the rear. “Agreed.”

Mydei leaned back to grab his half full cup from the shelf behind him. It was closer than the table. He held it out to his friends, and they repeated the gesture.

“To brothers in arms, bound by the blood we spill together, not the blood we share,” he said, looking squarely at Phainon as he spoke.

They all mimicked his gesture, waiting until Phainon joined them. Everyone else had empty glasses, so it was only he and Phainon who drank, but the sentiment was there.

Mydei felt his heart flutter looking at his family. It was still too much to hope that Phainon might be a part of it. There were insurmountable odds, laid plain and bare now, but something about the universal willingness in the room to climb that mountain gave him courage.

He raised his glass one more time and waited for the others to copy him before he said with a smirk, “to getting back to work.”

All the Kremnoans groaned aside from Krateros, who cracked his composure to laugh. “You heard the Crown Prince,” the old man said, chattering fondly in their native tongue.

Hephaestion helped herd them along, leaving Phainon and Mydei alone.

Phainon still looked bothered, conflicted, like he was holding the whole world squarely on his shoulders.

He didn’t know why, but Mydei wanted to share that weight with him.

“Deliverer,” he said as he stood and Phainon’s daze broke enough to look up, “if there is a way for me to return you to your home while still protecting my family and my people, then I will find it.”

Phainon’s face tilted, just enough to make his hair sway across his forehead and bounce around his ears.

“Why don’t you want to be King?” he asked softly, and the question stole his breath.

Mydei looked down at his now empty cup and slowly put it on the table next to the others. “It is hard to explain.”

“Try.”

Mydei looked up at Phainon and their eyes met. It felt like Phainon was looking straight into him. His eyes were like the sky, clear, pure, and infinite, held steady.

“Because the blood-soaked Crown of Strife cannot lead my people to the peace that I dream of for them.”

“Even if it’s a way to end this war and peaceably secure my freedom?”

“It is not the answer that Krateros thinks it is.”

Phainon went quiet then, back to his thoughts.

Mydei sighed. “Perhaps I should throw you back into the sea,” he growled and turned his nose up, arms crossed, eyes closed, “sleeping in, lazing about when the rest of my crew are hard at work!”

“Apologies, Captain,” Phainon said, and Mydei could hear the playful lilt in his words, “someone saw fit to keep me in his room for a time after my meeting. I could hardly refuse~”

Mydei felt his ears turn red, could hear Phainon pulling on his boots.

“If you are still here when I open my eyes, I’ll feed you to the waters beneath my ship,” Mydei threatened.

The scrambling got a little faster until he heard Phainon call from the door in a sing-song voice, “I’ll miss you too, Mydeimos. Don’t wait up for me.”

The door closed before Mydei could throw anything at him. He stood there in his room alone to catch his breath.

Well, mostly alone.

Fig Stew was still watching from Phainon’s hammock. The smug smile was back as he purred loudly enough to be heard from several paces away.

“If you have something to say, I would hear it,” he huffed at the chimera.

Fig Stew raised his tail and pressed it against the fabric to make the hammock swing, just a gentle sway. His expression never changed.

Mydei sighed and started gathering the dishes to take with him to the galley. A glimmer of guilt gnawed at his belly. In all that discussion he had thought of another solution, one that he had already been considering for a long time now.

‘No man or woman born, coward or brave, can shun his destiny.’

A thousand-year-old Kremnoan Dynasty. A crown he refused to pick up.

Mydei had already resolved himself to being the last prince of Castrum Kremnos, no matter how much his people wanted him to pick up the crown, to call himself King. They wanted him to lead them home, to resume the mantle of Strife, to follow the mad Titan to glory and conquest, to die. There was no future in that doomed life.

‘Okhema and Kremnos are doomed to hate until one of us is destroyed.’

Maybe that was the answer.

Why leave the crown there on the ground, waiting to be picked up, when Mydei could instead grind it to pieces forever?

chapters.title: Chapter 12: Homesick
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

New tag: Public Nudity

Home is where the heart is! ...right?

Chapter Notes

Thank you everyone for being patient while I tended to work obligations!

Phainon left the meeting feeling better but not resolved. Nothing had really changed aside from having all the nasty on the table where everyone could see it. The only peace came from knowing that no one was happy about the predicament, and everyone was on the same page wanting to work together to find an outcome that made everyone happy. The unspoken tension was the universal understanding that this peace was fragile. A decision couldn’t be avoided forever, and someone was going to get hurt when it was made.

Baby steps, Phainon had to remind himself as he stepped out into the light. Knowing that people on the ship wanted to kill him and how dismissive the others had been about it was the more immediate concern for him. But as he hurried to follow Hephaestion’s orders, bringing water to the men working the lines, he didn’t sense any animosity. Instead, the crew treated him with begrudging to open respect. Ulixes even hit him in the shoulder with an affectionate punch and praised him for his fight with Mydei the prior evening. Kremnoans really did respect strength. Even the older crewmen gave him a nod here and there, even if they looked like they had swallowed something sour while doing so.

Earned respect wasn’t the only thing that buzzed in the air. The crew was antsy, a little too eager to tend to the sails, many of them waiting by the oars one level down. Phainon tried to ask one of them in Kremnoan what was so exciting but after a very awkward exchange, the man had burst out laughing at something Phainon had said and walked away shaking his head.

He went looking for someone he knew could understand him after that.

“Perdikkas,” Phainon asked gently. The man was dumping waste over the rail.

“Someone giving you trouble?”

“The opposite. Is something supposed to happen today?”

“Oh, did no one tell you?” Perdikkas pointed to the horizon. They were following a shoreline. It was very far away, the kind of thing that was easy to miss if you weren’t looking for it. “We’re making berth soon. Good thing we put a rush on clearing the air before we got there. Ah, don’t get your hopes up.” Phainon’s face went from joyful surprise to cautious optimism. “It’s not an Okheman friendly place.”

Didn’t matter, it was still dry land, something solid. Phainon was excited until something else occurred to him.

“…will I be allowed off the ship?” he asked.

Perdikkas tried to keep the pity off his face. Emphasis on tried. “That’s-That’s something to figure out when we get there.”

And getting there didn’t take as long as Phainon had thought. Despite the delay from the Black Tide, the Chryseus Leo made good time, making it home with the late afternoon high tide. The wind was behind them, the current strong, the men pulled on the oars like their lives depended on it. The ship itself carried an air of urgency, that eager and powerful desire to curl up in a familiar bed after a long trip. It made Phainon homesick in equal measure with his sense of adventure.

The shoreline they were following was the same landmass that led to Okhema, albeit in a horrible zig-zag, spend-a-month-on-a-dromas, kind of way. Where the continent started to narrow was a collection of islands, perched on the biggest of which was a collection of buildings, too big to be considered a village but too small to be considered a city. Even from a distance Phainon could see the settlement was expanding, evidence of construction on the edges giving it away.

Phainon hurried to the bow, holding onto the shrouds so he could lean over the side to watch them come into port. Most of the crew were still on the oars, fine tuning their steering against the currents to avoid the islands’ reefs, a natural defense from seafaring invaders. Peucesta played music for them to give them instructions, relaying calls from Leonnius in the upper shrouds above to safely navigate.

Mydei was dressed finely, back in his usual regalia, looking every inch the King he should be as he watched from the upper deck. Phainon could feel his eyes on the back of his neck, gauging any reactions, but Phainon couldn’t be bothered to care. He was taking in the sights.

Up close it was easier to tell how much of this place was actually very old, especially near the docks. Newer buildings freckled here and there, but the core of the island home was many decades old at least, perhaps even pushing a hundred. He’d need to be up close to be sure, but he recognized familiar textbook examples of Kremnoan architecture. Older buildings had bronze fixings, both functional and decorative, making the old city into a recognizable fort with sprawling walls.

Mydei shouted orders to the men on the lines as they approached, turning to call to the men on the tiller as well. The sails were completely furled now, no need for the wind to carry them any further. Krateros shouted orders below and they gently coasted in close using their lingering momentum and the oars to glide expertly into place. People shouted from the shore and the docks, pointing to the big ship. One of them blew into a horn to call for more hands.

Perdikkas and Hephaestion rolled massive ropes over the side of the ship for them to grab on long hooks. After a quint of fine tuning between the oars, and their comrades pulling the lines from the shore, the Chryseus Leo was safely tethered between two docks. The whole ship lurched a little as she settled, sails furled tight, oars being tucked away.

Mydei was already heading down from the upper deck, talking to Krateros on the stairs and waving over Hephaestion to join them as he went. A couple men were removing a section of the railing to allow for the wide, sturdy ramp from the dock. They caught the ropes tossed up to them, pulled the ramp into place and latched it tightly against the deck so it wouldn’t slip. Within seconds men and women were pouring onboard to greet the crew with happy cheers and rough greetings.

“They’re all Kremnoan,” Phainon mused aloud.

“Yup,” Leonnius confirmed. He dropped down from above to land next to Phainon with a heavy thud. The man definitely felt that landing all the way through his knees if the look on his face meant anything. “Welcome to the new Kremnos, sort of.”

“Sort of?”

“Well, this is an outpost that Castrum Kremnos has had since our battle with Icatus like 70 years ago,” he explained, “when the Black Tide took over Castrum Kremnos, this was the only territory left that was safe. This is what’s left of our people.”

Phainon’s heart sank. “This is all that’s left?”

“Don’t look so sad. It’s a miracle so many people made it to safety at all and those we lost died honorably.”

“Then this is your home port?”

“For now, yeah, just until Mydeimos becomes King and then we’ll go back to Castrum Kremnos.”

Another sad tug pulled Phainon’s heart. Surely Leonnius knew how Mydei felt about that prospect? If the prince had been willing to answer when Phainon asked, surely, he had answered his friends? Had he given them the same answer?

“Leonn-“

“Deliverer!” Mydei’s voice cut him off.

Phainon turned to look at the captain who was gesturing for him to come with one finger pointed his way, curling and uncurling in an unmistakable summons. He gave Leonnius an apologetic smile and obeyed.

Mydei was standing next to the ramp talking to a tall and intimidating looking woman. She had two people beside her, another woman with long braided hair and a bald man who was already barking orders to the people down on the dock. Krateros and Hephaestion were standing there too, acting as liaisons between the crew and the dock workers. The entire exchange felt amicable and efficient. No small talk, only happy business.

“Yes, Mydeimos?” Phainon asked with as sweet a voice as he could muster.

Mydei reached out and grabbed Phainon’s chin, pinching his cheeks tightly to keep him from moving, making him blink in surprise at the sudden rough treatment. The woman looked him over. She was wearing armor, had a couple small scars on her jawline, and short hair. She also was not happy to see him.

She said something to Mydei in Kremnoan and Phainon caught a couple words. One of them was flattering, the other was not. Mydei responded somewhat flippantly, letting him go. They went back and forth like that, obviously discussing him with varying degrees of hostility. Inevitably, Phainon started to speak, eager to calm them, but Mydei’s gauntlet covered his mouth and grabbed his head so fast that he ended up floundering in place around the impromptu gag instead, clutching at Mydei’s unmoving wrist and tapping it like that would convince him to let go.

Mydei only released him when the woman sighed and turned to talk to the other lady, leaving behind a horrible, metallic taste on Phainon’s tongue. They must’ve settled on something because she barked another order and suddenly traffic was moving around them. The crew was already opening the hold to roll barrels and treasure onto unloading nets, eager to have the work out of the way so they could enjoy the short break.

“Your pretty face is already turning heads-” Mydei told him as he let go.

“You think I’m pretty?”

“You’d be prettier if you weren’t interrupting me.”

“I don’t think it works that way.”

“Phainon.” Something about the way Mydei growled out his name sent shivers up his spine and trapped his breath halfway down his throat. “This is a Kremnoan port. They have no love of Okhemans.”

“I have to stay on the ship…”

“I did not say that.” Mydei held a hand up to shut down any expected excitement and looked a little surprised when Phainon wasn’t ready with excitement to share. “I’m saying that when we go ashore, you must stay with someone from the detachment.”

“Someone like you?” Phainon teased.

“Yes.”

Oh. He didn’t expect that to be an option.

“Preferably me,” Mydei doubled down and Phainon felt weak in his knees, “I am the most qualified to protect you.”

“You know I don’t need protecting.”

“Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, you do here. This is not a matter of individual strength, it’s a matter of politics.”

Phainon could see the seriousness of Mydei’s words in the way he gestured with his hands, a finger sharply pointed his direction and a clenched fist.

“Alright,” he relented, “am I still a prisoner then?”

“Consider the port an extension of the ship. The same vow we made this morning applies there.”

Phainon chewed on the inside of his cheek for a second before asking, “what’s to stop me from running away?”

“Do you see any other way out of this port? There is only one other ship that makes berth here, a merchant vessel of ours that we use for trade and it is not here nor will it be in the time it will take us to make repairs and again disembark.”

Well, that would do it. Phainon wouldn’t get very far on a secluded island full of Kremnoans.

“You’re not going to want to run anyway, Phainon,” Hephaestion said with a gentle smile. He patted Phainon’s back with one very firm smack. “We’re going to drag you to the bath house and there’s always good food when we come back to port. The whole city wants to welcome back their prince!” He put an arm around Mydei’s shoulder and grinned.

“Go help unload,” Mydei snapped, but there was no irritation in his voice.

Hephaestion chuckled but obeyed.

“Should I help?” Phainon asked.

“No. We have a system; it will be better for you stay out of the way.” Mydei leaned forward over the railing to rest his weight on his forearms while he looked out over the town. He looked wistful, regal, but wistful. The breeze was nice here, it tugged at Mydei’s cape and earring and played with his hair like a comfortable friend.

Phainon watched him for a second, feeling his cheeks warm looking at that soft expression.

“Are you happy to be home?” Phainon asked. He stepped up to the rail beside Mydei.

“This isn’t home.”

“This is where your people are, isn’t that home?”

Mydei looked down to watch the people moving on the dock. A couple of kids were weaving underfoot, running to jump into a man’s arms, excited to see their father home again. His expression was guarded but there was a slight smile threatening to break through that composure. It was there hiding in the corner of his eyes.

“I suppose,” he mused softly.

“Hey, I meant to ask,” Phainon said light-heartedly. He mimicked Mydei’s pose so he could playfully nudge him with his shoulder. “Why aren’t there any women on the crew?”

“Why? Looking for someone?” Mydei retorted a little snippier than Phainon expected.

“Nothing like that!” he insisted with a laugh, “I was just curious. I thought Kremnoan women were as strong as Kremnoan men.”

“They are.” Mydei’s mood mellowed again. “I had a few on my crew for a time.”

“Did something happen to them?”

“They left of their own volition. Said they would rather help rebuild Castrum Kremnos from the shore than waste time comforting insecure men on a ship.”

Phainon laughed, “surely they weren’t talking about-“

“The crew? Yes. They were stronger than most of them, but I am glad I honored their parting. This island is only a success because of their strength and wisdom.”

“Then the lady from before…”

“Yes, her name is Empousa. She’s the harbormaster now.”

Phainon whistled. “She didn’t seem all that happy to see me.”

“No one will be,” Mydei admitted. It was cold but honest. “But most will be focused on the bounty we brought.”

“Right, why wouldn’t everyone be excited for their share of the pirate treasure.”

That was not the right thing to say. Even if Phainon meant it in jest, Mydei didn’t take it that way. He tensed for a moment and then leaned back, resting only one hand on the railing while he turned to look down at where Phainon was leaning with a frown.

“Do you really believe that is all there is of us? That we are simply thieves cackling over hoarded gold before we bury it?”

“No, I-“

“This island used to be self-sustaining before the population more than tripled. My people are trying, but they will perish without the goods we retrieve. That is what we are doing Deliverer. When we disembark we are looking for food, supplies, the means to survive. That is the treasure they are eager to receive.”

“And is that sustainable, captain?” Phainon fired back as he stood up to meet him, “piracy may be the easy answer now, but what happens when that’s not enough anymore?”

Mydei scowled irritably. “Go get your things,” he ordered instead, “whatever you need for a night on shore.”

Phainon let out a short and stiff huff of air to tell Mydeimos he wasn’t happy with the deflection but stomped off without a word anyway.

At first Phainon wasn’t sure what he needed to pack. It wasn’t like he had much to his name to begin with. He unlatched his drawer and opened it to check. Would it be too much to wear his full armor? …if he was already turning heads.

Phainon took off his exomis and got dressed in the familiar clothing, this time wearing all of it. As he tugged on the strap across this chest to tighten the leather, he felt a little smug. The pauldron, the fine stitching on his sleeves, the gold and blue of his half cape, the medallion set into the leather guard at his shoulder, it was all designed by Aglaea, and it filled him with confidence. It was also extremely Okheman. He checked his bracers, his boots, the thigh strap, and even his collar, wanting to make the best (or worst) impression. If he was already going to be accepted as an Okheman first, let him at least look the part and be ready to play ambassador.

He grabbed his two books and tucked them inside his coat. His sword was still hidden away, waiting to be summoned. Phainon had been a little surprised Mydei hadn’t tried to confiscate it again, but in light of everything that had happened maybe it was a calculated choice to let him keep it.

“What do you think?” he asked Fig Stew. The chimera was still in his hammock from earlier. He sleepily yawned in response and curled back up to nap.

“That’s not reassuring.”

“There you are!” Leonnius called from the door. The runner stopped and looked Phainon up and down.

“Too much?”

“You’re gonna stand out.”

“So, I should take it off?”

“Nah, I think it’s very you.”

Was that good or bad? Leonnius didn’t give Phainon a chance to ask. He was already across the room and pulling Phainon along by the wrist. “The dock crew are going to finish unloading and start on repairs which means we finally get to relax.”

“Don’t you do that all the time on the foretop?”

“This is not like those times,” he insisted, defensive, “how did you even know?”

“Everyone knows. You snore.”

Phainon was a little surprised to see the same happy group from this morning waiting on deck for him. They all seemed eager to be off with bags slung over their shoulders and wearing minimal armor.

“I am so ready for a real bath,” Perdikkas was saying as they approached.

“Shouldn’t we show Phainon the city first?” Hephaestion asked.

“Dressed like that?” Mydei asked. The prince’s eyes were unabashedly looking Phainon up and down, drinking him in.

“’When they had admired everything to their heart’s content, they went to the bath room and washed themselves,’” Ptolemy quoted. Everyone was giving him a deadpan look. “I’m just saying that in books they explore first!”

“He’ll see plenty of the town on the way,” Perdikkas groaned, “I want to be clean.”

“I’d like to see,” Phainon said happily. It might be his only chance, he realized.

“I’ll show him,” Leonnius offered, “and we’ll meet you guys at the bath house after.”

“Don’t take too long. Perdikkas might have boiled away into nothing by the time you catch up if do,” cautioned Hephaestion.

“Would you like to come too, Mydei?” Phainon invited. A couple of the guys flashed each other looks.

“Mydeimos knows the most about the city,” Peucesta finally weighed in. He made it sound so casual but there was insistence there.

Immediately, Perdikkas added on, “he knows about the history of the old town too.”

Mydei narrowed his eyes at the others. “What are you lot on about?”

“Phainon does love history, don’t you, Phainon?” Ptolemy said with a huge grin.

“Then it’s decided,” Hephaestion announced firmly, before Mydei could get a word in edgewise, “Mydeimos and Phainon will take the scenic route and the rest of us will head straight to the bath house.”

“Wait I was gonna-“ Leonnius didn’t get to finish before Perdikkas and Ptolemy each grabbed one of his arms, lifted him off his feet and all five of them sprinted off the deck and down the dock, laughing and stumbling and very nearly taking out at least twice as many people as themselves along the way. At some point between the ship and the shore Peucesta had ended up on Hephaestion’s back, playing a rapid melody that could be heard all the way until they vanished from sight in the crowd.

Mydei and Phainon both had to take a second to process.

“Do you know what that was about?” Phainon asked.

Mydei shrugged and sighed, “I have known them my whole life and they never cease to surprise me. Come along.”

The city was vibrant. That was the best way Phainon could describe it. There was a life, an energy, that reminded him of Okhema but perhaps with a different flavor, different colors. While Okhema was frequently abuzz, it was more reserved, polite, the sort of noise that accompanies peddlers shouting in markets rather than the charged excitement of the Kremnoans. They were more open and honest in everything they did, even when it made them seem too rough or too forward, the people here embraced it. Just like on the ship, disputes were settled with brawls that ended amicably, men and women alike were more willing to express their feelings with physical contact and had little concern for personal space. Phainon saw people throwing their arms over each other’s shoulders, playful punches, rough-housing children, impromptu arm-wrestling matches, and people standing close to each other when they talked or gestured.

And all of it was framed by a beautiful island town. Mydei led him on a winding route through the old city. Buildings crafted from stone and painted with old murals depicting glorious combat and Strife, were carefully placed to create chokepoints and strategic advantages should the city ever come under attack. They paused frequently so Phainon could ask questions that Mydei efficiently answered to keep them moving. They talked about the history of the town in between greetings with excited townsfolk and Phainon was pleased and surprised by how much Mydei knew of his people’s wants, needs, and history despite what he knew of Mydei’s past spent away from these traditions.

He also was made more keenly aware of Mydei’s people. Proud as they were and as comfortable as they seemed to be, there was a sort of longing in the way they saluted their prince. They revered him but it never felt like they were seeing Mydei so much as they were seeing Mydeimos the Undying, Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos, future King. His presence was so radiant to them that Phainon was thankfully overlooked or spared little more than a wary glance. All it took was Mydei to wave them away from him and they gladly turned their attention back to him, to their hope, avoiding any conflicts and giving Phainon a chance to perceive him in this new light.

To his credit, Mydei took everything in stride, he was polite and loving towards his people, but always from the pedestal they put him upon. As Phainon watched Mydei carefully take the hand of an elderly man in both of his gauntleted hands with reverence, he realized that the prince was trying very hard to step off that figurative raised platform, to meet them at the same level, to be one of them. But no one aside from his crew ever gave him the chance. That same old man bowed his head and knees to be lower than Mydei and after a brief exchange they were again walking and talking about the murals as though Phainon weren’t catching glimpses of the depths of Mydei’s soul.

He understood now why Mydei was so eager to captain a ship than lead his people directly. For as much as he cared for them, there was also a detachment, as though his heart already belonged elsewhere, but chose to return for a time out of dutiful love.

When they finally got to the bathhouse, Mydei’s demeanor changed. It was so subtle that Phainon almost missed it, but the second he heard his crew laughing loudly enough to be heard from the street, Mydei softened at the edges. The prince that his people wanted was happily put back inside the box and Mydei was able to just be himself again.

“You should avoid the bath we will be in,” Mydei cautioned as they entered.

“Why is that?” Phainon puzzled.

“It will be too hot for you.”

Phainon felt the twitch in his eye. “You don’t think I can handle it?”

“I know you can’t handle it. Did you not see the forges next door? This bath is resting on a natural hot spring but some of the pools still use the boiling water from our forges.”

That sounded awful. Phainon squinted at Mydei’s back as the prince led the way to the changing rooms. This part at least reminded Phainon of Okhema. While it wasn’t as ornate, bath houses tended to follow the same basic layout. There were places to rest, cubbies to store one’s clothing, stacks of folded towels, soaps, oils, the only thing Phainon couldn’t find was…

“Do you not have chitons for bathing?” he asked, turning to Mydei.

Mydei who was already very naked and tucking his clothing and boots into a larger storage space. Phainon’s cheeks and ears turned pink as he gave Mydei a once over before Phainon realized what he was doing and looked away entirely. Huh, those tattoos went a lot farther than he had previously speculated.

“No… are you shy, Deliverer?” Mydei jabbed. He had twisted enough to smirk over his shoulder at Phainon, eyes glittering.

Phainon was a soldier. There was no such thing as privacy in the barracks, and he had been to public bathhouses before. Nudity was not a big deal unless someone went out of their way to make it a big deal. That said, Okhema still expected some measure of modesty outside of smaller, private baths. He had simply expected the same.

“No,” he said a little too quickly.

Mydei laughed and walked up to Phainon, locking eyes with him and holding them there with his gaze. He reached around Phainon while the Okheman tried to remember to breathe, to grab a towel from the stack behind him. Staying far too close, leaving no space for Kephale between them, Mydei slowly wrapped the short towel around his waist, never once breaking eye contact.

“Take a minute if you need it, Deliverer,” he teased and then he was gone.

Phainon had no idea how long he was standing there short-circuiting. It was probably only a few seconds, but it felt like a full quint. He took a deep breath. Really, nudity was nothing, there were men coming and going around him and only about half were wearing towels and Phainon wasn’t in the least effected.

But something about Mydei.

Maybe it was the way he had leaned in with that simmer in his eyes, like the gold of them was melting. Maybe it was the way he flexed when he turned to look over his shoulder at Phainon. There was that smirk curling his lips like Mydei knew exactly what he was doing. Or the flashing glow of those tattoos that went all the way down his-

Phainon slapped both his cheeks hard, hard enough to leave red handprints if the heat of the bath and his own embarrassment weren’t already making him feel like a tomato. He was way too hot standing in the spillover steam of the baths, fully dressed, after that.

He shook his head and took his clothes off, feeling a little paranoid as he did, but every time he glanced at others changing, they weren’t looking at him, everyone was too focused on getting clean and getting home.

Phainon tucked his neatly folded clothing away and reached for a towel. He was halfway done wrapping it around his waist when he remembered Mydei’s jab about being shy and felt that spirit of competition curling in his belly. After taking the time to calm down while he undressed, Phainon didn’t really have anything to hide…

He very happily strode to the baths with that very towel draped around the back of his neck instead.

It was not hard to find his friends. All six of them were in the back of the spacious room sitting around and inside a square-shaped pool. Steam rose in thick curls, weighing heavily in the air until disturbed by splashing, laughing, and rough housing. They saw Phainon walking towards them and a couple of them whistled.

“We thought you got lost!” Leonnius called.

“Starting to take bets on if you had slipped and died,” Hephaestion weighed in. Despite how dark his words were, they all laughed, enjoying the mood.

“Mydei ran away so quickly,” Phainon dramatically lamented as he stood behind the prince, “it took me some time to figure out where he went.”

Mydei turned around in the bath to retort but it was his turn to catch his breath as his eyes traveled upwards to where Phainon smirked down at him. Mydei may have been aware of how he looked and the effect he could have on people, but Phainon could also play that game. The prince’s lips parted just a little bit as his eyes traveled up and down.

Hephaestion came to the rescue, splashing them both with water with a firm slap across the surface. Mydei raised a hand and turned towards his first mate with a chuckle, but Phainon was far less dignified. The moment the boiling water splashed across his legs and feet, Phainon squealed like a small child, recoiling with a leap from where he had been scalded until he was a safe distance away.

The others blinked at him for a long heartbeat and then all the Kremnoans were laughing so hard their roar could no doubt be heard from the ship all the way down at the dock.

“It’s his soft Okheman skin!” Perdikkas teased.

Hephaestion wheezed around tears, “I have never heard that sound from a grown man before!”

Ptolemy slapped them both. “Cut him some slack, what did we expect from the finest of the Okheman Navy!”

Even Mydei was cracking up at Phainon’s bruised pride.

He knew the teasing was all good fun, but it still gave him pause as he tip-toed back to the water, itching to prove them wrong, too competitive to listen to his body screaming for him to wait, that no one wanted boiled Okheman for dinner, least of all the Okheman!

“Deliverer, don’t force yourself,” Mydei said, a little more serious despite the chuckle in his voice and that was all Phainon needed to hear to firmly step into the bath.

It was absolutely the hottest thing he had felt in his life. This was what stew felt like. He was soup. This was soup. This was soup that needed to sit for twenty minutes to be safe to eat, that was what it was. But he managed to take a very painful seat in the bath, and everyone happily cheered for him, even if it felt a little condescending.

They were not in there long before Peucesta complained about wanting something cooler. Phainon suspected it was for his sake, but he was grateful for the excuse to y’know, live. Even so, he fought the urge to spring out of the water, waiting not so patiently until he was the last one out as though he had something to prove and then he was hurrying to the cold bath. The others laughed at him but followed Phainon all the same, trying different baths, different temperatures, until finally everyone felt clean, relaxed, and smelled nicely of soaps.

Phainon worked a floral smelling oil through his hair as everyone changed. He was already back in his pants and undershirt, checking himself in the mirror.

“You’re plenty pretty, Phainon,” Leonnius reassured him, “let someone else use the mirror.”

“’And he looked like a god as he came from the bath,’” Ptolemy agreed in quotes.

“I don’t know about all that, Ptolemy,” Phainon laughed.

“Relax, he’s said that about Mydei before too,” Hephaestion teased, and it was Mydei’s turn to blush scarlet. He had dried and dressed quickly but was taking his time with his hair like Phainon was, gently rubbing in a nice, sweet-smelling scent and braiding it carefully. For all their gruff, they took cleanliness very seriously when they had the opportunity to do so.

Clean, content, and feeling refreshed, Phainon followed them out of the bath house. They looped him in close, fussing with his hair, putting their arms around him, letting Mydei take up the rear to follow the pack in the dimming evening light. And as they walked, they pointed out landmarks and taught him more Kremnoan phrases while Peucesta played his lyre in the lead like an enchanted piper.

“Home sweet home!” Leonnius announced when they finally reached a building on the hill, nestled amongst other dwellings. It was an older home, had been there for a long time, sporting bronze fixtures and big stone pillars. Not quite the size of a palace but built for the general or dignitary that was expected to lead the city. Mydei’s home, Phainon realized.

“Wait do you all…?”

They nodded enthusiastically.

“There is too much space for any one man,” Mydei explained, “why would I not share it with people I trust?”

Leonnius took his wrist and dragged him inside, showing Phainon all the hallways but getting distracted when they got to a large, open receiving room connected to the balcony. Piles of cushions were shoved in two different corners. There were folded up screens set aside against a bookshelf along one wall. A big desk sat empty, pushed out of the way against the opposing wall. There were people there Phainon didn’t recognize, setting up food on a big, oval table surrounded by chairs and a pair of klines.

“Just in time,” Peucesta noted gratefully, and the music stopped so he could sit.

The others poured in behind them, shoving Phainon along until he was sat in the middle of a kline with Mydei sitting beside him on his left. Without ceremony, the Kremnoans started passing around plates full of fruits, roasted vegetables, fresh cheeses, herbed meats on delicate skewers, warm, fluffy bread, and of course fresh juices and creamy milk.

Phainon curled his nose a little when Mydei added milk to his pomegranate juice but after asking to try it and getting to sample a sip from Mydei’s own chalice, he was equally convinced of the merit of something that would seem otherwise strange.

They laughed, they joked, they told simple stories, and Phainon felt whole, so he was surprised by the aching in his heart when he stood on the balcony after dinner, changed into sleepwear that Mydei had loaned him, listening to Leonnius snoring, the quiet turn of pages while Ptolemy read, and the soft breath of the ocean breeze. The sky was dark, out of range of the Dawn Device he could see stars in the night sky, they twinkled as a reminder of days long past, and of how far away he was from his own home. A home he desperately wanted to share with the people resting quietly behind him.

This felt so safe. He felt so happy here with these men that he considered friends. Even felt privileged to have seen Mydei without his public-facing mask, to be able to jest with them, be vulnerable around them.

Phainon wanted so badly to introduce them to his family, to show them his city as they had done for him. He could imagine Ptolemy and Professor Anaxa arguing about a tome they had both studied while Perdikkas and Hyacine chattered about healing poultices. Leonnius might be able to stand a chance in a race against the triplets with those swift feet of his. Would Castorice love listening to Peucesta’s songs, wiling away the time in peace, humming along while she worked on her handicrafts? If anyone could smooth talk Cipher into parting with her goods for a fair price it would be Hephaestion.

What would Aglaea think of Mydei? Would she also catch her breath, appreciating his beauty, that quiet confidence, the way he cares about his people so much that he fights the destiny they want for him?

His heart twisted, feeling so far away. No matter how much he wanted to just magically fix things, build the perfect bridge between everyone, he was still a prisoner from that distant place.

And he was unbearably homesick.

Chapter End Notes
