chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei not putting a name to it yet but he is feeling something~

Chapter Notes

I keep telling myself the fluff is over and I focus on the plot now and then I think of something new and I can't help myself

They weren’t the usual nightmares, Mydei was used to those. Usually, the back of his mind would dredge up old memories of drowning, whispers from the Sea of Souls as he fought upriver again. No these were different because there was light this time.

It started very much the same, Mydei was drowning, but when he broke the surface of the water the dream changed, everything was bathed in red light, the glimmer of a gold sun breaking through smoke. He could feel Nikador’s battle cry rattling his bones, hear the titan’s voice in his head, beckoning to him between screams and when they fought it was with violence that cracked the world.

Mydei expected to be jolted awake when Nikador’s lance punctured his chest but there were hands on his back supporting him, pushing him forward, and when he turned to look over his shoulder: there was Phainon.

And in him was the courage to fight on.

Mydei woke up with Phainon’s name on the tip of his tongue, unspoken only because of the weight of sleep. Sunlight was pouring in from the balcony, barely missing his face but warming his chest and legs. He felt groggy and heavy, still flopped across the kline. Someone had covered him with a blanket which he promptly kicked off to spill onto the floor. It was well past Entry Hour and it was too hot to be covered.

With a soft groan he sat up and ran his fingers through his hair. Mydei was very rarely the last one awake, but… where was everyone?

He looked around the room, puzzled.

Where was Phainon?

Surely, the puppy was not dumb enough to go into town alone?

Mydei waited for that thought to comfort him and when it didn’t work, he was springing up off the kline and searching for his boots. Someone must’ve hidden them, determined to make him rest. Perdikkas did that sometimes when he felt like Mydei was overworking himself.

Instead, the prince hurried to the balcony, hoping to see one of his friends returning that he could call to but instead he found Phainon.

Not on the balcony of course, but down on the street. For the sake of space, Mydei’s home was surrounded by others, not nearly the same size, but what use did he have for an expansive property when he was barely even there? The people who lived around him were mostly families, older men and women of the Godshield Brigade that had been commanded to retired and settle down.

Phainon was playing with a ball in the middle of the wide path, surrounded by children.

Mydei couldn’t hear what they were saying from where he was on the balcony, but they were laughing and pointing at the ball in his hands that he was keeping above them, trying to balance it on one finger until two of the young boys jumped up and grabbed his arm, knocking the ball loose and then everyone, even Phainon, were chasing it. If Phainon slipped and fell (something he must’ve been doing on purpose) they tackled him while he laughed. Whenever he managed to steal the ball back, the kids teamed up to try and recover it. Anytime Phainon shouted at them in play, they laughed and had to stop to teach him how to say the Kremnoan words right while they pulled on his cape and coat tails.

It was shockingly domestic and Mydei found himself watching, no longer out of concern but out of curious amusement. Phainon getting along with kids shouldn’t have been a surprise considering he was just like them at heart, but it wasn’t something Mydei had considered until he saw it himself. Most of what they knew about Phainon was from embellished stories, he had been surprisingly reserved about himself on the ship, asking questions more than offering answers. Was Phainon so good with kids because he had his own?

Mydei’s gaze sharpened at the thought, remembering what Phainon had said yesterday about not looking for a woman. Did he already have one? Was that why Phainon was so eager to return home to Okhema? Mydei could have sworn that Phainon was interested in men, the way Mydei had caught him studying his body at the bath. If he did have a family waiting for him, it would make sense to keep it a secret, to protect them from people he only thought of as pirates.

For some reason it really bothered Mydei to consider that Phainon may have a wife and child waiting for him back in Okhema. A knot twisted in his stomach, clawing through his insides towards his heart, but Mydei shoved it back down with practiced force. He frowned as he watched them now, deciding his time was better spent away from the self-indulgent speculation that he despised so much.

He sighed and leaned away from the rail but turned back when something caught his eye. Left on the wide stone railing were a pair of books, nearly identical.

Mydei recognized them almost immediately. He reached out to scoop up the book on top. It was his favorite tale, printed in Kremnoan, a rare find stolen from Queen Gorgo’s personal collection when Krateros fled Eurypon. Sure enough, when Mydei flipped through the pages he could see his own scribbles in the margins, marking his favorite parts. His handwriting was instantly recognizable because it was barely legible; something Ptolemy had long mocked him for.

The book told the story of a warrior returning from a long war. Mnestia had spared him in combat because his wife had prayed to her for his safe return, but as the hero traveled home, he offended Strife by mistake. Thus, he was trapped, doomed to wander the world to atone until his family sought him out to return in glory together, saving him. Ptolemy quoted the book constantly, knowing that Mydei enjoyed it.

He jumped ahead to his favorite part, when the hero is finally found by his family. As a kid, Mydei resonated the most with that scene. It reminded him of the moment he had been pulled out of the sea. The detachment certainly weren’t his children, but they were his family, and the joy he had felt when the hero was found filled him with such familiar love that Mydei had underlined and labeled the passage multiple times. He paused over the words. Underneath his own scribbles were neat letters, elegant handwriting in Okheman Common.

‘This is my favorite part too.’

Mydei blinked. Maybe Phainon’s Kremnoan was better than they realized, but more impressive was how Phainon had been able to interpret Mydei’s atrocious handwriting.

He looked back over at Phainon, still having the time of his life playing with the kids. One of them had brought snacks, a melon that a parent must’ve cut into manageable slices. They were all taking turns trying to force feed the Deliverer while he sat on the ground, desperately trying to please the hoard despite his full mouth and the juice running down his chin.

Mydei turned back to the book. His favorite part too… Drastically different backgrounds, different cultures, and yet the human experience of wanting to be found by family, connected them. It was endearing.

And then Mydei remembered Phainon had a family in Okhema, and he closed the book with a pained, door-closing sigh and set it right back where he found it.

“Oh good, you’re awake,” Hephaestion said. The first mate tossed him a pomegranate from all the way across the room and Mydei had to step forward to catch it. It had already been cut so it was easy for Mydei to pull open the rind to start snacking while his best friend spread a couple of maps out across his desk.

“Has Phainon ever mentioned a wife?”

The desk screeched as it was pushed across the stone floor when Hephaestion tripped and stumbled into it. With a very careful, measured voice, Hephaestion over-enunciated, “What brought this up, Mydeimos?”

Mydei watched Hephaestion struggle to fix the desk, utterly unbothered by the reaction. “He had asked me about women on the deck yesterday and mentioned a family in Okhema when we were discussing his status as a prisoner of war. Do you think he has fathered any children?”

“I think that’s the kind of speculation you abhor, and you should ask him directly.”

That wasn’t going to happen. It was such a non-issue that didn’t change anything or directly affect anyone in the Detachment. Mydei was determined to see Phainon home regardless, so it didn’t matter.

Mydei responded with a non-committal hum.

“I have the reports from the dock crew,” his first mate said instead with a cough. He slapped a bunch of folded up papers onto the desk. “As well as the reports from the local scouts.” More folded papers landed with a whap! “And I have the inventory report from Ptolemy.”

“You have all been busy this morning.”

“Yeah, well, we had stuff to get done before we could leave, and you and Phainon needed the sleep.”

Mydei raised an eyebrow. “He slept in too?”

“Yeah, but I saw him playing outside on my way back. Leonnius was a little worried he’d wander into town if we left before he awoke.”

“I thought the same.”

“I know we joke about him being a dog, but he’s incredible, Mydei,” Hephaestion said with a smile, “we’d be very lucky if he joined the crew.”

The prince waved a hand dismissively, but he didn’t comment. Getting Phainon home in a way that didn’t jeopardize his people was the priority, nothing else mattered regarding the Deliverer of Okhema. He brought his breakfast over to the maps so he could look.

The situation was bleak.

The Black Tide claimed territory two different ways. The first was the horror that Phainon had experienced in his youth, the revulsion that claimed Castrum Kremnos, when the wave itself spreads like smoke or ink in the water. That’s the wave that they had felt in the storm, when the ocean turns black and corrupts ships that sail through it, turning whole crews into monstrous minions. When that wave hits land, it spreads like a mist, engulfing islands and turning their residents to those same monsters. At least when islands are taken, the monsters are generally landlocked, the mist retreats, and the monsters are left behind to hold the new territory.

The second way was via monster and bloodshed. Those roaming corrupted ships and monsters could persist away from the Tide itself, acting as any other army, expanding the Tide’s reach by conquest. Weak people, soft people, could be turned clashing with Black Tide creatures, but warriors like those in the detachment were safe from transformation during those clashes.

In their sailing, the Chryseus Leo had seen the aftermath of battles with the Black Tide monsters. They were brutal and bloody warzones, with no captives and no survivors. Sometimes it was hard to tell which method was worse. Written in blood or ash, it was all the same story of suffering.

The map had been updated by the scouts. They used multi-colored dots and lines to indicate sightings, skirmishes, and other notable encounters with the Tide and other city-states. For now, the rest of the world still didn’t know about them hiding here on this island, and Mydei was fine with that. When Phainon had told them that Castrum Kremnos’ recent history was all but unknown to Okhema, Mydei had been relieved. The last thing they needed was a war on two sides.

The Black Tide had expanded to the isle north of them, taking it over entirely. If the Tide continued to push from that direction, their island would fall within a month, finishing what it started in Castrum Kremnos.

The roaming monsters hadn’t found the island yet. For all their lack of humanity, they still harbored some leftover intelligence, enough to sail and to choose targets according to their master. One of the Detachment’s self-imposed tasks was hunting down these ships, killing the monsters, and burning the vessels to push back the arm of the Tide. Another task was to be, as Phainon was so fond of calling them, pirates. They were discouraging trading vessels from routes that crossed into Black Tide waters by assaulting and robbing them, convincing those routes to change out of necessity.

Mydei followed the line of one of those routes with his finger. As of the storm, that route was now in danger, anyone traveling that line would be turned and then they’d have more enemies to deal with.

He sighed.

“It gets worse,” Hephaestion told him, “we don’t have the ore to repair or make weapons. The forges are reusing what we can but…”

“It won’t be enough,” Mydei finished.

He started looking over the map, combing through it with a practiced eye, eventually resting his finger on an island to the northwest. “This fort.”

It was an Okheman fort. It was also the closest fort to the Black Tide line, in immediate danger. Mydei could go anywhere as a Chrysos Heir. He had that protection from the Tide due to his golden blood, but he was not going to bring his men into a place that may be underwater with the Tide. This fort was next, but there was still time. “They’ll have an armory.”

“It’s Okheman…”

“It’s a military outpost far away from Okhema, soldiers not civilians.”

“You’re the one that said we aren’t at war with Okhema anymore…”

Mydei pulled his finger back and sighed yet again, this time softly through his nose. He was gripping that pomegranate way too hard. Hephaestion was right but they didn’t have a lot of choice. It would take too long to get to any of the other outposts to restock.

“All the more reason to go,” Mydei said, “the Tide will take that fort within the week. If we get to it, not only will we be able to take the supplies, but we may be able to save the men by chasing them to safety.”

“Never beating the pirate allegations,” Hephaestion sighed.

“Good.”

They had done this a lot. It didn’t bear repeating out loud. Whenever they did don the pirate persona, it was in its entirety. They covered the lion figurehead, changed their flag, wore ragged clothing over their armor, Mydei even had a horrible tricorn hat that at least distracted their enemies enough to forget any distinguishing features. Because at the end of the day, it was better for them to see pirates than Kremnoans. Pirates were isolated trouble, Kremnoans might encourage Okhema to mobilize against their ancient enemy. It was safer for his people if Mydei played the part of a brigand.

“And after the fort?” Hephaestion asked.

Mydei leaned over and pulled out drawers in succession until he found an inkwell and his pen. He put his mostly abandoned snack down so he could open the little jar of ink and wet the end of the pen with his tongue. Then he delicately marked a line in dashes.

“The fort and the trade route.”

“Yes,” Mydei confirmed, “we will take the north passage to travel the edge of the Black Tide. Once we have taken the fort and claimed their armory, we will chase the Okhemans back to the trade route and then follow it back here.” He followed the line with the back of the pen as he spoke.

“Taking out any ships we find along the way.” Hephaestion nodded, “short trip.”

“Tell Ptolemy to plan for three weeks.”

“Mydeimos, this is barely a two-week trip. We should save space for any cargo we take.”

Mydei shook his head. “Plan for the worst, Hephaestion.”

-

Phainon never wanted melon again. He had no idea what kind of melon it was, but he had eaten so much of it at the hands of a gaggle of children that he was sure that he was going to be sweating sugar for a week. Kremnoan were relentless at any age, and it was hard to say no when they weaponized those huge, adorable eyes, and physically shoved sweet treats into his mouth before he could squeak out any words.

Eventually, the herd thinned, called away to do chores or training by their parents. Not every parent was happy to discover that their children were playing with an Okheman and Phainon had to scurry away from sharp insults and suspiciously accurate stones thrown at his head. He hadn’t expected the first one and it had slammed into the space just behind his ear. It had hit hard enough for him to take the warning seriously, but not enough to bleed. The rest he was able to dodge but it was hard to explain the hostility to the kids, so he opted for a lame excuse about his own parents calling him and removed himself to head back inside.

“Oh Phainon,” Hephaestion greeted, “done entertaining the whelps?”

“Ah, yeah, it seems their parents weren’t pleased with an adult stranger eating their snacks,” he laughed softly to himself, “it sounds worse when I say it out loud. Were you here to see Mydei? He was still sleeping last I checked.”

“The prince is awake,” Hephaestion confirmed with a grin, “we were just talking strategy.”

“Anything I should know about?”

“Maybe not this, Phainon.”

Phainon’s smile wavered only a little. If Hephaestion noticed he didn’t react. “I understand.”

“We will be leaving this evening with the tide, though. Best be back on the ship before then.”

“I will… Is there anything I can do to help until then?”

The Kremnoan tilted his head, a little puzzled with the request. “You know this is a break, right?”

“Heh, I know, it’s just hard to sit still when there’s so much to do!”

“The dock crew are working on the last repairs right now,” Hephaestion thought aloud, his voice dropped nearly to a mumble like he was working through the list for his own benefit, not Phainon’s. “There are still a lot of barnacles to scrape off the hull, if you really want to do that… oh, you said once that you dreamed of training at Castrum Kremnos as a child. The city may be lost for now, but the old masters are still here.”

Phainon brightened at that prospect. “Would they be willing to train with an Okheman?”

“I’m sure with your obnoxious tenacity you could win them over,” he laughed, “I’ll take you there myself, put in a good word.”

“I would appreciate that. Let me get my things, just in case I don’t get a chance to return here before we leave.” Phainon hurried down the hall but paused when Hephaestion called his name.

The Kremnoan’s eyebrows were pinched, mulling over his words carefully before he asked, “Phainon, are you married?”

The question caught him so off guard that Phainon almost fell over when he tilted his head to a full 45 degrees. “No? Why?”

“Maybe I have a crush on you,” Hephaestion teased.

“Aw, do you really?”

“Fuck no, go get your stuff before I leave you here.”

Phainon laughed and jogged through the house to get his books, pleased to find them exactly where he left them.

-

Mydei trusted Empousa, really, he did, but it was routine for him to personally check the supplies that were restocking his kitchen on the Chryseus Leo. It wasn’t that he needed a lot of ingredients, he just needed the right ones. This was when he started formulating recipes in his head and deciding if he needed to request anything last minute to round out the menu. It was very important to Mydei that everything his men ate was nutritious first and foremost, but a little variety and good tasting food boosted morale better than any other idea he had tried in the past.

He was reviewing their supply when the commotion started. Like a tsunami the disaster began with silence, an absence of people. It was that silence that made him curiously leave the galley to search the empty deck. The dock below was barely manned by a skeleton crew despite the pending voyage. Not a single crewmate was trying to sneak something extra on board. No one was fussing over the barrels still left on deck that needed to be secured. Honestly the only reminder that he wasn’t completely alone was the soft shuck, shuck of someone scraping off the rest of the barnacles from the hull.

This was the only reasonable time to do it. As the tide retreated, the ship settled onto stilts placed on the beach, keeping her from becoming stranded in the sand and resting upright. It also allowed access to her belly which is how they quickly replaced the damaged outer layer of the hull and removed aquatic pests.

Mydei puzzled over the quiet, searching the shore, but even the shoreline was devoid of people. The city could’ve been empty for all he knew. That’s when he heard the roar on the breeze, the collective shouting of many, many people. A little switch went off in the back of his mind, putting Mydei into combat mode, alert, ready for anything.

“Mydeimos!” Leonnius yelled. The runner came flying around the wall, sprinting towards the ship. He was panting, sweat dripped down his nose and splashed onto the dock when he paused to catch his breath. “Mydei!”

He leaned over the railing to look at Leonnius with a serious expression.

“You need to come quick!” he said, worried, “it’s Phainon!”

Mydei didn’t even use the ramp. He vaulted over the railing and hit the dock in a runner’s stance, already springing after Leonnius in a sprint. They rushed through the empty streets, panic and bile rising in Mydei’s throat. He pushed it back down, readying his crystals, prepared for anything as the sounds got louder.

The sounds of gathered people shouting and the noise of combat were not very different, the energy was very similar, and the smell of sweat was about the same. Mydei shoved through the crowd. Many of them parted willingly given enough time to recognize that it was him brushing against their shoulders, but he was in a hurry and most stumbled on contact.

They shoved through narrow, packed alleys until Leonnius and Mydei finally burst into the training grounds. Set up to emulate the coliseum of Castrum Kremnos in miniature, there was plenty of seating surrounding the hard packed dirt of the arena. All the seating was packed, overflowing to where people were watching from the tops of neighboring buildings and children were perched on their parents’ shoulders to conserve space. Every eye was watching two men circle each other.

Leonnius pushed further, closer to the edge of the arena with Mydei pressed in tightly behind him, until they finally could breathe. It was still packed tight but along the rail they could at least see what was happening.

Phainon was pacing, shirtless, wearing only that damn collar and his bracers above his belt. His hair stuck to the back of his neck with sweat and there were bruises forming across his ribs, right on top of the old yellow ones from the storm. A Kremnoan round shield was strapped to his left arm and he held a spear tightly in his right hand. Across from him was Herklas, one of the warriors that Mydei had tasked with defending the island, a seasoned warrior with a healthy bloodlust. The Kremnoan was dressed similarly but wearing a helmet where Phainon had chosen to go without. He was hitting his shield with the spear to draw Phainon’s attention before lunging and the battle continued in earnest while the crowd roared their approval.

On the sidelines, six other Kremnoans were waiting on a bench. One of them he recognized as Daidalos, former chief engineer of the Kremnos Arena turned General and Trainer. The others were warriors from the island. Three of them were tending to wounds or laying on the ground, already defeated, presumably by Phainon.

“Why is he shirtless again?” Mydei wondered aloud.

“You, of all people, did not seriously ask that,” Leonnius countered.

Mydei ducked under the railing, fully intending to stop the fight, to get to the bottom of this, when he noticed gold flashing in the corner of his eye and shot a glance in that direction. Perdikkas, Peucesta, and Ptolemy were working the crowd, taking gold coins and gathering them into a helmet.

His frown deepened and he stalked along the railing towards them while Leonnius followed.

“Round four!” Ptolemy called while Peucesta played an exciting chime on his lyre, barely even audible over the cheering and shouting.

“He IS just an Okheman,” Perdikkas was telling a man in the front row, “you really think he’d get lucky four times in a row? And against Herklas? It’s a safe bet that this is where the Okheman meets his maker.”

Gold coins changed hands.

“Okhemans train their bodies to be pretty more than strong,” Ptolemy was arguing with a lady a little farther down. “You can see it in his eyes and hair, he might have muscles, but does he really know how to use them?”

Yet more gold changed hands.

Behind them in the arena, Phainon and Herklas clashed again. Phainon’s spear glanced off the shield and he narrowly avoided the bite of a spear across his belly. Phainon slid under the shield this time, swinging the butt of his spear around to smash it against the back of Herklas’ head. The bigger guy stumbled but still twisted, lashing out to smash his shield against Phainon’s face. Golden blood streamed from his nose and Phainon had to retreat to brush it away with his thumb. It still flowed and he lapped at it absentmindedly with his tongue across his grin while those sunny eyes tracked his opponent.

Mydei stomped up behind Perdikkas who was still happily cheering to the crowd. Peucesta noticed the prince first, grabbing his lyre with an ugly twang to stop the strings from vibrating further while he wide-eyed flinched away.

“What?” Perdikkas asked and then he turned around.

Mydei must’ve looked like Nikador come to take them the way Perdikkas recoiled and hid the jingling helmet behind his back. Ptolemy slowly leaned forward, presumably to take it from him.

“Mydeimos! My prince! Are you not taking inventory?”

“What the hell is going on?”

“Mydei, it is not as it seems,” Ptolemy insisted over Perdikkas’ shoulder while Peucesta nodded furiously.

“It seems you are exploiting Phainon.”

All three of them started protesting at once, a combination of “we would never!” and “it was his idea!” and “it just kind of happened!” while they pointed fingers in every direction so Mydei wouldn’t noticed the helmet of coins being slowly tucked behind Peucesta’s boots. Of course he noticed. They were not subtle.

“Is this a hustle?” Mydei growled and the protests continued, impossible to follow.

“Mydei!”

Any anger immediately unraveled at the sound of that cheerful voice. Phainon had run over to them all smiles, blood still dripping from his nose, making a mess of his face while he licked his lips. Behind him Herklas was being dragged to the sidelines, barely conscious and groaning.

“Why are you here? Perdikkas said you usually check the ship inventory.”

Phainon was completely oblivious to the noise around them. Too excited to see Mydei. All of that adrenaline from the fight must’ve still been singing in his veins with the energy he had bouncing around, spear still in hand.

It made Mydei happier than he realized that this puppy had eyes only for him. His heart did a little confusing dance and then Mydei felt jealous. There were others fighting with Phainon? Having a good time about it? This wasn’t a more serious affair?

“Are you fighting for fun?” Mydei asked, incredulously.

“Daidalos thought it would be useful for me to spar to apply the techniques he was teaching me and Hephaestion had to go. I guess a few different people thought it sounded fun and agreed to help!” Phainon laughed. He was smiling so wide it was burning Mydei’s eyes in the best possible way.

He also knew that helping probably wasn’t the right word. This may have always been a fun and silly thing for Phainon, but Mydei was damn sure that it didn’t start fun for any Kremnoans that volunteered for a chance to stab an Okheman captive on home turf.

That said… it certainly took a ‘fun’ turn if the crowd was anything to go by. Mydei hadn’t seen this much life on the island in a very long time. There were still some upset people. He could hear curses thrown Phainon’s way, but the man was undaunted, just happy to be there; overjoyed with the prospect of learning something new and getting the opportunity to apply it.

“Mydei, would you like to spar with me?” Phainon invited and Mydei’s face cracked. His eyes widened, his lips parted, and it took him a while to find his composure.

He cleared his throat, coughing into a closed fist, and looked down, “Deliverer, this is not the best place for our rematch…”

“Then it doesn’t count.”

His golden eyes darted up again, to that warm and welcome smile.

Phainon repeated, “Then it won’t count. What do you say, Mydei? Show me how to use a spear properly.”

Mydei’s lips curled up into a smile and he shook his head with a wave of his hand. “HKS, I have been using a spear since I was a child.”

“I know,” Phainon teased, “we met with your spear under my chin, remember? It won’t happen again.”

“…very well, I’ll show you a few things, but tend to your nose first,” he said pointing to Phainon’s bloody face, “while I tend to some business of my own.”

Phainon smiled and trotted over to his trainer, who gave him a hearty slap on his back and handed him a cloth. They talked amicably, too far away for Mydei to hear but it still made him happy to see Phainon getting along with more Kremnoans. This man was single-handedly building a bridge between himself and these people who struggled to see past his affiliation.

If he wasn’t already Okhema’s Deliverer, he could almost be for the Kremnoans…

Mydei shook his head to chase away that hope and focused instead on retrieving those coins, but while the three of his men were still standing there feigning innocence, the helmet behind Peucesta’s boots had disappeared. He pushed past them to follow the tracks in the dust with his eyes, tracking where the helmet had been dragged and barely saw the heavy thing, laden with riches, disappearing around the corner in a flurry of fluffy orange and white fur.

They really were never going to beat the pirate allegations.

With a sigh, he turned on the trio again. “Does he know?”

They all shook their heads.

“The hustle is over,” Mydei ordered.

“Of course!” Perdikkas agreed with a not so innocent smile.

“Mydeimos!” Phainon called and the prince turned to see that dazzling smile again, pointing a spear his way, sun shining on his shield. “Will you keep me waiting, your Highness?” There was a laugh in the way he tossed his challenge, and Mydei grinned back, wide and unrestrained.

“You’re going to wish I had!” he hurled back.

“Then show me!”

-

Phainon missed watching the launch. Not that he hadn’t seen ships launch before, it was just fun to feel the breeze in his hair and watch the sails unfurl. It was usually an all-hands-on deck kind of moment, but Perdikkas had dragged him to the infirmary immediately upon boarding, leaving Mydei to take his things to his drawer.

The doctor was slapping salve on Phainon’s bruises with a big grin on his face.

“It’s not that funny,” Phainon whined, “it wasn’t even kind of fair.”

“You did last longer than we all thought you would,” Perdikkas tried to reassure him while he wrapped Phainon’s outstretched arm.

“If I was using my sword…” he grumbled under his breath.

The door creaked as it opened and in strode the proudest chimera. Fig Stew jumped up onto the bed where Phainon was sitting, put his front paws on Phainon’s thigh, and very carefully dropped a single gold coin into his lap.

Perdikkas choked on his own spit laughing while Phainon picked it up and bounced it in his palm.

“What’s this?” he asked suspiciously.

“It’s your cut,” Perdikkas wheezed.

Fig Stew gave Phainon a proud, tiny, “rawr!” and then bounded away.

chapters.title: Chapter 14: Crossroad
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

No new tags but bear in mind the archive warning "graphic depictions of violence" for this one.

I like to think Mydei can act when he wants to as long as he has a good reason

Chapter Notes

This one got away from me a bit. I have a sticky note on my monitor that says "keep it simple, stupid" and never read it when it matters.

Mydei liked to think they did a pretty good job of keeping Phainon in the dark. They were careful to only talk strategy when he wasn’t around, they avoided all his questions, kept him occupied with tasks, but Phainon wasn’t stupid. He was graciously looking the other way. Mydei could see it in the tight press of his lips when he was told this information wasn’t for him. He could see it when Phainon’s smile wavered as they grew quiet in his presence.

But Phainon didn’t push the topic. He held his tongue every time he caught small groups of men meeting with their unit leads in the galley to talk about the plan. He looked away when he saw them reviewing the armory, gearing the men despite no visible threat on the horizon. Phainon even hid himself in their room when they pulled the longboat up onto the deck to start packing it for the operation.

It was by Phainon’s own desire that Mydei had given the order to exclude him. Piracy was something Phainon wanted no part of, and the captain was determined to respect that request.

By the fourth day, it became impossible to keep Phainon completely out of the loop. They had beaten the Black Tide to the island, approaching from the far side just as the thief star dashed across the evening sky, burning red, and weighed anchor out of sight of the fort. With the operation beginning, it was no longer feasible to work around Phainon without locking him away entirely and Mydei wanted to trust him enough to not resort to that.

They had taken forts like this before. Most of them followed similar layouts but Mydei was always careful to have many layers of planning and protection, and good strategies required intelligence. War wasn’t just hack and slash like common folk believed. All five of Mydei’s closest friends commanded their own units during operations such as these, taking a handful of men to fulfill specific tasks best suited to their talents.

Leonnius was their best scout. Supported by his own hand-picked runners, they would go ahead first, taking a few hours to gather what information they could, and then they’d return to report and last-minute adjustments, if any, would be made.

Mydei saw them off, personally helping lower the ship’s longboat into the water with the four of them tucked inside. Each runner was wearing a small pack of supplies, including the means to communicate with the ship from the shore.

That’s when Phainon couldn’t take it anymore.

“Mydeimos,” he demanded, after Leonnius had departed. He cornered Mydei on the deck, stopping him by the rail where the prince was waiting to spot a signal in the dark with his arms crossed.

“I told you-“

“I know what you told me and that’s not good enough anymore.”

Mydei drummed his fingers on his forearms. “Deliverer, you don’t want to know.”

“Yes. I do.”

“Piracy,” he answered flippantly.

“I understand that. What specifically are you doing here? I know this island; I restocked here when I was hunting you.”

“Then you already know why we have come.”

Phainon was fuming, his voice strained. “I thought you said we weren’t at war with Okhema anymore.”

“We?” Mydei countered and Phainon’s face fell.

“As long as I’m on this ship, I’m one of you, we agreed.”

Mydei turned on him. “Are you offering to raise your sword against your own people? Steal from them?”

Phainon looked away with an annoyed tsk.

“Go to bed, Phainon. We will be moving on by morning.”

For a long second, Mydei thought Phainon would argue with him, maybe try to stop them entirely. In the dim light of the evening his defiant eyes glittered darker, somehow a richer blue, but he didn’t say anything else. Phainon scoffed to himself and stomped away with his shoulders tight and his footfalls heavy enough to speak to his displeasure.

It took two quints for Leonnius to respond. A fire lit on shore, a pinprick of orange glow that flashed green after a moment. Mydei smiled as the fire in his belly roared in response. He turned and shouted to the crew to make ready.

Slapping on disguises was something so practiced that by the time Leonnius and his scouts rowed back to the ship with their report, the Chryseus Leo was a different ship. The red flag emblazoned with the gold symbol of Strife had been replaced with a solid black square, the lions at the bow had been covered in a massive black sheet, and everyone had dressed the part. They were wearing dirty leather coats, using swords and spears without shields, and tying their hair back with cloth and worn hats. They used animal fat and ash to dirty their clothing and faces, hiding any identifying markers.

Leonnius climbed up the side of the ship first, followed by two scouts. The runners peeled off to brief Hephaestion and Krateros, while Leonnius followed Mydei to the captain’s quarters. Mydei was undressing down to his pants as he went.

“It is as we thought. They have a dock for merchant vessels waiting for inspection and another hidden in a cove on the other side of the island near where we are now,” Leonnius was telling him, “Only two triremes, both belonging to the fort, one is waiting in the cove, the other is at their public facing dock.”

Phainon stood up from his chair when they entered but Mydei physically pushed him back down as he strode past, motioning for his runner to continue with the other hand.

“The wall is tall but thin and there is a locked wooden gate on the side, reachable via island path.”

Mydei pulled open drawers and cabinets, throwing articles of clothing on as he went, moving swiftly with no wasted energy. Black leather boots replaced his golden armor, light gloves instead of gauntlets, rather than going bare-chested as he preferred, he pulled on a dirty, fraying tunic with an old cord around the waist for a belt. Over the top of that was a knee-length heavy leather coat, dark and covered in patches from prior battles. He strapped a sword around his waist by a thick belt that kept his coat from flapping and ran ashes from an amphora through his hair to darken it. Another dash of ash brushed under his eye with a thumb covered the red mark under his eye.

And the whole time Phainon watched with a deep, disapproving frown.

“No matter what you hear or feel, you will stay here,” Mydei instructed, commanding and firm. He studied Phainon for any sign of rebellion while he pressed his tricorn hat to his head, and finding none, he left.

“Leonnius, your unit will be with me, bring me Hephaestion,” he instructed and then Leonnius was gone, zooming ahead while Mydei paced the deck checking his troops for any last-minute adjustments. There was no need for a rousing speech, this was routine, nothing special, no one needed any more than that.

“Mydeimos,” Hephaestion announced his presence.

“Your unit will accompany me to the shore via longboat; we will be approaching the fort from the island. Krateros!” the old man jogged over, “there is a trireme docked, use it to breach the wall. We will meet you inside.” The old man nodded, and they clasped forearms.

“May victory be yours, Mydeimos.”

There was another flurry of last-minute orders as each of his friends addressed their men, reminding them to show mercy to those that flee. Ptolemy was reviewing with his men what supplies to look for and how to mark their locations with charcoal on the walls. Peucesta was organizing his archers. He had a horn at his side, a means to relay orders in the chaos of combat.

“Mydeimos,” Hephaestion called. They were already piling into the longboat, via the rope ladder thrown over the side, waiting for him.

The prince flashed Krateros a look from the railing. The old man was already on the upper deck, ready to take over command. They nodded once and then Mydei was vaulting over the side of the ship.

The longboat dropped nine ‘pirates’ on the shore before returning to the Chryseus Leo. The crew would secure the longboat and then meet them around the side of the island. They wouldn’t have time when they fled the scene to recover it otherwise.

Leonnius whistled once, sharp and short, and they all fell in line behind him, keeping low along the edge of the foliage. To run through it would provide cover but the movement would be more easily spotted from a distance, even in the cover of night they were too many to convince a good lookout that they were animals. Keeping close but staying on the beach allowed them to move quickly and quietly.

The island itself was not big. It was not meant to be sustaining, only strategically placed. This fort was little more than a storehouse and inspection point, entirely at the mercy of their own Navy’s traffic through the area bringing supplies and providing equipment and food as needed in turn. Mydei didn’t expect a full garrison of troops, but he didn’t expect a walk in the park either. Two triremes meant two crews which meant a couple hundred Okheman soldiers. Maybe enough to challenge the Kremnoan Detachment.

Maybe.

Not likely. This would be over fast.

Leonnius led them through the trees to a narrow dirt path and then to a dense patch of foliage for them to hide in while they waited. Mydei could see the wall ahead. The gate was little more than a pair of wooden doors, locked in the middle.

Mydei closed his eyes to wait, taking deep breaths in his low crouch. On every inhale he could smell the warmth of sunbaked loam and humidity and hear the distant chirp of insects. Hephaestion’s heartbeat was steady, right behind him, Leonnius’ in front. They too waited in reverence, contemplating the battle ahead, holding back that excited rush at the prospect of a proper battle. The adrenaline lurked under their skin like hounds waiting for the-Peucesta’s horn cut through the night like a knife. Two seconds later the whole island shook, erupting with the sounds of shouting and tearing lumber; the creak and snap of twigs magnified a hundred-fold, barely audible over the crunch of collapsing stone.

Before the dust had even begun to drift their way, Mydei had already started running. Crystal erupted from the ground to rip the doors from their hinges and toss them aside, still locked tight but now utterly useless. His crystals burst into glimmering dust as the Kremnoans surged through the gate and into the keep.

Leonnius claimed first blood from their group.

Mydei was fast but no one could beat Leonnius for speed. The runner had dashed ahead to clash with the first of the Okhemans that wanted a fight, swords clashed twice before Leonnius had dragged his blade across the man’s throat, already moving on to the next clash. Hephaestion was on his tail, cutting off the Okheman troops from the side as they tried to race to the courtyard, yelling all the while in desperate attempts to organize under the assault.

The courtyard was the pirate’s primary entry point so naturally the bulk of the fighting was happening there. Using their position as a pinch, Mydei and his small group were able to confront and pick off the Okheman reinforcements before they could join the main host, more importantly, they were running into individuals as they raced through the fort’s hallways and open courtyards between checking rooms.

Individual soldiers were easier to scare than those running with a pack. It was human nature to draw comfort and courage from your companions. Lone soldiers that saw Mydei and the others roaming showed more of a willingness to run, and that’s when the pirates showed restraint. The same training and control that made them efficient killers also made them compelling actors.

Hephaestion raced down a hallway after a young Okheman. The soldier was trying his best but the feral look in Hephaestion’s eyes made the point of his sword drop, easy pickings in true combat where only blood mattered, but the first mate’s sword glanced off the man’s cheek instead of slitting his throat. He kicked the sword from the Okheman’s hand and swung in painfully slow arcs, giving the man telegraphed swings to dodge until the fear finally bit at his heels.

“It takes so much more effort to let them go,” Hephaestion complained, while they watched the man run away.

Mydei patted him on the back. “Few Okhemans fight as well as our Deliverer.”

Leonnius ran ahead, back and forth, luring in enemies that saw him as easy prey only for Mydei and Hephaestion to chase them away when the Okhemans realized how out of their depth they were. Any soldiers that stayed and fought were granted swift glorious deaths. It was respect for them to honor the choice of those men who wished to be courageous in the face of death. Better to die by the blade than to become food for the Black Tide.

“The storehouse is up ahead,” Leonnius confirmed when he returned to them again. He had already mapped the place in his head. Mydei could see it in the gleam of his grin. “There is a long hallway that leads to island caves up a couple hallways down. That’s how they’re escaping to the cove.”

“Hephastion, secure the storehouse and armory with your men,” Mydei ordered, “Leonnius go to our main force and lead them there. If the way is clear tell them to begin loading supplies starting with the armory.”

They both saluted and hurried to their tasks without question while Mydei raced deeper into the fort, searching for anyone that may be left behind. True cowards would abandon their own if they believed them to be dead. If the ship left prematurely… It was important that the Okhemans sounded an official retreat.

Navigation rooms were in high places on ships, usually attached to the upper decks, but that was not necessarily the case for forts. As they did not move there was little need to check the maps to distant shorelines or glittering stars. Mydei found it next to their commander’s quarters and was only mildly disappointed to see that the commander was not there. Whether fled or gone to fight it was hard to tell but he left behind a very angry looking older man.

The Okheman reached for his sword, drawing it and throwing it at Mydei with admirable precision. He barely stepped to the side in time, and the blade embedded itself into the doorframe with a few of Mydei’s hairs.

“Pirate,” the man hissed.

Mydei held his arms out to the side and grinned a wild grin. “So I am.”

The Okheman reached for a spear leaning against the table beside him, but Mydei was faster. He dashed across the room and kicked the old guy in the gut, sending him against the wall. Experience gave him recovery unsuited for his age, and he reached for the hilt of another sword hung on the wall nearby, even as he slouched.

Mydei grabbed the spear before it could clatter to the floor and threw it like a javelin. The cold, impartial bronze cut through the Okheman’s hand, pinning him to the wall with a short, startled, and pained scream.

The prince drew his sword, spinning it in slow, measured circles, meant to intimidate. He was a lion playing with his food, drinking in the pain and fear as he stalked towards the guy. To his credit, the man was masking his fear well.

“Kill me then, make it quick,” he spat.

“Kill you?” Mydei crooned. He stabbed the sword into the wall beside the man’s head, slowly dragging it closer and closer to his neck with a screech that he felt in his teeth as it dragged through the wall. “I wasn’t going to kill you.”

Suspicion cut through the pain on the man’s face. This close it was easy to see he was terrified, but brave, using anger to bury any doubts that may shatter his defiance.

“You are not the commander of this fort,” Mydei observed allowed.

“The commander is dead,” he snarled.

“Oh? Then congratulations on your promotion.” The spear and sword ripped free. Mydei braced himself against the wall with a foot for the leverage to wrench them both from the wall at the same time, to let the man stumble. The new captain cradled his injured hand to his chest as blood flowed freely down his palm and wrist.

“Sound the retreat,” Mydei ordered, “sound the retreat and my men will let you go.”

“You will hunt us at sea, pirate.”

Again, the prince grinned, a wild and feral thing. He was a rabid animal, a bloodthirsty pirate, eager to leave bodies in their wake. Or so he wanted this man to believe.

“Do you not want the head start?” he crooned.

The man’s eyes darted about and then he slowly started to walk around Mydei, keeping his body turned to face him, expecting to be stabbed in the back, but the pirate didn’t move. The Okheman violently snatched a horn from the table as he fled and before Mydei could count to five he heard that crisp clear sound of a war horn, bleating out a code into the night air.

Mydei held still as he listened, still counting. When he got to ten, he turned and continued to chase. He needed to be that specter in pursuit, that was his role; he couldn’t let them regroup at their dock and try to take the fort back. It was so important that they finished chasing the Okhemans away.

He turned a corner into a long hallway, the one that led to the escape route to the trireme in the cove and scrambled backwards when he heard people rapidly approaching. Mydei hid behind the wall with his hand on the hilt of his sword, listening to the rapid patter of footsteps and shouts, waiting for them to thin so he could take up the rear, to chase them properly.

The horn sounded again, close. That guy should have been promoted earlier. It sounded like he was taking up the rear himself, making sure his people were retreating. That made things easier.

Mydei waited for the horn to pass and nearly stepped out, but one last straggler was trying to catch up. With a purr and a grin, Mydei listened to those footsteps until they had barely passed his hiding spot and then his sword was swinging at that last Okheman’s heels.

He had expected a squeal, a shout, maybe a stumble before the man scurried away. Mydei did not expect it to be countered. His blade clashed with another much larger one as they sprang away from each other, down either ends of the hallway.

Mydei’s heart dropped. Standing between himself and the waiting Okheman captain was Phainon.

-

He really tried.

Phainon knew. He knew on day one that they were planning something he wouldn’t like, something that would force him to confront his sense of morality, to balance it with what these men were like versus the things they chose to do. The kind of thing that tested the benefit of the doubt he gave them, the trust they had earned from him, that whatever horrible task they saw fit to exclude him from was for the right reasons.

They got quiet when he came near, dodged all his questions, and when he played along and let the subject change to small talk, he could see their relief as they believed they were playing him. But Phainon was no fool. If this was a campaign against the Black Tide then they would have told him the plan. No, whatever their plot, it was against people. Living, people. And when he had the chance to peek at the maps that they thought were so cleverly hidden, he knew that the Chryseus Leo was heading for the northernmost Okheman fort.

Phainon had been there before. He remembered it from when the Sol had resupplied there. It was not a well-manned fort and the people there were brave, soldiers true, but unpracticed. It would be a slaughter.

So, when Mydei shoved Phainon down, changed into wildly different attire to hide his identity, and then left, he didn’t know what to do.

Phainon really tried not to think about what was happening.

He stayed in that chair with his fists on his thighs, trying not to look at the stitching on his sleeves, the suns stitched into his leather armguards, or feel the weight of the shining cape over his shoulder. He tried not to think about the title hung around his neck like a noose. Even when the ship picked up speed and he braced himself for the impact he knew was coming, Phainon did his very best to stay in that chair. He closed his eyes tightly and covered his ears with his palms pressed tight to drown out the sounds of shouting and yelling. He kept them covered even when he was thrown to the floor when the ship collided with something big, pushing and shoving forward before it finally stopped.

He really tried.

He really tried to behave.

Phainon scrambled to his feet and ran out of the door before he could stop himself. He didn’t bother with a disguise; he didn’t consider anything except how that noose labeled ‘Deliverer’ could just as easily be used as a lifeline as long as he pulled the rope away from his own neck and tossed the rope to someone who needed to be saved.

The Chyrseus Leo was bigger than the trireme that they had rammed. At their speed and angle, they hadn’t plowed through the thing so much as just took its place at the dock by forcibly relocating the whole damn ship. It had been forced up the bank and into the fort wall, causing both the wall and the ship to tear in twain. The crew were already using the crashed ship as a bridge to run through the gap and begin fighting.

Phainon listened to the clash from the railing, scanning for his own entry point. A flash of light to his left and fine red dust on the breeze told him that Mydei had found an alternate way in. They were pinching the Okhema soldiers.

He swore to himself and instead followed the main host. He ran up the trireme and used it to vault up onto what was left the standing wall, crouching there to watch, to search for an opening, some way he could help.

The pirates did not hesitate to cut down those Okhemans that raised their voices with battle cries. He watched Perdikkas cut one such man down before moving to the next, his sword clashing with a man wearing a leader’s colors. Mityphon was a young commander but kind. Phainon recognized him immediately from the one time they had met.

Arrows whistled past his ear and for a heartbeat Phainon worried that they saw his clothing and the crew were targeting him by mistake, but then Ptolemy’s arrow lodged in Mityphon’s eye while he was locked in combat with Perdikkas and he stopped caring if they targeted him too.

Phainon cried out but it was buried under others to mesh with the cacophony of death.

An older soldier turned when Mityphon crumpled, calling to his men, ordering them continue to defend with all their lives while he ran in the direction of the commander’s quarters. That’s where Aglaea’s nymph would be, where any hope of rescue would come from.

Phainon saw Krateros advance on a young man, probably the kid’s first tour. The boy was shaking, taking a step backwards. He was about to intervene, maybe save someone, anyone, when Krateros pulled his swipe short, barely clipping the boy’s shoulder. It was enough to make him run, courage spent, and Krateros let him go.

Any Okheman that tried to retreat was allowed to, Phainon realized, but there was no mercy for those that chose to stand their ground. That was still too high of a price for Phainon. He had no tears for men he barely knew, but he had blood aplenty to shed on their behalf instead.

He dropped into the courtyard and summoned his blade, surging forward next to Perdikkas to expertly deflect a spear that was meant for his pirate friend. Adrenaline starting to flow, Phainon pushed his opening to shoulder charge the Okheman back and away from the others.

For a second nothing moved. Perdikkas was looking at Phainon with seriousness and worry, shaking his head and watching him with unblinking, burning eyes without saying anything. Phainon glanced away, turning from him to his own people instead.

They were caught between horror and awe. Phainon was framed by starlight and the glow of braziers, gold and silver outlining their Deliverer as he stood over them with his sword drawn, clean and gleaming. They recognized him and several of them smiled, cheering as they rallied, ready to fight once more, so their shocked faces cut him deep when he raised his sword towards them instead and yelled, “Flee! Leave this place! Now!”

Stunned, they made no attempt to move until the pirates again advanced and then they were clashing again as though Phainon had said nothing. A few even puzzled and murmured over whether they should be raising their swords towards him as well. Or at least they did until Phainon swung his blade to deflect an arrow meant for an Okheman and spun on his heel to face the invaders.

“Move!” he called to them.

One of the men, excited to stand shoulder to shoulder with their Deliverer, raised his sword to attack, but Phainon physically blocked him and the sword glanced off his pauldron with a clang. He put a hand on the man’s chest and shoved him back. “Run!”

This time two of them obeyed, turning to flee.

Krateros swung at a persistent Okheman archer, but Phainon was there to intercept that fury. The old Kremnoan scowled under his disguise, rage burning deep as his sword was forced away, but it softened almost imperceptibly, when the archer tried to retaliate, and Phainon shielded Krateros with his own body. The bolt sunk into his shoulder just under the protection of his pauldron and he hissed but did not cry out. Sweat dripped from his nose as he spun, ripping that great sword through the air to cleave the bow in two. He chased the arc to put his hand on the archer’s chest, to shove him back towards safety.

It was an uphill battle, Phainon lamented, one he was ready to climb, when he heard the horn. One long bleat and two short calls sounded a tactical retreat. The Okhemans responded immediately. Those in the back turned and fled, while the more experienced warriors on the front moved more slowly, covering their escape until Phainon physically got between the two forces again and then they were running too.

The vice commander, the old man that Phainon hadn’t recognized at first, was crossing the courtyard with the horn, still sounding the retreat as he scanned for his men. The pirates were still pushing forward, slowing to a crawl as the battle faded into recent memory, and whooped victory cheers.

Leonnius raced around a corner, stumbling when he saw Phainon. He shook his head and ran to Krateros, talking to him swiftly. Orders were barked and they surged into the complex to loot it, any desire to chase was gone as they moved with purpose instead.

Phainon saw Perdikkas reach for him out of the corner of his eye, but he ran before the Kremnoan could stop him, chasing after the Okheman horn, eager to obey, to retreat, to flee, to go home. The vice commander paused when he met Phainon’s eyes, the shock of seeing a ghost turning quickly to joy as they clasped arms.

“You live,” he said.

“Yes,” Phainon told him firmly. He let go to push the man along and he obliged, still sounding the horn as they ran into the hallway together. The pirates had peeled off, headed towards the main gate, the armory, and the storehouse. They were nearly at the exit, where the walls met the caves, when Phainon faltered and he almost paid for it with his ankles.

The flash of a sword reaching through the shadows barely registered in time for his instincts to respond. The clash lasted less than a second and then Phainon was bouncing back, putting himself between the Okheman vice-captain and their attacker.

Mydei’s eyes were wide and confused. He lowered his sword at the same time Phainon raised his own.

“Deliverer!” the vice-commander called from down the hallway, urging him to come.

And Phainon really considered it.

They would flee to Okhema, to report to Aglaea. To be safe under the Dawn Device. It was a straight shot home to return a hero. The way he had been greeted, Okhema must have thought he had perished in the waters, it would overjoy them to know he was alive and well, to hear him speak to the Goldweaver of the tale of his survival and triumphant return.

And it would condemn those Okhemans to do so.

If Phainon went with them, Mydei would have no choice but to pursue with purpose to destroy. As far as these soldiers knew, they were attacked by pirates; an isolated incident, something to report, lament, and then forget. But if Phainon ran with them, then the truth went too. They would know that these were not simple seafaring brigands, they were Kremnoans, the Crown Prince himself among them and even if their reasons could be justified, Okhema would never be able to look past the flag they sailed beneath.

Mydei’s expression changed as Phainon stood there at the crossroad. The surprise had melted into a frown. His grip on the sword tightened, the creak of leather giving him away. He was doing the same math as Phainon was, coming to the same conclusions.

The sword in Phainon’s hand disappeared and he bowed his head, turning away from the vice-commander to walk towards Mydei instead. He didn’t look at the man, didn’t want to see his expression. There was too much to explain so Phainon didn’t try. He stood a few paces away from the pirate and waited until he heard the footsteps behind him vanish into the night.

“…you did not go with them,” Mydei observed aloud. His voice was softer than Phainon had expected, no edge at all.

“How could I?” he asked. When Phainon looked up it was with a genuine smile and tired eyes with his hands held out to his sides. As much as he wanted to go home, he still wanted to do it the right way. He owed them both that much. “We haven’t finished our fight.”

Mydei studied him in the dark, his eyes flicking between Phainon’s own and the spreading gold on his sleeve. The captain closed the last few steps between them and reached for him. Phainon expected a soft touch, but Mydei forced him to turn around with a shove instead so he could break the arrow sticking out of his back, making Phainon yelp as the head moved in the tender flesh.

“Go back to the ship,” he ordered gently, “I think that’s enough piracy from you today.”

Phainon grimaced and nodded. Mydei left him standing in the hallway, trusting him to return on his own.

He walked slowly, eyes straight ahead. Phainon didn’t want to look down, didn’t want to see the bodies. There were some in the hallways with their throats slit and he wondered how many of them had been killed by his close friends. He puzzled over why that didn’t upset him more.

A few pirates were moving the bodies in the courtyard before they could finish cooling, setting them neatly to the side, more respectful of the dead than Phainon might have expected. Against orders, he stopped to help them.

He was supposed to be these peoples’ Deliverer, but even as he set his hands on each of their chests, sending them to Thanatos with a mumbled blessing, Phainon felt… fine, relieved even to not find any Kremnoans among the dead. Of course he grieved, of course he felt guilty and hurt to see his countrymen dead, but there was also an acceptance. He couldn’t save them all against their centuries long feud, but he had managed to sway a great many of them to escape unharmed. Perhaps it was Phainon’s newfound understanding of Strife, or maybe he simply did not know them well enough to mourn them as one might a close friend, but as he stood again and left the fort to climb back onto the Chryseus Leo it was with a sense of curious peace blanketed over his grief and unease.

There was no way he could choose to be like this all the time. But wasn’t this lifestyle of violence the same as the one he had already been living as a warrior for Okhema? How was this any different? Both sides were fighting for duty and for love; as Perdikkas had once described it: a reason worth living for.

Phainon watched from the railing of the upper deck as the crew loaded stolen goods from food to weapons to precious resources, everything except wealth. They were loading survival onto the ship, hope for the future of their displaced people.

It made him feel like he was still standing at that crossroad again, the same one that he had been trapped at from the moment fate put him under red sails in the mouth of a lion. The same crossroad that fate was going to decide in the purest way through combat. Phainon had told Mydei that he stayed to honor their duel, and he meant it with his whole being.

So why did it feel like he had already made his choice without it?

Chapter End Notes

chapters.title: Chapter 15: The Fine Line of Piracy
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

No new tags!

Chapter Notes

My friend pointed out that I keep taking Phainon’s shirt off. I’m not sorry. Consider it a call back to almost every trailer he's featured in.

Mydei was worried when he got back to the Chryseus Leo. It didn’t show on his face of course but Hephaestion could tell, and it wasn’t hard to figure out why.

Phainon was acting normal.

They were still anchored at the fort’s dock, the last of the supplies trickling in, getting ready to leave, and Phainon was on deck helping Perdikkas tend to the injured with that same soft smile as though they hadn’t just killed a bunch of his countrymen and robbed them.

“If Perdikkas isn’t worried…” Hephaestion tried but Mydei’s frown deepened.

Phainon was talking softly to calm one of the men who he knew could not understand him while he pressed gauze to a wound. Phainon’s right arm was in a sling, tied tightly to his chest to keep his own injury from worsening so he only had his left hand to work with. He had left his coat and cape in their room, but gold still soaked his shirt making it stick to his back over the bandages that had been swiftly slapped on. Crimson blood colored his palm and fingers, but he was still steady, unbothered by the way the soldier held tightly to Phainon’s wrist for grounding. He just… kept talking in soft whispers to put the man at ease until Perdikkas could get to him.

When the doctor took Phainon’s place, he moved to the next guy, fetching water, gauze, applying pastes, whatever was asked of him that he could do with one arm. He just wanted to help.

“He could have run,” Mydei wondered aloud.

“We would have had to hunt him, you know that.”

Yes, and Phainon would’ve also known that. He wasn’t stupid, but… “why didn’t he try?” Phainon was too hopeful, too positive, too determined to give up without a fight. It was in his nature to try.

Hephaestion turned around to lean his back against the railing, looking over the aplustre instead of studying Mydei as he had been since they got back. His hair was in a long ponytail, tied at the nape of his neck. He pulled it over his shoulder and ran his fingers through it.

“Did you want him to?”

Mydei’s brows pinched. His immediate response was ‘no’, but it was more complicated than that, so he kept his silence.

Hephaestion sighed through his nose and rolled his head, leaning on his elbows so he could stare straight up into the sky to say, “You better beat him, Mydei.” They both twisted in place, just subtly enough to catch the other out of the corners of their eyes. “When you settle his challenge. You better fucking win.”

-

Phainon was tired. It had been a long and miserable night, but his hurts could wait, people needed help, and he couldn’t sit still knowing there was something he could do for them. There were too many injuries for the infirmary, so Perdikkas had any man that needed medical attention stay on deck towards the bow, out of the way of where able-bodied Kremnoan pirates were moving goods.

It was an efficient system, practiced, but slower than Phainon had expected it to be. Everything they brought on board had to be inspected before it could be sent to the hold to be packed away for the journey. Peucesta and Fig Stew had final approval over every piece that crossed that ramp. It had seemed utterly ridiculous to Phainon that the chimera’s stamp of approval was required. Surely this was not the best time to entertain the animal’s antics.

And then he saw Fig Stew pull one of Aglaea’s golden threads out of a crate and everything made more sense. Even the pet on board had a job. The chimera had a nose for finding them and if he couldn’t reach one, he’d just scratch until Peucesta came to offer opposable thumb assistance. Fig even found, and ate, one of Aglaea’s nymphs, and finished sniffing the rest of the cargo with part of a wing stuck to the fur next to his mouth.

“Phainon,” Perdikkas called gently. He reached out to gently touch Phainon’s bicep with his still clean forearm as he stepped in close. “You’ve done enough. It’s late, please rest.”

“I’m okay, Perdikkas.”

“You fought twice as hard as any of us, playing both sides like you did.”

Phainon shyly reached to scratch the back of his neck and barely stopped himself in time to avoid bloodying his hair. “It was nothing.”

“No. It was a lot. You saved people, Okheman and Kremnoan. Maybe there’s something to that title you keep trying to ignore.” Phainon’s eyes went wide for a moment and then he looked away, but Perdikkas lightly kicked his shin to keep his attention. “Something to die for, yeah?”

“A reason to fight, to live,” Phainon corrected, “…I think I will go lay down.”

Perdikkas nodded and gently nudged him along, pushing Phainon towards the stairs. The crew still milled about, barely recognizable in their costumes as they unfurled the sails and raised the anchor.

He went to his room and closed the door with his foot. The wash basin water hadn’t been replaced yet, so it was still a little dirty, but it wasn’t egregiously murky. It darkened immediately when Phainon gently put his hand under the water to try and wash away the gore. Phainon had avoided the mirrors in the room. He knew there was red blood spattered across his clothes, his face, his hair, never mind what he had personally shed in gold.

One-handed it was almost impossible to get the blood off, no matter how much he splashed. He sighed and nearly gave up until a hand reached around to rest on his arm. Phainon flinched away and the hand retreated.

“M-Mydeimos! I didn’t hear you come in.”

“My apologies, I didn’t mean to startle you,” he said gently, like he was trying to soothe an upset chimera. Mydei looked different, but kind of attractive as a pirate. The hat suit him. It held his bangs just right to frame his eyes and drew attention to his signature braid that rested just over his right clavicle.

Phainon felt the heat rise to his cheeks. “I wasn’t startled,” he insisted with a cough, but Mydei didn’t push the issue.

Instead, he pointed to Phainon’s hand on the edge of the bowl. “May I help you?”

Dirty water slowly ran down the side of the basin while Phainon considered that question. Matching Mydei’s softness of voice, he said, “Yes… please.”

Mydeimos took off his hat, coat, and gloves and left them on the table. Then he lifted the washbasin to cradle in both arms, muscles flexed but not struggling. Water sloshed as he lowered himself to sit on the floor with his legs folded beneath him to cradle the basin in his lap. He gestured for Phainon to sit across from him.

Carefully, because of his bound arm, Phainon stumbled his way into a cross-legged position to match and offered Mydei his hand.

Gently, almost reverent, the prince took Phainon’s hand in both of his and guided it into the water. It made sense, because of his gauntlets, but Phainon was still surprised by how soft Mydei’s hands were without them. Where his were callused from swinging a sword, Mydei’s were not. The prince took very good care of himself.

Strong thumbs massaged Phainon’s palm in slow circles and long, firm strokes, then rolled his hand to do the same for the back, for each knuckle. He held Phainon still, palm up, with one hand cradled beneath while the other gave every individual finger attention, rubbing them each in turn to clean them. He guided Phainon to curl his fingers, to trace along his nailbeds to find the stubborn, offensive sanguine there, until it was only healthy pink skin beneath the swipe of his careful touch. Mydei cupped water with his hand to scoop it over Phainon’s wrist, to brush away the stray speckles that had tried to escape down his arm.

It was impossible to tell which drop of blood was Kremnoan and which was Okheman. It was all the same red. It all smelled like copper and dried dark. It all turned pale in water and it all washed away the same, leaving cloudy streaks in something that was otherwise pure and untarnished.

Even when Phainon was certain he was clean, Mydei didn’t stop taking his time to trace the lines on Phainon’s palm as though he was searching for the future there in the dim light, reading a book that no one else dared tried to understand but that he desperately wanted to.

And Phainon didn’t once try to take his hand back. He felt respected, maybe even a little worshipped. He was definitely blushing all the way to his ears at the quiet intimacy, but every touch carried relief and gratitude in equal measure.

“Why didn’t you go with them?” Mydei asked in a whisper while he massaged the soft flesh below Phainon’s thumb.

Phainon looked up at him, but Mydei was avoiding eye contact, focused entirely on Phainon’s hand in the basin while he waited. His expression was relaxed aside from the subtle arch of his brow, a curve of concentration and concern.

“You would have had to chase after me, to bring me back if I had,” Phainon answered in the same whisper.

“Is that the only reason?”

Phainon tensed but Mydei assuaged those feelings by twisting the Okheman’s hand to cradle his fingers as though he may raise them to his lips for a kiss. His thumb rubbed across Phainon’s knuckles.

“I told you,” the Deliverer mumbled, “we have to finish our fight.”

Mydei lifted Phainon’s hand from the water, holding it just above the surface. The little drips plinked in the water below.

“Are you angry with me?” the captain asked, while he used his other hand to scoop water over the both of theirs, to rinse them. “At the crew?”

“…I was at first,” Phainon admitted when he had a moment to consider it. He lowered his gaze from Mydei’s downturned face to watch the basin. “But I think you’ve earned my trust. I saw that you had ordered the crew to let them escape if they ran. And I saw the map; I knew the Black Tide was going to reach this fort soon. They would all be dead if you hadn’t picked this spot.” Phainon experimentally flexed his fingers and Mydei stopped what he was doing in case Phainon wanted to reclaim his hand, but he didn’t. He left it there for Mydei to hold. “In a way, I suppose I should be thanking you, for saving who you could.”

“Leave your hand right like this,” Mydei ordered. He tapped Phainon’s outstretched hand with one finger, leaving it palm up in the air so he could move the washbasin to his side, setting it on the floor and leaning over to reach for a cabinet drawer. Mydei fished around, body tilting at a funny angle as he strained to reach for a towel. Then he set the soft fabric in his lap, recovered Phainon’s hand, and the care began again.

“I expected you to be full of fury,” the pirate admitted as he delicately pressed the towel against Phainon’s skin. “So eager to be home that you would have taken any chance to be free of the shackles that I put around your wrists.” He pressed his thumb to the side of Phainon’s wrist as he said it. “When I saw you standing there between myself and your freedom…”

“I think… I think we should still let the fight decide,” Phainon admitted, “we swore an oath when we stood across from each other, to face each other fairly. What kind of man, what kind of Deliverer would I be if I could not honor my own word? Besides, I think I have done more good here, serving you, than I ever have playing court in Okhema.”

Mydei snorted, a light puff of air through his nose, perhaps a laugh in disguise. “Silver-tongued as you are, Okheman, I’d expect you to enjoy such boring endeavors.”

“And where were your boorish mannerisms tonight, Kremnoan brute?” Phainon teased, “when you let my people escape, saving them in ways they will never know?”

Mydei rolled his eyes and rubbed at Phainon’s hand a little more roughly while Phainon chuckled.

“Mydeimos,” Phainon said more seriously, “I’m not a pirate. I can’t do everything you do, even if it’s for the right reasons, but I still want to help. I want to fight.”

Mydei met his eyes for the first time sitting down, his face still guarded, but there was a tremor to his gaze when they looked at each other, when Phainon smiled with genuine warmth.

“HKS,” Mydei grumbled. He looked back down to continue drying Phainon’s hand. He gave it back when he was satisfied that it was clean. “Then perhaps you should be more careful. You have nearly doubled the number of injuries my ship sees per every three entry hours, and I cannot trust you by my side if you are leaving gold all over my ship every time I look away!”

Phainon laughed, “Perhaps you are not protecting me well enough, hm?”

“Are you a child? Do I need to be your keeper?”

“You could keep me,” Phainon joked but the look of shock on Mydei’s face had Phainon back pedaling. He took his hand back so he could cough into his fist. “I’m sorry, that joke was in poor taste.”

Mydei rolled his eyes and folded the towel so he could dip the corner of it into the washbasin to wet it. Roughly, he took hold of Phainon’s chin and held him still while he wiped his face. That grip loosened with every stroke until it was just the warm pads of Mydei’s fingers pressed under the bone of Phainon’s jaw, guiding more than demanding.

“You are a strong fighter Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,” Mydei praised, “not many can keep pace with me, and I like how it feels to fight with you, both at your side and against you. If we want to ensure our pending battle for your fate is fair, I think it best that we study the way the other fights.”

“Makes sense.”

Mydei set the towel aside and motioned for Phainon to turn around with a slow spin of his finger. He obeyed but still jumped and twitched at the cold of those gentle hands when Mydei slid them under the hem of Phainon’s shirt. He pressed a little more firmly in response, so that it wouldn’t tickle so much as they worked together to get the filthy fabric off his chest around his sling.

Water dripped and splashed behind him and then the cool of the towel turned washcloth wiped away the evidence of his willingness. The scarlet of life spilled by men, the same between nations, was starkly set apart from the two men. Did Mydei feel isolated from his people because he did not bleed the same as them? Did he perhaps see in Phainon a kindred spirit? Gold sparkled in the water, refusing to blend with the hematic price shed by common men until Mydei stirred the water with the cloth.

“When you are well, I would like to begin sparring with you regularly,” Mydei invited as he resumed his task.

Phainon’s smile widened. He knew Mydei could hear it in his voice. “I would be honored.”

“So eager to collect bruises.”

“Oh Captain, this won’t be anything like the arena.”

“Good,” Mydei purred, with an audible smile of his own, “I’m counting on it.”

-

The Chryseus Leo stopped chasing the Okheman trireme by Lucid Hour. The crew was too tired after the late-night prior and with how quickly their prey had fled on favorable winds, Mydei decided their goal had been achieved. Those soldiers would be safe in Okhema, and they had other plans to attend to.

True to his words, Phainon began to spar with Mydei daily, something they both looked forward to. Mydei found comfort in sparring with his old friends, but Phainon was always a challenge. They were there to learn from each other, sure, but Mydei learned day one that Phainon hated losing and their spars almost always escalated into fights that rattled the ship.

It got so bad that they lost the privilege of using the upper deck, where Mydei usually sparred, after Mydei kicked the tiller on purpose to make the ship turn unexpectedly tight. Phainon had predictably lost his footing when the ship caught on a wave and lost most of its momentum, but before Mydei could take advantage of the stumble and claim victory, a very angry Fig Stew came flying up the stairs. Displeased with the whiplash that had interrupted his nap, the chimera sank his teeth into Mydei’s elbow, just above his gauntlets, and then gave Phainon the same treatment with teeth in his hand when the Deliverer laughed.

They were more careful after that.
