Every time they clashed, Mydei felt himself getting stronger, properly growing, where before he had felt like he had hit a plateau. He could see Phainon improving too. His sea legs were getting better and somehow his disposition was even sunnier. It was easy to forget that one day they’d have to do this for real, for higher stakes, a topic that didn’t even come up when they bantered, finding a good give and take that carried into real fights too.

And there was no shortage of those.

Mydei had been right to plan for three weeks at sea. The storm had pushed the Black Tide into more of the trade route than they had predicted and the Chryseus Leo had to burn four ships in two weeks. Only half of those ships had been safe to loot after being corrupted.

Phainon was invaluable in every fight against the Tide due to his golden blood and righteous tenacity, but his true value came from what he meant to Okhema and her allies. As the Deliverer, he was instantly recognizable and as they had seen at the fort, his presence and a few carefully chosen words were all it took to end a fight quickly, to chase away those who may otherwise stand their ground and fall to the sword and spear when they did. It was Phainon’s own idea to weaponize his reputation for good.

Mydei had nearly sent him away when Phainon had strode confidently into his meeting with Hephaestion and Krateros. They were discussing plans, budgeting resources, and calculating their route with every intention of returning home at the end of the second week. Krateros had been the one to offer to hear him out and Mydei was so surprised and a little impressed that he agreed.

Which was why at the beginning of the third week since leaving the Kremnos outpost, they were already targeting another Okheman fort. Phainon had pointed it out on the map, not too far out of the way. He provided explicit details of its layout, its size, number of soldiers on duty, and even an estimate of supplies worth taking. He helped with every single step of the plan, something that Mydei considered very pirate. He kept that observation to himself.

It was a plan that only Phainon could’ve scripted, and it was something only he could pull off. When they pulled into that enemy port dressed as pirates and waiting for the signal from Phainon, the Deliverer walked right up to the gate to call his people. Regal and beautiful, fully on display in the Goldweaver’s handiwork, he shone like the sun under starlight. Phainon knew exactly what to say, exactly how to be himself, to get them to willingly open the gates. When the Kremnoans surged inside like a hurricane, ready to fight, Phainon was beside them, weaponizing the pirates’ reputation with his own. He never once summoned his sword because he knew exactly what words would make the Okhemans drop their weapons and flee.

To the mild disappointment of the crew, it was the first time they had won a military engagement without bloodshed, and the payoff had been substantial. Despite planning it, Phainon still refused to help steal, and excused himself to wait in the library, keeping to himself to study, away from the piracy that he felt he could avoid.

He only did what he absolutely had to do to ensure the fewest number of casualties. But for all his efforts to preserve peace, Phainon was still a savage warrior when he needed to be and was not shy of bloodshed. When they clashed with the Black Tide, Phainon and Mydei would race to leap to the corrupted ships, to steal each other’s kills, and pretend they didn’t see money change hands between their friends whenever they announced their totals.

They were in familiar waters, heading home under clear blue skies and warm sunlight, talking about the bath house and leaning against the rail side by side to watch the white caps when Phainon had another crazy idea.

“Have you ever considered going on the offensive?” he asked, cheerful, natural. Phainon had said it with the same casual cadence as asking what they were having for dinner.

Mydei turned his head to look at him. “Against?”

“The Black Tide.”

“Is that not what we have been doing?”

“Patrolling the line and burning ships that have already turned slows it down, but it isn’t the same as pushing back.”

“Deliverer, there is no way to ‘push back’, the Black Tide,” Mydei reminded him.

“What if there was?” Phainon’s eyes always glittered a brighter blue when he latched onto an idea. Like a dog with a bone, Mydei often thought when they gleamed with such resolution.

“Don’t waste your time dreaming.” Mydei turned around to lean backwards against the ship instead. He crossed his legs at the ankles and rested his elbows on the railing.

“I’m serious. If there was a way, would you take it?”

“Of course I would.”

Phainon turned to rest his weight heavily on one elbow so he could face Mydei completely. The sea spray clung to his bangs in tiny droplets that shimmered in the wind. “What happens to the Tide line if we reclaim its islands?”

Mydei frowned as he considered that.

“It already retreats,” Phainon pointed out, “after turning what it can.”

“Not for all of them.”

“But when it does... If we kill all the Black Tide monsters, would the Tide line retreat further?” Phainon was looking at him with excitement. Oh, if determination and sheer willpower could make it true…

“What if the Black Tide itself isn’t expanding?” Phainon asked, “what if it is just moving forward and trusting it’s monsters to hold its new territory? What if there is a limit to how far it can reach without its army?”

“We would not be able to verify that without sailing around it,” Mydei mumbled. He held his own chin between his thumb and curled pointer finger while he studied the deck in thought.

“But if I’m right, then it could be forced to retreat.”

“What is to stop it from surging forward again? When it realizes what is happening?”

“Then we don’t invite people to go to those islands yet. We clear them and just-“ Phainon shrugged his shoulders, “-see what happens.”

“It’s a curious idea, Deliverer,” Mydei agreed, “if the others see fit to gamble on your idea, then when we restock, we may test your theory.”

Phainon beamed but that smile faltered. He was looking past Mydei, out towards the horizon, suddenly very serious. The scout on duty noticed it at the same time and shouted from the topsail in Kremnoan, “sails ho!”

Mydei turned to look as the shout went out, squinting at the ship. The Chryseus Leo was moving quickly, less than a day away from home and a good night’s rest on dry land. They would easily outpace this ship but…

“Mydeimos, could that be one of yours?” Phainon asked, breathy and rushed.

“No.”

“They’ll find the isle-“

Mydei was already crossing the deck to shout, “Hard to starboard! Battle stations!”

Krateros and Hephaestion took up the call and started shouting more specific orders as the men hurried to obey. The ship twisted and the sails groaned as they started to turn. Mydei bent his knees just a little to brace himself as the deck tilted ever so slightly and was secretly proud that Phainon did the same without holding onto the railing. His sea legs were getting better.

“Mydei, we don’t know if it’s an enemy ship,” Phainon tried.

“Wait in the room, Deliverer,” Mydei ordered stiffly.

“I can help-“ “Not if they are Okheman Navy! Those sails are white and blue, you know there is a chance.”

“Then I can talk to them!”

Mydei stomped his foot and light rippled along his tattoos to intimidate, but Phainon met him with his own growl and a shine in his eyes.

“We don’t have to fight!” Phainon snarled in broken Kremnoan.

“Look at the ship, Deliverer! We are not playing pirate. We are a Kremnoan war ship nearly home! This is not only about us but the remainder of all my people… and you are the only exception I will make.”

No prisoners. His people needed to stay safe.

Phainon’s eyes burned, his closed fist was shaking, but Mydei was right and Phainon knew it. With an angry yell, the Okheman turned on his heel, cape flapping happily and as oblivious as an inanimate object could be at the tension in the air. He stomped out of sight to sulk, presumably waiting to crash the party anyway.

Mydei stretched his hands and shoulders by rolling his fingers and reaching across his own body to pull each arm in turn until he felt loose and ready to fight. The two ships were rapidly gaining on each other now that they were moving to intercept and not following the same path. With every passing second the ship on the horizon got bigger until Mydei could see her flag proudly on display in the swift wind.

Okheman Navy.

And then a black and orange bolt narrowly missed his cheek.

Well, they used to be Okheman Navy.

“Black Tide,” Mydei snarled over his shoulder and Krateros relayed the call to the crew.

Phainon would probably come out of hiding then. There wasn’t time to worry about him right now and if he wanted to stay sulking, fine. More for the prince and another win to hold over Phainon’s head.

Moving in broad daylight like this was abnormal and the sea was still a sparkling blue, rather than the ink of the Tide. There was no reason for this ship to move with such haste and energy.

Mydei climbed up onto the railing and held onto a line for balance as they approached. Another Black Tide arrow zipped his way, close enough to pull his half cape in its wake with the wind but he didn’t flinch, he didn’t move at all until the sides of their ships ground together and then Mydei was throwing himself onto the opposing deck in a spray of red crystal.

The monsters near him evaporated as he clawed through the air and jagged crimson materialized in a wave before him. Aside from the monsters, there was no other evidence of the Tide.

Mydei twisted enough to yell across, “Hephaestion!” They made eye contact. “Free to board!”

The first mate saluted and started shouting orders, and Mydei was turning back to the monsters with a feral smirk. He started running at a Black Tide archer but moments before his claws could connect, Phainon’s great sword tore through its chest. The steel stuck in the deck point first while the monster dissolved into ash.

Mydei spun on his heel in time to see Phainon land on the deck beside him.

“For the record,” he said, as he ripped his sword free and spun it in a circle, “I’m not happy about this either.”

“Then you concede?”

“I didn’t say that,” Phainon growled, and then they were both dashing different directions.

The entire fight was over in five minutes.

Mydei would have loved to personally take credit for the swift victory, but favorable circumstances were on their side this time. Phainon and Mydei could have single-handedly cleared the ship but having the rest of the crew on board to help was a boon, not a hindrance.

“23!” Phainon shouted from the ship’s bow.

24, Mydei thought but he lied when he shouted back with a scowl, “21!”

It was worth it to see Phainon fist bump the sky and dance to his own music the whole way back to the Chryseus Leo. Let the man be happy while he avoided the piracy he so abhorred.

“Let’s make this quick!” Hephaestion was yelling, “only grab what Perdikkas and Leonnius mark!”

The crew were pouring below decks to the cargo hold. There wasn’t enough room to take all the supplies, but they could get the valuables for now.

Mydei walked up to the upper deck first to bind the tiller and drop the anchor. He raised his hand towards the Leo as well and waited for one of his men to respond with the same gesture. The hand shot up a moment later, followed by the splash of the Chryseus Leo also weighing anchor so the ships wouldn’t drift too far apart while they searched for goodies. It looked like only the crew had been corrupted, so they could leave this one anchored here and return when they had more space for stolen goods to burn it then. This close to home they could probably just send their merchant ship to loot it on the way to market.

The maps spread across the table by the tiller were useless. Nothing they didn’t already have so he went to check the captain’s quarters instead. Unsurprisingly, Ptolemy had beat him to it and was perusing the two-shelf library there.

“Anything of interest?”

“The captain was a lover of romance,” Ptolemy acknowledged with a tone that screamed yes. His finger traveled along the spines in turn before he made a happy oo! sound and plucked one out to thumb through its pages.

Mydei grunted and started going over the man’s desk looking for orders. There wasn’t anything readily available to give their purpose away. His desk was neat and tidy, just another Naval war ship caught in the Black Tide’s net.

Mydei was about to leave when he saw the corner of fine parchment sticking out of a half-opened drawer and reached to retrieve it. The glitter of the broken wax seal was what caught his eye. The image pressed into the wax featured a pair of scissors crossed with a needle, the two bound loosely by a swirling thread and framed by laurels. It was Aglaea’s personal seal.

He turned the folded paper over a couple times before opening it to read.

Mydei’s eyes widened, and his head jerked up to check that Ptolemy hadn’t seen. The man was still engrossed in whatever book he had found. He turned so the bookworm wouldn’t notice him and then he read it again. Then he read it a third time.

His heart twisted twice, first with relief, and then with worry.

That fine script that curled effortlessly over the page in neat and simple lines were orders to the late captain from the Goldweaver herself. Orders of the utmost importance, a singular task to bring a particular pirate to justice.

Mydei folded the paper up carefully and tucked it inside his gauntlet, wedged in tight so he could keep it close, already feeling the weight of it. He’d have to tell them all eventually but first he wanted to get out from underneath the ink, to process this news himself.

“Let’s go Ptolemy,” he ordered.

“But I’m right in the midd-“

“Now!” So much for their fight.

-

From the desk of the Admiral Goldweaver of Okhema,

Herein I officially commission the esteemed Captain Theophis of Okhema with the singular task of bringing the pirate, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, Deliverer of Okhema, to justice.

All expenses for any additional supplies that may be acquired at sea will be compensated, to be paid from the Goldweaver’s private treasury.

Allies of Okhema must provide any and all resources as needed at the discretion of Captain Theophis until this criminal is apprehended and returned to Okhema to stand trial.

Refusal will be considered an act of treason.

Aglaea, Goldweaver

Chapter End Notes

I've said it before but I'll say it again: I treasure you guys. I love my readers and especially my commenters. You guys bring me such joy and relief to know that my silly idea was worth sharing! Even if I do get a little carried away and write way too much. Someday I will master the art of one shots, but it is not this day.

chapters.title: Chapter 16: Deliverer
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

No new tags Phainon has a really good idea Mydei also has a really good... well, it's an idea

Chapter Notes

Posting this one late cause it was actually a little tricky and it was running long. I was very adamant about putting specific things in this chapter so a couple scenes got a trim so the important parts could shine

I don't like swapping perspectives too many times per chapter but this felt right

“HKS,” Ptolemy said slowly. He was leaning against one of the balcony pillars, enunciating the word for their poor puppy. Phainon was sitting on a stool in front of him, trying to navigate petting Fig Stew while they practiced.

“High kas,” Phainon responded, equally slowly.

“HKS.”

“Hick ass.”

“HKS.”

Phainon’s eyebrows were pinched so tightly together while he concentrated that he was almost squinting. He licked his lips and tried again. “Hic is.”

Mydei was trying so hard not to laugh, but the smile slipped out anyway. Even though their last voyage was only a few weeks, he had ordered more than one day of rest back home. The ship was fine; she was resting at harbor. Mydei just wanted the time for… personal reasons.

Even as he lazed about on the kline on his balcony, watching his best friends desperately try to teach Phainon how to pronounce Kremnoan syllables correctly, that letter was burning a hole in his desk. The same desk that was in this room shoved against the wall. He had put it there when they got home and hadn’t had a chance to move it from where it was hidden under a stack of blank stationery.

Mydei wanted to show it to Phainon, needed to hand it to him, to let the man read it and understand how much had changed, this new gravity to the situation. He wanted to be ready on the heels of heartbreaking news with an invitation to his own family, to let Phainon know that he was wanted and loved, even if it was from pirates. Everyone in this room from Peucesta playing the lyre half upside down on a cushion, to Perdikkas who was slowly losing his patience with all the swear words flying around, to Hephaestion who was trying and failing to nap, wanted Phainon to stay. At some point since they pulled him on board, every single one of them had come to Mydei in private to ask if they could keep him somehow.

But not like this.

Please not like this.

Mydei wanted Phainon to choose them because he had that choice, not because it was taken from him in ink or because of the results of a fight that Mydei kept finding excuses to avoid.

“HKS,” Ptolemy tried again and Phainon groaned and flopped backwards off the stool to starfish on the cool floor with a whump. He tried to use the new angle to pet Fig Stew’s belly but the chimera bit him and then Phainon shouted his worst attempt at the expletive yet.

“For Nikador’s sake,” Perdikkas finally cracked, “that’s enough cussing for now!”

“This is important,” Ptolemy insisted.

“How is that important?”

“Do you not want him to be able to pronounce your name correctly?”

Perdikkas was across the room in an instant, tackling Ptolemy around the waist and scooping him up enough to throw him over the balcony and into the bushes below to the soundtrack of raucous laughter. He at least leaned over the edge to make sure Ptolemy was okay. The scholar-warrior must’ve been fine because Perdikkas snorted, clapped his hands together to rid them of dust, and returned to his lunch with a satisfied expression.

It wasn’t the first time someone had been thrown off this balcony. There was a reason Mydei had personally planted bushes down there. He chuckled lightly and raised his cup to Perdikkas in an approving salute who flashed a toothy grin his way.

The only one who was really alarmed was Phainon who scrambled to his feet to charge the railing, barely avoiding going over himself to call out, “Are you okay?”

“’Be strong, saith my heart; I am a soldier; I have seen worse sights than this,’” Ptolemy quoted back and Phainon relaxed.

Phainon who was too nice for his own good. Phainon who had weathered so much more than any one man of high moral standing should have to endure. Truly, he was the hero from the book, the one who Ptolemy most quoted.

“’Much have I suffered, labored long and hard by now in the waves and wars. Add this to the total - bring the trial on,’” Mydei mumbled under his breath, to himself, for himself, as he studied Phainon. The man was strong, physically and emotionally. Intelligent too. It would take him time to adjust to the news but there was no need to baby him, to protect him, and the longer Mydei waited to break the news the worse it would be.

“Did you say something, Mydeimos?” Phainon asked, twisting his head to look his way.

“Yes.”

“I didn’t catch it.”

“Because it was not for you,” he grumbled and hid behind his juice.

Phainon laughed, “keep your secrets then.”

Mydei’s heart twisted uncomfortably. “…Phainon, there’s something-“

“I got the new maps!” Leonnius announced. He jogged into the room with his arms full of giant scrolls. Ptolemy was a few steps behind still picking leaves and debris out of his hair and clothes.

“Well played, Perdikkas,” he said in a low tone, flicking one of the leaves in the doctor’s direction. It obviously didn’t get very far before it fluttered uselessly to the ground to be crushed under Leonnius’ hurried steps.

The runner took the maps to the desk and set them down before dragging the furniture away from the wall about a foot. That’s when Hephaestion got up to pick up the other end, so they didn’t have to endure the screeching protests of an inanimate object dragged across marble. They set it down near the middle of the room where the light was best and where everyone could gather around.

Mydei’s eyes flicked back to Phainon. The man was watching with increasing concern, head tilted, the sky of his eyes alight with curiosity. “Mydei?”

“Another time.” The knot in his chest twisted farther, almost unbearable. He got up to avoid Phainon’s persistence, to focus on this new curiosity. It helped for now, but avoidance wasn’t a long-term solution.

Perdikkas pulled the extra maps to the edge of the desk and held them with one hand to keep them from rolling. Leonnius had found the specific one he felt was most urgent and needed the space. The map smelled like fresh ink just barely dried, and it held itself open without help in the corners.

“This is just around the isle,” Leonnius said as everyone gathered to see, “what the island scouts could confirm and… it’s not good.”

“Fuck…” Perdikkas breathed, and no one called him out for his language. There was no better word for how they were all feeling.

There were two lines dotted on the map to mark the ebb and flow of the Black Tide as it fluctuated around the ocean. At ‘low tide’, it was quite far away, harassing islands too far to be of concern, but at ‘’high tide’… It was reaching the northern part of their isle.

“We have to start evacuating,” Hephaestion said in a whisper.

“That’s not possible. We’re too established here,” Ptolemy argued.

“We did it before when we left Castrum Kremnos,” Perdikkas reminded them.

“No, Perdikkas, we do not have the means to do so. There’s not enough food, not enough ships. We physically do not have the ability to get everyone off this island fast enough.”

“You shouldn’t have to, Ptolemy,” Phainon insisted.

“It was an inevitability,” Mydei said casually, but it did hurt. Moving his people again so soon… where would they even go? How would they even get there? The only place safe from the Black Tide was Okhema.

His thoughts drifted once more to the possibility of dissolving the Kremnoan Dynasty. Perhaps Okhema would accept them then, as refugees. If he personally went before the Goldweaver to negotiate… but after their adventures in piracy, they were more likely to be arrested. If Okhema was willing to arrest their golden boy and put him on trial, what hope was there for the Kremnoan people?

“What about my theory?” Phainon asked.

The Kremnoans looked at each other, puzzled.

“What theory?” Leonnius prodded.

Phainon told them what he had theorized about the nature of the Black Tide. Everything that he had told Mydei the day before on deck.

“Look,” he said as he pointed, “there’s a town right here on this island.” He pointed to a dot on the map, between the two Black Tide lines. The dot was marked in purple, indicating that it belonged to the Black Tide. It fell a little over a year prior, the whole town swallowed up and turned. For a long time, it had been unreachable, and with the way the Tide fluctuated it was rarely free of the black and it still might have been trapped under that corrupting fog. These maps were as accurate as possible but with something so malleable as the Black Tide, there was a chance that only Phainon and Mydei would be able to do anything to quell the swell.

“If we follow the Tide when it retreats and reclaim this island, I think it won’t be able to surge as far when it comes back again.”

“I don’t think that’s how the Black Tide works,” Perdikkas said bluntly.

“We don’t know anything about how the Black Tide works,” Ptolemy huffed.

“We know that every time it comes back it pushes farther,” Leonnius added unhelpfully.

“If it’s just an unstoppable force of nature,” Phainon started, “then why has it slowed down in recent years?”

Perdikkas shook his head, “what are you talking about?”

“I’ve been through all your old maps in the library,” the Deliverer said, “about five years ago the Black Tide’s expansion slowed down.”

Ptolemy stroked his chin. “Leonnius, down the hall-“

“I’m on it.”

Leonnius turned and jogged out of the room.

“I’m not saying you’re wrong, Phainon,” Perdikkas started to say, “I just don’t think it’s as simple as taking a sword to a hurricane.”

“…I better go help him,” Ptolemy grumbled, and he left too.

When they returned it was with way too many maps of various ages. A few were so old they almost crumpled when Mydei reached out to help take them. The paper was yellowed and faded with dark edges from years of handling.

“Careful!” Ptolemy hissed.

They very, very carefully sorted Ptolemy’s hoard by age and started to unroll and lay them on top of each other with the oldest maps on the bottom of the stack. It took all of them (except Peucesta who was still happily adding a suspenseful soundtrack to the room) to delicately layer each sheet and pin down the corners. The curl factor varied based on age so while the newer maps still remembered how to lay flat, the oldest one kept desperately trying to snap back into the scroll shape it was used to.

“Good grief, Ptolemy,” Perdikkas mumbled, “more than half of these are older than you!”

“Don’t start, my collection is about to prove a point.”

“…yeah, Phainon’s point,” Hephaestion observed. He was already flipping through the maps by one corner and just the little bit he could see was making a difference.

“There are more maps here than just what I had on the ship,” Phainon noted. He was preening under the praise, Mydei could tell from the way he carried his shoulders, but he was too focused to gloat.

“I can’t bring my whole collection on board.”

“Not that it hasn’t stopped you from trying,” Leonnius coughed into his hand.

Mydei reached out to gently take the edges of the stack. With Phainon’s help they pulled the layers back and then relayered them one at a time to watch how the Tide had spread throughout the years.

It was daunting to say the least. Stories claimed that the Tide was at least a thousand years old, but their records on the desk only went back about four hundred years. By that point the Tide had spread all throughout the North and was creeping through the ocean, eating civilizations that had almost been entirely forgotten. Even calculating how hard it was to track the Tide accurately, the pattern that emerged was consistently easy to follow.

The Black Tide had spread like a plague unhindered, getting bigger every jump, every new layer showed it spreading until around 80 years prior when it started to slow. The next map after showed stagnation, it wasn’t growing, but it wasn’t retreating either. Mydei went to drop the next map on top when Ptolemy stopped him.

“Wait.”

He reached into one of the drawers and pulled out a few sheets of paper and Mydei tensed. Aglaea’s letter was just underneath that stack, but Ptolemy didn’t see it. He closed the drawer, and the prince was able to breathe again.

Ptolemy tore a strip off the paper and folded it around the edge of that map to mark it and then he gestured for the next one.

The next map was a seven-year jump showing another surge of Black Tide activity. Again, it steadily spread through their rough simulation of the years, until it stopped for a time. Ptolemy marked that map and the next three maps that showed the Tide fluctuating, before they moved on. Anything that seemed out of the ordinary was marked until they again reached the present day.

“A force of nature would not have slowed down,” Leonnius pointed out.

“Or retreated…” Ptolemy mused as he flicked through his tabs and finally settled on the one, he wanted to look at first. Mydei helped him peel back the layers to get to the map from around 40 years back. There were three of them, all penned within a couple years of each other.

Ptolemy flicked between them rapidly to watch the Tide retreat in massive strides. “Do you guys know what this is?” he breathed, quiet, almost disbelieving.

Phainon sucked air in through his teeth. His eyes got wide.

“Kremnoans,” Ptolemy continued with disappointment, “you cannot tell me that the Okheman realized before the rest of you did.”

Mydei took a breath, realizing at the same time as the others as he reached out to run two fingers over a red and gold dotted line. There were notes in the margins, scribbled orders marked by arrows, circled isles, all in familiar handwriting. The air felt heavy.

“The Northern Campaign of King Eurypon,” Mydei said, breathy and tense.

“Krateros blamed the campaign for Eurypon’s corruption,” Hephaestion mused, “but he must have been doing something right.”

Ptolemy pointed to key locations on the map. “This is the isle where Chryseus Leo was recovered.” He flicked between maps to show the isle changing hands between the Black Tide and the Kremnoan army.

“Krateros would remember that campaign,” Perdikkas pointed out, barely above a whisper.

“He wasn’t on that front,” Hephaestion reminded them, “Eurypon had him running the campaign against Okhema at the same time.” The first mate leaned over to point at blue marks on the map, Okheman conflicts towards the South.

Mydei made a mental note to consult with his teacher later. The prince reached out to another tab and flipped through the maps to five years back. The time skips between each flip were not as long so it was easy to watch the Black Tide slowly engulf Castrum Kremnos. Just prior to the death of King Eurypon, the Black Tide was almost entirely stopped. It had been holding constant for several years and then it slowly started to creep forward again, not as fast as it had hundreds of years in the past, but dauntingly consistent.

“Did we do this?” Mydei asked the room in a hushed tone. Two of his fingers rested over the Castrum Kremnos of six years ago, waiting on the line of the Black Tide. Eurypon’s notes were everywhere in increasingly frantic script. Words were misspelled, the ink was thick and spattered where he had broken pens pressing too hard. Most of it was total nonsense. He had been trying to fight the Tide, Okhema, and three other nations at the same time, craving war anywhere he could find it.

“When I killed the old King,” Mydei continued, “did I take away our defense against the Black Tide? Am I the reason Castrum Kremnos was lost?”

It was quiet. No one knew how to answer that.

“Doesn’t matter. Take it back,” Phainon said, “there’s proof right here. Fighting the Black Tide works.” He flipped rapidly through the last five years with his thumb. Before anyone could argue with him, he asked, “When did you guys become pirates and start patrolling?”

“About five years ago, not long after Eurypon’s death,” Ptolemy said.

“Then it’s still working.” Phainon flipped through the sheets again so they could see. “Your patrols are keeping the Black Tide from spreading faster.”

“It’s not enough-“

“Then we make it enough!” Phainon’s energy was infectious. He was firm but excited, eager to make them see that there was hope. “It’s right here! The story of the Tide is right here! No other military force has tried to fight the Black Tide aside from the Kremnoan Dynasty and it was working. The island I mentioned earlier, we can start there, stop trying to slow it and start pushing it back.”

“Phainon, Eurypon went mad fighting the Black Tide,” Perdikkas reminded him, “mad enough to start infighting. He famously came home from the Northern Campaign a changed man. He became obsessed with his role as the inheritor of Strife, started trying to experiment on the Titan, demanding more violence. Mad enough to-“ he cut himself off with a glance towards Mydei.

“To feed his only son to the Sea of Souls,” Mydei finished for him with a nonchalant wave of his hand, “the Black Tide poisoned his mind.”

“Eurypon wasn’t a Chrysos Heir,” Phainon reminded them. Mydei shifted uncomfortably.

“You really think you two are enough to make up for the entire Kremnoan Navy?” Leonnius laughed, “the Kremnoan Navy at the height of its glory?”

“No, but it’s a start, and there are more Chrysos Heirs in Okhema. If we can contact Agla-“

“No,” Mydei cut Phainon off with an urgent growl that had Phainon blinking in surprise.

Hephaestion looked between them with narrowed eyes and then broke the silence himself. “For now, we should test the theory. We take a few islands from the Tide, clear out the monsters and see what happens.”

“We will have to time it right,” Perdikkas pointed out, “for when the Tide is focused elsewhere.”

“Better not feed it more people to turn,” Ptolemy agreed.

Behind them Peucesta twanged his support in a major key.

“It will work,” Phainon reassured them, and it was hard not to believe him, “we’ll save everyone.”

“Who better to try than us?” Leonnius sighed, “only Kremnoans would be this stupid to think we could win against the Black Tide.”

“Well, Kremnoans and one Deliverer,” Peucesta reminded them. Everyone looked over at the musician where he still lay, hair splayed in all directions while he strummed out a melody. “Who better to pick up a mad king’s broken torch, than a collection of fools that bleed red and gold, Kremnoan and Okheman?”

Mydei watched them scatter, invigorated by Peucesta’s words, to begin preparations for their fool’s errand, leaving him alone in the room. He flicked through the map tabs and pushed the layers off until he found the map from around 20 years prior. His father’s handwriting was legible and lacking any signs of physical strain, but his words were radical drivel focused on his reign. He scribbled poems in the margins praising Nikador, begging for the coreflame, for the strength to finish the enemies of Strife while the Black Tide consumed their Northern territories.

He brushed his thumb over the date in the corner. A month after this map was drawn, King Eurypon threw his newborn into the Sea of Souls to appease the Titan of Strife.

With a long sigh through his nose, Mydei covered the map and pulled out the letter that held Phainon’s fate. Phainon, who so desperately wanted to go home, who so desperately wanted to save everyone. The Deliverer of Okhema…

Mydei tossed the letter onto the desk as though it would burn him to hold it any longer. It settled on top, covering part of the Black Tide on the map. Aglaea’s seal glittered like golden blood and Mydei realized something important.

‘They call him Deliverer. From whom do you believe they want to be delivered from?’

Mydei had once selfishly believed Phainon could be their Deliverer, not Okhema’s, but what if that clever lady, ancient as she was, had considered the same.

But then why did the Goldweaver call for the arrest of the person she believed could deliver the world from the Black Tide?

-

Phainon absolutely felt like he had the advantage on land. Something about the predictability of where his feet were landing without the need for micro adjustments to keep his balance. All that training on the ship was paying off at least. It felt like he had so much more stamina as they raced through the town, scouring for Black Tide monsters.

Mydei and Phainon were leading the charge. The Tide had retreated just before action hour and wasn’t expected for another entry hour, so it was safe for the entire detachment to swarm the island. They left behind a few men to protect the ship and everyone else was given orders to raze the place.

This was the third island that they were trying to clear. The other two had felt like a warmup, little more than small villages with only a handful of monsters guarding their shores. They were on the way. This town was much bigger with a population near a thousand. The island had been rich in natural resources and was home to a small mine that would need to be checked before they left.

Phainon had every intention of taking on that task… if he could find it. They didn’t have any maps of the town’s layout so there was some learning on the fly, but Phainon had a good sense of direction and understood how to navigate difficult terrain. Aglaea very frequently chose him for difficult missions in dilapidated places for that exact reason. Who better to handle it then?

The sword in his hand flashed in the afternoon light, blinding a daemon before he leaped through the air with a shout to slice cleanly through its arm. A spin, a slash, and gold and ash gushed from its chest before it crumbled.

246.

In the distance, Mydei’s crystals surged tall enough to be seen over the tops of the buildings. The crimson shattered into dust just as quickly as it had appeared. Phainon whistled. From this far away he didn’t mind openly admiring Mydei’s handiwork.

The captain had been distant the last few days. Embracing the opportunity to unleash everything against the monsters would do him good. When they had leaped off the boat together and raced to get a head start on the other, they had both been grinning.

Phainon was still worried. If he had stayed by Mydei’s side like he wanted to, the captain would’ve undoubtedly scolded him for it. He’d scoff and say something about not needing an Okheman’s help, but there would be mirth in his expression and a lightness to his tone and he’d be right. Even distracted Mydei in combat was wildfire, all-consuming and untamable.

But something about him lately was… off.

They were both in great shape, healed from their injuries, but Mydei kept finding reasons to postpone their duel. Ever since the end of their last voyage, Mydei kept looking at Phainon like he was in pain and then denying it when Phainon tried to point it out and ask what was wrong. All their conversations now were short and professional, keeping only to the topic of the Tide except for one.

Before they fell asleep the night prior, Mydei had called to Phainon from his hammock across the room and told him in all seriousness that he was very happy to stand shoulder to shoulder with him, that he hoped they could continue to fight under the same banner. It had been so soft and so strange that Phainon had to ask Mydei to repeat it.

He had refused and Phainon had laughed and returned the sentiment.

But he still remembered the fear in Mydei’s voice, so subtle in that moment of vulnerability. He remembered the way Mydei had washed his hand, his face, and his back more than a couple weeks prior, the way Mydei had looked in that fort, like he was relieved when Phainon had chosen to stay.

It was a curious thing to feel that want from Mydei. Even if he didn’t say it, Phainon could tell that Mydei wanted more than anything to ask Phainon to stay, to join the crew. This awkward distance that Mydei was keeping felt like he was gathering courage to ask, delaying their fight to buy time, and Phainon was trying to decide how he would answer. It had been a joke at the time, but Phainon meant it when he said Mydei could keep him.

But… he still needed to go home. Okhema needed him, Aglaea needed him, but as Phainon rushed forward and slashed through the heart of a Black Tide blade creature (247), he felt genuinely sad. Out here, Phainon felt like he was saving the world and helping people as he had always dreamed of doing. If this plan to push back the Tide worked, he had every intention of winning the duel, stomping up to Aglaea’s desk and demanding her Navy come to Mydei’s aid.

But that meant convincing Mydei to finish their fight.

Phainon ripped through a pack of three more monsters. That was 250. He wondered how many Mydei was up to and then he was surging forward again.

In the end, Mydei had found and cleared the mine. The monster in there had taken him the better part of several quints to kill which gave Phainon more time to kill the small fry. After a heated argument about how many points the champion was worth, Mydei finally threw his hands up in defeat and let Phainon claim victory this time. A victory that Phainon happily celebrated at dinner with a deep bow and a victory fanfare provided by Peucesta.

With three islands cleared of the Tide, the Kremnoan Detachment plus Phainon retreated to safety at their home port and then it was just a matter of waiting.

A lot of waiting. After failing again to convince Mydei that it was time to finish their fight, Phainon had fallen asleep on a kline with his book over his face. Leonnius sliding around the corner so fast he slammed into the wall was what woke him up.

“Phainon!” Leonnius greeted excitedly. “Where is everybody?”

“Uh, bath house, I think.”

“Phainon, it worked!” the runner said. He was waving a scroll in his hand so animatedly that the poor thing was getting wrinkled and squished where his hand was squeezing it around the middle.

“What worked?”

“Your plan!” Leonnius eagerly unrolled the map across the desk to show Phainon the new Tide line. “It didn’t come back as far. It isn’t much but… Oh wait, there are some lines missing.”

Phainon got up and set his book down on the kline behind him so he could see the map. Leonnius had a spot marked with his finger. “Will you get a pen from the drawer?”

“Which one?” Phainon asked as he started opening them.

“I don’t remember.”

There were three drawers on the desk, all shallow, meant for office supplies. The first drawer was mostly empty aside from some sticks of sealing wax and a seal with the symbol of Strife on it. The second drawer was full of blank stationery. Phainon ran his hand along the back in case the pen and ink had rolled. No luck but the stationery wasn’t laying flat. He lifted the stack to check underneath and froze in place.

Hiding underneath was a folded letter with a broken seal in gold wax. He recognized Aglaea’s emblem immediately. Why did Mydei have a letter from Aglaea?

Phainon felt sick. His stomach had started twisting in loops. He felt dizzy. He didn’t even know what it said, and he already felt like he was going to throw up.

“Phainon? Pen?” Leonnius asked.

“…yeah, right.”

Phainon covered the letter and closed the drawer to fetch the pen from the third. The drawer slid open with a soft squeak and closed with the same sound. He handed Leonnius the pen and tried to focus on the good news as the Kremnoan finished drawing in the line.

“It’s not much, but it’s some,” he said with a grin.

Phainon gave him a strained smile. “I’m glad.”

Leonnius punched him in the shoulder. “Be more excited! You were right! With the right battles and enough people, the Black Tide can be pushed back!”

“I am excited! I’m just tired,” Phainon admitted, “but we should tell the others for sure.”

“Mydei especially will want to know,” Leonnius agreed, “you said they’re at the bathhouse?”

“Yeah.”

“Let’s go tell them!”

Phainon waved him off. “I’ll never be able to keep up with you, go on ahead.”

Leonnius squinted at him, but excitement won in the end and the Kremnoan was zipping out the door before Phainon could change his mind.

Phainon waited until the footsteps faded into the dusk and then the good news morphed again into dread. He took several deep breaths that didn’t work and reached for the drawer again, pausing when his fingertips brushed the knob.

Whatever was in that letter was probably what Mydei wanted to talk about the other day. Where did he even get it? Was it addressed to Mydei himself? Did Aglaea know what was going on this far from the Dawn Device? Why didn’t he share it with Phainon?

Phainon pulled the letter out and put it on the desk. He shakily ran a finger over the seal and then stopped without unfolding it. Breathing was hard. Every inhale felt like someone was sitting on his chest. It felt like he was sinking, spiraling out of control.

No, he trusted Mydei. If this was important, Mydei would have told him about it. He still might. Phainon didn’t know anything about this letter. Speculating would make things worse.

He left the letter there and stepped away from it, walking backwards like it might attack him until he felt the edge of the kline against his legs. Phainon sat down, bowed his head, put one hand on his chest, and just focused on breathing for now.

-

The Kremnoans were in fantastic spirits when they got back to the house, clean, refreshed, and ecstatic. It reminded Mydei of stories of the energy to be had at massive victory feasts of wartime. His boys were tackling each other, punching each other, shouting to everyone that they saw on the street that there was once again hope.

Hope that the Deliverer had brought to them.

Mydei grinned at the thought. Surely the man was losing his mind, happy to be living up to his title, but the house was eerily quiet and Phainon did not get up to greet them. When they came around the corner and saw him on the kline, Mydei’s first thought was that Phainon might be catching ill, and then he saw those blues look up at him above a frown, exhausted and guarded. It was the same expression that Phainon had when he had been made to kneel on the deck while men argued about his fate.

Then he saw the letter on the desk.

“Everyone out,” Mydei said firmly, and the partying stopped.

“Wait, what?” Hephaestion asked.

Perdikkas was looking between Mydei and Phainon with concern.

Leonnius whined, “I just brought you the best news in five years and you-“

“Now.”

Hephaestion threw Leonnius over his shoulder and grabbed Ptolemy’s arm, pulling him along and ushering the others away to leave Mydei and Phainon alone. The protests carried down the hallway until the front door slammed closed and then it was quiet again.

“Did you read it?” Mydei asked softly.

“No.”

His brow furrowed. “Why not?”

“Were you going to tell me?” Phainon asked instead.

They watched each other for a long breath and then Mydei walked to the desk. He picked up the letter and brought it to Phainon, standing over him and offering it. “Yes. I needed to know how I felt first.”

Phainon took it and Mydei could see the nervous tremor in his hands. “And? How do you feel about it?”

Mydei took a deep breath through his nose and then sat down next to Phainon on the kline. “That it doesn’t matter how I feel. It isn’t about me.”

Phainon gave him a puzzled look and then anxiously opened the letter to read it. He kept quiet, reading every line several times before he folded it back up and held the damned thing out to Mydei again. He slouched forward, resting his weight on his elbows on his knees, looking down, his face hidden by his hair.

He wanted to say something, to comfort Phainon, but he wasn’t sure what he could say as he took the paper and set it on the kline between them.

“I’m sorry, Mydei,” Phainon said carefully. It was so quiet, as though speaking any louder might shatter him. “I must retract my challenge to you.”

Mydei’s heart hurt listening to him. Phainon was starting to shake. He covered his face with his hands to hide his soft sobs.

“Deliv- Phainon,” Mydei offered gently, “I wanted-I wanted to extend this invitation to you under better circumstances…”

Was this really the best time? To ask Phainon to join the crew? When he was hurting, reeling from the loss of his homeland, something that Mydei understood all too well? Was it even something that Phainon wanted?

“Would you like to be left alone?” he asked instead.

Phainon was curling in on himself, wrapping his arms tightly around his knees and hiding his face in them to cry.

Mydei extended his hand to touch him but stopped just above his back. It just… didn’t seem right. “Will you promise me that you will still be here in the morning?” he asked.

Phainon nodded without looking up and Mydei respected his privacy and let him be to process his changed reality.

-

Phainon wasn’t sure when he fell asleep, but he woke with tears dried on his lashes and sunlight on his face. He still felt sick and utterly, horribly betrayed.

To read those words in Aglaea’s handwriting…

The letter was scrunched up in his hand, not that he needed it anymore, those words were stitched into the fabric his soul. He sat up, head heavy, and took a couple deep breaths. There was still so much pain, but he started pushing it down as he always had.

There is no room for sulking on my ship.

And, hey, Phainon had wanted fate to intervene to make the decision for him. What was this but fate? Had he not wanted to be of use? To be in the best possible spot to do the most good? Surely this was still okay? Even-Even if he wasn’t their Deliverer anymore, that title had always felt like too much for someone like him. Somehow in all this pain there was a sense of freedom too. Those high expectations were gone, and he could focus on saving the people who needed him most.

So why did Phainon still feel like his heart had been ripped from his chest?

He sighed and got to his feet. None of the others were within eyeshot. The house felt quiet, thoughtful. Phainon wiped his face with his sleeve and wandered the house to find them.

All six of his Kremnoan family were sitting in the dining room that they rarely used, sat around a big table made for too many people. Even Fig Stew was sitting at the head of the table, watching the Okheman with bright eyes. They looked at Phainon expectantly when they noticed him, and Leonnius sprang up to pull out a chair for him.

“Please,” he whispered when Phainon hesitated and he slowly sat down.

“Mydei told us about the letter,” Hephaestion started, “and we talked about it.”

“You guys don’t have to-“ Phainon started but Mydei held up his hand and shook his head.

“We talked it through and even if you do not accept, we consider you a part of the crew,” Mydei said, “and we look out for our own. One’s home is important, and we want you to be able to return to yours.”

“That’s not possib-“

Again, Phainon was cut off. This time by Ptolemy, “I looked it up. We are going to buy you a pardon.”

Phainon felt dumbfounded by the idea. There was nothing that the Council of Elders, that Aglaea, would accept in exchange for something so valuable except-

“We decided we’re going to Castrum Kremnos,” Hephaestion told him.

“When we send you back to Okhema,” Mydei said with a wild look in his eye and a reassuring smile, “it will be with the Coreflame of Strife in your hands.”

Chapter End Notes

Just so you guys know. My original outline planned for 19 chapters. The events of THIS chapter were originally the end of Chapter 5. Two things we learn from this: 1. I grossly underestimated my ability to yap. 2. This is going to be a long fic. I am so, so sorry.

chapters.title: Chapter 17: Heading Home
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

New Character Tag: Cipher

Chapter Notes

Should I put gambling in the tags? With all these silly boys making bets I'm wondering if I should xD

This was a dream. It had to be. Phainon genuinely could not think of another explanation for what he was hearing. The Coreflame of Strife aside, they were just… adopting him? On the spot? And what was this about a pardon? Did Okhema even give those?

Phainon reached up with one hand to rub his temple. The room was quiet while he processed. The other men ranged from nervous to resolute, even Mydei looked anxious at the silence.

Mydei who was so much more expressive than people realized. Who wore his feelings just underneath that thin, guarded layer, so that people who loved him enough to look could read him as easily as he seemed to do for others. Phainon could see that worry in the curve of his brow, the way he was second guessing his announcement in the twitch of his eye, the way he was watching Phainon, unblinking like a wild animal that he desperately wanted to befriend.

This was a lot to process on top of everything he had learned last night. Phainon’s whole world had flipped upside down with a single crumpled page and now these people were jumping to try and fix it for him. It felt so surreal.

“Phainon?” Perdikkas tried. The doctor was looking at Phainon with a soft, reassuring smile. “Maybe we should have waited until you were more awake.”

“No… no this is okay. It’s just a lot,” Phainon admitted.

“We think the soldiers from the fort must have reported what they saw,” Hephaestion theorized, “when you defended us and stayed behind, they didn’t know you were with us against your will.”

That made sense. It hurt, but it made sense. Phainon hadn’t thought to send a message with his countrymen. In retrospect, that seemed like a silly oversight. Why didn’t he send a message the second time either? All that planning and he was so focused on making sure everyone was safe, Phainon didn’t once consider what it looked like to see him, their hero, helping pirates.

“I did some digging through the library,” Ptolemy said, taking the floor. His eyes were a little too wide and dark, like he had yet to sleep. “And there is historical precedent for pardons as decided by the Goldweaver and the Council of Elders. Usually because of some heroic deed or a big donation. Bribe,” he coughed into his hand and mumbled around that last word, “We don’t have any treasure we can send with you, but it would be hard to say no to one of her missing coreflames and slaying a Titan is a heroic feat.”

Phainon shook his head, “Fighting a Titan is… and Castrum Kremnos is in the middle of the Black Tide.”

“Yes, but we proved your theory which means it’s possible,” Hephaestion reminded him.

“Taking back Castrum Kremnos would be a major victory in the war against the Tide,” Mydei pointed out, “it would be forced to retreat farther than it has since the time of Eurypon.”

“There’s also a chance that the Tide has corrupted the Titan,” Perdikkas theorized, “maybe even as far back as when Eurypon first returned from the North. Imagine how deep of a blow that would be to fell such a major piece.”

Phainon shook his head. “It’s so dangerous, that’s too much effort to go through for me.”

“We’d be doing it for all of us,” Leonnius insisted.

“Deliverer,” Mydei called and Phainon flinched at the name, “what do you want?”

The room was quiet as Phainon bowed his head to think. The wood grain on the table was lovely.

“…I don’t know,” he admitted, “I think I just want to help everyone, however I can.”

“Well, we want you to have the option to go home,” Perdikkas announced. The others nodded. “So you get to help us, help you.”

“Not to be the messenger of bad news but since that is my job, how the hell are we supposed to get the coreflame?” Leonnius asked, “Castrum Kremnos isn’t a small town on an island.”

“No human navy has ever been able to lay siege to Castrum Kremnos,” Hephaestion mused.

“Even if we got every single remaining Kremnoan to go with us, there’s no way we could clear the city. That deep in the Black Tide, we couldn’t even step off the ship,” Leonnius reminded them.

“Pushing back the Tide is working,” Perdikkas suggested, “we just keep pushing it back until we get home.”

“We’d all be in our sixties by the time we get there,” Hephaestion groaned, “that’s not an option.”

“I will go alone,” Mydei offered.

“No,” Phainon said too quickly, “I can’t ask you to do that.”

“Deliverer, this is happening,” the prince snapped, “do not reject our efforts to care for you, lest you offend us.”

“I’ll go with you.” There was a long silence before Phainon continued, “we both have golden blood, and we are both admirable warriors and… you shouldn’t have to face a Titan alone.”

“Assuming you get that far,” Leonnius bummed them all out once more, “population turned monsters aside, Nikador’s Titankin fill the inner city. Two people cannot do it alone, gold blood or not. I’m just saying, are we sure a strongly worded endorsement from the Crown Prince explaining that Phainon isn’t a pirate won’t work?”

“I’m sure the Goldweaver would love that,” Ptolemy mocked, “Don’t worry Miss Goldweaver, we promise he’s still a good person, you can trust the Kremnoan pirates.”

Phainon still felt heavy, grief still lingered, but the little ray of hope that they were trying to give him was thawing the ice in his veins. That they were here and even trying spoke volumes. Mydei was willing to go alone for Phainon.

How could he even begin to be worthy of such a gesture? Even his own people rejected their Deliverer. What could he hope to be for these people?

“You know, you never actually asked,” Phainon realized out loud, and the room quieted to look at him. Peucesta wasn’t even playing the lyre, they were so focused on him.

Phainon looked up at Mydei specifically, “you never actually asked me if I wanted to join your crew.”

Mydei’s eyes widened by a fraction and then he looked down and away. His hand was on Fig Stew’s belly, scratching with new purpose now to distract himself while the chimera purred loud enough to feel through the table. The others were doing some variation of the same, avoiding eye contact. Peucesta’s lyre plucked nervously, switching to a minor key while Leonnius picked at his chiton. Hephaestion crossed his arms and drummed his fingers, Perdikkas was trying to sink in his chair, and Ptolemy was suddenly very into artwork, studying the painting across the room from himself.

“Were you afraid I would say no?” Phainon asked.

“Would you have?” Mydei asked.

“No.”

The relief in the room was instant. Everyone was trying to hide their smiles. Ptolemy whispered something under his breath in Kremnoan that was too obscure for Phainon to recognize. Leonnius leaned back in his chair with both his hands behind his head.

“It hurts,” Phainon admitted, “knowing that I can’t go home. It’s not even the first time this has happened, but I woke up already accepting it. The last time I lost everything it took too long for me to find myself; it took Aglaea to make me a person again and I owe her my life for that. It would dishonor her for me to step backwards into that shell that I once was. But-“ he started to cry again. The tears beaded in the corners of his eyes, threatening to spill over as he held his chest, twisting his fingers in the fabric of his shirt as though he could claw out his own aching heart. “-I didn’t expect to feel like I was already home here. I don’t want people to sacrifice themselves for me, trying to restore something that I don’t-that I don’t need anymore.”

Tears weren’t a foreign concept to Kremnoans but emotional vulnerability like that was close. No one moved or said anything except for Leonnius who flailed a little awkwardly trying to decide what to do with his hands. What could they possibly say? Call him a bad name, punch his shoulder, and scold him? That did seem to be the popular Kremnoan response but they kept their silence this time in silent processing.

It was Fig Stew who decided to take charge. The chimera got up, grabbed Mydei’s finger gently in his teeth, and pulled until the prince had to stand up as he was dragged around the table, awkwardly climbing over other Kremnoans on his way to Phainon. Fig put his front paws on Phainon’s bicep so he could reach up and place Mydei’s hand right on top of that ahoge.

Both men shared the same alarmed expression, frozen. They didn’t know what to do until Fig Stew sat in front of Phainon on the table and put his paw on his own head to teach them the proper comforting etiquette here. Unwilling to argue with the chimera, Mydei relented and Phainon felt the tears spill over as that warm hand gently pet his head, eventually getting bold enough to run his fingers deeper through snowy hair, to massage gently at his scalp with comforting presses.

Mydei eased into it, half leaning, half sitting against the table so he wouldn’t be hiding in the Okheman’s blind spot while he provided that physical comfort. Fig Stew scooted forward and leaned in close to lick those shed tears from Phainon’s face with a rough tongue until Phainon’s hands gently wrapped around the animal to hug him. He melted into that touch, relaxing with half-lidded eyes into Fig’s fur.

It bought enough time for Hephaestion to find his words. “Phainon, our home was taken from us too. We chose to leave, but it was only easy to do so because that choice to return was still there. Even when we swore ourselves to self-exile and thought that door was closed, we didn’t understand the true loss until that choice was completely gone.” He drummed his fingers on the table and then crossed his arms. “We want you to stay, I think every single one of us wants that and we had planned to ask, we just wanted to invite you join us when you could make that choice for yourself. So no, none of us are asking yet, not officially, not until you get the chance you deserve. We want to take this risk for you and for us. So put that crazy optimistic brain of yours to work and help us figure out how to do the impossible.”

The hand in his hair didn’t let up until Phainon pulled away from Fig Stew to look up at Mydei. The Prince was looking down with wide eyes, curious, concerned, and a little bit afraid. He pulled his hand back when it looked like Phainon was feeling a little better and let out a breath through his nose. Pink had crept into his cheeks and chest and Phainon felt the heat rush to his own cheeks and ears at the closeness.

Rather than go back to his own seat, Mydei took the empty chair on the other side of Phainon, settling with a soft hrumph and crossed arms. Fig Stew stayed where he was, loafing comfortably with his eyes closed and Phainon’s hand resting on his back to give scritches between his shoulder blades.

A way to do the impossible… The biggest hurdle wasn’t Nikador. It was the Black Tide corruption. Leonnius was right, the biggest navy in the world wouldn’t be able to take Castrum Kremnos because it was entirely under the black. The only people that could safely get through that would be Chrysos Heirs. Phainon had a lot of faith in himself and Mydei. The Kremnoan was even immortal which could only work in their favor, but two of them against an entire city? Even if they tried to sneak in, they would need someone skilled in stealth or someone who could pacify any hoards that they couldn’t handle themselves… people like…

“I have an idea,” Phainon said.

Peucesta held his hand out across the table and Ptolemy angrily slapped a pair of coins into his open palm.

“But I don’t think you guys are going to like it.”

Peucesta slowly slid one of the two coins back towards Ptolemy.

“I’m not worried about being outnumbered,” Phainon admitted, “you guys are experienced Kremnoans after all. I’ve studied Kremnos fighting styles and I’ve seen Krateros with the crew. The crew could handle Titankin and monsters in any number given the right strategy and positioning.”

“Black Tide,” Leonnius coughed into his fist.

“Yeah, we need more Chrysos Heirs.”

Ptolemy laughed, “sure! We’ll just go to the market and pick up a few, Phainon be serious.”

“Our options are recruit Chrysos Heirs and go after Nikador with a small strike team,” Phainon said, “or we recruit a big enough Navy to push back the tideline. The only navy left in Amphoreus big enough to do that is the Okheman Fleet.”

“Either way, Okhema is involved,” Perdikkas lamented, “the only known Chrysos Heirs are under the Goldweaver’s care. She’d have our prince too if she had her way.”

“This is good news,” Phainon proclaimed. His cheer was coming back. He still ached, it would take time for that to go away completely, but having a purpose was helping. Having a purpose that helped the people he cared about was helping a lot. Mydei’s leg was pressed against Phainon’s under the table, anchoring him, giving him courage and comfort. Difficult didn’t mean impossible, and that was Phainon’s favorite kind of challenge.

He pressed back against Mydei and said, “I know all the Okheman Chrysos Heirs they’re still family. Given the chance, I could convince them to help.”

“Convince them to team up with Kremnoan pirates? While you have an active warrant for your arrest?” Ptolemy was still skeptical.

“Castorice and Hyacine would help for sure. Cipher can be paid off.”

“Paid off with what?” Lack of sleep was catching up to Ptolemy for sure the way his voice rasped and his eloquence fled.

“The treasury at Castrum Kremnos is untouched,” Mydei thought aloud, “this Cipher would be welcome to it if they offered their services.”

“But can we trust them? Wouldn’t they have the same oath to the Goldweaver that you have, Phainon?” Hephaestion asked.

“That’s why they’ll agree,” Phainon argued. Fig Stew gave a warning growl when his excitement led to a particularly rough squeeze. He apologetically patted the chimera. “Because we’re going after a coreflame.”

“Why can’t we ask the Goldweaver directly then?” Leonnius asked, “the whole goal is to buy Phainon’s pardon with the coreflame, so why not just tell her that and get her help first?”

“We’d be arrested before we even get the chance,” sighed Perdikkas, “and intention, actionable or not, isn’t the same as having the coreflame in hand ready to trade.”

“Even with her golden threads that know every truth,” Pecuesta agreed, finally weighing in, “she is no Queen.”

“Even if Aglaea-“ Phainon cut himself off thinking about her. The woman that he trusted, the woman that was demanding his arrest in the first place, who first called him Deliverer now considered him a pirate. “-um, even if Aglaea supported our mission, she would have to arrest us and take us to the Council. She can’t know what we’re doing.”

“You don’t think the other Heirs would tell her?” Perdikkas asked.

“I don’t and we need them. Castorice is the Demigod of Death, just her presence makes Black Tide monsters and Titankin sluggish, she’s a one-person army, and Hyacine is a healer. When I left, she was researching the Black Tide corruption and how to resist or even reverse it. She could be the key to letting all of you fight beside us without golden blood.”

Hephaestion uncrossed his arms to point at Phainon, wagging that finger up and down. “That would be worth it. Even if we couldn’t help you fell the Titan, we could keep the city busy if we didn’t need to fear the corruption.”

“Listen to yourselves for a moment,” Ptolemy whined. Bro needed to go to bed. “We would have to go to Okhema, sneak into the holy city, find these Chrysos Heirs, convince them to join our Kremnoan pirate crew, take them to Castrum Kremnos, our homeland that is drowning in Black Tide creatures and our own fallen Titankin army, so that we can sneak our Crown Prince and our former prisoner of war to the arena where they are going to fight and kill our god so we can then go back to Okhema to buy a pardon so Phainon can just have the option to go home? An option that we all want him to reject? Because we think it will make him feel better?”

“Yes.”

“Yep.”

“Mrreow!”

A single happy twang from a lyre.

“Absolutely.”

“Correct.”

Phainon shyly resumed petting Fig Stew.

They made it sound like Phainon’s feelings; his autonomy was the most important part of this scheme. It was humbling. It wasn’t like that was the only reason why they were braving such a feat. As they had pointed out, defeating Nikador could potentially push the Black Tide farther back than it had been in six years. Reclaiming Castrum Kremnos was not only an emotional and symbolic action, but a strategic one as well. If they did their job well enough, maybe Mydei’s people could also go home.

It wasn’t just Phainon’s choice that was the prize here. Everyone could win and the Coreflame of Strife was the ultimate bargaining chip not just for Phainon’s pardon, but for peace. It was a gift in good faith that could demand a place at the table, an audience with the Council and Aglaea, to officially end the war between their peoples. While they planned to press that coreflame into Phainon’s hands, Phainon was plotting on his own, to hand it to Mydei, to personally escort him to Aglaea, not as a pirate to be imprisoned, but as the Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos, representative of his people. That coreflame would pardon them all and usher in a new era of collaboration against the Tide.

Ptolemy pressed his hands together like he was praying, both elbows stretched across the table as he leaned over it. He breathed in sharply through his nose and pressed his hands to his lips before letting it all out in a long exhale. With a voice bordering on unhinged ferality he asked, “What are we waiting for?”

-

Mydei didn’t realize how much he enjoyed nighttime until there was no longer any nighttime. Honestly, only Phainon seemed unbothered by the unchanging sky under the influence of the Dawn Device. He was the only one on the whole ship that was able to sleep comfortably after the bright thief star would dash across the blue to announce the curtain-fall hour. The man saw the star, yawned, wished everyone good night and crashed, just like that.

How the hell did he do that?

Even Fig Stew was having a hard time getting comfortable. He constantly protested by making laps around Mydei’s hammock, leaving little scratches on his chest and belly in the process. Every time the chimera started to settle, he’d growl, mewl, and reposition, which might’ve woken Mydei up if he hadn’t already been awake the whole damn time because of that sunlight directly on his eyelids.

Inheriting the wealth of a nation via royal birth had nothing on the riches a curtain salesman must have from peddling his wares in Okhema. This was horrible and everyone was feeling it.

By day three, Mydei found members of the crew cannibalizing old clothes to make blindfolds for sleeping and nailing scrap sail canvas to the windows and portholes. Everyone had matching bags under their eyes. Hephaestion had passed out in the galley at one point, narrowly avoiding wearing his meal. Ptolemy was found willingly buried from the waist up in the library, finally sleeping in the shade of many suspiciously stacked books. Mydei knew they were in trouble when Krateros nodded off at the tiller and had to catch himself with the most frayed and head empty expression he had ever seen.

And all the while, the crew dog was as cheerful as ever.

Phainon was covering all the sleepy slack by himself. The lunatic was up early, rushing to help deliver breakfast, work the lines, clean the deck, cook dinner, even offering to cover other tasks so folks could take longer breaks. He never stopped moving and he never stopped smiling.

Mydei could tell he was suffering. He could hear it at ‘night’ when Phainon slept. Those tearless sobs and broken whines kept soft, even in sleep not wanting to disturb anyone that may hear him and be bothered by the noise. He was no stranger to nightmares himself so, sometimes, Mydei would get up and pet him to soothe those troubled thoughts, running his fingers through Phainon’s hair as Fig Stew had suggested and it would ease his sleep. Phainon was so responsive to gentle touches, just subtle reminders that he wasn’t alone.

And it wasn’t like Mydei was sleeping anyway with that fucking light turned on all the fucking time. Surely the Dawn Device had a lever or a wheel that could switch the thing off for a few hours?

Even when Phainon was awake and bouncing between people, chattering about how beautiful Okhema was and how you could see Kephale from so far away, and all those other fun facts that he had ready to go at the drop of a hat, there was misery there. Mydei could see it. Maybe it was because he was looking for it, but he could feel it most when they sparred. That pain was buried deep in the way Phainon’s banter felt flat and his swings were stiff. When Mydei’s claws cut a little too close and he didn’t take advantage of a stumble, the prince knew for sure. For all his outward excitement, Phainon was still trying to cope with the changes.

The closer they got to Okhema the more Mydei worried how Phainon would react. It couldn’t be easy to face this wound so soon after the knife had cut and twisted, but he seemed calm and focused when they finally weighed anchor in a sheltered cove a short walk from the holy city.

The bow was covered with the black sheet, and they took down their Kremnoan flag, choosing to fly no colors at all rather than go all in on the pirate costume that would give them away. They were far enough away to buy themselves time before discovery, out of immediate eyeshot and hopefully away from all but the most thorough of patrols.

Phainon had insisted that years of relative peace had made Okhema lazy and lax. This close to the city they were unlikely to find anyone particularly attentive as long as they didn’t draw attention to themselves. Which meant everyone, even around the deck, was dressed as plainly as possible. No visible armor, no obvious weapons, if anyone asked, they were a merchant ship waiting for orders from their captain and they would not allow any inspections until said captain returned from the market.

Mydei thought Phainon looked cute in disguise, standing by the railing, excitedly searching for the best path to get to the road once they made it ashore. Even with the hood of the heavy cloak pulled up his white bangs and brilliant blue eyes still showed brightly. He was a man meant for the spotlight, even hiding under rough dark linen.

“You cannot all go,” Mydei huffed. He and Phainon were matching looks standing there, waiting for the longboat. Mydei wasn’t comfortable going without his gauntlets and familiar wear, so he also slapped the cloak on top and called it a day, the same way Phainon was hiding his own armor.

The exact same cloaks that all five of his fellow Kremnoans were wearing as they fanned around him expectantly.

“What happens if you need back up?” Hephaestion asked and Mydei pointed right at him.

“You must stay because if Krateros is left in charge he will have declared war by morning.”

“Aw, sorry Hephaestion,” Leonnius said, “we’ll bring you back something from the market.” The other four shuffled forward and Mydei had to hold his hands out, spread wide to stop them.

“No. Only two of you may come with us,” he huffed, “a large group will be harder to hide.”

“Obviously I need to go in case one of them gets hurt,” Perdikkas argued.

“Don’t even start, you’re too slow,” Leonnius huffed.

Peucesta raised his lyre, itchy to argue with music but realized very quickly that the instrument likely would not help his case. He tucked it back under his cloak and tried creeping past Mydei instead, but Ptolemy yanked him back.

“We do this fairly, by chance,” he growled, and then Ptolemy was fishing around in his pockets. He pulled out a crumpled piece of paper, double checked that it wasn’t anything important and tore it into four strips that he then rolled into tight straws. Two of them he tore short and two he left long, then he mixed them together between his hands and hid their lengths behind his palm.

“Short stays, long goes, agreed?” he asked while offering just the tops of the straws to them. The other three nodded and all reached to grab one, snatching them up quickly and holding out the results.

Perdikkas grabbed a short slip, he would have to stay. He seemed more resigned than disappointed. It was hard to argue with chance after all.

Leonnius pulled long. He hissed a soft, “yessss” to celebrate and crumpled the paper in his fist.

Peucesta frowned and flicked the short slip back at Ptolemy. No field trip for the bard. His lyre twanged uselessly from under his cloak, muffled and pathetic at best.

But Ptolemy’s slip had been plucked from his hands at the same time as the others’. He stood there puzzled, trying to determine who had accidently grabbed two slips, stealing what he now knew was the second long slip.

“Oh my~ Does this mean I get tag a long?” purred a feminine voice. Standing beside them in the circle as relaxed as though she was meant to be there was a lean woman with a long tail. She waved the last slip of paper between them all, pinched between long nails painted gold. “That is what the long one means, right~?”

The ship erupted at once as Kremnoans fumbled to find weapons and turned on the woman on deck. Trying to stay under the radar left most of them with nothing bigger than a combat knife. Mydei reached to contain her on instinct, but Phainon dashed between them all, putting himself squarely in front of her with his hands held out wide and a shout on his lips.

“Must be my lucky day,” she crooned around a bouncy giggle, “a whole ship of wound springs and one missing puppy.”

“This is Cipher, she’s one of the Chrysos Heirs,” Phainon hurriedly told everyone, but the Kremnoans didn’t relax. Mydei rolled his fingers, trying to assess the threat.

Cipher was the Heir that Phainon had mentioned before. The one that could be paid to help them. She… wasn’t what he expected.

Cipher was dressed like a thief, wearing a hood that left space to cover her cat ears and a skintight body suit and thigh highs with just enough ribbons and flair to advertise the Goldweaver’s handiwork. She had gray hair that was barely long enough to extend past her hood and blue-green eyes that rivaled Phainon’s for clarity. Her tail was dark brown at the tip, fading into the gray of her fur that predictably matched the fur around her ears. It lazily swayed back and forth, held in an elegant curve to keep it from dragging across the deck. The tip of it kept twisting in tight curls like a question mark.

How in Nikador’s name did she get on board?

“Geez, brat, if you’re going to name drop at least do it with some pizzaz.” Her voice had a permanent roll to it, like a purr under the playful lilt of her words. It made every word sound like a tease, like a piece of cheese dangling in front of a mouse, both tantalizing and suspicious.

“Try something like Cipher the magnificent, or Cipher, the greatest of all thieves~!” She held her hands out to the side and slowly turned to show off her curves. “Or there’s the obvious, Cipher, the Demigod of Trickery!”

Nobody moved.

“Tough crowd, and after I won fair and square!” she purred as she waved the little strip of paper back and forth.

The tension was thick enough to cut with a knife and Cipher was swimming in it like a fish. She was the only one that didn’t seem even slightly bothered to be at the pointy end of a nervous Kremnoan Detachment.

“I really hit the jackpot finding you, Deliverer boy,” Cipher went on, ignoring the boring Kremnoans, even as they pushed in a little closer to try and corner her. Mydei could see Hephaestion trying to slowly shift towards the rail, watching the flank in case she tried to bolt. Ptolemy was trying to match him on the other side.

She put a hand on Phainon’s shoulder and spun in a circle around his arm as though she were dancing to swoon and drop in front of him. He predictably hurried to catch her. “Seamstress has been looking alllll over for you.” The cat walked two fingers up his chest and booped his nose and Mydei instantly felt angry. “She misses her favorite.”

“Miss Cipher-“ Phainon started to say but Mydei cut him off.

The prince surged forward to grab her, but she saw him coming from the corner of her eye and sprang over Phainon, vaulting over his shoulders to hide behind her fellow Okheman. Mydei barely stopped himself from hitting his friend.

“Easy, gold-hair, I’m not here for you~”

“You can’t be here for me either, Cipher,” Phainon told her. He turned around and stepped back to be beside Mydei.

The prince fought not to show how much the action filled him with joy and pride. Having Phainon beside him felt right, no matter who they were facing, friend or foe, this was how it should be.

She blinked, genuinely surprised by his serious tone.
