“Because we actually came here for you,” he said with a grin, that playful tone was back.

Cipher tilted her head back and laughed, at least, it kind of sounded like a laugh. She looked like she was laughing but that sound was closer to the dying cackle of a starving animal.

“Color me intrigued, golden boy,” she purred again, “how about we put down the prickly pieces and you can try to convince me why I shouldn’t take you back to our favorite motherly control freak.”

Phainon turned in place to look at Mydei with a soft, begging look. Those eyes glittered in the light, imploring, trust me.’ And he did.

Mydei turned enough to raise his hand and slowly lowered it, signaling to the crew to put their weapons down. They reluctantly did so, everyone still watching this cat woman carefully.

“Because I know you, master of mischief,” Phainon said with a playful tilt of his head and lilt in his voice, “and you of all people wouldn’t want to miss out on this.”

Chapter End Notes

I have been so excited to play Cipher. I know she shows up in HSR when Phainon is already crashing out, but I like to believe that in a world where she is more around, that they have a good rapport.

chapters.title: Chapter 18: The Protective and Perceptive Nature of Big Sisters
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

New character tag: Castorice

Phainon is a good boy with a big destiny but he's still the family baby and Mydei's about to learn what love means to one of them

Chapter Notes

Now that we're 100k words in I can really get started on the plot! :D

“What’s your plan to sneak past the seamstress?” Cipher asked.

“She should be asleep,” Phainon said as he stepped off the longboat and onto soft sand.

“You really think she’s been able to sleep worrying so much about you?”

Getting Cipher to agree to their crazy plan was easy. Phainon knew that all he’d have to say was ‘treasure,’ ‘Kremnos,’ and ‘this might be crazy but…’ and the cat was in. He didn’t even have to give her all the details of his awkward imprisonment and the experiments he had been doing on the Black Tide with their city’s mortal enemies. She was shockingly chill with those last two words, not even blinking when he introduced Mydei to her.

Cipher was a complex person in that she kept enough secrets to maintain a layered persona. There was a depth to her that Phainon knew was there but had never personally uncovered. The light-hearted and jovial prankster that had stood by Aglaea’s side every second that he had known the two of them was the only version she had ever shared with Phainon. And that side was predictable and agreeable as long as one knew what buttons to push.

The only hiccup he had anticipated was Cipher’s closeness to Aglaea. Cipher was old. Not quite Aglaea old but old enough and traveled enough to have built an airtight relationship with the Goldweaver. Aglaea had taken them both in when they were young, finished raising them, and gave them purposes on her flame chase journey. It made Cipher like Phainon’s much older sister where Aglaea was like their aunt that stepped up to mother them when things went south.

Phainon thought that ‘behind Aglaea’s back’ would be the phrase that made her walk away, but Cipher had purred at the idea instead and readily agreed. She was even leading their small group of four down the path towards Okhema herself, with her hips swinging back and forth with every step like she hadn’t just cracked Phainon’s resolve in sing-song a quint prior.

Aglaea was worried about him? Enough to lose sleep?

It was crushing to consider, especially with her written words still bouncing around in his head. Yeah, Aglaea was so worried she wants him arrested? He had a hard time reconciling both statements. If Phainon had a child out there committing crimes he’d be worried too but the image of Aglaea worrying at all was the hard part to picture. She wasn’t very expressive. But if anyone would know how Aglaea was feeling, it would be Cipher, who could read hearts and intentions at a glance and who was very near and dear to their Admiral.

The only other Chrysos Heir that was close enough to Aglaea to know how she really felt about something was Tribbie and hopefully all three triplets were also asleep at this late hour. If one of the triplets caught them sneaking into the city, no one would be sleeping anymore.

“Cipher,” Phainon asked as they walked up a hill to join the dromas road, empty at this late hour, “has Aglaea not been sleeping?”

“That’s still bothering you?” she cackled, “afraid of getting caught? Even if she is asleep her threads are all over the city, you’d have to be a chimera to get past them.”

Phainon could feel the Kremnoans behind him tensing up. Sweat started to bead at Phainon’s brow, and he pulled the hood down a little lower over his eyes. That wasn’t why he had asked, but perhaps Cipher wasn’t the best person to talk to about his worries. Aglaea was strong, she didn’t need Phainon fussing over an off-handed comment from a known trickster.

“Is there no way to sneak into the city unseen?” he asked instead.

“Oh, there are lots of ways,” she crooned. Cipher leapt onto the top of the waist-high wall along the road to walk along that narrow edge. Even in her heels she had perfect balance.

“Even from Tribbie?” Phainon asked.

“Oh, the big sis trio aren’t even in the city.”

“What?”

She paused to look back at Phainon. Every time he stopped the Kremnoans did too, bunching in close behind him to peek over each other’s shoulders in a line.

“All three of them have been flying allll over Amphoreus looking for your silly ass. They’ll owe me big for finding you first.”

Phainon’s heart twisted. Even the triplets were looking for him? He should have tried to send a message to them sooner, to reassure them. Maybe he could find a chance to write a letter while they were here, to try and start explaining things.

They started walking again.

“Not to be the voice of reason when Ptolemy is here,” Leonnius said from the end of the line, “but how are we getting into the city around the threads?”

“We can destroy them as we go,” Mydei suggested, “as we do at sea.”

“No news is still news,” Ptolemy sighed, “she will notice their absence will she not?”

“Phainon, how did you plan on getting around them in the first place?” asked Leonnius.

“Um…”

Cipher lost it, she was barely able to breathe, she was wheezing so hard. Disproportionately hard. No one else was laughing. “You weren’t, were you?”

“Deliverer.” Mydei grabbed Phainon’s shoulder, hard enough to stop him from walking, to make him turn to see the truth of it in his eyes.

Phainon held both his hands up in a gesture of surrender. With the hood pushing his bangs so much farther down his face, any reassuring smiles were coming out awkward and unconvincing. “I don’t think it’s possible to get around them entirely,” he admitted, “but if we move fast enough-“

“And what if the Goldweaver is awake?” Ptolemy asked, “we should go back to the ship for now, make a new plan.”

“We don’t have time for that,” Leonnius pointed out, “not that we’d even be able to tell with the sky barely changing.”

“Leonnius is right,” Mydei agreed, “Okheman patrols will find the Chryseus Leo before we have time to formulate an effective plan with the time to execute it. We must determine a route now.”

It felt really bad knowing he had put them in a tricky situation. Phainon could hear the trepidation in Mydei’s voice. It was so, so subtle, but it was there. This was Phainon’s home, surely, he could think of something?

“How badly do you want that silly piece of candy buried deep in Castrum Kremnos?” Cipher crooned. She stepped off the wall to sit on it instead, swinging her leg up in a wide arc to cross her knees, both of her paws resting over them in a misleadingly demure posture.

“The what?” Leonnius asked.

“She’s talking about the coreflame,” Ptolemy hissed.

Phainon immediately thought of the crew and the people of Castrum Kremnos, of peace within reach. He stepped towards her to answer but she yawned loudly and held her hand up.

“I already heard your pitch back at the deck, Deliverer brat. I wanna hear from mister royal lion here.”

Phainon stepped back to look at Mydei. Shining amber eyes were narrowed at Cipher from under his hood, but he answered, “I have already promised you the treasury of Kremnos. Is that not enough?”

She got up and sauntered up to him. “He must not have told you very much about me and my bottomless greed.” Cipher stretched, catlike, both of her arms outstretched to reach past Mydei’s shoulders before she relaxed, letting her forearms fall on either side of his neck to smoothly pull in closer to him. “I want the truth too.”

“I would pay as many of my lives as it takes to retrieve that coreflame,” Mydei said firmly. He made no move to push her away. Even when she ran a hand down his chest and shifted her weight against him, he was stoic, controlled, and unintimidated.

Phainon instantly was annoyed and his smile faltered. Her eyes darted in his direction, and their gazes met for half a second. That’s when she pushed herself away, keeping a hair’s width between herself and Mydei so she could still judge the Kremnoan up close.

“That’s a lofty price for something you’re just giving away.”

“It’s worth it. I want my crew to be happy.”

Cipher must have seen something surprising because the smile faded for a few seconds before she stepped away with a knowing cackle. “That’s gross. I’ll help you get in, buy you time, I’ll even keep the Goldweaver busy until your horribly disguised ship can get underway. But if anyone ever asks-” she chuckled, “I’m the one who found you first.”

And then she disappeared.

-

Mydei’s opinion of Cipher kept bouncing back and forth. He didn’t particularly care if she was overly friendly, she wasn’t really threatening, and Phainon seemed to like her. But she was snarky, sneaky, and her teasing felt like it was teetering on the edge of being malicious. She hadn’t done anything aside from randomly appear in the first place so it would be unfair to draw any lines, but he didn’t care all that much when Cipher vanished.

His gut reaction was, good riddance, until Mydei counted their posse a man short. Phainon was missing now too.

All three Kremnoans went wide-eyed, looking at the spot where he had been a moment ago. Nothing was left of him aside from a pair of footprints in the dust.

“What just happened?” Leonnius asked, breathy and tense.

“That’s a fantastic question~!” Cipher purred from behind him, “let’s find out together!”

Before Mydei could throw crystals in her direction, his fastest runner vanished at the same time as Cipher, once again leaving behind only footprints and a deepening sense of unease.

“Ptolemy.”

They immediately took up positions, back-to-back, the scholar holding his combat knife, blade twisted backwards, to rest along his forearm. Mydei let his gauntlets click as he rolled his fingers.

“She must be taking them somehow,” the scholar theorized, swapping to Kremnoan for some privacy.

“Well, I’m not evaporating them,” she crooned from where she was sitting on the wall, speaking in a perfect, albeit very old, dialect of Kremnoan. “That sounds like effort.”

Hearing those words from her mouth stalled both men long enough for her to dash to Ptolemy’s side and then he was gone too, leaving Mydei alone at the edge of the road. He lowered his hood so it would be easier to hear and crouched, just a tiny bend in his knees, arms outstretched like a coiled spring, a lion ready to pounce. Mydei closed his eyes and waited.

It was so soft, the gentle crunch of gravel underfoot as the cat reappeared. His crystals erupted from the ground, narrowly missing as he swiped at her.

Cipher squealed like a startled chimera and leaped backwards in a perfect back handspring over the wall to hide behind it.

“Good grief,” she whined, speaking Okheman again, “you know if you kill me, I can’t take you to your friends.”

She was right. He slowly lowered his hands and stood up straight, watching her tail swishing back and forth over the wall until she finally poked her head out, ears twitching and twisting.

“Where did you take them?” he demanded in a level voice.

“Relax, I took them past the guards to the Marmoreal Palace. You were never going to make it without my help.”

Mydei’s eyes narrowed at her.

“This is where you say, thank you, Cipher the Great.”

He did not say that. “Take me to them and I will.”

“Maybe in a minute.” Cipher vaulted back over the wall and stretched her arms up over her head with a soft mewl. “This is probably the last chance we’ll get to talk just the two of us for a while and I have to do my due diligence.”

“You already agreed to help.”

“And I already am! Have faith little gold lion,” she purred. Her arms fell back to her sides with a slap and then she entwined her fingers behind her back while she paced around him, wisely keeping just barely out of reach. He crossed his arms, refusing to dance with her.

“That Deliverer brat is like a younger brother to me,” she explained, “even if he never developed the right sense of humor, I still care about him.” Pacing turned into stretching after she made a full loop around Mydei, everything she did felt like it was meant to draw the eye, to distract. “He also was quick to skip over details back on your boat.”

“Ship.”

She laughed and waved her hand dismissively. “’We’re going to Castrum Kremnos to get the coreflame!’” Cipher purred in a creepily accurate impression, sounding exactly like Phainon, “’there’s treasure there if you help us!’ I get why he wants the damned thing, the man is too goody goody for his own sake, desperate to fulfil that ridiculous vow to Aglaea, but why is the Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos helping him?” She leaned against the wall and started rolling a gold coin between her fingers. Mydei had no idea where or when she got it, it was just there, and for some reason it felt… threatening.

“I told you-“

“Yeah, yeah, you want your crew to be happy,” she repeated, “but that brat isn’t on your crew.”

The way she was looking at him… This was a test. Mydei held her gaze a little too hard, searching for the right words but she read his silence.

“Zagreus’ purple balls, you stole my puppy,” she hissed, “you really did make him a pirate.”

Mydei’s frown deepened, and he hissed back, “No. Aglaea did. And he belongs to no one. You would do well to not speak of him as though he is a pet to be collared.”

He expected Cipher to react poorly but to his surprise she smiled and sighed, “Fine fine. I don’t believe for a second that he woke up one day and simply stopped being himself. You were keeping him against his will, right?”

Mydei shuffled. “It’s complicated.”

“And the coreflame will fix it?”

“It’s a start.”

The coin in her hand disappeared and she walked up close to Mydei again. He resisted the urge to reach out to grab her, to demand she take him to his friends. They were wasting time with this useless interrogation.

“And what’s stopping you from keeping that coreflame? It belongs to Strife, your god, you could finish Okhema with that power.”

“I have no interest in continuing our war with Okhema.”

“Easy to say now,” she crooned, “before you know what it feels like to have that power in your chest. You haven’t felt that heat that pressure deep inside your ribcage like a part of you that you never realized was missing.” Her voice was almost manic as she described it from personal experience, losing herself in the moment at the memory with wheezing breaths before she found her composure again. “The brat is so easy to use too, he’d do anything to make the people around him happy.”

Mydei’s eye twitched. He so badly wanted to grab her by the neck and shake her out for even implying that he could use Phainon like that.

“So long as he is on my ship, Phainon is a part of my crew,” Mydei said. He over enunciated every word, emphasizing how he felt with a low voice. “Nothing good will come of that coreflame except for the value it has to the Goldweaver. Value enough to buy that Deliverer’s pardon so that he can come home… where he belongs.”

Cipher’s eyes were darting back and forth like she was literally reading text behind Mydei’s eyes, delving into his soul and dancing there with emotions Mydei wasn’t even sure he understood. She was gleaning meaning from his tone; from the way he paused when he spoke of Phainon’s home. Her tail flicked twice and then the tip of it curled tightly when she mewled her way into a rolling laugh.

“Oh, I see, you love him,” she observed and Mydei deflated like a popped balloon.

“What nonsense,” he sputtered.

“He’s easy to love. I won’t tell him,” Cipher promised.

“There is nothing to tell! I am caring for him as I would anyone else on my crew!” Mydei insisted. His heart was racing at the implication; he could feel the heat in his ears, in his cheeks, behind his eyes. What the hell was she on about?

“Men really are so damn stupid,” she cackled, “you’ll figure it out eventually, I’m sure.”

Hrumph. Mydei crossed his arms.

“Or don’t,” she said noncommittally, her voice dropped low, “but when you get that coreflame and hold the ultimate temptation in your hands… if you betray him, if he gets hurt, I will bury you alive.”

The idea of suffocating over and over again was unappealing. Mydei had been there, done that, it wasn’t an experience he wanted to repeat but even without the threat, the potential for heartache alone was a deterrent.

Power had never appealed to Mydei. If it did, he’d have a crown on his head, a Kingdom to rule, people to order about, but even considering that option in passing made the bile creep up his throat. That wasn’t a future he wanted for his people. There was nothing left for them in Castrum Kremnos but bloodshed. Plenty of Mydei’s culture was worth preserving, the legacy of a corrupted, bloody king was not one of them.

“There is no power in this life that I could want aside from that which could protect my people. The Coreflame of Strife has more value in Phainon’s hands as a means to the happiness he denies himself, then it ever would to me or my kin, who would see it at the extension of a crown I have long rejected. Make your threats, I can feel in them the love you have for him, but rest assured, if that man is ever made to suffer by my hands again, I would sooner bury myself.”

They studied each other until Cipher started to laugh again. “Alright, alright, I believe you little lion. Just… make him happy, okay? My little brother deserves the world.”

Mydei blinked and then slowly nodded. He agreed completely, even if she was giving him horrible whiplash.

“Shall we go to him then?” Cipher offered. The threatening aura was gone, the rolling purr was back, and she waited patiently with one hand extended and the other behind her back.

Mydei skeptically reached for her hand. She snatched it and then the world blended into streaks of light and a rush of wind.

“You’re not gonna be sick, are you?” she asked when it stopped. The whole ordeal had taken maybe a second. Mydei had been on the road, blinked, and now he was… where was he?

The room was small but elegant, reminding him a bit of his home back on the island but with more frivolity in the architectural decorations. Kremnoan and Okheman architecture came from similar roots and shared a lot of their structural hallmarks such as balconies, columns, and love of open space. This room was no exception, with its own private balcony, a kline, a dresser, full-length mirror, a small desk and bookshelf. It even had its own private bath, though the water had long been drained. There was a light layer of dust on every surface except for the growing pile of discarded clothing behind the kline and perfect circles where amphorae and vases had been hastily shoved against the wall to make space for unexpected guests.

Phainon was frantically cleaning while Ptolemy perused the bookshelf and Leonnius was trying to calm the Okheman.

“It’s really okay, Phainon! We don’t mind!”

“I don’t usually leave a mess like this!” he insisted.

“You’re cute when you try to lie,” Cipher purred.

“Mydei!” Phainon called, brightening immediately. He kicked the pile of clothes under the kline. “What took so long?”

“Geez kid, not even a thank you?”

“I’m sorry, Cipher. Thank you for your help.”

“Good boy. I just got lost on the way,” she explained, “you know how big the palace is.”

Mydei caught her wink as she spun in a circle and watched her stumble when her spinning almost caused an accident. Her acrobatics saved her ankle and the amphorae that she almost tripped over. Phainon was already hurrying to scoop the thing up to carefully move it to a corner with the rest of his bizarre collection.

“Ugh, I’m realizing a little too late the missed opportunity to get rid of your trash while you were away,” she mused, “now, before I go~” She scooted in close to Mydei again with mischief sparkling in her smile. “What are you supposed to say, little lion?”

He sighed and rolled his eyes before mumbling, “Thank you, Cipher the Great.”

She squealed with glee and saluted the room, “Duty calls~ Better hurry.” Cipher was gone before anyone could blink, leaving silence and exhaustion in her wake.

“Okay but for real,” Leonnius said, “how does she…?”

“She flips a coin and can move really fast,” Phainon explained.

Mydei was already moving on. He wanted to focus on their mission, to trust that Cipher was doing her part to keep them safe from discovery. They didn’t have a lot of time to spare, and it was hard to tell with the permanent daylight how much of that precious resource they had left. But it was hard not to think about what Cipher had said. Love was a very loaded word. Now was probably not the time to open that basket of snakes.

Phainon’s room was still cluttered despite his rushed attempts to correct it, but it was honestly very nice. Phainon wasn’t a dirty person, he kept himself clean and was organized. It was refreshing to see that he was also very human. In the comfort of his own home surrounded by the fingerprints of a life lived, he was somewhat scatterbrained.

“I’m not usually here,” he was still trying to explain.

“Are you hoarding jars?” Leonnius was asking.

“No, no, I’m appraising them… Ptolemy did you just put one of my books in your pocket?”

“…it would go so well with my collection on the ship!”

Mydei tuned them out to look over Phainon’s walls. He had sketches and paintings and old advertisements hung up somewhat haphazardly. Anything that appealed to him he had purchased and kept as reminders of time well spent. That play he saw as a matinee, the announcement of a new sweet at his favorite bakery, a child’s drawing gifted to him, even a hastily scribbled receipt for a commission for a new sword with the start date left blank, payment pending, to name only a few. These were snapshots into the life of a man that wanted to experience everything, who wanted to remember all the joys in his life worth fighting for.

Maybe Mydei was feeling a little in love.

“We’re wasting time,” he said, quiet but forceful. They needed to get Phainon back to this life.

Ptolemy hurriedly grabbed two more books and shoved them under his cloak and then the four of them were peeking out of the doorway, heads stacked on top of each other and twisting to check both directions.

“The hall is clear,” Phainon observed.

Moving quietly in armor was a fool’s errand but Mydei made it work and there weren’t a lot of people around to hear them. …they hadn’t seen another soul at all.

“Shouldn’t there be guards?” Leonnius whispered.

“This is where the Chrysos Heirs live,” Phainon whispered back, “there isn’t any need to guard up here.”

“…Does the Goldweaver live here?” Mydei asked when he realized.

“Yeah.”

“So maybe we stop whispering,” Ptolemy hissed.

They moved in silence down the hall until Phainon stopped them in front of a closed door and motioned for them all to come in close. “Castorice can be touchy, so just, don’t be surprised.”

Mydei started to ask what that meant when a shadow moved down the hallway. The prince immediately shoulder-checked the group to shove all four of them into the bedroom and closed the door behind them with a soft click.

“Someone is coming,” he hissed.

The room itself was dark. Castorice had heavy curtains to block her balcony, leaving just enough light to see to not trample her things. Where Phainon’s clutter had been in laundry and antiques, Castorice had a thing for stuffed animals and handicrafts. Her desk was covered in fabrics and cotton stuffing, needles and thread, and projects that were missing their heads. Finished stuffed animals were piled in the corners, brightly colored and friendly looking.

Ptolemy had already moved to her bookshelf. It was smaller and mostly consisted of amateur bound manuscripts, packed with notes. He pulled one out to start reading but Phainon smacked his hand and swiped the book to put it back.

Mydei expected to find this Castorice sleeping, but the kline was empty.

“Does she sleep somewhere else?” Leonnius whispered.

“I have never actually seen her slee-“ Phainon cut himself off and dove into the pile of stuffed animals when the door handle started to turn.

Mydei almost followed him, but Leonnius beat the prince to it, wiggling into hiding and leaving no space for the other two. Ptolemy managed to get behind the curtain to hide on the balcony, but Mydei was left awkwardly behind the door, trusting the shadows and his hood to hide him from view.

The woman who let herself into the room was ethereally beautiful in the same way moonlight on bone was beautiful. The way flowers bloomed on decay in defiance of death or the sense of peace that comes from visiting the grave of a loved one long since mourned. She was pale enough to nearly glow in the limited light, wearing white clothing adorned with handmade ornaments in the shapes of butterflies and flowers to match the ornaments in her lavender hair.

Castorice paused when she closed the door behind her with her foot, listening to the ‘empty’ room with her arms crossed tightly over a pair of tomes pressed to her chest.

Mydei was holding his breath, trying so hard not to breathe. She was so close, close enough that he could reach his hand out and take her shoulder.

And it was a very good thing he didn’t. The feeling that crept over Mydei was so gentle that he couldn’t remember when it started. Had he always felt this relaxed? This tired? It was a little cold, the creeping sensation in his veins, a squirming that made his mind recoil, screaming for him to move, that this feeling was too familiar and wholly unwelcome, but his body felt so light and unresponsive. If not for his shoulder against the wall, he would have collapsed.

They had time for a nap, right?

Mydei barely processed that her rich purple eyes were looking right at him. Oh, there was some pink in there too. It was lovely, like someone had taken the oranges from a sunset and left only the purple hues of dusk.

“Castorice,” Phainon called. His voice was so far away, muted like he was calling from underwater.

Those beautiful purple eyes widened, and she turned, taking the hand of death, for surely that was what it was, with her. Mydei felt the clarity come back in a surge of warmth and put a hand against the wall for more support while he came to terms with how close that was.

Phainon was kicking himself free of her stuffed animals and stumbling to the center of the room. He lowered his hood and smiled at her.

“Lord Phainon?” her voice was gentle as a long rest, soft as the velvet of petals.

He nodded and held his arms open, and she dropped her books to the floor, utterly forgotten, to run to give him a hug.

It occurred to Mydei far too late exactly who Castorice was. Until he had felt it himself, he hadn’t put the pieces together nor remembered the tales of Aidonia’s Priestess of Death, a woman that could not touch nor be touched without taking life. She who lived without color, who knew not warmth, who danced with the dead, and conversed with spirits. The executioner of a culture that worshipped the grave.

Phainon’s Castorice was that very same Hand of Thanatos. So, when Mydei saw her run to him, he panicked and reached to grab her with no regard for his own life. He was too late.

Her arms wrapped around Phainon’s waist, and she pressed her cheek to his chest, holding him tightly with the happiest coo sound Mydei had heard. Phainon’s own arms wrapped around her shoulders, curling around her to be all-encompassing. He rocked them back and forth a few times before they finally pulled apart and she was quick to grab his sleeve as though she would perish without the contact.

“Lord Phainon… how are you here?” she asked. Her eyes darted back to Mydei who was still trying to figure out how Phainon was alive.

“It’s a long story and one I hope to tell you under less rushed circumstances,” he said softly, “but first, please, I want to introduce you.”

Phainon took her hand in his and pulled her towards Mydei, just a step. He held her hand firmly, offering comfort with a squeeze, and then motioned to Mydei with his other hand. Cautiously, the Kremnoan stepped out of the shadows and lowered his hood.

“Castorice, this is Mydeimos, Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos, and my very best friend.”

Best friend. That was the first time Mydei had heard Phainon refer to him as his friend using words. So much of what was between them was unspoken, shared through exchanged blows and hard work. To hear it said aloud felt different.

“Castrum Kremnos,” Castorice mumbled, she was also reeling from shock, Mydei could tell. “Lord Phainon, what an adventure you must have been on.” She gathered her wits and stepped up to Mydei to curtsy. “It is an honor to meet you, Prince Mydeimos. Do I have you to thank for returning Lord Phainon?”

“It is… more complicated than that, Miss Castorice,” Mydei responded. He bowed his head in a gesture of respect.

“If you are a friend of Lord Phainon,” she said, “then you must be a fine person. With your permission, may I touch you?”

Mydei was genuinely taken aback. “A moment ago, I could have been certain that you were Aidonia’s Hand of Death…”

“I was, Prince Mydeimos, until no more than few years past,” she confirmed, “my touch no longer brings death against my will, not since my ascension to divinity, but if it would make you more comfortable, I will refrain.”

Mydei looked between her and Phainon. The man was smiling reassuringly, still holding Castorice’s hand as proof that it was safe. This person, like Cipher, was very important to him.

He extended his hand to her. “Mydei is fine.”

She still hesitated. “With respect, Prince Mydei, I would like your spoken consent before I touch you.”

“You may touch me,” he said and then she was taking his hand. There was no ominous presence, no creeping dread.

“May I hug you, Prince Mydei?” she asked.

“You may,” he invited and then her arms were wrapped around his waist. She was warm, warmer than he had expected from a woman of her origins. His fingertips gently pressed between her shoulder blades when he raised his hand to reciprocate her gesture, and she must have understood his hesitation because she did not overstay her welcome. When Castorice pulled back, she took his hand again and then reached for Phainon’s, desperate to maintain contact.

“Lord Phainon, we must go wake Lady Aglaea, she will be so happy to see you!”

“Miss Castorice…” Phainon started, and she heard it in his voice and felt it when he let her go.

“…you are not staying, are you?”

Leonnius stuck his head out of the pile of stuffed animals to say, “Lady, have we got a story for you.”

Chapter End Notes

My twist on Castorice and coreflames is gonna be a little more original. This was something I decided on a long time ago, because half the joy of fanfiction is getting to provide happy endings and new twists wherein to explore a character. I love Castorice a lot in the game and her touch has defined a lot about her, she retains that history in this fic, but I'm so excited to explore how that history would effect her actions and perceptions of human connection when she is finally able to touch

chapters.title: Chapter 19: Bedtime Stories
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

The best stories, the stories that hurt the most, the ones we need to hear, are the ones that ring with truth.

Chapter Notes

I was looking for Phaidei fic recs on Twitter via threads of folks asking the same, and while I was looking through replies I found my own fic recommended and I lost my shit and called my mom freaking out excited telling her I officially made it! Idk which one of you it was but I am so honored. Thank you so much for enjoying my story enough to recommend it!

The sudden appearance of not one, but two additional Kremnoan men in Castorice’s room was enough of a jump scare to land Castorice in Phainon’s arms. Which was admittedly a funny reaction considering between the two of them, he was confident she was the stronger warrior. Castorice was a proper demigod with a coreflame in her chest, Phainon was just… well, he was just himself.

He very gently set her down and the other two greeted her warmly.

“My name is Leonnius, this is Ptolemy.”

“’But tell me, are you a goddess or are you a mortal woman?’” Ptolemy quoted when he bowed politely and pressed his lips to the back of her hand. Castorice turned a light shade of pink but before she could respond Leonnius was dragging his friend to the other side of the room while he protested, "I’m being polite!”

“Why is your polite always so weird!” Leonnius grumbled back.

“It may be best if you start at the beginning, Lord Phainon,” Castorice said, as she gathered the books she dropped earlier and set them on the bookshelf. Elegantly, and perhaps still a bit flustered with that dusting of blush still in her cheeks, she settled on a stool, hands in her lap while she waited to be regaled.

“Forgive me, but there isn’t time for the whole story.” Instead, Phainon told her the short version, like the one he told Cipher but minus the emphasis on treasure. He told her that he had been traveling with the Kremnoan Detachment, that they did not want to continue fighting with Okhema and had instead been fighting the Black Tide. He told her that they knew where the Strife coreflame was and were making plans to retrieve it, plans that needed her help to achieve success. He emphasized that he believed it was the first step towards defeating the Black Tide, the right step towards lasting peace for all Amphoreus.

“…this feels like something Lady Aglaea should know about,” Castorice mumbled when Phainon finished.

He shook his head. “Not until we have the coreflame in hand. I can’t risk any of us being arrested before then.”

It was Leonnius who leaned in to add, “if nothing else, help us get it for Phainon. We believe it will be enough to buy him a pardon and let him come home.”

Phainon bit his tongue to keep himself from adding that he wanted it to end their war. The way Mydei and the others had talked before, he didn’t believe they’d go through with it if they knew that Phainon intended to reject it as payment for just himself.

Castorice folded her hands in her lap, flat, one on top of the other. She looked down. “Lord Phainon, are you really a pirate?”

Out of the corner of his eye, Phainon saw Mydei step forward to say something but… this was something Phainon had thought about since he had read Aglaea’s words. He held his hand out to stop Mydei and was relieved when the prince honored his request and stepped back. The Deliverer knelt in front of her and took Castorice’s hand in his to look her in the eyes.

“Yes. I am.”

The three Kremnoans tensed in tandem, taken aback but he ignored them to focus on one of his oldest friends.

Castorice had arrived in Okhema not long after he had with a longer story to tell and a crushing curse. Despite her many years, she willingly accompanied Phainon to the Grove to study alongside him and they had grown very close to each other in that time. It was via study and research that Phainon and Castorice had been able to track and retrieve the Coreflame of Death together, answering questions that had haunted her as long as she had memory.

When Castorice ascended to divinity and had first learned to control her touch, Phainon was the first person who had reached for her. When no one else wanted to take the risk, he took her hand and held it to his face for her to feel. He had been her first hug, one that had lasted so long that she had cried herself into a stupor and had to be carried to her room, where she clung to him as though she was making up for hundreds of years of missed human contact.

There was a connection between them that he treasured. She had earned his complete honesty.

“And I want to show you why,” he continued with a tender squeeze, “please, come with us. I want you to meet all of them, to see what I have seen.”

She curled her fingers around one of his. Phainon had always had big hands, especially compared to her delicate ones. The other tenderly touched his cheek, holding him still with the palm of her hand so that she could study him and his smile.

“I trust you, Lord Phainon,” she agreed, “I will go with you to retrieve the coreflame.”

“That’s two,” Leonnius said cheerfully.

“Were you here for others, Lord Phainon?”

“Yeah, I was going to ask Hyacine to come. Her research into the Black Tide could save lives and Cipher already agreed to help us.”

Castorice pulled her hand away from his face and tilted her head. “Lady Cipher agreed?”

“Yeah.”

“Lord Phainon, I saw Lady Cipher and Lady Aglaea walking to the baths when I left the library.”

All four men went tense, winding even tighter than they already had been.

“If the Goldweaver is awake…” Ptolemy mumbled.

“Fuck,” Leonnius swore in Kremnoan and then he remembered there was a lady present, “sorry, sorry.”

“Time is short,” Mydei agreed.

“No that’s good,” Phainon told them, “She’s keeping Aglaea busy. Castorice, pack your things, only a small bag of essentials, while I go talk to Hyacine.”

He got up to move to the door, but Castorice caught his sleeve. “Lord Phainon, you should know, Lady Hyacine moved into the city to help rebuild the Twilight Courtyard. She does not sleep in the Marmoreal Palace.”

He groaned.

“Then we go into the city,” Mydei offered, “the Goldweaver is the only real threat, Okheman patrols are inattentive, they will be easy to get past.”

Phainon bit his lip.

“You do not like this plan,” the prince observed.

“No, it’s not that. I have some things to grab here at the Palace but if we go into the city…”

“We don’t have time for both,” Leonnius supplied.

“Castorice, could you take them?” Phainon asked.

“No need,” Mydei insisted, “tell us where to go and we will go. Give us a message or a token for this Hyacine and we will meet you at the Northeast dromas road.”

“Prince Mydei, it is no trouble. I can guide you.”

To Phainon’s surprise, Mydei took his place on his knees in front of Castorice, offering his hand to her for her to take. It was unexpectedly considerate of him to defer to her and her comfort. Phainon felt the heat rise to his cheeks as he watched Mydei gently hold her hand, ever conscious of his gauntlets and their sharp claws. Mydeimos must’ve been observing the way they interacted, noted their body language, probably took into account their closeness, and still decided to copy Phainon to put weight behind his words in the exact way he had, that he knew would reach her because of his exampled.

“I don’t know you very well, Lady Castorice, but we are taking you from your home, and in this I have experience,” he said gently, “I request that you take the time you need to gather your things and say goodbye in a manner that will bring you the most peace. It is easy now in the excitement of the decision to believe you will not need it, but I insist.”

Castorice was genuinely taken aback, so was Phainon. He tilted his head at Mydei, looking at the back of his head and that messy mane with genuine appreciation and a bit of a flutter in his stomach.

“Prince Mydei,” she said.

“Please, just Mydei,” he gently corrected.

“Lord Mydei,” Castorice said instead and Phainon smiled a little imagining the face Mydei must be making, with those subtle twitches in the corners of his mouth and eyes when he was trying to stay polite when he really wanted to say something. “That is… unexpectedly considerate. Thank you.”

Mydei patted her hand once more and then got up to face Phainon. “You will do the same, Deliverer.”

“Mydei, I don’t need-“

“You do. We will have you home soon, but until then, do what you need to do.” He put his hand on Phainon’s shoulder when he said it, holding them close, those golden eyes almost glowing in the dim light from the cracked curtain. That simmer in the dark made Phainon’s heart sing, that concern in Mydei’s voice, just for him!

What else could he do but nod?

“We’ll meet at the arches,” Phainon promised. He punched Mydei’s shoulder and the Kremnoan’s lip curled in a lopsided smirk.

“If you are late-“ “If I’m late, you better come and get me,” Phainon teased with his own sparkling grin.

“I will throw you over my shoulder and drag you back to the ship myself,” Mydei promised.

“You can flirt when we’re safe!” Leonnius scolded.

Mydei and Phainon broke eye contact at the same time, flustered at the accusation.

“You better hurry, Mydeimos.”

“My victory always be yours, Deliverer.”

Phainon left the room before Ptolemy or Leonnius could try cat calling and before Mydei could see his face adopting a deeper shade of red. Th-They weren’t flirting? That wasn’t flirting! That was just banter between friends!

The cloak almost tangled in Phainon’s legs as he shuffled down the hallway. Mydei had been right about his homesickness, Phainon really did miss these halls, but his longing to return was more complicated than he was willing to admit to Mydei just yet. It wasn’t that Phainon wanted to be back here, it’s that he wanted to show his new friends the beauty of Okhema. He so badly wanted to take Mydei’s hand and pull him through the market and show him good food and good music. He wanted everyone else to meet these wonderful, rough, rowdy, incredible men that Phainon had grown to adore. Kephale’s love was for all who walked across Amphoreus, not just Okhemans, and Phainon wanted so badly for Okhema to see and appreciate them.

That wasn’t the kind of homesickness that could be sated with a temporary goodbye, so he didn’t try. Instead, Phainon abandoned the idea of goodbye at all. As far as he was concerned the light promise to return in glory that he had given to Aglaea still held, even if he was returning in a very different manner than he, or anyone, had intended.

He paused to listen for movement in the hallways before he dipped inside Aglaea’s office. True to her words, Cipher was keeping the Goldweaver busy, and her office was empty. Her garmentmakers were hovering against the wall. If they noticed him enter, they didn’t care that he was there.

Phainon immediately noticed the subtle signs of Aglaea’s stress. Her office was visibly organized and immaculately clean. The kind of space that people might expect from a major political player in the largest standing city on Amphoreus. Which is how Phainon knew she was upset.

A happy Aglaea was inspired, constantly working on new projects, eager to create. It was only when she had too much on her mind that she cared about the organized clutter and sought to tidy her space in a manner befitting the desires of others. Her mannequins were empty, tools put neatly in their drawers, shelves dusted, letters organized, and so on.

It hurt to see.

“Oh Aglaea,” he mumbled to himself with his head bowed and a hand held to his chest, “I promise, I’ll make it right.”

Phainon hurried to her desk and started opening drawers. He knew where she kept things so despite the dozens of knobs, he only needed two. Her stationery was embossed along the edges long before she took pen to paper for that extra level of refinement. She applied it herself to set her words apart, something Aglaea felt was important when the Council of Elders had so much to say.

He dipped the pen in her gold ink and sat down to write. Phainon’s penmanship was neat and practiced, something he picked up from Aglaea. In his haste, Phainon left little speckles and tiny drips that made his perfectionism unhappy, but this was already more than he had expected to be able to say. He folded the letter but didn’t seal it.

Phainon tapped the paper as he looked for a spot to hide it, somewhere that Aglaea would find that Caenis or her goons wouldn’t think to look should the Council send spies.

He crossed the room in three long strides to one of her shelves and pulled a wide amphora down from the top shelf. It was decorated with scenes of lounging chimeras, snacking on cookies and sweets. It was on theme.

Phainon set it on the desk and started stuffing his pockets with the chimera biscuits that were stored inside. The crunchy treats were of the finest make, only the best possible ingredients. Aglaea traded high quality clothing for them as a long-standing deal with the oldest bakery in Okhema. These treats were especially made for Vigethos, (affectionally called Beagle Coconut by the children in town) Aglaea’s gray and white chimera, and Phainon knew the adorable monster went crazy for the things.

It was a good spot to hide the letter and if the daily treats were the best way to Vigethos’ heart, maybe they’d work on Fig Stew. Phainon was not above bribery to earn those belly rubs.

He had managed to cram more than half the jar into his pockets and tucked the letter inside when he went to put the amphora back. The second he lifted it; two bright blue eyes were looking right up at him from behind the jar.

“Fuck!” Phainon cussed in Kremnoan as he almost fumbled the pottery, “Cipher has been teaching you how to magically appear, hasn’t she?”

The chimera didn’t move. He was plain by chimera standards, all white belly and gray on top with a spade on the end of his tail and two uneven horns on the top his head by his ears. Aglaea had owned him since before Phainon had come to Okhema for the first time. He was a deceptively old creature with a spry demeanor and knowing look who had learned how to weaponize his cuteness against everyone except Aglaea. That’s why he was a little on the chubby side, because Trinnon kept giving him treats. The same treats nearly spilling from Phainon’s pockets.

He was also a little snitch.

“Hey, Beag,” Phainon crooned. He gently gave the chimera scratches under his chin. They were accepted but those eyes narrowed at him a little more with every pet. “Aren’t you so handsome?” The chimera had a lovely golden collar, just a delicate band barely visible under his fluffy white ruff. Phainon ran his fingers underneath it to scratch at the fur. “Did you miss me?”

The chimera purred and got up to sniff at his pockets, but Phainon quickly covered them. “You’re on a diet remember?”

Beagle sat down, his front paws neatly pressed together and opened his mouth for cookies.

Phainon gave him a pat on his head instead and put the jar back up on the top shelf, out of reach of the small terror.

“Sorry Viggie,” he whispered with an apologetic scratch behind the ears.

The chimera stomped his paw, but Phainon was already getting up to leave. So, Beagle escalated to plan B.

He screamed.

Phainon jumped on the chimera and jammed three cookies into his open mouth, silencing the animal in a heartbeat. There was a tense second of Phainon waiting to see if it worked and Beagle realizing he had a mouth full of delicious goodness before the chimera’s little mouth curled into a wide smile and his eyelids drooped in the most mischievous expression anyone had seen since Cipher had convinced the local fishing chapter that goldfish were made of actual gold. That was the face of a gluttonous animal that knew he had won.

And Phainon hated to lose. If he wasn't on a time crunch...

“This isn’t over,” he hissed to the smug animal as he stacked a little pile of cookies on the floor to keep the monster busy.

Phainon slipped out into the city via balcony to avoid Verax Leo and the only few guards that he knew would be at attention. They weren’t looking for people with active warrants, they were more like bouncers to keep sleepy drunks from wandering into restricted housing, but it wasn’t worth the risk that he’d be recognized under the hood.

He landed lightly on all fours and waited, listening, but nothing moved, nothing cared that he was there while the city slept.

Phainon wove through back alleys and hopped a couple walls, startling the occasional bird until he stood outside the door of a small home in a serene residential district. It felt like there was cotton in his throat and pressure behind his eyes. Now that he was here, Phainon felt very strongly that he needed to feel. He needed to remember and carry this weight, the same one that he had been holding onto for over a month, keeping close, buried deep as a new permanent part of him.

The longer he stood on the stoop the more risk there was that he would be seen, but it still took him a long time, nearly a quint, to gather himself to knock on the door.

It was late. No response.

Another knock, more waiting. Phainon checked down the path, hoping that none of the neighbors were up late.

Finally, the door opened a crack and Phainon shoved his way inside.

“Wha-! What in Kephale’s name are you doing?! Who are you!?” the lady yelled. She slapped his chest and tried to shove him, but Phainon barely noticed the physical protests. As soon as the door was closed, he lowered the hood and the assault abruptly stopped.

“Phainon?” she whispered.

“Xenia,” he greeted. Phainon tried to smile softly, but it was forced and weak.

She stared at him, pale and uncomfortable, and he wasn’t even slightly surprised when she slapped his face. It stung. He deserved it.

“You shouldn’t be here,” Xenia hissed, low, full of venom, and wavering with grief. Tears were flowing down her face.

“I know,” he managed.

“Mom?”

Both adults stilled when a little boy, maybe six years old, called out to them. The knocking must have woken him too. He was rubbing his eyes and covering his yawn, hair standing up on one side from sleeping too heavily on one side. The same side Phainon’s fallen first mate, Marcus, had slept on. The same dark brown hair, even the way the boy scratched at his belly was his father in miniature.

“Wha’sh goin’ on?” he mumbled, and she hurried to hug him.

“Nothing, just an unwelcome visitor,” she told him. Xenia gently pet her son’s head to fix his hair. It sprang right back up in defiance. “Go back to sleep, you have school in the morning.”

“Who’s that?” he asked instead.

“No one.”

“I was a friend of your father’s,” Phainon greeted, “what’s your name?”

“Don’t answer,” Xenia ordered with a shake and Phainon’s heart clenched, “go back to sleep, I’ll tell you more in the morning.”

The little boy looked suspiciously between the two of them, but he nodded and obeyed.

“He looks like his father,” Phainon observed softly, “Xenia, I-“

“Why did you get to come back?” she sobbed, “and not him? What happened, Phainon? What won’t the Goldweaver tell us?” Shaking hands covered her face as though it could stop the dam, hold back the grief that Xenia had probably been holding onto for a long time, that she had hidden away until now.

He reached for her but paused before his hand could touch her arm. Grieving people didn’t always liked to be touched but when Xenia stumbled, sobbing too hard to keep her balance, he stepped forward to catch her and held her tightly. Even when she slapped him again and pounded on his chest with her fists, he held her close until she finally accepted that she was not the only one in mourning. Her arms wrapped around his neck, and she sobbed into his shoulder while he held her, trying to convey in every firm rub across her back and shoulders the comfort that he knew she needed.

“The truth will not bring you comfort,” he told her, “but I owe it to you. Will you tell the others? The rest of the crew’s families?”

“Are you that much of a coward?” she growled but there was no bite in her tone, “that you will not tell them yourself?”

His hug tightened around her shoulders. Phainon felt that shame like a noose. “If there were not a people that still needed me, I would turn myself in to the Council in exchange for the time to tell them. Please, Xenia, meet me here in this middle ground, it is as far as I am currently able to go.”

She took a shuddering breath against his shoulder and slowly pushed away. Phainon kept his arms extended towards her, to catch her if she fell again but she found her footing.

“Then speak, Deliverer. Tell me the story of how you failed my husband.”

-

“Are they always like that?” Castorice asked just after Phainon left.

“It’s gotten worse since Phainon moved into Mydei’s room,” Leonnius noted blandly.

Castorice’s arm shot out and grabbed his wrist, making the man jump, slowly she turned to look at him with mischief and surprise painted in broad strokes across her face. “You must tell me everything.”

“There is nothing to tell,” Mydei grumbled.

I got you, Leonnius mouthed, gesturing to her and then back to himself with a few rapid nods.

“How do we get to the Twilight Courtyard?” Ptolemy asked and Castorice rose gracefully from her chair to walk to the balcony. Offensive daylight streamed into the room as she pushed aside the curtain and motioned for them to come see. All three of them piled in behind her to follow the line where she was pointing.

“Follow the road down the hill to the market,” she instructed, “when the path splits, go left until you see a forge to your right, then it’s another left and then your second right.”

All three of them nodded but she still studied them skeptically.

“…were my instructions clear enough, my lords?”

“We got it,” Leonnius reassured her. He was already walking up to the balcony railing to vault over it.

“When you are packing,” Ptolemy started to say, “will you bring a couple of those manuscripts? One of them looked interes-!” Mydei interrupted him to bodily throw him over the balcony.

Castorice jumped just a little bit in shock but when neither of the remaining men seemed alarmed she sheepishly held a hand to her mouth to say, “Does he truly want me to bring my works?”

“Please don’t listen to him Miss Castorice,” Leonnius reassured her, “he is simply a lover of literature and a hoarder of books, mostly harmless.” The runner saluted her and then jumped off the balcony.

“Miss Castorice,” Mydei gently cleared his throat to get her attention, “have you anything that I may show to Miss Hyacine? A token or a phrase?”

“Of course, Lord Mydei.” Castorice walked over to her shelf and pulled out a box of handmade charms. She fished around for a very specific one, a fat horse with tiny wings, lopsided and colored white, stitched from pieces of scrap fabrics of different textures. “Give this to her and she will know that I have sent you.”

He took it reverently and tucked it inside his cloak. “Will you be able to meet us at the gate? Or should I send Leonnius to escort you?”

“Respectfully, Lord Mydei, it is safer for me to move about the city than it is for you. I will be there.”

He walked back to the balcony and put a hand on it.

“Lord Mydei?” She was looking at him with awe and wonder that he didn’t expect from a demigod. “I hope we have more time to talk in the future. When Lord Phainon told his story, he mentioned you the most. I am looking forward to learning why.”

Mydei felt light-headed. He hadn’t even noticed. “I am sure it is nothing, Miss Castorice.”

She smiled knowingly and turned away to pack, leaving him to drop into the bushes beside his two friends with a whole new confusing feeling to push down on his list of priorities.

“Let us move quickly,” he whispered to them and then they were dashing down the street.

Okhema was very different from their Kremnoan settlement. While it had its share of twists and turns, stairways and covered roads, none of it was built with combat in mind. There was no strategy to it, no regard for defense, only a desperate need to make every empty space a monument to art. Every wall was covered in mosaics, every pillar sported colored fabrics, when stairs created awkward spaces between buildings, the people created water features full of colorful fish and bright flowers. Ivy was allowed to creep up the walls to add splashes of green to cream colored stone and pale marble. There were statues under each archway, colorful paintings and tapestries hung beside windows and doorways. This was a city for the wealthy, for those who had never known the horrors of combat, who had the luxury of wiling away the days dancing with spirits of creation and inspiration to enrich their lives.

It made Mydei a little envious. He couldn’t see his people indulging to this degree, but what could his people create, given the opportunity to express themselves without the constant threat of war. Would they embrace it? Or would they reject it in favor of the path they had always known, following Nikador’s footsteps to bloody ends?

“She said left at the fork, right?” Leonnius asked.

“Right.”

“Right?”

“No, left.”

“You said right.”

“Because you were right.”

“Oh.”

Mydei rolled his eyes.

“Did we miss the turn?” Leonnius asked, “how far down the road were we supposed to go?”

They were almost at the bottom of the hill and hadn’t seen a market, nor a fork in the road. Were they already lost? Mydei stopped to look around. This felt like a commercial district, but not a market. He sniffed the air. Forges could have distinct smells if they were close but all he could smell was fish and salty sea air.

“We must have missed the turn,” he said.

“Let’s try this way,” Leonnius offered and then they were running again, trying to guess the layout of a city that none of them had ever seen, following signs that kept leading them through confusing paths up and down stairs, through tight alleys, and almost into a pond.

“We don’t have time to keep guessing,” Ptolemy hissed.

“Quiet! Someone is coming!” Leonnius hissed. The three of them crammed into a doorway down a shallow alley.

Mydei peeked, careful to keep his hood low over his head. It was a single guard, half asleep, not even armed. If not for his armor, Mydei may have thought he was a normal guy just out for a late-night stroll.

“Even with the Black Tide,” Ptolemy huffed, “how did Eurypon fail to bring this city to heel? Their security is so unserious.”

Very slowly the man wandered away, continuing his rounds. They gave it another quint for good measure and then spread out into the alley for space to breathe.

“We agree we are lost, yes?” Mydei whispered.

“Yeah.”

“’But cease your sighing and lamentation- we have no time to lose,’” Ptolemy said in his deadpan voice that he saved for quotes.

“But you have time to recite literature?” Leonnius scolded.

“You could ask for directions.”

All three of them froze at the new voice. It was a rumbling growl, deep and gravely with a purr embedded in the sound. Mydei spun, claws ready but it was no guard at the end of the alley, just a stone statue. He scanned the walls, looking for a place where a trickster or thief might hide. Who else would be out at this hour aside from pirates and criminals?

Leonnius peeked around Mydei. “Uh, and who might you be, mysterious empty dead end?”

“Hahaha! How curious that you do not know of me…” mused the statue. Its eyes lit up when it talked but no part of it moved.

“Anyone else getting an uncomfortable sense of familiarity?” Ptolemy asked.

The statue was round and mounted to the wall, a simple relief of a lion’s head with its fanged mouth open wide, jovial eyes, round ears, and a fluffy mane. From base to top it was slightly shorter than Mydei was tall but for something that was all head it still made for an impressive display. Chryseus Leo was a special case but in a world as wide and magical as Amphoreus, Mydei wasn’t surprised to see that there were more like their beloved ship.

“Distant cousin,” Leonnius mumbled. He pointed between the statue and Mydei.

“And you will help us find our way, lion?” Mydei asked.

“Not for free~”

“Then we will find our own way.”

“Wait! Wait! I need to at least know where you are trying to go,” the lion insisted. He had the same mistrustful playfulness that Cipher had minus Phainon’s seal of approval.

“The Twilight Courtyard,” Mydei told him.

“Of course, I know where that is.”

“Then speak, lion.”

“Not without something in return.”

Ptolemy scoffed and waved his hand back and forth. The sleeve of his cloak swished dramatically as he did. “And what could a statue want?”

“Tell me why three cloaked figures are hiding from the guards,” the lion crooned, “and I will consider it payment.”

Leonnius tugged on Mydei’s shoulder to turn him around and the three of them locked their arms around each other in a huddle to talk with some privacy.

“We don’t trust this thing, right?” Leonnius asked. The other two nodded.

“If it’s like Chryseus Leo, then it may adhere to a code,” Ptolemy guessed.

“We don’t have the time to wander; the risk is great but what choice do we have?” Mydei pointed out. He broke away to confront the lion head again, peering at it from under his hood.

“I will answer, lion, and you will give us directions. Should you fail to honor your agreement or send us the wrong way, we will return and crush you into dust, is this agreeable?”

The lion head sputtered, fumbling for words, “th-there is no need for such violence, Lord.”

“Then we are agreed?”

“Y-Yes, we are!”

“We are hiding from the guards because we are Kremnoan pirates,” Mydei said with a smirk, “on a mission to steal away the Chrysos Heirs of this city that we may fight the Black Tide in Castrum Kremnos and slay the Titan Nikador that resides there.”

The lion was silent. Its eye would glow and then turn off, as though it were starting to speak and then lost the words.

“My lord, you must jest…” the Lion tried but Mydei waved his hand.

“I have kept my word. Now tell us where to go.”

“Th-The road, take a left from here and then another two staircases down. That hallway leads to the market, from there-“

“Forge, two streets over, got it!” Leonnius said. He grabbed at Ptolemy and Mydei to start pulling them along. A couple steps later he was letting go to run ahead.

“My thanks lion,” Mydei crooned and then he was running along.

“Mydeimos,” Ptolemy hissed as they jogged to catch up, “why did you tell him the truth?”

“Who could he possibly tell that would believe him?” Mydei laughed.

Leonnius slid around the final corner and slowed to a walk. The market was several blocks and a few streets and there nestled in the corner by a fountain was the important shop. The forge they were meant to use as a landmark was closed for the night of course, but Mydei still had to resist the urge to browse the wares. He recognized the name of the forge from the receipt slip that Phainon had attached to his wall. If the Deliverer trusted this shop, then it must be high quality.

Leonnius tugged on his sleeve, and they reluctantly moved on past multi-colored signs with bold advertisements for everything from fresh fruit to antiques, to books.

The Twilight Courtyard was poorly named. It was never twilight in Okhema and their ‘courtyard’ was a very small part of the alley where space between buildings widened by an extra foot. Multicolored awnings connected the two roofs, filtering the light onto a small water feature and far too many potted plants.

Mydei checked both ways down the path and lowered his hood when he was certain they were alone. The sign was brand new, no more than a week old. This was either a new establishment, or something had happened to the prior sign.

He checked the door handle first to see if it was unlocked, expecting a shop and not a residence, but it didn’t budge. There was no bell or knocker, so he gently tapped twice with the knuckles of his gauntlet and then pressed his ear to the door to listen. Someone was moving inside, but no one was coming to the door.

“Maybe they’re asleep,” Leonnius offered.

“No, someone is awake.”

Ptolemy leaned over and knocked instead, loud, booming bangs that almost knocked over a plant, and made him the center of attention.

“If we had time to be polite, we would’ve brought cake,” he grumbled.

It worked at least, the door opened a crack and a sleepy voice called from the dark, tiny and light, a woman’s voice. “Hello? Are you having a medical emergency?”

“Not yet,” Leonnius joked.

Mydei pushed him away from the door. “Are you Miss Hyacine?”

The door opened just a little more. The young woman was wearing a loose chiton, sleepwear, and rubbing her eyes. Long pink hair rested over her shoulders in big curls, the ends tipped teal the same color as her big, wide eyes. She was a tiny thing with a lovely, if currently sleepy demeanor.

“I am. May I help you?”

“Phainon sent us,” Ptolemy hurried to say.

The door pushed open, and she stepped aside, very suddenly awake. “I’ll make tea.”

Chapter End Notes

No Fig Stew cameo for a couple chapters. Hopefully the other gremlin will suffice! :3c

Also, I'm sure most of you forgot the super background characters who perished for the plot in Chapter one, but Phainon sure as hell didn't. ;w;

chapters.title: Chapter 20: An Answer to All Things
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

New character tag: Hyacine

This is the first and hopefully only time, that the perspective jumps to someone other than Phainon or Mydei. I really want them to be the center of this story but I also felt like this was the best way to speak to Phainon's state of mind.

Chapter Notes

I'll still try to post every 1-2 days this week but UH GENSHIN UPDATE AND THE HSR STREAM SOOOO I MEAN, PRIORITIES

Mydei had expected a little more resistance or at minimum some wariness from this Hyacine. She was a small thing, smaller than Castorice was, with a bubbly personality. Even just barely awake she was cheerfully welcoming them inside, seating the three of them down at a table and getting tea started at a kitchenette in the same room.

No questions, no concerns, just three very large Kremnoan men dressed like they were there to rob the place, and this tiny young lady alone in her sleepwear had let them inside, sat them down, and was treating them like honored guests.

“Is Phainon alright?” she asked.

“He could be better,” Leonnius answered, meeting her cheerfulness with his own.

“Is he hurt?” Hyacine prodded.

“Nothing like that,” Mydei corrected, “As a Chrysos Heir are you aware of his status?”

“I know the Council of Elders demanded Aglaea brand him as a pirate and write a warrant for his arrest.”

Ptolemy snorted through his nose, a chuckle in another time and place cut short by the urgency of the situation. “You know more than we do.”

“If you would allow us,” Mydei offered, “we have a plan to rectify that order, but we need your help.”

Hyacine carried four little ceramic mugs over to the table and passed them out, one for each of them. “Please, I want to know what I can do, but first, what should I call you?”

“I’m Leonnius, this is Ptolemy, and that’s Mydeimos.” He pointed at each of them in turn to match their faces with their proper names.

She blinked. The rapid response was not what she had expected.

“Sorry, introductions are for people with more time,” Ptolemy explained.

“Then, please, do not delay,” Hyacine requested.

The three of them tag teamed the story while she poured them a herbal tea. Ptolemy was the better storyteller, but he was more dramatic, including vignettes that were nice but probably not necessary for the more recent, pressing concern. Hyacine didn’t need every detail of Phainon’s stay and Leonnius and Mydei kept having to cut their bookworm off mid-sentence to hurry him along. Mydei especially didn’t want some details to make it to the surface until after they had convinced this woman to join their quest.

‘We want you to join our pirate crew! It’s okay, one of your friends and colleagues has been our prisoner for a month and he loves it! He’s only almost been killed twice!’ Honesty was the best policy and Mydei had no issues coming clean later, but this was not the best time.

Unfortunately, the result was a disjointed retelling of the last month that left Miss Hyacine visibly distraught and further confused. Phainon would’ve done a much better job explaining all of this.

When they were done fumbling over their explanation of the situation to her, Mydei took the little charm out of his pocket and put it on the table. She very carefully set her mug down to hold it while she thought.

The silence was deafening. Mydei was questioning everything they had said to her, wondering if a crucial detail had been omitted or if they had said too much and frightened her. Simply admitting that they were Kremnoans in Okhema would make the average young lady politely excuse herself to run for help, but Hyacine was surprisingly patient.

She handled everything in stride with the same composure that Castorice had, contemplating every word without jumping to conclusions.

“This was the very first charm that I made,” Hyacine said gently, “I wasn’t very good at it, but Cassie was so patient talking me through it.” Her fingers ghosted over the stitching. “I gave it to her when I was finished because I was so embarrassed and she wouldn’t let me throw it away.”

Leonnius shuffled awkwardly.

“If Cassie and Phainon trust you, then I do too,” she finally said after another pregnant pause. After how horribly they butchered their pitch, Mydei was impressed that Phainon and Castorice’s trust was enough to sway her, but then again, Phainon did sort of have that way about him.

“Just like that?”

“Would you prefer if I said no?”

“’You are the most admirable woman in the whole world both as regards personal beauty and strength of understanding,’” Ptolemy quoted. Immediately after speaking he ducked under Leonnius’ punch but collapsed when Mydei kicked his chair out from under him.

Hyacine very calmly looked Mydei in the eye and scolded him, “Lord Mydeimos, please don’t do that again.”

Brazenness aside, he hadn’t had anyone talk to him like that in a long time. He blinked through his surprise while Ptolemy laughed.

“Those chairs are expensive,” Hyacine finished with a playful grin, “I wouldn’t want them to break.”

Ptolemy’s laugh turned into a choked, “huh?” while Leonnius’ spat tea through his nose when his laughing and drinking disagreed on whose turn it was. She would definitely get along with the crew. Mydei made a note to introduce her to Perdikkas.

“Hyacine, we are pressed for time,” Mydei managed.

“I know, we mustn’t keep Cassie and Phainon waiting for long. I only need a moment.” She got up and hurried to another room.

“Why do you insist on flirting with everyone?” Leonnius coughed.

Ptolemy was using the table to recover his footing. He put the chair back upright and pushed it in without himself in it. It was safer to stand. “It’s not flirting, it’s being polite. Flirting is whenever Mydeimos talks to Phainon.” A hair’s breadth before Mydei could throw his mug at Ptolemy, the bookworm scooped it up from the table and held it out of reach.

“I do not flirt with him.”

Leonnius and Ptolemy shared a look.

“There’s nothing wrong with flirting, prince,” Ptolemy insisted.

Leonnius covered his mouth with his mug to whisper through gritted teeth, “except when you do it, Ptolemy.”

“There is no more elegant way to greet a Lady than with the words of fine poetry!”

“Just compliment them or punch them like a normal person!”

“Punching is not normal outside of Kremnos!”

Mydei huffed and crossed his arms to wait, eyes closed, determined to ignore their bickering. He did not flirt with Phainon. Banter was different than flirting. It was only flirting if there was intent, if there was love.

Oh, I see, you love him.

Mydei stood up fast enough to stop both of his friends mid-sentence. They gave him funny looks as he sulked around the table, gathering the mugs and taking them to the washbasin to clean them for Miss Hyacine.

He really hoped Phainon was okay. If he had been caught… The mug in his hand creaked in protest, nearly cracking when he squeezed too hard. Mydei tempered himself quickly and added a little soap to the water.

The lion did not concern himself with matters of the heart. That was a luxury for peacetime, perhaps when they retrieved the coreflame, when Mydei was able to set right this horrible situation that he had trapped the Deliverer in, then he could assess his feelings. Even if he was in love, and he was not admitting to himself that he was, none of that love mattered if it wasn’t reciprocated.

More speculation. He should just ask Phainon explicitly what they meant to each other and be happy with the outcome. They had already proven to each other that they were rivals and crewmates, Mydei didn’t need more than that. And if he were to ask, it needed to be at a better time, when Phainon didn’t have the weight of the world on his shoulders. It would not do to put either of them in a position where their trust in each other needed to be questioned, on the eve of a major operation.

He set the mugs aside to dry while Ptolemy and Leonnius continued to argue behind him until Hyacine finally emerged again.

She had changed into a red, white, and pink dress that covered her body and arms but stopped short mid-thigh. Stockings covered her legs, bows adorned her ankles over black shoes, and her hair was pulled into pigtails just behind and above each ear. She had a little hat perched like a tiara, away from her forehead, a pink cape as long as her dress, and a very full messenger bag slung over her shoulder. The charm he had given to her was clipped onto her belt.

“Are we to meet them here?” she asked.

“No, they are expecting us at the Northwest dromas road.”

“Many of the early risers will be beginning their days soon,” Hyacine cautioned, “and that is on the other side of town.”

“Then I guess we better run,” Leonnius mused with a stretch.

“I can carry you,” Mydei offered.

“Thank you, but there is no need,” she promised.

The door opened on oiled hinges as she held it wide for them, beckoning them out into the alley where they pulled their hoods over their heads once more. Hyacine closed the door behind her but left it unlocked and then she hurriedly led the way.

She didn’t run as fast as Leonnius or Mydei could, but her little legs carried her fast enough to make them jog to stay caught up as she dipped through back paths through hidden alcoves to stay hidden from any curious eyes. Hyacine didn’t take the scenic route, she didn’t slow down, and she focused entirely on the mission. Mydei respected that.

They popped out between two buildings on the edge of the road, the only soul in sight was Castorice who was standing next to one of the arches that marked the edge of the city. She was wearing a long shawl bunched around her shoulders and holding a big bag in both hands in front of her.

Hyacine waved at her, and she smiled back, a cute open mouthed, eyes closed kind of smile. They hugged the moment they were close enough to do so.

“They found you,” Castorice observed, “I am glad you were willing to come as well.” She playfully reached to pet the charm at Hyacine’s waist.

“They said that Phainon requested the both of us himself.”

“Where is the Deliverer?” Mydei asked.

Castorice shook her head.

“You didn’t say he returned to Okhema!” Hyacine noted with alarm.

“Ah, we must’ve forgot…” Leonnius apologized but now she was looking back at the city with concern. So was Mydei.

“We still have some time before the Entry Hour,” Castorice tried to reassure them, but Mydei was not reassured.

“Maybe he got lost?” Leonnius asked.

Ptolemy smacked the back of Leonnius’ head and said, “in his own city?” Leonnius came back up with a growl to tackle Ptolemy and they both went down wrestling on the road, completely ignored by the other three. Oh yes, these two Chrysos Heirs would fit right in.

“If the Goldweaver caught him,” Mydei said, and the pair stilled to listen, “where would she have him taken?”

“Does Aglaea not know that Phainon returned to the city?” Hyacine asked.

“…we may have been told two different stories, Miss Hyacine.”

Mydei scanned Okhema systematically, eyes darting back and forth to track any movement from birds, to a stray cat, to the rustle of leaves on distant trees. He trusted Phainon, but he also respected the Goldweaver’s diligence. It was already very likely that they had stepped on a golden thread, that she knew they were there or would know very soon. Mydei didn’t know how long Cipher could keep an omnipotent demigod distracted.

His brow wrinkled, only a little and only for a moment. “Where is Cipher?”

“Oh, Lady Cipher told me to give Lord Phainon a message,” Castorice reported.

“Is she not coming?” Leonnius asked from the road. Ptolemy was sitting on his chest with a foot on one of his wrists to keep him pinned.

Castorice shook her head.

So only two of the three Chrysos Heirs would be accompanying them. Four heirs were better than two but… Mydei had counted on more for their assault on Castrum Kremnos. That was a logistical problem for later. He shoved that down next to other problems that didn’t matter any time soon, like his feelings for Phainon and the old cookware on the ship he wanted to eventually replace.

Mydei crossed his arms, still watching the city and counting in his head. Searching for Phainon in a city he didn’t know how to navigate was not a wise strategic decision. The crew would undoubtedly fall to infighting between Krateros and Hephaestion if Mydei was caught and imprisoned alongside Phainon in a foolish attempt to free him, but perhaps Castorice could guide him through the city. Hyacine seemed to share Phainon’s eagerness to help, with a good plan to ensure the safety of his men and the populace at large, it wouldn’t be too hard to lay siege to Okhema with only the crew of the Chryseus Leo.

The plan was starting to come together in the back of his mind when Phainon stumbled out of an alleyway and jogged up to them, panting.

“Sorry,” he managed, “that took longer than I thought it would.”

Mydei scoffed to bury his own relief, “you’re too sentimental, Deliverer.”

Phainon laughed and rubbed the back of his neck. He was smiling but Mydei could see the hollowness of his eyes. Something had happened. Phainon looked tired, there were little dark spots on his shoulder and a redness to his cheek. That smile was shallow and forced, meant to reassure and conceal. It was too much like the smile Phainon had shared with him the first time they really spoke, when they shook hands and agreed to Phainon’s servitude on the ship, no more than a mask.

“Lord Phainon!” Hyacine greeted, and she rushed to hug him. He scooped her up and hoisted her off her feet to twirl her in a circle.

Mydei was jealous for the second time that night.

“When Aglaea told us-“

Phainon shook his head and let her go. “It’s fine, Hyacine. I can explain more later when we’re safe but… I’m glad it happened. Where’s Cipher?”
