“Lady Cipher told me to tell you, Lord Phainon, that she will not be going with us,” Castorice relayed with a slight tremor in her voice, “she came to tell me that someone would need to hide our absences, lest the Council assume we were kidnapped and try to pursue, or worse, assume we were traitors and try to harm Lady Aglaea. She also told me to tell you: ‘leave the treasury door unlocked’ and that you would understand what she means.”

If Phainon didn’t, Mydei certainly did. With that superpower speed of hers, she could empty the Kremnos Treasury at her leisure once Nikador was dead and the coreflame retrieved if the vault door were unlocked.

“We should go,” Mydei urged, “Leonnius, run ahead, tell Hephaestion and Krateros to make ready to sail. This city will be awake soon.”

Castorice reached for one of Phainon’s hands, but Mydei grabbed his sleeve, holding him back. Both heirs looked at the prince with puzzled expressions and Hyacine’s eyebrows shot straight up.

He cleared his throat. “Deliverer, a moment.”

Ptolemy offered both girls one of his hands each and they giggled and ignored him to hold hands with each other instead. They skipped ahead, heads leaning close to each other as they whispered among themselves.

“Alas, I feel I may have deserved that,” he mumbled, clearly unbothered as he followed them down the road.

“Mydei?”

“Phainon, are you well?” Mydei asked.

He laughed, “Should I not be?”

“You’re leaving your home again; you have every right to be upset.”

“What do you mean, Mydei?” Phainon teased as he started walking, “we’re going home right now.”

-

Phainon hadn’t expected Mydei to be so stunned by what he had said, but he did mean every word. Okhema was home in the same way Aedes Elysiae was still Phainon’s home. It was a place where a part of his heart belonged, but Phainon had always carried the bulk of that belonging wherever he happened to be at the time so long as it was with good friends. Writing his letter to Aglaea, explaining how he felt he realized that homesickness had shifted, and he found himself longing for the Chryseus Leo, her crew, and especially her captain.

Fortunately, Mydei was easy to break out of stunned silences. Phainon punched him hard in the shoulder, challenged him to a race, and then they were nearly overtaking Leonnius and burying the girls in dust as they ran past.

Mydei did win that one. Phainon was only a little upset.

“Just you know,” Phainon started to say while the Kremnoans got the longboat ready, “only about half the crew are going to be happy to see us.”

Neither of the girls seemed upset so much as a little confused.

“Aren’t they expecting us? Is it because we’re Chrysos Heirs?” Hyacine asked.

“No, Mydei bleeds gold actually,” Phainon said, gesturing to him.

“It is because we are from Okhema,” Castorice observed, “and they don’t trust us.”

“Yeah. It took me a long time to earn my place here with them and some of them still don’t trust me,” Phainon admitted, “but the whole crew knows the plan and why you’re here.”

It had been a very stressful meeting and subsequent announcement. Krateros especially had not appreciated being kept out of the loop, especially when that loop involved retrieving Chrysos Heirs from Okhema. Having one Okheman warrior on board was enough as far as Krateros was concerned. Mydei and Krateros had argued about it up until Hephaestion yelled over them both to tell the old man why, that this wasn’t an Okheman infiltration, it was recruitment to reclaim Castrum Kremnos. Krateros had shut up after that and listened intently. He still wasn’t happy, and they didn’t tell him about their intentions for the coreflame, but he at least agreed to continue to follow Mydei’s command.

Even better, Krateros responded well to Phainon’s warrant. Perdikkas had worried that Krateros would try to kill Phainon as soon he learned that their duel was cancelled, but the old warrior had simply shrugged. He still refused to accept Phainon as crew, but he promised to speak to the others and assured them that there was no longer a risk to Phainon’s life from within.

“Don’t worry, Phainon,” Hyacine beamed at him, “we’re here to help, whether they like us or not.”

Castorice smiled and nodded.

“Your chariot awaits, ladies,” Ptolemy called. Leonnius slapped his shoulder, but they still held the boat steadily.

Both Phainon and Mydei held out their hands to the girls, offering strong support as they stepped into the longboat with their things. They waited until the girls were settled and then clambered in beside them to take up the oars.

The anchor was already coming up when they pulled up alongside the Chryseus Leo. Two pulleys were tossed down for Phainon and Leonnius to catch. They hooked them onto matching clasps at either end of the boat and, once secured, Mydei whistled.

“Hold on,” he cautioned and then the longboat lifted out of the water. It was not smooth. It never was being pulled up out of the water like that, but it got the job done and spared them a climb.

Hephaestion and Perdikkas were there to greet them at the rail and pull the longboat in close. They held the edges of both watercrafts tightly together while Mydei and Phainon jumped to the deck. Like before, they held their hands out to the ladies.

“Watch your step,” Phainon advised, cheerful. The crew were torn between pausing to curiously peek at the guests and hurrying to get underway, only deciding when Krateros came along barking orders and making the decision for them. They were still in enemy waters and there would be plenty of time for gawking later.

“Phainon,” Mydei instructed, “will you take them to our room for now? We need to take advantage of this favorable wind.”

The girls pinched their lips tightly, fighting grins as they elbowed each other at Mydei’s instruction.

“With respect, Prince Mydeimos,” Krateros growled, “I want to meet them before we leave.”

The underlying threat took the shine from Phainon’s eyes. His smile stayed but he was ready to call his sword if anything went sideways. Mydei was ready to fight too, the shine of his gauntlets toyed with the light when he rolled his fingers.

But neither woman minded the hostility. Hyacine stepped forward first with an adorable curtsy. “Thank you for having us!” she greeted, “My name is Hyacine. I’m a Chrysos Heir from the Grove of Epiphany, living in Okhema to help establish The Twilight Courtyard there.”

Krateros blinked. His harsh expression had already dropped in the face of such a friendly greeting.

“And I am Castorice, the Demigod of Death and Chrysos Heir from Aidonia.” She matched Hyacine’s curtsy. “If I may, would it be alright if I greeted you with a hug?”

Phainon tried and failed to keep his smile contained but his pride shone through anyway. His clever friends had managed to circumvent the Okheman issue entirely, were charming, and most importantly, disarming.

Krateros had no idea how to react. But Peucesta beside him did.

“I would like a hug,” he requested in his usual clear but soft voice. Castorice happily set her bag aside and stepped forward to hug him, brief but warm.

“I am Peucesta,” he told her when they separated.

“I’m Hephaestion,” the first mate greeted. He stepped up on Krateros’ other side to sandwich the old man in. “I would also enjoy a hug.”

She smiled ardently and embraced Hephaestion. He squeezed her shoulders appropriately and then let her go to look at Krateros with a smug expression until the old man caved.

“…I suppose that would be alright,” he grumbled, that old man bravado crumbling under so many eyes and gentle expectations.

Castorice’s hug melted the man’s heart so fast that Phainon wondered how much of his own heartache in the last month could’ve been avoided if he had requested the same on his first day. Probably none of it actually. Phainon might’ve been executed if he tried that. He was a different kind of cute and Castorice was simply special in a way that he was not. Phainon loved everything about her.

Krateros’ tiny smile was priceless as he tentatively hugged her back, until he broke it off and she stepped away. He cleared his throat. “I’m Krateros,” he finally introduced, “if you need anything while you two are on board, let me know.” And then the old man was stomping away, barking orders as though he wasn’t an old grandpa at heart with a new favorite.

“Peer pressure always works,” Hephaestion said with a grin, “it’s an honor to meet you both. Anyone that can sway Krateros so completely is a someone that I’d like to toast.”

“After we are away from this place,” Mydei reminded him.

“Any trouble in Okhema?” Perdikkas was asking Leonnius.

“Homer over here wouldn’t stop flirting.”

Ptolemy almost dropped the line he was holding as they pulled the longboat inside the ship so they could set sail. “It’s not flirting!”

“’Oh, Miss Castorice!’” Leonnius impersonated in a voice much too high to be Ptolemy. He pressed his hands together and turned his eyes to the sky. “’Are you a goddess or a woman? May I steal your books?’”

“I don’t sound anything like that!”

Hephaestion was cracking up. “How many books did you steal, Ptolemy?”

Absolute silence. Ptolemy’s jaw slammed shut with a click of clashing teeth and his face turned red.

“I let him take a few of mine,” Phainon laughed.

“Yeah, they were offered, not stolen!”

“Oh, Mister Ptolemy,” Castorice picked her bag up again and opened it to show him several of her handwritten manuscripts, cheeks matching his shade of red.

Hyacine covered her mouth to giggle, “I think they’re going to be friends.”

“Phainon,” Mydei reminded.

“Of course, captain,” he crooned with a mock salute, “I’ll get them settled in.”

-

Aglaea –

Someday, I hope to be able to tell you all of this in person but hopefully this letter brings you comfort until that time when we are reunited.

I am alive and well and the last person who deserves your worry. When we last spoke, I swore an oath to you to sail into the world hunting the evil that threatened our people, that I would return in glory, worthy of the name you gave me. That oath still holds true for the greater part.

I am still sailing and hunting the worst threats to humanity, but I have failed you in one regard: my loyalty is no longer solely to Okhema and her beauty. Rather I have sailed beyond Kephale’s reach and met people as vibrant and lively as our own and equally worthy of protection. They are led by a man that reminds me of you.

I am no hero, but you taught me with words and by example how to be selfless, that our golden blood is a noble calling to set ourselves aside out of love for others. It is because of this that I must apologize for failing the responsibility you gave me. I cannot be Okhema’s Deliverer. That title is not meant for me.

When I first read your words and realized that I had been branded a pirate I was hurt, but the fall from captain to pirate wasn’t as far as I first thought. I am still me. More than that, I am a version of myself that is somehow more ‘free.’

I suspect that it was not your decision. Caenis and the Council have ever opposed the Flame Chase and they likely leapt at the chance to weaponize the law against you. Even so, did you know when you wrote those words, that I would feel that way?

You have always read my heart in a manner that I never could. Have you always known that I have harbored doubts? That I was afraid of letting you down? Did you know that when you made me a pirate that you were giving me the freedom to pursue a noble course? A course that has filled me with such passion that it has redefined for me what it means to be ‘home.’

If you did, thank you, Aglaea.

There is a man who I have found out here among the waves. He is the one I mentioned, a pirate captain, and the most honorable, noble soul I have ever met. Like you, he cares deeply, leads fairly, and keeps himself apart in quiet confidence so that he may best serve those under his command. I have found in him a kindred spirit, one that sings in combat and competition, but finds joy in peace.

You taught me to judge a man by how he treats others and Mydei elevates and inspires those around him, he serves them, loves them, and risks his life for their happiness. He is kingly, handsome, and he loves his countrymen so completely that he fights the destiny they want for him with an ardor that exemplifies the Titans of old. I have spoken to his crew, and not only would they die for him, but they LIVE for him, and he has proven to me time and again that he is worthy of that love.

I want you to meet him, Aglaea. Please be patient with me, as you always have been. When the two of us return to Okhema again it will be wreathed in glory, and I will present him to you as the hero he is. More than anything I want you to see what I see in him, this man who deserves the world, who is far more worthy than I of the title, Deliverer.

I believe that you will see into his heart as you have mine, feel the depth of his spirit, and fall for his charms as I have.

My vow to you is still binding and I will give all of me to the flame-chase journey, but I know now that it is at Mydei’s side that I may best achieve this purpose that you cultivated within me.

I will earn your pride and be worthy of you. Please continue to wait for me.

Phainon

-

Aglaea read the cookie jar letter three more times, her smile never wavering, never changing, with every pass, as she reclined on her kline with Vigethos curled up in her lap. Her perfectly manicured nails scratched under his collar and around his ruff while he snoozed happily in the peace just before Entry Hour.

Cipher’s distraction finally ran its course after bathing almost the entire night. Aglaea knew how much the cat hated the bath and had taken advantage of the opportunity in a heartbeat. And the entire time they soaked, and Cipher chattered to her of halcyon days long past, golden threads wove a symphony. It was a verse in vibrations, singing the tale of four intruders sneaking through her city and leaving with two of her own.

She had waited until they left along the dromas road to tell Cipher that she was tired and wanted to rest, freeing the cat from her soggy fate, believing her mission a success. In a way, Aglaea supposed it was.

“Agy,” Tribbie said by her side, “we changed the winds as you requested. Are you sure about this?”

“I am, teacher. Thank you for indulging me. I know it is not easy to command the winds in such a way.”

“We are the Demigod of Passages,” Tribbie confirmed, “it is our job… Is Snowy okay?”

The little demigod had her hands clasped to her chest; brows pinched with concern. Keeping them in the dark had been the hardest part of this plan. Aglaea felt so blessed to be worthy of the trust from her seniors.

“More than okay, teacher,” Agy said, barely above a whisper. She curled her finger in the air and the golden threads that bound the room made themselves visible. They wavered as they moved, glitter in motion, lining every letter on the paper so that she could ‘see’ every emotion that Phainon had left on the page in ink made of those very same threads.

Mnestia’s coreflame, buried deep in her chest, purred as she read the letter again to herself. The threads quivered vibrantly in their joy, allowing themselves this indulgence in a complicated web of Aglaea’s weaving.

“He is in love.”

Chapter End Notes

Technically Tribbie AND Trianne have made appearances now but I'm not going to add them to the character tags since those have been isolated to cameo style appearances. Aglaea gets one because she's been much more involved with many more appearances in the story than a lot of people realize :3c

chapters.title: Chapter 21: Coreflame Confessions
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

We should probably talk about coreflames...

Chapter Notes

Not a tag update but a chapter total update. My original outline is in sobbing shambles, the revised one was too optimistic for its own good, and I'm too determined to guess to just leave it as a question mark. No worries though, I'd rather move the goal posts than make cuts or ruin the pacing

They made it to the room eventually. Phainon had gotten distracted halfway there and left the girls by the rail to help with the launch. He was still a part of the crew, and he did apologize profusely for leaving them there while they got the sails unfurled but every time Phainon glanced over they seemed to be enjoying themselves. Neither of them were regular sailors but they had been passengers enough to know how to manage expectations. The two of them were shoulder to shoulder at the railing, pointing at eye-catching features on the horizon as the southern wind gathered them up and sent them soaring away from the holy city.

Castorice was gathering her shawl about her shoulders more tightly to combat the sea breeze when Phainon finally came for them again.

“I’m sorry about that,” he apologized with a grin, “all hands-on deck for the launch.”

“You’re really a part of the crew,” Hyacine observed aloud. She was thoughtful but mildly dismissive, clearly not wanting to start any kind of altercation.

“I’m glad you’re happy, Lord Phainon,” Castorice added to cover for her friend’s misgivings, “I have not seen you so eager to tackle a task since we were all students at the Grove.”

Memories begat smiles and lightened any lingering tensions.

“I want to give you the tour,” Phainon explained, “but I know the others will want to talk to you.”

“I think,” Hyacine started to say as she took Castorice’s hand and they exchanged a brief look, “I think we want to know everything first.”

“That’s fair,” he agreed. He motioned for them to follow and led them to the captain’s quarters, well, his quarters too. Now that Phainon wasn’t in any danger, would he have to move out to sleep with the crew? He hadn’t really considered it until now. Maybe if he didn’t say anything, Mydei wouldn’t consider it either and he could stay.

“This is where Mydei and I sleep,” he said with a broad, sweeping gesture across the room, “and where all the meetings happen, navigation… it’s an all-purpose room.”

The two girls spread out to explore, being polite and resisting the urge to touch anything.

“Do you two share a hammock?” Castorice asked. She blinked her eyes innocently at him.

“No, mine’s over here. The ship isn’t that small that we have to share.” Phainon moved to the far side of his room to his own hammock and put a hand on the edge of it. It peeped once and a sleepy Fig Stew stuck his head out, wiggling it under Phainon’s hand with a groggy sigh.

Both girls squealed.

The chimera squinted at them and leaned back but the assault he was expecting didn’t come. Castorice and Hyacine approached very slowly, very carefully, and they both offered their hands for Fig Stew to sniff before they tried to touch him, which he appreciated. Phainon scratched gently behind his ears.

“What’s their name?” Castorice asked in an awed whisper.

“This is Fig Stew. He is the ship’s chimera.”

“He’s so beautiful.” Hyacine had little tears budding in the corners of her eyes.

“Just don’t pet his belly. Only people he really likes can pet his belly.”

“Can you pet his belly, Lord Phainon? All the chimeras in Okhema like your belly rubs.”

Phainon sighed sadly, “I’m working on it.” He looked down at Fig Stew. “All the Okheman chimeras!”

Fig Stew sniffed each of them in turn, skeptical but curious, and then he sniffed the air, steadily picking up speed until his nose was moving a mile minute and he was standing up in the hammock, awake and on the hunt. He deliberated for about ten seconds and settled on staring at Phainon’s pockets.

“Oh, I stole these from Aglaea’s office,” Phainon remembered. He pulled a couple cookies free and held them up, watching Fig’s big red eyes widen.

“Lord Phainon…”

“I’m a pirate now, remember,” he teased. It still stung a little to say, but joking about it helped. Phainon had willingly embraced it even if it went against the grain he had been raised to follow for so long. Those little aches would probably linger for a while yet.

He handed each of them a cookie so that Fig Stew could consider his choice of offerings. All of them stood shoulder to shoulder, crowded around Phainon’s hammock, cookies held out on open palms, holding perfectly still.

With a connoisseurial flair, Fig Stew studied all three cookies. They each got a sniff, a tiny poke of a claw, and a lick. That little brain turned like a windmill until he concluded that they were the same and delicately took all three of them one at a time, beginning with Castorice and ending with Phainon. He dumped the biscuits onto Phainon’s bed and messily devoured all three at once, scattering crumbs everywhere while the girls fawned over his cookie conquest.

“He looks a little like Lord Mydei,” Castorice observed as she reached over to scratch between his shoulder blades with two fingers.

“I thought that too!” Phainon returned.

“Speaking of Lord Mydei,” Hyacine invited with a cough, “he isn’t what I picture when I think of Kremnoan pirates.”

“Really? It’s because of the cloak. He has the exact build you’d expect, and he has all the Kremnoan tattoos and that regal bearing from being their Crown Prince. How do I describe it,” he fumbled, “almost like if a lion was a person.”

“…do you like him, Lord Phainon?” Castorice prodded gently.

“Yeah, he’s a good captain. The crew loves him, and he takes care of everyone,” Phainon explained, “Mydei is also the ship’s cook, so he works just as hard as any of us, maybe even more so. I help him sometimes grinding the wheat for fresh flour and he checks on me a lot to make sure I’m okay. He’s strong too. As strong as we are. I know he bleeds gold so he’s technically a Chrysos Heir like us, but I believe he could stand up to you in a fight, Castorice.”

“You said he’s the Crown Prince?” Hyacine asked.

“Did they not tell you when they talked to you?” Phainon asked, genuinely surprised. He sat back on his hammock, nearly sending Fig Stew flying, but the chimera didn’t protest and instead scooted up close to Phainon’s side.

She shook her head.

“Lord Phainon, I think the stories we were told may have been different…”

“They tried to all tell me things at once,” Hyacine explained, “it was cute, but not very helpful.”

“And you agreed to come anyway?”

“Of course, Phainon. All I needed to know was that you were the one asking.” She smiled at him with sincerity that he had missed more than he realized and his heart melted.

“Well, let me tell you then, everything, the good, the bad, and how amazing this crew really is.”

-

Mydei, Krateros, and Hephaestion got the Chryseus Leo comfortably on course for home. It was the next logical step as it was a good halfway point between Okhema and Castrum Kremnos, they needed to assess supplies, and while there was an impending, unknown deadline with the Black Tide’s steady creeping, rest was also an important resource that needed managing. Mydei was not taking his men into the heart of the Tide unless they were rested and had chosen to go with full knowledge of the plan.

There also needed to be a plan.

And Mydei was not interested in a plan that was cooked up half-assed on exhaustion, which is why he really just wanted to sleep. But every time he paused outside his own door, he could hear three excited voices quietly chittering and giggling away. Phainon hadn’t seen his two friends in over a month. Until recently he wasn’t sure he’d see them ever again at all. It would be unfair for Mydei to interrupt a reunion when he himself knew how important those moments of reconnection were.

He pressed his ear to the door, trying to hear just enough to determine how long they’d be and all he could make out was Phainon’s polished voice in unintelligible murmurs. Mydei narrowed his eyes when he thought he heard his own name, but it could’ve also been the exhaustion.

“You know it’s your room,” Hephaestion whispered from directly behind Mydei. The prince swung a punch on reflex, but Hephaestion ducked in time. “Why are you sulking out here?”

Mydei skulked away from the door and walked all the way out to the rail. They would be away from the Dawn Device soon, not that they’d be able to easily tell with the new day already upon them. With this wind they were making amazing time.

“I’m giving them time to catch up,” Mydei explained.

“You know you could be in there catching up with them.”

The lion shook his head. “No, I want Phainon to feel as though he can tell them everything. He may not feel that way if I am there listening.”

Hephaestion leaned on the rail next to him. “Mydei, Phainon is the most understanding person on the ship. You’re still holding onto guilt that he’s forgiven you for.”

“Until I hear him say it-“

Hephaestion groaned loud enough to cut him off. “Mydeimos, my brother, I love you, but you are surprisingly dense when you get in your own way.”

Mydei frowned.

“If it wasn’t Phainon, would you be sitting out here?”

No. Mydei would’ve given anyone else the boot. He shook his head.

“Then why is Phainon different?” Hephaestion asked, poking at the heart of the matter, trying to drag that back burner thought back to the front. Did Hephaestion know? Could his first mate also see whatever Cipher had pulled from the depths of his soul?

“He’s not,” Mydei huffed, pushing it back down. He turned around and strode back to his own room with Hephaestion right behind him. The three Okhemans quieted when the door opened and the two Kremnoans stepped in.

“Mydei!” Phainon greeted and Mydei’s heart started doing jumping jacks. That smile was extra obnoxiously dazzling. All three of them had crammed onto Phainon’s hammock, the nature of the seating pressing them all tight against each other with Phainon in the middle. Mydei had to take a second to remind himself that close proximity was a friendly thing, that he was also very physical with his own friends.

“Hephaestion!” Phainon added when he spotted the first mate too.

“Heya, Okhemans,” he teased when Mydei said nothing, “I know this is a reunion you’ve been looking forward to, Phainon, but…”

“I know, it’s late,” Phainon finished with an apologetic furrowing of his brows.

Mydei looked between the three of them and sighed, “Deliverer, you and I will sleep in the crew’s quarters-“

“NO!” Castorice stood up and shouted and the whole room froze, wide-eyed at the outburst. Mydei stood still with his lips parted, he had no idea how to react to that. His fight-or-flight was holding the moment right in the middle of the two options in the space reserved for ‘what the fuck’ happenings and ill-conceived competitive challenges.

The only one that moved was Fig Stew, who rolled into the space she had just vacated from where he had been squished behind them. The chimera had a smug grin slapped on his face looking at everyone with a much too round belly and some kind of crumbs all over his fur.

“I-I just mean,” she fell right back into her soft, demure voice, gentle but insistent, “Hyacine and I don’t need our own room. We couldn’t possibly, when this is already your space…”

“Miss Castorice, I insist,” Mydei tried, tentative, like he was reasoning with a tsunami, “what kind of host would I be if I made you sleep with my men?”

Hyacine stood up next, a little too quickly, the balance in the hammock shifted and Phainon flailed to stay upright.

“Actually, Captain Mydeimos,” she said with that self-assured manner of speaking that Perdikkas used when he was taking charge of a room during a medical emergency, “as a doctor, I think it’s best that I immediately begin adapting to the atmosphere of your ship’s infirmary.”

“As her assistant, I should do the same,” Castorice insisted.

Phainon tilted his head. He was still trying to get out of the hammock. It was genuinely cute and simultaneously stressful. Part of Mydei wanted to hurry to his aid, the much larger part was enjoying watching his struggle knowing he wasn’t in any real danger. He’d figure it out someday, just like the sea legs he had finally developed.

“Since when?” the Deliverer asked.

“It happened while you were gone,” Hyacine said sweetly, and much too quickly.

“There are several beds in the infirmary,” Hephaestion offered, “I can take them so you two can get some rest.”

Hyacine and Castorice immediately locked eyes with Hephaestion and Mydei felt like they were up to something. Somehow. Already. With someone they had barely met. There was too much instant understanding for it not to be the most suspicious non-verbal exchange since Peucesta and Leonnius had set up that betting ring around Mydei and Phainon’s spars.

Mydei sighed, deep and full, defeated and open about it. He was way too tired for this right now.

“Alright, alright,” he relented, “make sure you speak to Perdikkas when he wakes so he knows you are staying there.”

Both the girls curtsied and gathered their things.

“We’ll talk more tomorrow, Lord Phainon,” Castorice reassured him. Not that he needed it. Phainon looked fine, just happy to have spent any time with them at all.

“Sleep well, Lord Phainon, Lord Mydeimos,” Hyacine said with a smile. It almost sounded like an order coming from her, the kind you wanted to obey without realizing it. Anything to make her happy.

Hephaestion closed the door behind them, leaving Mydei and Phainon alone.

Phainon groaned as he got up. The exhaustion was hitting him all at once now that the girls were gone and Mydei felt a little special to see him unwind. That public facing mask that Phainon wore was coming off in the comfort of his own space, a space he shared willingly with Mydei. Now that Phainon was no longer in danger, he probably could move to the crew’s quarters… Or Mydei could forget that he realized as much and never bring it up. They were comfortable, it would be a hassle to move all his stuff. Far more convenient if Phainon stayed where he was.

“I am glad to see them,” Phainon admitted, “but I am so tired.”

Mydei grunted and took his cloak off, starting the evening routine. “We are fortunate that we were able to retrieve them safely.”

“Yeah, Cipher must’ve pulled out all the stops to keep Aglaea from finding out.”

“…they’re cute,” Mydei mentioned quietly.

“Who? Hyacine and Castorice?”

“Yes.”

Phainon laughed, “do you have a crush already, Mydei? What happened when you went to find Hyacine?”

Mydei turned away to hide his blush. He did have a crush, it just wasn’t Hyacine. “HKS! Suggest as much again and I’ll toss you in my cookpot.”

Phainon’s chuckle was music to his ears. He could hear the man undressing, setting aside his armor pieces and putting them away in his drawer. “It’s okay if you do. Both of them are amazing, Cipher too. All three of them are like sisters to me.”

That was a relief. Phainon wasn’t dating any of them.

“I don’t,” Mydei insisted, “I have… other tastes.”

Phainon gasped like Mydei had said something scandalous. “Oh, Mydeimos, could it be that your crystal heart belongs to someone already?”

Mydei ignored him and shrugged out of his armor. Each gauntlet had their own space in an easy to access drawer so he knew where they were at all times.

“Oh, Mnestia, it does.” Phainon came up behind him and put an arm around his shoulders so Mydei couldn’t escape. He was only half dressed when he pressed in close. “Is it Hephaestion?”

“Persistent dog,” Mydei snarled. He punched at Phainon, but the man was learning, he dipped to the side to spare his gut the hit and swapped sides.

“Why won’t you tell me?” Phainon pouted, “who won the affections of our prince? Do I know him?”

“You will not live long enough to know if you do not go to bed this instant!” Mydei felt like he was on fire. He absolutely refused to look at his friend and rival, just in case he was as easy to read as he feared. If a stranger like Cipher could pluck truths from the depths of him, what could he hope to hide from Phainon?

Phainon gasped, “I do know him!”

“HKS! What did I just say!?” Mydei growled but Phainon took the hint and backed away to kick off his own boots and wiggle out of his trousers.

“Fine, fine, I’m sure I’ll find out eventually.”

“Phainon,” Mydei said, mostly under his breath, too much like a confession to his own burning ears.

“Hm?”

“…I’ll tell you who it is after we get the coreflame,” he promised. Mydei busied himself with folding his shed clothes as an excuse to keep his back turned.

“I’ll hold you to that.” Phainon’s grin was audible. “AW MAN.”

Mydei spun around, alarmed. Phainon was in his small clothes, holding his pants with the pockets inside out. They were completely empty but lined with toasty golden crumbs.

“How did you eat all of those already?!”

Fig Stew was smiling from Phainon’s hammock, eyelids heavy in the ultimate expression of full contentment, knowing he was the real winner of the night.

-

The tradition of waking Phainon up for meetings continued the following Action Hour when the chatter of several people woke him up. Perdikkas, Hephaestion, Krateros, Hyacine, and Castorice were there, sitting around the table with fruit, cheese, and juice. No yummy, captain cooked meals which made sense considering the captain was not awake.

For once, Phainon wasn’t the last one to the party. Mydei was.

He yawned, stretched, and very carefully swung a leg over his hammock to start the arduous process of sitting up in a sleeping arrangement that wiggled excessively every time he moved.

“Good morning, Lord Phainon,” Castorice whispered. She waved to him using Fig Stew’s paw. The chimera was sitting in her lap, partially on his back with her arm wrapped loosely around his chest so he could make biscuits in the air with all four of his paws. His big red eyes were watching her every move with very slow blinks, and he wagged his tail whenever she smiled back at him. Absolutely smitten.

Phainon managed a lopsided smile and another yawn. “Breakfast?” Hephaestion pushed one of the plates his way.

“It’s more like a late lunch,” Hyacine teased.

“We were up late,” he pouted. Phainon’s chiton had fallen off one shoulder while he slept and he didn’t bother fixing it. Modesty had long gone out the window with the Kremnoans and both Castorice and Hyacine had seen all of him before after a college prank went a little too right. Professor Anaxa had been far more embarrassed and upset than Phainon had been after that one.

He plucked a handful of grapes from their vine to keep in hand while he ate them one at a time. “You two met?” Phainon asked as he pointed between Hyacine and Perdikkas.

“I met them both this morning,” Perdikkas responded, “I didn’t expect them in my infirmary.”

“He thought we were patients,” Hyacine giggled.

“And I am relieved that you are not,” he added, “the two of you are welcome to stay there as long as I don’t have need of those beds for injured people.”

“Perdikkas was the one who stitched up my leg,” Phainon reminded them.

“Phainon showed us his scar last night,” Hyacine said excitedly, “your technique is incredible.”

“It’s just practice, Miss Hyacine.”

“Where’re everyone else?” Phainon asked.

Krateros answered, “sleeping or busy. Ptolemy is in the library reading, Leonnius is sleeping, and Peucesta is covering for the prince in the galley.”

Speaking of the prince… Phainon tip-toed over to his hammock to peek. The Kremnoan was out, wearing only a pair of shorts since he tended to run hot when he slept. He was curled up tightly on his side to face away from the room, leaning more heavily to one end of the hammock so he wouldn’t ruin his back with that position. The man was also crying, tiny tears beaded like pearls in the corners of his eyes. Phainon might’ve assumed they were just the usual sleep that gets rubbed away in the morning with a hearty yawn but there were tear tracks on his nose and cheeks and anxious tension in his brow.

He frowned, worried, and a little confused. Mydei was usually up before Phainon, rarely sleeping in, choosing small cat naps throughout the day instead. Those few times that Phainon was awake while Mydei slept, the man was like a rock. He didn’t thrash, he didn’t move, if he had bad dreams, he never physically expressed it… until now.

Phainon reached out to brush his thumb across Mydei’s eyes, to maybe provide some comfort if he could but he didn’t get that far.

“Leave him be,” Krateros scolded, “Mydeimos rarely gets the chance to sleep so heavily.”

He pulled his hand back and went to pick a seat instead, thoughts still drifting to his troubled friend.

“Okay,” Hephaestion started, to get everyone’s attention, “there are a few things we need to discuss before we can start making any real plans and that process needs to be moving. Perdikkas and I are doing inventory today so we can hand the list of things we still need to Empousa. So, what do you three need for the campaign?”

Perdikkas leaned on the table a little. He had a pen there, a small inkwell, and some loose paper ready to record.

“I suppose that will depend on what is requested of us,” Hyacine thought aloud, “Lord Phainon told us last night about his adventures here and about you all, but we didn’t have time to discuss what role you need us to play.”

“Do you need us to fight?” Castorice asked.

“Let’s start with the main problem,” Phainon suggested. He held his hand up to cover his mouth while he spoke, trying to multitask eating and contributing with at least a little bit of decorum. “Castrum Kremnos is very deep inside the Black Tide and it has been for five years.”

“So only Chrysos Heirs can go there,” Hyacine supplied.

“Not exactly,” Perdikkas said, “Phainon told you that we’ve been fighting the Black Tide?”

“He said that you had made strides and were able to push it back somehow,” she clarified.

“We can’t interact with the Black Tide itself,” the doctor continued. He used the pen to point between the three Kremnoans in the room. “But the ship can. Chryseus Leo is resilient to the Tide and as long as we stay on it, we’re safe. We can get a full crew to Castrum Kremnos.”

“The problem is we can’t leave the ship,” Hephaestion finished, “that’s where you two come in.”

“We have four Chrysos Heirs,” Phainon picked up what was now a practiced discussion, “the three of us and Mydei and Mydei is basically a one-man army. He is incredibly strong, and I told you last night about his immortality.”

“You told us a lot about Lord Mydei, yes,” Castorice confirmed, gently. She was slowly tracing little circles on Fig Stew’s belly, something that Phainon would be very, very jealous about later.

“He and I can fight Nikador,” Phainon said confidently.

“Just the two of you?” Hyacine asked, worry coloring her voice.

“Trust me, we’ve been sparring every day, and we are evenly matched. Mydei could probably take the Titan alone,” he praised, “there is no contest with the both of us.”

It was a fight that Phainon was genuinely looking forward to; one for which he had been preparing. He had some history with Strife, nothing as prominent as his deep-seated hatred and fears with the Black Tide, but Phainon had studied Nikador at length. It was one of his many side interests at the Grove when he still wanted to study combat at Castrum Kremnos, before duty and life had sent him in another direction.

“What we can’t handle, is Nikador and the armies of Castrum Kremnos,” Phainon admitted.

“You need me to use my touch…” Castorice mumbled. She hugged Fig Stew a little tighter and the chimera purred to reassure her.

“As the Demigod of Death, you could keep most of the city from interfering,” he told her.

“Hold on.” Hephaestion waved a hand in front of himself. “Aren’t all of you demigods?”

“Only Cassie,” Hyacine confirmed.

“I thought that was what the gold blood meant. That you were Chrysos Heirs and thus, demigods.”

Phainon shook his head. “Chrysos Heirs are people with gold blood, yes, but only Chrysos Heirs that have a coreflame in their chests are demigods. All demigods are Chrysos Heirs, but not all Chrysos Heirs are demigods.”

“Mydei isn’t a demigod,” Perdikkas reminded Hephaestion.

“Right, but I thought Phainon was.”

“Phainon and I haven’t been given coreflames,” Hyacine told them gently, “Lady Aglaea has unclaimed coreflames, but she said we weren’t ready to see them yet.”

Castorice put a hand over her chest. “Coreflames are alive in a way,” she explained reverently, “they aren’t power that can be wielded safely by anyone, like the Council believes, they have chosen their bearers across time. When Lord Phainon and I recovered the Coreflame of Death from Thanatos, it felt like nothing to him, but for me…” Her voice warmed at the thought. “It was like a part of my heart that I didn’t know was missing was restored. It was warmth and comfort and responsibility so great that I thought I would burst with the joy of it.”

“Aglaea told me that when she first held her coreflame, she knew it was hers,” Phainon recounted, “but it wouldn’t accept her right away. She said that knowing that the coreflame was a part of her but that she wasn’t ready for it was so heartbreaking that she almost gave up. She doesn’t want that for us, so Hyacine and I aren’t allowed to see the coreflames until Aglaea knows we’re ready and that we are paired correctly to the coreflame we’re meant to inherit.”

“Do you know which coreflames she has?” Perdikkas asked.

“Sky and Worldbearing,” Phainon said, unsure. He looked to Castorice and Hyacine for confirmation and they nodded.

“We used to guess which ones would be ours,” Hyacine shyly told them, “But not all Chrysos Heirs will get one, and that’s okay. We just want to help, and we can do that without coreflames.”

“Which one do you think is yours, Deliverer?” Mydei asked. The room jumped at his voice. It was hard to tell how long he had been awake. The tears had been brushed away and he looked groggy with wild bed head, but his eyes were alert as he sat up in the hammock and sluggishly twisted to look at them.

“It really doesn’t matter if I get one at all,” Phainon assured them, “I’m plenty strong without one, but I… I always thought Strife might be mine.”

Krateros inhaled sharply through his nose, but he held his tongue. His mood darkened and they could all feel the weight of it in the room, the sudden realization that Phainon had ulterior motives.

Mydei was undeterred. “That suits you. All the more reason to retrieve it,” he said.

Krateros leaned forward to snap, “Mydeimos!”

The prince held his hand up to stop the protesting they all knew was coming. “The greatest challenge will not be Nikador, it will be the armies between us and the Titan. Miss Hyacine, the Deliverer has spoken highly of your research. He claims you can heal Black Tide corruption; would you be able to find the means to allow my people to fight inside the city?”

Undeterred, Krateros stepped in again to shout, “No, you will not have a crew to fight for you if we do not discuss the coreflame!”

The threat lingered uncomfortably in the air. Mydei ran a hand through his hair and Phainon immediately wanted to do the same. Was it as soft as it looked?

“What use have we for it?” Mydei asked very seriously.

“I was led to believe that we were retrieving the coreflame for the glory of Castrum Kremnos,” the old man insisted.

Mydei sighed at the inevitability, “Krateros, that is not entirely true.”

The old man’s eyes widened as he looked between everyone seated there. Only the girls met his gaze, equally confused, the rest… “Was this the plan from the start? To give the essence of our Titan to the Goldweaver? So, your new favorite can play god?”

“This was always about Phainon’s pardon,” Mydei confirmed, “but we are not without benefit, Krateros, reclaiming the city and felling the Titan will silence the Tide and protect our people for many years to come. Is that not worth it?”

“This is the Crown all over again, Mydeimos! Will you reject the divine authority that should be your birthright too?”

“Did you not hear them? The coreflame chooses. For all we know that is what drove my father to madness, trying to force the coreflame’s decision.”

“This is not the future Queen Gorgo would have wanted for you!”

Mydei stood then with a growl. “My mother is dead!” he reminded his teacher, “do not use her to further your wants.”

Fig Stew cooed sadly, watching Mydei intently. Phainon looked over at the sound and saw the chimera’s eyes alight. Castorice was studying the chimera with a frightening intensity. He needed to stop this fighting, whatever it took.

“I won’t accept it,” Phainon said firmly, and the room went quiet, “if it is mine, I will reject it.”

“Lord Phainon-!” Hyacine started to say.

“Please believe me, Lord Krateros,” he said with a hand over his heart, “this endeavor is not to further my own ambitions. But I did keep my intentions from you and the captain and you are owed the full truth.” Mydei’s eyes narrowed, Hephaestion leaned forward with suspicion. “I know it was the plan for me to take the Coreflame to Okhema to exchange it for my own pardon, that is what Mydei, and the others wanted, but it was my intention from the start to petition not for myself but for the entire crew and for peace between Okhema and Kremnos. Even if the Coreflame of Strife is meant for me, I will reject it, to prove to you that this mission is not for me alone but for all our peoples.”

There was silence. Krateros was still shaking in fury, Mydei looked annoyed. Maybe that was a truth best kept to himself, but Phainon held his ground all the same.

“Do you really believe that I need the power of a Titan to lead our people, Krateros?” Mydei growled, backing Phainon up from another angle.

“With that power we could win our war with Okhema,” Krateros grumbled, but he sounded unconvinced.

“We have no war with Okhema!” the prince hissed, “our war is with the Tide!”

Krateros faltered under the reminder.

“Lord Krateros,” Castorice said and she commanded his attention, “I may understand more than most how you feel. Would it be alright, if we spoke in private?”

He looked at her and then down to where she was petting Fig Stew’s belly. The tension in the room remained but it plateaued. “So long as you know my mind will not change.”

She smiled and Phainon knew Krateros had no idea the kind of challenge he had just thrown to her. “I only wish to understand you, Lord Krateros.”

“…very well,” he agreed.

Castorice stood up on the spot, unwilling to wait. She delicately set Fig Stew down on the floor and then reached to take Krateros’ hand. Caught off guard by her gentle demeanor he took it, and they excused themselves to speak.

“Someday,” Hephaestion sighed, “he’s going to die in his sleep of old age, and we won’t have to worry about him anymore.”

Perdikkas smacked Hephaestion across the side of his head, hard, beating Mydei to it.

“That’s rude,” the doctor scolded.

“I stand by it,” the first mate grumbled.

“To answer your question, Lord Mydei,” Hyacine said. Her hands were in her lap as she fiddled with her thumbs. “I can heal corruption from the Tide, but I cannot prevent it. That was not my topic of study. A place as saturated as Castrum Kremnos… I don’t think I would be able to heal your men fast enough to allow them to fight and I know I wouldn’t be able to prevent the corruption.”

The Kremnoans tried not to show their disappointment, but Phainon saw it in their changed postures. Even Fig Stew slowly star-fished on the floor in chimerical grief.

“But I know someone who can,” she said, “and he’s a Chrysos Heir too.”

Phainon immediately brightened when he realized who she was talking about.

“Do we need to return to Okhema for him?” Mydei asked.

“No, he’s right where we saw him last,” she announced, smiling at her fellow graduate.

Mydei flashed him a puzzled look and Phainon grinned back to say, “we’re going to the Grove of Epiphany.”

Chapter End Notes

Krateros is not a bad guy. I LOVE him in the game but he's also a stubborn old man and stubborn old men need a lot of convincing to abandon the only course of action they've ever known

Also, Castorice and Hyacine aren't ENTIRELY self-inserts but they are certainly relatable

chapters.title: Chapter 22: The Grove of Epiphany
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

New character tag: Anaxagoras

The crew arrives in the Grove of Epiphany! Well, most of the crew.

The Grove of Epiphany had fallen to the Black Tide a couple years prior. Long enough ago to have already decayed into a shell of its former self with no hope of any population remaining but recent enough that Phainon had been at its downfall. He had helped with the evacuation and had even argued with the man they were going to collect, trying to convince him to leave with the rest of the scholars. A man that all three Okhemans insisted was alive, well, and probably very happy to have been alone for the last two years.

Mydei was having a hard time envisioning a man like that as someone respectable. All he could picture was a crankier version of Krateros, perhaps with a hunch, and thinner… with glasses, yes, there were definitely glasses involved somehow. Was this man eating? Bathing? Isolation without the Black Tide could drive a man mad, with the monsters and the mist…

“You wanted to speak with me?” Krateros asked from behind him. Mydei was on the top deck, leaning over the railing to keep watch over the rest of the ship. Lazy days meant more free time for the whole crew so only about half of his men were actively working on their chores.

On deck, Mydei could spot Hephaestion taking a nap with a book on his face, hear Peucesta writing a new song, and see Perdikkas buffing some dents out of his shield. Most of his attention was on Phainon and Leonnius who were playing games with the girls, some sort of team tag that involved running around the foremast and main mast.

“To apologize,” Mydei confirmed without turning around.

“There is no need.”

“Yes, there is.”

Krateros stepped up next to him. The old man had mellowed out considerably after talking to Castorice, neither of them were willing to divulge any details about the exchange and Mydei didn’t really care what was said. What mattered was that Krateros was calmer, more receptive, like he was at least trying to set aside himself for a bit to consider the bigger picture. He was still stubborn and grumpy, but at least he wasn’t egregiously obstinate anymore.

“You have been advising me my whole life,” Mydei said as he turned around to face his mentor, “since Phainon, I have been pushing you aside, kept you in the dark, for that I apologize.”

“I accept your apology, Mydeimos,” he said, still a little cold, but Mydei smiled at him and leaned back to hit his arm playfully anyway.

“What do you think of the two of them?”

“Miss Castorice and Miss Hyacine?” Krateros asked for clarification. He stepped up to the railing to watch them play too. Mydei nodded and rested his hand on the rail.

“I wonder how the Goldweaver managed to ensnare them. They are too honest and good for Okhema,” he said after a moment to think about it, “…perhaps Phainon is as well.”

“I did not expect you to change your opinion of him.”

“And I have not. Not yet,” Krateros reiterated, “but he keeps good company. Present company included and that is the mark of a wise man.”

“I am glad that Castorice has tamed your fire even a little.”

“Fig Stew has deemed her worthy.”

“A chimera’s word treated as law,” Mydei laughed once, a sharp bark like he couldn’t quite believe it even if such had been the case as long as he could remember.

“He was your mother’s,” Krateros reminded him, “for all I know, Queen Gorgo is still with us through him. And she trusted his judgement. How can I not do the same?”

It was silly but comforting to think about.

“Krateros… about the coreflame.”

“You don’t need to explain, Mydeimos,” the old man sighed, “I don’t believe that Phainon is worth this effort and I can’t be sure he will keep his word until I see the two of you return with the coreflame in hand, but that he is willing to set himself aside for the Kremnoan people… it speaks volumes.”

“After everything he has already done, he still hasn’t earned your trust?”

“Someone needs to be wary of the Goldweaver and her influence, if no one else will be.”

Mydei sighed and ran his fingers through his hair, eventually letting the hand fall to the railing next to the other. At least Krateros’ problem wasn’t with Phainon as much as it was the person that once trained him and held his leash. He leaned forward to rest his weight on his forearms to ask, “What will it take?”

“I suppose I will know when the time comes,” Krateros mused.

“Then I hope it comes soon,” Mydei admitted, “when we win and seize the coreflame, when we are sure that he has his free agency again, I intend to ask him to join the crew.”

The old man sucked a deep breath in through his nose, a sure sign that he was not surprised but still displeased and trying to control himself. “He is not Kremnoan.”

“He is the embodiment of Strife, Krateros,” Mydei praised, smiling at Phainon. How could he not with the pure joy that the man brought with him wherever he went? Leonnius had tackled him, and they were play wrestling. Both the girls were cheering them on like they had picked champions in a noble scuffle.

“He is Okheman.”

“Will you keep pretending he is then? His own introduction claims another homeland entirely and the Goldweaver rejected him as their Deliverer. Even if we restore his status, do you really believe a den of distrustful snakes would embrace him as such again?” Mydei asked, “he is as free as we are, and he is Strife as Nikador should be, strength, honor, reason, tenacity, and sacrifice used not for conquest but as a shield. The coreflame would be foolish to reject him.”

Krateros crossed his arms. “I know I can’t change your mind, but I urge you to consider what it means to your people, what they see when this creature of Aglaea walks away with a relic that is at the heart of our people. It is bad enough that we must wait for you to take up the crown, must we surrender our Titan’s spirit? Or do you expect us to follow it to seek solace in the arms of our once ancient enemy?”

Mydei pulled away from the rail and slowly walked to the apulstre where his favorite carving was. Fig Stew was on his usual midday napping crate there too, close enough to the carvings to see the resemblance with the faded lions beside him. He could hear Krateros following across the deck, staying close to keep their conversation but giving him space to be respectful of their stations.

Mydei put his hand on the carving of Nikador and Kephale. “In far more ancient times our Titans were allies,” he reminded Krateros, “of all the traditions and legacies we keep, let us not forget that most important one.”

“If Gorgo could see you now,” Krateros mumbled but his tone was measured, caught between disappointment and praise, like even he wasn’t sure which to feel.

Mydei scratched Fig Stew’s belly and the chimera purred and woke up enough to check who it was. Content, the critter rolled himself over to give his favorite person and those perfect tummy scratching gauntlets better access.

“I wish she could,” he dreamed aloud, “I would want to tell her about Phainon.”

Krateros huffed, angrily admitting, “I am sure she would be charmed by him and then would demand he stop distracting the crew from their duties.”

“Duties I must attend to as well,” Mydei agreed. He gave Fig Stew one last pat and then took a deep breath in through his nose and out through his mouth. “I trust you to keep her sailing smoothly while I am below.”

“As always, Mydeimos.”

Mydei walked quickly with purpose but not hurried towards the stairs that led down to the galley, stopping at them to yell at the squabbling crew.

“Deliverer!” They all froze and looked over at him. The tangle of limbs on the deck had at some point absorbed Peucesta as well. “If you have time to play then you have time to help me in the galley.”

“This is hardly play, captain!” Phainon called back.

“Yeah, he promised to teach us a lesson!” Leonnius yelled from the top of the pile.

“How are they going to learn if I am pretending at chef?”

“Give yourself more credit,” Mydei huffed, “but fine, stay the lines, Deliverer. Miss Castorice, Miss Hyacine, passengers earn their keep on my ship. If you are willing, I would be grateful for more hands, and perhaps you can teach me the trick to commanding this troublesome dog on my crew.”

Castorice looked down at Phainon who was still very stuck and trying to yell back but Peucesta’s foot somehow ended up under his chin and he was struggling to wheeze out any banter.

“We do know a few things we could share, Lord Mydei,” she called mischievously.

“Good luck, Phainon,” Hyacine teased and then she was trotting with Castorice across the deck to catch up.

The confused, playful panic on Phainon’s face was cuter than Mydei would ever admit out loud.

-

The Grove of Epiphany was several days away in the middle of the Black Tide’s massive tide lines but even without the added ick, it was an overgrown mess to sail through. They had to wait for the natural ocean’s high tide to even approach the island because of the mass of roots and growth that were hiding under the water. In the two years of abandonment the forest had overgrown beyond the natural pruning and care of her gardeners. Now she was a trap for any watercraft that did not plan accordingly.

The myth claimed that the forest that surrounded and covered the island was all part of a single tree. Its expansion even into the ocean to blend with the seaweed forests was regarded as a metaphor for the adaptive pursuit of learning even beyond natural limitations. Looking at the island from afar, Mydei believed the rumor. The Tree of Cerces was impossible to mistake. She stood above all other vegetation, a mountain among them with the great crown of foliage perched atop her face on the curling trunk, massive enough to cradle this small city of learning and her universities.

The crew were quiet when they first approached the island, observing with reverence this place of pilgrimage now fallen to ruin. Kremnoans may not have valued research and study as highly as other cultures, but they recognized a temple when they saw one. And it was always humbling to see the gem of a nation brought low.

“To oars!” Krateros called when they approached and the men hurried from the rail, even Phainon ran below, leaving the two ladies to watch with bated breath. Leonnius scrambled up the shrouds, taking position at the topmast to scan for shallow surprises.

The ship rumbled, it was very brief, but Mydei felt it through his boots. They were already brushing against underwater debris, and they hadn’t sailed into the tree line yet. Silently he dropped into a crouch to put his hand on the deck, eyes closed. It was so subtle, but it was there, the brush of roots against the hull.

Mydei immediately walked to the tiller, snapping once to get the helmsman to step away and he took the tiller himself. It wasn’t that he didn’t trust the helmsman, the man was an experienced sailor but there were some situations that called for a different hand.

The crew universally agreed that Mydei had the strongest connection to Chryseus Leo, more so than most captains may develop with their ships. Mysticism wasn’t the right word for that relationship, but no one really knew how deep that bond went to describe it, not even Mydei, and it didn’t matter most of the time. When situations called for a steady hand, the prince was quick to take control of their home.

The only sounds were relayed calls, the oars dipping shallowly in the water, and the creak of the hull. No animal sounds, no insects, not even monster calls. Mydei stared at Leonnius unblinking, noting the turn of his head, when he paused, to anticipate each shout and make micro adjustments as needed. He mapped the forest in his head as branches caressed the hull, slowly weaving them between trees, until finally they found the pier and came to a stop.

Mydei let out the breath he was holding and nodded at the helmsman when the man looped ropes around the tiller to secure it. The bay was at least cleared of debris, or perhaps it simply hadn’t grown this far in yet. There was room to maneuver around the long pier with their pick of moorings. Krateros suggested one towards the end of the long dock and Mydei agreed. It was safer to stay at the depth they knew was safe, than try to save time and run aground in their hubris.

It only took a few minutes for practiced pirates to secure the ship and lower the ramp. Mydei met Phainon and the girls at the rail, a pace away from their exit.

“Do you know where he will be?” Mydei asked.

“He had a lab up at the university,” Hyacine explained, “I was his teaching assistant, so I know how to get there quickly.”

“You don’t think he would’ve moved to Professor Socrippe’s lab?” Phainon asked.

“He likes when things are consistent.”

“Yeah, but he hated Socippe because he got extra funding to expand his workspace.”

“Lord Phainon, do you really think Professor Anaxa is that petty to steal his rival’s laboratory at the first opportunity?” Castorice asked. The three of them thought about that for a second and then they all nodded at once. “Saying it out loud, it does make sense…”

“We can check both places,” Mydei reassured them.

“Splitting up would be faster,” Hephaestion suggested. He had very suddenly appeared in their circle, fully geared, holding a spear with his shield strapped to his back.

“Yeah, we can take Miss Castorice and Phainon,” Perdikkas recommended. They were already starting to herd the two of them towards the ramp, Phainon excitedly taking the hint to skip ahead before Mydei realized what was happening. The vaguely hedgehog shaped hoard of Kremnoans were trying to sneak off the ship in a phalanx formation as though their shields were enough to hide them from his ire.

“No,” he said firmly.

“Oh, come on!” Ptolemy shouted from somewhere inside that collection of spears and feet.

“We only need a small group.”

“Welp, you heard him,” Hephaestion ordered as he started down the ramp after them, “everyone back on the ship.”

“Hephaestion, you too.”

“Mydeimos,” he whined, “I had to stay behind last time.”

“Someone needs to be in charge.”

“Krateros can do it! Who is he going to declare war on this time?” the first mate argued as he gestured to the empty shipyard.

Mydei sighed and turned back to the deck to call out, “Krateros!”

The old man’s head poked out of the formation that was already on the ramp. He was wide-eyed, trying to appear very small in the hopes that their commander in chief would forget that he had just asked for him.

Surprise stunned Mydei for half a second. “You too, teacher?”

“Your Highness, it has been a long time since the men have had a proper battle and the Tide’s mist has receded, how does this differ from our campaigns to push back the Tide?”

Mydei crossed his arms. This was a losing battle. The men were just going to swarm off the ship the second he left anyways. Almost the entire crew were trying to give him puppy dog eyes through the gaps in their formation. It was jarring, obnoxious, and it made Mydei want to say no but they were all dressed up as proper Kremnoan warriors, itching for a fight, and the distraction could help thin the monsters at the school.

“Fine, under one condition.” Everyone leaned in. “Ptolemy is confined to the ship.”

“What?!” Ptolemy cried. His head poked out next to Krateros’. “It’s a giant library, Mydei! Think of all the books that need rescuing!”

Ptolemy outing himself had the formation immediately turning on the man like a body rejecting a transplant. They scooped him up, passed him up the line, and tossed him back onto the ship into the waiting arms of Hephaestion and Leonnius. They were trying really hard not to laugh at their friend as they hurried to catch him before the book hoarder could leap off the ship against orders.

“It’s okay, Ptolemy!” Perdikkas snickered, “we’ll bring one back for you.”

“You heard him, Ptolemy!” Leonnius was trying to say around his wheezing, “this is for the greater good!”

“We appreciate your sacrifice, Ptolemy!” someone else called.

Another yelled, “You have plenty to read already!”

One man tossed them a rope.

“You’ll sink the ship with paper if you had your way!” yet another playful taunt.

The librarian kicked as he was dragged backwards towards the crew’s quarters by his arms, heels squeaking across the deck as he went, still yelling and pleading, “They’re sitting there UNREAD! They’re drowning in dust! They need meeeee!” Half the crew saluted, the other half roared with laughter and cheers.

“Lord Mydei, will he be alright?” Castorice asked, nervous. She was watching the door where the three men had disappeared and furrowed her brow when Hephaestion and Leonnius emerged without Ptolemy.

“We will untie him when we get back,” Mydei casually reassured her. “We would lose him to the shelves if he went.”

The crew were excitedly swarming off the ship, all spears and shields and excited war cries. Peucesta had already started playing an anthem at double speed. Phainon was in that hoard somewhere. What a lively mess. He followed them more slowly, offering a hand to each lady so they wouldn’t trip over the step onto the ramp.

“Only one rescue per day,” he joked with a serious expression.

“I’m not sure Professor Anaxa will see it that way…” Hyacine sighed.

Castorice matched her vocal expression with a gentle exhale of her own. “We can hope.”

-

Phainon’s memories of the Grove were complicated, just like they were for Castorice and Hyacine. There were good memories of falling asleep studying, the debate championships, finding exciting new reading material, college pranks, that time he tried out for an exclusive club and ended up getting caught by faculty while streaking across campus at night. Almost all of those memories featured his best friends. But those recollections had bittersweet edges when those same study halls, dorm rooms, and courtyards had been touched by the Tide, shadowing any fond feelings with frightened screams and flashing images of destruction.

The monsters had landed ahead of the roiling mist, giving many of the scholars a chance to escape. Phainon remembered a rushed and bloody day of racing through lecture halls searching for survivors and escorting them to the harbor. He was a more experienced hero then, but it had still been an emotional experience. Tearful and angry begging had not swayed every stubborn soul and Phainon’s hopelessness at the time had mirrored how he felt in Aedes Elysiae.

Okhema had welcomed everyone who had been displaced but many still regularly petitioned Aglaea for permission and protection to return for the Grove’s wealth. No other library in the world rivaled this library’s collection of knowledge, research, and readables.

Poor Ptolemy.

Phainon had felt bad watching his friend get pulled away from what was probably the man’s ultimate vacation hotspot, but he understood why Mydei made the decision. Ptolemy would’ve had them dragging whole shelves back to the ship, possibly sinking it in the process. As it was now, they had their hands full without having to babysit their own librarian.

The Kremnoans had descended on the Grove with excited voracity. Everyone had battle buddies that they stuck to, keeping in small groups or pairs as they roamed, slaying monsters as they came upon them. While the crew didn’t have all day to explore, they weren’t in a rush either. The Black Tide wasn’t expected to roll back over the Grove for a few Entry Hours, and low tide wasn’t until Curtain-Fall Hour.

Hopefully, it didn’t take that long to find the Professor but there was time to be thorough.

While most of the crew had spread to systematically clear the lower levels of the city, Phainon had paired with Perdikkas and Castorice to run directly to the school. Mydei, Hyacine, and Hephaestion had done the same but taken a different route to check other classrooms, leaving Phainon’s group to head directly to Professor Anaxa’s office. An unspoken fear lingered between the three of them as they ran along cracked walkways and collapsed pillars: was Anaxagoras still alive? Was he still himself?

Chrysos Heirs were not immune to the Black Tide’s corruption. Highly resilient yes, immune to small doses, maybe, but living in the Tide? Even if the mist pulled away for days at a time, it still returned and blanketed the Grove for just as long as it had been in remission with each surge. That’s to say nothing of the roaming monsters.

Castorice was more than capable of placating the monsters with her powers, but Phainon and Perdikkas still slew them as they found them. It was a mercy to do so as quickly as they could, when they could to free the tortured souls.

“How many stairs are in this Titan’s damned place?” Perdikkas huffed.

“It is not much farther,” Castorice insisted.

“Those scholars must have looked like warriors by the time they graduated with all this up and down!”

Phainon grinned at him, “Does the Kremnoan need a break?”

“Keep talking, Phainon, there are plenty of places around here for you to ‘trip.’”

It was a good warning as well as a threat. Phainon very nearly lost his footing on a raised root, but he rolled with his ankle and avoided lasting injury.

“Perhaps we should take it slower this close to the canopy,” Castorice suggested.

“We can’t,” Perdikkas insisted. He was still power walking around the growth, pulling ahead towards a door that was hanging off its hinges. Nature had ripped this one free as it grew unchecked. Phainon considered it a humbling reminder as they squeezed through the gap at how small humanity really was compared to the raw power of the Titans and the natural world.

“We can’t let Mydeimos find the Professor first,” Phainon explained.

“…men,” she sighed, but her pace quickened all the same.

Anaxa’s office was deep in a wing set aside for the Nousporist’s school. Even if each school of thought was embraced equally on paper, the Grove had gone out of their way to set this one apart from the others. Cerces valued all forms of academic pursuit, even blasphemous ones, but men were only begrudgingly tolerant of the blasphemy taught by Anaxa. The Professor found the entire situation humorous and embraced the solitude provided by the physical exclusion.

As one of the seven sages of the Grove, Anaxa still had a sizeable budget to fill his office with equipment, books, research materials, and even a small living space. Phainon remembered accidentally stumbling upon their professor late one night while he was heading back to the dorm after a late study session. The man had been dressed in a dromas themed onesie shuffling between the cafeteria and his office with murderous exhaustion in his eyebags and a mug of something that smelled suspicious in his hands.

“Well,” Phainon said as he walked slowly around the room. “It still looks lived in.”

“A Black Tide monster wouldn’t keep a human routine,” Perdikkas confirmed, “he may yet be himself.”

“That is wonderful news, Lord Perdikkas.” Castorice was speaking softly, her hands gently roaming over the spines of books and scrolls that were left in arbitrary piles. Phainon could see her out of the corner of his eye weighing a couple that were covered in dust, which did remind him to pick one out for Ptolemy before they left.

Phainon wandered over to the unmade bed and touched it, sliding his hand under the blankets. “Cold,” he reported and then he checked the chair at the desk as well. No dust but no warmth either. “He hasn’t been here recently.”

“Where else might he be?” Perdikkas asked. He was slipping a small tome into his pocket and trying to be sneaky about it.

“His lab. This way.” Phainon took the lead this time. The hallways were narrower, curved, with lower ceilings this deep inside the school. Monsters were around every corner, so they kept their silence to more quickly dispatch them.

Phainon paused around one such corner. This was a crossroads he knew, Anaxa’s lab was not far ahead but there was a lurking presence he couldn’t see down the other forks. He held his hand out to signal to the others to wait while he listened.

Black Tide monsters varied in size and strength. There were a few types that could be genuinely threatening, nothing that Phainon couldn’t handle of course but he was worried in close quarters about Castorice and Perdikkas. As a demigod, Castorice could assuredly deal with anything they ran into swiftly, but she couldn’t use her touch in these tight hallways without negatively impacting her comrades around her. Perdikkas was a solid fighter, but his shield and spear were designed for teamwork and practiced formations. In a hallway he was severely limited to what he could do.

Phainon squeezed the handle of his sword, doing the math in his head when footsteps from another direction caught his attention. One elite roaming monster he could handle but two at once? The angle of the hallway did not allow him to easily peek to see what they were dealing with, but it was glaringly obvious from the subtle breaths and shifting weight of presence that two of the other three hallways were occupied by something incredibly dangerous.

He turned to point, communicating with gestures that Castorice and Perdikkas needed to take the monster in the tight corner while he surged ahead to the farther hallway. When they both nodded their understanding, Phainon pulled his sword in closer to his side. He took a deep breath in through his mouth, nice and slow, no sound. Every muscle was coiled, ready. The air was charged but still. Each monster sounded like they too were waiting.

No time like the present.

Phainon slid around the corner with a battle cry, swinging his greatsword in a grand arc to clash right onto the back of Mydei’s gauntlet with a shower of sparks. It took all of two seconds for everyone’s shouts to turn into awkward echoes while they processed each other.

“Mydei!” Phainon broke the stunned silence with a cheerful greeting. This was a welcome surprise. “I thought you were a Black Tide monster.”

“HKS,” Mydei huffed. He slapped Phainon’s sword away.

“We almost skewered the both of you!” Leonnius growled. He pulled his spear up and tapped the floor with the butt of it. Peucesta and Leonnius had come pouring out of the third hallway. No monsters at all.

“Why aren’t you helping clear the city?” Hephaestion asked the pair.

Hyacine waved at Castorice and skipped up to her to trade information while the three groups mingled. Perdikkas was scanning everyone for injury, Peucesta was doing a head count with his fingers, and Mydei had crossed his arms to hide his embarrassment at mistaking his own people for enemies in the moment. Phainon could see the little bit of color in his cheeks and his ears.

“It’s done already,” Leonnius reported and Peucesta nodded, “there weren’t as many monsters as the other islands.”

“That makes sense,” Phainon added. His sword burst into bright blue dust as he tucked it away. “When we helped evacuate, the only people who were left to turn were particularly stubborn scholars.”

“Like your Anaxa,” Hephaestion confirmed.

“You didn’t completely wipe out the Tide before the mist came through, right?” Perdikkas asked. Phainon shook his head. “Then the army we are fighting is likely the leftover soldiers, abandoned by the Tide to keep control of this territory.”

“Did you find your man?” Mydei asked as he scanned the group.

“No, he wasn’t in his office,” Phainon noted with the barest hint of disappointment.

“We checked Professor Socippe’s lab,” Hyacine confirmed, “it had been picked clean but was covered in dust.”

“Leonnius?” Mydei asked, “have you seen any signs of life?”

“Non-Tide life? Yeah, lots of it. Your man is definitely here.”

Phainon grinned, “Professor Anaxa is the smartest person I know. If anyone could live among the Tide, it’s him.”

“The Professor’s lab is up ahead,” Hyacine confirmed. She pointed down the fourth hallway. It was one of the many paths carved from the tree herself, poorly lit and imposing in the wake of the Tide. Peucesta’s lyre twanged, only a few haunting notes to express displeasure but Mydei and Phainon were already stalking forwards, trusting the others to follow.

“I’m at 17,” Phainon purred in Mydei’s direction as they each fought for the lead with long strides.

“19,” Mydei coolly returned with a sideways smirk. He was slowly picking up speed, urging Phainon to match his pace.

“Hephaestion and Hyacine’s kills don’t count.”

Mydei scoffed, “I know that Deliverer! Or are you perhaps counting your companions kills for yourself?”

“Of course not, Mydeimos. You know I would never dishonor our competitions in such a way!”

“Perhaps you should if you are to stand any chance.” The Kremnoan started jogging, barely shy of a run.

“I can let you win this if you need the confidence boost.”

Mydei’s leg shot out to trip Phainon, but he neatly vaulted over the limb and turned around to run backwards, still keeping pace with Mydei’s jog. Was it showing off? Absolutely. But it was still nice to get to look Mydei in his beautiful eyes while he taunted his best friend. “We’re supposed to be hurting the monsters, your Highness, not each other~”

Phainon yelped when his heel caught on a raised root, and he tripped. All of his momentum shifted into flailing his arms like a drunken bird as he spun about in exaggerated steps to keep his balance. To his credit, he didn’t fall all the way to the floor and only lost a few steps as Mydei surged past him.

The prince was laughing as he broke into a run, “It seems you do not need help taking care of that yourself!”

Wounded pride pushed Phainon red-faced into a sprint to catch up and he finally overtook Mydei at the corner where the hallway split and the home field advantage swung in his favor. He took the left turn a little too fast and they both crashed together into the wall in a shower of tree bark before Phainon was able to slide into Anaxa’s lab ahead of Mydei with a gleeful, “I win!”

Immediately a bolt of green light shot in front of Phainon’s face, barely missing his nose and leaving behind the smell of burning hair. He yelped and jumped backwards into the hallway where Mydei slapped at his forehead to put out the simmering flames at the ends of his bangs before they could become a genuine problem. Phainon slapped back and they smacked at each other for a few seconds before Mydei eased up so Phainon could peek into the room.

“Professor Anaxa?” he called.

The man was standing on the far side of the room with a gleam in his eye. His custom-made weapon, a firearm, was aimed at the ceiling, smoke still curling from the barrel. He miraculously didn’t look any different from the last time Phainon had seen him. He still had the same sartorial preferences, the same pallid skin and hair that bordered on the unhealthy, and that same expression caught halfway between bored and annoyed.

Phainon slowly stepped into the doorway with his hands held up and a reassuring smile plastered on his face.

“Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,” Anaxa growled before he could say anything.

The man brightened at the recognition and then yelped when Mydei wrenched him back into the safety of the hallway by his cape, just in time to save Phainon from another green bolt that bounced past them down the hallway. The two of them pressed their backs against the wall for cover.

“Rule number one!” Anaxa yelled, "It's Anaxagoras!"

Mydei barked a single laugh from beside Phainon. “I like him already.”

chapters.title: Chapter 23: The Grove's Last Debate
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Words are a good start but pirate debater, Phainon has a couple tricks up his sleeve.

Chapter Notes
