If anyone was part of debate club in HS or at the collegiate level I apologize for my extremely shallow use of debate terms as I hide behind my "creative liberties" sign.

When instinct told Mydei to grab Phainon, he didn’t even question it. Mydei’s instincts had been honed by repeated deaths, at this point they had earned any and all benefit of the doubt. It was a damn good thing he did because some sort of glowing projectile ripped through the air where Phainon had been standing less than a second prior and proceeded to ricochet down the hallway.

“Whoa!” he heard Leonnius shout with unreserved surprise and then the runner’s head peeked around the corner where the hallway split …then Hephaestion’s, then Perdikkas’, then Peucestas’, and finally Castorice and Hyacine.

Mydei threw his hand up, gesturing for them to wait.

“Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,” the Professor was calling from inside the room. The man had a surprisingly smooth voice, not as deep as Mydei’s but not quite as gentle and jovial as Phainon’s.

“If I recall correctly,” he was saying, “you were an exceptional student.”

Mydei’s eyes darted to Phainon. The man was still pressed with his back tightly against the wall, nervous sweat beading on his forehead. The fear that flickered across his face was exactly the kind of thing Mydei wanted to poke fun of on good days but the way this Anaxa’s voice purred like poisoned honey, maybe Phainon was in the right to harbor that healthy wariness.

“So, what does it say about me, your teacher, that you cannot even remember the first rule of my class only four years after your graduation?”

Phainon very slowly leaned forward to peek back into the room. In the most apologetic tone, he could muster he called out, “Professor Anaxa, it’s not-“

Instinct saved Phainon again as Mydei grabbed him by one of the straps on the back of his outfit and once again pulled him behind cover. The shot pinged down the hallway, chasing after the last two. Mydei very carefully pinched out the budding flame at the top of Phainon’s ahoge. This guy was not pulling punches.

“How lamentable!” Anaxa mourned dramatically, “my former student retained nothing of my lessons!”

The follow-up shot bounced by before either of them had a chance to peek at all. Mydei admired the aggression, and was maybe a little afraid, but this was getting them nowhere.

“Professor Anaxagoras!” the Kremnoan called and there was silence from the room. It was impossible to tell if that was a good sign or not. Worst case scenario, his immortal body would take a painful hit from whatever that projectile was, so, Mydei confidently stepped into the doorway to get a good look at the guy who was trying to light his crush on fire.

Anaxa was… delicate, short, and visually young, especially from the far side of the room. He was wearing a cropped in the front, long in the back topcoat over long robes that made his shoulders wider, but the thick belt around his waist, tight sleeves, and formfitting vest gave the scholar away. The man was thin under the loose parts of his clothing. Everything he wore was intricate and fine with gold and red baubles tied in places too specific to be purely decorative. His left eye was covered with a wide patch that covered most of his cheek and almost the entirety of whatever parts of his forehead weren’t already hiding behind his too long bangs. Most of his seafoam green hair was cut at the chin but it was uneven, and a much longer section had gone untrimmed, left to hang over his right shoulder in a ponytail. No glasses, no hunch, no elderly persona.

Most important was the way the man was standing. His body language was open, confident, with his shoulders relaxed and his arm extended, holding the device that was presumably launching these high-heat projectiles pointed directly at Mydei. The other hand was raised to his eyepatch, hovering over it as though he would rip the thing off in a feral fit. His one eye was narrowed with suspicion and thinly veiled curiosity like Mydei had potential to be interesting if he didn’t prove himself a threat first.

“I am Mydeimos, Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos and Captain of the Chryseus Leo,” he introduced. No shooting yet, he must be doing something right.

“Oh?” The weapon drooped to point at the floor, but he kept his hand over his eye. “For what scheme could a Kremnoan possibly need my help?”

How the hell did this guy know they were here to ask for help? Was Mydei that easy to read? Did he tip his hand with his introduction?

“Professor!” Hyacine called. She stepped up next to Mydei so Anaxa could see her, but the scholar barely reacted to his former assistant.

Castorice came into the room next, taking up Mydei’s other side with a gentle, “It’s a pleasure to see you again, Professor Anaxagoras.”

He looked between the two of them, drinking them in with the careful assessment of a sommelier sipping fine wine before growling loudly, “see, Phainon? It’s not so hard to follow the rules. It’s a shame your potential is still so stunted by your glib tongue.”

Phainon peeked around the doorframe. “It isn’t that bad, Professor!”

Anaxa’s frown deepened. “If I had known there would be a class reunion I would have cleaned my lab.” The sarcasm in his voice had Mydei doubting that statement.

The lab itself was organized chaos, maybe three times the size of Mydei’s quarters on the ship and many times taller. Evidence of failed experiments peppered the entire space with burn marks, discoloration, broken shelves that never got fixed, scribbled out notes in heavy ink, and half destroyed cages. He had body parts in jars, suspiciously labeled baskets, books with pages ripped out and stuffed back in, and even half a Black Tide monster that he had somehow managed to preserve slumped in a corner. Arcane imagery was drawn on the floor and even on the back of the man’s own hand. The table he was standing beside had massive chunks missing from the corners and was completely covered in layers of notes scribbled on anything even vaguely paper in nature.

Behind him Hephaestion whistled. The entirety of their group was now piling in, driven by curiosity to roam around the lab, looking at everything from behind the safety of their shields.

“…you even provided the rest of the party,” Anaxa huffed irritably, “how kind.”

“Please don’t mind them, Professor,” Hyacine said, “they helped us find you.”

“You were not easy to find,” Hephaestion admitted.

“Consider that was intentional.” Anaxa’s scowl was bordering on murderous.

“Professor Anaxa…goras,” Phainon said as he took a few steps forward. He had one hand on his chest like he usually did when he was trying to put emotion into his next words. “We need your help.”

“Naturally,” Anaxa agreed without knowing any details or even any basics, “that does not entitle you to my input, nor give you the right to invade my home.”

“Respectfully, the Grove is a public university,” Phainon argued, “and the biggest standing library on Amphoreus. Would you deny us the pursuit of knowledge?”

Anaxa’s expression remained guarded, but Mydei was getting the sense he liked the pushback even if the man was still annoyed with the invasion of his privacy.

“Of course not, I encourage higher learning, especially for those who desperately need it,” Anaxa agreed, “but even if the university were still a functioning entity, this is my private lab.”

Phainon put on his more charming smile, “But Professor, three quints into the Lucid Hour is the first of your two office hours when you are available to answer your student’s questions.”

Anaxa’s head jerked to a circular timepiece mounted on the wall to confirm. He very slowly holstered his weapon and turned back to study Phainon with his arms crossed. It felt like an invitation to continue, as though the humor of a silly argument was entertainment enough to be worth the effort.

The rest of the room was quiet as everyone watched these two debate. Mydei saw Peucesta and Perdikkas quickly pull each other close to whisper between themselves before they turned back to watch with significantly more interest than before.

“I don’t see any students in my lab,” Anaxa countered, playing along, “only three alumni who should be out in the world conducting their own research not cowering behind their former teacher’s skirt.”

“But we are, Professor! Was it not you who instilled in us the desire to always be learning? What kind of a student would I be to not follow my professor’s teachings to pursue higher education and seek guidance from the most intelligent sources, especially when it pertains to my current area of study?”

“Really, Phainon? Flattery?”

“It’s not flattery, Professor,” Phainon insisted, “it’s an assessment of available resources to deduce the best logical choice of whom to request advice.”

“Flowery language and an appeal to ego may work on the Council of Elders but I am not so easily cowed.”

“You misunderstand, Professor, it is an appeal to ethos.”

“…I’m listening.”

“Not my own, but yours,” Phainon explained, “there is no other expert qualified to advise us on the nature of the Black Tide.”

Anaxa drummed his fingers on his arm as he contemplated Phainon’s words. Mydei found himself at a genuine loss as well. He had heard that Phainon was a debate champion, and the man was very well-spoken and self-assured around the ship, but to see him excel in yet another element... Mydei was a little turned on. Phainon was incredible on all kinds of battlefields.

Next to him both the girls were smiling, delighted to see Phainon shine again, and his men were still watching intently. The prince narrowed his eyes at them and slowly meandered close to lean into where Perdikkas and Peucesta were keeping personal council to whisper, “five on Phainon.”

“And what interest do you have in the Black Tide?” Anaxa finally answered, betraying his enthusiasm for the topic.

“We want your help preventing Black Tide corruption,” he admitted.

Anaxa scoffed, “start smaller, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, your ambition has led you to unattainable goals and it will crush your spirit to pursue this line of inquiry. A mind such as yours is best spent on other, more achievable things.”

“Don’t doubt yourself, Professor,” Phainon responded cheekily and Anaxa’s eye narrowed, “this is why we came for you.”

“Blind faith in my own work. It has been two years Phainon, what makes you think I have continued my study when it was little more than a pet project, a means to bring variety to my lab?”

“Necessity. You remain here in the Tide line and have managed to avoid corruption, even as a Chrysos Heir, no one can live within the Tide without eventually succumbing. That you are here and yourself is proof that you have been continuing your research on the topic.”

“An appeal to kairos.” Anaxa sounded mildly impressed. “That’s a difficult angle, Phainon, are you sure that’s the method of persuasion you want to play?”

“If anyone can appreciate the quid pro quo of this particular opportunity, it is you, Professor.”

“Then sway me.”

“We have made some discoveries of our own that contribute directly to your research,” Phainon explained, “through experimentation fighting the Black Tide and mapping its expansion over the years.”

“You are not the first researcher to map the Black Tide’s movements,” Anaxa pointed out, “a great many here at the Grove with our vast collection of records have noted the Black Tide’s movements.”

“Then you are aware of the effect that the Northern Campaign of King Eurypon had on the Tide?”

“I am. The Tide’s retreat has yet to be replicated, a single piece of uncorroborated proof is not enough to draw a conclusion.”

Phainon gestured to Mydei and his crewmates, “we have, on a small scale, managed to replicate the results. We have been able to prove King Eurypon’s hypothesis and have been keeping diligent records to prove it.”

For the first time since they arrived, Anaxa started to smile, like a cat that cornered a mouse. “Then you have no need of my research. If the Tide can be made to retreat by force, then you don’t require a means to resist the corruption.”

Phainon shifted his weight, “Not so. Proving that the Tide can be made to retreat is a valuable conclusion, but it is only a driving factor for the specific endeavor we have resolved to pursue.”

“For someone who once told me their lifelong pursuit was to be a hero, should it not be the end goal?” Anaxa asked.

“It is, but our specific task of great magnitude requires bolder, more foolhardy steps. A good scholar must never be overly cautious, right Professor?”

“And what is this endeavor that you have thus far refused to speak of in plain terms?”

“We are going to Castrum Kremnos to retrieve the Coreflame of Strife from the corrupted Titan Nikador.”

The man paused, properly surprised and then he laughed. It started small and then slowly turned maniacal, until Anaxa had to draw a deep gasp for breath. “You need my research to allow an army to lay siege to a fortress city that is drowning in the Black Tide, and you believe that I will eagerly join your efforts because it provides me the opportunity to run experiments that otherwise would be unavailable to me here at the Grove.”

“I do,” Phainon said confidently.

The Professor started to clap, slow and deliberate applause. “Congratulations on another win, Phainon.”

Perdikkas and Peucesta shoved five gold coins each into Mydei’s outstretched palm.

“Then you will come with us?” Phainon asked, a little too eager, too excited.

“No.”

The coins were quickly retrieved and Mydei frowned at both the loss of the gold and the loss of a valuable resource they were here to collect. This trip could not be for nothing.

“Now what?” Hephaestion asked Mydei, but the prince didn’t have an immediate answer.

“Are you not even a little bit interested?” Phainon pushed, even stepping forward a little closer to the Professor in his surprise.

“Naturally, I am, but I have already pursued that research as far as I intended to and have already turned my attention back to my truest passion,” Anaxa explained, “a good opportunity means nothing to me if I have no interest in the initial inquiry.”

Hyacine stepped forward into the space between the two debating men. “Professor Anaxagoras, have you already solved the issue of Black Tide corruption?” He didn’t answer, so she pressed harder. “It is not in your nature to stop researching until you are satisfied with an answer. Are you not interested because you already found that answer?”

The whole room turned to look at Anaxa. His face was as stone, frustratingly blank. He uncrossed his arms and set one hand down on the desk beside him. “I have.”

“Will you give it to us?” Phainon asked.

“No.”

Mydei tsked. An answer to Black Tide corruption would make their nearly impossible task of retrieving the coreflame into something difficult but feasible. Mydei was still willing to go and fight with just the Chrysos Heirs they had already assembled, but a means to minimize the risk to even themselves was not an opportunity that they could pass up.

He crossed his arms and tucked his head to think. Perhaps Anaxa could be swayed in other ways. Phainon may have other angles of debate that he could employ but the Professor had admitted defeat on that front and still refused. He didn’t seem like the kind of guy that could be swayed by an emotional appeal, otherwise Phainon might have tried that already. Time wasn’t on their side for an extended stay either, there was no way to win through a battle of attrition. The only other easy option was…

“Miss Hyacine,” Perdikkas said to get her attention, “do you think you could come up with a solution without the professor?”

Anaxa turned to look at them warily. His former assistant was looking between them, face wrinkled with thought before her shoulders slumped and she admitted, “not in a time frame that would help.”

“He is our only chance of fighting beside Mydei and Phainon in Castrum Kremnos,” Peucesta observed, breaking his silence with a mournful tone. His words hovered in the air for a heartbeat before sorrow quickly morphed into resolve.

“Well,” Hephaestion said beside Mydei. He tapped the butt of his spear on the ground, calling the other Kremnoans to attention. “I guess we have to do this the hard way.”

Anaxa scowled, irritably, “brutes always turn so quickly to violence. Torturing me will not give you the answers you want.”

“We’re not going to torture you,” the first mate reassured him, “we’re going to rescue you.”

The other pirates immediately caught on and started spreading around the room, Phainon too. They were strategically cutting off any means of escape.

Mydei sighed. He didn’t like this, but there weren’t any other, better options that could be considered in the time they had left. And they were, after all, still pirates.

“Rescue…?” Anaxa was too surprised by the suggestion and focused on the men surrounding him to be upset when Leonnius interrupted his curious musings.

“Oh no! Do you guys hear that?” the runner shouted through the lab.

“I don’t hear-“ Castorice started but Perdikkas cut her off.

“It sounds like the Black Tide has already returned!” he called as he reached for a discarded rope on the floor.

Anaxa unholstered his weapon but Peucesta had already pounced, tackling the professor to the ground. Less than a second later the other four men were on him in a flurry of protests, dust, limbs, and rope. When the Kremnoans plus Phainon pulled away, Anaxa was bound to a pair of spears with his arms at his sides and the bindings wrapped around his torso from his shoulders to his waist. His weapon was tucked under Peucesta’s arm. Phainon and Hephaestion each grabbed an end and hoisted the man up like a prized hunted animal strung up between them with his poor legs dangling uselessly above the ground and the most annoyed expression on his face.

At least the protesting stopped. Professor Anaxa didn’t waste his time on people who wouldn’t listen, regardless of the circumstances. Instead, he let out the most irritated, long-suffering sigh, accepting his fate and not happy about it.

“Is this really necessary?” Castorice asked, judging by Hyacine’s expression, she had similar concerns.

“Don’t worry, Miss Castorice, it’s a pirate thing,” Leonnius explained.

“We practice catch and release,” Perdikkas reassured them, “we’ll put him right back where we found him after we get the coreflame.”

Mydei joined the caravan of people hurrying from the office with their prize, with a pointed, “What happened to no prisoners?” Not that he had any intention of stopping them, but considering the last month, it felt responsible to at least acknowledge the line that they were crossing.

“He’s not a prisoner,” Leonnius insisted, “besides we already broke that rule with Phainon.”

“I’m not still a prisoner,” Phainon said, aiming his words at Anaxa as though that would be comforting while he carried his old teacher down the hall. “It’s a long story.”

“This is still a kidnapping,” Castorice calmly observed.

“It’s not a kidnapping, it’s a rescue!” Perdikkas clarified.

“It does look like a kidnapping,” Hyacine added. Her voice was laced with concern but the spring in her step was playful.

“Kidnapping is only for kids, it’s in the name,” Hephaestion explained, “and besides we’re just borrowing him. Kidnapping is when you keep the child.”

Anaxa sighed and corrected, “the word you’re looking for is abduction. I am being abducted.”

“Wow, you fancy scholar types pronounce the word ‘rescued’ funny,” Leonnius teased.

Mydei made a mental note to properly apologize to Anaxagoras later.

- Phainon really did feel bad about abducting the Professor. He genuinely thought that Anaxa would come willingly after a little bit of buttering up and the presentation of what would’ve been an incredible opportunity for experimentation. In retrospect, he should’ve skipped the subtle praise that Anaxa generally hated and gone straight to appealing to the man’s insatiable curiosity.

It was Hyacine forcing the Professor to admit that he had completed his research and refusing to elaborate at all that made Phainon jump on board the ‘rescue’ plan without hesitation.

Completed research didn’t guarantee a positive outcome. That lesson was learned after a very frustrating assignment had saddled Phainon with repeated failed results. After losing sleep every night, spending hours redoing the experiment, begging for help from Castorice and Hyacine, even talking to students from the other schools, Phainon almost took the zero, not wanting to submit something that had so completely fallen apart.

He turned it in anyway with a heartfelt cover letter on his assignment insisting he had tried everything and would benefit from an extension to try again. Anaxa had given him full marks and pulled the struggling student aside to remind him that failure was a result and that all knowledge was useful. Phainon had carried that sentiment into every aspect of his life, treating failures as opportunities.

So why was Anaxa so reluctant to share his findings? Why not simply say that all his attempts to resist the corruption had failed? If there was ample evidence that it could not be done then they would know for sure, and they could try to find another way to infiltrate the city.

Except that Anaxa was proof that the corruption could be resisted. Even Chrysos Heirs would show signs of the Black Tide’s influence after consistent exposure for so long, but as Phainon carried his professor back through the university down to the shipyard and up the ramp to the Chryseus Leo, there was no sign of it on his body. Hyacine would know for sure after an examination, but Phainon couldn’t feel any trace of the Black Tide on the man, so he must have found a way and simply did not want to share it.

They took Anaxa to the infirmary, still bound for now, while Peucesta used a horn to call for the rest of the crew to return to the Leo. An experienced crew, there were no casualties and only minor injuries, not including the general disappointment of how unorganized and infrequent the Black Tide monsters had been. They had been hoping for a more exciting skirmish.

Krateros stood at the top of the ramp taking a head count but the collection of stolen readables could’ve also sufficed. Every single member of the crew had grabbed a tome or scroll for Ptolemy as an apology for leaving him behind. Although, looking at the list, Phainon worried that the substantial offering was a double-edged sword. Many of the books retrieved had volume numbers printed on their spines. The bookworm was unlikely to be happy to start a series on book three with no hope of seeing the first two.

They only cut Ptolemy and Anaxa loose when the ship left the Grove of Epiphany and cleared the submerged forest. Mydei handed command over to Krateros once the bow was pointed towards home and then the captain met Phainon at the rail.

“Deliverer,” he greeted and Phainon flashed him a smile.

“Sorry we broke the no prisoner rule, again.”

Mydei sighed and rolled his head forward, defeated. “He is your professor. If there were another way, I am sure you would have stopped them rather than helped.”

“I genuinely believed I could sway him with words,” he lamented.

“You did. It was a pleasure to watch.”

“A pleasure? Really, Mydeimos? You liked watching my silver tongue wag?” Phainon teased.

Mydei scoffed and shrugged. “It looked like another battlefield to me.”

“It’s not as fun of one as your regular battlefields.”

“You shine on those too.”

Phainon slowly turned to look at his friend with a coy smile. There was pink in Mydei’s cheeks and ears, and the man was avoiding eye contact. “Careful, Mydeimos, too many compliments and you’re like to perish.”

“I am no stranger to giving praise!” he protested, “but if you would prefer that I nag you for your faults we may discuss how your kill count lost to mine again and you nearly snapped your neck trying to show off.”

“That is barely a fault! On flat and even ground I can run backwards as fast as you run can forwards!” Phainon insisted, ignoring the indisputable win that was added to Mydei’s tally.

“Prove it.”

“The deck is not flat and even ground!”

“It is devoid of roots!”

“The ship rocks, Mydei!”

Leonnius popped up beside them to say, “if you two are done flirting-“

“Not flirting,” they emphasized in tandem.

“…yeah, okay, so Hyacine says that the guy we rescued doesn’t have any corruption, but, uh, there is something you two should know.”

Phainon felt his chest tighten up. A thousand worries lanced through his bones all at once and he hoped it didn’t show on his face. Mydei was a picture of composure. How did he manage to do that? The man was always so in control of himself. Phainon knew that Mydei had strong feelings about things, but he schooled his control with such enviable ease.

“They are down in the infirmary, waiting for you two.”

“Thank you, Leonnius,” Mydei said sincerely and started heading that way immediately. Phainon nodded politely to his friend and lightly punched him back when Leonnius tapped Phainon’s chest with his knuckles.

“Phainon, that was pretty damn awesome today.”

He chuckled and shook his head to chase away the blush from the praise, “I had a good teacher.”

“Yeah, well, talk him into spilling his secrets, yeah? We want to be there for you too.”

“I’ll do what I can,” Phainon promised, sincere, before he chased after Mydei.

Anaxa was sitting in a chair in the middle of the infirmary floor when Phainon arrived. His coat was sitting on the bed, set aside for the examination that he undoubtedly tried to decline. He had his arms crossed, one finger tapping furiously at his arm while he tucked his chin. Once, a long time ago, Anaxa had admitted to reciting equations and proofs in his head when he was particularly bored. With his eye closed and his legs crossed at the knee, those equations were almost visible dancing around his ears.

“Hyacine,” Phainon greeted. Castorice was there too, seated beside the first mate behind Anaxa. He nodded in her direction then repeated the gesture for Hephaestion. Aside from Mydei, no one else was present.

The healer offered him a little half wave and then hurried to close the door which immediately put Phainon on edge.

“What is it?” he prodded.

“Professor,” Hyacine invited, “would you like to tell them, or shall I?”

He sighed and rolled his head back to look directly at the ceiling like this was the most obnoxious moment of his life.

“Does this have to do with your research…?” Phainon asked.

“I told you at the Grove that you would not get answers from me that you want,” Anaxa repeated as his head rolled forward again, “because I did find an answer and the solution to your problem is not accessible to this crew.” He paused in case someone tried to interrupt. The Professor hated when people didn’t let him finish speaking. That was rule number two. “My golden blood did prevent the Black Tide from corrupting me for a time but after only a month I had to try something a little more extreme to protect myself. I was able to reverse the early stages and prevent further corruption to my own body and soul by taking the Coreflame of Reason and embedding it within my own chest.”

There was a pause while that information sunk in. Phainon saw the defeat on Hephaestion face and the subtle downturn of Mydei’s gaze. For someone so vocally opposed to Aglaea and Titans as a whole, Phainon was more surprised that Anaxa, the blasphemer, had even considered the option.

The coreflame itself was supposed to be given to Okhema when the Grove was lost but in the rush during the evacuation, they had failed to retrieve it. Aglaea had yet to send anyone for it, deeming it a loss as long as the Tide extended too far to risk anyone but her Chrysos Heirs.

“It has been theorized that Titans are corruptible,” Anaxa continued with a wave of his hand, gesturing to the side as he tilted his head, “but as a Demigod I have seen no such evidence in the short time that I have had this coreflame in my chest.”

“Professor,” Phainon managed to say after the shock processed in his own heart, “I thought you hated the Titans, why would you have taken the coreflame?”

“The Coreflame of Reason has long been held in the Grove as a focal point of the Grove’s founding; a curiosity wrapped in myth. Regardless of how I feel about Cerces and my colleagues’ love for the Titan, the coreflame is still a proven source of power. There is no mysticism there. It was that woman’s lapse in judgement to not have it retrieved sooner for her collection. Perhaps she believed it was safe until she was ready to claim it, in any case, it was left behind and I had no reason not to use it for personal experimentation.” He spat his contempt for Aglaea but otherwise spoke candidly about his blasphemy.

Castorice tucked her hair behind her ears and leaned forward when she asked, “Professor, did the Coreflame accept you?”

“You’re worried that I may have forced it to attain divinity. No, I did not, nor did I take it into myself with the desire to achieve godhood. It was a successful experiment to determine the nature of corruption on my golden blood, nothing more. Anything I may have gleaned about the coreflame itself was an unintended byproduct.”

“But we’re still back to square one,” Hephaestion sighed.

“In your research, have you found any proof that an individual could be shielded from corruption without a coreflame?” Mydei asked.

“I have not,” Anaxa admitted.

“Have you found definitive proof that it cannot be?” Phainon tried.

The professor’s lip curled ever so slightly. “I have not. I ceased my research into the possibility when I found the solution that worked for my own body and then I resumed my preferred topic of research.”

“Maybe we can formulate a strategy that lets us help you from the ship, Mydei,” Hephaestion offered, trying to keep their hope afloat.

“Castrum Kremnos is inside the Black Tide,” Anaxa corrected, “your crew will turn long before you make it to the fortress.”

Mydei shook his head. “No, this ship is able to sail through the Tide. My men are protected so long as they are on it. What we need is a way to ward them individually so they can come ashore.”

Anaxa froze. His finger was still raised, mid-tap, trapped in time as he considered that. “You have tested this?”

Phainon nodded, “they found me inside the Tide. I lost my own ship and crew, but the Chryseus Leo and her crew were unaffected.”

“We sail through Tide waters all the time,” Hephaestion confirmed, “it’s how we have been able to pursue her ships and push back the Tide line.”

Anaxa’s finger started tapping again, double his original speed, and he tossed his head back again as he started to laugh that same maniacal laugh as before.

“Professor?” Hyacine asked, “Are you okay?”

He stopped laughing and leaned forward with a terrifying gleam in his eye that Phainon recognized from his school days. Either they were all about to have to write a ten-page essay, or Anaxa had figured something out.

With a happy, low purr, he said, “I have some follow-up questions.”

Chapter End Notes

Ethos is an appeal to credibility Kairos is an appeal to context or opportunity. It is not an official form of persuasion but I figure, fictional world, they probably have a bunch that we've never heard of

chapters.title: Chapter 24: Song of Recollection
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei and Phainon both reflect and Castorice has a very important question for Mydei.

Chapter Notes

I almost posted this last night but I'm glad I let it cook cause this was a very important one and we had a minor family 'emergency.' My spouse took the sailboat out yesterday and our search and rescue drone, Eous, went overboard. Fortunately, my husband recovered it this morning with his dive gear and we learned a very important lesson about naming inanimate objects and getting attached to them. My kitchen is full of big bowls of rice and buried electronics. RIP Eous.

Mydei’s proper apology had been promptly rejected, and the prince still had no idea if Anaxa was still angry about the abduction or if it simply didn’t matter anymore. The professor’s attention had shifted so rapidly after their discussion in the infirmary that it was hard to follow his thought process at all. The man refused to elaborate on what he was doing or what he was looking for and the only hints Mydei could glean came entirely from the questions he asked as the man wandered the ship.

He asked about her history, about Chryseus Leo, about the figurehead, the type of wood, the nature of the markings, until Mydei couldn’t keep up and Krateros took over. The old man had been a part of the ship’s history for its entire life and was eager to help when he overheard one of Anaxa’s snide comments about the Goldweaver. It was a bonding moment that no one expected but everyone appreciated.

Anaxagoras took samples, he raided Ptolemy’s library, and he didn’t sleep. Maybe it was a demigod thing, but he declined a hammock of his own and refused the meal that Mydei made, taking interest in the food just long enough to recognize the level of sophistication of his kitchen onboard. A kitchen that had been promptly co-opted into being Anaxa’s new lab.

Overnight Anaxa had completely reorganized everything, created a massive mess, started three fires, laughed loud enough to wake everyone up several times, and somehow deeply offended Fig Stew. And that was with Hyacine and Phainon’s supervision. Mydei had checked on the man in the morning, saw the state of his beloved kitchen and had to be held back by four people, an exhausted Phainon included. Very, very few things could challenge Mydei’s restraint, the abhorrent assault on his kitchen was one of those things.

Winning his morning spar with Phainon calmed him down and Mydei reluctantly agreed to hand over control of his galley in pursuit of the bigger picture. It was only for the few days between the Grove and the Kremnoan settlement. What could go wrong?

He stood at his favorite spot at the railing, flopped over it at the waist like a wet towel, watching smoke curl out of the galley with a deep frown. Hyacine and Phainon were busy assisting with an experiment of some sort, leaving Mydei without his favorite combat partner and he was too worried about what was happening down there to find another one, leaving him to sulk irritably.

“Lord Mydei?”

He twisted his head and slowly pulled himself up to rest on his forearms. “Miss Castorice, did the professor not need you?”

“No, he seems to be doing just fine on his own. Professor Anaxa is brilliant but eccentric, the best way for me to help is to stay out of his way.”

Mydei hummed in agreement and turned back again to pout at the smoke. The way it curled out of the vent in varied colors was unnatural and unsettling.

“I’m sorry that he has taken your kitchen from you.”

“It’s in service to our mission,” Mydei huffed but the slight whine under his voice must’ve come through because Castorice stepped up beside him and put her hand on his forearm to comfort him.

“Lord Mydei, if you have a moment, may we talk?”

Puzzled, he looked up at her from where he was leaning. Castorice was a master of keeping a measured voice, even better than he was. It was hard to determine from just her words and expression what kind of discussion this would be. “Is something wrong? Is it an issue with the crew?”

“Not at all.” She squeezed his arm. “But I would like to speak in private, if that is alright?”

Extra puzzled, Mydei set aside any speculation and instead put his hand on hers with a soft squeeze. Always mindful of the sharp claws on his gauntlets, he delicately scooped her hand up to hold her fingers over his own so he could guide her as the Lady she was. While he had never been one for stuffy royal etiquette, nor had the need to use it, Krateros had still taught Mydei in his youth how to act as a Crown Prince and eventual King.

“Will my room suffice?” he asked, “or would you prefer the library?”

“Ptolemy is still in the library,” she reported and then added sheepishly, “that may partially be my fault. I enlisted his help as a reader to find any errors in my latest manuscript.”

“My room then.” He got the doors for her along the way and closed the final one behind them. This close to home he didn’t expect anyone to be in here. Any remaining navigation could be done without maps while they followed the familiar coastline.

Mydei let her go to pull out a chair for her and invited her to sit, taking a seat across from her for himself. He settled in with his knees slightly spread and his arms folded across his chest while she took a second to delicately settle with her hands clasped in her lap.

Castorice still harbored habits from her time as a cursed woman. Her body language was tight with her legs tucked under the chair and to the side, eliminating the risk of someone accidently tripping over them or bumping into her foot. She kept her shoulders down but not relaxed, rolled in to make herself narrower, with her arms pressed in close and her hands folded so neatly on top of each other it was as though she only had one. Very slowly she settled in, carefully unwinding one thread at a time, keeping her posture but any remaining rigidity had softened.

Mydei extended one of his legs in her direction, leaving it there as an invitation without forcing any contact. She noticed immediately and curbed her surprise with a soft exhale; her own legs extended to cross at the ankle so she could lean them against his boot without sacrificing any modesty.

“Lord Mydei, I know from my limited time here that you do not care for small talk,” she started, “so I will start with the first of two things I wanted to ask you about. Have you recently lost a loved one?”

Mydei was taken aback by the question because it felt like the answer should be obvious. “I’ve lost many. I am Kremnoan, my people live for battle and fight with the intent to perish in glorious combat.”

Castorice reached up with both hands to play with a strand of hair. It was clearly a nervous gesture, a reason to look away from him directly while she fumbled with her words. “Someone closer, such as a sibling or a parent?”

He frowned and admitted, “both of my parents are deceased. My mother died when I was an infant.” Castorice already knew about Eurypon. Phainon had admitted to telling both the girls the whole story their first time on the ship to catch them up to speed on the world news that had been denied them in Okhema.

“Any siblings? Perhaps a sister?”

Mydei shook his head, “not by blood. I have lost crewmates before but those closest to me, that I would consider my brothers are yet alive.”

Castorice was braiding her hair and then deftly undoing it while she chewed on the inside of her cheek.

“Why do you ask?”

She tucked the hair behind her ear. “As the Demigod of Death, sometimes I can sense lingering spirits that resist the natural current of the Sea of Souls. Strong souls can sometimes project themselves, appearing in dreams or through relics or mediums. You simply seemed haunted, Lord Mydei, and I was curious.”

“In dreams?” Mydei wondered and he raised a hand to his chin, resting his finger there to think. “There are only two people that appear regularly in my dreams and one of them is alive. The other is my mo-“ He cut himself off when the pieces clicked in place.

“Your mother passed away when you were young, yes?”

“She was killed by King Eurypon, I barely knew her… but sometimes I dream of what could have been had I not been cast away and she had not been murdered,” he admitted.

Those dreams were less frequent now, but when he was a child in the Sea of Souls it was almost as though Queen Gorgo were there with him, helping him, raising him in spirit. Each one was sunshine and fresh air in an ocean that collected his lives, full of warmth and arms that held him tightly and wiped away his tears. She instilled in him courage before he even knew what that meant, to keep fighting, to always press on through pain. Her voice was the lifeline of his foundation, the reason for his resolve. Her example was one of strength and love, unsure of their own destinies as Kremnoans, joyously contemplating something more for her son.

The dreams had become more transparent over time, and he had even talked to her as clearly as though they were memories of another life. The woman he could not remember in life had become his everything in death. Whenever he woke with tears in his eyes, they were not from pain or fear, but from the emotional well of peace that speaking to his mother brought to his storming heart.

Get up, my son!

“Lord Mydei?”

He jerked a little when Castorice put her hand on his knee. “I’m sorry, I did not mean to get so lost in my thoughts.”

“Do you know very much about her?”

“Krateros raised me on stories of her adventures.”

She nodded gently and took her hand back. “Was she very strong?”

“The strongest.”

“I know this is cliché to say, but I believe she may be watching over you.”

It was the kind of thing that Mydei had heard from old Kremnoans his entire life. Hollow words that are said at funerals that people cling to for comfort alongside other such anecdotes as ‘she fights beside Nikador now’ or ‘her soul has strengthened Nikador’s blade more than any who has come before.’ Mydei had lived in the Sea of Souls, he knew that it was foolish to believe that spirits could so casually linger to watch from a higher plane. Once they crossed into the Netherealm, they were gone.

It was different to hear it from Castorice, the Demigod of Death, the Hand of Shadow, the Executioner, because if anyone, anyone, would know the truth of such a statement, it would be she who guides the river and keeps the souls of the dead. Which is why when Castorice said those loaded words, Mydei genuinely felt moved.

It was a dizzy sort of feeling, full of love and warmth that spread to his toes and fingers, the kind that cradled rather than strangled his heart making it feel so full that he worried it may burst. The threat of tears lingered behind his eyes as his throat felt tight. Instinctually, he raised a hand to his chest, pressing over his sternum to hold all those feelings back around ragged breaths.

“I’m sorry, if I said something inappropriate,” Castorice whispered, and he shook his head.

“No, it is good to hear. You’ve brought me a comfort I did not know I wanted,” he told her in a whisper.

She smiled warmly and clasped her hands before herself as though to pray. “I am glad. If I may, I had one other thing I wanted to discuss with you.”

He took a breath to center himself and blink away that pressure behind his eyes. What remained was a warm comfort, the eternal reassurance of a mother’s love.

“It can wait until another time, Lord Mydei, if you would like time to contemplate what I have already said.”

Mydei shook his head and gestured to her. “What is it, Castorice?”

“Are you in love with Lord Phainon?”

Mydei’s entire body went into fight or flight mode and got trapped in the middle of the decision-making process. Half of him wanted to jump out the window into the ocean and the other half was trying to evaporate on the spot. The blood was rapidly rushing to his face against his will making sitting uncomfortable and his face and chest turn red which probably answered her question better than his silent, opening and closing mouth was now that words had stopped working entirely.

Bless her heart, Castorice waited patiently for him to calm down enough for him to wheeze, “Love is a strong word.”

“Lord Mydei, I see the way you look at him.”

He looked away, embarrassed. “It cannot be so obvious.”

“I think he likes you too,” she said gently.

That warm feeling came back and he brightened, wide-eyed as he looked back at her. “Did he say…?”

“No, but I know Lord Phainon very well and he is not good at vocalizing his own desires. He simply doesn’t consider himself,” Castorice explained.

Castorice was right, Phainon never looked inwards. Mydei was reminded of a man that risked his own life to fight two sides in an Okheman fort, a man that was nearly lost to the sea fighting a storm to save a crew he was just barely coming to know, a man that saw an opportunity to have his freedom and honor back and wanted to reject it in favor of the means to save them all. Phainon was too perfect for a flawed man like Mydei, who willingly carried the pirate mantle and fought for a people that he could only disappoint.

“But I see the way he looks at you and the way he talks about you,” she giggled and put her hands back in her lap, “he is not a shy man. I think he mentioned your body and strength three separate times in the first quint of his storytelling.”

Mydei tsked but the blush stayed. “HKS, has he no shame at all?”

“He’s a catch,” Castorice admitted.

“…is there no one in Okhema waiting for him?”

“A lover you mean?”

Mydei shyly nodded.

“Not that I know of,” she reassured him, “Phainon is friendly and open, but I’ve never seen him take such interest in another person before.”

“Not even during your time in the Grove?”

Castorice considered her next words very carefully. “Lord Mydei, did Phainon tell you about his past?”

“He has in small doses, and I have heard pieces from my friends who have discussed it with him. I know that his home was destroyed by the Black Tide and that he was left, the only survivor, to wander until Aglaea found him and gave him purpose.” Mydei paused for a moment to consider aloud in a quiet voice, “And I have seen for myself what he will not say, that he is still angry and fearful to the point of breaking at the Tide. I have seen the same embers of vengeance in the bones of my own men, in Krateros especially.”

“Then you have seen the walls he has built inside himself.”

Mydei knew exactly what she was talking about. He saw them on the day they met and wondered now as he replayed their time together if they had ever completely come down. Perhaps that day in the galley, just before Phainon had thrown his challenge, and again when he had read the letter, but he was skilled in hiding himself again.

Castorice continued, “most people don’t see it. They see how friendly he is and assume that he is a trusting fool, but his friends know how deep his soul is and the sorrow and rage he keeps in those depths. He loves, he does, very deeply, but Hyacine and I worried that he would not be able to pursue a romantic love until that fire was tamed, so you see why we were excited to learn of you.”

That was a humbling thought, and he was glad for the distinction. There were many types of love and Phainon had demonstrated no shortage of familial and brotherly love towards the crew. Perhaps it was a love that he gave more freely, a natural byproduct of being a friendly person, of a Deliverer destined to save the world. But a man who had shunned romantic love, falling for Mydei?

“If you have feelings for him, will you tell him?” Castorice asked.

Mydei had never bothered trying to describe himself but pressed to do so he may have once said fearless, confident, or composed, but confronted with such a simple question it was hard to feel any of those things. The thought of taking Phainon’s hand in his own and admitting an all-encompassing attraction to the man filled Mydei with a fear that he had never known before, because admitting such a thing was opening the floodgates to change. Even knowing that Phainon may return his sentiments, Mydei was worried about what he may say.

“He suspects already,” Mydei admitted, “I told him that once we had the coreflame I would confide in him the secret of who held my affections.”

“You want him to have every choice available to him, before you ask.” Castorice was very good at seeing into the heart of things.

“Yes,” he said gently, “I would want the chance to court him properly as he deserves. I want him to join my crew because he wants to, not because I bound him to this fate. I would want the chance to win his love as he has already won mine.” Mydei sighed and reached up to rub his face. “I had hoped that he would see the Coreflame of Strife as a courting gift, the first of many, as a gesture of desire not only from myself but from my family that also want him to be one of us.”

“But Lord Phainon does not see it that way,” Castorice supplied, lamenting with Mydei over the confusion, “he sees it as a means to save you and your crew. Can this not also be a gesture of love in the same way?”

Mydei hummed, “It will not matter until we retrieve it. What matters the most is that Phainon is happy and if he is too busy taking care of others to care for himself, then I will simply have to take up that task.”

Castorice smiled and started to speak but the door slammed open, jumping on its hinges, slamming loud enough to have Mydei on his feet with his body between this new threat and his new friend.

It was just Phainon.

“HKS!” Mydei scolded, “have you no manners! I was ready to attack you!”

“Mydei!” Phainon panted. He paused when he saw Castorice in there too and tilted his head in confusion, brows furrowed like he was processing complex emotions all at once before he remembered why he had come. “Professor Anaxa has a prototype. He’s ready to test.”

- Finding an island that was inside the Tide line wasn’t difficult. In the time it had taken the crew to go to Okhema and the Grove, the progress they had originally made had been lost. It was still a slow creep without the monsters that the Tide desperately needed to hold the line, but it was dauntingly consistent. The last town they had cleared was eerie, devoid of life and movement but swimming in the Tide’s fog.

Phainon was having a harder time facing it directly than he thought he would. Facing monsters was easier than facing the surrealism of the fog. It was so different at sea when the ocean turned black around corrupted ships and it was different fighting in places where the Tide had retreated entirely. The aftermath of destruction was different than standing in the presence of the master behind the madness.

He blinked and his breath stuck as images of Aedes Elysiae flashed. Instead of stone buildings and a grand pier he could see farms and storehouses on fire. In the distance, someone screamed and he gasped.

“Deliverer?” Mydei’s voice snapped him back to reality with a harsh jerk and Phainon twisted his neck to face him sharply enough to hurt.

“Mydei!” he greeted cheerfully with a wide smile.

The captain’s eyes drifted towards Phainon’s hands on the railing. He was gripping the wood so tightly that it had splintered and gold was pooling around one of his nails. Phainon hadn’t even noticed.

At the concerned look in those pinched Kremnoan brows, Phainon laughed and let go of the rail to wrap his arm around Mydei’s neck, affectionately pulling the man in close to tussle his hair. Of course, his best friend roughly shoved him off and followed up with a punch that would bruise his shoulder.

“We’re about to see Professor Anaxa change the world,” he laughed while rubbing the budding sore spot.

Mydei still studied him, reading so deeply into his being that Phainon was starting to feel naked but if the captain found something worth addressing, Mydei didn’t say. That courtesy was one of the many things Phainon liked about Mydei. He turned back to the rail to look at the city, this time putting his forearms on the ship so he wouldn’t give away his misgivings so readily.

“Do you trust him?” Mydei asked. As guarded as he tried to be, Phainon could see the subtle tells of cautious concern. His braid was ever so slightly uneven from when he wove the strands this morning, his chiton was tied tighter at the shoulder, his necklace was unpolished. They were little things that most people wouldn’t notice, but Phainon did. Phainon always noticed when Mydei was upset.

“Well,” Phainon managed to squeak out and Mydei’s fiery eyes started to bore into the side of his head at the hesitation, “I trust that he is brilliant… but I also know he’s not shy of failure.”

“Are my men in danger?”

Should he lie? No, not to Mydei, but the truth was always yes. There were absolutely risks. “I trust Professor Anaxa to take every step that he can to ensure the safety of his subjects.”

Mydei was still unconvinced. It was written in the tension of his shoulders and how tightly he held his crossed arms to his chest.

The crew was mostly gathered on deck now. They were hesitant to lower the ramp and were relying instead on the anchors to keep them close to the dock. Black mist clung to the wooden planks like a dense fog, pouring over in places to drip to the water below, ink black and devoid of light.

Anaxa and Hyacine were standing next to the removed section of the rail, waiting impatiently. The Professor was holding a hastily carved, plain wooden pocket, no bigger than a small book in his hand with a slot carved into one end and sealed with wax. Beside him, Hyacine waited with her staff under her arm and her familiar, Ica, beside her. The miniature Pegasus was more marshmallow than flying unicorn these days, but he was cute and comforting with his trills and doots. Something about fat, brightly colored animal sidekicks tended to put people at ease.

“I need a volunteer,” the professor yelled to the Kremnoans, “before I choose a man at random.”

Mydei tapped his foot twice and then called to the crew in Kremnoan, “This man is going to test a means to repel the Tide, but he needs someone who is not of golden blood to take this talisman to the dock. I will not force any of you, regardless of what this scholar says.”

Hephaestion immediately stepped forward, “Mydeimos, I will do it.”

Phainon could see the worry and the pride flash across Mydei’s face as the first mate stepped up. It was worry that he shared with Mydei. These were his friends too, family to Mydei, and if this didn’t work…

“No, Hephaestion.” Peucesta stepped forward, his soft-spoken voice resolved. “I am the better pick.”

“Peucesta-“

“Please, I have touched the Tide before,” he reminded them all, “ever since, I have craved the means to hear it again. I want this.”

For a very brief moment, it looked to Phainon like the man would decline, pull rank, and force Peucesta to cede this risk to himself but instead Hephaestion clasped arms with Peucesta. They leaned in to press their foreheads together, holding each other there for several seconds with Hephaestion’s hand on the back of Peucesta’s neck and their eyes closed. It wasn’t a common practice in Okhema and even on the ship, Phainon had only seen it a couple times among the older crew, but he knew it as a deeply intimate Kremnoan farewell reserved for family members or lovers.

They broke apart and Peucesta repeated the gesture with Mydei and that second goodbye caused the truth of how dangerous this was to settle in his belly. Phainon’s proposition, this risky experiment… they were sending Peucesta to his death and not a kind one either. Peucesta was potentially sacrificing his free will to painfully transform into a monster that would need to be killed by his family on this ship. For a Kremnoan, to be denied the opportunity to die a glorious death as himself…

Phainon clenched his fists tightly at his sides and looked away before he could step in and ask them to find another way. But he knew, he knew that this was still the best option. Success would grant the wish of the crew to fight beside their beloved Prince on their homeland again. This was about all of them and Peucesta knew it.

The bard broke away from Mydei but leaned close to whisper something in the prince’s ear and then he stepped back. Peucesta smiled at Phainon from where he was and nodded his head, a gesture Phainon returned in a quiet and solemn salute.

“Take heart, my friends,” Peucesta told them, “When I return as myself it will be with a greater understanding of the sweetest songs.”

Despite his impatience, Anaxa was surprisingly respectful. Phainon recalled the tenderness with which he treated his past test subjects, the only exception being students as they were rarely exposed to his more dangerous ideas. Famously, Anaxa preferred himself for testing but that wasn’t an option this time.

“My theory is sound,” Anaxa explained as he handed the wooden block to Peucesta, “you should not need it, but Hyacinthia will be sending her familiar with you.”

“Little Ica helps me heal,” she explained, “if the corruption begins to harm you, he will do his best to slow it before you turn, to buy us time to get you back to the ship.”

“You understand that per the nature of this experiment, that Ica is a distant safety net, not a crutch,” Anaxa cautioned, “He will not help you unless the situation is dire. It’s possible that you will turn before we can get to you.”

Peucesta nodded and tucked the wooden block inside his chiton, pressed against his belly.

“We will lower you by rope,” Mydei explained.

Another nod.

“May victory be yours, Peucesta,” Hephaestion said firmly with his hand over his heart.

There was a pause so that everyone could breathe through the weight and then Mydei waved his hand for the rope. They looped it around Peucesta’s waist and a second loop under his thighs. He slowly lowered himself to sit with his lyre in his lap while the crew held his weight.

After a testing bounce, he gave them a thumbs up, and the crew moved the pulley arm out over the dock. Peucesta didn’t wait for a push or any help, he kicked off the deck and out into open air, floating there over the mist while the crew very slowly lowered him. Ica fluttered around his descent in excited circles, eager to work and oblivious to the tension.

Phainon leaned over the railing, with sharp wire around his heart. He wasn’t sure he could watch and turned away to look at Mydei instead. Perhaps he shouldn’t have. Mydei was holding his hand out to Ptolemy, who reluctantly handed their prince a war bow and three bolts. He waited to ready them, leaving each arrow leaning against the deck wall, bow unstrung unless there was no other choice.

Their beloved bard twanged his lyre as he was lowered, playing something sweet and cheerful, a reassurance in a major key that made Ica twirl and dance in the air. And he kept playing when his feet touched the dock, ankle deep in corrupting mist.

“Oh!” he exclaimed in soft surprise, only audible because no one on the crew could bring themselves to breathe. His song stuttered as the Black Tide licked at his knees, swirling around him, trying to engulf his body, but he regarded it all with fascination rather than fear, as though greeting an old friend.

Peucesta paused his playing and crouched to touch the mist with his hands. It swirled all the fiercer like sharks thrashing through chum at the surface of the ocean, but he was yet undaunted, calm and composed. Instead of calling for help or screaming in pain, he closed his eyes and rhythmically twisted his head back and forth, listening to something that only he could hear.

And then he began to play again.

The song was hauntingly beautiful. It was a lonely lullaby sung in sorrow, a prayer of ancient grief longing for peace long past. Mournful regret and hope in tandem sang harmonies beside the deepest longing of ages. And when Peucesta hummed the melody over the careful glide of his fingers, Phainon felt tears spill unbidden over his cheeks.

Overwhelming loss robbed Phainon of his strength and he slowly dropped to his knees with one hand clinging to the rail for support and the other covering his mouth, afraid to make any sound that may mar the beauty of the enchanting melody.

Someone put a hand on his shoulder, but it only barely registered before it drowned in the rush behind his eyes. All he could see was his home burning to ash while warm blood coated his hands. His mother’s dim eyes were watching him, face contorted in agony while behind her body, Phainon’s father was morphing before his eyes. Still that melody played over all other sounds, and while Peucesta was only humming, Phainon could hear the whispering words of the song in his head in a language he could never hope to understand. He remembered every lyric desperately singing from the black depths of the sea in a raging storm. Longing with such force that nothing else remained but infinite heartbreak and suffering, pleading for something known and lost.

Phainon came back to himself when pain stung across his cheek and the flashback faded away into the cheers of the crew on deck. Mydei’s ember eyes were watching him, he had dropped to his knees beside Phainon and was holding his face in one hand. The other was slightly raised after the slap but hurried to cradle the other cheek, to keep him steady.

Around them the cheering continued, directed at the dock where Peucesta’s song had changed. He was playing a drinking shanty to show everyone that the experiment was a success. They were already pulling him back onboard, blissfully unaware of Mydei and Phainon in their own bubble.

Phainon grabbed onto Mydei’s wrists for support, and he felt the thumbs of Mydei’s gauntlets stroking his cheeks.

“Breathe,” the pirate ordered and Phainon realized he hadn’t been, not properly. He was panting so shallowly that his lungs were starving for air and he felt dizzy. Mydei took one of his hands away from Phainon’s face to grab his wrist, to press his shaking hand against Mydei’s warm chest, just over his sternum. He kept it there in an abiding grip and took slow, deep breaths, giving Phainon a tactile example to follow.

He closed his eyes and leaned his face into Mydei’s hand, letting his friend help hold Phainon’s weight while he focused on that strong, fast heartbeat under his hands. Slowly he matched the pace of every inhale and exhale until the ache in his heart was distant and he could open his eyes again.

Mydei was watching him, face as stone, unblinking, until Phainon gave him a few weak nods. Only after Mydei was sure that Phainon was himself did he stand and pull him up to shaky feet.

Peucesta landed delicately in the crowd of his comrades with his lyre raised in one hand and the wooden block in the other. He had a big grin on his face but when he flashed a look at Phainon, he saw the shine on the Kremnoan’s cheeks and the hollow look in his eyes.

Whatever that was, Peucesta had felt it too.

Chapter End Notes

I actually have a specific song in mind but I can't share it here cause it will IMMEDIATELY give away the plot LMAO. That said, by this point, some people may have some semi-accurate theories about the Black Tide. I will not confirm them in the comments but you're welcome to share them with me if you theory crafters want your ideas on the record in case you end up being right~ :3c
