chapters.title: Chapter 25: Truth Hiding in the Harmony
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Anaxa theorizes and Mydei confronts Phainon

No new tags but mind the existing ones

Chapter Notes

I feel very strongly about mental health. PTSD and treatments are different for different people. My fic is not meant to be an example of good coping habits or what therapy should look like. Please bear that in mind as we continue to follow Phainon and Mydei on this journey!

Even if it didn’t show on his face, Mydei was trying to balance a wide array of emotions standing on that deck. The cheers and excitement of the crew had replaced his anxious trepidation and solemn resolve. He wanted to celebrate this success alongside them but Phainon…

Phainon looked like he was going to be sick. He was pale as a sheet, eyes wide and glassy, and shaking like a leaf in a summer breeze. The way he was staring ahead and fighting for every breath as though it may be his last reminded Mydei of old Kremnoan soldiers returning from campaigns they weren’t ready for. Those men were haunted and changed, as though their minds or souls were injured. Most of them healed with rest and returned to the front lines, but some of them did not and were unable to fight again.

Mydei reached out to grab Phainon’s arm just above the wrist and the man flinched, but he at least looked him in the eye and offered a weak and broken smile.

“Sorry, I don’t know what happened there,” he laughed and reached up to scratch the back of his head apologetically. “Peucesta is really moving when he plays, yeah?”

Mydei didn’t know what to say, not all men liked having attention brought to their weaknesses, but injuries to the soul needed care and attention as much as injuries to the body.

“Deliverer-“ “Anaxa’s experiment worked!” Phainon exclaimed. He was trying to turn the conversation away from himself.

Not this time. Mydei tightened his grip on Phainon like a vice.

“M-Mydeimos!”

All protesting was ignored. He half-led, half-dragged Phainon across the deck, detouring only briefly to catch Perdikkas’ confused expression to beckon for the man to join them. Then he pulled Phainon down the stairs through the belly of the ship and to the infirmary where he finally let go.

“Sit,” Mydei ordered.

“Mydei, I-“

“Sit.”

Phainon rolled his eyes but kept his smile as he dramatically pulled up one of the chairs and took a seat. “Mydei, I don’t feel sick.”

Mydei crossed his arms and stood between Phainon and the door until Perdikkas finally caught up.

“Mydei, what’s going on?” he asked, “everyone else is looking for you and the professor wants to talk to Phainon.”

“Shouldn’t keep the professor waiting,” Phainon announced brightly. He stood up but Mydei roughly pushed him back down into the chair.

“Where were you back there, Deliverer?” Mydei asked.

“Hm? I was on deck.”

“Where were you up here?” he asked again this time pressing the tip of a claw to Phainon’s forehead.

Phainon’s eyes glittered and his jaw tightened. Mydei saw his throat bob as he swallowed. The man was angry and trying to hide it, but he answered in a deep, dark voice, “Aedes Elysiae.”

Perdikkas’ mood shifted to something more serious, and he stepped back enough to close the door. “Has this happened before?”

“There’s nothing wrong with me,” Phainon insisted, already back to being cheerful.

“I’m not saying there is,” Perdikkas said gently as he walked in closer to take a seat on the bed next to Phainon, “this happens to a lot of people.”

Phainon leaned back in his chair with his arms crossed and one of his legs bouncing up and down. “It only happens sometimes. There is nothing to worry about.”

“How often is sometimes,” the doctor prodded, “does something trigger it?”

The leg stopped bouncing as Phainon thought. “It happens sometimes around the Black Tide.”

“Have you known about this for awhile?”

He sighed and admitted, “Aglaea knows. It was worse when she found me, when I was more… angry and hollow. It hasn’t happened like this since before Aglaea took me in.”

“You were tense on deck when we got here and mostly fine until Peucesta started playing,” Mydei noted.

Phainon leaned forward and put his hand on his face to cover one eye. “That song was just… so familiar, it sounded just like the song I heard in the ocean when I went overboard during the storm.”

“Did you have the same visions during the storm?”

“Not as clear but, yeah.”

“And before then?”

Phainon thought aloud, “I felt it briefly a couple years ago when we were evacuating the Grove and a couple times before when fighting the Tide.”

Mydei nodded and said, “if you are seeing visions of your home then that is the source of the injury, and the Black Tide is ripping it open.”

“We fight the Tide all the time without incident,” Phainon pointed out, “and I’m not injured.”

“Not on the outside,” Perdikkas agreed, “Phainon, there’s nothing shameful about lingering trauma like this and it may come and go. You went through something awful as a kid, that can take a lifetime to recover from, especially if you’ve never had the chance to face that trauma or work through it.”

“I don’t think that really applies to Chrysos Heirs,” he laughed.

“It does,” Mydei corrected, “it happened to me.” Phainon went quiet at that, looking at Mydei with concern and perhaps a little bit of awe. “I spent my childhood drowning,” he reminded them casually, “it took many years of working with Perdikkas and Krateros for me to let that go. The nightmares still linger and there are times when I feel fear looking into the heart of the black ocean, but I have embraced that part of me and learned how to let it go.”

“We’re not saying you have to fix it right this moment,” Perdikkas told Phainon, “nor can you. It’s not the kind of thing that can be magically corrected but if you’re willing, will you let me teach you some techniques? So, if those flashbacks return you can come back to yourself more quickly?”

Phainon still seemed a little upset at the implication that he needed any kind of care as he let his hand fall back to his lap.

“Do it because I want it,” Mydei said quickly, and both the other men looked up at him in flabbergasted shock.

If he is too busy taking care of others to care for himself, then I will simply have to take up that task. What better way to get Phainon to take care of himself than to convince him he is doing it for someone else?

“HKS, what use are you to me if you break down at the sight of the mist?” Mydei growled dismissively, “if you are going to watch my back in the battle against Nikador, then I must know you can handle yourself. Or must I always be there to show you how to breathe?”

Phainon blinked and then exhaled into a half chuckle. “Alright, alright. I will do my best.”

“We can meet after your Kremnoan lessons in the evenings,” Perdikkas invited.

“I’ll be there,” Phainon promised.

-

Phainon still felt uneasy when he left the infirmary with Mydei and Perdikkas. As much as he wanted to push everything back down and focus entirely on the task at hand, he was still very shaken. But mostly, he was ashamed. The reassurances from his friends that what he was experiencing was normal, that Mydei had also endured similar stress, was comforting but it didn’t eliminate the worry that somehow this made him less of a person. What if someone got really hurt because he broke down?

Years ago, when he was still barely himself, Aglaea had taught him how to manage his rage and fear to control himself in the face of the Tide. These episodes had stopped with her care over the years and Phainon had been able to successfully lead many expeditions against the Tide. He really believed they were behind him but the closer they got to the Tide the more those old wounds were reopening. Lessons from Perdikkas seemed more like a good idea the longer he thought about it.

His stomach was still churning when he walked down the steps into the galley. Anaxa was furiously taking notes as he studied the wooden block that Peucesta had taken to the dock while Hyacine checked Peucesta for any lasting damage or corruption.

Little Ica trilled happily at Phainon and zoomed up to collect his nose boop which Phainon happily bestowed with a wide smile and a single pointer finger.

“Is my man well?” Mydei asked as he stepped past Phainon. The pirate was tense. He still wasn’t happy about losing his kitchen to this endeavor. His expression matched Fig Stew’s glare who supervised Anaxa irritably from the open, cold oven door.

The bard was sitting on one of the preparation tables, lyre set aside by the cubbies. Phainon could see the exhausted hollow of his eyes still but the tear tracks had since been wiped away. Hyacine was standing in front of him with a gentle blue-green glow coming from her palm.

“He is perfect,” she announced, “no corruption at all.”

“That is not entirely accurate,” Anaxa mumbled from the opposite countertop. He held up the wooden block without turning around. The wax seal had been pulled free and something inside the pocket clunked about as he waved it. “He was corrupted but this removed it as quickly as the stain was accrued.”

“Then it worked?” Phainon asked. His heart fluttered at the good news.

“It will need some adjustments, but yes.”

“What kind of adjustments?” Mydei prodded.

“Ideally, the talisman would absorb the corruption before it can touch the man but drawing it out is an excellent start.” Anaxa dumped the contents of the pocket out into his hand and held it up to the light.

The red crystal was polished but cut unevenly into an irregular polygon. What mattered was that it was flat enough to fit in the wooden sleeve. Phainon had removed it from the crystal lion figurehead himself with a hammer, chisel, and a dozen apologies to the Chryseus Leo. The piece had come free like broken obsidian, clean, thin, and sharp. Now as it shined red in the light everyone could see the fine black staining the edges.

“…where did you get that?” Mydei asked.

“Ah, don’t be mad at the professor, Mydei,” Phainon hurried to say, “I broke it off the figurehead.”

Mydei twitched irritably and his hands clenched into tight fists, but he kept to himself with an annoyed huff.

“This ship has developed a means to absorb the energy of the Black Tide,” Anaxa explained as he set the crystal down. “Corruption happens when living beings absorb this energy and fail to purge it before they transform, but this ship is neither living nor wholly inanimate. The lion that has become one with this vessel is alive enough to absorb the effects of the Tide, but stone cannot turn into a monster. This is what protects you when you sail through tainted waters.”

“Absorb not reflect?” Perdikkas asked.

“Correct.”

“Does the ship have a limit to how much it can hold?” Phainon asked.

“Yes.”

“But it doesn’t matter does it?” Pecuesta realized softly, “because the corruption can be washed away.”

The corner of Anaxa’s mouth curled up, pleased with this new astute student. “Correct.”

Phainon inhaled sharply when it all came back to him, an afternoon spent caring for the lion, singing songs to him to heal his spirit, and the tender respect of a dutiful first mate repairing even the smallest dents. “All those times you went to sing to the ship…?”

“We knew the ship was resistant,” Mydei explained, “we didn’t realize it was absorbing the corruption.”

“This ship is in remarkably good shape,” Anaxa praised, “that care and love that you spend keeping it clean and in good repair may not have been intentionally meant to purge the Tide, but it did so all the same. Okhema has known for hundreds of years that minor corruption can be removed. Phainon, when that woman first brought you to Okhema, what was the first thing she requested of you?”

“She made me bathe. Twice.”

“The bathhouse in the Chrysos Heir’s bath glimmers gold with Mnestia’s power. It cleanses Black Tide corruption. Your golden blood may have kept you from turning, but it does not make you immune to the stain.”

Phainon searched through his memories. “I knew that the Black Tide could linger on a person. Every time Castorice, Hyacine, or I returned from missions where we fought the Tide, Aglaea would have us bathe. It was routine.”

Anaxa picked up the crystal and took it over to the washbasin. He dropped it in the water unceremoniously with a plop and droplets scattered across the countertop. When he took the crystal out of the water, the corruption remained but then Anaxa picked up a washcloth and reverently began to wipe it dry. Slowly, the black faded back to red.

“Care,” he announced, “it is not so simple as a bath. It is not the magic of clean water and soap. The answer is care.”

Peucesta had a soft smile on his face and Phainon could feel the warmth of those memories. His very first lessons on the ship had been to love and care for one’s home. The Chryseus Leo was a part of the crew as much as any other man onboard. Even if they didn’t realize what they were doing, even if they didn’t know that their love and respect for the ship was making a meaningful difference, it was that reverence that protected them.

“Even if it didn’t help, I would sing for this ship all the same,” Peucesta said proudly.

Perdikkas grinned. Mydei cracked a small smile.

“It means that this talisman is reusable,” Anaxa announced. He held the crystal aloft, pinched between his thumb and forefinger. “Acting as an extension of the ship, they will act as a sponge to absorb corruption until they are at capacity. This is not a permanent solution. At most it buys time until the crystal can be cleaned.”

“It is still something,” Mydei praised.

“Thank you, professor,” Phainon added with his hand over his heart, “but if they are already working as intended, why do you need to make the adjustments you mentioned.”

“I want to extend the time and prevent the corruption from passing through the individual before it is allocated to this crystal, or they will be exposed to the Tide’s song.”

Phainon felt his blood run cold and Peucesta looked down. Anaxa’s eye narrowed in on Phainon but he didn’t look surprised.

“What song?” Perdikkas asked, “the one Peucesta played on the dock?”

“Have you heard it too, Professor?” Phainon asked softly.

“Yes.”

“So have I,” Hyacine admitted quietly, “I-I recognized it when you played it.”

Anaxa tapped his fingers on the countertop. “Hyacinthia, you were exposed during a research trip if I recall.”

“Yes, I was a young healer at the time and didn’t know how to dispel the corruption,” her voice wavered as she remembered. She raised a hand up to her chest as she bowed her head. “I took it into myself instead, but it wasn’t enough, and my patient turned. As he was transforming, I heard distant singing, but it went away when I returned to the Grove, rested and bathed.”

“And you, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae,” Anaxa invited, “you were exposed as a child.”

“Yeah, but I don’t remember singing,” he said very slowly. Phainon had to really think about it, had to force himself to recall the details of the destruction that altered the course of his humble life. Revisiting it now, he was starting to shake but a hand on his shoulder immediately grounded him.

Mydei’s hand squeezed firmly and when their eyes met, the pirate gave Phainon a genuine smile and subtle nod. Reassured, Phainon closed his eyes to think and as he relived that awful moment he realized that there had been a voice that day, buried under the screams and sorrow. The Black Tide had sung to him in the background of his dazed mind the entire time he had fought his turned family and friends, adding soundtrack to the numbness as he buried them and dragged himself away from fields of gold turned black.

“There was a song,” he whispered, “and I heard it again during the storm. Peucesta and I talked about it while we cleaned Chryseus Leo.”

“Then you have heard it as well? I suspected as much when you volunteered on deck,” Anaxa noted when he turned to Peucesta.

“Several years ago, I was nearly lost to the Tide,” he recounted, “I slept beside Chryseus Leo and spoke with the lion daily until the song was gone. I have tried ever since to revisit the melody, to understand that voice, but I could not recreate it until today when I heard the song again, more clearly than I ever have before.”

“And I heard it in the Grove,” Anaxa confirmed, “before I realized the song was a symptom of the corruption, I entertained it as a curiosity to study. Only after I took the coreflame into myself and the song ceased did I realize the truth of it.”

Mydei took his hand back, brows furrowed. “I have waded through the Tide before, and I have not heard a song.”

“I didn’t hear it until after… after the danger had passed,” Phainon admitted.

“The corruption would have needed time to take root in a Chrysos Heir,” Anaxa explained, “far longer than a brief military conflict at sea. The extended exposure as a child likely made you more sensitive to it, Phainon, creating a stronger association that allows you to hear it at the slightest contact with the Tide and solidifying the association you have between the song and your childhood trauma.” The drumming on the countertop quickened. “Extenuating circumstances aside, Chrysos Heirs are more resilient to its allure it would seem. You said on deck that you wanted to hear the song again, that you have been longing to recreate it.”

“I would say it is my love of music that drives my desire,” Peucesta said, “but that would be a lie. It is enchanting, a melody of temptation.”

“Like you need to go to whomever is singing it,” Phainon whispered, and the room quieted.

“I know the feeling,” Hyacine added, equally soft, “I remember crying when I heard it. All I could feel was…” she trailed off like it was too hard to say the words.

“Loss,” Phainon supplied and she nodded. Shakily, he admitted, “Earlier, when you were playing on the dock, Peucesta, I collapsed hearing it again. I could hear the words in my head even though you weren’t singing them… and see my home burning. All I could feel was overwhelming grief, fear, and loss like I felt back then.”

“I have long theorized that the Black Tide is a form of energy,” Anaxa offered, “perhaps it is one weaponized by emotion.”

“But… belonging to what?” Perdikkas wondered aloud.

“Or who?” Phainon asked instead.

No one had an answer.

-

The nature of the Black Tide was an engrossing mystery but one best left for another day. Mydei’s list of concerns was growing with every new discovery but the priority was still the upcoming battle at Castrum Kremnos. As long as they knew enough about this eldritch enemy to protect themselves during the fight on the horizon, everything else could wait.

Gossip amongst the crew agreed. Word of the discussion and subsequent hypothesis about the Tide had spread like jam on bread, but Mydei got the vibe from the others that most of them considered the information above their paygrade and only cared about the impending battle. The battle and how tired everyone was after all the detours.

Only so much could be done on the ship and Perdikkas and Hyacine both agreed in their professional medical opinions that everyone needed rest and prescribed relaxation, which Anaxa promptly ignored. The eccentric professor kept working until he was satisfied with the tests and by the time they turned around to sail back to the Kremnoan settlement, he had a shopping list and a step-by-step process for making the protective charms. It would take time to gather the materials, but having a plan was already a huge step in the right direction.

Until then, the anticipation of a major battle made the air onboard buzz with excitement that overflowed to the rest of the settlement when they finally made berth again in the form of a classic Kremnoan celebration. It was tradition to party and spend time with family before a major campaign to allow the people to bid farewell to their warriors. There were feasts, fights, drinking, singing, and as long as they didn’t hurt themselves, Mydei didn’t mind.

He preferred the men get the partying out of their system now. More than a week at sea would sober them up with plenty of time to prepare and be ready to fight.

Most of his immediate family were happy to engage in the festivities, eating their fill and drinking sweet wines. Under the protective care of Hephaestion and Perdikkas, even Hyacine and Castorice were scooped up into the excitement. It was getting dark when the house finally settled. Most of the crew had gone dancing after dinner with the promise of a visit to the bathhouse afterwards. The only ones left behind were Mydei, Phainon, Anaxa, and Peucesta.

The Professor had excused himself to the library, disappearing among the tomes, determined to keep to himself. Mydei had expected nothing less, his worried attention was instead on his remaining wayward friends. The two who had taken the discovery the hardest, who still wrestled with their inner demons

Peucesta and Phainon were at the balcony railing facing opposite directions. Phainon was looking out over the city with his book in hand, reading it with one thumb pressed between the pages to keep it open while he leaned on his other arm. Peucesta was sitting on a stool with his back against the rail to strum his lyre. He was playing the song of the Tide, humming it quietly and striving for something more nostalgic than haunting. Carefully lending the same melody his own voice, to turn it from something sad into something hopeful.

“This one,” Phainon mumbled to Peucesta as Mydei approached. He was holding the book up to the bard, pointing at one of the words. They were reading from the Kremnoan tome, Mydei realized.

Peucesta pronounced the word twice for him and added, “it means ‘recoup’.”

“Thank you, oh, Mydei.”

“Deliverer. Peucesta.” Mydei kept his voice quiet to match the mood. “Do you not want to go into town?”

They both shook their heads and Peucesta changed the song to something sleepier and less emotionally charged by way of an answer. Phainon folded the corner of the page in his book to mark his spot and set it aside.

“Are you both well?” Mydei asked instead.

“Yeah, it just,” Phainon mumbled. He struggled to find the words. It hurt to see Phainon of all people struggle to speak.

“The song still bothers you?”

“It doesn’t bother me,” Phainon assured him, “it just changes things.”

Mydei frowned. “Do you no longer want your pardon?”

“I do! I still think retrieving the Coreflame of Strife is the right step.” His words trailed off again. Phainon’s hands were slowly clenching into fists on the railing. “This pointless rivalry between Okhema and Kremnos feels so small when I think of the Black Tide,” he explained, “the more we learn about it, the more I want to go farther than Castrum Kremnos. When we get the coreflame and take it to Okhema, I’m going to tell Aglaea everything and ask for the Okheman Navy to help us fight the Tide.”

“That is a very ambitious plan, Deliverer,” Mydei observed aloud.

Phainon sighed at the name and with a waver in his voice said, “No other choice but forward.”

Mydei could see the doubt that Phainon tried to hide, the struggle of worrying that he wasn’t enough. That something inside him was broken. Even after a few days at sea, days that felt normal and relaxed, Mydei suspected that Phainon was still thinking about the way he had collapsed on deck.

“Come,” Mydei ordered.

“What?”

“Come!” he repeated and then Mydei jumped over the railing. He landed beside the bushes and then jumped over the small wall around his yard to get to the street. Above him, Phainon was still standing on the balcony, confused. Mydei flashed him a smirk, gestured again and then took off running.

Mydei didn’t turn around, he didn’t need to. He could hear Phainon’s boots on the stones on the road behind him. He ran faster.

The hills on this island were steep, but Mydei had found natural paths through the foliage and hidden places that provided ample escape. Leonnius and Hephaestion knew of them too, had even helped Mydei map routes to some of the prettier places. Mydei led Phainon down one such path, behind a waterfall, along a small cliff, under trees with leaves the same size as they were, until they reached the beach.

He stopped running when they broke free of the trees to the sound of crashing waves. The waterline on this side of the island didn’t break on sand, instead it crashed across wide, massive rocks, smooth and flattened by the tide. The waves lapped at the sides of the stone at low tide, slowly eating away at rounded gaps and occasionally spraying the surface with salty droplets.

Mydei walked out onto the plateau, stepping around puddles that were left in the shallow basins in the uneven surface. They glowed like mirrors holding the moonlight. He took a deep breath in through his nose and held the sea air tightly in his chest until it hurt to keep. The breeze picked up and a misty sea spray left tiny droplets like diamonds in his hair and on his clothes and chest.

“Deliverer,” Mydei called, turning enough to see his friend still hiding in the tree line.

“Why do you keep calling me that, Mydeimos?” Phainon asked as he slowly stepped out onto the stone, keeping several paces between them. He sounded tired, maybe even a little annoyed, like the weight of the world was starting to get to him.

“Because that is what you are.”

Phainon snorted. “I haven’t been since Aglaea labeled me a pirate.”

“Are you so sure?” Mydei asked.

“Yes. Especially now.”

“Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, you do not get to decide,” he said.

Phainon’s face twisted in surprise, “Huh? What does that mean?”

“It means you are still the Deliverer, and you have no say otherwise.”

“I don’t think that’s how it works, Mydei.”

Mydei’s tattoos started to glow, just a ripple from his base through his back and chest up his arms to summon several shards of crimson crystal. “It is, and as the stronger fighter, what I say goes.”

Phainon twitched. “You are not the stronger fighter.”

“Prove it.”

Blue flashed in Phainon’s hand as he summoned his sword, a serious look on his face. He paced further out onto the stone to stand down the shore from Mydeimos.

They waited in silence until a particularly strong wave bashed against the stone sending a column of water up in the air beside them and then they were racing to close the distance.

This far away from the settlement, Mydei let loose. He opened with a massive wave of crystals aimed at Phainon’s left side. Phainon predictably dodged to the right, towards the ocean, but when Mydei rushed to meet him, his claws tore at empty space. He barely managed to raise his gauntlets in time to catch the sword that dropped from above.

They clashed, Phainon’s sword weighed heavily in the cross of Mydei’s gauntlets with all of Phainon’s body behind it as he dropped from his leap. The force pushed Mydei back on the smooth stone. Sparks bounced through puddles, disturbing the water’s peace.

Mydei broke the stalemate. He dropped one arm and pushed with the other to cast the sword aside, creating an opening for him to reach for Phainon’s chest, but Phainon had spun with the momentum, bringing his sword around in an arc to force Mydei’s retreat. The tip of the blade narrowly missed Mydei’s nose.

Phainon let the sword finish its swing and neatly spun it into another sweep, following Mydei’s backstep with that blade gliding along the ground. He slowed its assault with crystal but couldn’t stop it entirely, instead using the opportunity to leap over the blade, towards Phainon with his claws extended.

They broke apart, bouncing away from each other when Mydei landed. He flashed Phainon a toothy grin and licked the gold from his claws. A drop of blood slowly rolled down Phainon’s cheek.

“Apologies Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, it looks like you will need to stay our Deliverer after all,” he taunted.

Phainon shouted and surged forward, moving faster than Mydei had expected. He raised an arm to intercept the sword, but Phainon was strong and the force still launched him towards the tree line. Mydei slid on one knee. Gold shimmered dark in the moonlight as it ran over his gauntlet and the tip of Phainon’s sword. The blade had bitten him on his bicep, just above the armor.

“That’s more like it,” Mydei growled with glee.

Mydei and Phainon exchanged blows with increasing fervor until their roars echoed around the stone arches and sparks from their clashes fell on moonlight in equal measure as the splashing sea. They were evenly matched in every way, pushing each other to heights that Mydei could have only dreamed of before Phainon.

It was the same feeling as the first time they had fought but cultivated into something far more intimate. Mydei didn’t need to waste time trying to read his friend, because he already knew. He knew that Phainon was ambidextrous, that he favored movements in threes, that he preferred to lead with his right foot but was willing to use his left if he thought there was an advantage to be seized. And Phainon knew things about Mydei that he couldn’t hope to understand. Mydei knew this to be true because when they fought it felt like dancing, like they were a single being relishing in the true joy of Strife and inspiration through challenge.

And the longer they fought the more Phainon relaxed and let himself meet Mydei at every step. Mydei could see the confidence coming back, feel it when that blade reached for his flesh, and when he was sure that Phainon was more himself than he had been in days, he finally spoke again.

“You should be more honest with yourself,” he told Phainon, “as you are right now.”

Steel screeched against the rocks as Mydei kicked the sword away, but it sang on the return as it swiped from above.

“You think this is me at my most honest?” Phainon laughed.

Mydei grabbed the blade, pinching it between both of his hands to stop it above his head. “I know it is.”

“Will you still be saying that when I win?”

Mydei scoffed, “If you win.” Mydei’s foot connected with Phainon’s stomach, and the Deliverer was sent flying, disconnected from his weapon. Mydei tossed the sword to the side and ran at Phainon to tackle him. They went down in a flurry of limbs, rolling until a rock stopped them.

Phainon panted beneath Mydei, his wrists pinned beside his head, hair spread across the rock and shining with the water from the puddle beneath him. The moonlight caught in the water, making his white hair glow and stealing Mydei’s breath away.

The Kremnoan wiggled a little to settle over Phainon’s lap, boxing him in with his knees and weight while he looked down at that surprised smile that made his heart leap into his throat.

“Phainon, I-“ Mydei caught himself mid-confession, instead saying the last thing Phainon wanted to hear, the last thing he wanted to say, “I want you to stay here.”

“What?” he breathed, disbelieving.

They were still for several heartbeats and then Phainon surged beneath him and they rolled again, this time Phainon had Mydei pinned with a hand on his chest. Seawater dripped from his hair onto Mydei’s face. The moonlight caught the shine of the droplets, casting colors across the white before they fell.

“Do you think me that weak, Mydeimos? That I will break when it matters most?” Phainon asked, with hurt in his words.

It’s because I love you.

“Don’t be absurd.”

“Then why would you request that of me?!” he snarled.

Mydei rolled his hips to buck Phainon forward so he could pull his legs up for the leverage to roll them again. He looped his thumb through Phainon’s collar and pressed his hand to the stone beside his neck, holding him there by the accessory and a hand splayed on that strong chest. Phainon’s hand came up to grab him by the chiton’s fabric across his chest. The other held tightly to Mydei’s bicep, just below the metal band there.

“Will you not let me do this for you?” Mydei asked with a strain in his voice that made Phainon’s eyes go wide and his heart race below Mydei’s palm.

“No, we should do it together,” Phainon breathed.

“And what if something happens to you?”

Phainon scoffed. “To me? What about you?”

“I am immortal.”

Phainon’s hands let go to fall to either side, entirely at Mydei’s mercy, completely surrendering to him with a cheeky smile. “I have to go. It’s my duty as the Deliverer.”

“Then you concede?”

“Just this once, Mydeimos.”

“A shame, I would have liked to pummel you unconscious.” They had never needed to fight all the way to such a drastic win condition. Someone usually came by to stop them before they could.

Phainon chuckled softly and Mydei felt the butterflies in his stomach take flight. He wanted so badly to kiss this man who glittered like starlight, whose eyes were the sunny sky and whose heart beat out a rhythm of confidence with which Mydei longed to harmonize.

“You are not weak, Deliverer,” Mydei crooned, “your inner demons do not scare me.”

“They scare me,” Phainon admitted and Mydei tilted his head with how easily Phainon admitted such a weakness. Phainon brought a hand up to gently push Mydei off so he could get to his feet and brush the dust and sand from his pants. He offered Mydei a hand and pulled him up so they could stand together. “But I’m ready to fight them now, because you have my back.”

“HKS,” Mydei huffed. He punched Phainon in the shoulder, hard, and that damn man laughed his perfect laugh that made Mydei’s knees feel weak. “Together then.”

Chapter Notes

This was almost the longest I've gone without updating and it's all Anaxa's fault. I have no idea why he was so hard to write this chapter.

Even after drafting the help of the craftsmen from the settlement, creating enough charms for the entire crew took two days of focused labor. Anaxa concluded that the solution to both of his problems was in the size and shape of the crystal removed from the figurehead. Mydei offered to provide his own crystals instead of chipping away at the lion, but Anaxa refused. Crucially, the crystal had to come from the ship itself, as an extension of Chryseus Leo.

Unfortunately, the wood also had to come from the same source and whole sections of railing were removed and cut into cubes instead of flat sleeves to accommodate the larger sections of crystal. The crew insisted on handling that part, while their Kremnoan friends from the shipyard installed new railings. The smooth new rails were a lighter color than the worn wood and far less interesting without the unique carvings running the length.

“I can’t tell if it’s poetic or weird to be going into battle with a cross section of a story tied to my belt,” Leonnius mused aloud. Phainon was next to him holding a cubical rough section himself. They were sitting on the deck in groups of four each responsible for various stages of the process. Phainon’s group was finishing up the last of the hollowing out process.

“It’s tragic,” Ptolemy grumbled, too upset to even think of a quote, “these designs were carved by shipbuilders and artists that fell to the Tide. Some of them may still be roaming Castrum Kremnos as monsters.”

That was not a pleasant thought. Phainon gently brushed shavings from the inside of his cube with two fingers. They were not small considering the width of the railing. Twine would be wrapped around them so they could be carried like oversized pendants or too full coin sacks at the belt. The twine would hold the crystal inside too with the right wrapping technique.

The girls were in that group. They were happily chatting between themselves as they expertly wrapped the cubes and checked that the crystal chunks were secure. High-stakes arts and crafts somehow fit perfectly in Castorice’s element.

Phainon turned back to the cube in his hand. The goal was to leave the remaining walls the same width as a pinky. Hollowed out too thin and the wood may not be sturdy enough to survive a battle. This one was almost done. On three sides it had carvings of men carrying shields and spears, marching towards the cutoff. He held it up to see the faded images a little better and Hephaestion, sitting next to him, held his up too so those marching figures had somewhere to go. They did not match and somehow those warring soldiers ended up marching into a bathhouse.

“It isn’t the worst place to end a march,” Phainon chuckled.

“It’s definitely where I’m going after dinner,” Hephaestion agreed.

Leonnius leaned over to see what they were talking about and then held his own cube up between theirs. He had part of a feast on his. The front half of the roast pig had ended up on another cube somewhere, but he still had the curled tail carved just under a group of men raising their glasses in a toast.

“There we go,” he added, “the perfect itinerary.”

“It’s awful that we must do this. It is like losing Castrum Kremnos all over again,” Ptolemy lamented. He was still very focused, unwilling to be there any longer than they had to be. Every time he pressed the knife into the wood he winced like he was carving up his own flesh.

“Kremnos’ history is us,” the first mate reminded him, “it doesn’t end because some faded carvings are repurposed.”

“Isn’t this an ideal situation for them?” Phainon offered. Ptolemy flashed him a glare. “I mean it. Broaden your perspective, Ptolemy. We will be carrying snapshots of history, a part of the ship with us into battle to reclaim your homeland. What better place for Chryseus Leo than protecting his crew even when ashore? If the lion had a choice, wouldn’t he want to fight too? In this way he, and the legacy of your people, can be a part of one of the greatest battles since you were last at Castrum Kremnos.”

“Well said, Deliverer,” Mydei praised as he passed by. The man was coming from the bow with a basket of crystals that he had carved from the lion himself. It was a solemn duty, but Mydei refused to let anyone else chip away at that regal mane, not after he begrudgingly forgave Phainon for doing so once before.

Phainon watched Mydei walk by and his eyes traced the tattoos that spanned his back, his huggable waist, the way his muscles flexed carrying that heavy basket. He wondered what it would feel like to trace those lines with just the press of his fingers, with his tongue…

Leonnius smacked Phainon upside the head. “Ogle on your own time.”

“Damn it, Leonnius,” Hephaestion growled, “you are ruining my strategy.”

“If you’re gonna compete, at least keep it fair.”

Apologetically, and blushing profusely, Phainon got back to work, and in the end, he still won. By the time they finished hollowing out their pile of cross-sections, Phainon’s tally was twelve and Hephaestion had finished eleven. Leonnius came in third at eight, proving his hands weren’t as fast as his feet. And Ptolemy was last with only four. He had spent too much time mourning and wincing to be efficient. It was a closer race than Phainon had intended as he had been easily distracted by Mydei and the bittersweet of repurposing these old carvings.

“Perdikkas!” Ptolemy shouted from where they were still sitting.

Across the deck Perdikkas leaned back to see around his own pod of workers. He was on sanding duty.

Ptolemy raised his arm to point dramatically down at Phainon, Perdikkas scowled and ten seconds later a gold coin slammed into Ptolemy’s face with suspicious accuracy. It fell in his lap, leaving behind an imprint but the book worm still chuckled under his breath as he scooped the coin up and rolled it between his fingers.

“’Let heaven give victory to whom it will,’” he quoted as he pocketed the coin, already feeling better now that victory was soothing his emotional wounds.

Phainon knew better than to ask for details. He figured out awhile ago that people were gambling on their competitions. It didn’t stop him from doing his very best at every opportunity.

“Have you finished your assignment?” Anaxa asked as he came to stand over them. The professor had been supervising the entire process, pacing as though he were searching for cheaters in the middle of a test. All four of them held one of the hollowed out cubes up for his approval but he didn’t linger long enough for full inspections and walked on.

Leonnius leaned in and Phainon and the others instinctively mimicked him, getting in close to huddle. “Is he always like this, Phainon?”

“I think the isolation made him nicer.”

All four of them broke the huddle to look at Anaxa’s back, watching the man closely until he paused and quickly spun around to glare at them and then they were hurrying to reconvene.

“That man would snap in a strong breeze and has a literal blind spot,” Hephaestion confided, “so why is he so damn scary?”

“If you have time to gossip like children, then you have time to help others with their tasks,” Anaxa called from above. He had slightly closed the distance to lean over their huddle, making them all flinch in place.

“We were just about to, Professor Anaxa!” Phainon reassured him.

“Anaxagoras.”

“That’s what I said.”

The angry Demigod stalked off to check on the others.

“I need to check with Empousa about our cargo allotment,” Hephaestion said as he got to his feet.

“I’ll find her.”

“Thank you, Leonnius. Ptolemy?” He helped the bookworm to his feet.

“I’ll help the girls. Phainon- Phainon?” Ptolemy turned in time to see Phainon already carrying the big basket of their hollowed-out cubes over to the next station to help with the sanding.

He set them down right in front of Perdikkas and squeezed in between the doctor and Krateros. The former handed him a sheet of sharkskin, already worn but with enough life left to be effective.

“Did you really bet against me?” Phainon teased and Perdikkas groaned.

“Hephaestion dabbled in whittling,” he explained, “got good at it. I thought maybe that gave him an advantage.”

“He did?” Phainon asked. He looked up in time to see Hephaestion leave the ship, presumably to find Empousa as he had previously declared.

“Yeah, Krateros taught him.”

The old man could clearly hear them but refused to engage in the conversation while he sanded away, careful not to damage the images. Every once in awhile he would stop and Phainon thought he may say something unprompted, but each pause was meant for Fig Stew who was dozing on his back in the warm sun. The temptation to reach for Fig’s belly was right there but Phainon had learned from that morning that his worthiness to scratch the royal fur was still in question and they didn’t need blood smudges messing with Anaxa’s perfect formula.

“Krateros, you whittle?” Phainon asked.

“Woodworking was a hobby of mine when I was younger.” Gruff words landed flatly between them and Phainon took the hint.

“I wouldn’t have expected that,” he offered politely but didn’t push the topic, instead they fell into a comfortable and drowsy rhythm with the shushush of sharkskin on splintery edges.

Phainon made a point to work at every station. When they were done sanding, he helped with the waxing, then on to polishing and shaping the crystals to fit them neatly inside each box, ending next to Castorice and Hyacine who showed him how to properly tie the twine. The rough cord wrapped around all sides of the cube multiple times to cover the missing side and hold the crystal in place. The light coat of wax along the inside hollow helped keep each piece from clattering around but there was still some give to them, and they rattled with muted thuds when shaken.

Phainon put the last charm in the shallow crate just as the thief star dashed across the sky, brilliant white and twinkling good night.

“How did we do, Professor Anaxa?” Phainon asked.

“…”

“…Professor Anaxagoras.”

“Passable.”

In a world that was mostly pass or fail, Phainon took that as praise.

Anaxa took one off the top and ran his hand over each side. He shook it violently for a few seconds and then bounced it gently between his hands, letting the talisman roll as naturally as possible. Satisfied with their durability he put the piece back where he got it and pulled the lid over the top. The box would be stored safely in Mydei and Phainon’s room until it was time. They didn’t want to risk losing any on the journey through hostile waters.

Most of the crew had left the ship as the number of tasks to complete decreased to tend to last-minute plans and packing. The partying had not persisted past their first night on shore, but the town was still very alive and bright. Streetlamps were staving off the dark of dusk, glowing gold under navy blue and dying orange. The hum of people talking carried across the dock like the distant buzz of a beehive, indiscernible as words but thrumming with life.

Castorice and Hyacine had already excitedly left to find food, leaving Phainon and Anaxa alone on the deck. Mydei was around there somewhere too and Phainon was eager to meet up with him, but thinking of Mydei also brought up memories of their fight on the beach and the things that Mydei had said.

Even if Phainon had swayed the Kremnoan in the end, it still stung to recall that Mydei had wanted to leave Phainon behind, even after insisting that Phainon retain the symbolic title, ‘Deliverer.’ A name that Phainon still wasn’t so sure about after Aglaea’s warrant and his own willingness to reject it.

“Will you be coming with us to Castrum Kremnos, professor?” Phainon asked.

Anaxa was using both of his hands and little bunny hops to push the lid down. He was a strong man but too small to benefit from the same leverage literally any other full-grown man on the ship had. Phainon stepped up to help, pressing down until the lid wedged shut.

“Of course. I want to see this success with my own eyes.” He waved a hand down at the box, indicating that said ‘success’ was not the retrieval of the coreflame, but rather that his design performed to his personal high standard. “But that’s not really what you want to talk about, is it?”

“…nothing ever escapes you.”

“I didn’t spend all those years teaching you for nothing.”

“Lately, I’ve been thinking about the name Aglaea gave me, that’s all. I’ve been wondering why she chose me to carry it,” Phainon explained.

“And you think I’d have some perfect answer to lay your concerns to rest, Deliverer of Okhema?” Anaxa sounded more annoyed than bored, but Phainon knew that of the two, bored was worse.

“Do you?”

“No, I don’t.”

He sighed and looked down, “I thought so.”

“Because it’s a ridiculous question to be concerned about in the first place,” Anaxa scoffed, “Why are you fretting over that woman’s choice on her behalf? Or is it that you are afraid that you cannot live up to the expectations that have been attributed to a single word? Are you only you because Aglaea gave you a fancy title? Listen up, I’ll say this once. There is value in rising to expectations but not because others have challenged you to meet them, but rather because you have chosen to accept that challenge, to match those expectations with those you have for yourself. If you truly want to be worthy of being the Deliverer, then stop wasting time wondering why she chose you, and prove to yourself that she was right to.”

Phainon considered that thoughtfully. He didn’t tell Anaxa that Aglaea had rejected him as their Deliverer, that his concerns stemmed from Mydei refusing to let Phainon throw the mantle away. But the advice was still sound regardless, and Phainon did want to be worthy of the title for Mydei’s sake. It was the Kremnoan that was throwing the challenge to encourage Phainon to be the best possible version of himself, and who was Phainon to deny Mydei?

“Thank you, Prof. I’ll keep that in mind.”

“See that you do.” Anaxa didn’t wait around for Phainon to keep asking questions. The professor already seemed annoyed at the one so Phainon didn’t try to stop him when the man walked away to leave the ship.

Choosing the title himself… Phainon had a hard time with stuff like that. It wasn’t something he ever really considered and something as grand as the “Deliverer”? He was just Phainon, the son of a farmer, turned warrior by circumstance. A fancy title didn’t magically make him amazing, but it didn’t take away from who he already was either. Rejecting the title, or embracing it, Phainon still wanted to defend people, to fight for them and their dreams.

“Deliverer,” Mydei called and Phainon looked up as his thoughts stalled. The captain was on the forecastle deck, looking at Phainon with his head tilted. “I thought you had already left.”

“I was about to,” Phainon shouted back, “come with me?”

Mydei shrugged and leaped over the railing, skipping the stairs to save time as he walked up to Phainon. “Food and then bath.”

“Aye aye, Captain,” Phainon teased.

Challenge accepted. He would be the Deliverer, because Mydei believed in him and that was enough.

-

Chryseus Leo’s sendoff was no grander than any other departure. They left early with the tide, pointed the bow North, and made great time with a favorable wind. Free time was spent preparing, polishing shields, sharpening swords, and quiet moments of meditation. But even though the crew went through the motions of a stereotypical journey the air was charged with anticipation.

Mydei could feel it on every single one of his men. It practically dripped like condensation from the sails and clung to every word in every exchange as they crossed into the Tide line. The days still turned and stars still glittered at night, but at all hours the ocean was black as the shadow in the hearts of evil men. A lesser crew may have turned and run, abandoning any notion of success, but Mydei’s pride was in the resolve of every single crewmate, not one of which decided to stay behind.

This crew had not set out on a more personal endeavor since they sailed for Castrum Kremnos nearly six years prior to kill Eurypon. Homecomings were not supposed to be met with steel and blood but what other choice could there be for Kremnoans? It was poetic in a twisted way.

Mydei watched the men work from where he was sitting on the railing. The Black Tide kept reaching for him in splashes, but it fell short every time. Some of these men would not survive this fight, he knew that. That held true every time they donned their armor and leapt into battle with eager roars and what better way to say goodbye than embracing what they loved, what they genuinely believed in?

He wasn’t so sure. Krateros saw this campaign as the first step towards a renewed Kremnoan Dynasty, that they were following their King into battle to reclaim their homeland so that the Kremnoan people could return in glory and begin anew in the ways of Strife. Exactly what Mydei didn’t want.

“You look like you swallowed a bug.”

Mydei huffed and slowly turned towards Hephaestion.

“The protein is good for you,” the first mate added, “…Mydei, you don’t have to worry about us.”

“I never have.”

“Not out loud.”

Mydei grunted.

“…we wanted this too,” Hephaestion reassured him.

The prince turned his head back to look over the ship again, not ignoring his first mate, but not exactly eager to discuss it either.

Undaunted, Hephaestion leaned against the railing, hanging on the shrouds with one hand. “It is not lost on the crew how important this campaign is. For many of them it is returning home and to fight what may be the hardest and glorious fight of our entire lives.”

“We will not be able to purge the Tide from the city,” Mydei cautioned, “routing the enemy is not the goal of this campaign.”

“Mydeimos, we know.”

“This is not a permanent return.”

“Not this time.”

“Not ever,” Mydei growled and Hephaestion let go of the shroud so his arm could fall to his side.

“You still won’t pick up the crown.”

Mydei looked down. “Does that bother you?”

Disappointment was all over Hephaestion’s face and his heart burned to feel like he was letting his people down, but long hair waved back and forth across his shoulders as Hephaestion shook his head. His features softened and he smiled to say, “Maybe a little. It was always our hope that you’d lead us back someday as King, but we trust you, Mydeimos, and still follow you even unto death with or without your crown.”

“It is a comfort to hear you say that, my friend.”

“I would continue to tell Krateros that you are still deciding though,” he joked.

Mydei didn’t laugh.

“Have you given anymore thought to how you will propose to Phainon?” Hephaestion asked instead.

Mydei lost his balance and fell off the ship. He caught the railing with one hand as he fell and scrambled his way back on board to flop on the deck with Hephaestion’s help.

“Titan’s, Mydei, I was kidding!” Hephaestion laughed.

Mydei punched his shin and the first mate dropped to the deck beside him, still chuckling but now within strangling reach. Just before Mydei could get his hand around Hephaestion’s neck, the first mate wrapped his arm around Mydei’s and the two of them rolled, wrestling all the way across the top deck to slam into the side of the tiller to get yelled at by the helmsman. Mydei growled low in his throat when he finally got Hephaestion in a chokehold.

“Alright, alright, bad joke!” Hephaestion wheezed. He frantically tapped Mydei’s arm until he was released to chuckle through his coughing.

They sat on the deck just enjoying each other’s company for long moment while Hephaestion ran his fingers through his hair to try and fix it after the brawl.

“Don’t die, Hephaestion,” Mydei ordered in a soft voice that completely caught the man off guard.

Hephaestion snickered a little, “I don’t think you have a say in that, Mydeimos.”

“I am your Prince and Captain; you have to do as I say.”

“Don’t be a child, Mydei. It would be an incredible honor to die fighting for Castrum Kremnos.”

“You self-exiled,” Mydei reminded him.

“And you never lived there,” Hephaestion turned it around, “the heart still longs for our homeland.”

“Reminiscing about the past doesn’t change anything,” Mydei grumbled, but Hephaestion was right on all accounts, especially that it was disrespectful to worry. He trusted his men as his family. There were no stronger fighters in Amphoreus than those that belonged to this crew.

“If I should die,” Hephaestion told him, “do not mourn.”

“All weakness, grief, and grudges will be settled on the battlefield,” Mydei agreed.

“And promise me you will make Phainon your first mate.”

“If he accepts the invitation to join the crew,” he promised.

“Oh, Mydei,” Hephaestion laughed, “he will. The moment he has that pardon in his hand, ask him, and he will say yes.”

“And you will be there to see it.”

Before Hephaestion could snap at Mydei for his stubbornness, a low rumble across the water brought them back to standing. It was still Action Hour but had been overcast since they crossed into Black Tide waters, softening the light with gray clouds. But the way ahead was darker, navy blue and black like the sky was bruised and the distant thunder rolled without rain or lightning.

“The Lance of Fury,” Hephaestion mumbled in airy awe.

Mydei’s eyes narrowed as he scanned the horizon. The wind was changing, the sails fluttered and popped as the canvas was teased and there in the black was a glimmer of gold light.

“We will be there by the next Entry Hour,” Mydei observed, “gather the others for the war council.”

Hephaestion took a long second to obey, too focused on that same distant point. Most of the crew felt the ripple of Nikador’s call to arms and were getting antsy. It was unlikely anyone would be able to sleep tonight.

Mydei slapped his arm to get him moving and then followed him down the stairs where they went separate directions. In anticipation of everyone meeting, Mydei wanted to be mentally prepared. Krateros had already helped him determine a strategy over the course of the past several days, so the maps were already spread across the table in his room.

Fig Stew was waiting there, grooming himself on the map when Mydei entered the room and walked over to offer the chimera scratches.

“Now that I am here,” Mydei confided in the animal, “I worry I may have been too ambitious.”

Fig Stew cooed at him and stopped his grooming to lean into Mydei’s hand, accepting the scratches to his face, his back, and finally his sensitive belly.

“Perhaps I should I have done the normal thing and started my courting by gifting him a shield or perhaps flowers as Okhemans do,” he sighed.

It was more than that of course. What may have started as fetching a gift for Phainon meant much, much more now. This wasn’t just about Mydei’s personal future, it was also a resolution for the older crew, finishing what they started when they were last here. It was a military step towards safety for their island under siege. A chance to lay to rest their broken Titan in a manner befitting Strife. And it was those and a hundred other reasons that made this campaign important enough to weigh like the world and be worth the blood they would undoubtedly pay.

The door opened and the first of Mydei’s friends entered. They offered him warm smiles and firm nods as everyone picked their favorite chairs and squabbled over the less squeaky stools. The Chrysos Heirs arrived together. The girls were giggling about something under their breath while Phainon protested in flustered whispers.

He was cute when he was flustered. The pink in his cheeks and ears was just a shade darker than rosy and the way Phainon danced in place made Mydei want to pounce on him, hold him down and feel the heat of Phainon’s face with his lips. Krateros closing the door behind him snapped Mydei from the early stages of an inappropriate longing.

The captain’s quarters were not small, but it was struggling a bit with this capacity. All five of his Kremnoan unit leaders (and best friends), all four Chrysos Heirs, Krateros, and of course himself and Fig Stew.

“Krateros,” Mydei invited and the quiet chattering in the room stopped.

The old man stepped up to the table. Anaxa hung back, so did Peucesta for now, but the others crowded around the map. Displayed on the table was a detailed layout of Castrum Kremnos. The map on top was of the outer city, the map below was the inner city, but Mydei didn’t need to review the latter, as he would be personally escorting the small group that was delving that deep into the city.

“Krateros and I have discussed the best strategy for this campaign,” Mydei announced, “as a reminder, the purpose of this mission is to slay Nikador and retrieve the Coreflame of Strife. The city is too vast and too populated to rout with a small crew and the Black Tide’s constant presence, but the fall of the Titan should weaken the Tide’s hold in this corner of the world all the same.” Mydei opened a couple of shallow drawers to fetch a few generic figurines that he placed on the table. “To this end, we have decided that it is best if only Chrysos Heirs breach the inner city, while the crew remains behind to hold the bay. Phainon, Castorice, and I will take the first opportunity to sneak into the city while the crew holds the attention of the Tide’s forces and the corrupted Titankin.”

“Lord Mydei,” Hyacine called softly, “do you not want me to accompany you?”

“No. I have faith in Professor Anaxagoras’ creation protecting my men, but we cannot be sure of our timeline nor ignore the risk that they may be parted with that protection,” Mydei explained, “I would rather you stay with Peucesta’s unit to administer aid as needed.”

“Not Perdikkas?”

“I lead my own unit in combat,” Perdikkas explained, “we do not have dedicated medical personnel on simple campaigns like this.”

“What do you do if someone gets hurt?” she asked.

“Everyone is trained in basic field medicine,” Hephaestion explained, “a friend binds the wound so the man can continue fighting.”

“We do not fear death by the sword or spear, Miss Hyacine,” Leonnius explained, “we fear the shameful death of succumbing to wounds or illness.”

Phainon put a hand on her shoulder to stop her protests. The two heirs looked at each other in silence, Phainon reassuring, Hyacine questioning, until she relented and nodded her understanding. “I will do my very best to ensure that you are all able to keep fighting then.”

“If any man is parted from his talisman, then they are to be rushed to Miss Hyacine,” Krateros ordered and was met with a wave of mumbled agreement.

“Miss Castorice,” Mydei said next, and she stepped forward, happily squeezing between Phainon and Hyacine so she could see the map. “Phainon and I will have no trouble safely navigating the inner city on our own, but I worry about our escape. I have been told that you are an army unto yourself.”

“I will hold the line, Lord Mydei,” she promised, “wherever you tell me to draw it.”

He nodded and then gestured to Krateros.

The old man leaned forward and gathered several of the figurines to set them in places across the map. “We will be assuming a formation for defense, not an assault,” he instructed, “with the Chryseus Leo as our designated target to defend at all costs.” The veteran pointed to a few roads on the map, addressing the Kremnoans. “If you recall, when we last led an assault on this city we left behind barricades in these three places to manage our escape. It is possible that those barriers were removed but if they remain it would be in our best interest to reinforce them and if they are not, then they need to be replaced using the surrounding structures here and here.

“Hephaestion and Leonnius will take the West roads, Ptolemy and Perdikkas, the East. That leaves my unit and Peucesta to manage the North and command.”

Krateros used his hand and the pieces to clearly indicate the areas that each unit would be responsible for keeping. Both the West and East zones contained four roads each with instructions to limit that access to two chokepoints at most and, if it was safe and reasonable to do so, narrow that down to one. The largest road to the shipyards and bay was from the North. There was no hope of blocking that route, which was why the bulk of their forces would be stationed there under Krateros.

Their primary goal was the protection of the ship; their secondary goal was to make noise to attract the Tide. The distraction would clear the way for Mydei and Phainon. If Castorice’s prowess as a Demigod of Death was not understated, then the forces they had to worry about would only be a problem at the start when they were on fresh legs and arms. By the time the crew would start to feel fatigued, Castorice would begin fighting from deeper within the city, creating a war for the Tide on two fronts.

“Changes in plans will be communicated to both fronts through Peucesta’s horn,” Krateros reminded them, “if your side needs reinforcements, communicate in kind. Leonnius, will you choose runners for all three groups?”

“I already have three in mind.”

“You are drawing the line far enough into the city to allow room to fallback, so take advantage if you need to,” Mydei reminded them, emphasizing the line that Krateros had already marked, “when we return with the coreflame, Peucesta will sound the retreat. Emphasize to your men the importance of heeding that call, the Leo cannot wait for those that may fall behind whether it be to death or bloodlust. Krateros, if something changes and the hour grows late, retreat without us and move the Leo away from the dock to rest and care for the charms.”

“As you command, Prince Mydeimos. Valorous death before glorious return,” Krateros said firmly to the table.

The Kremnoans nodded their agreement, caught up in the excitement of the moment.

“May victory be yours, Mydeimos,” Hephaestion added with a closed fist over his heart in salute. The others did the same, repeating the words and bowing their heads ever so slightly in respect. Even Phainon held his hand over his heart, smiling at Mydei in such a way as to fill him with courage.

Mydei resisted the urge to correct them. It was right to wish victory towards their commander as a representation of all of them. In honoring him, they were wishing for success for the mission as a whole, so he accepted the gesture with grace, returning their salute, but he did not repeat Krateros’ words as he was expected to.

Instead, he muttered an order, “Get some rest.”

chapters.title: Chapter 27: The Assault on Castrum Kremnos
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

No new tags, but I did have to push the chapter count back again... Forgive me for my inability to self-assess my yapping. @.@

Everyone says goodbye and the operation begins!

Chapter Notes

Edit: If this chapter reads funny it's cause it was funny to write and rereading it I was like... why does this feel off? And then I posted it and was organizing my notes and it explicitly says "Phainon's POV through CK" so, uh, oops? I'll leave it up for now but uh, I might spend tomorrow rewriting the last half and sneaky replacing it with Phainon's internal dialogue instead cause I feel like that will fix the funny feeling in my head. If you read it NOW, the plot and dialogue won't change, the story is still the same, you just get the little bonus of Mydei's POV for now and there's no need to revisit after I fix it unless you really want to.

Edit 2: I FIXED IT. IT WAS A FAST FIX. Goodness that feels so much better.

No one slept. How could they when the Chryseus Leo was anchored within spitting distance of Castrum Kremnos, listening to the rolling thunder of Strife who waited in the city for them? Phainon had laid in his hammock listening to Mydei’s breathing, knowing that he was also awake and contemplating the day in their silence. Part of him wanted to spring out of bed with his excitement and encourage the crew to leave early! If no one was sleeping then what were they waiting for?

But still he lay until the Entry Hour and that feeling of beginning that dawn so frequently carried in its wake. All the good poems and stories spoke of noble deeds beginning at dawn, and what else could this be but a noble, heroic pursuit?

So, they waited in the dark quiet until neither of them could bear it any longer and even then the silence followed them to breakfast where the crew drifted in and out like ghosts. They were quiet as they walked back to the room, and it was quiet while they got dressed in their most iconic signature looks.

“Mydei,” Phainon softly said, testing that first break of their comfortable silence Mydei grunted.

“Don’t forget when we get the coreflame,” he paused, lingering for dramatic effect, “you have to tell me which pirate stole your heart.” Phainon flashed him a cheeky smile and the consequential blush in Mydei’s cheeks was worth the ice breaker.

“HKS,” the man huffed but he chased it with a sigh to say, “I will. Deliverer, will you be alright?”

“Of course, Mydei.” Phainon flinched just a hair when Mydei grabbed his wrist.

“Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, are you sure?” he asked again with burning in his eyes and a steeliness to the way he clenched his jaw.

It would be an easy thing to play and tease but Phainon and Mydei knew each other better than that by now. Mydei would see through the deflection, keep his quiet, but close himself off to be upset at the dishonesty. Even if Phainon did it to reassure, it was still hiding, and he didn’t want to hide from Mydei at this critical juncture.

“No,” Phainon said instead, his own anxiety laid bare for Mydei’s inspection, “but I have been working with Peucesta and the song no longer calls to mind those horrible visions and Perdikkas has taught me more techniques alongside the ones I learned from Aglaea.” He twisted his wrist in Mydei’s grip so he could hold the prince’s hand. “Most of all, I have you, and you give me courage.”

Mydei broke eye contact and pulled away. “Don’t be so sentimental, Deliverer. There will be enough of that today without your honeyed words.”

“Of course, Captain.”

“Finish getting dressed,” Mydei ordered, “I’ll meet you on the top deck when you have finished preparing.”

“Of course, Captain,” Phainon repeated with the same playful, reassuring lilt in his voice.

Mydei gave him another once over, punched Phainon lightly in the shoulder, and then excused himself.

Alone, Phainon let his smile fall to gather himself under the weight of emotion. He really wasn’t afraid. Even with those lingering flashbacks that haunted him at the worst times, he wasn’t worried. Thinking of Mydeimos was enough to stave off all his fears, leaving behind excitement, the thrill of the battle lurking under his skin. Today, they would end the war between their nations with the death of a Titan. Today, they removed Strife from the world and pushed back the Tide from this corner of the ocean, saving the last of the Kremnoan people from the same fate as Aedes Elysiae.

The chill that ran up and down Phainon’s spine jumpstarted his movements and he ceased his delay, getting dressed carefully but with confidence. Then he left to find Mydeimos.

Phainon found Mydei on the top deck as promised but he wasn’t alone. He was meeting with his unit leaders, the five friends that had welcomed Phainon into their family on the crew. They stood beside and around their Crown Prince, each taking turns meeting with him. Phainon hung back, waiting on the stairs to not intrude.

One at a time they exchanged quiet words with Mydei, grasped forearms and touched foreheads in intimate Kremnoan farewell. For each one of them, the captain held them close with his free hand around the back of their necks, resting firmly to decide himself how long each embrace should last as they silently conferred blessings without words.

When the last man, Hephaestion, pulled away, Perdikkas called softly to Phainon.

He jumped and hesitantly approached the group. “I did not intend to intrude,” he apologized.

“Intrude?” Perdikkas questioned.

“If anything, you are late,” Hephaestion told him. The first mate extended his hand to Phainon.

It took him a second to realize what Hephaestion was doing and then he held both hands up, palms out to say, “Oh, no I really couldn’t, this is sacred to Kremnoans…”

Hephaestion’s hand lashed out to grab Phainon’s raised arm, clasping him tightly below the elbow before stepping forward into his space. His other hand hooked around the back of Phainon’s neck, and he pulled the man forward until their foreheads bashed together. Phainon stared at Hephaestion’s closed eyes, feeling a little awkward at the closeness.

“I know, Phainon,” the first mate whispered, “and you have more than earned it.”

He held on until Phainon gripped him back and closed his eyes, basking in the moment of shared respect, the well wishes for the battle ahead, the understanding that this could be the last time they see each other alive, and that was okay.

“May victory always be yours, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, my brother,” the first mate said firmly, leaving Phainon at a loss for words.

Hephaestion let him go and Perdikkas took his place, holding Phainon’s arm and leaning forward to press his forehead to Phainon’s.

“Take care of him,” the doctor whispered, “and yourself. You both are precious to us.”

Humbled, Phainon squeezed Perdikkas’ arm and said, “I will.”

Leonnius was next with a playful, “When we win, you’ll show us Okhema proper, yeah?”

Phainon laughed and their foreheads bumped together. Neither of them closed their eyes like they were supposed to, too mischievous for that. “I promise, Leonnius.”

The runner pulled away but took a second to wrap his arm around Phainon’s neck to pull the man down for a solid hair ruffle, neatly undoing all of Phainon’s hard work trying to comb it this morning! Phainon still laughed and shoved the man playfully away.

“I told you once that ‘a friend with an understanding heart is worth no less than a brother,’” Ptolemy told Phainon as he stepped up and took the man’s arm. They leaned in and touched foreheads, and Ptolemy squeezed a little harder. “I meant every word then. I mean it even more now.”

“I have no words to express how honored I am, Ptolemy,” Phainon told him.

“Then show me with actions, as you have been, Deliverer.” Ptolemy smiled at him when they pulled away and stepped aside with one last pat to Phainon’s back.

Peucesta twanged three notes, the first three of the Tide song, before he tucked the lyre under his arm and offered his hand to Phainon, inviting rather than grabbing as the others had. Phainon didn’t hesitate to reach for it and even moved to hold Peucesta’s neck as Hephaestion had to him, holding them close for a second before he let his hand fall between them.

“Give me something more to sing of, Phainon,” Peucesta said in his soft whisper, “let me sing of the heroes that brought Nikador low.”

“For no other reason, than to give you your epic,” Phainon promised, and then the bard stepped back to join the others, leaving Phainon feeling full. These were goodbyes, he should feel sorrow, knowing this was a Kremnoan parting, a salute with the expectation of death, but instead Phainon felt sustained, like he was no longer a lone hero but a part of something bigger. They had willingly offered up a part of themselves and graciously accepted a part of him, a reminder that he would not be fighting this battle alone, even if they should fall, he carried them in every swing of his sword.

Phainon looked for Mydei next, half-expecting the captain to want to exchange the gesture as well, but he was set apart, standing several paces away to say goodbye to Krateros in the same manner.

“Well, duty calls,” Leonnius said to the small group.

“And we will answer,” Hephaestion added before herding his companions away, leaving Phainon to wait.

Krateros and Mydei whispered for a couple minutes and then the old man bowed and hurried to tend to his last-minute duties, giving Phainon a window to approach. When Mydei turned back to him, Phainon already had his hand extended.

Mydei looked at it, then up at Phainon’s face, then back to his hand. He slapped it away.

“M-Mydei!” Phainon felt genuinely hurt.

“HKS, what did I say about sentimentality? That is a farewell,” Mydei scolded, “and you will be fine and by my side the entire time.”

He walked to the railing and Phainon followed, the both of them studying the giant blade over the city. The sky was dark with rolling black clouds but the light from Nikador’s sword made the city feel as day.

“Phainon, when I called you Deliverer,” Mydei started but Phainon put his hand on Mydei’s shoulder to stop him.

“I know.”

“…do you?” Mydei prodded, “Do you presume to know what I wanted to say?”

“That you call me Deliverer, because you believe in me, not as an omnipotent savior but as an ally in battle that you can trust to do right by you and your people?”

Mydei’s eyes widened by a fraction, eyebrows raised, and his jaw dropped just enough to part his lips. He scowled to hide his surprise and turned away from Phainon entirely with his arms crossed. “A lucky guess.”

Phainon chuckled and put his arm around Mydei’s shoulders to pull him back around. “Or maybe I just know you better than you think I do.”

Mydei’s demeanor softened. This close Phainon could smell the sweet scents that Mydei liked to comb into his hair and add to the washbasin before wiping himself clean of the day, could feel the way Mydei leaned into him, the way Mydei’s eyelids drooped even though he was still trying to pretend to be mad. Mydei’s foot bumped into Phainon’s as he stepped in closer to keep his balance and it took genuine strength to not kiss Mydei right there.

The feeling caught Phainon by surprise and he let go to lean on the railing instead. His imagination thought Mydei seemed disappointed but that couldn’t be, not when Mydei was already in love with someone. It had to be Hephaestion, maybe Perdikkas? Phainon tucked those thoughts away when the curiosity was outweighed by the churning sickness in his stomach and he realized that imagining Mydei with someone didn’t make him as happy as he thought he would be. He cared about Mydei, they were best friends, it felt wrong not being happy for him.

“My Prince,” Krateros called. They both turned around enough to look over their shoulders at the veteran. “It’s time.”

Mydei nodded and pushed away from the side of the ship to walk to the top of the stairs to stand beside Fig Stew who was perched, waiting on the railing. The whole crew was on deck, armed to the teeth with shining steel and bronze. Even the Chrysos Heirs stood near the back, Anaxa reunited with his firearm, Hyacine holding her staff. Phainon stood just behind Mydei, not wanting to be in the way, feeling out of place standing beside Krateros as though he were someone of importance.

“Sons and Daughters of Strife!” Mydei called them and Phainon’s heart swelled when he realized that included himself and his friends. “Words have already been said of the importance of this campaign and the weight of that which we now shoulder, not only for our own glory but for that of all Kremnoans, Okhemans, and Chrysos Heirs. What we do here, what we accomplish today, will set in motion the course of the future for all of Amphoreus, a brighter future free of the threat of the Black Tide.” Mydei bowed his head for a moment and reached one hand out to rest on Fig Stew’s head. He pet the chimera reverently before lifting his gaze again with fire in his eyes and roaring in his growl. “I know I need not ask of you to give your all in the coming conflict, so instead I swear on my own golden blood that I will give a thousand of my own lives to celebrate this triumph beside you all. Fight for that future, and when fate’s inescapable grasp comes for you, resist it with the strength of your mighty will that we may raise our glasses over the Coreflame of Strife and toast this most valorous victory!”

Fig Stew roared his tiny roar and the crew followed suit, cheering with renewed vigor and an eagerness that carried in their chant, “The son of Gorgo will be crowned in blood!”

Mydei let them cheer for him three times before he raised his hand to silence them and then he nodded at Krateros who took command, shouting in Kremnoan, “To oars! To lines! Raise anchor!”

The crew hurried to get the ship moving, to close the final gap between the open ocean and the dock. Phainon stepped up beside Fig Stew and Mydei with a pat on the chimera’s butt. He tried to sneak a scratch at the animal’s belly, one last try for luck but the low growl stopped that idea in its tracks and Phainon turned to Mydei instead.

“And they say I’m a wordsmith,” Phainon teased.

“Deliverer,” Mydei said very seriously, “do you have my back?”

“Always, Mydeimos.”

- It wasn’t lost on Phainon as they raced through the back streets of Castrum Kremnos that this was a dream come true in the weirdest possible way. He had longed to visit the city of warriors his whole life, but he had imagined bright skies and a brighter people, the full glory of the Kremnoans he had come to love on display under crimson banners and guarded by the glittering bronze, blue, and white of the fabled Titankin.

But this… this was the wrong kind of life. Crumpled stone and long shadows of near eternal night painted the backdrop for the twisted orange glow of the black Tide. The only other light was from the Blade of Fury that glinted from the bronze fixtures above doorways and capping columns. Grass and vines desperately tried to grow from tears in the stone beneath their feet, choking on the smooth Black Tide that whispered its sweet song with every step.

Phainon could hear the whispers under the distant sounds of battle that they left behind as he and Castorice followed Mydei into the depths of dilapidation. Every monster they came across crumpled in seconds as they raced, too focused to even keep score, too worried about removing another monster that would otherwise be racing to the noise to slam into the barricades to attack their friends.
