The moment they had made berth, the three had left the others behind, war horns and the cacophony of battle the only hint they had that everyone was okay, embracing the battle, and fighting to their hearts content. And there was plenty to fight. Phainon could feel the vibrations of rumbling footsteps on the main road not far from where they were running.

They didn’t slow down until the Black Tide thinned and a massive wall rose in front of them and then Mydei switched to a brisk walk. This far from the fighting and the noise, Phainon could hear the song louder in the back of his mind, threatening to pull him back to darker days but every step made it easier to ignore, not only because he had Mydei’s back to watch, but because of the city he wanted to see.

This path that they had run had taken them through courtyards, around dry fountains, under massive arches, and glorious atriums. Everything was built to last with thick columns and dense walls that could endure the mightiest armies and navies. Only the Black Tide could’ve felled this mighty city, no work of man could’ve brought her low. Even as they trampled through the fog, making the Tide curl and churn around their boots, Phainon wondered how such a mighty dynasty could have fallen.

“Lord Mydei,” Castorice spoke softly, lest they be discovered once more. “Is this where you lived?”

“I was not raised in Castrum Kremnos,” he told her, “If I had, I would have lived in the inner city.”

“Are you sure you know where we’re going?” Phainon asked.

“Five years ago, this is the path I took to meet my father. I will not soon forget the way.”

Phainon could hear the pain in Mydei’s voice. It was subtle but there. Even though he wasn’t raised here, Mydei still respected and loved his culture and heritage. This city was still a part of him and the last time he was here it was still vibrant and alive. He couldn’t imagine that pain, couldn’t imagine what it would be like to see Aedes Elysiae again after all this time.

“Be wary as we near the acropolis,” Mydei cautioned, “we will also have to contend with Nikador’s Titankin.”

“Have they also turned?” Phainon asked.

“No, but they will have still succumbed to depravity like their Titan. Smashing them to pieces would be the greatest mercy.”

Phainon almost slammed into Mydei’s back when the man came to a sudden stop. Was their path taking them over rooftops? Or perhaps much of the city was built underground, either way the way was lost, one of the footbridges collapsed, hanging limply on the far side of a sizeable drop and within eyeshot of a distant, massive gate.

“I had higher hopes for the master masons of Castrum Kremnos,” Phainon teased as he stepped up beside his friend. “Seems even Kremnoan craftsmanship can be unreliable sometimes.”

“The outer city was built by convicts,” Mydei explained.

“Maybe they were taking their grievances out on you.”

“Doesn’t matter. There’s no shame in resistance here.”

“Is there a way around?” Castorice asked.

“Undoubtedly,” Mydei confirmed, “but it may take time to find a safe route, and I am unfamiliar with the surrounding streets.”

“We could split up,” Phainon thought aloud, but it would be hard to find each other again to communicate a discovery.

Castorice shuffled and then quietly offered, “I will ask Pollux for help. It is nearly time for them to join the fight anyway.”

“Pollux?” Mydei started to ask but Phainon was already grabbing his arm and pulling him out of the way. Phainon had met Pollux twice before and learned both times the importance of distance.

The air around Castorice grew heavy and dark, wind spiraled around her, chasing away the mist of the Tide like fog against the rising sun. She gathered herself and stretched her hand into the empty space before her; petals condensed in the air and gathered rapidly at the Demigod’s command forming a scythe in a flash of light. The elegant curve sliced the air as she spun, tearing into space itself.

“So, this is the might of the Demigod of Death,” Mydei mumbled beside him. Phainon’s hand pulled at his chiton again, pulling him further down the road to make space as massive claws reached from within the void to pry the gash open into a gaping wound. The dragon burst free in a shower of butterflies and flower petals that somehow worked with Pollux’s natural grace. Castorice had told Phainon once that the petals were from the land of the dead, that there grew the most beautiful blue flowers that the dragon slept beside.

It was quiet like its counterpart, Castorice, with scales the same purple hues ranging from the sky at night to the lavender of fresh flowers and a surprisingly soft appearance bordering on cute. Castorice patted the beast’s nose and whispered to it softly while Mydei and Phainon returned to her side.

“To think you command such a creature…” Mydei praised.

“I do not command Pollux,” she corrected gently, “they are my companion in death, the other half of the Coreflame in my chest, and the keeper of the Netherealm in my absence.”

The dragon rumbled, content to be called upon. Castorice very rarely called upon Pollux, it was hard for it to keep form away from the Netherealm and it frequently had to retreat to rest so they were only for emergencies, or the occasional treat. Phainon knew that nose could happily pierce the veil for nuzzles and cookies whenever Pollux wanted them.

Its wings fluttered in the breeze when it craned that mighty head over the trio to see the bridge that had collapsed under the passage of time.

“Can Pollux not fly us all the way to Nikador?” Phainon asked.

“I do not think Pollux would mind,” Castorice offered but Mydei shook his head.

“Nikador’s lance is especially deadly when thrown. Any approach from the sky is doomed to fail.”

Phainon frowned to himself as he remembered stories of Nikador’s thrown spears. They were said to appear like rain, thrown from such a distance and with such accuracy that many that fell beneath those golden blades never knew that Nikador approached. But then why didn’t…

Pollux shifted and Phainon was pulled from his thoughts. One massive leathery wing laid flat across the gap, creating a means for them to cross and both he and Mydei were able to reach the far side safely.

Castorice was the last, but she paused before taking a step. The sounds of screeching were getting louder, the drag of flesh on stone no longer a distant murmur. Pollux twisted its head to track the sounds with curiosity and the low rumble of a warning growl.

“Lord Mydei, is this far enough?” she asked.

Phainon looked to the Kremnoan. He wasn’t sure what lay beyond, how much farther they had to go. The sounds of angry screams, metallic and ugly, doubled in number and volume as the first of many monsters ripped down the hallway and into Pollux’s fire.

“Yes,” he confirmed as the heat of those flames blasted past them.

“Then I will make my stand and cover your advance,” she promised.

“Castorice!” Phainon called across the gap, “please be safe!”

“And you, Lord Phainon.”

Mydei grabbed Phainon’s sleeve and pulled him along and together they raced to the broken gate, the sounds of combat fading behind them as they ran. It was there that Phainon slowed to a reverent stop and Mydei let go of him to stumble a few paces ahead along the platform.

High above the city, no longer blocked by tall walls here beside a cliff, was the Blade of Fury, pointing straight down at the arena ahead and oh did it take Phainon’s breath away. The weapon that felled a hundred nations, no longer descriptive words on a page.

“I always wanted to see it,” he mumbled.

“Even if the world lay shattered, it would still hang high above everyone’s heads,” Mydei agreed.

“It’s magnificent.”

“You haven’t seen it at its most magnificent. It’s not just a weapon, it’s the faith of the Kremnoan people and where heroic souls that died on the battlefield go to temper the blade, becoming a part of the god-king’s power. Even in death, they embrace eternal glory.”

Phainon’s thoughts drifted to the detachment. He couldn’t hear them from here, just the soft melody of the Tide and an unsettling thought.

“Mydei, I have been thinking,” Phainon said quietly.

“Don’t hurt yourself.”

Phainon punched him in the arm. “Are you sure that Nikador is here?”

“I am. When we killed the old king, Nikador was here in Castrum Kremnos, standing at the ready beneath Kremnos Arena. We had no reason to confront them, and they had no reason to pursue. The Titan has not been seen in five years. There is nowhere else that they could be.”

That didn’t seem right… but he followed Mydei to the Janus Passage without saying another word and they crossed the first canyon to push deeper into the city, slaying Titankin as they went with disappointing ease. Every time Phainon closed the gap to cleave a monster that unsettled feeling got worse. Every pile of dust that made his heart want to shout victory only twisted in his gut.

A hulking Titankin stood up ahead, shifting its weight as though on guard and even though it looked right at them, the monster made no move to defend itself. So, he missed. Phainon pulled his strike to the left, far enough to drop from above all the way to the stone in a shower of sparks.

Mydei’s footsteps quickened behind him and Phainon hurriedly stretched out his arm to stop him, relieved when the prince skidded to a stop with Phainon’s arm across his chest. Together they studied the creature, waiting side by side for …nothing.

“Mydei, none of these Titankin have put up a fight,” Phainon said seriously.

“Of course they wouldn’t, we have been killing them too quickly.”

“No, I think they won’t.” The sword vanished into blue light, still the kin did not attack. “Something isn’t right.”

“What are you thinking, Deliverer?” Mydei’s frown was audible.

“I’m thinking that there are no Black Tide creatures in the inner city, and the Titankin have made no effort to stop us or attack. The stories of Nikador tell of a Titan with the strength to level city-states in a single blow, that the Blade of Fury was great enough to strike even Aquila from the sky. You said yourself that the lance of Nikador is deadly when thrown, so why did they not strike the Chryseus Leo while we slept at anchor? Were we not within reach of his mighty blows?” Phainon paused to shift uncomfortably under the weight of his new theory. “If the Tide had claimed such a powerful minion, why has it not used it to further its ambitions? Why has Nikador stayed here all this time?”

“Eurypon was corrupted by the Black Tide,” Mydei insisted, “this we know to be true. He brought this corruption home and passed it on to an already crumbling Strife itself.”

“Professor Anaxa said that becoming a Demigod stopped the corruption inside him at the Grove, that it even healed what he had already taken in. Mydei, was Eurypon a Chrysos Heir?”

“Yes,” Mydei said softly with the weight of someone wrapped in uncomfortable nostalgia.

Phainon took a shuddering breath and started walking, advancing forward as they talked, no longer bothering to kill the Titankin that waited unmoving, covered in the dust of neglect beside extinguished forges.

“Eurypon was exposed to the Tide for years, like Professor Anaxa was, but without a coreflame,” Phainon thought aloud.

“Perhaps he reasoned that claiming the Coreflame of Strife would heal him and give him the strength to continue his bloody campaign,” Mydei added.

“So, he lured, or trapped, or somehow brought Nikador here and started his famous experiments.”

“While the Empire crumpled to ruin around him from the infighting.”

“Mydei…” Phainon said as another thought occurred to him, “What if Nikador hasn’t been corrupted by the Black Tide?”

“Our mission has not changed,” Mydei reassured him, “Even if Nikador is not corrupted by the Tide, they are still a mad god in the wake of Eurypon’s tampering. Even before the old King brought his violence against his own Titan, Nikador craved bloodshed with equal fervor to Eurypon. Now, with their divine body hollowed by the hands of madness and their dignity as a warrior forsaken… there is no place in a peaceful world for a Titan of Strife that has abandoned their reason.”

“It’s sad really,” Phainon mourned aloud as he paused before a mural. Kremnos was not known for its artists, but Nikador was lovingly depicted in tile leading troops in a story told in pictures, their glittering spear catching the light in artistically embellished rays. He reached out to touch it, to feel the grit of age and wear under his fingertips, trying to see this exact picture in unfaded colors, feel the message behind the artisans longing for triumph. “I wish I could have seen this place before Eurypon, when it still had its glory.”

Mydei stopped behind Phainon. He could hear the softness of his breath that kept Phainon grounded in the present, bleak and broken as it was. What would it have been like to have been here? To have been raised alongside the other Kremnoans? Would he too have left at the rumors of their beloved prince, alive and waiting to be found?

“To survive, my people have migrated, and our traditions have faded. But glory? Even crumbling beneath the mist of the Tide, Castrum Kremnos has never forsaken the glory of its warriors.”

The ground beneath them shook, the tiniest tremor, the barest reminder of those very same warriors fighting towards an end. They were relying on Mydei and Phainon.

“Deliverer,” Mydei started.

“I know.” And then they were running again.

Phainon followed Mydei down narrow hallways and chambers, out into the open air once more, and across giant chains, spanning the chasm that separated the Kremnos Arena from the city. The Blade of Fury was close enough now to charge the air with the smell of ozone and storms, of iron and blood, and a brutal desire for violence. The feeling permeated Phainon’s skin, making him feel more alive than he ever had as the adrenaline rushed with electricity to every corner of his being, keeping him on the knife’s edge until a bolt of lighting pulled a gasp from his lips. Still, they ran, even when Phainon chanced a look back at the city below, searching for his friends in the dark.

He saw nothing and did not slow.

They raced past Titankin standing at eternal attention, slid past armories of untouched masterpieces and treasuries full of gold and precious stones. It wasn’t until they crossed through a cold forge that Phainon realized where they were. Mydei was taking him beneath the arena, under the Blade of Fury itself and Phainon could feel that power turning his breaths ragged as he realized how close they were to a fight he had thought about since his vow to Aglaea to join the flame-chase.

“We’re so close to the death of a Titan,” Phainon breathed when they slowed to a jog, “it feels surreal.”

“Don’t think of them as a god. It’s just you, me, and them – warriors in a fight to the death,” Mydei growled.

Phainon felt the pressure the moment they crossed the threshold, stepping from a staircase into a massive, open atrium. It was a brutal call to arms, chanted in the voice of a Titan with weight so great that the air felt oppressive. It warped and rumbled, loud like a battlefield, filling Phainon with bloodlust and a battle high that clawed at his buried rage so carefully put away and forced it to the surface with the taste of blood. It was excitement and adrenaline and hatred that overwhelmed the song of the Tide until Phainon felt like he was about to lose control.

And that scared him more than anything. More even than the Titan itself waiting in the center of the room.

Nikador was a creature of long limbs, animated bone and armor, gilded in gold and blue. They were an elegant figure clad in a flowing cape that dragged on the ground behind them as they hunched forwards to lean on a golden spear many times longer than Phainon was tall. Even as the Chrysos Heirs stepped into their territory, the Titan did not move.

Neither did Phainon. Every step was too heavy, too fearful. The next step would strip him of his will, he could tell, remove from him all that made Phainon himself, and leave behind the shell of his youth that longed for nothing else but revenge against the mist. He slowly raised a hand to his face to hold himself, pinching his eyes shut to try and block that voice in his head.

“This feeling… it smells of blood and the cries of lost souls,” Phainon struggled to say. His breath kept getting stuck in his throat and chest but to his credit, he stayed upright. This was no ordinary battle, and he could not pretend it was.

“Show me your resolve, Deliverer.”

Phainon looked up at Mydei with agony, all the fear of inadequacy of failure, rising with the terror of losing himself as he realized he was not ready for this. They had misplaced their faith.

“How can you stand there with such confidence?” he asked with a shaky voice, “can you not hear it? The voices of suffering and your corroded homeland?”

“Of course I can,” Mydei told him with a low growl, “All the anger and regret I feel right now, I have learned to control them, hone them into a razor-sharp weapon for my use. Come, Deliverer. I need you in this fight. Let us be as beasts, give in to that primal desire, the purest form of Strife and fight with intent to kill. And if you cannot do that for yourself, then do it for those that stayed behind to give us this noble opportunity.”

Phainon fought to picture the faces of their friends, remembered the way they held him on the ship and took a deep breath, then another, and finally stood straight once more as he found his resolve. Their confidence in him weighed more than his own doubts. Even if it was borrowed strength, it was enough to know that he was not alone, that he was more than his past.

“I would trust no other in this fight,” Mydei reminded him with a soft smile and Phainon let out his held breath. That wonderful, beautiful face and strong voice returned to him his wavering agency and Phainon instead embraced this gift the Titan was giving them. Let him feel it all and keep himself.

“Then let us end this, Mydeimos.”

Mydei grinned a wild grin and the excitement returned in waves. His best friend started walking towards the Titan, towards the deity of his people with confidence and command in his footsteps. And Phainon followed, watching Mydei’s back.

“Hear me, broken god!” he called as he walked towards the Titan. The figure on the platform twisted as it awoke. Phainon watched it move with suspicion. There was no fine layer of dust, no creak in its joints as though it had been at rest for years as he had anticipated.

“We are sons of Kremnos, inheritors of the Coreflame of Strife, and have come to meet you in glorious combat worthy of your name and mantle!”

The Titan unfolded, leaning forward to scream in a language that Phainon couldn’t understand, that mighty spear resting lightly in its spindly fingers. He raised his sword beside Mydei, pointing it at their foe while his blood sing with joy at this legacy that Mydei was sharing with him.

“Are you still afraid?” Mydei asked Phainon with a playful growl as he took up a battle stance, turning his back to Phainon to protect.

He smiled at that feeling of ferality rising to the surface, blue eyes glittering as the Titan roared at them again at a pitch that rattled the entire room and rippled through the Tide that pooled around their feet.

“No.”

Chapter End Notes

I originally considered letting them be competitive as they were in 3.0, fighting titankin on the way but the mood didn’t seem right. In the game they didn't go after Nikador with a crew of friends at their backs.

chapters.title: Chapter 28: The Inheritor of Strife
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

No new tags but please mind the ones that are already there!

:)

Chapter Notes

If my original outline is to be believed, this was supposed to be the beginning of chapter 9 out of 19... So wooo halfway point~!

:)

When Mydei read grand epics and studied historical conquests in his youth, battles were always embellished to make them seem desirable. He had learned through experience that there was joy in combat that his Kremnoan blood knew every violent dance and song but before Phainon, the challenge was minimal. His friends were noble and powerful, more experienced, classically trained, but there were limitations to their growth and Mydei always felt like he could be more, like something was missing.

Realizing that Phainon filled that empty space with his presence, his sword and understanding was a revelation for the ages. It was a feeling that Mydei had felt budding inside him, but it wasn’t until Castrum Kremnos that he knew for sure. Phainon was the harmony to his melody, or perhaps it was the other way around, it didn’t matter. The solo that Mydei’s heart had been singing in every conflict, every battle, every sea breeze, every journey, was meant to be a duet.

And their song was one of struggle and victory, singing over the Titan’s battle’s cries.

Nikador’s pressure, that which warped the air and twisted all intentions into a desperate need for bloody carnage was no more than a lion’s roar, formidable but conquerable. It was adrenaline and desire fueling both he and Phainon as they clashed against this mighty foe. There would be no need to embellish this tale, it was the grandest of conflicts in truth.

Mydei felt in Phainon’s presence, in every swing of his sword, an extension of himself and in turn, he felt like an extension of Phainon. They needed no call, no shout to know where the other was or how they would move. All their training together, fighting the Tide beside each other, was building an understanding that Mydei could not have fully appreciated until they were facing a true challenge and there was no greater challenge than Nikador.

To compare Nikador to an army would be a disservice to their strength. They were a hurricane blotting out the sun, a force of nature that could not be overwhelmed, only weathered. Every time that lance struck, lightning shook the atrium and rattled Mydei’s bones. Every step that clattered across the stone was the crashing of towering waves. They were fools to assume they could win against this god-king of Strife.

And Mydei had never felt so alive.

Phainon dashed in from the right and Mydei immediately followed, giving his partner room to move to swing his sword. At the last moment, Phainon feinted to the left, swiping his sword at Nikador’s ankle in a shower of sparks and giving Mydei the window to hold course. Mydei’s fist, wrapped in crystal, slammed into Nikador’s shoulder and the Titan lurched, still Mydei held on. His feet against that massive bicep, scrambled to hold for just a second more while Mydei used both hands to force his crystals to sprout from that divine shoulder.

Nikador’s swung around to face Mydei, that long horn that extended well past their head sliced through the air, but Mydei held his ground, full of faith. That horn glanced off the flat of Phainon’s blade, deflected when the warrior sprang between them. The lance spun in Nikador’s hand and both Phainon and Mydei bounced away.

Mydei skidded across one of the bridges, a little too close to the edge for comfort, coming to a stop in a runner’s stance. He glanced across the room to where Phainon had come to rest in the same pose, different bridge. They briefly exchanged looks, taking note of the next verse.

Phainon dashed first and Mydei paused, letting him lead in this arpeggio. Phainon’s sword flashed blue and orange flickers every time the blade met the unbreakable bronze of Nikador’s spear. The god was fast, jabbing and slicing, advancing on Phainon whose every effort was in deflecting, dodging. If they clashed, Nikador’s superior strength would win, and Phainon knew it.

Mydei waited until the tempo increased at Strife’s bidding, even the chanting in his head quickened with every jab. He waited and trusted Phainon’s abilities, until the Lance of Fury chipped the edge of Phainon’s sword and gold blood dripped to the floor. A wave of crystal slammed into Nikador’s side, sharpened edges stabbed up into the Titan’s chest, taking advantage of the gaps to pin the god to the lattice.

Phainon rushed in, gold blood turning his hair yellow where it streamed from his ear and cheek. His blade whistled in the air as he dropped from above to slice at the Titan’s joints. The steel dragged across the god, leaving behind a shallow scratch.

He was mid-leap when Nikador shattered Mydei’s crystal, throwing the prince back with the force. The Titan screeched and jumped onto the statue in the back of the atrium. They clung there like an insect, long limbs gripping the statue’s sword as they readied their lance to throw.

Mydei and Phainon rushed in close so they would be harder to hit, and the instinct saved one of Mydei’s lives. The lance cut by his shoulder like light, too fast to track with mortal eyes.

Phainon leaped after the Titan and Mydei sent crystals ahead. The crimson shards grabbed at Nikador’s feet while the god summoned another lance, pinning them in place so Phainon’s sword could swipe again at that scratch. This time, the crack was audible. It was punctuation at the end of a long sentence, a staccato note in a legato refrain.

Mydei hurried to follow up, taking Phainon’s place when the swordsman bounced back to jab his claws into the opening Phainon had created. The war armor splintered and Nikador screeched loud enough to shatter the statue. Long cracks ripped across the atrium’s ceiling and plaster and dust rained down upon their shoulders.

Long fingers wrapped around Mydei’s leg as he was falling but Phainon’s sword cleaved through one of the digits and they both fell to the platform.

Nikador pressed their advantage.

A broad swipe of the lance thrummed in the air above them, nearly claiming their heads before the two warriors were able to drop beneath it. The ground underneath them was vibrating with the intensity of the fight. Mydei could feel it through his gauntlets when he crouched.

Phainon was moving again, shouting in a wordless snarl that betrayed the man’s excitement. He was feeling the bloodlust, that vicious desire to fight and kill, with no concern for his own injuries. Mydei briefly realized that Phainon probably didn’t know he was bleeding at all.

More dirt rained around them. There was a platform here, a way to raise this battle into the arena above but Mydei had a better idea. He turned on his heel and raced to the wall, leaving Phainon to contend with the Titan alone for a short time, to hold that divine gaze. Ledges and statues facilitated his climb as Mydei hurried, as close to the ceiling as he could get before crystal erupted above them.

The ceiling exploded.

Mydei fell alongside the dust and cacophony of his own attack and the massive blocks of the collapsing atrium. Through the debris he could see the flash of blue and white as Phainon pushed away from Nikador to dodge the environmental hazard and Mydei lost him in the chaos. The roar of the cave in drowned out all other noise, any attempts to shout for Phainon were lost until stone settled and the dust began to clear.

“Mydeimos!”

“Here!” he called, and relief washed over him. Cracked open to the world, the atrium was flooded with light from the Blade of Fury above and it was infinitely easier to see the destruction. The Titan was buried under the rubble, but Mydei could still hear chanting in that ancient tongue, reverberating in the back of his mind. Nikador was still alive.

Mydei sprang backwards to the edge of the arena. The collapse had filled the space below, leaving them in a crater of debris, the once grand colosseum no more than a bowl in the ground now. Phainon bounced across the arena and landed beside Mydei, sword still ready, eyes searching for movement.

This pause, this rest in the melody was unbearable. The tension was winding tighter with every passing second as they waited.

It was Phainon who sensed it first. Energy gathered above them and Mydei might not have moved in time, but Phainon’s shoulder slammed into his chest, and they both rolled. For a brief second, Mydei remembered the storm and a falling beam. He immediately reached for Phainon, eyes searching his leg for injury, but the man was okay, nothing damaged aside from a new tear in his cape. The torn fabric was pinned beneath a golden spear, an acceptable substitute for flesh.

The ground ripped open and Nikador pulled themself free with a jerky jitter.

Mydei’s resourcefulness paid off. Nikador’s armor was cracked and golden blood streamed over those lanky limbs in rivulets to pool beneath those gangly feet. The Titan twisted and screamed.

“This isn’t over,” Mydei cautioned with a happy purr as he and Phainon got back to their feet, dirty, bruised, and still very eager to fight.

The hollow crack of Nikador’s back was different than the rolling peal of thunder above. It was wetter. With a squelch that made Mydei’s stomach turn, a golden figure ripped free of Nikador’s back. The bloody heart of the unarmored Titan was missing its face, and sections of its arms and shoulders. Long blades stood out of their hunched back, all that remained of grand wings. They squealed and chanted as their upper body stretched, free of the confining armor. The pale body of Nikador still moved, still attached below the waist of the bloody, aurum god, but the spear in its hand was guided now by the detached arm of the exposed flesh.

One golden hand reached for them, gesturing in mirror with the white armor beneath it to grab at Mydei and Phainon. The tug on his soul was immediate. Mydei felt a piece of himself ripping away, saw it in a white shimmer as his vitality was drawn in towards the god and left speared in the ground.

Beside him, Phainon panted, holding his chest. Their ghosts, pieces of their souls were side by side, lifeless and shimmering pearlescent. Mydei and Phainon exchanged glances of shared confusion and then lightning cracked the sky and this four-armed Nikador was upon them.

They could have been fighting for days or minutes, Mydei genuinely didn’t know. The world was moving in a blur. Everything was flashes of red, gold, and blue, give and take, dance and song. Three times the god pulled from them their spirits to weaken them. Three times Phainon and Mydei hurried to smash those spears and reclaim that vitality and three times Mydei felt his endurance wane.

This fight could not last forever.

Mydei was tossed aside when the flat of the spear slammed into his chest, leaving a long cut across his belly as the weapon finished its arc. He paused to catch his breath, but Nikador surged after him, the tip of the spear reaching for his chest.

It stopped when Phainon dashed between them and the divine weapon slammed into the flat of Phainon’s sword, locking them both in a clash above Mydei. Phainon’s legs were shaking, his arms straining to hold back the Titan and then the unthinkable happened, Phainon’s sword shattered. Pieces of the blade rained across them both and the spear tore through Phainon’s pauldron, sinking deep into his shoulder with a pained cry and a hot gush of golden blood.

The sound of angry pain cut through Mydei like a knife, filling him with a newfound rage. Phainon was holding tightly to the weapon, shouting Kremnoan swear words at the golden god in a voice that cracked and rasped, broken and tired.

Crystal erupted around Nikador’s feet and the spear ripped free, Phainon’s blood dripped across Mydei and spattered on the ground. It burned hot and horrible like the surging hatred that uncoiled in Mydei’s gut. He turned on the Titan with ferocity unbridled. Thunder rolled as Mydei fought the Titan alone, faster and faster, until he stopped processing every action, surrendering entirely to the beast within him that wanted to kill this creature that hurt what was his.

The Blade of Fury shimmered above them, bearing witness to this final Kremnos Festival, as Mydei ripped Nikador’s head free in a shower of glittering gold and the Titan of Strife lay still. The pressure in the air stilled, the chanting ceased, and all that was left was a regretful silence.

Mydei panted. His heart was still racing, the battle high still lingered. Even without the Titan’s living presence pumping it into his veins, that bloodlust still fluttered in every breath. It took a conscious effort to rein in that rage to find himself buried in the violence and as soon as he did, Mydei was hurrying to Phainon’s side.

“Deliverer!”

Phainon was sitting up, eyes wide, breathing heavy. There was gold on his lips and pouring over his fingers where they pressed into the wound at his shoulder. His injured arm hung limp, the hilt of his broken sword still half resting against his palm.

For a fearful moment, Mydei thought his mind was gone. Phainon’s eyes were so haunted, so deep in that trance that it looked like Phainon was lost, but then he took a shuddering, wet breath and said, “that was amazing.”

“HKS,” Mydei scolded but he could not hide his relief nor his agreement and smiled his way to tired laugh.

He reached for Phainon’s wound to check it himself, but Phainon hissed and flinched away. “Leave it, please. We need to get back to the others. The coreflame?”

Mydei tilted his head towards the body where it lay and then helped Phainon to his feet. The sword clattered away spent and useless, and the broken shards crunched underfoot as Phainon found his footing and walked with reverent purpose towards Nikador’s corpse.

Was this something that they should do together? Mydei stayed back. Where before he was eager to retrieve the cursed thing to present to Phainon as a gesture of promise, now he wasn’t so sure. In the aftermath of combat, actually here beneath the symbol of their faith, standing across from their dead Titan, Mydei felt a sort of fulfillment, like he had passed some test that he didn’t know he was taking. It felt like he was being watched, when he would’ve preferred that feeling shift to Phainon.

Phainon who was kneeling beside the body, shoving his good arm down the god-king’s severed neck to pull the coreflame from their heart and in doing so achieve a destiny that he had been groomed for. Aglaea must have intended for their Deliverer to become a Demigod and what better coreflame than Strife? Phainon could save the world with that coreflame, be what Strife was always meant to be, a protector, a defender, not a tyrant.

Mydei humbly watched from a distance as Phainon pulled away from the corpse, hands dripping gold around the relic. It looked small in Phainon’s hand. Purple and bright with shimmering white glitter that looked like the night sky and the crest of Strife prominent within, etched the same color as their blood. Even from several paces away, Mydei could feel its warmth and call beckoning him to come closer.

“Mydei…” Phainon said, so small, so full of wonder that quelled all the residual bloodlust inside them, “It’s not mine…”

Those words hit Mydei with the weight of a mountain and the dread of staring into the unknown. It was the way Phainon looked at him, with awe and worship. The way Phainon held the coreflame out to him as he stumbled over uneven ground, trying to hand the coreflame to Mydei.

And something inside of the prince desperately wanted it. His heart ached for it and when Phainon very, very gently tried to put it in Mydei’s hand, Mydei heard Cipher’s words crooning from memory.

…like a part of you that you never realized was missing.

“It’s yours,” Phainon said so gently, so pure, and with the most genuine, happy smile that little tears were beading in those perfect blue eyes.

…they have chosen their bearers across time.

The coreflame was so warm in his hands, so small and seemingly so fragile. This tiny thing that could save them, save all of them. This was the strength to conquer, to ensure victory in every battle.

It was warmth and comfort and responsibility so great that I thought I would burst with the joy of it.

Mydei took a deep breath through his nose and slowly grabbed Phainon’s wrist. He pulled it up and cradled the man’s hand in his own so that he could give the coreflame back, making Phainon take it so he could step away from that power.

“Mydei?” Phainon’s confusion dripped from him like blood. “What are you doing? This is yours. It belongs to you.”

“No.”

Phainon took a step forward and Mydei recoiled. “It chose you.”

“I don’t want it.”

“No one else can take it!”

“You can, Phainon!” Mydei insisted. He closed Phainon’s fingers around the coreflame with both of his hands. “As we planned. You can take it back to Aglaea to buy your pardon.”

Phainon shook with frustration, exhaustion, it was all the same now as he tried to push the coreflame to Mydei’s chest. “This is a part of your heart, Mydei! You need it!”

“I don’t!” Mydei held tightly to Phainon’s fist with both hands so his best friend could not let go of the coreflame.

“How can you say that? Now that you know, now that you’ve felt it, you’ll never feel whole again without it!”

He closed his eyes and looked down, away from Phainon’s begging lest that pleading face make him relent and accept this horrid gift, heavier than any crown. “That’s not true!”

“It is!”

“It’s not, because I have you!” Mydei shouted.

The silence was deafening. Beneath his fingers, Phainon was still quivering. Mydei looked up at him, at those wide searching eyes. The tears that had beaded there were spilling over, leaving trails through the grime and blood on Phainon’s cheeks.

“What?” Phainon whispered.

“I don’t need the coreflame to feel whole,” Mydei repeated and then he smiled to say, “because I have you. And if you make me take it, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, I will tear it from my chest and drag you and that damned thing to Okhema to see you free.”

“Mydei-“

The ground rumbled hard enough to nearly send them to their knees. Something thick and horrible dropped from the sky beside them, a heavy goo that dripped like rain around the Titan’s body. A tearing laugh, otherworldly and bone chillingly shrill rolled over Castrum Kremnos. In the distance, Mydei thought he heard a horn, Peucesta calling for a retreat. The mist started to pool and rise around them again, where the Titan’s screams had dispelled it before, in Nikador’s absence it swelled and thickened.

Phainon stumbled and Mydei hurried to steady him as they started putting together the pieces. Nikador wasn’t corrupted. They were not an agent of the Tide.

They were the dam.

The pooling mist surged to the body of Nikador, filling the bones of the Titan, until the husk started to twitch and move. Mydei saw Phainon widen his stance preparing to fight and knew that he would not survive another round.

None of them would.

Except maybe Mydei.

This was no longer Nikador, this was the Black Tide unleashed and if someone did not hold it back, then Phainon, the crew, and his distant people would die.

“Deliverer!” Mydei snapped, “You’re the captain now.”

“What-?!”

“Listen to me!” he growled, grabbing Phainon by the front of his armor to capture his attention, to make the man meet his eyes, “take the coreflame, earn your freedom, but first please, save my family. I trust you. I trust you more than anyone to lead them. Get them to safety and I will cover your escape.”

“I won’t leave you!” Phainon snarled.

Mydei ignored the declaration and dragged him close, one hand holding Phainon’s arm that clutched the coreflame, the other hooked around the back of Phainon’s neck to pull him in until their foreheads were pressed tightly together.

“It was you, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae!” he shouted as though to announce it to the world and then softer, only for them, “it was always you. The pirate that stole my heart.”

“Why are you saying this now?!” Phainon cried. He was trying to pull away, to get out of this Kremnoan farewell but Mydei held him tightly so he couldn’t escape.

“I promised.” He squeezed Phainon’s arm, reminding him of the coreflame still held tightly in his fist. “Save them, Deliverer. I beg you.”

The Tide churned behind them. Mydei could hear the song now, it was soft and peaceful, a stark contrast to the twisted, headless form of the Titan it was nearly done assimilating.

Phainon was sobbing but he nodded and Mydei took that as a promise. He rubbed the back of Phainon’s neck, squeezing reassurances before he closed the last of that space between them.

Their lips met, rushed and desperate. Mydei could feel Phainon reaching for him with his injured arm, taste the blood on his lips as the man reciprocated, longing for Mydei, begging him without words to stay with him, to return to the ship together.

Mydei’s instincts screamed. The spear glittered in the corner of his eye. He grabbed Phainon by his armor and threw him.

-

Phainon’s heart was racing. He was dizzy, light-headed, and not from his injuries. To hear Mydei’s confession was everything, but it crumpled away as that love was replaced with loss so much worse than that which the Tide had sung.

He screamed Mydei’s name as he was tossed down a long path and tried to find his footing faster, to run back to that fight so that Mydei didn’t have to struggle alone. The Tide was sticky and boiling under his feet as he ran but a massive wall of crystal blocked his path and Phainon slammed into it with reckless abandon. Again and again with helpless screams and sobs he rammed his body uselessly against the barricade, refusing to abandon his best friend, refusing to accept that intimate goodbye, angry to collapsing that Mydei had been so selfish as to deny Phainon the chance to say the words back.

The words that Phainon didn’t even know he needed to say. The words that sprang to mind along with the singular, overwhelming desire to be selfish, to want for himself.

I love you. I love you!

He could still feel that goodbye on his lips, the hope that Mydei had left with him, knowing that this horrible, cursed fire in his hands was Mydei. This was a part of Mydei’s heart, given willingly with complete, implicit trust and love to be casually sold for what? For freedom? For something Phainon already had standing at Mydei’s side?

The ache in his arm was getting worse, the Tide was surging, building. This was not a gentle Tide that took in its own time. It would overwhelm the crew, push its way across the ocean and take take take.

What the hell had they done?

Phainon screamed and pounded on the crystal until his voice broke. He could hear the combat beyond, knew that Mydei was fighting. How long could he keep it up? Immortal as he was, Mydei could fight for days, weeks even, but with the weight of this corruption…

It was a tug on his cape that cut his next harrowing plea short. Phainon twisted, tears and blood flying with the sharpness of the action.

Standing in the mist, tugging with all his might, was Fig Stew.

The chimera was in bad shape. His paws were muddy and scratched, splotches of bloody fur were nearly black in the dim light, red eyes were glassy and tired. Purple goo clung to his tail and ears, the corruption trying to wear away at the beast, eager to recruit such a noble soul to its legions of monsters.

Even when Phainon just sat and watched, unmoving, Fig Stew tugged and tugged. His nails left marks on the stone as he fought to move the mountain, an impossible task without Phainon’s consent, but the effort was everything, an ultimate example of resolve. The chimera was already tired from his trek through the city, ready to collapse, but like his master his spirit exceeded the limitations of his body, and he pulled and pulled until his legs gave out and then he shakily got back up to pull again.

And Phainon cried.

Fig Stew needed him. The crew needed him. Mydei needed him. Phainon made a promise to protect, to save Mydei’s family, his family now too.

Following Fig’s example, fighting the exhaustion, Phainon shakily crawled to Fig Stew to scoop the suffering chimera up to cradle in his arm. The tired animal clung to him with his paws, tail resting loose over Phainon’s wrist beside the coreflame. He got to his feet and caught his breath, almost choking on the heavy Tide. He turned back to glare at the wall that Mydei had made, at the Sword of Fury beyond it, and growled low under his breath, “Don’t die too many times.”

And then he ran.

Getting back to the ship was harder than anything Phainon had ever done. The city was almost empty now between the efforts of Castorice and the crew, but it wasn’t the monsters that made the sprint difficult. It was moving farther away from where Mydei was fighting and dying. It was knowing that they did this, they messed up. It was the aching desire in his chest that loved to the point of pain. It was Fig Stew’s quiet whimpers as they ran from the dense might of the Tide on their heels.

He tripped over the Kremnoan barricades, abandoned along with their dead… and there were dead. Phainon recognized Ulixes, the taskmaster, as he fell on the street beside the man’s lifeless body, gutted with his sword in his hand, and the flashing rush of memories threatened to trap him here, to die beside them.

The coreflame in Phainon’s hand burned, bright enough to keep the mist at bay as it tried to roll over him where he curled around Fig Stew on the ground. He held it tight and thought of Mydei and the coreflame flickered brighter, reassuring, reminding him that Mydei was alive, strong, and counting on him. It was courage in the darkness and Phainon took deep breaths, letting that courage give him the strength to stand again, to limp the rest of the way to the dock, where the crew watched from the railing.

The ramp had been pulled up to keep the fog from chasing the crew in their retreat, but as Phainon hurried down the wooden dock he heard shouts and saw them throw him a rope. He looped it around Fig Stew first, letting the chimera be carried to safety while he watched the city slowly disappear in inky smoke.

He looped the rope around his chest when it was thrown again and tried to hold on as he was pulled up roughly over the rail.

Phainon let the rope go, tossing it aside when his feet touched the deck. It was a struggle to stand, and he leaned heavily on the railing as chaos erupted around him. Perdikkas was by his side immediately, pressing a warm, wet cloth to his shoulder. Hyacine too was trying to get to him and Phainon felt some strength return with a quiet ‘doot.’ “Where is Mydeimos?” Krateros shouted and Phainon felt like collapsing all over again. The crew was shouting, crowding him.

“Give him space!” Perdikkas demanded and Ptolemy was there to help them push the crowd back. Both of them were hurt, he could see it in the way they limped, the bandages on their bodies.

Where was Hephaestion? Phainon dimly wondered after the first mate and then Krateros was in his space, sword drawn. He had bandages wrapped around his chest and leg, dried blood clinging to his jaw, the man’s eyes were wild, still crazed from battle and eager for answers.

Phainon slowly opened his hand showing the coreflame of Strife to a round of gasps from the crew. A couple of them shouted, the start of a victory cheer, but those few were quickly silenced.

“He told me,” Phainon started, and his words cracked. He had to pause to swallow, still his voice was raw and broken as he fought to yell loud enough to be heard by all, “he told me to take his place as the captain.” Gasps and whispers moved like ripples through the men.

Krateros’ hand lashed out to grab Phainon’s coat, pulling him close, holding him still while that still bloody blade pressed cold against Phainon’s throat. The deck erupted into chaos and tears rolled down Phainon’s cheeks again, not for fear of death, but for fear of failing in this critical task assigned to him and sealed with a parting kiss.

“You left him,” Krateros accused with a tremor in his voice. Rage and anger could not hide the grief in the old man’s expression. The steel bit into Phainon’s neck and he felt warmth run over his collar, but he did not plead for his life, even as the crew turned on each other. This old veteran was a mirror, Phainon’s own grief reflected in those watery eyes as Krateros lashed out the only way he knew how.

“I’m sorry,” Phainon whispered and waited for the end.

A hushed silence settled on the deck. It startled even the old man who relaxed his grip to look with curiosity at the chimera. The crew parted for Fig Stew, lowering their weapons to watch the chimera struggle with determined purpose, limping to Krateros’ and Phainon’s feet. He howled, low and mournful until Krateros stepped back and lowered his weapon, leaving Phainon to Fig Stew’s judgement. The chimera mewled and then slowly lay down to roll over, presenting his belly to Phainon.

The crew held their breath as Phainon slowly knelt, resting on both knees. His injured arm still hung uselessly and the other still clutched the coreflame like a lifeline, still Fig Stew waited. With a shaky sigh, Phainon let go of the coreflame, setting it reverently in the space between himself and the chimera. Phainon’s bloody hand felt too dirty, too stained to gently scratch that perfect white belly fur, but Fig Stew didn’t mind. Even in pain, even in mourning, Fig Stew still purred.

Krateros dropped his sword. The steel clattered on the deck, shattering the silence. With humility and exhaustion in every movement, the old man slowly knelt beside Phainon, head bowed and his fists tight over his knees.

“What should we do, Captain?” he asked, genuine.

Phainon didn't have the strength to marvel at the change of heart, at the power that Fig Stew had over the faith of the crew. Everyone was looking at him for guidance, anxious and afraid. They needed him to be the Deliverer, the person that Mydei believed in, that Mydei loved.

The coreflame pulsed, encouraging, filling Phainon with confidence to give his first order, “We need to go home.”

The crew scattered in silence to obey, to get underway before the rolling Tide could catch up to them. With Krateros and Perdikkas to help, Phainon got back to his feet, cradling the coreflame like it was the only thing that mattered. Ptolemy scooped up Fig Stew, holding him within reach so they could still hear his purring.

He turned to look at the city falling away behind them, all but that mocking Blade of Fury hidden in the Tide’s polluted grasp, pointing at the still fighting Mydeimos the Undying, Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos, Inheritor of Strife.

“We’re coming back,” Phainon hissed, low and angry so only those beside him could hear, “we’re coming back for him.”

Chapter End Notes
