chapters.title: Chapter 29: Aftermath
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

No new tags! In the wake of unexpected loss, the captain has some decisions to make

Chapter Notes

Thank you all for your patience! I had a wonderful week attending my first con! I spent way too much money but I am content if a little tired. Hopefully, I'll be back to regular updates now!

Phainon tried to help the others the moment Chryseus Leo got underway. A cursory glance at the injured on deck and basic math told him that only a skeleton crew would be left to sail the ship. Three rows of men lay in various stages of dying, from the eerily still to those howling and writhing in pain. They needed everyone that could stand working the lines.

But the second he stepped away from the rail Phainon collapsed heavily into Perdikkas and Krateros’ arms. All of his remaining strength was in keeping Mydei’s coreflame held tightly to his chest with nothing left to keep his shaking body upright.

“Stay with me, Phainon.” Perdikkas sounded so far away.

The deck twisted and blurred, his vision failing as the adrenaline finally settled, leaving him feeling cold and numb.

“’m fine… where’s Hephaestion?” he asked but he didn’t even recognize his own voice with the slur of the syllables.

If they answered, he didn’t hear it. Instead, they pulled him along, half dragging, half carrying him across the deck to an open pad to lay him down beside the other injured Kremnoans. Every sensation was muted as his body started shutting down to rest, focused entirely on the warmth in his arms and the flowering pain in his shoulder where the Lance of Fury had pinned him to the stone.

Someone was talking to him, but he couldn’t see who it was with the black creeping along the edges of his vision. Hands were pulling on his clothes, undoing the straps and buckles of his armor. A sharp pain ripped through Phainon a moment later, and that was enough to crush what was left of his consciousness.

-

Phainon woke to the pitter-patter of rain on canvas and opened his eyes to a gray and solemn world. The ship wasn’t listing like it might during a heavy storm, just the gentle sway of a ship at rest, likely moored in a protected cove. Above him was stretched the fabric of one of the top sails, angled to dump the rainwater over the railing to keep the deck dry. The red of it looked like drying blood, dark and cold, wrapped in the same gloomy filter that blanketed the rest of the world in soothing mourning.

It was you! It was always you.

Time passed differently laying there, listening to the distant roll of thunder while the petrichor tickled his nose. Phainon felt too numb to think, too tired to feel beyond the voice of memory, a mercy perhaps considering the emotions that he knew were waiting for him. Emotions that still manifested in watery eyes and quiet tears that spilled over his cheeks while he stared blankly ahead and slowly tried to process.

Save them, Deliverer. I beg you.

The ache in his shoulder was still there, a brutal reminder that the nightmare was real. The corresponding arm was strapped tightly across his bare chest to keep it from moving. Just below, over his belly, was a foreign warmth, one that breathed in tandem with himself. Fig Stew’s little heartbeat was slow, at rest. He too had endured and lost.

Men moved around the deck, keeping quiet, tending to their companions when one of them moaned or whimpered in their pain, until the rain was once more the only soundtrack.

What should we do, Captain?

A shadow passed beside him and then a small hand was pressing on his chest, just below his collarbone. Her fingers were warm, even through the bandages.

“Lord Phainon?” Hyacine whispered, “Are you awake?” Without moving his head, Phainon’s eyes slowly shifted to meet hers. “Can you speak?”

He swallowed and opened his mouth to try but all he could manage was an exhausted croak. She reached up to press the pads of her fingers to the side of his throat. A soothing, cooling sensation spread from her touch and he shivered.

“It’s okay if you can’t right now,” she reassured him gently.

Phainon still tried, testing his jaw with a couple stretches before he managed to whisper, “what happened?”

“Krateros took over after you passed out,” Hyacine told him, “We got as far as we could before the rain started but he didn’t want to risk being on open water during a storm. We spent the night anchored in a cove while we tend to the wounded and assess our situation.”

He pulled at his bound arm and a sharp pain twisted in his shoulder, ripping a gasp from his lips. Hyacine rested her hand over the wrap with a concerned expression, but he nodded at her reassuringly and used his other arm instead to feel around for the coreflame.

The doctor pushed down on him more urgently when he started to panic, unable to find the only part of Mydei he had left. Phainon shoved her off, fighting to sit up, sending Fig Stew into an alarmed roll when he bucked and kicked at the heavy blanket that was holding him down.

Where was it?

Where was the coreflame? Where was Mydei’s heart?

Hyacine threw herself across his chest to hold him down, but even exhausted, his thrashing was not so easily tamed. She failed to subdue his recklessness until Perdikkas joined her, jumping onto Phainon to straddle his lap with both hands on the man’s chest to push him back down, panting.

“Phainon, what the hell?” he snapped, “do you know how long it took Hyacine and I to get you stitched up?”

“Where is it? Where is Mydei?”

Perdikkas drew in a sharp breath. “Mydei is gone, Phainon. He’s still at Castrum Kremnos, remember?”

Phainon’s hiss made Perdikkas and Hyacine flinch, “How can I forget?” He still tossed, trying to get Perdikkas off but the doctor held firm and even managed to pin Phainon’s remaining good wrist across his chest next to the other. “Where is the coreflame?”

“Relax and I’ll tell you.” It took effort but Phainon took a couple deep breaths and slowly resumed his supine position. “Peucesta has it, he is keeping it safe beside Chryseus Leo.”

Something about that didn’t sit right. There was a possessive feeling lurking cold inside his belly, that hated the idea of someone else holding onto it, of keeping it safe. That was Phainon’s job, but the longer he lay there with his two friends watching him with wary, fearful expressions the more he realized how silly that was. They had every right to worry and care just like he did, and Phainon needed to be the captain, to take care of them until such time as he ceased to embody that role.

Slowly, Perdikkas let go and eased off Phainon’s lap to kneel at his side opposite Hyacine. There were questions in those tired eyes, worry and loss eating away at them all. Exhaustion weighed heavily over the deck.

“Perdikkas,” Phainon started, he swallowed and whispered, “back there-“

“Not right now,” Perdikkas scolded. He looked down, shaking but dry eyed, “I-I want to know, really, I do, but you need to heal first. Are you in pain?” Phainon shook his head but gasped and cussed when Perdikkas lightly touched his shoulder. “Let me get you some poppy.” He started to get up, but Phainon caught his sleeve to stop him.

“Not this time,” he whispered.

“You don’t need to punish yourself,” Perdikkas reassured him, “if you’re in pain…”

No, it wasn’t that, Phainon thought to himself. He just wanted to remain clear-headed, to be able to make important decisions without the influence of the drugs, but… pain was already clouding his mind. Grief was already driving his actions. Perhaps, in a way, Perdikkas was right, reading the depths of Phainon’s soul.

“Please,” he still whispered.

“Water at least?”

Phainon nodded, already feeling the fuzzy of exhaustion creeping behind his eyes. Before Perdikkas returned with a waterskin, Phainon had already fallen asleep.

-

It took Phainon one Entry Hour to recover enough energy to get to his feet, against the advice of his physicians. His arm was still tightly bound to his chest to ease the strain on his shoulder, but he had strength enough to help furl the sails and get them moving towards home. They were falling behind in a race with the Tide to get to the settlement, cursed to sail on inky water until they made up the sea that that they lost.

Krateros sat beside Phainon as soon as the new captain felt clear-headed enough to take in the report and had patiently walked him through the bleakness of their situation.

They had lost seven men in Castrum Kremnos, the names of which were recorded on paper and handed to Phainon to read, along with reassurances that Kremnoans had no need to grieve. But it didn’t stop Phainon from tucking that piece of paper under his chlamys to keep close to his heart. He would respect their culturally held desire not to be openly mourned but the weight of their sacrifice was something he wanted to appreciate in private.

Nearly every man had sustained injuries during the battle, but only a few were confined to their beds or the infirmary with wounds that prevented them from working. Hyacine had been a miracle on the field, saving the lives of nearly a dozen men that would have undoubtedly perished, something that several of them grumbled about. Only Kremnoans would so openly regret surviving a major battle.

The worst part of the report was news of the Tide. Even with fair winds to carry them, the Tide line had kept pace with the ship and any advantage they had was lost when the rain forced them to moor for an Entry Hour. According to their maps and predetermined timeline, the Tide should’ve been in retreat, but it had changed course unexpectedly and was surging with renewed vigor.

Phainon, Krateros, and Ptolemy equally agreed that the surging Tide would take the settlement within fourteen Entry Hours and had begun discussing the possibility of an evacuation. A topic that Phainon felt was best decided when everyone would be able to listen and contribute.

That moment came five Entry Hours after they had left Castrum Kremnos and finally started to overtake the Tide line. The promise of beating the spread filled the crew with new life even as they focused on nursing their wounds.

Phainon had ordered Ptolemy to fetch the others and meet at the infirmary, leaving him alone in his room with Fig Stew to get ready. The chimera had healed quickly, shrugging off the corruption like a champ, but he was still emotionally distant. He had the same brave façade that Phainon had been wearing, pretending that everything was alright, but Fig was clingy, refusing to leave Phainon’s side for even a second, and in that action Phainon saw through him.

“Would you like to nap with him today?” Phainon offered, referring to the piece of Mydei they still held onto so tightly, and Fig Stew tilted his head.

The Coreflame of Strife was a revered treasure amongst the crew. Phainon insisted on keeping it at night ever since he was able to return to his own bed, cradling it and Fig Stew together in a tight curl to sleep, the warmth of it a comfort in the lonely gloom. He frequently would wake when it flickered and caught himself looking over at Mydei’s hammock, expecting the Kremnoan to be there, sleeping as though nothing had happened. That was the miracle of this coreflame, so willingly given to Phainon. Keeping it close… it felt like Mydei was still there.

Which was why, during the day, Phainon made sure to share.

It hurt every morning, handing it to members of the crew with reverence, but Mydei’s family needed their Prince and the comfort that the coreflame brought, even if they didn’t know yet why it felt that way. Phainon had not revealed the truth of the coreflame’s nature. Something he intended to do at the meeting today.

He fixed his hair in the mirror and then crouched down to one knee to hold his arm out to Fig Stew. Carefully, the chimera climbed onto Phainon, paws clinging to his chlamys with his chin on Phainon’s shoulder. That strong arm scooped under Fig’s bum and tail, holding him secure while they walked to the infirmary.

Most everyone was there already, waiting in solemn silence. Krateros was leaning against a wall, arms crossed. He nodded politely to Phainon when the captain entered, a gesture mimicked by Perdikkas, Ptolemy, and Peucesta all sitting on chairs.

“Hello, Lord Phainon,” Hyacine greeted from the desk beside Perdikkas. Behind her, Anaxa was ignoring them, reading a book and sitting on a bed beside Leonnius. The runner had twisted his ankle during the battle and was on bedrest until Perdikkas said otherwise, but he had the strength to sit up, with his legs thrown over the side of his resting place.

Castorice raised her hand in a small wave from where she sat beside one of the beds and Phainon moved towards her. He set Fig Stew down at the edge of the sheet that covered most of Hephaestion’s body.

“Thank you everyone for being here,” Phainon addressed the room, careful to sound at ease, “It makes me happy to see everyone looking better.”

“Everyone?” Ptolemy grumbled.

“I do miss Hephaestion,” Leonnius lamented dramatically.

“Me too,” Hephaestion agreed in a tired but playful voice from his bed.

“Not everyone can pull off the corpse look with such vitality,” Perdikkas praised.

Leonnius whistled, “That’s not what you want to hear from your doctor.”

Phainon looked down at Hephaestion and offered the first mate a small smile. Hephaestion really did look horrible even when he tried to smile back. Better than before even with a pale countenance and too weak to sit up.

Fig Stew crept up across the bed with delicate steps to curl against Hephaestion’s side, purring gently.

“He’ll be fine,” Ptolemy huffed as he waved a hand back and forth, “Hephaestion is not fool enough to perish in his bed, succumbing to injury. The embarrassment of such a thought alone will sustain him.”

Hephaestion tried to laugh but it came out as a whimpering bark. “Surely, I am immortal now,” he mused, “if ever there was a fight in which to give my life, that would have been the one.”

“I am sorry you missed your shot at glory,” Phainon apologized.

“No, you’re not.”

Phainon tilted his head with a wide grin, “no, I’m not, because I need you. All of you.”

He slowly sat down on the edge of the bed beside Hephaestion, and Castorice reached out her hand to take his own with a reassuring squeeze.

“I know you all want to know what happened-“

“Phainon, wait,” Hephaestion wheezed, “where is Mydei?”

The question felt like a punch to his gut. Hephaestion had been in and out of consciousness since his emergency surgery, no one had the chance to tell him yet.

“Perhaps, captain,” Krateros said, and Hephaestion stiffened, “you should start at the moment you and the Prince entered the city.”

Phainon took a deep breath and then he told them a story of valor and loss.

He told them almost everything, from their sprint through the city to when he and Mydei left Castorice behind. He described their climb surrounded by lightning and what it was like to hear the voice of the Titan. Phainon told them how he faltered under that crushing weight, that bloodlust that Nikador demanded with their presence, but how Mydei spoke to him in earnest, giving him courage to persist.

The battle was harder to describe in detail, as most of it faded into a blurred memory, so he stuck to the highlights and absentmindedly reached to touch the new nick in his ear as he recounted the blood they spilled. He told them about the ceiling collapsing, their near deaths and the breaking of Nikador’s armor, revealing the true spirit of the god-king that crawled from their shell like a cicada. Phainon recounted in detail how Mydei rose to the challenge and killed the Titan when he was too injured to continue the fight himself.

Then he told them about the coreflame, about their discovery of its nature. That piece of Mydei’s heart was resting in Peucesta’s lap where he sat across the countertop. The bard curled more tightly around it when Phainon told them the truth of what it was, to whom it belonged, and the weight of it being apart from their Prince.

Phainon started to tell them about how he fought to give it to Mydei, but the words caught, and he changed the story only slightly to keep that world-shattering confession to himself. Instead, he told them that there had been no time for Mydei to ascend to divinity, as the Tide surged. He revealed to them the truth that they had discovered, that Nikador’s ‘corruption’ was not of the Tide but of necessity and Eurypon’s madness, that the god was a dam, slowing the flow of this mighty swell. Mydei’s continued sacrifice was the only thing keeping the Tide from surging faster than they could sail.

Then he shared with them Mydei’s last orders to Phainon, to assume the role of captain, exchange the coreflame for Phainon’s pardon, and get his family to safety. He told them about Mydei throwing him aside and blocking his return in crystal, to cover their retreat. His fingers carded through Fig’s fur as he recounted aloud the chimera’s bravery in coming to find them, to retrieve Phainon from his own desperation that would have destroyed him.

“I know I am not Kremnoan,” Phainon said, “and if it is the will of those here, I will gladly give the title of Captain to another.”

Ptolemy stood up, walked over, and punched him square on the jaw. The whole room jumped. Phainon blinked, stunned as he slowly reached up to rub at the warm spot spreading across his cheek.

The bookworm shook his hand out and said casually, “I had to since Hephaestion can’t right now.”

“Thank you, Ptolemy,” the first mate managed after a loud swallow.

“The young Prince chose you,” Krateros said firmly. If there was anyone on board that should be the captain, it was Krateros. “It would betray our love for him, to not honor his wishes.”

“Do you not want to be captain, Deliverer?” Peucesta asked in his soft, attention commanding voice. He was still holding the coreflame delicately, his lyre set aside, within reach but less important than the heavy burden he cradled in both hands.

Phainon’s eyes drifted down to that fragment of Mydei’s heart, heavy with the weight of that name on his shoulders. “I want to do what I promised,” he said after a long moment of thought, “to take care of his family.”

“Then believe in yourself the way he does,” Perdikkas offered with a smile.

“You are more than enough,” Hephaestion offered from behind him.

“If we have finally established the chain of command onboard the ship, there are more urgent matters that need discussion,” Anaxa huffed, ever condescending.

“But I didn’t get a turn to kiss the new captain’s ass yet,” Leonnius crooned.

Anaxa’s painfully loud sigh was met with chuckles.

“’If he were to return and look after my affairs I should be both more respected and should show a better presence to the world,’” Ptolemy quoted absentmindedly before asking, “Alright, captain, what is the plan?”

Phainon took a breath to steel himself and the coreflame flickered encouragingly. The regret that he felt for trying to reject this responsibility handed to him, died in the embers of hopeful support and Mydei’s love, leaving behind only a stubborn, renewed resolve to be the Deliverer that they needed.

Krateros’ report played on a loop in the back of his head, taking precedence. Hephaestion will have not heard the report, it was worth reviewing.

“Hyacine, how many more men need bedrest?” he asked. The energy was returning to his voice.

“Five, they have been moved from the deck this morning and are settled comfortably in the crew’s quarters and these two wonderful patients here.”

Phainon looked down at Hephaestion. “How long will Hephaestion be bedridden?”

She glanced over at Perdikkas who wrinkled his nose.

“It’s hard to say,” she admitted, “if he is to fight again, perhaps a couple weeks?”

Hephaestion made an annoyed snorting sound.

“For now, I want Krateros to be my first mate,” he announced.

“Captain,” Krateros protested, “I served his highness as an advisor.”

“Excellent, I expect the same from my first mate.”

The old man’s eyebrows shot up as he studied Phainon, but he slowly nodded.

“I saw the list of people who died, is there a funeral ceremony that needs to be performed on their behalf.”

“No,” Ptolemy answered, “I have already recorded their names for the histories.”

“I know one of them used to assist Mydei in the galley… Who has been covering the kitchen?” Phainon asked.

“I have, Lord Phainon,” Castorice offered, “myself and the Professor.”

That was a genuine surprise. “Professor…?”

“Wipe that dumbfounded look off your face, captain,” he grumbled with a dismissive wave of his hand. The other was keeping his spot in his book; thumb stuck between the pages. “It is a small price to pay to retain some control over my lab and I have yet to hear any complaints.”

“Would you two be willing to continue serving in the ship’s galley?”

“Anything I can do to help, Lord Phainon,” Castorice agreed immediately. When Anaxa didn’t respond, she added, “I am sure Professor Anaxa will help.”

“Not if you keep calling me that,” he hissed.

“We are two days from the settlement,” Krateros said, to get them back on track, “and the Tide is on our heels like wild dogs.”

Ptolemy raised his hand but didn’t wait to be called upon to say, “Krateros, Phainon, and I checked the maps. It’s impossible to say for sure but it is highly likely that the settlement will be under the Tide well before we can push it back.”

“We discussed it among the three of us, but… how long would it take to evacuate?” Phainon asked and the question hung in the air for a long breath as everyone processed the grief of losing their home again.

“A couple days?” Perdikkas offered with a heavy swallow.

“If I gave the order to evacuate the city, would the Kremnoan people listen?”

Again, silence hung in the air. Ptolemy and Krateros had already had the time to process the inevitability of this decision and even they were hesitant to answer. The bookworm drummed his fingers on his knee.

“We will make them listen,” Hephaestion said firmly when no one else dared to speak.

“Lord Phainon,” Hyacine offered, “if anyone can get them to listen, it’s you.”

“A silver-tongued Okheman, what could go wrong?” Leonnius chirped.

Krateros tsked and said assuredly, “they will listen.”

“But where can we even go?” the runner added. He shifted uncomfortably on the bed and Anaxa nearly smacked him with his book for bouncing the thin mattress up and down.

“There is only one place safe from the Tide,” Castorice reminded them all.

“The Dawn Device extends well past Okhema,” said Phainon, “there are lots of places that we can lead them for now that will keep Okhema and Kremnos apart.”

“Can we not take them to the Holy City?” Hyacine asked, “was that not the purpose of this bloody campaign? To end the war between us? Aglaea would accept the Kremnoan people as refugees…”

The coreflame flickered under darting gazes and Phainon’s shoulders slumped.

“That…that is the one thing Mydei told me to do that I hesitate to obey,” he admitted.

Immediately five Kremnoans started protesting at once, a combination of accusations, reminders of the blood spilled for this specific purpose, words reminding of Mydei’s desires, of their desires for him. Words that turned into arguing with each other when calls of support clashed with the others. He let them shout until he saw Castorice slowly move her hands to her ears and then he stomped his foot and barked once, “Enough!”

They quieted, still fuming as the room tried to be more polite in their discussions.

“Did we not just say that it is a betrayal to not obey Mydei’s wishes?” Krateros growled, “you who claim to love him as we do, would spit in the face of his sacrifice?”

“Phainon just told us that the coreflame is a part of Mydei,” Hephaestion tried to growl but he barely managed to get his sentence out before he started weakly coughing. Castorice reached to comfort him, resting her hand on his forehead.

“But he knew that it belonged to him when he told Phainon to exchange it for his pardon,” Perdikkas reminded them, “he knew, and he still wanted this.”

“I agree,” Ptolemy added onto Perdikkas’ statement, “we should honor our Prince’s wishes and do as he said. He wanted his people to be safe, what is safer than the protection of the Dawn Device and the end of our peoples’ war?”

“Miss Castorice,” Peucesta called gently, “you described once before what it was like to bear a coreflame, that need to feel whole when you realized a part of you is missing.” The bard had a captive audience, and he knew it, pausing to gather his thoughts while he rolled the coreflame in his hands to see the symbol of Strife as it flashed inside. “When we return for our Prince, he will be needing this piece of his heart.”

I don’t need the coreflame to feel whole, because I have you.

Phainon swallowed around his secret.

“If,” Leonnius said harshly, “if we return.”

Perdikkas rose to his feet, knocking over his chair. Behind him, Phainon felt the sheet shift as Hephaestion squirmed in his uselessness.

“How can you say that?!” Perdikkas snarled.

“You think I want to say it?!” the runner motioned quickly to himself, to Phainon, and then Hephaestion, “Does this look like a crew that can repeat what we just did? Now that the Tide is stronger? Faster? Have you looked at the talismans, Perdikkas?”

The doctor winced and looked down, fists clenched at his sides. Anaxa’s charms had saved them from corruption, but barely. Even with the increased capacity, they had filled too quickly once Nikador had perished and the Tide had been unleashed in full force. Phainon had learned that the only reason they had survived was because Peucesta had noticed them breaking and sounded the retreat early.

Phainon closed his eyes and replayed his final moments with Mydei again, all the way up to that desperate, hasty kiss.

I don’t need the coreflame to feel whole, because I have you.

“We will evacuate the settlement to the mainland,” he finally said, “it is a long route, but Okhema can be reached by land, and the Dawn Device reaches over the plateaus and fields between. It will not take long to ferry the people and supplies and get them moving.”

“Phainon that will take months…” Ptolemy mumbled.

“It gets them moving on a predictable, safe path with plenty of options to stop and rest maybe even settle, and we will sail ahead to Okhema,” he took a breath and let it out before saying, “where I will exchange the coreflame for the pardon of all Kremnoans and end the war between our peoples.” In the corner of Phainon’s eye he saw Krateros shaking, angry, but respecting the decision with reluctance by holding his tongue. “And I will petition for reinforcements to go back for Mydei.”

The quiet was shattered by Anaxa’s laugh. “A single coreflame to end a generations long war, buy the forgiveness for an entire crew of pirates, and access to Okhema’s golden fleet? A tall order and too small of a purse.”

“That’s why you will come with me, professor.”

Anaxa frowned and then schooled his expression once more as he quickly realized Phainon’s intentions. “Ah, you would offer two coreflames and abuse my relationship with that woman to appease the Council of Elders.” He laughed again and all the Kremnoans shuffled uncomfortably. “If I decline your request?”

“We are practiced rescuers,” Phainon said simply, and three different people snorted in lieu of laughter.

“Fine, I will acquiesce under the condition that you do not present me as your primary offering. A skilled barterer does not empty their pockets at the beginning of negotiations, and I would rather not be presented to those peacocks except as a last resort.”

“Do you think that little of me, Professor Anaxa?”

“It’s Anaxagoras, and you have given me reason to be worried in the past,” he admitted, “prove to me that you are worthy of this faith that so many others have entrusted to you.”

Phainon nodded humbly and held a hand to his chest, “I will do everything in my power to secure the means to save Mydei from his eternal battle. He deserves nothing less than our very best.”

“I abhor the idea of allying with Okhema,” Krateros admitted, “…but what they lack in military might they make up for in other ways. The Goldweaver alone could turn the Tide.”

“Aglaea, Cipher, and Tribbie, are all powerful Demigods,” Castorice reminded them, “so long as Lord Mydei continues to fight, we are not without hope.”

“Even if I have to go alone,” Phainon told the room with resolve reverberating in his declaration, “I will return to Castrum Kremnos and bring Mydei home.”

-

Phainon stood at the rail watching over the deck from Mydei’s favorite spot. The wind played with his hair and tugged at his clothes, nearly knocking Fig Stew off the railing with one gusty burst. The chimera huffed and jumped to a barrel instead for a more secure foundation. He rolled onto his side and Phainon willingly obliged, giving that soft belly gentle scratches.

“How often did Mydei take your advice?” he asked without turning around.

Krateros stepped forward, one hand resting idly on the hilt of his sword, the other relaxed at his side.

“Less frequently than I wish,” the old man admitted, “but he is wise beyond his years. Mydeimos will be the greatest of Kremnoan kings, a worthy successor of Gorgo.”

Phainon had to give the old man credit for his quiet positivity. The Kremnoans had absolute faith in their Prince, in Mydei’s resolve, endurance, and his immortal body.

“Did he ever reject your words and regret it?”

“I cautioned him once as a child not to eat jellyfish,” Krateros recalled and Phainon heard the fondness of revisiting a pleasant memory in that gruff voice.

“He didn’t…”

“Stubborn to a fault.”

Phainon chuckled at the image that came to mind of a young Mydeimos determined to find a recipe that called for stinging jellyfish.

“It was ever my purpose to guide not control,” Krateros said. He stepped forward to pet Fig’s belly. That old hand, covered in scars and rough skin long damaged by years in the sun knew all the right places to scratch and Fig Stew happily wiggled away from Phainon into that more experienced touch. “I had promised his mother as such.”

“What was she like?” Phainon asked, quieter now that they were closer.

“Radiant and strong,” he said simply, “just as the young Prince is.”

“I know that you have reservations about me, Krateros, but I appreciate your guidance.”

The old man snorted and pulled his hand away from Fig Stew’s belly. “Okheman sentimentality has no place on this ship.” Phainon smiled behind Krateros’ back as the old man turned to leave. “For all his questionable judgements, and his unwillingness to listen when I have spoken reason, I am glad that he did not heed me when I advised him about you.”

Phainon chuckled and twisted his head to look over his shoulder. “Oh, so Kremnoan sentimentality is allowed?”

Krateros huffed, loudly, indignant, and hurried away to manage the crew without another word.

“I’m glad too,” Phainon whispered to the chimera.

“Awoo!”

Chapter End Notes

Just so every knows, I have had a list in my notes of every character that is doomed to die and WHEN they will die from the very beginning. I KNEW that Hephaestion would be fiiiine but it was so endearing all the same at how many of you all commented in horror begging for him to be okay. It's funny because he's probably the only one disappointed that he didn't get to perish in glorious combat befitting a Kremnoan warrior.

Chapter Summary

No new tags? I personally find losing a home to be traumatic but it's already been mentioned in this fic so I'm not going to tag it

The evacuation doesn't go as smoothly as they hoped and Phainon finds someone who was almost left behind

Chapter Notes

TWO LOVELY PEOPLE HAVE BLESSED ME AND THIS FIC WITH FANART NOW. This is a literal dream come true so now I am going to share: Link - Lissain Link - Yanli1ruu My Pirate agenda is spreading :)

Convincing the Kremnoan Settlement that evacuation was the only option in the face of impending danger came with a sobering revelation. Phainon had already anticipated the language barrier. His Kremnoan was still laughably atrocious, even with extra help from Ptolemy and Peucesta, practicing exactly what he needed to say to the Kremnoan people. But when he finally stood before those who gathered at the dock, Phainon remembered that “captain” did not mean “Prince”, nor did he want it to. Mydei entrusted the ship and his people to him, but the farmer’s son was not of noble birth, nor did the settlement see him the way the crew did: Kremnoan in spirit.

As he stumbled over his words, speaking to Empousa and Daidalos, trying to remember every syllable with confidence, it slowly sunk in just how out of his depth Phainon really was. A crowd had gathered, eager for news of the battle, and met him with resounding disappointment and thinly veiled disgust.

Who was this Okheman that stood in the place of their Crown Prince, stumbling over words in a language he barely understood to demand they leave their home? Even when he tried to go off script, begging and pleading with more heartfelt words, they struggled to accept the shock of the crew’s bitter return. He could not tell them about the Coreflame of Strife, lest they tear themselves apart to get to it, to try and become its master out of fear of the impending Tide. He could not tell them Mydei’s final words in full, knowing they would not believe him. And Phainon struggled to admit to them that he was wrong, the Tide was not pushed back as they believed, and for that hubris, their people would suffer.

Krateros, dutiful, grumpy, highly respected, Krateros, was the one that rallied the people. He stood beside Phainon and spoke to them loudly in Kremnoan in words simple enough for Phainon to understand.

He stood at Phainon’s shoulder on the dock, vouched for him as a man who was Kremnoan at heart, hand chosen by Mydeimos the Undying. He reminded them of Phainon’s strength in the arena, spoke to his courage and tenacity serving the ship, and then he repeated the order: the settlement must evacuate or perish. There could be no valorous death against a foe that tears from them their identity, not yet. The old veteran did not mince words, he did not hide from them the danger, nor their limited timeframe, and urged them to spread the message to the city. If there were any doubts, he invited them to settle the grievance with their spears, a challenge that none dared rise to meet.

With the crew’s help, word spread like wildfire through wheat and packing began in earnest. The Kremnoans had two ships, the Chryseus Leo, and a merchant ship that they used to trade in faraway markets. The latter was a large trireme, commandeered a few years prior but with limited capacity for defense. She was not built for speed despite her oars and was wider and longer than the Leo, with fewer decks and sails.

Her primary cargo was left in the shipyard; stolen goods were no longer the priority over people and necessities. Even as half the city debated the validity of the threat, Perdikkas and Ptolemy worked with Empousa to send supplies across the sound to the mainland via their merchant ship, sailing back and forth at all hours.

Phainon personally helped everywhere he could, something that got easier when he was finally free of the sling. He couldn’t lift heavy things but there were plenty of ways to help, especially when Krateros took over the coordinating. The people listened to the leader of the former Godshield Brigade, they recognized him as a local hero, but not once did he ever try to assume command, deferring to Phainon at every opportunity to show the people that the Okheman was worthy of the same respect. It was during this time, meeting with local leaders, veterans, and helping pillars of the community, that Phainon realized how adaptable the Kremnoan people were and how prepared they already were for this outcome.

A lifetime of hope and experience had left them without permanent roots. Phainon saw with every passing Entry Hour of preparation that the Kremnoans had been waiting for the chance to leave. For many adults it was simply a habit formed after years of military campaigns to not put down roots, to be ready to follow their King or Titan on long excursions across the ocean at a moment’s notice. But overall, they as a people had never seen this island as the final destination for the sons and daughters of Kremnos, especially with their Crown Prince returned to them. There had always been an eagerness lurking under the streets for Mydeimos to take up the crown and lead them back to their homeland. To send them instead to shelter under the protection of a foreign god, they viewed as a temporary step on a long road home.

That preparation and willingness to work together as a people saved most of them when the Black Tide arrived ahead of schedule. The fog engulfed the northern half of the island in the dead of night, spreading rapidly like a tsunami, turning all those who had stayed to keep watch. The speed at which the Tide poured over the Kremnoans was unprecedented, slowing only as the fog broke against the inland hills, and even then, still it crawled with hungry purpose. Phainon and the rest of the city were awoken in the night to a light from the North as fire licked at the forest and illuminated the mountainside, bearing down on the city as those poor souls that had been claimed by this eldritch enemy stormed the streets to meet their ends on their former comrade’s spears.

The last of the evacuation began in earnest. Phainon could hear distant battle cries as Kremnoans fought monsters in the streets and made use of the city planning to seal off routes, creating bottlenecks that funneled the Black Tide creatures into kill zones. A city of warriors was well prepared for combat against flesh, but the creeping Tide still flowed, driving them back to the ships even as they slew the Tide’s vanguard.

The smoke stung Phainon’s lungs as his boots clicked on the stone road. Aside from the crack and pop of the fire slowly taking this street, it was quiet. Not a soul in sight as he hurried into burning buildings, calling for any who may have been trapped in the urgency. A few he found dead in their beds, crushed by falling debris, but no one answered his call until he fell back a couple streets and then his combing paid off.

Further from the quick moving fires Phainon heard a muffled peep. It was so soft and intermittent that Phainon wasn’t sure he had heard it at first and very nearly moved on but when he closed his eyes and systematically took in each sound, filtering through the noises of destruction he heard a tiny whimper.

“Is there someone there?” he called, sticking to Kremnoan.

A gasp. His head whipped around in the direction of the sound.

The alleyway was a tight squeeze, even without his armor, Phainon’s broad shoulders had to twist sideways to fit and his chest and back scraped against opposing walls as he crept between the two buildings. The glow of the fires was only just beginning to spill over the top of the opposing home, raining tiny embers and ash into a small, open clearing between several homes. Children had built a little fort here, old flags and thrown away sheets were stretched over lopsided sticks for cover and a collection of toy swords leaned against one wall.

Phainon squatted down and peeled back the fabric of the tent to peer inside and very nearly lost an eye.

“Whoa!” he yelped as he leaned away from the wooden sword. The point of it chased him backwards, swinging wildly at his outstretched hands, slapping his forearms, his fingers, and wrists when Phainon’s back hit the wall. He snatched the swinging weapon, holding it by the dull ‘blade’ while the child fought to free it from his grasp.

“Hey, hey, it’s okay!” They didn’t understand and let go of the sword to throw themselves at Phainon instead. Little fists punched at his thighs and groin until he managed to catch a wrist and gently pulled the child away before any real damage could be done. Still, they struggled in his firm grip.

In the dim light, it was hard to tell if the child was a boy or a girl. They had chin length, mousy brown hair that was matted with ash, dark eyes, and were dressed like most other children Phainon had seen around town in a rough, sleeveless tunic. Mud and dust were smeared on every inch of exposed skin aside from two tear tracks down each cheek, already long dried.

Furious, they babbled in Kremnoan, presumably demanding that Phainon let them go while they whined, but the words were too slurred and Phainon was too new to the language to have any hope of understanding.

“Hey, it’s okay,” he tried again, dimly aware of the fire above, steadily reaching down the walls. The smoke was starting to settle in the cramped space, so he lowered himself to sit on the ground to buy some time.

The kid was still yelling at him, slapping him with stress in that small voice. Phainon could hear the rasp of a dry throat under the babbles and feel blunt nails trying to tear at the skin above his bracers. When the little kid managed to cut him, he winced but held on. The gold startled the child who ceased fighting to admire the new distraction when it glittered on their fingertips in the orange light.

Phainon gently let go when the kid stopped fighting. He let the toy fall to the ground and they seemed to recognize the truce in the action, taking the opportunity to retreat and keep a safe distance from this stranger.

“Come with me?” he asked.

The child looked up at him and then back to their fort. They crouched down to get their wooden sword from the ground but didn’t use it to hit him this time. Instead, the kid flinched and pointed it at one of the alleyways when part of a roof collapsed into the gap, sealing off one of the fort’s escape routes.

Sweat dripped down the back of Phainon’s neck and beaded on his brow. This narrow side yard was heating up fast and the ceiling of smoke was getting lower. Distantly, Phainon heard a warning horn, the first of two from Peucesta.

“What’s your name?”

The child babbled back in Kremnoan and Phainon gave up. He would need a translator for sure, his own sentences were missing the proper words, so he tried to keep it simple.

“Help me?” Phainon asked. He pretended to be scared of the fire, leaning away from it and covering his eyes, and the child reached out to put a hand on his arm.

They babbled again and then grabbed his hand to pull him towards another alley. It was wider than the one he had come from and full of heavy, black smoke that left him at the mercy of this child until they were on the street and the rest of the roof slid into the gap behind them.

Phainon didn’t wait for permission this time. He scooped the kid up in his arms and started running, lungs complaining with every step. At first the child protested, yelling at him and trying to slap his face. That wooden sword smacked the side of his head repeatedly while he tried to orient himself downhill towards the ship.

He slid around a corner, and a massive paw swatted him out of the road. Phainon and the kid were sent flying and fortunately landed in a fabric stall with Phainon taking the brunt of the blow. The child was holding tightly to his chest now, stunned by the very sudden appearance of a monster.

Kremnoan children were trained from birth to be warriors, it was a cultural thing to shrug off fear and pain even at this age, but Dark Sun Gryphons were a league of their own. The monster’s screech made the kid yell and bury their face in Phainon’s shirt and while they didn’t cry, their grip was white knuckled.

He wrapped an arm under the kid to hold them close while he staggered back to standing, no easy feat with the slip of silks underfoot, the soreness of his recently healed wound, and the ragged ache of his burning lungs. The gryphon was already advancing, swooping in at them wings wide and mane sharp. Phainon dodged at the last second and the Tide monster slammed into the stall, quickly becoming tangled and buying them precious time.

“I need to put you down,” Phainon said in Okheman, knowing the child probably didn’t understand his words but hopefully understood the action when he bent down and loosened his grip. The child scrambled to hold on tighter, wrapping their arms around his neck and their legs around his waist. The wooden sword smacked against the back of Phainon’s head when he tried to dislodge them and by then the monster was lunging again.

Phainon instinctually called for his sword, but nothing happened. The broken hilt was still in Castrum Kremnos, pieces of the blade scattered across the crater under the Blade of Fury. His thoughts drifted to Mydei as he sprang sideways away from the gryphon. It slammed into the building behind them, showering the street with plaster and debris. Phainon covered the child’s head as they screamed, more from the shock than fear.

What would Mydei do right now? Phainon tried to picture the Kremnoan standing here in the street alongside him, ready to fight. He could picture those broad shoulders and the flex of his biceps. Mydei would curl his fingers, halfway to a fist, and widen his stance with a pointed taunt.

Let me show you how it’s done, Deliverer.

When the gryphon shrugged off the stone and turned again, Phainon stood his ground. The child turned enough to watch, wide-eyed as the monster ran at them, swiping with a massive paw. Phainon dodged in and to the side, narrowly avoiding those sharp claws to get in close enough to slam his fist directly into the gryphon’s flat face with an angry shout.

There was a moment when time seemed to stop, the smack to what Phainon hoped was the monster’s nose had the creature stumbling while it processed what happened. Mydei surely would have done the same… but Mydei wore gauntlets and had more experience fighting with his fists. The skin on Phainon’s knuckles split with the blow and he felt the vibrations all the way through his arm to his shoulder with a tickle that made his teeth grind together.

It was the child that started the clock again. With one arm still wrapped around Phainon’s neck they leaned back and slapped the gryphon with the wooden sword with a brave thunk. The gryphon reared, and the child swiped again but Phainon was already moving. He put his hand on the child’s back to support them and raced away.

The gryphon pursued, swiping at his heels and occasionally leaping over Phainon’s head to cut off any retreat. Every time, Phainon found a way to evade, dodging down side streets and once, he successfully ran along the wall around the gryphon, something he wished Mydei could’ve seen.

The horn of Peucesta’s second warning reverberated through the air, comfortingly close. Phainon dipped between two buildings to run along the shore. It was more open along the wharf, no more hiding from the gryphon, but more importantly it brought the beast and himself into eyeshot of the crew. Phainon took the turn onto the dock just a tiny bit too fast and nearly threw himself and the child into the water, narrowly keeping on track as they surged towards the ship. He could see the crew ready to pull the ramp up behind them and then the dock shook.

The gryphon failed on the turn, claws tearing into the wooden dock and ripping it free from the shore. The monster flailed, tearing out planks as it dragged itself after them while its back half splashed helplessly in the water below. A younger Phainon would’ve surely faltered on that listing dock, but compared to a ship during a storm…

He leaped onto the ramp taking it in two strides to roll onto the deck, removing himself from the line of fire as a volley of arrows and one bright gunshot whistled on their way to the depths with the sinking, dying gryphon.

Phainon curled around the kid. They were shaking, holding tightly to him with a racing heartbeat, but not crying or yelling. Krateros was already shouting for the ship to get underway, and the sails above fluttered as they unfurled and caught the wind. The deck was already packed with people and Phainon knew that the hold wasn’t any better. The last of the city was on board, ready for the ferry to the mainland where the others were waiting, already organizing the caravan for the upcoming exodus.

“Phainon!” Ptolemy dropped to one knee beside Phainon and immediately got his hand whacked by a toy sword.

The child babbled at him and Ptolemy’s brow wrinkled.

“Can you understand… her?” Phainon asked. He had to lean back a little to see her face better but in the lights hanging around the ship, it was easier to tell that this fierce, courageous child of Strife was a girl.

“She has baby voice but yeah.” Ptolemy got swatted again and this time he grabbed the sword and scolded her in her native tongue, “stop that! I am not your enemy!”

She fought to get her weapon back and he let her have it which calmed her down a little bit, enough to look around and stress. Phainon sat up with her and she squirmed to get comfortable in his lap, propping herself up on her knees on his thighs to look around with increasing concern. She mumbled to herself while she carefully took in the chaos of the deck, still clinging tightly to Phainon’s shirt with her good hand. A couple of very small babies were crying and there was a general buzz of people, to an overstimulated child it was probably a lot but then again, this was a Kremnoan child. She was probably desensitized to loud noises as an infant, in preparation for the cacophony of combat.

“Do you see your parents?” Ptolemy asked her and she shook her head and settled back down, retreating from Ptolemy to lean against Phainon’s chest with her toy sword still swinging wildly around while she got comfortable.

“She was near the Tide line,” Phainon reported, “in a residential district.”

“What’s your name?”

She shook her head and leaned into Phainon.

“Phainon, will you ask her?”

He struggled with the pronunciation but repeated the question and she reluctantly babbled something.

“Ask her about her parents and her age.” Ptolemy helped him get the syllables right, while the girl was warming up to the bookworm. She still didn’t answer when Ptolemy asked but she was starting to smile mischievously waiting for Phainon to repeat the words she already recognized from her kinsman’s lips.

Phainon stumbled over the words, but she still answered, and Ptolemy understood. He rubbed his eyes. “Her name is Chironome, she’s five. Give me a bit to track down her parents.”

“Is there someone that can take care of her until we find them?” Phainon asked and they both looked down at where this little girl fiddled with her sword. She didn’t understand them when they spoke Okheman, but Phainon got the feeling she wouldn’t listen to the Kremnoan either.

“Maybe when we meet up with the others.”

Chironome waved at Ptolemy to get his attention and started talking to him again. Her little voice was still strained from the smoke, and she kept pausing to cough, but she motioned eagerly to Phainon and tried to sound authoritative while she told a story.

“Did you understand what she said?” Ptolemy asked.

Phainon shook his head. “It’s hard to understand when she doesn’t enunciate.”

“She says that you were very brave but that you still need a lot of help but it’s okay because she’s going to take care of you since you asked so nicely before and that’s what heroes do. She also says that you need to get a sword because your punch wasn’t good.” Her little voice suddenly got louder as she added very quickly another string of words. “…you can’t have her sword because it’s her favorite. You need your own sword.”

She had twisted in his lap so she could rub Phainon’s arm, offering comfort, he realized. He smiled at her reassuringly and she smiled and patted his cheek like one would pet a dog, proud of her ability to make him feel better.

“I can keep an eye on her until we get across the sound,” he offered.

“Maybe get out of the way while you do,” suggested Ptolemy. He turned to the little girl to say, “this is Phainon, you did a good job saving him, but he needs more help, can you keep helping him?” Chironome nodded. “Good, can you take him down there to the doctor?” Ptolemy pointed to the stairs that led below and after a very short nervous gasp she found her courage and nodded again.

Determined, she got up and brandished her sword in one hand, narrowly avoiding smacking Ptolemy in the head, and with the other she grabbed Phainon’s hand.

“This way, Fine!” she ordered with a solid tug, still slurring a bit but she was getting easier to understand the more he focused on her particular brand of little kid accent.

“Tell Hephaestion I said hi.” Ptolemy patted Phainon on the back and then hurried to help the others with the sails.

Chironome was short for a five-year-old, or so Phainon assumed, while he loved children and had on occasion helped babysit back in Okhema, his grasp on child raising was notably limited. He just loved the whimsy of kids, their wild ideas, the silly things they said, the sort of imagination they still retained. They were joy and curiosity with infinite potential, and this little girl had the added bonus of being fearless.

She took her job very seriously, pulling Phainon along and swinging her sword around to clear the way. When Chironome wasn’t sure where to go she looked up at him expectantly until he pointed and then she was back to pulling him along and yelling at everyone that dared cross her path.

“Move! Fine needs help! Move!” she shouted in Kremnoan.

Phainon mumbled soft apologies any time someone got slapped by the sword, but the crew were mostly amused, shook their heads, and got back to work after letting them pass until she finally found the infirmary door. It wasn’t locked but it was guarded by Leonnius who was sitting on a barrel just outside. He saw them coming and was trying so hard not to laugh.

The runner was healing nicely but his ankle was still tightly wrapped to keep it stiff. With his limited mobility, guard duty was the best Leonnius could hope for until the sprain healed. He raised a hand in greeting and very nearly lost it to the swing of the toy.

“Fine, needs to see the doctor,” she announced.

“Fine?” Leonnius bit his lip to hold back the laugh.

“It’s a long story,” Phainon said cheerfully, albeit a little raspy from the smoke inhalation.

“Okay, okay, little warrior,” Leonnius told her in Kremnoan, “you can go inside.” He reached up to grab the latch so he could push the door open for her.

She started to walk in, stopped so suddenly that Phainon very nearly tripped over her, and turned to say, “thank you.”

The second they stepped inside the infirmary, Chironome forgot that she had a job. She gasped so loudly that Phainon thought she might have been hurt and then followed up with a high-pitched squeal, startling the locals as she rushed to Hephaestion’s bedside to croon over Fig Stew. Alarmed by the sudden assault and the reaching hand, the chimera hissed and fluffed himself up, turning sideways to look bigger and hide the coreflame behind him. Hephaestion’s quick reflexes saved the little girl from a nasty bite when he caught her hand enroute to those fluffy cheeks.

Phainon was a second behind, grabbing her by the back of her tunic to hoist her aloft. Rather than being indignant or upset, Chironome squealed happily at that too and laughed while he bounced her up and down to keep her distracted.

“What in Nikador’s name is going on?” Perdikkas asked from one of the cabinets.

“Lord Phainon?” Castorice inquired with a tilt of her head. She blinked from her chair where she was peeling an apple. Two more waited in her lap but she had almost forgotten the small knife and half prepared fruit now that this new hellion was loose in the infirmary.

“I’m sorry, I didn’t know she would react like that,” he managed. He swapped back to Kremnoan to ask, “Will you be good if I put you down?”

She tilted her head in confusion and Perdikkas sighed. “Phainon, you got the pronunciation… hold on.” The doctor put the bandages he had in his hands back in the basket in the cabinet and closed the door before he wandered over to repeat Phainon’s question. It sounded notably different from how Phainon was saying it.

She nodded and started excitedly talking to the doctor, talking too fast and too slurred for Phainon to follow but Hephaestion chuckled and Perdikkas nodded politely. Very slowly, while she still rambled, Phainon set her back down on her feet. She was so engrossed in her storytelling that she didn’t even notice.

“You can’t pet him if you are holding the sword,” Perdikkas told her firmly.

She stomped her foot and started scolding Perdikkas, trying to explain something to him in earnest while Phainon crept around her to go to Hephaestion’s side. The man was well enough to be propped up on a gentle recline, sitting up to eat simple foods. His breathing was still very rough and wet but that was to be expected.

Hephaestion’s chest injury would’ve been fatal if Hyacine had not been standing next to him at the time. Both doctors had given Phainon the list of medical issues that the man had to overcome but it mostly boiled down to damaged lungs, ribs, and a few smaller organs. Little Ica had tended to him day and night after they still almost lost him in recovery, but the man was a fighter and refused to perish in such a shameful way.

“Ptolemy says hi,” he reported while he gently pet Fig Stew. The chimera was still fluffed up and unhappy but when Phainon’s hand gently patted the raised fur back down, it at least didn’t stand back up.

Hephaestion snorted. “What’s with the kid?”

“I was doing a last pass, looking for survivors and found her near the Tide line,” he explained, “Ptolemy is going to track down her parents when we get across the sound.”

Phainon gave Fig Stew one last pat and then reached over the little body to place his palm on the coreflame. It was snug between Hephaestion’s side and the chimera, safe and warm.

“Earlier tonight it went dark,” Hephaestion reported in a hushed voice, “it flared back to life quickly, but…”

Phainon’s eyes grew wide, and he snapped his head to look over at Castorice. Her eyes were a little darker than usual as she met his with a slow swallow.

“Lord Mydei is fighting very hard,” she said and Phainon’s heart sunk into his belly. The Tide’s surge, the coreflame losing its light… How many lives had Mydei already lost to buy them time? How many did he have left?

“Phainon, can she pet Fig Stew?” Perdikkas asked from behind them and Phainon scooted over to make space.

Chironome was much quieter now, she had surrendered her weapon and was trying to be more respectful of the chimera’s personal wants.

“Let him sniff you,” Hephaestion ordered, and she held her hand out.

Fig Stew leaned forward to sniff and when she stayed quiet, he gave her fingers an accepting lick. Chironome reached out to pat his head. Encouraged by the purrs, Phainon let out his held breath and went to sit down on a chair beside Castorice. Compared to the fight at Castrum Kremnos this hadn’t been as physically taxing but Phainon was emotionally spent. He had avoided any traumatic responses, but his heart still ached at the familiarity of a burning home, of Black Tide creatures tearing through streets. And knowing the high cost of every passing quint.

Castorice gently put her hand on his arm to get his attention and when he turned his tired expression to her, she held an apple slice to his lips. He happily took the sweet fruit, chewing slowly as he sank into his chair far enough to rest his head against the back of it to close his eyes and just rest for a moment.

The ship swayed underfoot, he could feel it in his wide stance as he braced himself to stay seated. An ache was starting in his hand, cool air stinging his knuckles where they had split. Sweetness on tongue lingered from the apple slice and even seated apart he could feel the warmth of Mydei’s presence in the room.

Phainon may have fallen asleep if it wasn’t for tiny hands on his thigh. He kept his eyes closed as Chironome climbed into his lap again, her knees dug into the meat of his legs enough to make him wince, but he kept his hands folded on his chest to resist the instinct to remove her. She settled with a quiet oof and babbled at him.

“Fine, Fine,” she demanded and he hummed in response, only opening his eyes when he felt that sweetness against his lips again.

She had seen Castorice feeding him and decided that her charge still needed help, hopeless as he was. One of her hands was on his chest so she could lean up enough to reach, the other holding the apple slice so tightly that juice dripped over her fingers to drop onto his chin. Phainon obediently parted his lips, and she alternated between shoving apples into his mouth and politely asking Castorice for more as they tag teamed his care.

“Do you understand her?” he asked Castorice right before a hand on his cheek demanded his attention again.

“Not in words,” she admitted. The knife made a soft, crisp sound as it glided through the fruit’s flesh. Cas handed the slice over, but this one went into Chironome’s mouth, now that Phainon had been fed, she was realizing her own hunger. “Children of this age can be surprisingly generous. They long for connection and are keenly aware of what is happening around them. She saw me give you a bite of the apple and wanted to be the one to take care of you.” Castorice offered a slice to Hephaestion, but he politely declined with a raised hand.

“Do you need me to look at that?” Perdikkas asked over his shoulder and Phainon followed where he was pointing to his knuckles.

“Oh, no, it’ll be alright.”

“Mydei makes it look easy,” the doctor teased and Phainon’s smile turned sad, at least until Chironome gently took his face in both of her hands, scooting up his chest to reach.

“You are okay,” she said in her baby voice. His heart lurched a little at her tenderness and he really believed it even when she added, very seriously, “but you won’t be if you don’t get a sword.”

Hephaestion started coughing when a laugh got stuck in his damaged chest and Perdikkas hurried to check on him while he mouthed ‘I’ll tell you later’ to Castorice.

Oblivious to the chaos around them, Chironome wiggled off Phainon, crashed her way back to her feet and fetched her wooden sword from where Perdikkas had put it on the desk. She brought it back to him and put it in his lap with reverence. “You can share mine,” she offered and then seriously again, “for now.”

Phainon put his hand over hers and smiled. “Thank you,” he said, and it sounded correct.

“I’ll get her cleaned up, Lord Phainon,” Castorice offered, “if you would like to rest.”

“I can translate for you, Cas,” Perdikkas added.

“I can do it,” Phainon insisted.

Perdikkas roughly shoved Phainon back down when he tried to get up and Chironome punched Perdikkas for it.

“He needs to go down for a nap! Or else he won’t be able to fight anymore!” the doctor huffed at her. The child contemplated that and then she also pushed against Phainon until he finally relented with a wave of his hand.

“Alright, alright, just a quick nap.”

Perdikkas scooped up Chironome who looked very displeased to be in someone else’s arms. “We’ll wake you when we make it across the channel,” he promised.

The chair wasn’t comfortable, but he was planning on only closing eyes for a few minutes. Phainon nodded and leaned back again. “Okay… thanks.”

The last thing he heard was the quiet click of the infirmary door closing and the soft purr of a content chimera.

Chapter End Notes

Note: This chapter is so late because I ended up playing phone tag with my niece, my father, my mother, my sister-in-law, and my brother doing research for this chapter cause I could not remember what five-year-old kids were like. Her name is from a readable in game. Super, super side character but I did try to give her the same personality as the NPC so fun easter egg.
