chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

No new tags

Phainon and Krateros get a chance to bond

Chapter Notes

Notes: Don't mind me trying to very sneakily adjust the chapter count. I think this is the last time I will have to do it, I say hopefully knowing I have a lot of plot left ;w;

Phainon dreamed of Mydei. Like most dreams it was hazy around the edges, fluid and non-descript. The environment around them didn’t matter, the context of the company ceased to be, but Mydei was there beside him. They didn’t talk, didn’t touch, they just sat beside each other, smelling the sea breeze and the warmth of the distant sun.

Peace.

“Phainon,” Mydei said, as gently as he could with that natural purr in his voice. He turned to see him, but Mydei was blurry and fading away at the edges.

“Phainon…” Mydei repeated and then Phainon was gasping awake. He blinked a few times and started to sit up, the immediate ache in his back and neck reminding him of how stupid it was to fall asleep in a chair.

“Phainon,” Perdikkas repeated as he put a hand on his shoulder to stop him from rising, holding a finger to his lips before pointing at Phainon’s chest. Chironome was curled up there, sound asleep around the coreflame of Strife. Someone had covered them both with a blanket at some point while they were sleeping.

He slowly reached up to wrap his arms around her and the coreflame so he could reposition for the sake of his aching back without dumping this precious cargo onto the floor.

“The ship is already unloaded,” the doctor reported with a whisper and Phainon tried not to jump with alarm.

“Why didn’t you wake me?”

“You needed the rest. So did she.”

Phainon looked down at the little girl. They had found her clean clothes, an oversized old shirt that went just past her knees and tied at the waist with a bit of extra cord, and wiped the grime from her arms, legs, and face. Without the ash in her hair, the hue was less brunette than Phainon had originally thought, rather walking the fine line between a light brown and a dusty blonde.

He gently pulled the blanket up over her shoulder after it slipped, hiding her from the dangers of the world. Not that he needed to. Her toy sword was on the chair beside him, ready to be pointed at any monsters with the courage of a child that had not yet learned to fear those things that go bump in the night. Or perhaps her parents had already quelled those fears in a way that only a father or mother could.

“When we came back,” Perdikkas whispered, “she saw you getting restless in your sleep. Hephaestion told her to bring you the coreflame to ease your nightmares and she insisted on supervising until you were at peace.”

“I don’t remember any nightmares,” Phainon admitted, but this was probably why.

Mydei’s coreflame flickered warmly in her arms and Phainon wondered what he would think if he knew that little hands were holding this part of his heart. Did Mydei like children?

“Perdikkas, does Mydei like kids?” he asked softly.

“I think so,” the doctor admitted, “we don’t get a lot of chances to meet them when they’re this age but he’s very good with the infants.”

“Infants?”

“As the Crown Prince, many Kremnoans seek his blessing for their children. Even if he has never placed much value in such traditions, I’ve never seen Mydei decline, and he always holds them with such care. Someone who does not like children wouldn’t hold them with such soft hands and eyes.”

The tender image of that wild lion cradling a tiny person in his gauntlets made Phainon smile.

“I need to get her to the caravan,” Phainon murmured after a quiet moment, “will you grab the coreflame?”

Perdikkas’ steady hands surgically removed the coreflame from Chironome and she stayed sleeping, fussing only long enough to turn more into Phainon’s chest to drool on his shirt with her head tilted back. The doctor gently squeezed her wooden toy sword in between them to take its place and Phainon mouthed, ‘thank you.’ He wrapped the blanket around her nice and tight, even pulling it up over her head like a hood to keep out the early morning chill, and stood up with her cradled carefully in his arms.

Beside him the doctor was tucking Mydei’s coreflame back in beside Hephaestion who was out cold, sleeping heavily. If not for the very slow rise and fall of his chest, Phainon may have assumed the worst.

He carried the little girl past the working crew. It was still very late; dawn had not yet begun to paint the sky. Black smoke would’ve hidden the rosy and lavender hues anyway. Across the sound their island still burned and glowed but the sea beneath them had yet to turn murky. The Tide would take some time to chew through the settlement before it came to crash against the mainland. It gave them time to rest.

Half the crew were sleeping, the other half were loading the Chryseus Leo for the journey to Okhema, moving quietly so as not to disturb the others. Down the ramp it was a similar story. The Kremnoans were trying to organize, letting as many people sleep as could be spared while others packed carts, packs, and struggled to take inventory. The heaviest items were loaded into two different trains of carts to be pulled by two of four dromas. The long-necked gentle giants were dozing in their harnesses, grumbling softly as they awaited the morn.

Phainon scanned through piles of supplies, sleeping people, and hurried runners in the dark trying to find someone he recognized when he heard his name.

“Deliverer,” Krateros greeted once more as he approached.

“Krateros.”

“We are very nearly finished here and should depart with haste.”

Phainon pulled the blanket back to show Krateros Chironome, and the old man’s harsh gaze immediately melted. He leaned in to put his hand on her forehead; to pet the child ever so gently the way a doting grandfather might fawn over their first grandchild.

“And who have you brought to me today?” he asked in a slightly higher pitch and Phainon tilted his head in confusion at the question. Krateros made it sound like this was a habit of his to scoop up small children or other critters to present to the man for approval.

“Her name is Chironome,” Phainon whispered, “Ptolemy was supposed to find her parents amongst the evacuated. Have you seen him?”

“He was speaking to Daidolos when last I saw him.” Krateros’ brows pinched and his tone turned serious once more. He scratched absentmindedly as his beard before saying, “I recall one of the crew mentioning a newborn daughter named Chironome. This was many years ago when we left Castrum Kremnos after Eurypon’s death.”

“Five years ago,” Phainon observed, “she told us she was five years old.”

“Pray that I am wrong,” Krateros lamented, “He was one of those that gave their lives a week ago when we retrieved the coreflame.”

Phainon winced. “A mother then?”

Krateros contemplated that and then motioned for Phainon to follow without answering. He must not have known. Despite Phainon’s best efforts to bond with every crewmate there were a sizeable number of them that kept their port lives private, something that the others respected without judgement.

They walked swiftly over uneven ground. The beach gave way quickly to jagged rocks and then to uneven plains, where many were resting. That was where they found Ptolemy, still talking to Daidolos. He greeted them with a wave and then they quieted when they saw Chironome.

“Ptolemy did you-?”

“Yes, and it’s not good news.”

Phainon rubbed the little girl’s arm with his thumb, a gentle back and forth to offer comfort that she was too asleep to realize she needed.

“Her father was Militiades,” he reported and Phainon recognized the name from the list of those they lost in their return to Castrum Kremnos. “And her mother was on duty tonight in the northern guard towers, she didn’t make it.”

His heart dropped at the news. This little girl was going to wake an orphan.

“She was left alone? Does she have any other family? A neighbor?” he asked.

Ptolemy shook his head. “Her mother was working short shifts, leaving after her child was put to bed and returning before she woke.”

“My lords, with respect, I can take her for now,” Daidolos offered, “I know this child. Chironome has been attending classes at the arena for over a year now. She will recognize me as her teacher, and I can care of her until we find a family or unit that will take her.”

“A unit? She’s so young to already be learning to fight,” Phainon wondered aloud before remembering how different Kremnoans were. Ptolemy was the one that told him Kremnoans began learning how to fight from the moment they could hold a spear.

“This is no strange thing,” Krateros confirmed what he had already recalled, “Kremnoan children are stronger than most, it is important to begin training them as early as possible to refine that strength and courage.”

Chironome stirred in his arms, blinking her eyes and squirming to get closer to Phainon. He bounced her a little, swaying gently before holding her out to Daidolos who stepped forward to take her in his strong arms.

The change was immediate. She whimpered once and then shouted at Daidolos, something in sleepy nonsense speech. Chironome fussed and fought to get free, reaching for Phainon again. Her toy sword fell on the ground as she kicked and protested. Phainon bent down to fetch it while she finished waking up enough to realize she recognized the man holding her now and settled into an irritable stew while she babbled sleepily.

“You cannot go with him,” Daidolos said firmly, switching to Kremnoan.

More mumbles, urgent, stressed, and insistent.

“He does not need your help.”

Chironome didn’t cry but her bottom lip stuck out and her whole body started to shake like she wanted to weep and simply couldn’t. When the pouting didn’t work, she tried to hit Daidolos who caught her wrist and held it tightly the entire way to the cart nearby. He set her inside and scolded her, more like a drill sergeant than a father. It had Phainon second guessing his decision, but Krateros and Ptolemy didn’t seem bothered and it wasn’t his place to try and change their culture.

Phainon walked up to the cart and peered over the edge to where Chironome was sitting with her knees pulled up to her chest and her arms wrapped around her legs. The shirt looked even bigger with her curled up so tightly, head down, hair splayed wildly over her knees while she sulked. The blanket pooled around her, bunched up around her back where it fell.

“Chironome,” he called gently, and she looked up with a tiny gasp and hurried to her feet so she could wrap her arms around his neck, hugging him so tightly he was sure that she would hang from him above the ground if he pulled away now.

She baby talked at him, something like, “I don’t want to go, Fine.”

He gently reached up and pried one of her hands away so he could hand her the sword. “You have to protect them,” he tried to say, and it was hard to tell if he said it correctly because she smacked him in the head lightly with the sword and then leaned forward to press her forehead to his.

Phainon wasn’t sure if she really understood the Kremnoan farewell or if she was mimicking what she had seen adults do. Chironome could have simply been tired and wanted that physical connection. With one of her hands holding the sword, there was only one left to cling to the high collar of his shirt.

The last time he had done this was with Mydeimos. There were things he didn’t say back then, things he wanted to say, needed to say, and just didn’t have the time.

He very carefully pried the other little hand away and stepped back before she could grab him again. She reached, leaning over the side of the cart and called for him with increasing panic that hurt to hear. Daidolos reached out a massive hand to block her from Phainon, before she could leap from the cart and potentially hurt herself.

Upset, she threw her sword, and it clipped Phainon’s shoulder hard enough to bruise before it clattered to the ground, sticking in a patch of sand before the weight of the hilt flattened it in the grass.

“Chironome…” Phainon sighed. He again crouched down to retrieve the weapon but when he stepped forward she had already turned away to pout, yelling between her fingers.

Phainon looked at Ptolemy who politely relayed, “she says she doesn’t want it anymore.”

“Okay,” he said softly, turning to look at the top of her head. The rest of her had sunk back into the cart to be angry on her own. “Then I’ll keep it until she’s ready again.”

“’The blade itself incites to deeds of violence,’” Ptolemy quoted as he watched Phainon tuck the toy into his belt as though it was a holy weapon. “I am sure she will find another when the time comes, but this is a time for tools of rebuilding rather than conquest, I suppose.”

There was a solemn silence between the men for a breath at that thought and then Phainon turned to Daidolos with last minute reminders. “Keep moving inland, as far from the coastline as you can get until everyone is inside the range of the Dawn Device. Don’t go all the way to Okhema. I will send a messenger when it’s safe to send representation to the city.”

“All will be well, Lord Phainon. We have Ptolemy’s maps to guide us.” They clasped arms and nodded to each other, not quite a formal farewell.

With Chironome’s dry sobs and the soft chirp of a nymph in his ears, Phainon turned and led the way back to the ship.

-

Phainon stood in Mydei’s spot with his torn armor in hand, still damaged from the fight with Nikador. The break in the metal pauldron would need a smith to repair, a very skilled one too. These pieces had been crafted by Chartonus, Okhema’s Master Smith. His skill could only be rivaled by the Kremnoan masters and what few of them remained were lost in the wilderness, several days of sailing behind them. The coat, also torn was thrown over the railing, leaving Phainon in his favorite shirt while he pondered the best way to fix what was broken. And no, he wasn’t just considering his clothing.

When confronted, Phainon was cheerful, albeit a little short. He was sleeping alright and still putting his best foot forward, but his thoughts drifted regularly to Mydei, still fighting, still dying, and, on occasion, to a little girl with no parents who had been the essence of courage and care in the face of overwhelming loss.

“Captain,” Krateros said behind him and Phainon glanced over his shoulder.

“Is something the matter, Krateros?”

“Ever since we left the young Prince behind you have seemed less yourself.”

Phainon tilted his head and turned more fully to the man. “…are you worried about me?”

“Do not misunderstand, I prefer this version of you to the carefree puppy that once wreaked havoc on this ship,” the old man admitted.

“Then why the concern?”

“Is it not my duty to tend to the needs of my captain? Perhaps you would prefer another first mate?” he huffed.

Phainon waved a hand back and forth in front of himself and put the pauldron on a crate beside the railing to give the old mentor more of the attention he deserved. “Of course not, Krateros, I value your input. What would you like me to do?”

“When Mydeimos became stagnant his mood would be diminished. I have not seen you practice your spear work since before we retrieved the Coreflame of Strife.”

“…you want me to practice my spear forms?” Phainon asked for clarification and Krateros sighed so deeply and so loudly with such a slump of his shoulders that Phainon immediately felt bad for whatever transgression he had committed in misunderstanding.

“I am inviting you to spar.”

He really didn’t mean to laugh but the words were so surprising that Phainon let out two soft barks before he realized Krateros was serious. “With you?”

The old man crossed his arms and turned his nose up to hide his wounded pride. His armor creaked as he did so, his sword was in the armory, but the decorative straps at his belt still swayed and light glinted off the clasp of his chlamys.

“Is it so difficult to believe that I am an accomplished warrior? For all your battle prowess, captain, my experience is many times that of your own.”

“I do not doubt that Krateros,” Phainon insisted, trying not to be condescending, “but I have only seen you command the others. I had assumed that your combat days were behind you.”

Krateros snorted. “My combat days will be behind me when my corpse is cooling on the battlefield.”

Phainon wanted to vocalize a wish otherwise, but the Kremnoan would probably take it as an insult and this peace between them had been nice. He didn’t want to shatter it by saying something so insensitive, which also meant the only right answer to the challenge was ‘yes.’ Anything less could be deeply offensive.

“Alright, Krateros, show me the right way to wield a spear,” Phainon ordered, and the man seemed pleased. The exercise would do him good. Even if it was just simple forms or a relaxed spar. Phainon had every intention of going easy on the old man, using the fight as a chance to practice his restraint, something that had felt a little harder to hold onto since losing Mydei.

The old man was prepared and walked only a short distance away to fetch two spears and two shields from where they rested against the railing. The upper deck was as good of a place as any for them to face each other. It was where Phainon and Mydei had spared most frequently and in the early days of Phainon’s stay, was where he had seen Mydei train with Hephaestion.

He caught the spear as it was tossed to him and twirled it experimentally to get a firm grasp of how the weight was balanced and what the weapon felt like when it moved. Daidolos’ lessons of the basics started to zoom through the forefront of Phainon’s memories as he adjusted his grip and opted to forego stretching. It was unlikely he would need it.

Krateros started to toss him a shield too but stopped at the beginning of his swing when Phainon held up a hand.

“I won’t need it,” he said confidently and Krateros raised one eyebrow.

“The spear is only one half of the weapon, the other is the shield,” he scolded, offering it again.

Still Phainon declined. “I will not need it to focus on my form.”

Krateros set the disc aside and put his own shield on his arm, tightening the straps with practiced ease. It fit perfectly, round and small and very old. The same way the younger crew had favored weapons, arms crafted for them that they had come to learn as an extension of themselves, the older crew had favored shields. The old guard had broken more weapons than Phainon had ever handled in his entire lifetime and through experience had come to appreciate the symbolism and reliability of defense. This was the same shield that Krateros had carried in Eurypon’s campaigns, when the old man had overseen the line against Okhema. Phainon distinctly remembered it from when he lost the fishing bet and had to shine all the shields in the armory. The task had become infinitely more pleasant when his appraiser’s eye realized the age, value, and craftsmanship of the shields of the old guard.

To stand across from it now…

Phainon felt the familiar tingle of excitement that preceded a fight. It would be both an honor and a horrible shame to be the one to break the relic.

“Very well,” Krateros replied calmly. When he was ready, he stood in front of Phainon with the shield held lightly in front of his belly and his spear pointed down. “Whenever you are ready, captain.”

Phainon started to pace around Krateros, surprised when the old man did not also begin pacing. Where Mydeimos would have mimicked his footwork to find an opening, Krateros did not. Instead, the veteran held still, tracking Phainon with his eyes, even when Phainon paced to Krateros’ left where his eyesight was the weakest.

It was then that Phainon experimentally lunged, jabbing at the space above the shield. The weak attack was effortlessly blocked and a very sharp point dragged across Phainon’s side, tearing his shirt and ghosting lightly over his skin, enough to be felt, but not enough to draw blood.

He bounced back and patted at the tear, looking for gold and finding only that shallow scratch. At first Phainon snorted to himself, praising his luck, but then he realized how little of a role luck had played at all. Krateros had struck with surgical precision and chosen not to punish his arrogance.

“I expected more from Mydeimos’ chosen,” Krateros lamented.

The corner of Phainon’s mouth twitched and he rushed in a little faster, swiping up as though the spear were his greatsword. The shaft clashed against the man’s own weapon and then Krateros’ spear dipped, spinning around his own in a way that forced a painful twist of his grip until the weapon pulled free entirely. It clattered on the deck and Phainon dove to retrieve it, but a heavy boot kept it pinned and sharp bronze tapped the side of his neck.

Frozen in his crouch, Phainon looked up into disappointed eyes. Krateros had the bearing of a demanding but patient father trying to coax greatness from a failing son. It made fury and fear rise in Phainon’s belly and chest. Fury at being looked down upon when he had already accumulated noble feats, not the least of which was the conquer of Nikador, and fear that perhaps Krateros was right.

“Do you think me fragile, Deliverer?” Krateros taunted. He pulled the spear away from the flutter under Phainon’s collar and moved his foot. Slowly Phainon stood back up with his own spear in hand. “Have you forgotten who trained the Crown Prince? Who trained the crew? I can feel in your pathetic attack the hubris of a foolish youth who judges only the surface of a man.”

Those two feelings combined in Phainon’s throat into humility, and he nodded. Taking those words to heart. This time when he lunged it was with the respect that Krateros deserved and a feint to Krateros’ left, to force the man to move his shield and create an opening. The veteran called Phainon’s bluff, and the shield deflected the blow meant for Krateros’ shoulder.

Still Phainon pushed, utilizing the momentum to follow the swing, treating the spear more as a lance, a style closer to the sword he was more familiar with. Krateros followed the momentum too, finally moving from his rooted stance to chase the spear rather than breaking upon it when the arc carried the blade around again. Exposed, Phainon got a close look at that legendary shield when it slammed into his face and sent him staggering.

Krateros did not allow Phainon to recover and a swipe at the Okheman’s legs had Phainon jumping right into that shield once more. To his credit, he did not fall when he stumbled, and when Krateros pushed again, he dodged every pointed jab in his retreat. The shield came around again and Phainon leaped backwards, he rolled towards the rail to give himself some space and to retrieve the shield he had originally declined.

“Better,” Krateros praised. The old man was smiling now too and Phainon caught a glimpse of the past in those aging bones. A lion does not lose his regality in his old age. When his ribs begin to show and his mane clings to him in patches, he still carries himself with the grace of majesty and a survivor’s heart. He is as deserving of admiration as the young lion that rises to take his place.

Properly armed, their clashes no longer felt quite as one-sided, but Phainon still failed to draw blood and the longer they fought under the harsh sun the more Phainon felt like the mouse trapped between paws. Every advantage he thought he had was met by experience until he found himself thinking more than relying on instinct.

Where fighting against and beside Mydeimos was a dance that Phainon felt in his soul and heart, Krateros was a puzzle to be solved. The veteran not only knew how to move with the flow of battle, but he also knew how to direct and command it. Phainon found himself needing to think multiple steps ahead to find openings that Krateros was deliberately leaving him, subtly encouraging learning until every other clouding thought fell away into nothing.

There was no room for Phainon to worry over things in the future or the past, all that mattered was solving this pattern that Krateros was weaving for him in the moment and processing the subtle corrections. Somehow, Krateros was able to defend, attack, and still find the time to use the butt of his spear to correct Phainon’s form, leaving little bruises on his ankles and wrists, even through his boots and bracers.

But for every humiliating strike, Phainon was also blessed with praise whenever he did something noteworthy from a particularly powerful, well executed jab to a rolling block, to even the use of his surroundings when he made use of the railing during a vigorous part of their bout. In this way Krateros was cultivating the good while removing the bad and doing so amid practical application. Where Daidolos would have had Phainon stop to discuss his form, Krateros simply let the man make mistakes and see the results of those mistakes as they happened to give feedback in real time.

It was exactly what Phainon had imagined training in Castrum Kremnos would be like when he read of the warrior city in his books as a child. The surge of excitement when he realized how true this was, that not only was he standing in the presence of a master, but Krateros was training him in a way that only future Kings would have been trained. This was the same way Mydei had learned, had become the warrior that made Phainon’s heart sing. It was arguably the highest honor that Phainon had received from Krateros, more so even than the veteran’s deference the day he had become the interim captain. So, when the Okheman finally dropped to one knee, exhausted, it was under the weight of that humility and gratitude.

Krateros spun his spear and tapped the butt of the weapon against the deck twice, a signal that Phainon did not yet know but from context concluded it meant the end of their training. The old man had a shine to his skin, but sweat did not bead along his brow, nor did he collapse with exhaustion. He simply moved his spear and shield to one hand so he could offer the other to Phainon.

Sweat dripped off Phainon’s nose and onto the deck when he took that hand and let himself accept the help to stand once more. The old man roughly smacked Phainon’s arm and laughed, the first real laugh that Phainon had ever heard from him.

“There may be hope for you yet, Okheman,” he praised, the title feeling affectionate, and then he walked to the railing to set his weapons aside for the time being.

Phainon followed him on shaky legs, somewhat bewildered by the man’s endurance. As soon as he set his own spear and shield beside the others, he collapsed to sit on the heavy lid of the bins that held their fishing supplies.

“How…?” he managed to squeak out around heavy breaths.

“I learned in my second tour the value of conserving energy and stamina,” Krateros explained, “no movement in combat should be wasted.”

The old man sat beside Phainon and held out his hand palm facing them so Phainon could see the subtle quiver there. It was in his knees as well, proof of exertion that Phainon took as a compliment even if it did not match his own notably worse state.

“You are on the heels of emotional exhaustion and injury as well,” Krateros reminded him.

“I didn’t just lose my home again,” Phainon said gently. There was a question there.

Krateros frowned and leaned back, he patted along the bench until he found a waterskin and after a short drink he offered it to Phainon as well. “I am not unaffected by emotional duress,” he admitted, “as I am sure you know from past experience.”

Phainon recalled the moment he returned without Mydei, how ready Krateros was to lash out and take his life in his grief. He remembered too the haste at which Krateros moved to act on his distrust and anger many times in that month of sailing before they found mutual acceptance.

“I admit that I am prone to emotional outbursts,” Krateros continued, “and I too miss Mydeimos with my entire being. To see what Kremnos has become, after witnessing her glory with my own eyes in days long past…” he trailed off but aside from a distant look, there was no sign of grieving. “Resilience comes with age and experience. It takes time to build and may falter in those moments of intense and unexpected duress, but it holds truest in the service of my brothers and sisters.”

“…that’s why you won’t take command,” Phainon realized aloud.

“I am at my very best in the service of the crown to which I have sworn the greatest of oaths, when I have left behind my own wishes in the ship’s wake.”

Phainon thought about that and then he started to laugh. It was a weak thing, exhaustion still weighing on him after an excellent fight. He stopped when Krateros’ annoyance had turned into a face of deep concern lest the veteran believe him to be a mad man.

“I’m sorry, Krateros, I just think it’s funny,” Phainon explained, “of all the people on this ship that I thought I would never be able to please, never be able to understand… Aside from Mydeimos, how is it that you are the one with whom I am the most alike?”

Krateros’ concern fell, turning more contemplative.

Phainon offered the waterskin to him and he took it, taking another drink. They passed it back and forth until it was empty and then they simply enjoyed the sounds of the sea in comfortable silence with their heads resting back against the smooth railing.

“Krateros,” Phainon said and was met with a gentle hum. “These new railings need stories to tell.”

“So they do, captain.”

“Will you teach me?”

“To tell stories?”

“To carve them,” Phainon specified.

Krateros paused, surprised that Phainon remembered from a passing comment that the old man was familiar with woodworking and carving. After a moment of consideration he grunted and said, “it would be easier to teach you to use a carving knife than a spear, hopeless as you are.”

Phainon chuckled, “I hope so, Lord Krateros. There are too many stories that need to be told.”

Chapter Summary

No new tags

Phainon tells Okhema a story

Chapter Notes

My cat made every effort to keep this chapter from happening. After that week long vacation she has been unbearably clingy

Happy FFXIV patch day to all who celebrate~ And heck that floor 99 boss~

Phainon wore every piece of his armor, even with the metal torn and the fine stitching in his cape ripped. The wear of a well-traveled journey was the only part of him that went unpolished and it was by far the most honest. Castorice and Hyacine helped him with his hair and washing his face, Anaxa went over talking points, and Peucesta helped him wash the salt and grime from his clothing to make him more presentable. When Phainon approached the gates of Okhema from the dromas road to the Path of Parting, unarmed and alone, it was with the bearing of one who had walked the world and found therein a glorious and heavy purpose.

“Are you sure you don’t want us to go with you?” Hyacine asked for the fourth time.

“Not until I know it’s safe.”

Ptolemy waved his hand dismissively. “We told that lion we were kidnapping the Heirs, they have no reason to be suspect.”

“Caenis is smarter than that,” Phainon reminded them, “if it were true, what’s to stop Castorice from freeing herself with the Hand of Death?”

The coreflame was wrapped in fine fabric and tucked in a messenger bag over Phainon’s shoulder. He walked with one hand resting on top of it to keep that precious cargo from jostling. It still didn’t feel right carrying Mydei’s heart to the Holy City and away from its proper keeper.

The irony of this lonely march was not lost on Phainon, who had dreamed of this moment ever since Aglaea had begun training him to live it. How many times had he imagined himself walking along the golden road, clad in the garments of a noble hero with a shining sword on his back and an air of undeniable righteousness? He had pictured the blood of Titans on his boots and the light-headed joy of victory as he presented the fruits of his labor to Aglaea. Her lips would’ve curled in a genuine smile, and she would whisper words of praise, bringing honor to his vow to the Flame-Chase journey. And then he would bathe in the golden waters of the Marmoreal Palace, under the watchful gaze of Kephale and the comfort of a peace hard won to wash away the aches while feasting on figs and fine meats.

“If I don’t return by Curtain-Fall Hour,” Phainon told Krateros and the barely standing Hephaestion, “then flee.”

“And leave you?”

“Yes,” he ordered, “If that happens, Hephaestion, you’ll be the captain.”

Krateros’ eyebrows raised and they shared a knowing look. He nodded politely in gratitude, and they clasped arms in farewell. “May triumph always be yours, Phainon.”

How different this walk was from Phainon’s dream. He was not a golden hero from storybooks, just a tired pirate, worn from the sun and salty sea spray. He did not return in glory, but pleading on his knees for a people that were now his own. The grand battle against the Titan had not been fought in picturesque temples with perfect results but paid for with the blood of good men in a place of sorrowful ruin. This coreflame was not to be given willingly, but with incredible pain and humility at the sacrifice and promise of the one who had surrendered it for love. Any bath he may be allowed would be to wash the stink of hard work, loss, and Tide from his skin, not the glitter of Titan blood. And this coreflame may serve Aglaea’s Flame-Chase, but it was not Phainon’s vow that bore it to her, but dire necessity for a proud people who were strong enough to endure when profound evil sought to devour their pride.

Phainon was still the Deliverer, but no longer Okhema’s alone.

They saw him from a distance, as he made no attempt to hide and as recognizable as he was, Phainon was swiftly surrounded by a half dozen of Okhema’s finest men in shining armor. He recognized several of them from his time in service to the guard. They had trained together, dreaming of epic battles and earned accolades. The messenger bag was taken from him at sword point, slung over the shoulder of one of the soldiers and Phainon had to fight the urge to forcibly reclaim it. But they did not open the bag, nor treat it with roughness and there was pain in their eyes as they reached for his offered wrists and bound them with manacles and chains. Phainon could see and feel the shaking in their hands as they carried out the justice they were sworn to uphold.

They muttered apologies and asked for answers as they paraded him through the streets to the wide eyes and whispered buzz of a troubled crowd. He offered them nothing aside from idle pleasantries and soft reassurances, a gentle smile still on his face to put the populace and his anxious friends at ease. A deal had not yet been struck and until his pardon was secured he was a pirate, a criminal that needed to be brought to justice. But that did not erase their history, their respect, and confusion. Even in chains between them, Phainon knew these guards were deserving of kindness.

With nothing left to say, he kept his peace when they brought him through Marmoreal Palace to stand before the Goldweaver. They retreated then with soft and pleading expressions, putting his bag on the floor between himself and his fellow Chrysos Heir. For the first time since Phainon started his journey, he was alone with Aglaea. He did not fight his restraints or cow under the tickle of her threads as they reached for him. Phainon could feel them at his neck, his wrists, and his legs.

Aglaea was as unchanging and beautiful as the sky. Her office was still neat and tidy, organized without fault. Breakfast waited on her desk, barely touched aside from a suspicious, chimera sized bite from one of the cakes. The letter he had written for her was beside the plate and open to the world as though she had just been reading it. She was standing on her balcony with her back to him, looking over the waking city with a cup of tea in one hand and a little saucer in the other.

“To your credit,” she said, voice slow and sharp, “you did not lie to me in your letter.”

The smile he wore for the guards faded into something neutral and guarded. He swallowed stiffly and reassured her, “I have never lied to you, Lady Aglaea.”

“Because you never wanted to?” she challenged, “or because you couldn’t?”

Phainon said nothing, watching her at attention, head held high. She didn’t turn around, and he felt a little sad. After all this time, and she was so disappointed, Aglaea couldn’t bear to look at him.

“You said in your letter that when you returned it would be at the side of a man you had come to admire,” she said.

Phainon’s eyes flicked downward, and he clenched his fists to keep from shaking. The chains between his wrists clinked like heavy windchimes.

She let him stew in the thick silence for a moment and then turned to walk to her desk. Her dress flowed around her like morning mist, as light as her every step. The teacup settled on the saucer when she set it down, soundless when the fine ceramic met its match. Beside him a garmentmaker moved, floating in close to pick up the messenger bag to hand it to Aglaea directly and she in turn set it on her desk. With a sort of sad appreciation, she pulled the flap back and pushed away the suffocating wrap to free the Coreflame of Strife from its careful packaging.

“This was not the manner in which you intended to do so,” she observed and Phainon realized she knew that the Coreflame had already met its bearer.

“How long have you known?” he asked sourly.

“I was not sure until you entered the city,” she admitted. Her eyes settled on him, hazy and somehow piercing all the same. The yellow of them glowed through the emerald. “Did he give it to you willingly?”

Another painful swallow. Another fight to hold his composure. “Yes.”

Her long and perfect fingers hovered over the coreflame, appreciating its warmth before she gently covered it again.

“The coreflame is not a gift,” Phainon told her firmly, “nor is it a fulfillment of my vow to you. It was given to me with purpose, and I will only surrender it if those needs are met.”

“If it is within my power alone to give, you shall want for nothing,” she promised.

Hopeful, he said, “the Coreflame of Strife is a peace offering from the Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos, to be a physical manifestation of a permanent truce between nations.” She didn’t react so Phainon continued, “And with this peace, our new allies in Okhema will see fit to issue pardons, absolving the Kremnoan people, especially the crew of the Chryseus Leo, of their crimes under Okheman law.”

“A clean slate for a crew of pirates,” she stated.

“Yes.”

“And the end of a centuries long war.”

“Yes,” Phainon insisted firmly.

“Our new allies in Okhema,” Aglaea noted gently, “spoken like one who is outside of her beauty.”

“Yes.” He said it without hesitation, without faltering or looking away. He needed her to see how much he had changed since they had last met, that he was a better man in every way for his experiences, even if it may hurt her to see how far away from her side he now stood.

She raised a hand to her chest, pressing a delicate finger to the space below her throat, and closed her eyes. Aglaea was statuesque, elegant and crafted from fine marble by a master’s hand to be the image of cold beauty. It was his hope, when she finally moved again, that it would be to grant his wish on behalf of the Kremnoan people, his people, but when she opened her eyes it was with predictable disappointment.

“You know such a wish is beyond my power alone to grant. For all my authority, I am not a monarch and Kephale’s will is not mine alone to interpret.”

Phainon sighed with the tiniest chuckle in the exhale. The Council of Elders would need to be swayed. “I expected as much.”

“You must have quite the tale to tell, Phainon,” she mused.

“It is an epic for the ages,” he confirmed, “but there are many heroes in this story, and I am not one of them.” Phainon lifted his bound hands just to let them fall again. The metal complained with loud clanks when it was jostled. “I am the messenger who speaks on their behalf.”

The shadow of a smile passed over Aglaea’s features, so fleeting that Phainon worried he had imagined it. She put her hand over the messenger bag again and the Coreflame at rest there.

“How are Castorice and Hyacine?” she asked.

Phainon’s eyes narrowed just a hair. “They are well. This success belongs to them as well.”

“And you?” She asked with a tenderness that very nearly spoke of emotions that the Goldweaver may have once had, that remained in minute amounts buried deep within her.

“I am well,” he said with equal softness and the golden threads between them trembled.

“If you could do it again,” Aglaea wondered aloud, but she changed her mind before finishing the question and instead shook her head and asked, “Was it worth it?”

Phainon thought of a burning island, a displaced people, of countless injuries, and a surging Tide. He remembered the crew of the Sol and the sobs of a widow living in this very city, of his divisive presence tearing apart a crew that sailed as a family. His mind wandered to thoughts of a naval outpost, looted, with the bodies set aside unburied, of a Crown Prince left behind in desolation with the dead he had once sailed beside.

And then he thought of warm nights with good food and a happy crew listening to Peucesta’s tales whiles they taught Phainon the language of another world beside his tiny corner of existence. Good men told him stories, competed with him, filled him with courage and curiosity, sharing their culture with him and inviting him to explore alongside them as a part of their family. He thought of the blood shed between comrades fighting the Tide, trust built during a storm, a child’s compassion in a time of loss, and a hurried kiss. Phainon thought of Mydei, the crew, and the hopes that they had entrusted to him, a hope for peace that they had never considered possible before now. A peace that he would secure with a story, the kind that bards would immortalize in song beside those of the Titans. As they should, because if any people deserved to have their story told it was the Kremnoan Detachment and the Chryseos Leo.

“Yes. Without question.”

Her nod was subtle, but the bounce of her perfect curls was not. “Though they move with glacial stillness on the best of days, the Council of Elders wishes to convene this afternoon to try you. Political theater at its finest. They are eager to use your arrest to sway the people against the Flame-Chase and have already begun to invite the entirety of Okhema to witness.”

“Will I be given the chance to speak?” he asked her.

“Yes.” The smile was back, this time with a glimmer of mischief. “Will you tell your story to the people?”

“With pleasure.”

-

Phainon was taken by the Council’s guard shortly thereafter. Aglaea kept the Coreflame despite their insistence it be taken to the Council, but she refused to part with it until such time as it could be presented during Phainon’s trial. Even on opposing sides, Phainon was grateful for her intervention. If the guards had taken it he wasn’t sure he’d ever see it again.

They took him directly to Dawncloud from the Marmoreal Palace, marching him through the Sacred Path with noisy stomps and a mountain dweller escort to draw attention from the elders and scholars that studied there. The guards at each arm pulled and pushed at Phainon to keep him off balance to instill in him a sense of shame but every time he stumbled, the pirate rose again with a gentle smile and his head held high. When the citizenry stared, he pleasantly waved back, treating this parade as an opportunity to instill in everyone a sense of curiosity.

Come! He said with his smile and gentle nods. Come and listen to a tale that will shake the foundation of Okhema! Come and hear the words of the Deliverer turned pirate as he faces judgement under Kephale! Come and see the beloved Chrysos Heir of Aglaea, the man of the people, the hero of epics, beg on his knees for forgiveness!

He was kept in a small enclosure to wait, just barely tall enough for him to stand and wide enough for him to sit with his legs fully extended no matter which wall Phainon leaned against. The cell on the Chryseus Leo was only a pace larger and when he considered his first bed on the ship, Phainon didn’t feel so cramped, rather he smiled at the fond memories of meeting Fig Stew, making a deal with Mydei, and even that cold morning when Leonnius dragged him from the safety of the bars to fish.

He ignored the taunts of the Council’s men, and the curious looks of passing people that could see him from the hallway. Phainon was not hidden by any means, no, Caenis wouldn’t miss the chance to humiliate him before they could put the man on Trial. At least his cage was not in the center of the walkway where he could be openly mocked but Phainon was quite alright with the opportunity to watch the populace as they went about their day.

Okhema was truly a beacon of light, clean and beautiful, the city itself a temple to Kephale. Dawncloud especially, was the district closest to the Titan, built underneath the god where they bent under the weight of the Dawn Device. Dawncloud extended to the mountains at Kephale’s feet reaching the peaks where the Worldbearing Altar rested beneath their giant, silent face. It encompassed this place of learning where Phainon was now kept and it was the home of the Demigod Council, an amphitheater laid out like an arena not for combat but for words. It lay perched on a giant basin, a lake surrounded by giant torches where facsimiles of the coreflames glowed.

It was there that the guards brought Phainon, two quints past the Action Hour to face the Council of Elders and the whole of Okhema under Kephale. In the forecourt, across the wide bridge to the center of the arena, they removed his chains and gave him a moment to collect himself.

“Snowy!” called a playful voice and Phainon’s day immediately brightened.

“Lady Tribbie,” he greeted cheerfully while he rubbed his wrists, “what are you doing here?”

“Agy asked us to bring the coreflame,” she explained from a few steps above him on the stairs. He didn’t see the bag with her.

“Trianne and Trinnon are here as well?”

“Yes, we are waiting but we wanted to see you before,” she explained, “because we missed you and we worry about you.”

His heart softened and he held a hand to his chest. “I have missed you too, Tribbie, but I am also excited to share a story with Okhema and with you.”

“They are ready for you, Snowy,” she said after a slight pause.

“Well then, I better not keep the world waiting.” His voice was light and confident, buoyed by the strength of many others.

She reached out her hand for his and held it the entire way up the stairs, floating along so he wouldn’t have to crouch while they walked. Tribbie left him at the edge of the arena to fly away to the stands, presumably to meet up with her sisters and Aglaea.

“…proof that Lady Goldweaver’s Flame-Chase experiment has failed,” Caenis was saying to the crowd, “if her chosen hero, the Deliverer of Okhema as she calls him, could stoop so low as to ally with pirates and engage in piracy against his own people! Today justice will be done against this heretic that dares raise his blade against the Holy City!”

Oh, this was more than an indictment, he realized. Aglaea hadn’t been kidding, Caenis intended to deal with him now entirely.

“You finally deign to grace us with your presence, Deliverer,” she taunted as though she hadn’t been the one who ordered him caged since the Entry Hour.

“Elder Caenis,” he greeted politely and stepped forward with a slight bow of his head. His opinion of Caenis was not positive, but if she wanted political theater, then she would get political theater.

“Behold the traitor,” she told the people with a flourished gesture his direction and stepped back to be more in line with the other Elders on the Council where they sat on the front row of the curved bench.

Phainon humbly moved more into the center so all could see him.

“Elder Caenis there is no need for grandstanding,” Elder Callictis cautioned before continuing, “Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, you have been arrested and brought to stand before this Council to be indicted and tried in compliance with an arrest warrant that was issued on the order of this Council after evidence of your wrongdoing was presented and reviewed. It is the wish of this Council that we proceed directly to trial while this Council is convened today. Have you any objections or statements you would like to make at this time?”

“I have no objections but would make a humble request,” he said, loud enough for people to hear him. “I will willingly submit to the judgement of this Council but only after I am given the opportunity to speak at length regarding my time away from Okhema and of the noble task which was entrusted to me.”

Caenis narrowed her eyes suspiciously while the Council leaned in to discuss among themselves. After a short moment they leaned away and turned their attention back to him.

“This is permissible as part of your testimony. We will henceforth commence the Trial of Phainon of Aedes Elysiae. Elder Caenis, if you would,” Elder Diogena invited.

Caenis raised her voice to announce, “Phainon you stand accused of depredation, acts of violence against Okhema and her people, destruction of property, kidnapping, and treason against the Holy City. Do you deny these accusations?”

“I do not.”

The crowd did not expect that, and whispered confusion rippled through the crowd, a low buzz of many voices that kept clear phrases from coming through. Phainon paid them no mind.

“Then you confess?” Caenis prodded with a widening smile.

“Not to every accusation,” he specified, “I am not a traitor to Okhema, but yes, I am a pirate, and it is because of that allegiance that I am able to bring this Holy City that I love mixed tidings.”

“Settle down!” Elder Callictis called to the crowd. He waited for the din to quiet before he addressed Phainon, “confessing to being a pirate is treason in the eyes of Kephale. Would you like to retract your statement?”

“No,” he said firmly, “but I plead with the Council, not for my sake, but for the sake of Okhema to allow me the opportunity to explain what I have seen in my capacity as a pirate on distant seas.”

Caenis opened her mouth to say something, but Elder Diogena spoke instead, “Make your case, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae.”

“Then allow me noble brothers and sisters to tell you a story worthy of Kephale.” Phainon took a breath, then he began to reveal to them the truth, beginning with his commission from Agalea and as he spoke he walked in a slow circle so that it was clear he spoke to the people, not the Council. He told them about his own trepidation when he received the call and the horrors of pursuing pirates across the sea. Phainon spoke highly of the crew, who were invaluable in tracking the pirate ship across the ocean beyond the reach of the Dawn Device and their courage in the face of the destruction they had witnessed.

“When I first laid eyes on that ship with red sails I knew we had found our mark. It was before the Entry Hour and Aquila’s eyes were closed beyond the Dawn Device. These pirates were turning to flee when we approached at speed, leaving behind a merchant ship, recently plundered. Hopeful to aid any survivors, I ordered my men to approach the burning ship and jumped across to search for any who survived this brutal attack.” He held a hand to his chest and paused. “It was the last time I saw my crew alive.”

He spoke from his heart as he described how helpless he felt in the hold, listening to the tearing of the ship’s hull, the screams from above as ink slowly swallowed the merchant ship and the Sol. He relayed how he was the only survivor pulled from the water by the pirates who had sent these two vessels to the depths, where he fought for his freedom and for vengeance only to be stopped by a man of incredible strength and nobility.

“The truth of what transpired that night came during the Entry Hour when I spoke at last to the Captain of this pirate crew. He was a man of harsh words and harsher means but honest and honorable. Perhaps you, my fellow Okhemans, would consider it strange to hear me refer to a pirate in such a way, but I choose my words because they are true and to speak otherwise would diminish the character of one who I now call my friend.”

The crowd murmured but Phainon paid them little mind.

“He told me of what I did not know and opened my eyes to a truth that Okhema has learned and then denied, that there is a need for pirates on the sea, for such men are the first line of defense against the greatest antagonistic force to poison Amphoreus, the Black Tide.”

Shouting and angry words were thrown in his direction, the crowd refused to believe him.

“I know! For I too struggled to believe that the Tide had reached so far and that pirates were hunting those monsters! But if I had known, if I had not willingly forgotten the Tide as a distant enemy, then my crew would still be alive, for when they fell to the blades of the pirate crew, they were no longer themselves but beasts, howling in pain.

“Thus began my time aboard a pirate ship, captive in name only for they accepted me and taught me and through them I learned not only of the threat that ever creeps through the seas but truths that have been denied the people of Okhema, truths of an enemy that haunts our recent history, Castrum Kremnos.”

The mumbling began in earnest and the crowd shuffled fearfully, still he raised his voice and spoke through their fear.

“The pirates that we have been taught to abhor are no brigands, they are Kremnoan, and they care nothing for our ongoing war, but act as protectors of their own people and the innocent alike. While they do not shy from bloodshed, every action is with purpose in defense of a greater good that Okhema has not been able to see, beginning five years ago, when, by the hand of their Captain, Crown Prince Mydeimos the Undying, Inheritor of Strife, that King Eurypon was slain.”

Phainon looked Caenis in the eye as he said it and saw the truth of it there. They knew. The Council knew and kept the truth hidden for mysterious, unknown ends.

“Lies!” someone yelled, and the chant began until the Council called for order once more.

“If it pleases the Council,” Aglaea offered smoothly behind them, loud enough for others to hear, “I may attest to the truthfulness of his story thus far.”

“There is no need, Lady Aglaea,” Caenis insisted, but the crowd’s chants grew in earnest, demanding that she use her threads to prove his words until the Council relented under the pressure.

The golden threads shimmered, visible to the crowd as Aglaea gave them form. They wrapped around Phainon’s hand when he offered it, palm up, and then bound him to the ground in a wide, circular array in the center of the Demigod Council.

“If he lies,” Aglaea told them, “then the threads will vibrate. Phainon, please repeat what you have said clearly and concisely.”

Emboldened, firm, and with his head held high he announced, “Crown Prince Mydeimos slew his father, King Eurypon of Castrum Kremnos five years ago. He sails as the Captain of the Chryseus Leo, a pirate ship, in defense of his people and all peoples of Amphoreus. He is not the enemy of Okhema.”

The string held firm and unmoving, and chaos erupted once more. This time the Council could not calm them as the implications of what Phainon had said passed through the shock.

So, he raised his voice instead and the arena slowly quieted to listen. “If you would lend me your ears once more, great people of this Holy City, I would tell you more of this story so you may know more of the allies that wait for you.”

And then he told them more. He told them nearly everything, laying his heart to bear as he recalled those gentle moments with each member of the crew. He told the people of Okhema about each of them in turn and how every interaction had shattered his preconceptions of them and what he had been taught to believe about their former enemies.

He told them about Ptolemy, a Kremnoan scholar who embodied the reason that so many of them believed their foe to be without. Kremnoan words spilled from his mouth as he demonstrated his learning and the patience of the bookworm, who treasured his history with such care that he chronicled the journeys of his people with his own hand with indifferent acknowledgement. This man who pursued knowledge and history with the fervor of any Grove Sage had been forbidden from visiting the Grove itself because he surely would’ve sunk the ship with the knowledge he longed to recover.

Phainon described for them Perdikkas and the honor that the doctor demonstrated in his every action. This man who could have let him die, an Okheman that was his enemy, but treated him fairly as one of his own at every turn. He told them about Perdikkas’ organization of his infirmary, the patience with which he kept his space clean, and the eagerness to learn what Phainon knew of medicine, as limited as it may be in the hopes it could improve his life-saving care. These were not men of needless violence, Perdikkas had taught, they were men of passion who had found their reason to live and to die.

From Leonnius, Phainon learned tenacity, not only in the face of physical trial, but in the face of grief and loss. He told the people of their fishing competition and the daily challenge that pushed him to improve and grow beyond his limitations. He told them of Leonnius as a voice of humor and honesty, pushing them through difficult times. Phainon recalled aloud the darkest moments of his voyage when he realized he was their captive and later when he learned of his warrant. He spoke to Leonnius’ tenacious logic and humor to carry them forward always, never stagnant, always moving.

Phainon spoke to them of Peucesta’s grace and quiet strength, the embodiment of courage during dark days. He told them how the man had once become tainted by the Tide, how he had recovered and found in himself new purpose, the courage to be kind. In a pale comparison to Peucesta’s voice, Phainon sang to them the melody of the Tide, something that was only known because of his willingness to test a means to save them all at the risk of his own painful death. He emphasized that because of Peucesta, the Tide could now be survived and therein was a method to resist. Because of Peucesta and the hard work of others, Okheman sailors could brave polluted waters without fear.

He told them of Hephaestion, the last of the tenants of Strife, the embodiment of sacrifice. Not the sacrifice of the flesh that Kremnoans chased in their bloodthirsty pursuit, but the sacrifice of one’s time and love. Phainon shared his first day working with Hephaestion, when he learned through example the value of respect for the ship. He recalled for them the conflict in the wake of his duel with Mydei, when Hephaestion stood between Phainon and Krateros to defend his enemy with Kremnoan blood. He told them of the assault on Castrum Kremnos, where Hephaestion almost lost his life and how willing he was to lay it again on the line to see his people safe from the Tide.

Phainon told them about Krateros. About how long it took the prickly old man to accept Phainon. How it took the approval of a chimera to finally win him over. He spoke of Krateros’ stubbornness of his rigid belief that there could be no peace between Kremnos and Okhema. And then he told them how even that man’s icy heart was melted by hope when Phainon, an enemy, and Krateros, emblematic of the old might of Castrum Kremnos, crossed spears not as bitter foes but as an old warrior and the rising generation.

Finally, he told them about Mydei. Phainon spoke about Mydei more than all the others because he was the perfect embodiment of Strife, Kremnoan in his entirety, not as their people were described to Okhemans, not as the old soldiers of the Holy City remembered from warring days, but as they were meant to be. He spoke at length about his time training with Mydei, sparring with him, learning of him, coming to understand his story, and all the while Phainon’s prejudices were shattered on distant shoals. Mydei was no King, he refused to wear the crown, but still he led his dwindling people with fairness, kindness, and honorable strength.

He told the people of their conquests against the Tide as partners, as a crew. And he told them of the Settlement, of a people that had long abandoned their war with Okhema. Phainon’s voice stayed loud and true so all could hear him as he told them of that fateful meeting in Mydei’s house where they agreed to chase the Coreflame of Strife into a land unreachable. He expressed with earnest the way they longed to accomplish this task not because they wanted power, but because they cared and loved in a way that Okhema had not seen since Kephale’s sacrifice. And then he told them in detail about the Battle at Castrum Kremnos and the fall of a Titan, speaking to Mydei’s composure in the face of Strife and then again, his resolute calm when the truth of Nikador’s mission came to light.

Phainon held up his unbound hand and called Tribbie who flew to his side at his humble request with the messenger bag in hand.

“Lady Tribbie, if you would?” he asked gently, and she smiled at him and removed the Coreflame of Strife from the bag so everyone could see it. The collective gasp gave Phainon pause so everyone could appreciate what they were seeing.

“This Coreflame belongs to Crown Prince Mydeimos. He is its chosen bearer, the true Inheritor of Strife, and still he has parted with it and remains even now in the heart of Castrum Kremnos holding back the Tide,” Phainon explained, his voice breaking for only a moment before he steeled his resolve. “This is the sacrifice of Castrum Kremnos! A man that could have power unrivaled, the means to claim victory for his people, chose instead to reject that power in favor of peace.”

The threads held true, they did not waver once.

“This Coreflame of Strife is here to facilitate an exchange,” Phainon said, “The end of a centuries long war between our peoples, the promise of peace and an alliance against the greater threat posed by the Black Tide, in exchange for the absolution of the Kremnoan people, including the charges of piracy.”

The Council was watching with varying degrees of interest and Caenis scoffed. The people’s responses seemed mixed. Many seemed undecided still trying to process earlier revelations, others were angry and yelled that Phainon demanded too much, others shouted that pardons were a small price to pay for peace.

“These golden threads are proof of the truth of my words!” Phainon reminded them all, but Caenis was not swayed.

“Is that all?” she mocked.

“No, I also would plead for the use of Okhema’s Navy,” Phainon said, “As newly realized allies, I beg for the strength to return to Castrum Kremnos, to rescue Mydeimos from his cruel Fate endlessly fighting the Tide. I would gladly submit myself to any punishment, pay for all my crimes as this Council deems fit, if this one wish would be granted.”

Her laugh was a mixture of bark and cackle, loud enough to make the crowd uncomfortable and push them to silence. “And why would you agree to something like that?”

Phainon answered immediately, “Because I love him.”

The golden threads held still.

Chapter End Notes

By now I'm sure some people have noticed but at the very beginning of the story I chose a tenant of Strife and assigned them to each of the Kremnoan 5. They have been embodiments of those traits from the very beginning~ :D

Chapter Summary
