Phainon faces judgement at the hands of the Council of Elders

Chapter Notes

This fic is now in the top ten longest fics for this pairing in any language. I did not intend to do that. :’)

I’ve seen an uptick of kudos and idk if people are just finding this fic by accident or if people are recommending it but if you are, thank you! It is a massive honor to have written something worthy of sharing.

Because I love him.

It wasn’t what Phainon had intended to say but he made no effort to retract his statement, nor did he break into flustered giggles at the confession. This was the truth that Phainon had carried into this meeting, the answer to all things: love. What better place to announce it aside from shouting from the rooftops?

Beside him Tribbie held the Coreflame in both hands, looking up at him with the biggest smile. She held that precious piece of Mydei with the care he deserved and Phainon was all the more grateful for her presence by his side.

Caenis scoffed again and then laughed, “For you to have stooped so low. These are the words of a captive, brain washed by time and the exertions of his captors. The threads do not quiver because it is his truth, a truth that will not apply to Okhema.”

Phainon’s gentle demeanor shifted just a little towards anger. “Perhaps if the Lady Caenis had experienced love in her lifetime she would understand.”

The crowd laughed and Caenis’ scowl deepened.

“If the Kremnoans wanted peace, why did they not send a Kremnoan to barter for it? Why did they sneak into the Holy City and steal away the Chrysos Heirs?” she asked.

“Do you think so little of Castorice and Hyacine?” Phainon turned it around, “could the Hand of Death not choose to escape on her own?”

“Then the Heirs were complicit, traitors to the Holy City as you are.”

Phainon could tell from her voice that Caenis was planning on leveraging this against Aglaea. Maybe not today, but the Flame-Chase was on the chopping block on bad days, and he had given Caenis an edge. One step at a time.

“Again, I must insist that the acts of piracy that we have committed are not treason,” Phainon said, “and I know how that sounds, but please remember my story. Treason is malicious intent to destroy, to undermine, and we have done nothing to that end.”

“I heard your words, Lord Phainon,” Caenis said smoothly, “and the many confessions you have made therein.”

“And I have confessed,” he agreed, “to fighting to protect Okhema and people who needed me.”

“Kremnoans, enemies of Okhema.”

“Good people!”

“What you have done is illegal!”

“What I have done is right!”

“People of Okhema and my fellow Councilmembers,” Caenis continued, turning her back to Phainon, “Phainon pleads for forgiveness for crimes that he admits to committing and offers in exchange a trap for Okhema. What use do we have for a Coreflame? The already claimed Coreflame of Strife no less! Such a trinket matters only to Aglaea’s Flame-Chase which has consumed resources and lives for an idle collection while Okhema has enjoyed peace and prosperity without their influence. Even the Kremnoans have not dared to raise their blades against Okhema proper in five years because of our strength. They can only manage these cowardly pirates that intercept our merchant ships, slaughter good Navy men, and raid our forts in distant waters. ‘The Black Tide did it,’ Phainon claims to justify his evil actions.”

He shook, annoyed. Even with the thread to prove his honesty, she refused to believe. Or perhaps she did and chose to sow these seeds of doubt. What Phainon brought in his truth was the means to shatter this illusion of perfection that the Council of Elders fought to preserve.

“Yet, there is good news in his story,” she teased, “The Kremnoan people are without leadership and weakened, no longer a threat. We have no need to call an end to this war in exchange for your pardon, because it has already ceased now that the warring brutes have cannibalized their own culture and people.”

“For the sake of Okhema, you cannot abandon them!” Phainon insisted.

“For Okhema?” she taunted.

“Yes! The threat of the Black Tide will not stop at the Dawn Device, not for long,” he passionately insisted, “I have heard its song and seen its face. The steady creeping that has claimed so many city-states before will come for Okhema and we need every ally, especially those with the strength and willingness to form an alliance to repel it.”

“How dare you speak such blasphemies against Kephale? To doubt the power of the Dawn Device, to doubt the strength of the Dawn Father…” she shook her head and tsked like she was scolding an animal.

“Kephale gives strength to those who seek strength,” Phainon said, fighting the growl. She wanted this rise out of him, to make him angry enough to appear rabid and frightening. “They never meant for us to become lazy and self-centered. Does their love not extend to every person that walks Amphoreus? Do you, Elder Caenis, dare to claim that they care only for Okhemans when nearly half this city is loved by refugees that have made her into the shining beacon on the hill? I have witnessed the strength of the Tide; it will break upon the Dawn Device and seep into the light if it is not stopped.”

Caenis didn’t falter, still on the attack, even mimicking his style of debate. “Did you not admit yourself to strengthening the Tide with your own actions? When you retrieved this Coreflame, did you not unleash a stronger Tide per your own admission? This rescue that you demand, trading Okheman lives to save a single man, the Crown Prince of our enemy, would that not increase the flow of this primordial force? Is it not better to leave the man as the dam? Okhema will be saved from the Black Tide, and our centuries long conflict will end if we simply do nothing but enjoy this peace we have built!”

“Mydei’s sacrifice slows the Tide, it does not stop it,” Phainon cautioned.

“Then he has bought Okhema another hundred years to contemplate a distant and minor threat.”

Caenis wasn’t going to budge. He knew that she would be the biggest obstacle coming into this, but the other members of the Council were more agreeable, and they had yet to offer their opinions. They very likely wouldn’t vocally weigh in as Caenis liked the sound of her own voice and would speak on their behalf, but she did not hold unilateral power, and the others could be convinced.

“I have come to you to offer peace, valuable allies, and an answer to a threat, and you respond with disdain, ignorant accusations, and closed-mindedness,” he huffed, “the people of Okhema will see the wisdom in my words and choose to step off this path of complacent destruction that you would have them follow.”

The Council leaned close to each other to whisper amongst themselves while the crowd grew restless where they were sitting. Phainon had already taken the better part of the hour to tell his story, a one man show for their entertainment while Caenis sowed seeds of doubt disguised as reason. The Coreflame of Strife wasn’t the only thing in his pocket he could offer but if Caenis rejected the first coreflame, there was little chance she would care for two. Anaxa was, thankfully, safe for now. He shifted his weight to ease the pain in his foot from standing still for so long.

“Order please,” Elder Etro demanded, and the crowd settled for the second act. “We have decided that the trial will continue. This discussion of your proposal is entwined with the charges brought against you; thus, we will announce our decision on both counts at the conclusion of these proceedings. Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, if you have finished your opening remarks, do you yield your time?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Then we will proceed to analyze the charges and give you the opportunity to defend yourself. Is this acceptable?”

“It is more than fair,” he agreed politely, though internally he seethed. It felt like they were deflecting, like they had already come to a decision about the Coreflame of Strife and this critical exchange. The people of Okhema and Kremnos needed this deal, accusations of piracy aside, pardons aside, they needed this guarantee of peace to move forward.

The threads around his palm warmed, comforting, and he felt them take away that emotional disturbance, filling him with peace to continue with clear-headed confidence.

“The kidnapping charges will be dropped,” Elder Callictis announced, “in light of recent confessions regarding the missing Chrysos Heirs. On the charges of depredation, acts of violence against Okhema and her people, destruction of property, and all other acts encompassed under the pirate flag, we will proceed to the indicting incident: the destruction of the Okheman Naval Base on the Pyrian Isles.”

Phainon remembered it. That was the first time he had seen the Chryseus Leo crew hide their identities as Kremnoan, the night where Phainon had stood at the crossroad and made the decision to stay with the crew to honor his agreement with Mydei. It was the first time he had been forced to confront the reality of what his capture entailed for both himself and the Kremnoan people. The first time he had to raise his blade against both sides to save them.

“Were you present when pirates attacked the fort?” the Elder asked.

“Yes.”

“Were you allied with the pirates?”

“No.” The thread stayed still and he continued, “At the time I was still a hostage. Mydeimos forbade me from leaving the ship.”

“Were you imprisoned?”

“No. I was ordered to stay behind but I was not confined,” Phainon explained.

“Then you willingly chose to engage in piracy?” Elder Caenis prodded.

“…yes,” he admitted, “but-“

“A confession!” she announced cutting him off, “he willingly chose to join the pirates in the sacking of an Okheman fort.”

Phainon took a deep breath to keep his composure, “I joined the fight on behalf of the Okheman troops. I did not personally engage in any destruction of property nor theft, but I did raise my sword to save lives. When Mydeimos and the crew attacked the fort they did so with the intent to chase the Navy from the island, to save them from the encroaching Black Tide.”

“The Black Tide again-“ Caenis huffed dramatically.

“It’s the truth. Mydei and the Kremnoans have been tracking its progress, studying it, to find a way to stop it.”

“Elders of the Council, if I may,” called a vaguely familiar voice from the populace. Phainon turned his head with the rest of the arena to see an older gentleman stand and step through the crowd. He waited patiently at the edge of the innermost bench to be acknowledged. The man looked different in the light, with dark brown short hair and matching eyes, clean and without the stress of combat but he looked familiar wearing the Okheman Navy uniform and a rich, bright blue chlamys to mark his rank. He raised a hand to his chest and the knotted scar through his palm gave him away before his words could.

For the sake of the crowd, the man raised his voice and announced, “I am Commander Hapries, though at the time I was Vice-Commander. It was my testimony of this attack that led to Lord Phainon’s indictment.”

Phainon’s eyes widened just a hair, and he barely kept his mouth from falling open. He had never expected to see this man again after that night. Mostly, he was relieved that the man had made it safely to Okhema after their parting.

“This Council recognizes Commander Hapries,” Caenis invited, “your report was invaluable.”

“And it was woefully misinformed,” Hapries declared. He stepped a pace closer, to be a part of the trial rather than left on the fringes. “When I gave my report to this Council it was from a narrow lens.” The man turned towards Phainon with sad eyes. “I am sorry Lord Phainon, it wasn’t until many weeks after I told them of your betrayal that I learned what you had done for us.”

Phainon smiled at him gently, trying to be reassuring, but kept his silence.

“What you saw was this man fighting against your own soldiers, killing them, and then choosing to follow the pirates when given the chance to flee!” Caenis reminded the officer, but he did not balk under her biting words.

“Not once did I say that Lord Phainon had killed any of my men,” he said firmly, “and I have brought with me soldiers that can testify to that truth, who were there at the battle until the last of us had fled.” Hapries turned and gestured behind him where three others stood to indicate their readiness to speak on Phainon’s behalf. “I did plead with Lord Phainon to run with us when we escaped, and I was confused and angry when the Deliverer of Okhema chose pirates that had killed our people over his own kin. But in the weeks that followed my testimony I have learned that the fort where we were stationed had been swallowed by the Black Tide shortly after the fort was lost.” Gasps rippled through the crowds. “Now that I have heard Lord Phainon’s story, and the trials he underwent I believe I have a greater grasp on what transpired that night.”

He looked to Phainon when he spoke next, searching for forgiveness, understanding, or both Phainon couldn’t say but he gave this man his full attention as he told his story.

“I was a young soldier when Okhema last clashed with Kremnos, I know the strength and ferocity of Kremnoan warriors. They are disciplined, expert fighters. The man that drove a spear through my hand could have just as easily driven it through my chest, but he let me live to sound the retreat. At the time I believed him to be a cruel man, enjoying the pain he caused but as I have had time to reflect I know now that these Kremnoan pirates were willingly restrained.

“’Sound the retreat and my men will let you go,’ he had said to me, and he spoke only truth. They only killed those brave soldiers that were determined to fight to their last and gave each of them every chance to flee. As a warrior, I know the desire to die on my own terms with a sword in my hand and if Phainon had not been there, I may have perished willingly with my men that night just as Commander Mityphon did. Those that died did so with honor and those that fled, their lives were saved. If these pirates, these Kremnoans, had not come to our station, we would not be here to speak on Lord Phainon’s behalf.”

Hapries paused to look at Phainon for some kind of confirmation that he was right. Phainon smiled and gave him a subtle nod, and the soldier returned the gesture. He turned on the Council with new confidence.

“That act of piracy saved our lives from the worst of fates,” the soldier said firmly, and the crowd buzzed again at the implication.

“These pirates still stole Okheman property!” Caenis accused and Hapries waved his hand.

“Those goods would have been lost to the Tide with the noble men who were ordered to guard them.”

“If this is true, if these Kremnoans targeted the fort to save men, then why did they attack without warning?” Caenis insisted, looking for holes in the argument.

“Commander Hapries,” Phainon said, and attention shifted back to him, “I am sorry your promotion came under such heavy circumstances. I knew Mityphon, he was an honorable man and died a warrior’s death.”

Caenis rolled her eyes, but Hapries pressed his fingers to his chest and bowed his head in respectful gratitude for the sentiment.

“If a ship bearing the mark of Strife approached the fort, would you listen to them speak?” Phainon asked.

Hapries contemplated that for a moment and then shook his head. “No. I would not wait to hear the words of Castrum Kremnos, they are not known to treat with their enemies, and I would be hard pressed to believe they come in peace.”

“If you had and they told you that the fort needed to be abandoned to save all the lives therein, would you leave?”

“No, I would believe it a ploy to secure a military victory, and perhaps request reinforcements in response,” he admitted.

“Elder Caenis, the prejudices of Okhema would’ve cost her many fine soldiers. There was no other way for them to save the people than to disguise themselves as brigands and chase them to safety,” Phainon insisted.

Caenis’ mouth curled into a foul smile, and she asked, “Commander, if the Deliverer had approached your gates and relayed to you the dire nature of your situation and ordered a retreat, would you obey?”

“…I would,” Hapries admitted.

“And we did!” a young voice added. One of the three men that had come with their Commander shuffled past his companions to walk down the stairs to stand beside his commanding officer. The young man bowed politely to the Council and then as a second thought bowed to Phainon too. He had light brown, short hair and energy that came only from inexperienced youth.

“My name is Amorphis, my lords and ladies,” he said, “forgive me for speaking out of turn, but I was also there that night. I am an archer, and my life was saved by the Deliverer when I-I shot him. My arrow was meant for one of the pirates, er, Kremnoans, but the Deliverer got between us, he took the arrow instead-“ he motioned to the place on his own body, too vague to be specific but Phainon remembered where that arrow had stuck in his back, “-when he used his sword to break my bow, I thought for sure he was a man possessed and that I would die, but he pushed me back and ordered me to run, saving my life.”

“Your testimony does not add-“ Caenis started but the young man waved both of his hands frantically and talked over her.

“My lady please! To your question, I had the fortune and misfortune of fleeing from the same pirates twice.”

Caenis blinked. Phainon blinked. The Commander was the only one that wasn’t surprised.

“And the second time, it was as you said,” Amorphis confirmed, “after we fled the first, many of us were left at the nearest fort while Commander Hapries returned to Okhema to report and receive instruction from the Admiral. While we were there, the pirates came again, but this time it was during Action Hour and the Deliverer came before them. He told us that there was no need for bloodshed, that our lives were in danger if we stayed. The Deliverer said that pirates were here to take the fort and many of the men laughed, but I and the others told them of the night our fort was lost and convinced them to flee. Not a single soul was lost to Thanatos that day. It wasn’t until later that I learned that fort too had been consumed by the Black Tide.”

The young man looked between the Commander, Caenis, and Phainon before Hapries patted his back reassuringly and gave him a nudge to return to his seat.

“Elder Caenis, I will take no more of this Council’s time except to say that this man’s illegal actions served Okhema in ways that few could ever hope to understand, if it were up to me, I would retract my initial testimony and see these charges dropped,” Hapries said clearly and firmly for everyone to hear.

“Noted,” she said shortly and after an awkward shuffle to realize he had been dismissed, the man returned to his seat amongst the chatter of the audience. They conversed at every level, too muddled to hear anything but isolated and meaningless phrases.

Oblivious to the buzz of the crowd, Elder Oenone consulted her notes, unrolling the scroll farther to read, “Beginning with your indictment and the issuing of your warrant, Okhema has lost two naval warships, the wreckage of which washed up on friendly shores with evidence of battle. While bound by the golden threads, can you assert that you, Phainon, and the pirate crew with which you sailed had no part in those ships’ destruction?”

“I cannot. I know those two ships, and we did destroy them,” he admitted, “the crew and ships had become corrupted by the Black Tide and would’ve caused unspeakable damage to innocent people had we not raised our weapons against them.”

The threads stayed still. Phainon could see the Council members looking between each other, trading quiet looks while Oenone rolled the scroll up tight. Caenis was scanning the immediate crowd, judging their reactions carefully. While any decision would be up to the Council alone, they frequently weighed the public’s opinion and nearly all Okhema had come today to see what would become of their Deliverer.

Eventually her eyes settled on Aglaea. With a sneer, Caenis invited, “You are quiet today, Lady Goldweaver. Will you not say something on behalf of your favorite Chrysos Heir?”

The crowd murmured excitedly as Aglaea stood and stepped away from her place in the front row to be more easily seen. She shimmered in the light of the Dawn Device. “There is nothing I can say to sway the people to Phainon’s defense. They already know by his own works that he is a man who chooses good regardless of the law.”

“Good intentions should not absolve a man of guilt!” a woman called. She was pushing through the crowd; face twisted in anger.

Phainon took a deep breath through his nose and then mumbled under his breath, “Xenia.”

Her short blue hair had been combed but only just and her gold eyes were dulled to bronze. Phainon’s words to her had not brought her peace, rather they left her feeling hollow and angry. He could see the exhaustion in how she moved and the way her eyes shook. Depression had rooted deeply in her heart and driven her to become a shell of the woman she had once been.

“I was resolved to hold my tongue, certain that justice would be done as this man’s crimes became evident, but I hear the crowd contemplate forgiveness and not once has this Council addressed his greatest sin,” she explained, curling in on herself. Her chiton shifted as she spread her stance for balance, arms held to her chest as if to hold her heart back while she struggled to contain her angry tears.

Caenis moved to her side and put a hand on her back for comfort. The Councilmember gently guided her forward and offered a hand for her to hold while she found her quivering voice again.

“It does not matter how many people he may have saved by breaking the law,” Xenia managed, “more have been lost to his neglect! My husband, Marcus, was this man’s first mate aboard the Speeding Sol and was lost to the sea when his captain’s reckless behavior drove them to their deaths. Pirates? The Black Tide? It doesn’t matter!” She glared at Phainon with so much pain and anger that his own face fell into grief with his aching heart. He wanted to hold her, to comfort her, but she needed more than he could hope to provide as tears spilled over, and she had to take a second to sob. “I am one of many women and men who have lost their loved ones, not only on the Sol but on the two ships sent to retrieve this criminal to bring him to justice. Far more have died for his adventure, for his epic, than have been saved.”

She turned to everyone in the crowd, now silent with the weight of her pain. “When my Marcus held me the night before his departure, he told me with pride what an honor it was to serve the Lady Aglaea at the command of the Deliverer. He admired this man more than any in the city as the hero that we had been taught to believe in, that many of us have seen him embody… but good deeds from a young man do not make him qualified to lead men to their deaths!”

Xenia held more tightly to Caenis’ hand. Her knuckles were white, but the Elder didn’t wince or flinch. “His arrogance, his recklessness has denied my son his father, and then he has the gall to stand here and blame the Black Tide? He stands here and tells a story of a lone survivor choosing to honor the sacrifice of his men, men that trusted and loved him, by joining pirates. Phainon may not have killed any Okhemans, but he supports and loves the men who did while he ignores the blood on his own hands!”

On stumbling feet with tears flowing freely she turned again to Phainon. “They trusted you completely! Believed in you! Did you even mourn them? Did you honor them with funeral rites as we did here? While we were praying to Thanatos to bear them safely through the Sea of Souls, you were falling in love with the very same pirates you were hunting, that my Marcus longed to bring to justice.” She turned her head back and forth to plead with the crowd to understand. “Had this monster died with the Sol, how many more Okhemans would yet live? Even if there was no hope for my husband there would have been hope for Captain Theophis and his crew. The pirates would have still chased away and saved Commander Hapries, and this fool would not have unleashed the Tide in a manner that may threaten Okhema. I don’t care if the Council dismisses the charges of piracy, I don’t care if they choose to end the war with Castrum Kremnos, none of that matters to me as much as seeing the Scales of Talanton balanced for the sake of the crew you abandoned!”

She stumbled in close to Phainon so he could see the hatred in her eyes, her desperate longing as she told him, just him, “a good captain would have gone down with her ship.”

The crowd mulled over this new information while Xenia eyed him with such vitriol that Phainon was starting to get weak knees. Shame filled his consciousness with an uncomfortable itch that settled around his heart and neck to strangle him, and he knew she could see into him just as Phainon could see into her. Hatred and anger were easy emotions. Grief was infinitely harder to grasp with grace. How many times had Marcus reassured her before they departed, that he would come home to her and their son in glory? How many times had he kissed her and his boy and told them what an honor it was to serve his city? When he praised Phainon as a captain he was excited to serve, did he do so with absolute faith, convincing his beloved wife and son that the Deliverer would protect him as they did what they believed was right?

When she looked at Phainon she saw a vicious pirate that stole from her the man she treasured above all else. She saw a thief that took away a father and a future. And most of all, she felt betrayed, because a part of her that could not look past the truth of circumstance felt as though Phainon’s failure made her husband a liar. How many dreams had they shared as a couple? What hopes did they have for her son? These angry tears that spilled down her cheeks and dripped from her jaw and chin were not shed for Phainon, they were meant for the man she wanted to see most in the world.

This weight of loss was crushing her completely and he longed to make it right.

“Thank you for your testimony, Xenia,” Caenis praised with shallow compassion. She gently pulled the mourning woman away from Phainon to face the crowd again. “If this were your decision, how would you balance the scales?”

“His life is all that I would accept,” she said firmly, “He was the captain, those men and that ship were his responsibility. He failed them and should have perished with his ship. It is justice to demand he pay for this sin now.”

Phainon’s hands tightened into fists and the golden thread pulled in response. He felt horrible and for a moment he agreed with Xenia, that perhaps he should have perished but her sentiment came from a place of malicious grief. She was searching for revenge, not justice, and while Phainon had made mistakes, he had also played that fateful night in his head many times since. There was no action that he would have taken differently with the information that was available to him at the time. Information that was severely limited, even with Aglaea’s threads.

If Okhema was not so focused on complacency, on hiding from the world at large and pretending that there is no conflict in Amphoreus, then perhaps Marcus and the others would still be alive. For as eager as Aglaea was to accept refugees, to send the Heirs and her Navy to save people from the Tide, he had not once seen the Council approve the means to track the Tide nor research it. Phainon wanted to say as much, to shift the blame where it belonged, on the Council that insisted on keeping secrets and fueling prejudice to ensure that Okhema stays picturesque and perfect without struggle. He should out the Council and tell the people that if they would simply look beyond the Dawn Device perhaps he would’ve known the extent of the Tide as an immediate threat and not an enemy of distant city-states.

But he couldn’t because that’s not what Xenia needed right now. That’s not what any of them needed right now. Pointed fingers would not move the city forward out of stagnation.

“Xenia,” he gently said, and she turned on him with heartbroken malice, “I will not plead for my life for my sake, but for yours. My death will not bring you peace.”

“It’s a start,” she hissed.

Before Phainon could say anything else Caenis pulled her away, guiding Xenia to sit beside the Council in the front row. Then the Elder turned back to the crowd to ask, “Are there others in agreement? That for his crimes, incompetence, and neglect, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae should offer up his life?”

The response was an overwhelming disagreement in the form of boos and angry shouts. For as torn as the people were, they still held Phainon in high regard.

“What think you, Lady Aglaea?” Caenis taunted, “Will you exercise your influence to save his life?”

“I will not.”

The crowd and Caenis paused, stunned by that total disregard for the life of one of her own. Phainon could not bring himself to look at Aglaea when she said that, but he felt in one tiny thread around his finger a tiny tremble when she added, “I have no love for a traitorous hero. Do with him as you please.”

While her words stung, rife with indifference, Phainon clung to that thread like a lifeline. It quivered on every word, soft enough to be felt but subtle enough to not be witnessed by the others. There was reassurance in her lie as Aglaea distanced herself from him and he saw in Caenis’ face revealing disappointment. Caenis’ hatred of the Flame-Chase would ever dominate her desire for fairness and justice. If Caenis could find in Phainon’s trial a chance to punish Aglaea, she would do it. It was kindness to push Phainon away.

Still the crowd boiled with discomfort at the implication. They expressed confusion and worry with many more beginning to shout and yell for Phainon to be freed. Despite Xenia’s emotional plea that pushed many of the crowd to indecision, too many Okhemans weighed this heavy mistake against the rest of Phainon’s testimony and what he had said about the Black Tide. He had recounted for them the story of the Sol’s demise, and while the thread had not borne witness to the truth of that part of his tale, they had no reason to believe he lied about the futility of the crew’s end and did not believe he should be held responsible for the tragedy.

Caenis turned and walked back to the other Elders, and they gathered together to deliberate. All the while the crowd roared, eager to have their opinions known until they were silenced by Elder Callictis rising to his feet to address the people.

“This Council has decided on the topic of Phainon of Aedes Elysiae’s proposal, to reject it in its entirety. Castrum Kremnos has crumbled to dust, there is no need to ally ourselves with her people, what remains of their military might pales compared to Okhema’s Navy. Okhema has no reason to send men to die to rescue the leader of our enemies. Okhema is protected by the Dawn Device and has no need to concern ourselves with the Black Tide. As to the matter of the Coreflame of Strife, it will be seized and taken into the care of the Lady Goldweaver to prevent this power from returning to our generational enemy.”

Phainon pulled at the threads. They felt more binding than reassuring now.

Elder Callictis continued, “In the trial of Phainon of Aedes Elysiae, this Council has decided on a guilty verdict. Regardless of any noble intentions, the accused broke the law and facilitated the breaking of the law leading to the deaths of Okhemans. He willingly conspired with the enemies of the Holy City and for this act of treason we sentence him to death by beheading. The execution will be held one quint past Entry Hour at the Worldbearing Altar with this Council serving as witnesses. There will be no public access.”

The crowd erupted into chaos.

Chapter End Notes

I apologize for how uniform everyone sounds. I try to give each character distinct speaking patterns to distinguish them from each other and Phainon even has two patterns, one for debate and one for his everyday life, but unfortunately the NPCs I grabbed from the game don't have enough to go off of and I didn't care if Caenis' syntax was unique as long as she was a bitch soooo yeah :')

chapters.title: Chapter 34: The Dangerous/Miraculous Power of Truth
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

New Character Tag: Tribbie New tag: Temporary Imprisonment

Phainon, the hero, gets the chance to play the damsel in distress. Too bad his prince is off slaying dragons.

Chapter Notes

I’m genuinely happy that some people are able to predict some parts of the fic. I know some people don’t like predictability but it means I’m writing my characters well and managing my foreshadowing! Ready to see if you guessed correctly? :3c

The shock of the announcement hit Phainon with a crushing sense of failure, not for his own life, which he cared little about, but for the people who had been relying on him to secure this victory. As soon as his sentence was read, Phainon hurriedly looked at Aglaea, an instinctual response, he was sure. Phainon didn’t know what he expected to see. Comfort? Anger? Disappointment?

She had her eyes closed and her head bowed, face guarded and neutral, like she didn’t care. It made him feel hollow to see her like that until Phainon realized Caenis was studying Aglaea as well, searching for a reaction that the Goldweaver refused to give. When the golden threads tightened around Phainon’s wrists and ankles, visibly restraining him so he couldn’t run from his fate, Phainon realized that Aglaea had to play a long game, even if it meant sacrificing him for a greater good. More than anything, he trusted her.

The assembly was erupting around them, worsened by the Dawncloud guards that rushed to secure the safety of the Council and surrounded him with weapons drawn. The crowd was furious with the decision and as the shock settled, more joined the chorus of voices that demanded a retrial or simply shouted for him to be freed. A scuffle was breaking out in distant seating as the populace disagreed with the sentencing, but Phainon never got to see the outcome.

He was swiftly placed in the Council’s chains to replace the glimmering comfort of Aglaea’s threads as he moved from her care to their confinement, and the Council took no chances with the Deliverer. As they locked the manacles around his wrists, ankles, and neck, Phainon really did consider fighting back. These men stood little chance against his strength, even unarmed, he doubted they could best him if he tried to escape, but there were too many people there and Phainon would never risk the collateral damage against an innocent populace if he had the choice.

As the golden threads gave way to steel, he held his tongue, held his peace, waiting for an opportunity that didn’t come. A guard pulled roughly on the chain attached to his neck and Phainon stumbled forward with a shout and growl. They gave him little time to recover, and he was half dragged, half led from the agora to the shores of Dawncloud.

Only the assembly was perched over the lake, the rest of Dawncloud stretched over the plateau beneath Kephale at the far side of the water, and along the beach where sprawling buildings connected to Marmoreal Palace. It was there that they took him, back through the places of study, past administrative offices, through the maze of stairs, balconies, and courtyards up high to the Council’s prison.

Okhema had two jails. The other was in the city proper and was more what one would expect from a prison meant for the rare long-term inmate. This one was smaller, set high above a cliff overlooking the lake, run by the Dawncloud guards directly under command of the Council rather than the police that answered to Aglaea. There were only two cells here, meant for temporary holding. There was no bed, no place to relieve himself and nothing that could offer comfort. A small, barred window was set high in the wall opposite the door to let in daylight and a restrictive view of Kephale, but otherwise it was a plain, dark box carved out of stone.

Phainon resisted going in. He dug in his heels and held his breath as five men wrestled him into the small space. He managed to elbow one of them in the face, breaking a nose and his boot cracked the rib of another before the new collar at this throat dug too deep and he saw stars. Cold stone slammed against his face as he was pressed against the wall by an arm across the back of his neck and a fist in his hair. Another man had a shoulder against Phainon’s back, digging hard enough to bruise between his shoulder blades. The chains rattled as these men locked the links in place and then they finally let him go to cough and rub his sore throat.

If he had been anyone else, this would have been overkill. The door was heavy wood, locked tight, the stone walls would not easily fall, and the chain around his neck was firmly connected to a ring on the wall. Even if Phainon had the strength to barrel through the door, the chain around his neck was too short to reach it. The length was barely enough to let him sit on the ground.

He pulled at the chains still holding his wrists together, testing the strength of the metal at the locked clasps and hissed when the cold steel bit into his skin. Every time he shuffled his weight the chain between his ankles dragged across the ground, too loud in the confined space. Phainon shouted in frustration and tried to pull the chain free from the wall, but it didn’t budge, and the thick collar settled heavily on his collarbones.

Slowly he sank to his knees and the short chain tugged at his neck. Phainon’s feet still hurt from standing in the agora for so long. The Trial had eaten up the entire afternoon, and Curtain-Fall Hour was fast approaching, not that he’d be able to see the thief star from here…

How did it all go so wrong? He really thought that the people of Okhema were on his side. They were on his side! They were ready to start a fight when he was dragged away from his people and family. Phainon thought for sure that at least part of what he had advocated for would have passed the Council’s shrewd judgement. Even if they didn’t let him go, still held him accountable for the crimes he had committed at sea, he had thought for sure that ending the war on paper would be an easy victory for everyone. What governing body would decline the opportunity to take credit for lasting peace, claiming victory over a generational enemy?

He slammed his fist into the wall. Then again. Phainon punched the solid foundation until his knuckles cracked, and golden blood spattered on the wall in tiny droplets and dripped down his fingers. Then he tried grabbing the chain and pulling and tossing like a wild, desperate animal until warmth seeped down his neck from where the harsh metal cut into the soft skin under the hinge of his jaw. Still, he fought, clawing at the manacles and kicking at the walls and locks with snarling shouts and pained, frustrated cries until his voice cracked and his strength was spent.

Phainon sank again to his knees and leaned forward until his forehead pressed against the cold wall. He panted helplessly and whispered soft apologies inside his head. The Kremnoan people were walking to Okhema for help, unaware that they were walking into waiting spears. Okhema would see their approach as an army come to invade their homeland, without the official peace that Phainon had asked for.

There was morbid poeticism in knowing that Phainon would die beneath the visage of his Titan, just as Mydei would under his. While Mydei fought the Black Tide at the peak of Castrum Kremnos, Phainon had fought beneath Kephale for the same lasting peace of which they together dreamed. He prayed in soft, rough mumbles that the crew would find a way to save their Prince. Phainon wasn’t afraid to die, but how could he go to the next life while Mydeimos struggled endlessly, not knowing how he really felt? At least the crew would be safe, he reasoned, but the thought of never seeing them again squeezed his heart with such agony that tears rolled free.

Phainon didn’t know how long he knelt there with the Dawn Device illuminating his cell with bright sunbeams. No food was wasted on a man doomed to die. No guards came to taunt him. He was simply alone.

“Woooow, they must really be afraid of you, brat.”

Phainon’s eyes widened and he stumbled back to his feet, looking for Cipher.

“Ew, I don’t like the new jewelry though. It’s so not your style,” the cat crooned from the window. Her face was blocking half of the light as she peered through the bars. She was holding tightly to the metal rods for balance.

He stepped back as far as the chain would let him go so he could see her better.

“Oh, Zagreus’ oversized purple balls,” she huffed, “if you’re crying I’ll just come back later.”

“Wait! Cipher, stop!” he called to her, “I’m not anymore.”

“Maybe you should be since you feel so badly about-“

“Ciphy, he doesn’t need that right now…” scolded Trinnon. Her soft, tired voice preceded her little head popping into the remaining space in the window, blocking the rest of the light aside from the halo around each of their heads. It was oddly fitting considering the angelic comfort they were bringing him with their presence. He could never tell Cipher that. She would be so offended.

“Trinnon!” he greeted cheerfully.

“Snowy, are you okay?” she asked.

“I-I am.”

Cipher rolled her eyes so hard she almost fell and scrambled to hold onto the bars. She leaned back enough to look straight down at something he couldn’t see. “Damn it, Bartholos stop squirming so much!”

“Your tail is in my face, Boss!” Phainon couldn’t see Cipher’s best friend and sidekick, but his high-pitched, whiny voice came through the window just fine. That explained how she was up so high. Cipher was good at climbing, but she couldn’t fly like Trinnon and Bartholos could.

“It’s okay if you aren’t okay,” Trinnon reassured him.

Phainon looked down, hanging his head in shame. “I just… I don’t know what went wrong.”

“What did you expect for telling the truth like that?” Cipher said casually and Phainon looked back up at her with a confused tilt of his head that rattled the chains. “Oh, come on, brat, isn’t it obvious?”

“Ciphy…”

“You told the truth,” Cipher repeated, “You told the truth that the Council didn’t want anyone to know.”

And he did it in a public space, more than that, he was the Deliverer, people listened to him. Xenia had said it herself, they trust him and believe in him, so when he came home and broke the news about the world beyond the Dawn Device, he became the biggest threat to the Council’s carefully tailored society built on ignorance and complacency. As long as he was alive, he held the ears and faith of the people. There was no other way to silence him than to demand his head. It all clicked so hard that his eyes got wide and his shoulders slumped. Cipher tapped her nose when she saw the light turn on in his head and smiled her cat-like smile.

“Now you’re getting it.” She yelped as she dropped a couple feet from the window, leaving thin, long claw marks on the stone as she scrambled to hold on, and bright light shined directly in his eyes. He flinched away with a turn of his head and blinked until he could safely squint again.

“Snowy,” Trinnon said, unbothered by Cipher wrestling with her ride, “you still did the right thing. We loved your story and Okhema loves it too, even if some of them are scared.”

He looked down again, still contemplating the futility of the situation but Trinnon didn’t let the guilt settle in his heart.

“It wasn’t your fault,” she reassured in that soothing voice, “we know you took Xenia’s words deep inside you, but you have to know it wasn’t your fault.”

The tears beaded at his eyes again. He didn’t realize how badly he needed to hear those words. No matter how many times he tried and failed to forgive himself for what happened, knowing that someone else was there with answer, helped so much. He clung to her sentiment; let it dampen the guilt that lingered so he wouldn’t fall into crippling despair.

“UGH,” Cipher complained, she was finally back in the window, eyeing his tears, “stop that, you have more important things to worry about.”

Phainon tugged on the chains again. “Can you get me out?”

Trinnon raised a hand to her mouth to think. “Snowy, Agy told us not to take sides, and we agree with her. We cannot help you.”

“I’m not part of that we,” Cipher reminded Phainon, “but I’m not sure I want to help you after what you did.”

Phainon was again confused. It was all over his puppy dog face as he puzzled over what she said. He hadn’t even been around to do anything that might have upset her.

“Fucking Titans, you don’t even remember?” Cipher complained.

“He doesn’t remember??” Bartholos echoed in squeaks, “so much for the score of a lifetime.”

“Use that brain of yours for a second brat,” she commanded, still scowling down at him, “what did you forget to do, when you went to Castrum Kremnos?”

His immediate thought was Mydei, and his heart hurt again but after a long minute of trying to remember what Cipher had to do with Castrum Kremnos he remembered their original deal, the one this money-loving cat had made with them both.

“…we didn’t unlock the treasury door,” he groaned.

“Imagine my surprise when I made that long run with a big bag to fill with beautiful treasure and those big doors were still locked!” she complained.

“Tell him about the Tide!” Bartholos chimed and Cipher smacked her head on the top of the window with a yowl when he jumped.

She let go of a bar to presumably slap at him and she jostled about back and forth with flailing arms to keep her balance. “I would if you’d stop moving around you swollen grape!”

“Hehehe.”

It took her a second to settle again. “Whatever beasty you woke up on that island has the Tide all kinds of messed up,” she reported.

“Wait… you were there while Mydei-“ Phainon started to say.

“Yeah, I saw him,” she confirmed. Her voice had dropped in pitch to her more serious voice. “The lion was still fighting when we got there. Not sure how much of his humanity is left the way he was throwing himself at that thing.”

“And a good thing too,” Bartholos added. Phainon still couldn’t see the spirit creature, but Cipher’s involuntary bouncing and annoyed facial expression gave him away. “That kraken could eat whole islands if it wasn’t for that crazy guy keeping it busy.”

Phainon felt his body double in weight and his breath stuck like sludge in his chest. Suddenly his own skin was uncomfortable and itchy, the steel on his neck was too tight. He reached up and slipped his fingers under the collar to pull it down and move it from side to side as though that would alleviate some of the discomfort, but sticky warm blood trickled down his throat and made things so much worse.

Did Bartholos say a kraken? Is that the form the Black Tide had taken to fight Mydei? How could he hope to compete with that? With Mydei’s history in the Sea of Souls, fighting monsters… this was a horror meant to break him at every level.

“I need to get back to him,” Phainon mumbled.

“…what did he say?” Bartholos called.

“He says he needs to go back,” Cipher reported.

Trinnon’s face twisted into deeper concern. It didn’t look right on her child-like face, even with the flower veil she wore to cover her eyes, the crease of her brow was visible between her ruby bangs.

“Can’t he just open the treasury when he goes back?” Bartholos suggested.

“I am… deeply sorry that we forgot, Cipher,” Phainon said, genuine and with a small voice, “we had other things on our minds.”

Her cat ears twitched and they sat in silence for a while until Cipher sighed, “Well, you can’t exactly make good on your promise if the Council puts that pretty face of yours in a box, can you?” Another exasperated sigh, like this was the worst inconvenience of her life. “Let me see if I can get you out.”

“Can you just pick the lock?”

“Just-Just pick the lock?!”

“Did he tell you to pick the lock?!”

“No appreciation for the art of the heist! I thought I taught you better than that, brat,” she lamented.

Phainon was starting to get impatient, but he pushed it back down.

“Ciphy…” Trinnon whined, and Cipher softened.

“Give me some time to figure it out,” she said, “I know I make everything look effortlessly easy, but you don’t exactly fit in my pocket, do you?”

“…thank you, Cipher, truly.”

“Ew, sentimentality, I liked you better when you were on the other side of the world,” she complained, already leaving. Her voice faded as she finished the sentence, not giving him a chance to retort. The teasing was nice, comforting in an otherwise bleak situation. Even if she couldn’t save him, it meant everything that she was trying.

Trinnon rested her chin on both of her hands on the windowsill. “We can stay with you, Snowy, if you need us.”

He smiled warmly at her. “Thank you teacher, but I don’t want you to get in trouble too. I’m sure Aglaea has a plan and will need you.”

“Agy is very smart,” Trinnon agreed, “we will keep watch over you from a distance then, as we always have.”

As we always have. Phainon remembered the fair winds on his journey when the skies were clear, always exactly what they needed, when they needed it.

“Thank you, Trinnon,” Phainon said with all the heart he could muster, and then she was gone.

He waited in silence, looking at the window until the light hurt his eyes and then Phainon slowly sat back down with his back against the wall. The loose links of the chains settled on his shoulder and lap, but he gave them no concern.

Phainon’s mind and heart were across the ocean, with a blonde-haired Prince who needed him at his very best.

-

Hephaestion had been explicitly told not to sit out on deck for too long, but he was too happy to have some semblance of freedom back to obey Perdikkas and the anxious discomfort of experienced battle instinct was making that infirmary feel cramped. The compromise was the little fat pegasus had to keep him company, providing a steady stream of healing the entire time that gave him the energy to feel normal again. Hyacine’s healing magic couldn’t replace the pieces of his lungs and stomach that had been destroyed when he got hurt, but it could let him pretend that he was back to at least 50% of his strength and maybe, maybe with time, he could fight at everyone’s side again.

He tapped his fingers on the railing while Krateros paced. Fig Stew was prancing behind him, jumping into every imaginary footprint in turn. It was the nature of Kremnoans to leave all grudges on the battlefield and Hephaestion was no exception, despite their frequent fighting and fundamental disagreements, they both worried about Phainon. It was impossible to know if he was doing well in whatever meeting, debate, or engagement they were holding for him.

Anaxagoras had insisted that Phainon was charming to a fault and had a rapport with the people of the city that would garner him some protection. Then the scholar had muttered about that woman being a big support in a pinch too and that Phainon was probably going to be fine. But when Curtain-Fall Hour arrived, and the thief star flew overhead, Krateros was still pacing, and Hephaestion was still sitting by the railing tapping his fingers. Peucesta was playing something generic and quiet in the background while everyone waited in uneasy silence like the night before a battle.

There was still no word from Phainon.

“So, are we weighing anchor, captain?” Leonnius asked. He was lying in the shrouds with his legs dangling just barely out of reach of Hephaestion’s head. The title lingered, unsure, between all of them.

Hephaestion grunted, non-committal.

“Phainon told us to run,” Perdikkas reminded them but there was no command or urging in his vocalized recollection.

Another grunt. What would Mydei do? Would he put the crew at risk for something that was probably nothing? For all they knew, Phainon was giving a victory toast at an Okheman feast and lost track of time. Or he was in prison, and this Council or even the Goldweaver refused to listen to him at all. They didn’t know enough about Okhema to make an informed decision.

“I could go ask someone, Lord Hephaestion,” Castorice offered.

“We still don’t know if they consider you a hostage or a runaway,” Hephaestion said gently, “we don’t want to lose you too.”

He scanned the horizon. From their sheltered cove there wasn’t a lot to watch aside from the path up to the road. Hephaestion saw a distant glimmer and squinted. Something was sparkling just above the ground, a glimmer of gold at first but now a red dot was flying rapidly towards the ship.

He stood up and snapped at the others to get their attention and held his hand out for Peucesta’s bow but Perdikkas snatched it before Hephaestion could and drew it himself. If they weren’t potentially in danger, he’d be more annoyed by the doctor’s interference. Even if his wounded chest took priority over his wounded pride.

The others were slowly wandering over to the rail to look at the approaching… something. Leonnius had twisted in the shrouds to watch, even Fig Stew jumped up onto the railing, too curious to resist.

“What is that?” the runner wondered under his breath.

Perdikkas drew the bowstring back, and pointed with his finger beside the arrowhead, tracing a path at the oncoming… something… was that person? A tiny person?

Little Ica made a trilling sound and Hyacine hurried to Perdikkas’ side with a gentle but firm, “Wait! Wait!”

Castorice too gasped when she realized who it was. “Lord Hephaestion, that is not an enemy!” she insisted and then a breath later Tribbie was landing in Castorice’s arms for a happy greeting hug.

They spun on the deck, squealing like schoolgirls that hadn’t seen each other all summer while the Kremnoans still tried to process what was going on. Perdikkas slowly relaxed the bow until he could safely put the arrow back in the quiver and handed the weapon back to Peucesta. The bard tucked it away while he balanced the lyre on his leg so he could keep playing one-handed. The tune changed from something ominous and troubled to a curious brightness.

“Lady Tribbie!” Castorice greeted her, finally setting the girl down.

“Lady Tribbie!” Hyacine echoed while Fig Stew and little Ica hurried over to investigate with sniffs and happy chirps.

“Little Cas! Little Cinny!” she cheerfully greeted and Hephaestion decided he was just going to be lost and he accepted that. This person was half the height of the other two, a child, so the honorifics were confusing at best.

Bright, short red hair framed big blue eyes that rivaled Phainon’s for depth of color, made brighter by an adorable and stylish knee-length dress that matched her winged boots, flower themed headband, and black gloves. The accents and patterns were the same hue as her tiny golden wings that hovered over her shoulder blades behind her back. This Tribbie person had all the hallmarks of a well-kept child, with a tiny ponytail that only held back a very small portion of her hair, an inconsistent, half-forgotten braid in her bangs, and so many matching flower accessories pinned to her dress that there couldn’t be any left behind in the box. But she was clean, happy, and very respected by the two women on board.

“Tribbie? As in Tribios?” Krateros asked beside Hephaestion, and the new captain was genuinely surprised to see recognition and shock on the old man’s face.

“You know her, Krateros?” he asked.

“It has been decades,” the veteran admitted, “but she has not changed.”

“We age differently than humanity,” Tribbie confirmed as she, no, they, finally stopped playing with Hyacine and Castorice to turn to them, “but we remember you, Krateros of the Godshield Brigade and when you came to us for advice.”

The old man’s eyes widened.

“Uh, okay, that’s creepy, what’s going on?” Leonnius interjected.

Ptolemy’s gasp was a partial answer, and he finished the rest with excitement, “wait, wait, Tribios, the Holy Maiden of Janus? Demigod of Passages, the first Chrysos Heir?”

“How in Nikador’s balls do you know that??” At least Leonnius had the courtesy to swear in Kremnoan when he was in gentler company.

“Because I know how to read you cock-shaking nincompoop!” Ptolemy too swapped to Kremnoan to be polite.

Peucesta strummed a few notes and sang in his gentle, attention-grabbing tenor, “Sing to me muse of she who stepped through the first crossroads, who defied the gods to speak for humanity the will of fate. Sing of the first heroine who became many voices to reach every corner with a message of lasting hope.”

“Please, there is no need to sing our praises,” Tribbie insisted with a humble blush, “we are simply Tribbie, messenger of the Chrysos Heirs.”

“Have you brought us a message, Lady Tribbie?” Hyacine asked and the child, the Holy Maiden, wilted. Their wings drooped and their shoulders dropped even as they raised a hand to their chest and turned to face them all.

“Yes. It is about Snowy…”

“Snowy?” Perdikkas asked.

“Snowy is what Lady Tribbie calls Lord Phainon,” Castorice explained, “is he okay?”

“For now, but the Council of Elders has passed judgement on him,” Tribbie said gently, “they put him on Trial and have sentenced him to die at the Entry Hour.”

Peucesta’s lyre twanged an ugly note when his hand slipped, Castorice gasped, and then it was silent on deck while the news sank in. There was a long story there but right now those details didn’t matter.

“Lady Tribbie,” Castorice asked in a quiet, worried voice, “do you know where he is? Can you use your gate to save him?”

Sadly, Tribbie bowed their head. “We are only here as a messenger. It is our duty to share news, but we must remain neutral to the will of the Council, or things will be harder for Agy. We want to help,” they admitted, voice wavering, “but we know more than most that losses are a constant on the Flame-Chase journey.”

Something about that didn’t sit right with Hephaestion and he frowned deeply.

“Heh,” Ptolemy chuckled, and everyone looked at him with frustrated confusion, even Tribbie who seemed hurt, until he added, “then it is well that we are not on any Flame-Chase journey. We get to rescue Phainon for real this time.”

Perdikkas snorted through this nose and Leonnius snickered. Tribbie’s eyes glittered with knowing mischief that briefly had Hephaestion wondering if this was what she had hoped for from the beginning.

“Even this legitimate rescue is breaking who knows how many laws,” the doctor lamented.

“I will look up every last one when we are sailing away from this place,” Ptolemy promised.

“It is a good day to be a pirate,” Peucesta mused softly with a few accompanying notes.

“Gear up,” Hephaestion ordered, “we don’t have a lot of time.”

“Awoo!”

-

The last time the crew had visited Okhema only a small group had taken to the streets but when Hephaestion called the entirety of the Chryseus Leo to the deck to tell them that Phainon was in danger and needed saving, the outpouring of volunteers turned a quiet rescue mission into a ‘fuck it, we do it our way’ kind of affair, long-term consequences be damned.

The two groups sort of formed on their own. Originally Hephaestion only wanted one group, but when word got around, Anaxagoras had insisted on going into the city himself for an errand unrelated to the rescue. The scholar had been mostly isolated, keeping himself in the galley, pouring over his research as he worked on improving the Black Tide talisman. It had become an obsession of his, so it was surprising to see him on deck at all.

When Ptolemy had tried to argue with the guy against a separate mission, Anaxa had cracked his knuckles, opened his mouth, and Hephaestion still wasn’t sure how in the Netherealm he had convinced every Kremnoan onboard that he needed an escort to raid the Dawncloud Institute. He vaguely remembered big words describing Black Tide research and something about proper alchemical supplies. Krateros was a willing volunteer for that side quest. The old man recruited a few willing veterans, and they eagerly set out to approach the city from another route, to more easily visit hot spots around town that Anaxa thought ‘had promise’.

Hephaestion’s group was comprised of all the people that he couldn’t say no to. Ptolemy, Peucesta, Perdikkas, and Leonnius, of course, insisted on coming along, fully armed, fully geared with even their plumed helmets on their heads. They were imposing Kremnoans ready to storm the streets, but the two remaining Chrysos Heirs after Tribbie had departed had insisted on coming as well. Hyacine refused to let her recovering patient out of her sight for any strenuous activities and Castorice believed she could keep Aglaea off their tail in the event the golden threads made an appearance. Even Fig Stew, wearing his own little helmet, ran beside them as they hurried to the city in full regalia, bright red and gold colors on display.

The first sign that something had changed was at the gate, where the road turned from dirt to carefully cared for tile, when their group crossed into Okhema and ran into the city guard. Hephaestion had ordered their men to avoid killing anyone, they had a mission to do, and restraint would go a long way for future relations (if those could be salvaged at all), but it wouldn’t do to allow an alarm to be raised at the start.

There were four men waiting there armed with swords at their hips and shields on their backs. Hephaestion and Leonnius hurried to disarm their foes, but all four guards looked directly at the group, then turned around to face their backs to them. Confused, the two Kremnoans stumbled to a stop a pace away, spears pointed at the ground, but ready in case this was a trap.

“You heard then about the Deliverer?” one of the Okhemans said loudly to his friends, wanting to be overheard.

“Oh, the trial earlier,” his friend said back equally loud, “ridiculous if you ask me!”

“My brother is a guard at the Marmoreal Palace, he says those cowards of the Dawncloud Guard are keeping the Deliverer near the Council’s Administration District high in that gaudy tower.”

Hephaestion and Leonnius exchanged looks while the rest of their group caught up. Leonnius shrugged when Hephaestion tilted his head in confusion far enough for his long hair to spill over his shoulder. When the guards refused to acknowledge them any further, he waved to the group to keep moving. They slowly passed the Okhemans who kept turning in place as they passed to keep their backs facing the Kremnoans.

A third Okheman guard weighed in after quickly checking that this invading force was still nearby, “those arrogant Dawncloud soldiers are traitors if you ask me, all one hundred of them walking fixed patrols on duty tonight.”

“Incompetent traitors,” the last guard agreed, raising his voice and shuffling backwards to stay in earshot of the Kremnoans, “They don’t even bother to check the service routes for the Dawncloud staff!”

Hephaestion and Leonnius lingered to listen while the others hurried down the street. Briefly, Hephaestion’s eyes met with one of the guards. They nodded to each other with mutual respect and then the Okhemans quieted again, resuming their posts and leaving the two of them to catch up.

“Did you hear them?” Hephaestion asked the others as they rejoined the group, and everyone picked up speed.

“What’s Dawncloud?” Leonnius asked.

“It’s the district under Kephale,” Hyacine explained, “up on the plateau, where all the priests live.”

“The route to get there is through Marmoreal Palace,” Castorice added.

A guard on the road ahead spotted them and jumped in surprise. It would be impossible not to be startled by a sizeable unit of shining Kremnoan warriors shaking the road as they ran through the Holy City. The man pulled the horn from his belt. Peucesta reached for an arrow at his side but had barely strung the bow when the guard dropped the horn on the ground and smashed it with his foot. He pointed towards an alley as they approached, guiding them, and not a single person in their group slowed down when Leonnius turned on his heel and raced in the direction the man was pointing.

“Why are they helping us?” Perdikkas asked as they ran.

“Lord Phainon is very beloved in Okhema,” Castorice told them.

“What in Nikador’s name did he say to the city?” Ptolemy wondered aloud.

“The truth,” Peucesta guessed, “what else could he have said that could win the hearts of so many men, to look past what we are for what they know we are here to do?”

“Then let’s not let them down,” Hephaestion ordered as they surged between buildings, heading uphill, “let us do what they cannot and save the Deliverer.”

They broke free of the narrow alley and ended up in a wider street. If they were trying to be sneaky, the best option was to take the indirect route through more narrow side streets, but Fig Stew was done wasting time and the chimera booked it up the main road ahead of them. Peucesta followed next and then their crew were racing in the open.

He didn’t expect traffic this late at night, even with the glow of the Dawn Device making night feel like day, surely Okhemans still slept, but even trying to be quiet they made noise as they ran and there were people that peeked through their curtains. Every time he saw a shuffle on a balcony, those curious eyes watched not with fear but with relief and those few that did not hide reacted favorably.

One man, up late, raised his glass to them as they passed. Another clapped, briefly, but definitively. Every guard turned away and pretended not to see. And still they climbed unhindered.

“Lord Hephaestion,” Hyacine called, “don’t push yourself too hard. If you start to feel short of breath, tell me, and we can catch up to the others when it is safe for you to do so.”

He didn’t answer her to conserve strength. Now that they knew the city guard wouldn’t try to stop them, it was a reasonable request. Hephaestion had every intention of pushing himself beyond his limits if need be to save their brother, but it was nice to know he wouldn’t have to sacrifice his health for victory. His lungs were already fighting to keep up, every breath burned, and they were never quite deep enough, but there would be time to rest when Phainon was safe.

Chapter End Notes

I wrote two versions of this chapter. In the other one, Cipher is the one that tells the Kremnoans what happens and she jump scares them into long strings of robust and clever profanity that I couldn’t censor with “they swore in Kremnoan that Phainon didn’t understand” cause this is Hephaestion’s pov AND HE DEFINITELY UNDERSTANDS. Ptolemy reads lots of things. He has a very colorful vocabulary.

There are two types of people: Cipher - The heist must be elegant and clever and sneaky~ Kremnoans - What if we just break everything? :D
