chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

No new tags but I think this is the last time I'll have to adjust the chapter count now that I've finished pulling apart what's left of my original outline's carcass.

The crew brainstorms on how to get Phainon free...

Chapter Notes

I said it on Twitter, so I’ll say it here too. If this fic breaks 1k kudos before I finish the main plot, I’ll let readers request/vote on additional chapters/one-shots that can be anything from post-plot fluff, five years later, in-character Q&A chapter with questions from my readers, adventures of Fig Stew, prior chapters from other povs, etc. I would retain veto power of course and I won’t write anything that would change the rating, but it seems like a fun way to celebrate if that happens to happen. This is already my most successful fic by a longshot, and I am eternally grateful to all of you who made it this far! I am so content with the love that has already been shared so this would be entirely a bonus for you all as I am already as happy as I can possibly be~! :D

Waiting can be hard. Waiting patiently when you’re hoping to be rescued the night before your scheduled beheading is impossible. Phainon tried napping, he tried pacing, he sang songs under his breath, he crafted his afterlife apology to Mydeimos, tossed a pebble he found up in the air until he dropped it and it bounced out of reach, and all of that took him less than a quint. The misery of waiting to die was compounded by the anxiety of Cipher’s pending rescue attempt.

It was not for lack of hope. Phainon had absolute faith in Cipher! But he didn’t have absolute faith in her punctuality and without any knowledge of her fledgling plan the stress was eating him alive. This was a “better late than never” kind of cat, a sentiment that was notably not applicable to his current situation.

Eventually he sat back down with his back to the wall, legs outstretched, and his head tilted to stare at the ceiling while he dozed. Even if a good night’s sleep was an option he didn’t want to wake up to Bartholos’ giant black eyes and ghost claws in his face, or worse, Cipher’s teasing grin. But as the hour ticked by Phainon found his consciousness drifting along that top layer of sleep, the thin membrane that separates the waking world from the depths of deep dreams. It was the kind of snoozing that lasted for only a few minutes before the dip of the head jerked Phainon back to reality, only to nod off mere seconds later.

It went like that until Phainon lost all sense of time and zoned out watching the dust slowly float by in the beams of light through his window. They glittered as they caught the warmth of Kephale’s light, stars that he could see during the day. He watched the sparkling little dots drift back and forth and started to get frustrated when tiny vibrations disturbed them. He was so annoyed with the disrupted flow of dust that Phainon barely registered the shaking floor as heavy footsteps until he also heard muffled voices and the clank of steel on stone.

Still sitting against the wall with his head tilted back, Phainon’s eyes drifted to the door and narrowed suspiciously. Was it time? Surely Cipher would be lighter than that on her feet and smart enough to not banter with her sidekick the entire way? But the voices mumbling outside his door were too soft to make out and too animated to belong to only a pair of thieves.

The room jumped when something crashed nearby. It wasn’t a distant sound but not in Phainon’s immediate vicinity either. They were the sort of clunks and dinks that one might hear when a neighbor was working on their house next door with invasive construction sounds that felt closer than they were. There was more mumbling, the clang of metal on metal, and the dull hum of noise shifted closer.

Something slammed against his door this time, not particularly hard but with definite purpose. The voices picked up, talking over each other as the latch on his door jiggled experimentally, then a little more insistently, and finally the whole cell shook when it was assaulted a second time.

The heavy wood didn’t budge but Phainon did. He slowly pulled himself to his feet and adjusted the chain around his neck to be more comfortable where he stood against the wall while he watched the door with cautious optimism.

There was quiet on the other side, a few more mumbles, something that sounded rhythmic, and Phainon pieced together what was happening with the instinctual unease of his reliable battle instincts. He retreated towards the corner as far as the chain would allow him to go and pressed himself against the wall in the second before the door was ripped violently from its hinges and thrown across the room to slam into the space that Phainon had been sitting in. It shuddered and clattered down at an angle, eliciting a gasp when it caught the chain on one of its corners as it fell, ripping him forward by his throat while he clutched at the metal to keep his neck from breaking with the impact.

“Pay up,” Ptolemy ordered and Peucesta and Perdikkas passed over a few coins each while Leonnius proudly rolled his shoulder and slapped the dust from his hands in the now open doorway. Splinters were still rolling across the stone floor and one pathetic hinge squeaked as it swung back and forth where it was still hanging onto the wall by one last, bent nail.

They were all shining armor and hope with those glorious red plumes on their helmets waving and cheerful expressions partially visible around the curve of the cheek guards. Phainon held tightly to the chain to keep from choking but through the struggle he smiled at his friends come to save him.

“Phainon/Lord Phainon!” Leonnius and Castorice shouted simultaneously. They both hurried to his side but were promptly cut off and shooed away by Perdikkas. The doctor took note of Phainon’s discomfort on his knees immediately and pointed at the door.

“Make yourselves useful!” he huffed and Leonnius and Ptolemy hurried to lift the door so it would stop pulling on the chain. They put it unceremoniously against the wall it used to be attached to with a thunk.

The relief was instant and Phainon let go of the cold steel to put his hands on the floor while he caught his breath. The doctor was already brushing his hair away from his neck to look at the damage and inspect the locked clasp. Dried blood cracked under the prod of his fingers and Phainon winced at the tickle of a bead of warm gold slowly creeping into the hollow at the base of his throat.

Hephaestion came to him next. The man was the epitome of exhaustion quivering on his feet as he crouched in front of Phainon and put a hand on his shoulder. He took his helmet off and set it on the ground when Phainon looked up at him and they exchanged crooked smiles. It was so nice to see him out of bed. This wonderful man, too thin and lean in his Kremnoan armor, pale as new snow, lightly shining under a sheen of sweat with bandages still clearly visible under the fabric that stretched across his chest between his polished pauldron and shiny belt. He clearly needed to lay down for another week.

“Absolutely useless without us,” Hephaestion said softly, “must be a pre-requisite for a Captain.” He was oblivious to his own condition or firmly in denial, Phainon couldn’t tell either way.

“I told you to run,” Phainon said firmly.

“Pffft,” the first mate laughed, “we didn’t listen to Mydei either. You’re not special.”

Phainon leaned back to sit on his heels and everyone but him glanced down with thinly veiled rage at the clinking chains when they dragged across the stone.

“How did you even find me?” he asked as Castorice slipped into the tiny cell again while Perdikkas was distracted so she could get to him for a reassuring hug. Phainon reached up to gently touch her arms that were wrapped around his shoulders from the side opposite where the doctor was still assessing the damage. The extra bodies were not helping the claustrophobic nature of the prison, but he was grateful for the contact all the same. Yes, even when Hyacine and Peucesta appeared in the doorway to push the cell further past capacity.

“It’s a funny story,” Perdikkas said. The doctor was scooting over to make space for Hyacine who smiled at him, squeezed his arm by way of greeting, and then gently took his hand in hers so she could see how badly he had injured his knuckles. She hummed something under her breath, a lullaby perhaps, too soft to be for the room like a shared secret between doctor and patient while she rubbed his hand reassuringly and dabbed at the bloody tears with a cloth.

“If I may?” Peucesta cleared his throat from the hallway. There wasn’t enough space left for him to feel comfortable crammed between everyone else, but he could be easily heard from where he stood in the doorway even with his soft voice. Phainon expected a lyre and an already composed song about their adventure through Okhema, but Peucesta was shockingly very concise and unaccompanied with few parts waxing poetic.

He started with the crew on deck, eagerly waiting for news as the time of departure came and went. Hephaestion had taken command as ordered but bid them wait. It was well that he had because a heavenly messenger, Tribios, came to share the news of Phainon’s pending execution and the crew needed no other details to mobilize in a moment. When Peucesta’s story moved to the Holy City, Phainon listened with obvious awe when he heard about the guards and populace who stood by in blatant opposition to their upbringing.

“They let you pass?” he asked for clarification.

“Phainon, they told us where you were,” Hephaestion confirmed with so much love in his voice that Phainon worried he might burst.

“More than that,” Leonnius added, “every guard we passed pointed us the right direction, the first group even told us how many Swancloud troops were on patrol.”

“Dawncloud,” Ptolemy corrected.

“That’s what I said.”

“That is not what you said!”

“I think I would know what I said!” Leonnius insisted as he stepped into Ptolemy’s space.

Hephaestion sighed and stood up straight so he could get between them before it came to blows, but Kephale above, Phainon was just so happy to hear them banter. He was so, so grateful and humbled that as bleak as this situation had been, they loved him enough to come for him and they were acting like this was just another adventure, another epic tale to share over fine wine. It filled him with relief and the purest joy that could not be dampened even with the heavy chains keeping him trapped in this horrible place.

“But Dawncloud is run by the Council’s men,” Phainon wondered aloud, “it’s a maze, how did you…?”

Perdikkas smiled. Castorice’s hug turned into a back rub with one hand, the other resting gently on his forearm as she answered meekly, “Aglaea.”

“We made it through Marmoreal Palace much the same way that we did getting through Okhema,” Hephaestion explained when Phainon’s face tilted in confusion. He had a hand on Ptolemy and Leonnius each to keep them apart while they continued to glare at each other, itchy to fight. “But beyond the palace we noticed the guards wearing different colors and assumed we found the right place.” The first mate paused for a deep, struggling breath and let go of his companions to press both of his hands to his chest. Hyacine let go of Phainon to move to Hephaestion’s side, gently urging him to sit with Leonnius’ help.

When Phainon started to get up, worried, Perdikkas and Castorice both tightened their grips on his arms to keep him from making a fuss and he settled back down on his heels. He watched Hyacine check Hephaestion’s pulse and listen to his breathing while Perdikkas picked up the story in his stead.

“The guards at the gate, the first guards we saw, mentioned something about unguarded service tunnels, but we didn’t know where those were until Fig Stew led us to another chimera, a little gray and white thing with horns and a spade tail. It was holding the end of a very fine golden thread in its mouth. We thought if it was a trap at least there’s a chance they’d take us to the same cell block as you and save us the trouble of looking.”

Vigethos… “You followed the thread,” Phainon summarized.

“Led us right here,” the doctor confirmed, “I’m not sure where Fig Stew went, he and that other chimera had a very intense conversation barking and chirping at each other and then they both ran off when we started following the thread.” He gave the cuff around Phainon’s neck an experimental tug and Phainon winced. “And they think we’re barbaric…”

Ptolemy leaned over to inspect where the chain was connected to the wall. He gave it an experimental tug and tapped at the stone around the baseplate with a calculating expression and even held his finger to a spot just above where the padlock connected with the confidence of a navigator marking a spot on a map. “Hand me one of the shields?”

Peucesta leaned around the doorframe to grab one of the round shields that had been left in the hallway. They really had stormed the city prepared for war.

He passed it over and Ptolemy held it in both hands nice and tight to bring the edge of it down on the heavy padlock with zero ceremony and a whole lot of yelling and unbridled rage. The clang was loud enough to wake the entire tower but none of the Kremnoans seemed to care about that half as much as how ineffective the blow was. Only the Okhemans even flinched at the loud noise.

“You didn’t hit it hard enough,” Leonnius critiqued, and Ptolemy scowled.

“’With the same strength that I had when I killed the bravest of our foes,’” Ptolemy quoted out of context, “This is going to be a brain over brawn puzzle, I fear.”

“Just not strong enough,” the runner coughed. “The dust in here is just wow,” he explained when Ptolemy turned on him with a glare.

“Let me try,” Hephaestion offered, and four different people said ‘NO.’ He pouted, dejected, from where he was sitting in his own corner like a child that was enduring a punishment for breaking a rule. Little Ica landed on his head and trilled to offer comfort.

Phainon empathized. He knew what it felt like to not be of use, to be too injured to participate. Hephaestion’s frustration was almost palpable, especially remembering the days after the storm when Phainon was confined to a bed and only wanted to help. Oh… so this is how Mydei felt when he was upset with Phainon for risking further injury for the sake of service.

“Do you have your spears?” Phainon asked.

Ptolemy snapped his fingers as he guessed where Phainon was going with this. “Proper leverage may suffice.”

Peucesta passed a spear from the doorway and Phainon slowly got to his feet. Castorice and Perdikkas helped him up. He didn’t need it, but the moral support was worth keeping his silence and he knew what it meant to them to feel like they were helping.

Ptolemy contemplated how to get the spear through the links with little nods and shakes of his head that were easy to track with the way the plume on his helmet wiggled back and forth, up and down with every contemplative movement. Unfortunately, the weapon was a hair too wide to fit through everything aside from the ring on the wall and that was firmly bolted down. He stabbed it through anyway and put both hands on one side to hold it tight while the butt end of the spear pressed into the wall.

“Wait, wait,” Perdikkas waved his hand and left Phainon’s side to take the spear from Ptolemy so he could swap the end they were pulling on so the very sharp blade was against the wall and not flailing around where it could hit someone.

“So much for brains,” Leonnius coughed again, and Ptolemy let go to jump on him with an annoyed shout. They both went down scuffling and wrestling and they kept it up even when Peucesta firmly dragged them out by their ankles into the hallway to get it out of their systems. A crew of tense Kremnoans storming a city looking for a fight were going to find one somewhere even if it meant with each other. They’d be fine.

Phainon took Ptolemy’s place next to Perdikkas, and they both grabbed onto the spear with both hands to pull. The weapon bowed as they leaned back, slowly bending. Steel and wood creaked at the fulcrum when they hit that point of resistance, their strength versus that of the craftsmanship. For a second it felt like the piece would give. One of the bolts started to wiggle and then the spear snapped and both men fell backwards in a shower of splinters and the pathetic ding of the spearhead clattering against the floor.

Perdikkas looked at the end of the spear in his hand then back at the base of the chain and tsked. “Let it never be said that Okheman smiths are incompetent.”

“Mountain dwellers,” Phainon explained.

“That would do it.”

Hyacine tapped her staff in her hand while she brainstormed aloud. “Cassy, do you think Pollux could pull this free?”

Castorice tilted her head at the thought and then nodded. “Yes, I think they could.”

“We should have led with that,” Hephaestion mused from his time out corner. He was looking a little bit better under Ica’s ministrations.

The room got colder as Castorice closed her eyes and pressed her hands together as though in prayer. An energy gathered around her while they waited for Pollux to respond and then it occurred to Phainon how bad an idea this was.

“Castorice, wait-“ he started to say as she waved her hand in a broad stroke. A thin purple line stretched through the empty space from the floor to the ceiling and three seconds later everyone was shoved into Hephaestion’s timeout corner on top of him. Phainon’s chain tugged painfully against his throat at the end of its reach, and he made a gurgling sound against Pollux’s scaly side. Someone’s arm was in his belly; his foot was in someone’s thigh. Castorice was somehow across his shoulders, and he could hear Hephaestion’s groan turn into a squeak… or maybe that was Little Ica. The pegasus did have the appearance of a squeaking dog toy.

“Oh…” Castorice wheezed.

Pollux whined, only a small part of them made it out of the rip in space and the rumble made the whole building shake. The dragon was trying to cram more of itself into the extremely limited space, clawing at the floor and threatening to bring down the whole building while they puzzled out what was happening.

“I forgot they have to – oof! – squeeze in beside you!” Hyacine lamented, muffled under someone.

“Please stop squirming,” Perdikkas begged with his voice a few octaves higher, “someone’s boot is in in my groin.”

“Sorry, Perdikkas,” Hephaestion gasped from the bottom of the pile.

“Sorry, Pollux, you can go back now,” the Hand of Shadow peeped mildly, and perhaps a little embarrassed.

The dragon hummed and Phainon felt his whole body vibrate with the sound until the purr fully retreated inside the tear and the gate to the void winked out of existence once more. The whole crew peeled themselves off the wall in turn. It was amazing how much bigger the room felt when there wasn’t an oversized death dragon in there with them.

Perdikkas whimpered and limped away from poor Hephaestion who let out a breath with a squeaky moan. Hyacine had somehow ended up on top of him, and she was apologizing profusely and checking for any further damage from where she was kneeling over his lap, but aside from poor Perdikkas everyone seemed okay. Phainon rubbed at his neck and twisted his head back and forth uncomfortably while he glanced at everyone to double check their statuses.

“I think,” Leonnius said from the doorway, having witnessed it from a safe distance, “we might be stupid.”

Ptolemy scoffed and stomped back into the room. He had lost his helmet in the scuffle and just left the thing in the hallway, trading it for a sword. “Proper leverage will work,” he insisted. With the sword still sheathed he wedged it against the ring where the spear had been earlier and tugged. When the metal didn’t budge, he put a foot on the wall and pushed, straining with angry growls and constipated noises that got even more gross and undignified when he added a second foot. The combination of pushing with his feet and pulling with both hands left him parallel with the ground in an impressive defiance of gravity until the sword gave up and bent, dropping the bookworm on the floor.

“And how is that working out for you?” Perdikkas asked, snarky, with his knees still held tightly together to protect his recently bruised manhood.

Ptolemy rolled over and got to his feet again. He held up the sword now bent in the middle at a 45-degree angle to inspect the damage. “Relax, it’s only Leonnius’ sword.”

Leonnius gasped and there was some noise in the hallway as Peucesta tackled the man aside before the rising tensions could cause any real trouble. They had a personal limit to how many fights the men could get into with each other on a mission.

Phainon ran his fingers over the clasps at his wrists and then over the one at his neck. He could feel the little keyhole under his fingertips and the joint opposite it. Those would be the more fragile part of the chain.

“Can someone break the hinge?” he asked. Ptolemy and Perdikkas both leaned over to look at the ones on his wrists. “Right here.” Phainon pointed to where the cuffs would have to bend to open.

“That does look like a weaker part of the ensemble,” Ptolemy mused.

“Stomp on it hard enough and it might break,” Leonnius offered from over Peucesta’s shoulder.

“We’re not going to stomp on him!” Hephaestion growled and then started coughing.

Hyacine scowled at him and started scolding in her firm doctor voice that made everyone feel guilty for being disobedient, “Lord Hephaestion, what did I say earlier?” He stuck out his bottom lip and pouted.

“If we’re really careful with the flat of a knife I bet we can get the little pin out of this hinge,” Perdikkas suggested.

“Yeah I can see it,” agreed the Kremnoan.

Ptolemy reached behind himself and drew a knife from his belt and Phainon leaned forward to watch. A hair’s breadth away from the knife touching anything, Perdikkas sensibly thought of something important. “Phainon maybe you should sit down.”

“Oh.”

“Yes, that would help,” Ptolemy agreed.

The three of them sat down and Castorice scooted in close to watch. Phainon held onto his wrist to keep it steady in his lap while Ptolemy tried to get the blade of his knife in the non-existent spot between the pin and the hinge. He slipped and narrowly missed cutting Phainon and all four of them drew in sharp breaths through their teeth.

“What? What?” Leonnius asked urgently from the doorway. Peucesta’s frown deepened as they watched from relative safety.

“Lord Ptolemy if you hurt Lord Phainon…” Hyacine started.

“He’s fine!”

Maybe this was a bad idea, Phainon considered very briefly. “Let me try,” was what he said instead.

Ptolemy handed him the knife, and the chains clinked together as Phainon tried to get the right angle on the joint. He had a decently steady hand, but the pin was smaller than he realized and after scratching the metal thrice and slipping twice, Phainon slapped at it uselessly with the hilt to achieve the same results.

While he was working on that Leonnius had crept around the others to keep inspecting the collar at Phainon’s neck. Phainon could feel the runner’s fingers gently prodding around the soft flesh and slipping under the collar to gauge the space between the metal and skin.

“Y’know, I think we could squeeze a spear in here.”

“Against my neck?”

“The ring on the wall is too heavily bolted down but this collar is hammered thin, and the lock isn’t very strong. Ptolemy’s leverage idea might work better on this.”

“…”

Hyacine slapped her own face like she couldn’t believe what they were suggesting and Castorice asked, “Is that really the best idea, Lord Leonnius?”

“If it’s that weak we could just pull it apart,” Hephaestion suggested with another wet wheeze. He wilted a little when Hyacine turned on him with a disapproving look.

“I tried that,” Phainon admitted with a shake of his head.

Perdikkas shoved his fingers under the collar too, and Phainon resisted the urge to gag when the pressure on his throat increased and black spots peppered his vision. “We wouldn’t be putting anything sharp in there…”

“As long as we break the chain on his neck, we can deal with his wrists and ankles on the ship,” Peucesta reminded them. His gentle tone did not match the eagerness with which he handed over another spear.

“Okay, okay,” Phainon relented.

The crew was halfway through tag teaming awkwardly shoving the butt of the spear through Phainon’s collar while his eyes were bugging out from the tight squeeze when an exasperated awoo from the doorway stopped them in their tracks. The whole room froze in the middle of what they were doing to look wide-eyed at the chimera in the doorway.

Fig Stew looked horribly unimpressed with those bright red eyes half lidded under his helmet. He studied them all, making a judgmental show of looking at the claw marks on the floor, the broken spear, dented shield, time out Hephaestion, bent sword, and their current weirdness of too many people dog piling Phainon with the worst idea they had yet. The chimera sighed and turned his head to chirp over his shoulder and Vigethos walked up to sit next to him.

“Aglaea…” Phainon mumbled under his breath. He hadn’t expected to see her chimera here. Even when he was mentioned earlier, Phainon never would’ve thought the rotund critter would come to see him.

“Huh,” Leonnius managed, still mostly frozen like the others in their confusion, “I gotta be honest, I really pictured her as a woman.”

Ptolemy snorted but didn’t get a chance to say anything before the chimeras stole the spotlight again.

Fig Stew motioned with a paw towards the group. “Awoo! Aoo, awoo!”

“Awoo.”

“Aoo. Awawaoo.”

Beagle nodded when Fig Stew sighed and they chirped between themselves while everyone else watched with confused silence, unwilling to interrupt even though no one had any idea of what was happening.

The gray chimera pointed at Phainon with a paw and turned to chirp at Fig Stew again who sighed with a short, “Awoo.” Beagle patted Fig Stew on the back in a gesture of comfort.

“Awoo?” he asked.

Fig Stew slapped Beagle for whatever was said and Beagle cackled.

“Awoo! Awoooo! AoAwo!” Fig Stew insisted with a purr.

Beagle shrugged and relented with a soft chirp and reassuring, “Awoo.”

Fig Stew half mounted the other chimera to nose his way into Vigethos’ ruff, pawing at his collar, while the other held perfectly still beneath him. The gray chimera looked entirely too pleased to have Fig Stew necking him like that and Phainon was incredibly close to yelling at them to save such inappropriate behavior until after a date and definitely not in front of people. But well before he could fully process what was happening and the blush in his cheeks, Fig Stew pulled away with a golden thread between his teeth.

The two chimeras leaned away from each other, tugging to stretch the thread between them until it broke and the key that was tied to it dropped to the floor, bouncing with high-pitched clinks until Beagle pounced on it like he was catching a particularly slow fly. He slapped it twice to be sure it wasn’t gonna bounce away anymore and then gently batted it towards Fig Stew.

“Awoo?” Fig Stew asked, surprised, perhaps a bit honored as he pressed a paw to his chest just under his ruff.

“Awoo!” Beagle confirmed politely with his paw outstretched towards Fig Stew and his head bowed.

Fig Stew proudly leaned down to pick up the key in his mouth, nearly slapping Beagle in the face with the plume on his chimera helmet as he did so but Beagle didn’t seem to mind. He just leaned away until Fig Stew was upright again and then he took a seat with an audible flop to watch the orange chimera trot regally up to the awkward crew to slap the stupid spear that was clearly a bad idea and drop the key into Phainon’s lap.

They all blinked at it.

“Key,” Phainon said aloud as he picked it up, “none of us thought of trying to find a key…”

Perdikkas and Hephaestion both slapped their own faces, Leonnius chuckled, Hyacine sighed, Peucesta had crouched down to give Beagle an appreciative pet, and Ptolemy grumbled to himself in ancient Kremnoan so no one would know the specifics of his personal scolding.

“That does remind me, Lord Phainon,” Castorice said shyly, “I had forgotten, Lady Cipher taught me how to pick locks with a hairpin.” The whole room slowly turned to look at her, and she blushed, embarrassed, with both hands held up to her face to hide.

It was Fig Stew that broke the ice in the room with a huff as he walked back to Beagle, gestured broadly at the room with a paw, and chirp-trilled in what could only be interpreted as: do you see what I have to deal with?

Something about that was just so funny to Phainon. Still in chains, still in a tiny cold box, exhausted, emotionally spent, and filthy with blood, sweat, and lingering failure, he started to laugh. It was a genuine thing, a little rough on his sore throat and the way his friends looked at him, he must have seemed like he had gone mad in all the stress.

“Lord Phainon?” Castorice asked. She was peeking at him through the gaps in her fingers.

“I’m sorry, it’s just,” he started to say but his need to recover his breath got in the way. Phainon took a second to find his voice while he bounced the key in his hand. There was so much he could say about how awful this day had been, how seeing them come to his aid didn’t fix everything but it was enough to give him the strength to hold out hope. He wanted to take each of them in turn and tell them what they meant to him, how much he treasured these bonds between them. He wanted to laugh at how silly they all were, struggling to find a solution and in their exhaustion forgot about the most obvious answers. They tried to cram a dragon in this tiny prison cell before they considered picking the lock, a suggestion he had even brought up with Cipher earlier that Curtain-Fall Hour!

Here he was, the failure, surrounded by his new family, supported by his old family, and all he could feel was love. How do you even begin to tell people all of that? Where were the words for that?

Don’t be so sentimental, Deliverer.

He smiled at the memory of Mydei and closed his hand around the key to hold it to his chest and simplified everything he was feeling into one, single statement, “I am so happy to know you all.”

chapters.title: Chapter 36: The Heart of the Solution
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Heh, chapter title is a pun, heh. New tag: Beagle Coconut

Now free, Phainon has one more thing he wants to do before leaving Okhema.

Chapter Notes

Some of you saw this coming :3c

Phainon kicked the last chain across the floor into a pile with the other links and took in a deep, full-bodied breath to release in a satisfied sigh. He rubbed his wrists in turn and dried blood flaked off and flittered to the floor. Ugh, he wanted a bath. There was gold and black under his fingernails and a layer of dusty sweat that made his clothes stick to him uncomfortably.

“We should go before someone comes to check on you,” Ptolemy said while he put his helmet back on. Fig Stew agreed with a chirp and a wag of his tail. He turned to Beagle, and they met noses, staring at each other with their tails vibrating and noses wiggling like they were having their own conversation.

“If they didn’t come running when they heard the noises, I’m not sure they will,” Hyacine observed. She was helping Hephaestion to his feet, a task that Phainon hurried to help her accomplish. The first mate felt so much lighter than before with an arm slung over Phainon’s shoulders, and Phainon not-so-secretly worried about him as he slipped a hand around the man’s waist to hold him up so he could find his footing.

“The Dawncloud Guard are lazy,” Phainon said simply, “they have the most the important job in Okhema and have never once had to exercise their power of protection.”

“Ugh, big men with no experience who like throwing their power around,” Ptolemy grumbled sarcastically, “my favorite.”

Castorice delicately picked up Hephaestion’s helmet for him, but he shook his head at the thought. He was supporting the bulk of his weight just fine, but every inhale was labored, and shallow and each exhale had a wet, sourness to it. The restrictiveness of a helmet felt like yet another bad idea on a night of lesser quality brainstorming.

“Hephaestion, do you have any attachment to that helmet?” Phainon asked.

He shook his head and Phainon gently shifted his friend’s weight to Hyacine so he could take the helmet from Castorice and leave the shining piece of armor upright on top of the chains. Peucesta whistled and Phainon knew he appreciated the implied message of a Kremnoan helmet resting on top of loose chains and an empty cell.

“I was under the impression you didn’t want to be in here any longer than you had to be,” Leonnius teased when Phainon lingered to inspect his work.

“I don’t. Let’s go.”

Phainon was pleasantly surprised and wildly disappointed with how easy it was to escape the Dawncloud Administration District. As was advertised, the service tunnels and narrow hallways that weaved through the ancient architecture were mostly unguarded and those few courtyards, rooms, bridges, and walkways that were entertaining late-night traffic were predictable. The guards that paced did so on strict timers or had given up entirely and were napping at their posts.

This wasn’t the first time Phainon had been through here. As Aglaea’s envoy, Phainon had spent a lot of time in Dawncloud and while he wasn’t familiar with every route he did know that guards were supposed to be few and far between, stationed only in public areas. To see so many, incompetent or not, was a surprise and he reasoned that perhaps the Council had expected something like this.

It made sense of course, Phainon turned himself in, naturally that meant his pirate allies were nearby. The Council were corrupt and self-centered, but they weren’t stupid, increasing patrols was the correct response. Too bad the people they commanded were so inexperienced.

They took it hurried but not sprinting. Hephaestion was doing alright and insisted he was okay, but Phainon could see the struggle in the way he moved even without his spear and shield. The others had opted to carry his equipment for him as they were now down a spear, sword, and shield after their repeated failed attempts to free Phainon with weaponized stupidity. Phainon almost, almost offered to carry the man but he didn’t dare threaten Hephaestion’s pride like that when the man was doing his very best and was focused.

The humidity of the baths was a definite indicator that they had left Dawncloud and returned to the Marmoreal Palace. If what the crew had said was true, and they had no reason to lie, their escape was all but guaranteed, it was only a matter of getting back to the ship but…

Phainon slowed from a jog to a stop and the others passed by him, turning a corner before they realized he was no longer keeping up and then they were back tracking. Heads popped back around the wall in turn, giving him puzzled looks.

“Lord Phainon?” Castorice asked. She hurried to his side and took his hand to pull him along, but he stayed rooted with their arms stretched between them.

“We can’t leave yet,” he insisted, and Cas let go.

“Phainon, this isn’t a good time to be homesick,” Perdikkas cautioned.

The whole group was slowly meandering back to where he was standing to stop a few paces ahead of him, beckoning.

“Mydei,” he said, “they took the Coreflame of Strife from me during the Trial.”

Ptolemy cursed under his breath. “Even if you did not get your pardon, did it at least buy peace?”

“No.”

Leonnius cursed under his breath.

“Even so, I don’t think Mydei would be happy if we all got caught and killed trying to retrieve something that he willingly gave away,” Perdikkas reasoned.

“The coreflames are a part of a Demigod,” Castorice reminded them, “to know that a piece of you is somewhere else… it is an emptiness that is hard to describe.”

Mydei’s final words to Phainon played in his head, the same loop that had given him comfort and grief in tandem since they were spoken at Castrum Kremnos. Perhaps it was a little selfish then, to want that Coreflame back enough to reject Mydei’s insistence that he didn’t need it …because Phainon did. Phainon wanted it. And as horrible as it felt to want for himself, as much as he rejected that impulse, abhorred it so much that the bile rose in his throat and his gut twisted in discomfort, he still did.

That heart was entrusted to him with purpose, and it was his duty to protect it and the wants and wishes of the man to whom it belonged. If it couldn’t be traded for peace and pardons, then Phainon wanted the damned thing back. And if Mydei still rejected it, then it was going in Phainon’s pocket for the rest of their lives.

“I’m not leaving without it,” Phainon insisted. He turned around and started walking swiftly down the hallway and footsteps followed, hurrying to catch up.

“Phainon, wait,” Hyacine begged and he paused, twisting in place just enough to look back over his shoulder.

Hephaestion was leaning heavily against a pillar with Hyacine’s hand on his back. His long hair had fallen over his shoulders and was hiding his face like a partial veil the way he was hunched forward but Phainon could see the tremor in his shoulders and the heaving way he panted. He coughed twice and dark red clots speckled the floor in fine beads. When he rubbed his mouth with the back of his hand it came away dark with wide streaks of blood.

Phainon took a step towards him, but Perdikkas cut him off and gently guided Hyacine away from their patient. “I’ll take him,” he insisted, “we’ll go straight back to the ship.”

Hephaestion waved a hand as though insisting he was alright, but he couldn’t find the words and eventually gave up with a begrudging nod.

“Leonnius, try to find Krateros and tell him we saved Phainon and are returning to the Leo,” the doctor ordered, “Ptolemy and Peucesta, help me get Hephaestion back to the ship. We’ll let the Heirs find the coreflame and return to us. Anyone opposed?”

Ptolemy raised his hand, but he was ignored when Hephaestion flashed a tired thumbs up.

“Great then let’s do it.”

“Wait, none of you are staying?” Phainon asked. It wasn’t that he was unhappy to be with his college study group again, it was just weird to not have any Kremnoans around.

“Don’t worry, Lord Phainon,” Hyacine teased, “they will be fine without us.”

“I think Fig Stew wants to accompany us,” Castorice observed.

The chimera roared his agreement, a soft, growling sound that was echoed by Beagle Coconut.

“Vigethos wants to come too?” Hyacine bent down to scratch under his chin, and he purred.

“That’s its name??”

“Titan’s, Leonnius,” Ptolemy sighed, “you didn’t think this was actually Aglaea did you??”

The runner huffed and grumbled, “well, I know now.”

Phainon smiled at their antics. Peucesta was getting underneath one of Hephaestion’s arms to support his weight while Perdikkas did the same on the other side. A part of him felt like he should be more worried splitting up, but even as Ptolemy and Leonnius bickered the whole way down the hall and his friends disappeared around a corner, he didn’t feel that shadow of doubt. Absolute faith left no room for fear.

“Let’s go.”

He turned again and started running towards Aglaea’s office. It wasn’t far from where they had separated, and the door was unlocked when they got there. He stepped inside, slowly looking for the woman herself but she was absent.

“It’s clear,” he whispered and they piled in.

“Lord Phainon, do you know where she keeps them?” Castorice asked.

He shook his head. “She must have a hidden vault in here somewhere…”

Beagle chirped insistently and ran to the shelf, jumping on his hind legs and slapping his front paws together. He was staring at the amphorae on the top shelf that held his treats.

When Fig Stew trotted over to ask his new friend what he was doing, Beagle awoo’d back and then they both were jumping and begging.

Hyacine sighed and pulled over Aglaea’s chair to stand on so she could reach the jar but moments before her fingers brushed the clay it was snatched away by cat claws. The healer yelped and jumped backwards, falling off the chair, but Phainon dove to catch her, and she landed safely in his arms.

“Of all the nerve, brat,” Cipher hissed, “I promise to break you out of your cell in an elegant heist for the ages and when I got there all you left for me was a mess.”

She fell off the top of the shelf like a liquid, elegantly twisting in the air to land perfectly on her feet with the jar in her hands and two eager chimeras sitting in front of her licking their lips.

Phainon put Hyacine down when she mumbled a polite thank you and then all his focus was on his apology. “Cipher, it just kind of happened…”

“Save it. You have no idea what kind of a night I have had,” she whined, “I came up with the best plan to get you out, flashy but not overly so, the kind of heist that would have honored dolos… and when I went to that gaudy ship of yours to recruit sidekicks they were already all gone.” Beagle pawed at her leg. The two animals were sitting still with waning patience; mouths open like baby birds waiting to be fed. Without looking down, Cipher pulled off the lid and held it in her palm to free up two fingers to toss a single treat between them.

“So, I ran alllll the way back to town,” she continued with her tail swishing. The fur was puffed up so Phainon knew she was at least a little bit mad for real. “And I asked every guard I saw if they had seen any Kremnoans and every single one of them lied to my face!” Her voice deepened in a mocking recreation to say, “’Of course not Lady Cipher! Kremnoans haven’t been in Okhema in years! I think we would have noticed any Kremnoans!’ But ohoho, I knew that they tore through town! Even that guy at the antique place you like with all those ugly amphorae lied to me when it was obvious he had just been robbed! Who loses their entire stock to pirates and then lies about it? And the defaced Aglaea mural? The facial hair was a nice touch but please, signing something so uninspired?”

Phainon tilted his head in confusion and then opened his mouth to refute something that didn’t sound like his friends, but she was very suddenly in front of him with a finger on his mouth to shut him up. “I’m not done. Those Kremnoans were so damn unpredictable that I gave up and decided to just save my baby brother who was hopelessly rotting in a cell waiting for me and guess who wasn’t there?”

He shyly pointed at himself, and she patted his cheek with her free hand. The cookies in the jar she was holding rattled as she shifted from side to side. “That’s right.”

“Awoo!” called Beagle and Cipher paused her ranting to look down at where he was gently poking her leg. The single cookie she had dropped to them before had not been wildly devoured like Phainon would’ve expected, instead it was at Fig Stew’s feet where the chimera was waiting patiently to share.

Cipher took a second cookie from the jaw and dropped it for Beagle and he awoo’d a thank you, picked the treat up, and brought it over to Fig Stew so his buddy could have two cookies. All four Demigods watched them with mild amusement, the tension in the room defused by their adorable antics.

“Lady Cipher,” Castorice cleared her throat with a soft cough, and they were dialed in again, “I deeply apologize. We had no idea that you were on your way to save Lord Phainon.”

“Lady Tribbie told us that he was going to be executed,” Hyacine explained, “and we didn’t really think past our desire to save him.”

“Little red, huh?” Cipher purred. She put the lid back on the jar and passed it to her tail to hold so both paws were free to cross her arms. “Maybe the old seamstress is up to more than I gave her credit for. If you are trying to escape, why did you come here?”

“The Coreflame of Strife,” Phainon answered. He stepped past Cipher to continue his search, reaching for Aglaea’s desk drawers.

“She doesn’t keep those in here,” Cipher crooned.

Phainon froze. “Cipher, you know where Aglaea stores the coreflames?”

“Of course I do~ How do you think I got mine?”

“Will you tell us, Lady Cipher?” Castorice asked, “it’s very urgent.”

Cipher laughed, “really embracing this piracy thing, aren’t you?”

“Please,” Phainon insisted a little more softly, “it’s for Mydei.”

His earnestness caught her off guard and after a wide-eyed twitch of both ears, Cipher relaxed again. She put the chimera cookies on the desk and sighed. “Geez, you can stop with the puppy eyes, brat. Fine, I’ll help you if you just stop looking so damn pathetic.” He brightened immediately and she scowled. “That’s worse. Turn around so I don’t have to look at your face.”

Phainon immediately complied and Hyacine slapped her own forehead. There was a lot of that going around tonight.

“Lady Cipher? The coreflame?”

“Follow me~”

Cipher was polite enough not to leave them in the dust as they ran through Marmoreal Palace. Late at night the baths were empty or being cleaned by the sparse few attendants on duty, but a pro thief already knew how to avoid them and not a single soul witnessed the four Demigods and two chimeras. Which meant there was no one to yell at them for running through hallways between the pools and sliding around corners in the variable humidity.

Marmoreal Palace was more than just a bath house, but the crown jewel of the complex was still the Overflowing Bath, the largest and most open of the public baths. The pool was massive with tables and fountains interspersed in the water and stretching almost the entire length of the hall. The ceiling so far above them that it was impossible to appreciate the detail in the artwork was held up by pillars wider than several trees each that lined the length of the pool. At the far side, to where they were running, the wall had long since been removed so bathers could look out across the plateau and the harbor. Had it faced Kephale, the baths may have been too warm in the direct light from the Dawn Device but angled away the bath took advantage of the indirect light to fill the space with a warm glow that rippled in the water without harming the eyes.

There was a path there past the balcony, lined with small fruit trees, carefully manicured flowers, and a small stream that wrapped around the Marmoreal Palace to a separate pavilion that was always guarded. The Chrysos Heir’s bath was not open to the public and carefully removed to prevent anyone from straying in by accident. Even drunken guests would be hard pressed to get in there by mistake whether by the main path that snaked through the garden, or by any of the service entrances for approved bath attendants.

“The Heirs’ bath house?” Phainon asked.

“You’ll see~”

Cipher led them to one of the services entrances and the others followed her very closely. They crouched in the bushes, listening for any movement but there was nothing but the sound of insects chirping and the gentle trickle of tamed water. They still stayed low as they crossed the open yard where clean towels were drying in the light overnight and tried the door. Locked.

Cipher’s tail was already swishing back and forth, the tip twitching happily as she produced a lockpick from her sleeve and expertly opened the door as though she had the key and not an illegal facsimile. “Someday I’ll find something challenging to steal again.”

“Like the Castrum Kremnos treasure vault?” Phainon asked.

The cat went rigid and slowly turned her head to glare at him. “Too soon.” He offered her an apologetic smile, but she was already slipping inside.

They were standing in a neatly organized laundry room that Phainon recognized. He liked to get his towels directly from here rather than from the bins beside the bath. They were always so warm coming off the drying line outside.

“There shouldn’t be any guards inside the bath right?” Hyacine whispered.

“Nah.”

“There shouldn’t be any attendants left either,” Castorice reasoned.

“Not unless Aglaea is bathing,” Phainon grimaced.

Hyacine winced at the thought, “that might be possible considering what happened to you.”

“She didn’t seem all that upset at the trial.”

“Lord Phainon, with respect, you of all people should know that the Lady Goldweaver does not show the Council how she is feeling.”

Yeah… he did know. Phainon considered instead how Aglaea had been that morning, before the Council even took him into custody. She had been very professional, very focused… but her office was still devoid of projects and her words had that hint of second guessing herself. Those were sure signs that she was having a hard time and her favorite way to relax was with a bath.

“Would she stop us if she was?” Hyacine asked.

They all considered that for a moment before Phainon confidently answered, “Yes. She’d have to.”

“I’m not so sure about that,” Cipher mumbled to herself in a sing-song cadence. Phainon shot her a suspicious look but let it slide.

“It is possible that she has already laid traps inside the vault,” Castorice cautioned, “to prevent any Chrysos Heirs from turning on her.”

“Or from retrieving coreflames they aren’t ready for,” Phainon added sadly. Hyacine also looked down, and he steeled himself at her downtrodden expression. It was so rare to see her slip out of her perfect bedside manner. “But we aren’t here for us, we’re here for Mydei.”

Fig Stew agreed with a chirp.

“If you’re done speculating,” Cipher said from where she was sitting cross-legged on a spare kline, “then we can go get your candle flame. Seamstress isn’t here. I saw her earlier in Dawncloud when I was looking for the Kremnoans.”

There weren’t a lot of reasons for her to be there this late at night. Phainon frowned at the thought, but the girls were already moving on at the good news.

The hallway was still brightly lit like it always was with Kephale’s light filtering in from the skylights above. It was pleasantly warm with a humidity that one could feel and taste but not dense enough to see. It clung to Phainon’s clothing and made him feel sticky. He couldn’t imagine how uncomfortable Cipher was with her fur. She looked like she was holding back complaints as they passed the changing rooms to get to the baths.

The water here was visibly different from the water meant for the general populace. It glittered and swirled with gold, Mnestia’s divine power, Phainon had always assumed, though Aglaea had never confirmed his suspicions she didn’t deny them either. It flowed from a spout above the centermost pool and spread to the others in tiers until all five of the circular baths nearly glowed as the light caught on the water and made it sparkle. The baths curved around the room in a half circle surrounded by tiled walkways and in the very center of them all was a fountain.

The fountain itself was not particularly fancy. It was multi-tiered with smooth and even edges so the water would pour in quiet sheets so consistently that Phainon could almost see himself reflected in the sheen as though it were glass. Set into the floor without a raised edge or bench, the piece stood taller than Castorice but shorter than Phainon and was remarkably easy to run into. His first day, he had stepped into the shallow basin around its base and expected a firm correction, but Aglaea had smiled at his accident and waded into the fountain herself, beckoning him to feel the silk of the falling water as it splashed onto their feet.

It was that fountain that Cipher stood beside with a cheery, “Here we are~!”

She was met with blank faces.

“Oh please, you can’t tell me she never brought you all here before to ask cryptic questions.”

“I’m sorry, Aglaea,” Phainon said, relaxed after his bath. His voice was light and happy even if she was frowning beside the fountain. “I’m not sure what I’m supposed to be feeling.”

She made a harumph sound under her breath and mumbled, “it will come in time.”

Phainon frowned at the memory and stepped in closer. There was a definite tug that he hadn’t felt before, a sort of urgency that was hard to describe. He waded into the water and felt it immediately start soaking into his boots. They were water resistant, not waterproof, so he expected the sudden discomfort of soggy socks and lukewarm water, but his focus was not on his own well-being right now. The driving desire to retrieve this coreflame was starting to burn inside his chest, becoming a creeping obsession, a desperate urge to get into the vault that he now knew was nearby.

Aglaea stood at the top of the spiral staircase and watched Phainon carefully with a finger pressed to her lips.

“You are certain?” she asked him.

A young Phainon nodded, weary, tired, feeling almost nothing at all and she sighed and turned away. The stairs rose as she walked towards the changing rooms, becoming one with the floor around the fountain once more.

“There’s a staircase here,” he said aloud as he remembered. Phainon followed the footsteps of the memory, walking over the giant, wedged tiles that circled the fountain. These were stairs, he knew they were. He stepped on each one in turn until he stood where the Aglaea in his memory once had at what should be the top of them.

“There you go,” Cipher teased.

He twisted his body to match how she had stood but nothing happened at least not on the outside. The longer he stood there, the more urgent Phainon felt. It was an antsy nagging feeling in the back of his mind, not quite a longing but something bordering on hunger, on a need.

Hyacine shifted uncomfortably and started to pace, eyes narrowed at the water. She too splashed into the fountain and dark spots appeared on her stockings where she got wet. It barely registered for her, and she didn’t hesitate to feel along the edges of the layered basins, letting even more water flow along her arm to soak her sleeves and dress.

“There must be a way to open it then,” she reasoned, voice strained, “Lady Aglaea must have sealed it with her threads. There must be a way to tell the threads to open!”

“Two for two!” Cipher announced.

“Lady Cipher perhaps now is not the time…” Castorice tried to say as she watched her friends with a measure of concern.

“You know how to open it, Cipher,” Phainon breathed, it came out more accusatory than he intended but urgent nagging was turning into aching loneliness and a paranoia like he was forgetting something very important, something that he needed to live. There was something missing from him and it was waiting just behind this obstacle.

She sauntered over to him and snatched his hand, pulling him closer to the edge of the fountain so she wouldn’t have to get wet. Cipher turned his palm up and then pushed back his sleeve to see where the chains had rubbed his wrists raw. She pressed where the skin was the thinnest, where it had already bled that night until the gold flowed anew and he hissed at her in annoyance.

“Cipher!” Hyacine scolded, voice tight.

“You wanted me to help, right?” the cat purred. She let go when Phainon recoiled, splashing in the shallow water as he retreated. Beads of blood dripped from his wrist into the water, the same color as the gold that swirled in the pools already, visually unnoticed, but something recognized it, recognized him. He didn’t care if it was golden threads, the fountain, or Kephale themself what mattered was the shift in the tiles around the fountain as they slowly started to drop into the ground.

Phainon reached for Hyacine’s hand as the tiles moved behind her and the water in the fountain spilled over the edge. She held onto him tightly and splashed her way closer to Phainon and the top of the spiral staircase.

“After you,” Cipher purred.

Phainon barely heard her, his heart was already racing into the dark below. It pounded in his ears, demanding a hasty descent but reverence tempered his movements as he led the way down.

The space beneath the bath house felt primordial. It was the best way for Phainon to describe it in a single word. It was a cave first and room second with a tiled floor much the same as Okhema above, but the walls and ceiling remained natural stone, smoothed by the flow of water many years ago that still filled the space around the circular platform and the lake beside which it was built.

Light from the open staircase refracted through the water that flowed from the fountain above, filling the room with a pale glow to rival the blue that glimmered from the depths of the small, underground lake. Bioluminescent moss grew in water so clear and still that it was hard to perceive that it was there until the ripples of the water above disturbed the surface and invited the light within to dance on the ceiling in mesmerizing patterns.

But for Phainon these observations were secondary to the singular item in the room: a deep basin resting on a pillar, filled with water to the brim, and glowing like trapped sunlight.

He paused at the bottom of the stairs and Hyacine robotically came up beside him with a whispered, “do you feel it too?”

And he knew exactly what she was talking about.

Phainon approached the basin as though it were a wild beast, something unpredictable with teeth, even as his heart screamed at him to embrace it, to dive into this bowl headfirst to willingly, happily drown. And when he peered inside and saw the coreflames resting inside, he understood why.

He slowly put both hands on the side of the basin, letting his thumbs dip into the water to feel the familiar warmth. It was sunshine on wheat fields, warm stew after a cold day, it was Mydei’s subtle smile, and the feeling of his body hovering above Phainon’s own while they sparred on a distant shore. It was the wholeness of belonging, the good ache of knowing what it means to love and be loved. It was responsibility and expectations with the support and courage to meet them all.

Tears flowed freely, something he only noticed when they dripped from his jaw to disturb the water below. It startled him and he reached to touch them with surprise, rubbing one between his thumb and forefinger as he looked back at his fellow heirs.

Hyacine was weeping too, her face full of shock and something purer, happier, like she was recalling a memory so sweet that her body couldn’t hope to contain the emotions that had built up inside her. She was shakily walking towards the basin to stand beside him to peer inside with a soft gasp that brought her hand shakily to her lips.

Phainon watched Hyacine with total understanding as he realized this shared experience was not for him alone. When he turned again to look at Castorice, she was smiling at them, standing apart with a hand held to her chest to allow them this moment that she had already experienced years ago. Cipher too was uncharacteristically quiet, sitting on the stairs to watch them with a sort of pride that only comes from one who led the way.

Aglaea’s Flame-Chase Journey had been ongoing for nearly a thousand years; its history shrouded in mysterious origins long lost to everyone aside from those that had experienced it for themselves and that was history that they treasured just the two of them. In that time, five coreflames had been discovered and given to their new bearers, three were missing, one remained with their Titan, an ally of humanity, and three were here, waiting.

The Coreflames of Strife, Sky, and Worldbearing flickered with greeting, as though they had a will of their own, as though they too could not contain their joy.

“I always thought Strife would be mine,” Phainon whispered. The shining sun symbol of Worldbearing glowed brighter at his voice. “When it chose Mydei I didn’t think… I never thought…”

“I know what you mean, Lord Phainon,” Hyacine whispered. Her voice was cracking. “It’s like a reunion… but with someone I’ve never met. How is that possible?”

Phainon’s heart reached for his coreflame and in that moment he realized what Mydei had felt in Castrum Kremnos when Phainon had tried to hand him a heartbeat, a drop of weighty power and completeness.

I don’t need the coreflame to feel whole, because I have you.

The tears dripped again as Phainon fully appreciated that statement in a way he couldn’t before, now that he knew what it felt like to be this close to his heart, and what it felt like to reject it.

When Phainon reached into the basin with both hands, spilling the water over the sides in smooth, splashing sheets, it wasn’t to get his coreflame, it was to get the one he came here for first, the one that belonged to the only person that made him feel whole. He cradled the Coreflame of Strife in both hands and stepped away from the basin to check it, to watch the light of it dim and glow like it was breathing. A part of him ached for his own heart still submerged, but looking at this one in his hands, Phainon realized Mydei still held a piece of him across the ocean, and the Coreflame of Worldbearing could only hope to fill that space.

I don’t need the coreflame to feel whole, because I have you. Oh, how true that was.

“You know,” Cipher called, and her voice felt too loud in the echo, “you can take all of them.”

“Aglaea…”

“Would have stopped us long ago if this was not her intent,” Castorice reminded him. When he still hesitated she added, “Lord Phainon, are we not pirates?”

Phainon looked between his fellow heirs and then back down at the Coreflame of Worldbearing. It glowed brighter under his gaze, a promise of power, a promise of deliverance. He let out a breath on the tail end of a gentle chuckle as all the puzzle pieces clicked at once.

“Of course we’ll take them,” he said gently, looking at Hyacine’s shiny wide eyes and full smile.

She hiccupped a little bit and wiped away her own tears before she reached up to catch his with a gentle touch and the voice to what he just realized himself, “Lord Phainon, I’m sure of it now. This is how we’re going to save Lord Mydei.”
