Chapter Notes

I know I said I wouldn't pov swap outside of Phainon and Mydei very much, but I think you all will forgive me for this one. :3c

When Anaxa and Krateros entered Okhema it had been with express intent but only a fool was narrow-minded enough to resist choice opportunities as they presented themselves. With the help of a dozen men at his command and a surprisingly docile Okhema, those opportunities were too bounteous to ignore and Anaxa was eager to indulge. They had zig-zagged through town, filling sacks and bags with lots of things he needed and some things that he wanted from alchemical ingredients and curiosities to various containers, piled high on the backs of willing Kremnoans who were too enchanted by the piracy to question what he ordered them to grab.

Not that the citizens weren’t willing to relinquish their goods after only a brief exchange. It barely counted as piracy at all when they were giving stuff away. Phainon’s rescue was so easy to exploit. All it took was mentioning the Kremnoans and shopkeepers tripped over themselves to provide whatever Anaxa requested if it would save the Deliverer. It was so easy that he genuinely considered leveraging this newfound cheat to secure the dromas egg that he had always wanted… Alas, not the time nor place. It would be unfair to the perfect hatchling if they emerged at sea far from solid earth to eat. Besides, he had more urgent concerns, like planning three steps ahead while everyone else got them back to net zero rescuing Phainon.

Krateros was a professional and willing participant which came as no surprise. The man had no love of Aglaea, nor the Holy City and even indulged when Anaxa took the time to deface any mural or statue of her with charcoal as they passed. Nothing so violent as destroying them of course, but he didn’t mind taking the time to tease that arrogant woman as they made their way with purpose to Dawncloud.

In truth, aside from those moments where he was looking at her visage, Anaxa thought about Aglaea very little until he was finished with his primary goal and was confronted on the path to the Dawn Father by the woman herself as they were leaving the Worldbearing Altar.

What an image they made, Anaxa standing in front of a unit of Kremnoan pirates, recently stolen amphorae filled to the brim with blasphemy strapped to their backs. Even pious Krateros looked faint after what they had just done and Anaxa couldn’t blame him for his anxiety, not everyone had the courage to do whatever it takes in pursuit of the unknown. The professor himself was drenched in sticky gold standing a few paces from the Goldweaver, still dripping onto the road.

“Let me guess,” she crooned, her voice like a scalpel, “it’s not what it looks like.”

Anaxa scoffed and crossed his arms across his chest, a smirk slowly pulled one corner of his lips up into a curl as he responded with equal sharpness, “It’s exactly what it looks like.”

Her face stayed statuesque, emotionless, unchanging, but her words dripped with venom that made the Kremnoans behind him shuffle uncomfortably and tighten their grips on their spears. “You have gone too far, Anaxagoras.”

“Please,” he purred, “can I really be the Great Blasphemer as you so affectionately called me once, if I do not take action to reassert the title?”

“Defacing murals of me I can tolerate as behavior befitting a child throwing a tantrum, but cutting into the flesh of the Dawn Father? Inexcusable.”

“Lord Anaxagoras,” Krateros said with his voice low, quiet beside Anaxa, “if it comes to blows, it is unlikely we will be able to hold her for long.”

“Relax, Krateros,” he reassured the old man, “she will let us pass unhindered.”

“Cocky,” Aglaea accused.

“Confident,” he corrected with a demeaning tut, “so much so that you can take your men and go on ahead, Krateros.” The old vet seemed unsure, but Anaxa calmly extended a hand to the side to direct them around her. “She won’t stop you.”

Aglaea stayed quiet. Gold threads shimmered in the air, but the Kremnoans were able to cautiously pass by her with their precious cargo.

“Lord Anaxagoras,” Krateros called from behind the Goldweaver.

“I will be along,” the professor promised, “tell the others to wait at the ship for me.”

The veteran lingered, perhaps contemplating the theme of the night: opportunity, as he studied the Goldweaver’s back and drummed his fingertips on his sword. But that thought lasted only for a moment before he gestured to his men and they jogged away, eventually disappearing down the road.

“I have not missed your sharp tongue and foolish arrogance, professor,” Aglaea enunciated sharply when they were finally alone.

“Nor I you, Aglaea. So where does that leave us? Will you bind me in your threads, execute me beside your prized Deliverer?” Her eyes moved, just a hair to the side when he mentioned Phainon and Anaxa’s half smirk spread into a full smile. “So, they already freed him. Curious how foreigners found his cell so quickly.”

“I couldn’t possibly know what you mean,” she said, dismissive, harsh, “and I don’t appreciate the accusation.”

“Oh Aglaea, Aglaea, don’t insult me.” He made a tsk, tsk sound to drive home his point.

The shadow of a smile crossed her features and then faded just as quickly when she crossed her arms. “What do you want with the blood, heretic?”

“You haven’t figured it out?” he teased, and she immediately turned it around, unphased.

“Have you?”

His smile faltered only a little bit and his arm twitched.

“Oh…” she said, the edge of her voice softened by a thread, the very same thread that Anaxa felt around his arm like the ghost of a stray hair. “You have.”

He tsked and plucked it from his sleeve, tossing it aside with a roll of his thumb and forefinger, disgusted by the intrusive nature of it. Beneath the fabric the bandages itched around his wrist.

“It’s a versatile substance,” he admitted, unwilling to give her specifics.

“Still willing to defile your own body. How much of your blood have you spilled to use for your experiments?” Aglaea prodded.

“Enough to be sure that my pinnacle creation in this ridiculous journey has been perfected. Enough to know that I am right,” he snapped, tightening his crossed arms around his chest and squeezing them tight to stop the itch, “enough to know that you have let Phainon believe a lie.”

“I have never lied to him.”

“Lies of omission are still lies,” Anaxa scolded, “he told me that it is Mnestia’s divine power, your power, that cleanses the Tide in the Chrysos Heirs’ bath, but it is Kephale’s blood, is it not?”

She stayed silent. A confirmation.

“And you call me a blasphemer.”

“What I use is freely given-“

“Only for the use of you and yours, eh, Aglaea? How is this any different?” he asked.

“I have never taken a blade to the holy body,” she hissed, and the edge was back to her voice.

“Add this sin to my tab,” he laughed, “these accusations are pointless. You already intend to let me go.”

She hummed, “then tell me how I came to this decision.”

“Because you know that this is the best way to see your Flame-Chase Journey come to an end,” he reasoned.

“Go on.”

For a second he considered telling her no, but when would he get the chance again to call her out and perhaps confirm a few of his theories?

“Piracy has always plagued the free peoples of Amphoreus, but you sent Phainon to investigate the Chryseus Leo, knowing they were Kremnoans. You knew that the young Prince of Kremnos was a Chrysos Heir and an inheritor of one of your missing coreflames,” he paused to judge her reaction, to see if he was right but she didn’t move at all, not even a twitch. “You knew that Phainon could convince them to retrieve Strife for you, perhaps even find a weakness in the Tide.”

She let out a soft laugh, short on a single quick exhale. It felt a little too fake, a little too scripted and lacking any authenticity. “It’s not like you to give me so much credit. You really believe I predicted this outcome? Predicted Phainon and Mydeimos’ partnership?”

“As loathe as I am to admit it, yes. I believe you saw all of this.”

“I am no seer.”

“But you have been watching,” he accused, “and you understand desires, Demigod of Romance. The same way you knew that I would eventually relent and take up the Coreflame of Reason and thus chose to leave it unclaimed in the Grove when the Tide swallowed the isle.” Her smile returned but she kept silent. “And there is no one else that you have so carefully watched and cared for than Phainon of Aedes Elysiae. You intend for him to take up the Coreflame of Worldbearing, do you not?”

“I do,” she purred, “and he has.”

Anaxa’s eyes narrowed a little at the declaration and then he laughed, long and loud, “I see. I am not the only opportunist in Okhema this Curtain-Fall Hour.”

Aglaea started walking, giving him plenty of space to step around him as she walked towards the Worldbearing Altar and out of his way, no longer blocking his escape.

“Aglaea,” Anaxa said sharply. He turned sideways to look at her, and she stopped walking, back still facing him. “Would you send these young Heirs to solve the riddle of the Tide on their own?”

“With someone as clever as you, have they need of me at all?” she posited, turning just enough to ensure he heard her. He huffed to himself, resisting the urge to gag at the two-faced praise.

“You know what the Tide is, don’t you?” he asked, pointed, accusing. The threads in the air gave her away, they trembled, glittering from invisible to shining gold when they caught the light.

“I… have my suspicions,” she admitted.

Anaxa studied her with a narrowed eye. “Is it related to the missing coreflames?” he asked.

Something about her changed from perfect composure to the shadow of an emotion.

“Yes,” she said, and her voice was soft and quiet, like someone about to cry. Aglaea turned more fully to him, dry-eyed and stoic her tone of voice back to emotionless and biting. “Tell me this, Grand Performer, are your motivations purely selfish?”

“Of course, I cannot pursue the topic of my personal interest until the Tide is completely removed from this world,” he confessed freely, she would be able to tell if he lied anyway.

“Because until such time your experiments on yourself are tainted,” she said as a matter of fact and Anaxa schooled his expression, meeting stone with stone, knowing with knowing. She was peering deep into his heart, sensing what he had kept from the others.

“I will not discuss an ongoing experiment with you.”

“Your willingness to save Mydeimos is not altruistic, you need to see what has become of him after his time fighting the Tide and what happens when he accepts his coreflame.”

“Leaving him to fight the Tide without its protection for an extended time was an unintended but ideal experiment. But he is not the only source of valuable information waiting in Castrum Kremnos,” he admitted.

“Eurypon,” she said, low and deep.

“The Mad King kept detailed descriptions of his experiments on the Strife Titan’s corruption and his observations fighting the Black Tide. It’s possible he found the answer years ago and lost himself before he could act upon it.”

“A great number of his works are not stored in Castrum Kremnos but at a library that once belonged to Gorgo,” Aglaea thought aloud and Anaxa contemplated that hint in silence.

They watched each other for a long moment while the breeze played with their hair and clothes. Kephale above bearing witness to their standoff as Anaxa confidently waited for Aglaea to find what she was looking for and drop her threads. She must have found it because she closed her foggy eyes and turned away.

“I have nothing but faith in Phainon and the other Demigods,” she said, “make good use of what you have stolen today, heretic, you will not get more from Kephale. Hopefully you do not bleed yourself dry before you discover the truth of the Tide.”

“Would that really be such a loss?” he laughed.

“I suspect you will be more troublesome when you die,” she bit but her footsteps were light as she walked away and left him standing alone in the road.

Anaxa looked down at his hand, still bright with Kephale’s blood and his own seeping through his sleeve where the wound had opened beneath the bandages. He must have squeezed a little too hard. Oops.

“Thoughts?” he asked the air and a voice whispered beside him.

“I have to hand it to you, your theory about the Black Tide may be correct.”

“Just a little more proof, Cerces. The answer and corresponding solution are within reach.”

The Titan of Reason hummed in his ear. She had long since stopped appearing beside him, a specter only he could see and hear, but Anaxa had found in her companionship a wealth of information. She was proof that the coreflames retained limited sentience, that they were alive in a sense as a symbiotic part of their chosen Demigod, or perhaps this was simply the power of his particular coreflame, his ‘wish.’ That was the more likely explanation, but he had a few different theories, nothing to carve in stone just yet.

“Will you go the library as she suggested?”

Anaxa thought about that as he started to walk through Okhema, leaving behind squelching footprints as he passed the Dawncloud guards that had already been rendered unconscious the first time they had passed. “Why not? I’m sure it would not be difficult to convince the captain to make a detour after we rescue the Crown Prince.”

“If there’s anything left to rescue…”

“I would invite you to have faith, but the irony would make me sick,” Anaxa laughed, mumbling to his coreflame, “from a logical standpoint we have no reason to believe he is lost. We’ve already proven between the two of us that the River of Souls has a cleansing effect on the dead. An immortal Kremnoan Prince has the best chance of surviving without succumbing to the Tide song.”

“And what of his humanity? Enduring such repeated agony?”

“Ah, yes, I suppose how much of that remains we will have to witness for ourselves.”

- The temptation to take the coreflame into himself was not as powerful as Phainon had thought. Simply carrying the Coreflame of Worldbearing was enough to feel a measure of comfort and completeness but whether it was because he carried his own heart or Mydei’s it was impossible to tell, and he honestly didn’t care. What mattered was that both coreflames were tucked carefully into a laundry bag slung over his shoulder and held tightly to his chest.

Hyacine was loathe to part with the Coreflame of Sky and carried it herself while Little Ica kept trying to sniff at it. She too wanted to contemplate the implications of this power calling them before she took it into herself.

Phainon had expected Cipher and Castorice to be pushy about their ascensions but neither of them teased or insisted either way. Cipher especially was shockingly reserved when she was facing a very serious topic, and it gave Phainon reassurance that he was making the right decision to wait.

But hadn’t he waited enough?

As they hurried through the familiar city streets and back alleys, faster than a walk, slower than a run, Phainon slowed down to consider that heartbeat in his hands. The glow of the two coreflames was clearly visible through the weave of the canvas sack, happy to be along for the journey, but he couldn’t stop thinking of the many times where Aglaea had asked him if he felt anything and he hadn’t. He bathed in those shimmering pools daily, sometimes twice a day if he felt particularly sticky after a workout and until today he had never felt the pull of a piece of him literally under his feet.

“Why now?” he wondered aloud and the three girls ahead of him paused to give him their attention. He caught up in a few long strides and stopped beside them.

“Why what now?” Cipher asked.

“If the coreflames choose their bearers through time and it has always been mine, why now?” He looked up at Cipher for the answer, and she seemed contemplative, like she was worried she might say the wrong thing if she spoke too soon. Something in the way she searched his face, her eyes darting back and forth before settling on the coreflame in his arms, worried him. She was rarely this serious, this thoughtful. He’d take a joke at this point.

“Because you need it now,” she said simply.

“And I didn’t need it before?” he asked, genuine, pleading, “if I had already been a Demigod when Mydei and I-”

“Then what?” Cipher growled, “what exactly would be different? And don’t give me any of this ‘oh he’d be safe!’ nonsense, because you don’t know that.” She got in close when he looked down, arching her back and leaning in so she could stay in his line of sight. “Would you have been able to bond as equals?” she asked and Phainon’s mouth fell open to answer before it shut again when words failed him. “That adventure that you told the whole city about, yes, don’t seem so surprised, I heard every word, do you really believe any of that would have happened if you had that light in your chest? Do you really believe you could appreciate this power, this responsibility if you hadn’t struggled to be worthy of it? Trust me, timing matters and the truth is that you don’t know for sure what would have been different, and it doesn’t really matter does it? You have it now, it sees you now.”

“Well said, Little Ciphy!”

All four of them almost jumped out of their skins.

“Hehe, surprised you didn’t I?” Trianne greeted them as she settled both feet on Phainon’s shoulders and her hands on top of his currently dusty, silver hair.

“Hello, Lady Trianne,” Castorice and Hyacine said in tandem.

At their feet Fig Stew started to growl until Beagle pulled his tail and after a brief exchange of awoos and paw waving, Fig Stew was okay with this new friend and chirped a greeting.

“Snowy, are you worried about your coreflame?” she asked. She stood on his shoulders and leaned over his head to look at him upside down.

“Uh… It’s not that teacher,” he stammered, “I was just wondering why it waited so long to choose me, if it already knew.”

“You weren’t ready yet silly!”

“Surely it is not that simple, Trianne…” Phainon tried to argue.

She tilted her head, and it was a miracle her flower ornaments stayed attached to her hair upside down like that. “Why not? Aren’t some things that simple?”

Maybe it was the way she said it in her little kid voice or that she was the first Demigod and was misleadingly ancient, but something about that statement just clicked. Maybe it was just that simple. Phainon simply hadn’t been ready until now.

“Coreflames are really cool,” she told him. Trianne flew over his head to sit on his arm instead and he held it out for her to be comfortable facing him like the weirdest bird ever. “They give you special powers and make your wishes come true so it’s really important that the people who get coreflames have good wishes!”

“I’ve always had good wishes…” he pouted.

She put her gloved hands on each cheek and pushed them together to squish his lips and then she tugged on them to stretch them out. “Yeah, but Agy still had to teach you important things first. And you had to learn some important things for yourself first!”

“A-Am I the same way, Lady Trianne?” Hyacine asked, nervous.

“Yup!” she answered cheerfully, “think of all the things you learned Little Cinny that you can put to even better use now! There’s joy in the journey!”

Aglaea had said once that she had known about her coreflame and wasn’t ready for a while to receive it, that it took her some time to learn what it meant to be the Inheritor of Romance.

She had genuinely believed that knowing there was a coreflame waiting for her had made her miserable and probably delayed her ascension as a Demigod.

He thought about how easy it would be for Aglaea to use her powers to shortcut her dressmaking but still chose to do everything by hand. He could picture an impatient and frustrated young Aglaea pricking her fingers on needles, swearing at stiff fabric, stressing over colors, wanting her coreflame for the shortcut and learning instead to love the process.

Phainon was looking at this coreflame as a shortcut, as an answer, and it was, but if he had it before this journey had started… it was like Cipher had said, he never would’ve bonded with the crew, never would’ve fallen in love. It would have been a very different story, one lacking in personal growth. The person he was when he left Okhema was not the same person that held the coreflame now, that was ready to appreciate it as a comforting tool and not the end all, be all fix.

“If someone with good wishes gets a coreflame before they’re ready, bad things happen…” Trianne insisted. She stopped playing with Phainon’s cheeks and instead fussed over his hair and the dirty streaks on his face.

“What kind of bad things?” Hyacine asked.

Trianne held a finger to her lips and frowned, eyes squinting as she struggled to retrieve a particularly distant memory. “I don’t remember…”

Had it happened before? Was that why Aglaea had been so careful with him and Hyacine? Castorice had taken her coreflame almost immediately after they had retrieved it together, but she was also considerably older than Phainon. Cipher had stolen her coreflame but as the Demigod of Trickery perhaps that was all the coreflame really wanted to see from her to decide she was worthy. Every coreflame was different, with different powers and unique manifestations for their bearers.

“But that’s enough about that!” Trianne insisted, already happily moving on, “you’re ready now and the coreflames chose both of you! More importantly, I’m here with a special delivery!”

Cipher’s tail swished back and forth excitedly. “Oh? Why didn’t you lead with that Little Red?”

“It’s not for you, Ciphy!”

The cat was notably less interested now. “Oh. Boring.”

Trianne hopped off Phainon’s arm and landed right in the middle of their haphazard circle of Chrysos Heirs. She searched her pockets with little hands and then pulled out a way too big of a box from the left side of her dress. If the Flame-Chase didn’t work out, the Demigod of Passages could do very well working birthday parties. The box was almost the size of her head, wrapped in bright red paper with a big yellow bow holding it closed. She set it down in front of Phainon.

“Agy said that you needed this,” Trianne said cheerfully, “sorry, Little Cas, Little Cinny, Little Ciphy, if you break your things then maybe we will have something for you next time too!”

Castorice held her hands up to her mouth to hide her unladylike snort when she held in a laugh.

“Break something?” Phainon asked with a pout.

Trianne was already opening the box, letting the yellow ribbon fall across Beagle and Fig Stew who happily chased and batted at it, oblivious to the rest of the happenings there in the middle of a tiny, sleepy alleyway courtyard in Okhema. She pulled the lid off with a cheerful, “ta da!”

Just like her pockets, the box was much bigger on the inside, making use of their powers, their wishes, to bring to Phainon a replacement set of clothes. He pulled the pauldron out and held it up to the torn one on his shoulder with a sigh.

“I looked ridiculous up there today didn’t I?” he asked.

“Yes,” Cipher said immediately.

“Little Ciphy!”

Cipher stuck out her tongue.

“You look like you’ve been on a long journey, Lord Phainon,” Castorice reassured him, completely glossing over how tidy the girls looked. They had been on the same ship and looked just fine.

He crouched down to run his fingers over the neatly folded fabric, identical to what he was wearing aside from the character. This pair of pants didn’t have lopsided hand stitching from where a piece of wood had torn through it and into his leg during a storm. This new coat didn’t have a tiny hole from an arrow that went into his back defending Krateros. The cape was whole and shiny, not torn at the bottom where a Black Tide monster had ripped it. The leather straps and buckles were shiny and perfect having not had to endure the salty sea spray. It just wasn’t him, without those memories.

It wasn’t that Phainon liked looking a little worn, but the pauldron was the only thing he kept, tucking that into his bag. It was the only piece of his armor that was detrimental to its effectiveness when torn and he would be wise to replace it but the rest…

“Thank you, Trianne, but this outfit I’m wearing was given to me by someone I respect,” he said with a warm smile, “and I’m quite fond of it.” He thought he sounded sweet with just the right amount of heroic sentimentality and that signature wide smile.

“Agy said you broke your sword,” she said blandly in response, and he turned red.

“Well, I, yeah…”

Trianne pushed him back to his feet and shooed him away from the box so she could dig around inside, shoving clothes out of the way to grab the hilt of a sword that was buried towards the bottom of the magical gift. She had to fly to pull it all the way out.

Phainon recognized it immediately. Well, sort of, it looked like a better version of the idea he had sketched when he was working for Chartonus, the master smith in town. This was the sword that he had been trying to earn enough cash to commission!

It was a greatsword nearly as tall as he was with a wide blade and balanced grip. The fuller had been dyed the same blue as his cape, like the sky above Kephale. The treatment of the blade had left it in various stages of gradient from the shining silver tip to a dark gray around the golden hilt and stylized guard, designed to look like a sun curving over the full length of the black leather grip to the gold pommel.

Cipher whistled.

“Trianne,” Phainon whispered, it was hard to breathe looking at it, “I barely managed the first payment, I can’t afford this…”

“Please take it from, Trianne at least!” she whined. Her little wings were straining to hold it up and he hurried to take it from her. It was the perfect weight, the exact right balance, and it just felt right. He studied it in awe and couldn’t help giving it a few experimental spins.

“This is how Lord Phainon looks at Lord Mydei,” Hyacine observed with a giggle as she stepped backwards to give him space to play with his new toy. He immediately felt self-conscious.

“Chartonus said to tell you that it’s called Dawnmaker,” Trianne instructed, “and that it’s already been paid for.”

“But I didn’t,” he started to say but Trianne cut him off by shoving a note against his lips.

“Please take it, Snowy,” she insisted with a pleading whine.

He pulled the note away and opened it with his thumb to read it. It was short and simple, and it played the strings of his heart with expert precision. The warmth in his chest spread to his fingers and toes and his throat clenched tight when he tried to swallow around the new light-headedness. He tucked the small strip of paper inside his coat pocket with reverence.

“Alright, Trianne, I will. Thank you for delivering it to me,” he said genuinely. The sword vanished in a shower of blue, tucked away and waiting to be summoned when he called for it again.

“Aaaany other crises waiting in the wings?” Cipher grumbled.

“Nope!” the red head announced.

“Not you, Little Red, I’m asking the pirates.” Castorice shook her head. Hyacine checked with Little Ica and then they both shook theirs in unpracticed tandem. “Well, Deliverer? Anything else you’d like to second guess before skipping town?”

Phainon looked down at Fig Stew and Beagle Coconut. They both awoo’d at him in encouragement.

He put his hand over the coreflames and said resolutely, “No. Let’s get back to the ship.”

-

Phainon wasn’t surprised to see that he and the girls were the last ones to make it to the Chryseus Leo. Entry Hour was fast approaching, and the ship was already getting ready to leave, just waiting for their wayward captain and friends. What was surprising was the suspicious collection of new cargo sitting on the deck. It was the first thing Phainon noticed when he stepped on the deck and bid the girls goodnight.

Anaxa was standing next to many various antique and replica amphorae that were sealed tight but still had gold around the seal and splashed over the sides. There were fingerprints everywhere and the whole situation just looked bad. Collecting whatever that was, it looked like blood, oh Kephale that is so much blood, please do not be blood, must have been a messy hassle.

“Professor?” Phainon asked as he beelined over.

“Oh, good, you’re safe,” Anaxa greeted, monotone, bored, covered in yep, that’s blood.

“What in Kephale’s name is this?” he asked, gesturing to the jars and to Anaxa.

“Don’t ask questions you don’t want the answer to.”

“Where did you get these jars? Did you steal these?”

“I’m not repeating myself.”

Dumbfounded, Phainon had no idea where to even begin addressing this, but his first mate came to his rescue. Phainon turned when Krateros coughed twice into a closed fist to get his attention and directed his questioning gaze to the old man instead, but Krateros just shook his head and hurried to change the subject by physically leading Phainon away by the arm.

“It’s good to have you back, captain,” he said, “your orders?”

Phainon shook his head to clear the lingering fog, the exhaustion of the day was quickly catching up but he very clearly told Krateros, “get us going towards Castrum Kremnos. Where is Hephaestion?”

“In the infirmary, Perdikkas said to tell you that Hephaestion is fine but needs his rest.”

“We all could use some of that,” Phainon said with a laugh.

Krateros at least cracked a small smile and nodded once in agreement and then he was stepping away to bark orders. The wind was favorable; they’d all be able to sleep when Okhema was in their wake.

Phainon walked up the stairs to the top deck with the coreflames so he could watch the city get smaller behind them. As tired as he was, there was still a longing to look back both literally and figuratively. There was a haunting sort of feeling now looking at Kephale and the Dawn Device, a sort of kinship that Phainon would never have considered before he was holding the Coreflame of Worldbearing. It was a heart of a past being, given to Phainon to share. Talk about big shoes to fill.

“Well, I wish I could say it’s been fun, but you did leave me hanging,” Cipher said. She was in the shrouds, hanging upside down to be nose to nose with Phainon as he stood near the railing.

“You’re leaving already?” he teased.

“Uh, yeah, duh, I’d much rather be somewhere dry,” she hummed.

“Cipher, if you’re leaving, I actually need a favor,” Phainon said sheepishly.

“After standing me up?”

Cipher feigned annoyance but he saw the way her tail swished, content, excited at the prospect of something interesting to do.

“It’s important.”

“Alright, alright, let’s hear it.”

“The Kremnoan people are marching to Okhema,” he told her, “at my insistence.”

She whistled through her teeth and slipped through the gaps in the shroud to be upright, hanging above the deck from her hands for a moment before dropping to the deck without a sound. “You were counting on that coreflame to end the war,” she supplied, “so the city would take them as refugees.”

He nodded and rested his hand over Strife. It was colder than the other coreflame, flickering faintly, desperate to keep burning while its owner struggled on his own so far away.

“The Black Tide has taken their home twice and now they’re heading towards a city that will assume the worst.” Phainon could hear the grief in his own voice, feel the exhaustion as he thought of Chironome and the others.

“You need someone with quick feet to keep the world from burning down before you have a chance to fix it.”

“I’m really counting on you, Cipher.”

“Of course you are,” she teased, still playful, still purring. “Some things never change. Don’t worry about them, go save the man who gave you his heart and when you do, don’t forget to unlock that damned door.”

He winced and then promised, “I will. Cipher, take care of yourself.”

“I’m supposed to be saying that to you, brat. Try not to have too much fun when you finally eat that coreflame,” she teased and then she was gone.

Phainon sighed and looked over at Fig Stew. The chimera had followed him up to the top deck and jumped on top of his favorite crate to show Beagle Coconut the best sunning spot on the ship. The gray chimera had a harder time climbing up there but he made it after a couple of leaps.

“She never did like long goodbyes,” Phainon sighed, “I’m sure she got it from you.”

He reached over and scratched Vigethos’ chin, around his horns and then down to his scruff to pull the golden thread out from behind the chimera’s collar.

“She did, didn’t she, Aglaea?” he told the thread. Phainon pinched it between his two fingers as he leaned over the railing and watched the city shrink. The coreflames pulsed brightly through the bag over his shoulder and he patted them gently with his free hand before retrieving the note from his coat pocket to read it again.

He read it a third time, then once more, committing it to memory before folding the tiny piece of paper up and wrapping the golden thread around it. He pressed the bundle to his lips.

“From the moment you took me in, until now, thank you, for everything,” he whispered and then he held his hand out and let go. The same wind that pushed them forward into deeper waters snatched up the note and dropped it into the sea.

They were pirates after all. He couldn’t let the Goldweaver see what happened next.

-

I am, and always have been, proud of you, Phainon. You were always worthy of the title. -A

chapters.title: Chapter 38: Again

Chapter Summary

No new tags but please mind the ones that are already there

Welcome back, Mydeimos

There were a lot of things that didn’t matter anymore when Mydei threw Phainon to safety and blocked the man from returning.

The passing of time was a big one. With the sky above Castrum Kremnos permanently full of black clouds and rolling thunder, each Entry Hour passed by without acknowledgement nor fanfare. He had no concept of mealtimes, no time to rest or sleep, there was no reason to count the passing of weeks or years, because he had no idea how long he had been fighting, and it simply didn’t matter.

How many times he had died was another silly nonissue to forget. The first time the Tide gutted him, he considered starting a count, but something about the thought filled him with anxiety more than humor and he didn’t need that weight on his chest. Unnecessary baggage like that would ruin the fun of an otherwise good fight.

It was getting easier to ignore the constant hum of the Tide Song in the back of his mind, the volume adjusted on its own with every death. If Mydei paused to listen to it, he could sing the lyrics by heart. He didn’t understand them, but he could feel the underlying message: give up, join us, so you won’t be lonely again. But even that too was something that simply didn’t matter anymore.

What an absurd request. Giving up was never on the table, it wasn’t even a temptation because of the only thing that did matter, and that was Phainon. Of course, Mydei wanted to protect his people and crew too, but Phainon was at the forefront of every second of this struggle that would surely last through the eternities.

However long it takes.

Every time he died it was with Phainon’s name on his lips. Every time he sucked in air again he was calling for his Deliverer. Every long swim upstream through the River of Souls was spent picturing Phainon’s goofy grin until he couldn’t quite remember the details of his smile anymore. But even that didn’t matter as long as he held tightly to what it felt like to be side by side with the person he loved most in this world and any world after.

It was the heart of those memories that tried desperately to fill the void inside his chest, that eternal ache that hurt worse than every broken bone, every gasp for air, and stabbing wound. Phainon had been right about the coreflame. It was truly a missing part of him, a near literal removal of a part of his chest. It was a pain that he felt like he could speak to, especially after the second time sharp claws ripped his still beating heart from him and threw his body aside to break on the dilapidated remains of his homeland.

But Mydei had also been right when he pushed it away and made the lofty and perhaps naïve claim that the coreflame couldn’t compare to Phainon and the feeling of completeness that he had around the man, like a piece of him that he had never known was missing had come home. Which was why the pain was so immense now, fighting the Tide, because not only was his coreflame gone, but so was Phainon.

When his throat was slit and his body grew cold Mydei could imagine the feeling of Phainon’s warm frame wrapped around him, trying to protect what was left of that life before it faded away with his capable arms.

The first time the Tide had pinned him to the ground and choked him to death, he had felt phantom tears on his cheeks and a tight squeezing in his chest as though someone were mourning him and holding Mydei tightly to keep him together.

When his legs had been severed and tossed to the side, leaving him to bleed out yet again, he thought he heard music, not the Tide song, but the soft tenor of Peucesta’s lullabies. A memory he was sure, but he had felt the melody deep in the void that had once been his heart.

When he was choking on the ash of monsters he had defeated, buried under the severed limbs of the Tide’s kraken, panting, exhausted, he could feel the fears of the people he loved, their worry for him carried over the waters, and Mydei fought harder to reassure them and himself that this was nothing. Their worries were wasted on him. How could they forget so easily the joy that Mydei felt in battle? His only regret was not sharing it with the person he loved!

He prayed that those silly sentiments would carry across the waters, that Phainon would be the smart, strong, noble Deliverer that he had seen every day of their journey together. He knew that the man would be okay, that Perdikkas and Hyacine would see him well again and that he would step up to this request that Mydei had made of him. There was no one better to take care of his people while Mydei corrected their mistake.

It was his idea to retrieve the Coreflame of Strife. Had he known that Nikador was the last line of defense, would he have taken a different path for Phainon’s redemption? No. Nikador was not themself at the end.

Even if it was not the Tide’s corruption, Nikador was not the Titan of eld from stories anymore. Whether it was Eurypon’s influence or something else entirely, Nikador had still become something rabid that needed to be put down. If the Tide had not kept the Titan’s attention for such a long time, that spear would undoubtedly have torn across Amphoreus. That same spear that ripped through Mydei’s belly and left him dying, again and again as the Tide played with its new toys.

I swear on my own golden blood that I will give a thousand of my own lives to celebrate this triumph beside you all.

He meant every word. Mydei’s arms and legs were shaking as he revived. The Tide still clung to his spirit, he felt so heavy. Each death purged much of the corruption, but he could still hear the song when he stood again. His boots were caked in the blood of past partings, turned into a paste when the gold met ash. They weighed him down more than the flashing memories of a traumatic childhood.

Whether the Tide knew of his history fighting tentacled creatures in his youth or not he did not know but it gleefully took this form, enjoying every fight as he lost more and more of himself to his personal demon.

All weakness, grief, and grudges will be settled on the battlefield.

They were his mother’s words that he had repeated over the years, but every time he threw crystal at that monster’s beak and ripped into squishy flesh with his claws it was hard to let that weakness go. He was a kid again, flailing wildly, little more than a monster himself, a beast in the water, drowning, drowning and then it grabbed his ankle and threw him against the Sword of Strife, snapping his neck.

He was dead, again, before he hit the ground.

Get up, my son!

Mydei spat at the monster as it roared at him, getting frustrated. His wounds were knitting back together. It itched but he paid the process no mind, such little pains meant nothing to the lion of Kremnos. The kraken roared and squealed, a sound that was grating and unnatural above the ocean surface like a spear scraping against smooth marble. The kind of noise that you felt in your teeth. Sometimes it would retreat and send monsters to entertain Mydei in its stead, but it always came back, reaching for him eventually.

He stomped on the tentacle that slithered towards his foot and crystal erupted around it, spearing up the arm and holding the beast tight while he grabbed for another wriggling limb to rip it free in a gush of ink and song.

On and on they fought and Mydei left more and more of himself behind, freeing himself of the past to embrace that excitement that flowed in the veins of every Kremnoan when they look their end in the eye and greet it with glee.

Fight for that future, and when fate’s inescapable grasp comes for you, resist it with the strength of your mighty will.

He laughed as he grabbed a piece of Phainon’s broken blade from the ground. It cut into his hand, but he couldn’t feel it through the bloodlust, through the excited high of an eternal battle and when the kraken came for him again he met it eagerly.

Mydei didn’t know how long he had been fighting this time when the sky above rent in two. He was too focused on fighting his monster to notice the change until the kraken was recoiling from the light. The clouds above ripped open as though they had been cut with fine shears and multi-colored light poured across Castrum Kremnos, illuminating the city of warriors in a way that it had not seen since Eurypon’s fall.

The light was blinding but rejuvenating and Mydei threw himself at the Tide with renewed vigor, ripping and tearing like a rabid animal even when another beast joined him at his side. He could see the flash of gold and blue in the corner of his eye, an angelic creature of grace and destruction with beautiful wings, a long pair of tails, and a golden halo. Mydei could feel its heat when he dashed in close and with it came explicit joy and a surge of competitive elation. Bruised, bleeding, and broken, he launched himself at the kraken’s face to tear at its eyes while it screamed until a massive sword ripped across its body and its form frayed at the edges, slowly turning to ash.

It thrashed, throwing Mydei to the ground beneath the Blade of Fury where he felt his body break further, but he still stumbled to his feet with wild eyes and a toothy grin to spit blood and watch the kraken in its death throes. And as it faded so did he. The relief of a battle well fought, the end of a struggle paid for with many lives was often followed by exhaustion. It was not unexpected.

“Mydei!” a familiar voice shouted, and with one word he was himself again.

The Prince chuckled as his knees buckled, and he collapsed onto a strong and warm arm, a presence that flooded his dull senses with familiarity, comfort, and wholeness.

“I was prepared to fight til the end of time,” he rasped around his broken throat as those arms gently lowered his body and rolled him to face the sky. They held him close, supporting his head and shoulders, not letting him touch the ground. Phainon was hard to see through his blurred vision, he looked different, but he felt the same.

Mydei reached up with a shaking hand to press his palm to Phainon’s cheek and felt soft lips on his fingers. Someone else was shouting far away but black was creeping in along his vision and nothing else really mattered than what was here in front of him.

“What took you so long, Deliverer?” he sighed with the breath he had left.

And then, he died.

-

Mydei stood on the shore of the River of Souls. He needed to get back, to defy death once more but… he was tired.

He didn’t dare sit, lest he decide to stay, but knowing that the battle was over for now, that his body was in Phainon’s arms, brought a measure of peace. As eager as he was to return his spirit to that man’s side, Mydei was also exhausted and needed a moment to himself, to pick up the pieces that had been torn from his body and scattered across the battlefield. He needed this silence to put aside cohesive thought and simply be before the weight of who he was fell upon his shoulders again.

The air was cold here, quiet. Sometimes the spirits of the dead whispered to him as they haunted the fields of flowers that lined the shore. He had long surmised that this was where he visited in his dreams. Where he had talked to his mother in his youth.

Perhaps if he lingered here long enough she would appear, and he could tell her about their adventure, the things he had learned, and even the things he had yet to consider the weight of. Would she be upset with him for giving away the Coreflame of Strife? Would she be proud to know he did it for Phainon?

“Valorous death before glorious return. My son, you refused to fall in combat and insist on returning to the mortal world. Do you still dare call yourself a Kremnoan?”

The voice was muddled, more of a lingering thought than a true phantom. Mydei didn’t turn around. He recognized Eurypon’s words, this was not the first time he had heard them.

“Think you still have the right to sit upon the throne of the great kingdom you destroyed? I don’t think so.”

“…shut up,” Mydei mumbled. It was hard to talk down here; it took too much of his strength to fight the pull of abyss.

“Since when did the Kremnoans grow so weak as to become someone else’s quiet support? After all, you and I both thrive on strife and fear…”

For a moment, Mydei considered entertaining his father, asking why he did what he did. What drove a great King to sacrifice his only son? Maybe he would answer this time. Or maybe that too didn’t matter anymore.

“Get lost.”

Mydei gathered himself then and waded into the water, starting the journey upstream back to the world of the living, shrugging aside his father’s taunting, that madness that followed him even unto death. He needed to get back to Phainon, to the crew. Mydei still didn’t know how many, if any, survived their assault on the city. How long had it even been?

Don’t stop moving forward. I don’t remember ever teaching you to be “weak.”

The cold pulled at his muscles, stung at every cut, but still he swam until the cold of the afterlife gave way and Mydei felt warm again.

He kept his eyes closed. Mydei didn’t have the energy to open them. He couldn’t move his arms or legs, trapped in the limbo of someone not quite ready to wake up, so he didn’t. There was a voice, Phainon’s voice, he couldn’t understand it from this far away, but it was all-encompassing comfort. He could feel the rock of the ship and fur under his hand, both hands… that was curious… and smell sweet things. It was enough to feel safe, so he slept.

When Mydei finally felt the exhaustion fade away and wakefulness gave him the strength to open his eyes he focused first on the familiar. The ceiling above was that of his home at the Kremnoan Settlement, at least what he could see of it in the gaps between pinions and the limited light. He was surrounded by dark blue and bronze-gold feathers belonging to a pair of wings that had encompassed him and the person he was lying against as though they alone could keep out the world.

There was a heartbeat that was not Mydei’s own, beating strong and solid against his back inside a broad chest that rose and fell rhythmically with each deep breath between whispers. Phainon was spooning Mydei, keeping him close, letting him rest on his back across Phainon’s belly and chest while he read aloud in Kremnoan from their favorite book by candlelight. Mydei could follow along with where he was at with his eyes as Phainon used Mydei’s blanket covered chest to rest his arm holding up the book so he could keep the man secure while passing the time. One of his arms was wrapped in clean bandages, all the way from the wrist to the middle of his forearm, but it didn’t seem to bother him as he turned the page.

Mydei’s own arms were at his sides, bent slightly at the elbows where two chimeras, Fig Stew, and one he had never seen before had curled up with him on either side. Why they preferred his hard musculature over the plush of the cushions surrounding them he’d never know. Phainon had created a sort of nest out of bedding, far more than Mydei usually kept in the big room, but this was more enjoyable than the bedroom he supposed as he listened to Phainon’s horrible pronunciations butchering his favorite parts and smelled the light breeze as it passed over the balcony and into the open room. If he closed his eyes to listen, he could hear others snoring softly and knew that despite Phainon’s efforts to create a private bubble for them, his other friends were nearby as well.

He tilted his head back and looked up at the underside of Phainon’s chin. The man was wearing sleepwear, a light chiton and clasp-less chlamys over his shoulders like a shawl. His hair was clean and still damp from a recent bath, glowing in the candlelight. He could see it fanning over his ears like misplaced fine down. It made Mydei realize his own hair was damp too, cool against his scalp.

Mydei reached up with a hand to gently brush his knuckles along Phainon’s jaw, and the man finished his sentence, he actually finished the sentence before he closed the book with one hand and looked down at Mydei.

There it was, the smile that Mydei had fallen in love with. The one that carried him so many times from death to life. He ghosted the rough pads of his fingertips against Phainon’s temple and cheek. He looked so tired, how long had they been apart?

Mydei wordlessly sat up, letting the still sleeping chimeras roll away to snore on the pillows, and the wings fluttered around them, Phainon’s wings. They loosened around the pair to give Mydei space but only just enough to not feel claustrophobic as he turned around. Phainon was unwilling to remove the feathers entirely, leaving them curled in a way that was selfish, to keep Mydei to himself. He twisted to rest on his knees between Phainon’s legs, and the blanket fell off his shoulders, leaving his chest and shoulders bare.

Phainon pulled a leg up, bending at the knee so he could nudge Mydei’s side, perhaps a little playful, definitely grounding, possessive even, and he felt warmth in his cheeks that spread to his ears and chest. He set aside the book, leaving it on the blanket with a hand still resting over its aging pages. The other reached up to catch a lock of Mydei’s hair, giving it a gentle tug.

Mydei very slowly reached for Phainon’s face with both hands and coaxed him into sitting up and away from the pillows he was propped up against, eager to meet him on equal ground where they belonged together. He sat back on his heels and gently traced Phainon’s lips, under his eyes, and along his jawline with his fingertips until Phainon melted into one palm, leaning into where Mydei cradled him with his fingers wound in silken strands and his thumb resting on the soft space beside Phainon’s blushing ear and cheek. The other hand brushed the bangs away from Phainon’s eyes so he could see them better, to ponder how much Phainon had changed since he had seen him last.

The blue of them flashed gold and Mydei blinked and tensed in surprise, a movement that made Phainon look down. His wings fluttered and drooped to lay flat against the blankets and cold floor and he raised a hand to tenderly grab Mydei’s wrist to pull away as though ashamed, but Mydei held tighter, firmly tilting his head back with the press of fingertips against the underside of his chin until their eyes met again.

“It’s still you,” Mydei whispered, so softly he thought his voice might break, “I can tell, it’s still you.”

Phainon’s eyes turned shiny, and the threat of tears started to bead at the corner of his eyes and Mydei couldn’t wait anymore. He tilted forward at the same time as Phainon and their lips met, softly testing the waters, but building in confidence with every racing heartbeat. Phainon’s hands moved to Mydei’s shoulders sliding up his neck to hold him at the hinges of his jaw, keeping him close even when they parted for breath, their foreheads pressed tight and noses still touching.

Mydei’s fingers tingled, and his chest felt tight, no, full. There was a bubbling warmth in his stomach that rivaled the heat between them and made him want to wiggle in place, run around the building, or hit something, at this point it was a toss up which one he wanted more. All he knew was that he was full to bursting with love and adoration and couldn’t keep the little gasping chuckles from escaping between breaths. The smile on his face was hurting his cheeks but he couldn’t stop drinking Phainon in.

He memorized every blink, every stray hair that got in his face, the little breathy giggles that tumbled from his lips, the way Phainon looked at him with those eyes that couldn’t decide if they wanted to be blue or shine like golden sunlight. They could talk about that later, when Mydei returned to the earth from this heaven he had found himself in, this heaven he never believed he’d get to hold again. He had resigned himself to fighting forever, to be alone, oh how happy he was to be proven wrong.

“Mydeimos,” Phainon mumbled with Kremnoan pronunciation and Mydei couldn’t help but kiss him again. One of his hands drifted deeper into Phainon’s hair to gently hold him by the roots, to keep this man where he wanted him, as their lips parted and closed with inexperienced but eager kisses. He tightened his grip, just enough to pull a gasp from that pretty mouth and was rewarded with Phainon’s soft tongue licking across his lips with a shy, boyish expression that made Mydei’s heart race.

“My disobedient, ridiculous puppy,” Mydei mumbled in his native language as he let go of Phainon’s hair to press his thumb to his Deliverer’s lips, “I told you to leave me, could you not obey me even the once?”

Phainon reached up to take Mydei’s wrist, pulling it away to reverently kiss his palm. “Not even once.”

Mydei leaned in again to kiss him, but Phainon put a hand on his chest and pushed him back. Those wings fluttered up again, encompassing, not wanting Mydei to leave but keeping him at arms-length for some reason and Mydei tilted his head, confused at the response.

“I’m still mad at you,” Phainon explained.

“Mad enough to kiss me?”

“That was because I missed you.”

Mydei sighed and let his hands fall away from Phainon to rub his own face. He was still sore, he felt clean, but the ache of fighting still lingered. “You are angry because I did not let you stay and fight…”

“I’m angry because you didn’t give me the chance to say it back.”

He looked up at Phainon with unwarranted surprise. The man had kissed him, they had just kissed, surely that was enough for him to know that Phainon shared these feelings with him. But Phainon looked genuinely upset, like there was more than just this single thing on his mind.

“Phainon…” He brushed his knuckles against Phainon’s cheek. To his relief, Phainon did not recoil.

“I wanted to say it first,” he grumbled, “and you didn’t give me the chance to say it all.”

“I’m sorry,” Mydei said gently, “would you like to say it now?”

“No,” Phainon pouted.

“Then I will say it again.”

Phainon’s hand slapped over Mydei’s mouth, and he chuckled before kissing it as Phainon had done for him.

“When I can do it right,” Phainon promised, “I’ll say it out loud.”

He took his hand back and Mydei chased it with his own to clasp his rough fingers in their laps between them with his own. “Deliverer-“

“Not now, Mydei. It’s late, there will be time to answer all your questions in the morning.”

“Allow me a few?” the Prince asked, “so that I can rest more easily.”

Phainon visibly contemplated that and then nodded.

“How many did we lose?” Mydei asked softly, and they both crashed back to reality. It took Phainon a moment of puzzling. The candlelight over his shoulder made his hair glow along the fringes like a halo as he struggled to answer and Mydei got the sense that more time had passed than he realized, enough at least for Phainon to have to distinguish between events to understand the context of the question.

“Seven,” he answered sadly, “we lost seven the day we slew Nikador.”

Mydei’s gut twisted in knots as he asked, “and since that day?”

“None.”

He sighed, relieved it was not worse, and then shakily asked, “who?”

Mydei listened carefully as Phainon told him the names of his crewmates that gave their lives in combat, who undoubtedly joined that great blade in the sky that Nikador would never again wield. Names that Phainon had memorized, taking his role as captain very seriously in Mydei’s absence. His heart swelled with pride knowing that he had picked well and while he silently wished his fallen crewmates glory in their passing, he knew they would not tolerate mourning, especially from their Prince.

“How long has it been?” he asked next.

Phainon swallowed, the bob of his throat distracting as he said, “Twenty-seven Entry Hours, give or take a couple. Ptolemy kept better track than I did.”

Mydei slumped forward, his forehead resting on Phainon’s shoulder as the relief washed over him and took the tension with it. He shook very briefly with a soft laugh.

“Mydei?” Phainon asked, concerned. He felt strong hands on his back, massaging their way up to squeeze lightly at the back of his neck before they curiously played with his hair.

“I thought it had been years,” he confessed, “that perhaps you had forgotten about me.”

“Forget you? Like I’d ever.”

Mydei leaned back again to study the look in his best friend’s eyes. “Then why do you look like you carry the weight of a century?”

Phainon looked away, his voice shaky when he whispered, “You died in my arms, Mydei…”

“HKS, is that what this is about?” he teased.

The glare that came Mydei’s way was full of hurt. Phainon didn’t appreciate Mydei being dismissive of his feelings, but this was a nonissue and there was no way Mydei was going to let the love of his life stress over something so ridiculous.

“I held you while you died.”

“Deliverer, death cannot keep me for long,” Mydei reminded him. He gently took Phainon’s hand and held it to his bare chest so the man could feel his heart beating. When he let go, Phainon’s palm stayed flat against that firm muscle to feel and be reassured but the look in his eyes was still haunted.

“You have even now witnessed for yourself that I will always come back,” he pushed, “and if you have any idea how exhausting it is return from a protracted battle, then you should know that pointless arguments are the last thing I want to get into now.”

Phainon kept his mouth shut. He nodded and then it was his turn to lean forward to rest his forehead against Mydei’s chest, right over where his hand still counted heartbeats. Those wings shifted when he did, curling in tighter, wanting to keep Mydei safe and secure. The Kremnoan wrapped his arms around Phainon and felt the other warrior do the same, pulling him in as close as he could manage without pulling Mydei down on top of him.

“…you’re still upset,” Mydei observed.

“I know it is nothing to you,” Phainon murmured, “but it was everything to me. Even knowing that you would come back, to see you there, covered in blood, with no shine to your eyes or beating of your heart… You took a piece of me with you.”

The ache in Phainon’s voice had Mydei second guessing his casualness. His lives always felt cheap, even to his family and crew that had seen him perish and return several times it was almost like an inside joke, something to tease him about when a foolish idea snatched away a life. Perhaps it was a result of their cultural upbringing, to disregard death as simply something that happened, something to be desired under the right circumstances. But Mydei was one of very few Kremnoans to reject the idea of valorous death over glorious return. He wanted a future wherein his people valued every breath and fought to protect each other rather than to mindlessly march to their deaths like insects.

Who was he to devalue his own? Especially when someone dear to him was hurting.

“You’re right,” he relented, “and if it is everything to you, then it will be to me.”

Phainon’s arms around his shoulders and back tightened in a reassuring squeeze and then he let go when Mydei pulled away. Again, Mydei pressed his palm to Phainon’s cheek as though it would hurt him to not keep in contact.

“I can’t promise I will never die again,” he said firmly and Phainon’s expression turned sour, that guarded expression that he wore to mask his grief, but Mydei saw through him. “I would cross the River of Souls over and over again if it meant you could be safe.”

“That’s not fair,” Phainon hissed and Mydei let his hand drop, “you are my equal in everything Mydei. You don’t get to be the only protector here.”

“…fair enough.”

“We can talk about it more in the morning,” Phainon said after a minute of heavy silence, “a lot happened while you were holding back the Tide.”

“So, I see,” Mydei reached out and brushed his fingers against Phainon’s wings. They shivered under his touch, and Phainon gently brought them in closer for Mydei to feel. They weren’t like a bird’s wings with many interlocking feathers. Rather they were wholly unique, branched like a tree with only a few large pinions per branch. One entire wing was dark blue, almost black in the candlelight, and the other was golden bronze. There was an edge to them, but they weren’t sharp nor cold. Each feather had its own heat like laundry that had been left out in the sun to dry and warm. When Phainon wrapped them around Mydei it was as though he was surrounded by the memory of harvest days, of long naps in the shade of tree with the smell of warmed grass tickling his nose. It made him smile.

Mydei offered that smile to Phainon but the one he got in return was tired, happy and relieved, but still haunted.

“We should sleep, Mydei,” Phainon suggested. He was already falling away, laying back against the pillows but Mydei followed him, leaning over Phainon with his hands on the cushions to either side. His hair fell around his face to cage them in more intimately than Phainon’s wings had before.

“One more kiss,” he demanded, “one more kiss and one more secret.”

Phainon thought about that for a moment and then reached up to touch Mydei’s cheek. He lifted his head from the pillows to chastely press their lips together and they held it until Mydei’s shaky arms demanded he quit.

Regrettably, Mydei rolled off Phainon to lay beside him and Phainon turned to his side with a curious expression.

“You are right, we are equals, and I do trust you, Deliverer,” Mydei began. He paused, trying to find the right words to share this secret with the person he loved most. “And it isn’t fair if I don’t let you protect me too.” He reached out to futilely brush hair from Phainon’s tired eyes. Those bangs fell right back into place but still he tried. “My tenth thoracic vertebrae. That’s my weak spot, and the only way to kill me.”

Phainon’s eyes widened then narrowed, and his mouth opened but he didn’t say anything, not right away. As usual, the Deliverer had to process what he had just been told and his face cycled through a series of emotions in rapid succession until, in true Phainon fashion, he started to laugh.

“I share with you my greatest secret and you laugh?” he hissed around his whisper.

“I’m sorry, Mydei,” Phainon managed as he calmed down, “I just remembered something. Before I followed you into Castrum Kremnos you asked me something.”

“I did.”

“Do you remember what I said?”

“…I do.”

“And I meant it,” Phainon promised. The pain behind those beautiful blue eyes alleviated somewhat in the comfort of responsibility and trust. Mydei worried he might regret sharing something so intimate out loud, but it was worth it to see Phainon at ease. It was worth it to hear Phainon fall into a deep and restful sleep.

“Deliverer, do you have my back?”

“Always, Mydeimos.”

Chapter End Notes

I worry a TINY bit about what this jump will do to the pacing. I'm HOPING that after a couple more chapters folks will see the vision. Hopefully. I'm experimenting. Yay growth! Basically, if it feels like there's a chapter missing, that's intentional. I want it to feel that way because MYDEI feels that way.
