Chapter Summary

New tags: Implied/Referenced Self-Harm (changed from Cutting), Eye Trauma, Body Horror All very minor but please protect yourselves if you are sensitive to even references of these things

Phainon tells Mydei what happened

Chapter Notes

Shoutout to my beta reader, Bane. She's my co-author on my other long-fic and I made her read this one so she could read over my shoulders and help me find the things I missed. She doesn't even go here and already had to help me fix something I realized in a panic at like 11 pm :')

Writing is hard sometimes guys. Especially when your original outline is crying in a ditch somewhere.

Phainon woke up before Mydei but after everyone else and was relieved to have the room to himself. Everyone knew how he felt about Mydei now, word got around fast, and no one was surprised when many of the crew heard Phainon confessing to Mydei’s corpse over and over between sobs. He had rocked back and forth on his knees with Mydei held tightly to his chest apologizing and telling him how much he loved him in both languages as if that would wake him up faster. It didn’t.

He gently brushed bed head hair out of Mydei’s eyes as he slept and smiled at the memory of their kisses late last night. It was so very tempting to wake the man with another, but Perdikkas had warned Phainon that Mydei would probably need more rest than he usually did after coming back from the dead. It was hard to know how many lives he lost and couldn’t recover from before they came to his rescue and his body and spirit could finally, finally let their guard down to sleep.

Mydei’s hair was still a little sticky between Phainon’s fingers. They had tried to bathe him when they got to port yesterday but he’d need another. Side by side like this Phainon could still feel the corruption lingering on his spirit, another perk of his coreflame perhaps. He wanted to burn it away from Mydei, to take it upon himself. It wouldn’t be so bad, he thought, to hear the song one last time, something that may never happen again now that he was a Demigod.

He ran his fingers over Mydei’s shoulder and down his back, tracing tattoos as he went. The man had ended up sleeping on his stomach, a position that Phainon now recognized as a gesture of trust. Starting at one, Phainon counted the bumps of Mydei’s spine until he got to ten, brushing over that sensitive spot that made Mydeimos shiver in his sleep, little more than a reflexive twitch. He pressed a little harder with two fingers, circling that bump on his back with firm rubs.

I share with you my greatest secret and you laugh?

Phainon hadn’t known how else to react, he was so overwhelmed at the time. Happy to hear Mydei’s voice again and still angry with him for his callousness, but now that it was quiet, that he was rested, that Mydei was okay, the weight of that secret could properly settle. He didn’t like thinking of it as the only way to kill Mydei, this was the best way to protect Mydei and Phainon was humbled and honored to be trusted with such an important job.

“Awoo?”

Phainon grunted when Beagle pounced on him and knocked the wind from his belly. His tail was straight and his whole body was on alert. Those big blue eyes peered out from under Phainon’s arm as he rubbed his head and horns on the sore bicep.

“I’ll feed you in a minute.”

Fig Stew chirped at that sentiment but stayed put beside Mydei. The orange chimera was stretched out happily in the little spoon spot against Mydei’s side and Phainon suspected any attempts to move him would result in violent protest. Beagle purred and made biscuits on Phainon’s abs and then stotted over to his chimera boyfriend to lightly headbutt Beagle’s side and then sprawled on top of him. Fig’s peep was anything but distressed and Phainon took the hint to leave. They were making him jealous.

Breakfast was easy, bread, figs, and cheese had already been set aside and Phainon sliced up some of the cured meat they had on hand. Beagle was teaching Fig Stew how to have an appetite so Phainon piled the plate a lot higher than he normally would. When he considered how long it had been since Mydei had tasted food, Phainon added even more until the plate was an accident waiting to happen. The chimeras had their own water dish in the other room, so he grabbed the pitcher of juice for himself and meandered back, pausing in the doorway when he saw the empty pile of bedding.

Mydei was standing on the balcony petting Beagle Coconut and Fig Stew in turn. They were sitting politely on the railing, not demanding attention but eagerly accepting it when given. The chiton they had dressed him in was still tied around his waist, leaving his back and shoulders bare. Phainon watched him for a minute, studying the way he looked at the city with a tired slump and ran his fingers through his hair like he usually did when he was stressed.

“Mydeimos,” he whispered, just loud enough to be heard and Mydei turned those beautiful amber eyes to watch Phainon walk across the room where he set the plate and pitcher on the railing.

Mydei looked at the food with obvious want and then turned those hungry eyes on Phainon. He saw Mydei look for wings, which were put away for now, then to his eyes, and finally they dropped to Phainon’s lips.

“Was it a dream?” Mydei asked, his voice gravelly and hoarse from disuse.

Phainon leaned forward and pressed his lips to Mydei’s giving him every opportunity to step away but Mydei closed his eyes and pushed into it, even reaching a hand up to take a handful of Phainon’s chlamys to keep him from pulling away before he was ready to let go. He only stopped when Phainon’s smile broke the kiss.

“…not a dream,” the Kremnoan mumbled to himself.

“No, it wasn’t.”

“Good, I didn’t want it to be.” He turned back to facing the ruins of the settlement and reached for the food, curling his lip back to show his teeth when Beagle tried to snatch a piece of meat from him. The chimera pouted and took a step back, but Phainon stepped in to prevent a fight. He handed each of the chimeras bites of food when they waited patiently, acting as the intermediary between them and the plate so Mydei could eagerly take what he wanted, what he needed after going so long without.

“Was it the Tide?” Mydei asked.

“Yes.”

“The silence here is stifling… The city feels so unfamiliar now.”

“You’ve exchanged thousands of blows with the Black Tide…your ears are probably just not used to this peace and quiet,” Phainon tried to be light-hearted about it, but it didn’t feel right, “we would have lost everyone, Mydei, if it wasn’t for you.”

Mydei’s hands on the railing slowly curled into loose fists.

“I can call the others,” Phainon offered, “we can tell you what happened since Castrum Kremnos.”

“I want to hear it from you.”

“Mydei, there are parts of the story I don’t have…”

“Then tell me the parts you do.”

Phainon started with a shameful admission, beginning the story from the very moment the crystal blocked his way back to Mydei’s side. Fig Stew purred at the mention of his heroism and the well-deserved credit that the chimera had earned when he pulled Phainon away from crippling grief. The chimera puffed out his chest and rolled onto his back so Phainon could scratch his belly when Phainon described the tension on deck when he returned without Mydei. He ran his fingers through that plush fur as he recalled the first time Fig Stew had allowed such affection in detail.

“He accepted you,” Mydei repeated softly as he watched with a guarded expression. He reached over to pet Fig’s belly as well and their fingers met.

“Yeah, convinced the whole crew too.”

“Krateros.” It wasn’t a question.

“Yeah.”

Beagle very firmly put his paw on their hands and chirped, annoyed. He slapped them both across the knuckles when they lingered a little too long and then he set about grooming the tummy of a purring Fig Stew with more focus than Phainon had seen from the monster in his whole life.

Phainon moved on to talk about the crew’s injuries, how hurt he had been, how hurt Hephaestion had been. Mydei reached for Phainon’s chlamys and pushed it aside to trace the scar with his fingertips while Phainon described the lingering pain. He had been there when Nikador’s spear ripped open his flesh, but it was different, seeing it now when there was time to process how serious the injury had been. When Phainon started elaborating on the first mate…

“Mydei? Where are you going?”

“Where is Hephaestion now?” he asked while he pulled on his sandals.

“Perdikkas is staying with him in a home near the bathhouse.” Phainon’s own sandals hit his chest and fell into his arms. He saw where this was going, slipped the footwear on and reached to grab his bag beside their messy pile of cushions. Phainon added his book from last night and a couple of easy snacks, then secured it over his shoulder and rested his hand over the bag while Mydei finished getting dressed. The red chlamys only covered his shoulders and part of his chest. Phainon didn’t mind. He liked the flash of tattoos as Mydei moved.

“Tell me more as we walk.”

The roads were solemn and quiet. They took it slow so Mydei could take in the devastation as Phainon recalled the evacuation. He described for Mydei the Black Tide as it raced the ship in unpredictable bursts, how it stalled for a time, allowing them to ferry supplies and people to the mainland across the sound. The fires and monsters had blanketed the last of them to escape in the night with heavy ash. He almost told Mydei about Chironome, that sweet orphan child with a heart of a lion, but he paused and decided in that moment to keep the memory of her to himself for now.

Mydei reached up and squeezed Phainon’s arm, stopping in the road next to a collapsed stall. The city felt gray, even with the bright blue sky above them and the rising sun trying its best to splash color against the remains, but the ash still clung to every surface, dampening the brightness that had once been.

“That must have been hard for you,” Mydei observed when Phainon did not continue right away. There was worry in his leonine eyes, he must have thought the hesitation was Phainon recalling a particularly difficult memory.

“It’s your home that was lost,” he chuckled sadly, “and you’re worried about how I feel?”

“This was never home,” Mydei said simply as he started walking again, and Phainon vaguely remembered him saying as much once before.

Phainon matched his pace and told Mydei about the journey to Okhema. He had to tell his story about Krateros twice when Mydei didn’t believe him the first time. Even though the Kremnoan insisted he wouldn’t believe it until he saw it, Mydei still smiled when Phainon listed his positive interactions with the man. He especially emphasized to Mydei that Krateros made an excellent first mate but still dramatically complained about the veteran, describing Krateros as a terrifying taskmaster at every lesson whether it be sparring or woodcraft and Mydei laughed in mutual understanding.

The sounds of the crew got louder as they approached the bathhouse and surrounding buildings. Several of the structures had collapsed but a few still stood proud. Mydei and Phainon walked in silence when they heard the crew. The sound carried in the empty city, but the mumbling of distant voices made it easier to remember that there were more than ghosts here, that the Kremnoan people still lived despite the Tide’s best efforts.

“-I mean we could ask but there’s still some from Okhema,” Perdikkas’ voice carried. They rounded the corner in time to see the doctor talking to Peucesta. The two of them brightened immediately when they saw Mydei and Phainon.

“It’s good to see you on your feet, captain,” Perdikkas greeted and Phainon had to close his mouth before he responded. There would probably be some muscle memory there for a while as he readjusted to his role as crewmate, but Mydei still looked at him expectantly, as though he wasn’t sure anymore to whom the title belonged.

“It is good to see you on your feet,” Phainon agreed, silencing the debate before it could start.

Mydei turned back to their friends and nodded which was all the permission his men needed. Perdikkas and Peucesta scooped him up in a hug between them and Mydei’s eyes widened in shock.

“HKS! You fools! What is this? Has the Deliverer taken from you your pride?” he scolded but they didn’t let go of him.

“You were missed, Mydei! Let us love on you!”

“Nikador’s glory, he has! Phainon of Aedes Elysiae! Your sentimental foolishness has corrupted my crew!”

“It won’t happen again!” Phainon promised with a playful chuckle and then he joined the group hug while Mydei cussed at them more creatively in Kremnoan until they let him go.

“You need another bath,” Peucesta observed when they pulled away and let Mydei straighten his clothes to try and recover some of his dignity.

“Not now,” Mydei huffed, “where is Hephaestion?”

Perdikkas nodded and then gestured with a wave for them to follow and he led Mydei to one of the intact houses. The home did not belong to them, it didn’t belong to anyone anymore, but there were warm blankets and basic amenities that Hephaestion needed.

The first mate was sitting up on the kline when Mydei pushed aside the curtain to see him. Hyacine was tending to a long, wide scar across his chest while Ptolemy cracked jokes. There was a book in Ptolemy’s lap with his thumb between the pages to keep their spot but judging by the company that story had long been abandoned in favor of good conversation. The room brightened further when they saw their Prince.

“Mydeimos…” Hephaestion greeted, and the captain immediately stepped up to his side.

“Lord Mydei,” Hyacine acknowledged politely.

“Hephaestion, are you…?”

“I am not in danger, Mydei, don’t look so distraught.”

“Phainon told me you had been severely injured…”

Ptolemy huffed and shot Phainon a glare. “Storytelling without us?”

“You are welcome to repeat the tale,” Phainon invited with a flourish.

“’Why cover the same ground again? It goes against my grain to repeat a tale told once, and told so clearly,’” Ptolemy quoted with a shrug.

“If it helps, I haven’t finished telling him everything.”

Mydei took a seat on the kline near Hephaestion’s feet and gestured to Hyacine and Perdikkas, “tell me of Hephaestion’s condition, then I would hear more of what happened in my absence.”

The doctors told Mydei about the details of Hephaestion’s injuries and what it could mean long term. Phainon had heard it all before and it still hurt to know, but Hephaestion reassured Mydei with a soft, if tired smile, and even light-heartedly complained about not being allowed to help more with the all the new chores on the ship.

“What chores?” Mydei asked.

“Replacing all that wax, painting the ship, cleaning up all that blood from the talismans,” Ptolemy listed and Mydei frowned. “…Phainon is not as far in the story as I thought.”

Phainon pulled up a dusty stool and sat down to begin again, continuing where he left off on their arrival in Okhema. This was where the story diverged so Phainon focused only on his side. He glossed over his encounter with Aglaea and then described the Trial. Some details he kept to himself, as Phainon had the first time he recounted what happened to the others. They didn’t need to know about his confession to the city, not when he still wanted to say those words to Mydei himself when the moment felt right.

Mydei kept his reactions muted as Phainon talked until the story reached the Council’s decision and then his knuckles turned white where they squeezed his crossed arms. There was fury in his eyes as Phainon described how he felt when Caenis rejected the Coreflame of Strife and with it any desire for peace between their nations. He saw Mydei’s body tremble with anger when he revealed the Council’s judgement and had sentenced him to death.

That’s when Phainon took the bag off his shoulder and opened it in his lap to show Mydei the Coreflame of Strife. It was bright and strong in his hands, the gold almost overpowering the purple crystal in the presence of its keeper. He held onto it still when Mydei didn’t reach for it, keeping it close like the gift it was. He told Mydei about the rescue and how they used the chance to not only recover Strife but to seize the coreflames that belonged to Hyacine and himself.

“Worldbearing,” Mydei repeated thoughtfully, “it suits you.”

Phainon blushed and looked away.

“It does, doesn’t it?” Hyacine teased.

“Then you are both demigods,” Mydei confirmed aloud.

“Yes.” Phainon put his hand to his chest. “I wanted… I wanted to wait, to take that step with you, to do what you did for me and offer my coreflame to you, but…”

Phainon looked up when Mydei’s hand gently brushed his knee. “You came for me, Phainon. That is everything. But your pardon-”

“I don’t need it. I’m not sure I even want it anymore. The people that mattered most to me still believe in me, are still here with me. I meant it when I told Okhema that I am a pirate.”

“And my people?” Mydei asked.

“I sent Cipher with a message. They no longer march towards Okhema for safety.”

“They’re strong Mydei,” Hephaestion reminded him, “they’ll make a place on the plains and wait until we return to them with glad tidings.”

“You said the Tide took over the Settlement,” Mydei recalled.

“We cleared it after we saved you,” Perdikkas filled in, answering the question hidden in the statement, “well, Phainon did.”

“After we left Okhema we went straight to Castrum Kremnos,” Phainon continued, “Hyacine and I-“ he looked over at her when he said her name and she smiled warmly, making the whole room feel sunny, “-we talked to Castorice a lot about becoming Demigods before we accepted them.”

Phainon remembered what it felt like to take that burning fire inside his chest. The comfort of candlelight had felt like wildfire when he accepted it, burning him alive until he couldn’t bear it. On the deck of the Leo, he had taken his new sword to his own body, clawing at his chest and belly, trying to rip the coreflame free while the crew backed away in terror. That first transformation had been made so much worse by his confused panic, by the blood thrown across the sails as it crystalized and ripped him apart, filling him with power too great to contain.

He remembered worrying that he wasn’t ready after all, that this was the end of him and then the breeze had caught his feathers, colors had felt all the brighter, the deck was far below him and everything had felt right. Castorice had compared him to a butterfly, finally achieving a form he was meant to be after the painful process of breaking apart inside a chrysalis. And then he had willed himself back to his prior appearance and she retracted her metaphor with an annoyed grumble.

Hyacine’s hadn’t been much better though she handled it with more grace than Phainon had. Where he had panicked, she calmly waited for the Coreflame of Sky to settle inside her. She had fallen to her knees on the deck, talking with soft reassurances to those who gathered around with concern while she cried purest, glittering blood. Her eyes had rolled wildly until she shakily removed them herself, speaking softly as though comforting a patient and not enduring this horror herself. The wild, multicolored eyes of Aquila had taken the place of her own, pulsating wildly, moving independently until Hyacine found herself, blinked, and it was as though nothing had happened.

Perdikkas had fussed over her more than he had Phainon, wiping her bloody tears away with his own handkerchief while Castorice apologized profusely for not predicting something so ghastly. But Hyacine waved them both away and tended to Phainon who was still whimpering like a child with his new wings and embarrassing, self-inflicted wounds.

“It was a lot,” he summed up and everyone in the room silently agreed that no more needed to be said right now on that topic. “Hyacine used her authority as the Sky to part the clouds for us and I hurried to meet you. The Professor was able to improve on the talismans. They did work the first time but after Nikador…”

“The Tide was strengthened,” Mydei remembered.

“Yes. Anaxa dipped each protective charm in Kephale’s blood-“ Mydei’s eyes narrowed but he didn’t interrupt to ask where they got that, “-and then sealed them in wax to give them another layer of protection. It was enough, and the crew were able to follow us into the acropolis.”

“Good thing too with the number of trips we needed,” Ptolemy grumbled, “no one is allowed to give me grief for my love of preservation again. That Professor is many times worse.”

Mydei tilted his head and Hephaestion laughed a little before saying, “Anaxagoras wanted as much of Eurypon’s writings as possible. Most of the crew were combing through records for anything with his handwriting on it and hauling it back to the ship.”

“There is nothing to be gained from the ramblings of a madman,” the Prince huffed.

“That… might not be entirely true, Mydei,” Phainon admitted, “Anaxa believes King Eurypon had learned things about the Black Tide and the coreflames that no one else had discovered during his campaign. He believes there is information there that can confirm his theory.”

“His theory?”

“That aggravating man will not discuss it yet,” Ptolemy huffed.

“He’s always been like that,” Hyacine said but it wasn’t reassuring.

“After we loaded the ship and unlocked the treasury we came here,” Phainon explained, “the Tide had retreated after our battle, farther back than before and we agreed this was the safest place for you until you came back to us.”

Hyacine scooted over closer to Mydei so she could press the back of her hand to his forehead, and he obediently held still. “You still look a little pale… the Tide still clings to you. Do you hear its song?”

“Yes,” Mydei admitted, “if I listen for it, it is there.”

“That settles it then, I’m prescribing you a bath,” she instructed.

“You better go with him, Phainon,” Perdikkas added, “doctor’s orders. There will be time to talk more later.”

-

The sturdy bathhouse had escaped the Tide’s assault but in the absence of a regular attendant the complex still suffered. It had taken a fair number of them to get a few of the pools cleaned enough to be worth bathing in and there was no hope for a boiling bath like the one that had nearly broken Phainon the first time they had brought him here. The memory made Mydei smile and blush at the same time, a foreign combo that made it hard to recognize himself in the mirror as he changed.

It took time to bounce back from death, Mydei knew that, but looking at himself now… He looked and felt frazzled, burdened, and still very, very tired. His eyes darted to watch Phainon in the mirror. The Deliverer still looked the same, but he felt warmer, more confident with that coreflame inside him. He kept his back to Mydei as he shrugged out of his clothing and set each piece aside in a cubby, reverently working around the Coreflame of Strife that he kept close. It wasn’t something Mydei had expected to ever see again, and it wasn’t something he wanted to think about just yet, but Phainon insisted on its presence, prepared to even bring it into the baths with them.

“Phainon,” he called, and the man looked up at him with bright, expectant eyes as blue as the sea that crashes against the shore. “Leave the Coreflame in here.”

“Do you not want it?”

“Not yet,” Mydei said softly and when Phainon’s expression morphed into one of longing, Mydei turned and pressed his palm to Phainon’s cheek to remind him, “must you hold it instead of me? Am I not enough?”

“Okay, okay,” Phainon chuckled, and he pulled away to tuck the coreflame in the cubby with his clothes, choosing the book instead. There was a tiny tug in Mydei’s chest when he did so, like a pull on a string around his heart, but it faded when Phainon smiled and Mydei was again so sure that the coreflame meant nothing compared to Phainon’s fire.

Mydei was patient and obedient when Phainon led him to the bath, passing other crewmates that were in a similar state of relaxation, towards a smaller, warm pool of water that shimmered brighter than the others. He paused at the edge and studied it with confusion while Phainon set towels, soap, and his book on a stool beside it. The Deliverer waded in when he was ready, but Mydei rejected Phainon’s offered hand when the man stepped inside first and reached for him.

“Mydei?” Phainon followed where Mydei was looking and then waded closer. “It’s okay. This is how we bathe in Okhema to cleanse the Tide.”

“HKS, my caution is not fear,” he huffed, defensively.

“I know, Mydeimos.”

Mydei waded into the water after Phainon and followed his lead to sit beside him, letting the water soak to his bones and ease the aches and pains that still lingered. Phainon snatched the soap first to wash himself and Mydei tried not to stare. Neither of them had bothered with towels or bath wear but Phainon still had that damn collar on. Maybe it was the coreflame inside him, but the sun mark on his neck glittered brighter than he remembered.

“You mentioned Kephale’s blood,” Mydei said after a moment and Phainon shook water from his face and hair, “is that what you added to the bath?”

“Yeah.”

Mydei caught Phainon’s arm below the elbow, holding him tight to see the fabric bandage that was wrapped around his wrist. He remembered seeing it last night too. “…only Kephale’s blood?”

Phainon pulled his arm free and immediately started to soap up Mydei’s hair to change the subject, making him growl. “Oh, don’t act like you don’t enjoy the attention,” he scolded and Mydei huffed, settling down with his back to Phainon.

The once Okheman hummed while he worked and Mydei listened in silence, letting him massage the grime and oils from his hair. Mydei could do it himself, but something about being doted on was nice and he was content to doze and soak while the floral smell of the soap added another layer to what was left of the Tide song that lingered in the back of his mind.

“I don’t want the coreflame,” Mydei said after what felt like a long time. Phainon’s fingers paused in Mydei’s hair. “I meant what I said, it’s not a power that I want for myself and my people.” He raised a hand to look at it, not sure what to expect and finding nothing out of the ordinary when he did. “There is an expectation there, akin to the crown.”

“The future you don’t want for them,” Phainon supplied.

“Yes.” Once again Mydei entertained the thought of crushing the crown underfoot, of leading his people the rest of the way to Okhema, to demand the end of the war so his people could find a life of plenty and peace safe from the Black Tide.

“And what if it was the best way to secure their futures?” Phainon wondered aloud. Mydei twisted his head to look over his shoulder and up at Phainon. “Okhema, Kremnos, all people’s of Amphoreus, there is no future for anyone if the Tide cannot be defeated. Aglaea always believed the coreflames were the secret to destroying the Tide, that’s why she pursued them so relentlessly. Now that I have one and have wielded it against that evil... I won’t make you take it Mydei but consider instead what good you could do as the Demigod of Strife, not as Strife became, but as what it was meant to be, the Titan that I have learned so much about on this ship.” Phainon chuckled a little to himself and teasingly tugged at Mydei’s hair. “We could be as Nikador and Kephale of old, the ones carved on the Leo, who were friends and comrades. Maybe Peucesta will write songs about us.”

“He already does,” Mydei grumbled and turned back around. He let Phainon resume washing his hair. Soapy water trickled from his temple down his cheek, a tickling sensation that made him curl his toes.

No man or woman born, coward or brave, can shun his destiny.

Phainon was right. Mydei had been looking for an answer, a way to protect his people, what better way to inspire change than to tear down the old Dynasty and show them what Strife needed to be, not what they wanted it to be.

“Then we will go after the Tide,” Mydei said firmly.

“Isn’t that my decision now?” Phainon teased and Mydei’s shoulders tightened. He slowly turned around to fix Phainon with what he hoped was a commanding glare but the man booped his nose and left behind a little cloud of suds that undermined his entire air of authority. “You did make me captain.”

“A temporary measure,” Mydei growled, “but if you would like to fight me for it, I will oblige.”

Phainon chuckled, “No, no, sir, the Leo is yours, of course. I was never more than a passenger after all.”

His frown deepened and Mydei wiped the soap from his nose and stood in the bath to look down at Phainon. The man leaned away, rightfully intimidated and doing a shockingly good job at keeping his eyes up as Mydei leaned over him to slip a finger under that collar. “A passenger? No, you are my prisoner, if I recall.”

Phainon smiled, cheeky and teasing with a tilt of his head that bordered on coy. “Oh, captain, you have died too many times. The Chryseus Leo doesn’t take prisoners, remember?”

Mydei snorted and rubbed his thumb over that sun marking on his neck. “Join my crew, Phainon of Castrum Kremnos,” he demanded, diving to the heart of the matter.

Phainon’s breath caught when Mydei spoke, he felt it under his fingertips and the subtle bob of his throat when he swallowed and finally said, “With all my heart, Mydeimos.”

“What did I say about sentimentality, Deliverer?”

“That you love it and want more of it in your life?”

“HKS. What a ridiculous puppy I have on my crew.” Mydei let him go, turned around and dropped heavily into the water up to his nose. Phainon’s hands followed, once again scrubbing at his hair. A few soapy bubbles floated by and they fell into a comfortable and quiet rhythm, relying on gentle taps and gestures to finish washing Mydei’s hair and face.

“Any better?” Phainon asked when Mydei resurfaced again after another rinse.

Mydei brushed the dripping hair from his eyes running his fingers through that mane to shake away the glittering water and any residual soap and then he paused to close his eyes and listen. The song was still there, faint but relentless. He sat along the edge of the pool in answer and settled in to soak a little longer.

Phainon flashed him a sympathetic look and climbed out of the bath. “Would it be alright if I practiced reading to you?” he asked as he wrapped a towel around his waist.

“I welcome it,” Mydei invited, “I can correct your horrible pronunciations.”

“Have mercy, Mydei,” Phainon whined, “I am improving!”

It was still Mydei’s favorite story, the same one that he had almost ruined with his notes in the margins, the same one that Phainon had clung to since the day Ptolemy had handed it to him in the library on the Chryseus Leo with its faded pages and missing corners. It was the story that Krateros would read to Mydei when he was sick, the one that Mydei would read after bad days. To know that Phainon loved it too was another special thing they shared.

Mydei closed his eyes and listened to Phainon struggle to tell of the hero as he began his voyage home and the trials he would have to face. He listened to the soundtrack of the Tide song as it blended with Phainon’s words as he read of the hero preparing for a particularly dangerous part of the journey with daring curiosity. In the story, the clever hero asks his men to tie him to the mast and fill their ears with wax as they sailed past a notorious stretch of ocean so he could listen to the…

Mydei’s eyes snapped open, and he turned in the bath with wide eyes to look at Phainon who immediately tripped over the rest of the sentence before he gave up and tilted his head in concern. “Mydei?”

With the notes of the next refrain playing in his ears, he firmly declared, “I know what the Tide is.”

Alternative chapter title: The Lion does not Concern Himself with Footwear

Mydei has a theory, Anaxa has opinions about that theory (like he does about everything), and there's some déjà vu.

Chapter Notes

Sorry for the delay on this one. The 3.7 livestream had me so stressed all weekend there was no chance of me writing.

“Mydei, think about it for more than a second!” Phainon insisted as he followed his captain down the road. The Kremnoan hadn’t appreciated Phainon’s skepticism and was now stomping through the city looking for Anaxa, still soaked from the bath, barefoot, with his hair unbraided and dripping. Thank Kephale that Mydei had at least wrapped his chiton around his waist on the way out of the bathhouse, but he was still mostly naked. Well, more naked than usual.

“I’m not saying you’re wrong, I just think maybe you should think it through before telling anyone else!”

Mydei continued to ignore him as Phainon pursued with one sandal untied on his foot and the other under his arm. He was still trying to get his bag in order after the hasty exit and constantly flexing his foot to keep the one piece of footwear doing its job without being left behind. Phainon had at least used a towel before throwing his clothes on in his hasty pursuit. Mydei’s chiton was so soaked it was almost see-through, and it clung to his ass and thighs, leaving nothing to the imagination. The man didn’t seem to care that everyone who stumbled on them could see the perfect curve of his muscles and how that fabric hung low enough to see where the bathwater still dripped down the small of his back…

Phainon slapped his own face and hurried to catch up with a series of awkward hops and hobbles.

“Look out!” someone shouted and Mydei bounced backward, narrowly avoiding an accident and crashing into Phainon who was now out of breath for two reasons.

A child-sized stone sphere crashed down the crossing road in front of them bouncing along with a happy dragon in pursuit. The whole ground shook when Pollux ran by and then it shook again when they returned with the ball in their mouth, delicately held between sharp teeth and that beak-like snoot. They paused to sniff in Mydei and Phainon’s direction and then wagged their tail and fluttered the long petals in their ruff when the recognition clicked behind those bright white eyes.

“Pollux!” Leonnius shouted and the runner came sliding down the road a second later. “What’s the hold up? Come on, buddy. Mydei, you’re awake! Phainon! …why are you wet?”

Phainon and Mydei leaned forward enough to peer around the buildings to look uphill where Castorice and Peucesta were waiting beside an unloaded catapult. Castorice waved when she saw them.

“Fetch?” Phainon asked and Pollux wiggled at the word and whined around the ball in their mouth.

“Yeah we were taking a break from assessing the state of the armory-”

“Anaxagoras.” Mydei demanded urgently.

Leonnius reached up to scratch at the scar over his brow while he thought aloud, “still on the Chryseus Leo, I think. I saw him head down there with Ptolemy earlier.”

Mydei didn’t wait, he ducked under Pollux’s belly and kept going in the straightest possible line towards the docks while the others watched. The dragon craned that long neck to watch Mydei upside down along the path he walked between Pollux’s legs.

“…Phainon?”

Phainon sighed and started after Mydei again, going around Pollux like a polite person should and still trying to get his bag situated while he hopped on one foot to put the remaining sandal on. “Mydei thinks he’s solved the riddle of the Tide,” he called over his shoulder in answer and then he was hopping away before elaborating.

“Damn it, Mydei, slow down!”

Mydei picked up speed, very nearly crashing into Perdikkas when he took a turn down another street. The doctor’s hands were full of little sealed packets inside a basket that barely fit under one arm.

“Mydeimos?” The doctor reached out to grab Mydei with his free hand on instinct but the Prince expertly dodged around and kept powerwalking away. “I guess he’s feeling better… Phainon?”

“Perdikkas,” Phainon greeted with a smile and a panting breath as he caught up to the second almost incident. He hopped in place and finished tying the second sandal, eager to pursue Mydei but trapped by good manners. “Raiding the storehouses?”

“Yeah, most of what we had we sent with the others… Are you chasing Mydei?”

“Yeah, Mydeimos is convinced he’s figured out what the Black Tide is,” Phainon sighed, “I really need to…” He gestured vaguely in the direction Mydei had run and then hurried after him. The truth was as good of a reason to end the conversation as any.

Any response was left behind in dust as Phainon ran to catch up. At least barefoot Mydei didn’t dare try to sprint or even run with all the debris, so it was easy to catch up.

“I’m serious, you can’t just storm in there half prepared! Anaxa will eat you alive!” Phainon insisted as they jogged along the pier to the shoddily repaired dock, functional was more important than pretty and it was not pretty. It was still partly in shambles from when Phainon had run away from the Black Tide Gryphon, but Mydei didn’t slow down at all.

“Let me at least help you draft a proper argument!”

Mydei stormed up the ramp onto the deck of the Chryseus Leo and finally paused his powerwalking to look around, searching for any sign of the professor. There were half a dozen crewmates at work washing the deck, checking the sails, and moving cargo under the diligent eye of Krateros. Those who noticed him looked up in shock at the prince, who was clearly on a mission, his chiton hanging low and tight around his hips, scanning over them with curious urgency.

“Maybe I can get you a shirt?” Phainon offered cheekily instead when he saw Krateros’ confused expression. He was predictably ignored.

That’s when everyone else caught up. He had been so focused on Mydei that Phainon hadn’t noticed the procession of people that were curious enough to tag along too until Perdikkas, Leonnius, Castorice, and Peucesta were bunched up on the ramp behind him with an upset Pollux trying to figure out how to get down the flimsy dock without breaking it. The dragon kept putting a paw down on the wood and then pulling back to whine when it creaked, leaving the excluded beast stranded on the shore.

“What are you all-” Phainon started but he didn’t finish.

“Anaxagoras!” Mydei called and something crashed in the galley. He immediately turned and resumed storming in that direction with a curious pack of people on his heels.

Phainon was not prepared for Mydei to see the state of his beloved kitchen just yet. Anaxa had a month to make it his own lab and any semblance of what it used to be was limited to the things Anaxa couldn’t move like the ovens and firepit. The pantry had been reorganized to make space for alchemical ingredients, the cubbies were full of jars of things that Phainon didn’t want to know about, and Mydei’s pots, pans, tools, and even his apron were hidden in the captain’s quarters to protect them from the purge.

He scrambled to get in front of Mydei at the top of the stairs. “Mydei, listen, you just woke up, it’s been a long morning already-”

Mydei physically picked up Phainon under the arms and set him to the side but before he could walk past, Phainon grabbed his arm and twisted it behind Mydei’s back to steer him the other way. Angry gold eyes peered over Mydei’s shoulder, fixing Phainon nervously in place.

“Do you really want to do this, Deliverer?” he asked, low and threatening.

“Come now, Mydeimos,” he chuckled, “you’re still recovering, it wouldn’t be much of a fight.”

Behind them Perdikkas leaned in close to Peucesta to whisper in his ear. The bard whispered back and then they were suddenly much more invested.

“Is this really the time?” Castorice asked.

“Is something wrong with the prince?” Krateros asked, still playing catch up.

“I’ll break them up,” Leonnius offered but Perdikkas was on him in an instant with an arm over his shoulder to stop him and Phainon couldn’t take the second to consider that or answer Krateros before Mydei’s elbow slammed into his temple.

He stumbled, dazed, and shook his head to clear the stars behind his eyes but Mydei gave him no opportunity to recover. The Kremnoan looped two fingers through Phainon’s collar and started pulling him along down the stairs by the neck and all Phainon’s remaining coordination belonged to the nearly impossible task of staying upright and not being strangled. He was still wheezing when Mydei half-led, half-dragged him into the galley proper, where he finally paused to take in the results of Anaxa’s labor.

The professor and Ptolemy had covered every surface of the kitchen with reading material from Eurypon’s study. Scrolls were shoved into the cold oven, maps were blanketing piles of tablets, and books were stacked haphazardly on the floor. Half of the preparation table was covered in glass bottles, vials, and flasks all shoved together to make space for more reading material. Loose sheets of paper of various ages were being held down by hoarded trinkets including a series of prototypes of the protective charms now reduced to paperweights.

Phainon watched Mydei like a hawk, anticipating the inevitable murder attempt but the man was handling himself suspiciously well. Any irritation that he harbored was neatly tucked away and didn’t show in his body language or on his face.

Ptolemy raked over the whole party piling in with his eyes. His hands were full of shards of a broken jar that he unceremoniously tossed in a waste bucket. “How was your bath?” he asked.

Mydei let go of Phainon’s collar and gave him a small shove, enough to get Phainon out of the way so he could state clearly and confidently to Anaxa’s back, “Siren. The Black Tide is a siren.”

Phainon slapped his own face. Ptolemy’s eyes narrowed. Behind them Peucesta gasped, the others stewed in puzzled silence.

Anaxa didn’t react right away. He was leaning over a pair of books and making notes in the margins with one hand while the other fidgeted with one of the improved, blood-soaked talismans. The red crystal inside kept making clunking noises as he pushed it around with a finger. It was the only sound for what felt like an unbearably long time as Mydei waited patiently, arms crossed across his chest, for Anaxa to say something.

Phainon hid his face in his hands, expecting the worst.

“I concur.”

“…what?” Phainon mumbled, breathy and shocked. Mydei flashed him a smug smirk. Perdikkas swore under his breath and passed Peucesta a couple coins.

Anaxa stood up straight and twisted in place so he could look at Mydei without straining his neck. His powder blue eye glanced briefly over Mydei’s state and took in the accumulated audience without a single change in facial expression.

“I’m with Phainon on this,” Leonnius chimed in, “sirens aren’t real.”

“The world is vast and much of it remains unknown,” Anaxa reasoned, “common truths told through stories and songs become sensationalized, eventually becoming legends but the truth does not stop existing as truth because humanity chose to treat it as a children’s tale.”

“’If any one unwarily draws in too close and hears the singing of the Sirens, his wife and children will never welcome him home again, for they sit in a green field and warble him to death with the sweetness of their song,’” Ptolemy quoted softly, mostly to himself. He had a look of concentration on his face like he was putting pieces together and wasn’t very happy about it.

“This is why I generally refrain from sharing my hypothesis until after I have enough proof to draw a satisfying conclusion,” Anaxa grumbled when he looked over everyone’s telling faces, “The Tide itself is not a siren, but there is an argument to be made that it is a siren’s song.”

“It is a desirable thing,” Peucesta mumbled, overwhelmed by the revelation, “even unto death.”

“I had plenty of time to listen to it,” Mydei explained, “I understand now the pull of it.”

Phainon frowned. He wanted to refute this theory but didn’t he just that morning wish he could pull the corruption from Mydei to take it for himself? He had wanted to hear the song again, however briefly. Peucesta had risked his life as a test subject when there was a chance of hearing it again and no one who had heard it and lived would argue against its sweetness.

“Do you still hear it?” Anaxa asked Mydei and the Kremnoan bowed his head and closed his eyes.

He waited a moment, listening, then confirmed, “I do, though it is faint.”

“Have you claimed your coreflame?”

“No.”

Anaxa hummed to himself and raised his hand to press the palm against his eyepatch, a gesture that Phainon remembered seeing a lot during his days at the Grove. “But you have bathed in the golden blood?”

“I have.”

“Twice,” Phainon added.

“Was I talking to you, Phainon of Aedes Elysiae?” Anaxa snapped, “rule number two!”

He peeped and involuntarily took a step back behind Mydei with a mumbled apology and Leonnius snickered until that discerning eye turned on him next and then Leonnius was also cowering behind Mydei to hide from the academic.

Perdikkas raised his hand and Anaxa, pleased, invited him to speak. “I thought that siren song was supposed to beckon men with personalized temptation. Everyone who has discussed the song with me have described the same thing.”

“The song that Peucesta plays is indeed the same song I heard when I entertained corruption in my self-imposed exile at the Grove,” Anaxa confirms, “it does not vary, but our understanding of sirens comes entirely from a myth that does not explicitly state that the sirens sing of personal wants, only that the song is beautiful, enchanting, and drives men to their deaths.”

Ptolemy cleared his throat to get Anaxa’s attention and waited for the Professor to acknowledge him before he added somewhat skeptically, “if we treat the story of the returning hero as fact, then the sirens of eld were confined to a single island, one that was easily passed with wax in one’s ears. That is nothing like the Tide.”

“I agree,” Anaxa said, “therein is one of the questions that needs to be answered. If this is the work of a Siren, then why is their song manifesting as the Black Tide? By what power could a song become a transformative, persistent horror?”

There was no power in this world that could do that, Phainon considered. It came crashing down at once and he hurriedly raised his hand and waited to be called on when he realized the only thing that could even come close was, “A coreflame.”

“A reasonable hypothesis,” Anaxa praised and Phainon preened under the praise. “But this is still rampant speculation, and a theory needs supporting evidence before a conclusion can be drawn.”

Mydei stepped around the walking hazards that waited in every corner and reasonable walkway in the room to get to the table where he peered over at what Anaxa was studying.

“…you’re looking at my father’s research into the corruption of Nikador,” he observed.

“I am. The answer to this riddle is not only in a bedtime story. It is also in the study of the most ancient powers on Amphoreus. Unfortunately, Eurypon’s hoarded works alone are not enough which is why our next stop is the Library of Garbaniphoro.”

The Kremnoans in the room winced and Phainon tilted his head. “The Kremnoan royal library? Isn’t that a part of Castrum Kremnos.”

“It used to be,” Mydei grimaced.

“Part of the building still is,” Ptolemy corrected, “a very, very small part of the royal collection that we may have picked clean when we visited five years ago.”

Mydei started scanning over the mess while he elaborated, “the library has always belonged to Kremnoans but was maintained by a conquered nation after the island separated.” He waded through the mess when he found what he was looking for: a map of the northern seas.

Phainon hadn’t forgotten about that piece of trivia from his youth. Castrum Kremnos, the fortress island, was famed in ancient days for being impossible to lay siege to because it moved. The island was not attached to the earth beneath dark waters after Nikador carved it from one of the northern continents after Georios rampaged across Amphoreus, sinking whole landmasses. The Castrum remained untethered for nearly a thousand years until half a millennia ago when a Kremnoan king used giant chains to bind the city to another, rooted island, where it remains today, the same chains Phainon had seen with his own eyes.

“The library didn’t sink into the ocean?” Phainon asked, “When Georios sank the mainlands during the War of the Titans?”

Mydei shook his head. “Krateros has been there.”

They all turned to look at the veteran who had been listening quietly as he tended to do during serious discussions.

“I have,” he confirmed, “but even before the Black Tide claimed the ruins, only one wing was left. Part of the library burned to the ground after an accident and what remains has not been tended to for nearly fifty years.”

“Aside from the Grove it is the oldest repository of knowledge in Amphoreus,” Anaxa said with crossed arms, “and the only one that may still hold records of the Northern Kingdom of Hyperborea.” When everyone blinked at him in confusion the professor sighed. “The Kremnoan Dynasty once divided the Kingdoms of the north and those of the south. The Grove, allied with Okhema, primarily hoarded knowledge that pertained to the southern sphere of influence, while information and studies of the north gathered in the Library of Garbaniphoro. As the Tide stems from the north, it is to our benefit to study the Kingdoms that once existed there.”

“Hyperborea fell roughly a thousand years ago,” Phainon thought aloud, “I can’t imagine much will have survived that long.”

Mydei tilted his head. “A thousand years ago? How did it fall?”

“Scholars have debated that topic for centuries,” Anaxa lamented.

Mydei shook the map out and laid it on top of the flattest surface he could find and checked the date twice before he started searching for the tiny island that housed the library. The map showed the advance of the Tide Line, but the captured island wasn’t the only thing Mydei was looking at.

“The Black Tide came from the north,” he observed and somehow pointing out the obvious was revelatory to everyone there except Anaxa, who mumbled about having just said that very same thing.

“Y’know,” Leonnius mused, “these maps are very outdated.”

“If for no other reason than to update them…” Ptolemy agreed.

“Captain?” Perdikkas asked. He was looking at Mydei, but Phainon still had to resist the urge to answer.

Mydei traced his finger along the northernmost edge of the map. It was mostly blank, colored in dark as lost territory, forever inaccessible due to the Tide. Phainon watched the man slowly form a fist with that same hand to lightly press his knuckles to a tiny island, very far away, surrounded by black. “We will go to the library when the crew are rested and the Chryseus Leo is restocked for a long journey.”

“Finally,” Anaxa purred, “some hope for answers.”

-

It felt like it was only yesterday the last time Mydei had participated in a send-off celebration, and for him it almost was. The feasting before they had left for Castrum Kremnos to retrieve the coreflame nearly drained the city’s stores. This one was far more humble and intimate, reminiscent of days spent relaxing in the evenings at sea, only instead of the deck of the Leo, they feasted in Mydei’s open home on the hill, drank what wines they could find, and told stories, dressed in their familiar finery once more.

Surrounded by the crew he cherished, Mydei listened to them regale him with tales of the moments he missed, not to make him feel poor for his absence, but to eagerly include him. Everything from the name of the new chimera that had stolen Fig Stew’s affections, the details of their daring debacle of a rescue, of Captain Hephaestion and First Mate Krateros, and the many complaints about the food they had been made to endure the last month. They even let Phainon show off his new sword with a tacky name.

They relentlessly teased Phainon, especially when rosy cheeks from too much drink fueled rough-housing and the former interim captain was thrown over the balcony railing to cheers and toasts when Mydei announced the most excellent news of Phainon the Pirate’s official debut as crew. He had rejoined Mydei’s side with leaves in his hair, a scratch on his face, and the biggest grin.

“Shall I make him my first mate?” Mydei had teased when he took a moment away from the festivities to share a break with Hephaestion.

“That was only if I died, Mydeimos,” he laughed.

“If I should be so lucky.”

“Alas, I had orders not to.”

Mydei bumped Hephaestion with his knee. “I will not make that mistake twice.”

“Titans above you better not.” They laughed and then Hephaestion leaned forward over the balcony railing, breathing deep of the cool air of Curtain-Fall Hour before saying, “Phainon told me to leave him in Okhema, I’m sure he told you.”

Mydei grunted in confirmation.

“After we saved him, Phainon asked me if he made the right choice leaving you, since in my limited time as captain I chose to disobey him when he gave me the same order you gave to him.”

“Circumstances were different. You made the right choice, so did he.”

Hephaestion laughed softly and put a hand on Mydei’s shoulder. The man felt so much frailer and older now. The chlamys over his shoulder barely covered the scar on his chest but even with these shallow breaths, Hephaestion was full of mirth when he responded, relieved, “that is exactly what I told him. Come, we must toast to victory, the one we have achieved and the one yet to come.”

“We must,” Mydei agreed, and they both went back inside.

As promised in Mydei’s remarks before they went to battle, every crewmate toasted their victory over the Coreflame of Strife while it flickered on bold display in the middle of the table, glowing brightly in the presence of its master and practitioners. They toasted the Chrysos Heirs, honorary crewmates on the eve of another voyage, who raised their own glasses with equal fervor. They toasted those that had gone to that great blade in the sky, and to those that remained on distant shores.

They danced and laughed until the hour was late and those noble men and women departed to bathe, rest, and prepare themselves for the morrow until it was quiet aside from the strum of Peucesta’s lyre, revisiting the Tide song on the balcony and Phainon, who listened in quiet contemplation.

Mydei listened and watched them with a pleasant sense of déjà vu and quiet resolve.

He quietly set down his cup on the table between now empty plates and listened to Peucesta play in time with the song that still lingered in the back of his mind. A siren’s song. He was sure of it. Mydei had listened to that song the entire time he had been dying, a month of listening to sad sentiments, the longing of something deeply, profoundly alone and desperate. And he sympathized even as his muscles twitched and ached at the memory of death with such familiar honey in his ears.

Mydei let the world settle until the song began to repeat and then he accepted that it was time for action. He stood up and cracked his neck and stretched his arms. It just felt right to be back in his familiar clothes, armor, and jewelry, like he was himself again, the regal lion that his people considered him to be.

With the time for hesitation behind him, Mydei reached for the Coreflame of Strife. A cornered Leonnius had spilled the details of Phainon and Hyacine’s ascensions and Mydei expected such brutality from Strife. He had no desire to take this thing into himself here surrounded by sleeping crew. Instead, he tucked it back inside its bag and slung it over his shoulder.

“Phainon,” he whispered as he approached, and the man moved as though the word had roused him from sleep. He dreamily turned to Mydei with those sparkling eyes, blue as day against the moonlight glow of his hair in the dark. Phainon’s smile wavered when he saw the bag over Mydei’s shoulder.

“Mydei?”

“Come with me.”

When they ran through the jungle paths, behind the waterfall, along the cliff, and under trees the same size as they were for the second time it was the spirit of competition. Phainon now knew the way and raced Mydei at every step, pushing him to be faster and stronger, to consider the boundary that he once reached for and to push through it entirely.

They broke through the tree line and this time it was Phainon who walked ahead across the smooth stone where they had once fought. He walked with confident strides and broad shoulders and Mydei looked at that man’s back with adoration.

“Are you ready then?” Phainon asked over the crash of waves that showered them in fine mist.

Mydei walked closer, stopping several paces away to take the bag from his shoulder and reach for the coreflame within.

“I stand by what I said, Deliverer,” Mydei told him as he tossed the bag to the side and held the coreflame aloft. It shone in the night like a bonfire, bright and desirable. “You are enough to fill the space that this power left.” Phainon’s head tilted ever so slightly, and he put a hand on his hip. Mydei’s heart lurched at that smile. “But it fills me with indescribable anticipation when I think of meeting you in our full glory as Demigods.”

Phainon’s eyes flashed gold, the symbol of a sun inside the blue until none was left except the bright of burning flares and when he spoke it was strained with barely contained excitement. “I can think of no better way, Mydeimos, for two warriors to share in this moment, than to clash with all our power.”

The shiver that raced through Mydei forced his toothy grin. It lit his blood on fire before the coreflame had even touched his skin and he felt in his bones the same eagerness that Phainon was struggling to hide. There were beasts inside them thrashing at their cages, desperate for release to run, not to flee, but because they were free. That bloodlust that boiled in Mydei was not a desire to kill it was a desperate need for this man before him, to feel as they had the first day they stood across from each other, to feel as they had again here on this very shore. He wanted that thrill of meeting his match, of fighting until he collapsed, spent, and content knowing that his partner felt the same way after giving their all in return.

Mydeimos was ready to stand as equals beside this fellow Chrysos Heir to confront all the Black Tides of this world, unstoppable, indefatigable, and infinite. Strife and Worldbearing once again standing as allies, as friends, as lovers to be the envy of all other gods.

With Phainon watching, waiting, he made his choice to wield the fury of man to seize the authority of Titans.

Mydei pressed the Coreflame of Strife to his chest.

The agony was instant and unlike anything he had felt before. This was the pain of a thousand deaths compounded into a full body torture that dropped Mydei to his knees, fingers curled into claws as he fought the urge to rip the coreflame free as his insides twisted and burned. Something was crawling inside him, crushing his bones like kindling and remaking him from within. Crystal grew in his muscles and sinew, cutting through his body as they pushed through his skin.

Mydei’s teeth clenched tight, he had stopped breathing, and his voice broke when his pained grunts and groans gave way to a scream that he could not contain. He threw his head back as facets sprouted across his whole body, keeping his hands from closing into fists, tearing though his flesh to add gold to the salty sea spray.

Growling around each ragged, desperate swallow, Mydei tried to flex and felt the crystals respond, power surged through his blood. Light rippled through his tattoos, and he heard the voice of Strife roaring inside him like an uncaged lion. Those claws tore at the inside of his ribs and bit his heart until he just… let go.

Mydei stopped fighting it and instead he listened, embracing those calls of conflict that screamed over the lingering Tide song, and let the lion loose. He roared himself and shattered the crystals in his palms so he could close his fists and toss an arm to the side to guide those shards where he commanded, letting them erupt around him and not from within him. Still the beast inside fought until more than just the familiar red was bursting forth. Something long and horrible was ripping from his back, he had no hope of standing with the crunch coming from his legs, and still that lion ate his insides.

He didn’t know how long it took for that first transformation to run its course, nor could Mydei point to the moment when the pain turned into something more pleasurable, becoming instead a buoying power that made him sing. But he came to himself again with Phainon’s hand on his shoulder and those familiar wings curled around them.

Phainon’s Titan form was simply himself with a breaking, burned body, golden eyes, hair dyed blonde by the purity of his power. He had a long train from skintight robes, like twin battlefield banners frayed and torn at the ends, the same dark blue color as his left wing. A sun shaped halo floated behind his head, and shards of golden bismuth broke through the flesh of his right shoulder. He was radiance incarnate on his knees to comfort Mydei who was still struggling to even process what he was feeling.

He had expected the pain of taking his coreflame, especially as the Inheritor of Strife, suffering was simply a part of the package. What he didn’t expect was for his divine form to differ from that of the former Titan.

“Trianne said that coreflames grant wishes,” Phainon said gently as though he could read Mydei’s thoughts, “maybe Strife knew, that you wanted to be different than Nikador.”

His body was still mostly the same from the waist up. Mydei was still himself, tattoos and all, though his hair was longer, wilder, untamed, and his ears had changed, round and fuzzy. They twisted to hang on Phainon’s every word.

It was the waist down that was so different. Mydei’s bottom half had been replaced with a lion’s body like the centaurs of old myths and heroic stories but with paws instead of hooves and blood-red fur streaked with golden marks akin to his tattoos instead of the sorrel of horses. Golden armor adorned the lion’s back and front paws, glimmering gold fabric blanketed his flank with the shining symbol of strife, and behind him hovered metallic wings with feathers like blades, waiting, detached from his shoulders.

Phainon gently cradled Mydei’s face in his burning hands and Mydei realized how hard he was panting in the silence left behind by the silenced song. One of Phainon’s thumbs brushed under Mydei’s eye, tracing a shape so deliberately that it must be a new marking on his skin. Phainon followed it with the pad of his thumb under Mydei’s left eye from his nose to his temple and then back again along his cheekbone. The other thumb pressed between his lips to feel the fangs there with genuine curiosity.

Mydei licked Phainon’s thumb until it retreated and then he took a few deep breaths. The coreflame inside his heart stirred, excited, filling him with an unexpected fullness, of knowing that here, in this moment he was complete.

“Take your time,” Phainon said as he pulled back to give Mydei space, but the Kremnoan reached for him and caught his hand, holding tightly until Phainon pulled Mydei to his feet, all four of them.

The sensation was insane, not only was he feeling his new limbs, but Mydei’s senses had expanded. He could almost smell Phainon’s impatience, his longing to fight, even if it didn’t show on the worldbearer’s face. He could sense the sharks in the water looking for food, feel the predators of the forest as they hunted by moonlight in the purest form of violence. Mydei’s awareness and understanding of the world around him was accompanied with a newfound clarity that was too much to unpack right now.

He shifted on his paws, flicking water from one of them as the fur soaked up the moisture. There was a glow about him, the red of his fur, the bright gold of his claws, even his tattoos on his arms and chest glowed red and shimmered like sunlight. He twisted at the waist to inspect himself, to feel along the back of the lion body and shudder as he felt it. Another shiver traveled from his tail to his head when Phainon teasingly grabbed onto his wing. Even detached he felt the touch that made his fur stand on end and he growled a proper growl before swiping at Phainon.

Crystal erupted from the ground to chase the arc of his swipe, but Phainon hovered out of range to dodge the attack and slowly floated down to sit on the peak of those facets with one knee pulled up so he could rest his elbow upon it. His cheek rested in his hand as he peered down at Mydei, as casually as though it were any other day on the ship and Phainon were teasing him from the shrouds. That cute smile and squished cheek, and the mirth in gold eyes were a comfort, a reminder that they were still the same inside, no matter what may have changed with their newfound divinity.

“You know I’ve been meaning to ask,” Phainon crooned, “where did your crystal powers come from?”

“Not every question has an answer,” Mydei responded. His voice was raw and hoarse with a permanent growl.

“Don’t let Professor Anaxa hear you say that.”

Mydei walked forward, relieved to find that he was not as helpless as a newborn, that the coreflame came with the instinct to know his new form as though he were always this way, as though this familiarity was a reunion and not a first meeting. His front paws climbed the crystal to raise him up to eye level with Phainon who kept smiling and watching until they were nose to nose and Mydei was reaching for him.

Phainon waited patiently while Mydei’s fingertips felt the cracks in his ashen skin, the sharp points of the collar that rested heavily against his collarbone. He traced the open gashes across Phainon’s chest, and his fingers came away gold with blood that didn’t spill naturally from those wounds that would never heal. He left bloody fingerprints on Phainon’s cheek as he gently pressed that tender flesh, feeling the heat of him like a burning sun, a seraph trapped between the giant paws of a predator.

“How do you feel?” Phainon asked, light, teasing.

“My bones have turned into steel, and my blood is seething and ablaze. There is a tempest within me, like I could fight a thousand years and not fall.”

Phainon’s wings vibrated when he shuddered at the thought. “How about we start with just tonight, Strife?”

“At your ready, Worldbearer.”

Chapter End Notes

I am a huge fan of biblically accurate Mydei with Nikador’s body and arms but I am also a fan of lion-taur Mydei and for the context of the fic it made more sense to go that route. I apologize if that is not the image of Strife some of you were expecting.

Did Mydei have his crystal attacks in the game BEFORE the Trial of Strife? I can’t believe it just occurred to me that his crystals are not an inherent ability.

chapters.title: Chapter 41: The Actions Louder than Our Words
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

New tag: Implied Sexual Content

The boys have a "talk" and the crew arrives at the Library of Garbaniphoro

Chapter Notes

It's not writer's block, it's writer's perfectionism I swear. I'm taking these last chapters a bit slower because I want to be so careful to not miss any of the loose ends that I have left as we're now working towards the culmination of the plot. Also all the 3.7 stuff has me laying facedown in a ditch sobbing. They better be okay I swear to Kephale.

Phainon had expected Mydei’s transformation to be magnificent but what his crush became exceeded all his wildest expectations. Mydei’s presence was weighted. Light bent around him like the shimmer of a mirage on a hot day carrying that call to arms and surge of adrenaline that Phainon had felt from Nikador. He was so different and yet wholly familiar, like this was just what Mydei had always been on the inside and finally everyone who beheld his glory could see what he was meant to be.

But the pure honesty of what they were, Phainon felt most when they clashed. When Mydei’s summoned lance met Phainon’s transformed Dawnmaker, the shockwaves tore the leaves from the trees along the beach and pushed back the ocean. When Phainon retreated to the skies and Mydei followed with those beautiful wings spread wide, the clouds parted.

Where Phainon had two wings, Mydei had six. They unfolded like a Titankin construct when Mydei had leaped into the sky. Each wing was stiff and metallic, detached from the sphere that centralized them. The sphere itself hovered behind the small of Mydei’s back, in the curve of where the lion and man met. On the ground they crossed over the lion body, folded neatly aside from the topmost pair that had extended above him like a crown. Now as Mydei climbed into the sky to meet Phainon in the air they lined up along his body at intervals, reaching out like sunbeams in different directions to effortlessly carry his weight.

Every clash of claws on steel, every time their wings collided in a shower of sparks, light erupted and rippled through the vibrations. They chased each other as high as the clouds and then back to the island to shatter stone while the ocean churned and rolled. They were a maelstrom in motion, every wingbeat stirring distant tsunamis, and every meeting of blades shook the firmament with thunder.

Phainon barely noticed the effect of their divinity on lesser things. Nature meant nothing to them like this, locked in glorious combat not for rage but for joy. The grin on Mydei’s face no doubt mirrored Phainon’s own, minus those sharp, elongated canines. Every time they clashed and leaned in close, Phainon could see the shimmer of the new gold tattoos alongside the familiar red ones, feel his breath and the rumbling purr in his chest, and be mesmerized by the eager ferality in his unchanged eyes.

He'd be happy to fight like this forever. He’d also be happy resting on top of that soft fur, playing with Mydei’s fuzzy ears, and massaging those adorable and dangerous paws. Or even just holding Mydei in his arms as they used to be, changed back to human, Phainon didn’t care as long it was Mydei, his Mydeimos.

They were so engrossed in their sparring that Phainon was genuinely angry when Pollux pounced on Mydei to drag him back to earth. The dragon was like one of Anaxa’s projectiles hurtling through the sky to knock them out of it and Mydei was no less pleased. He shouted at Pollux the whole way down, paws flailing and kicking at the dragon’s side. Phainon hurried to help, caught up in the excitement of a foe they could fight together but a tornado erupted around him, catching his wings like sails in a storm and throwing him out over the ocean.

He dashed back, skimming the surface of the water to leave a rising wake. Little Ica swirled at him again, but Phainon grinned at the challenge and rolled out of the way, testing the limits of his agility in the air, until he was able to jump on Pollux’s back to pull at the dragon’s ruff. The night sky turned to day above them, a spotlight that made the three warring divinities freeze when the light turned scorchingly bright. It defused the tension enough to allow rational thought to creep along the edges of Phainon’s war-addled mind.

“Are you done now?” Hyacine asked with a sleepy huff.

Phainon held a hand up against his brow to block the light and he still had to squint to see Hyacine’s glowing Eye of Twilight watching them from the dark beyond this pocket of daytime she had so casually opened. She and Castorice were still in their sleepwear. They both looked annoyed.

“Thank you, Miss Hyacine, Miss Castorice,” Leonnius grumbled behind them.

Pollux bucked beneath Phainon, sending him bouncing along the beach where he lay face up for a second to let the bloodlust settle around his racing heart. The spotlight turned off and Mydei shoved Pollux away with both his hands and front paws so he could get up and stretch. His wings folded up behind him.

“Y’know, I think I would appreciate how cool you look way more Mydei if you didn’t just almost sink the island,” Leonnius complained.

“Stretching new muscles, Lord Mydei?” Castorice asked.

Mydei’s lion rump sat down with a whump and he expertly spun his spear around his body until it settled on his shoulders with his wrists draped across the shaft. “Yeah.”

Phainon slowly floated back over, hovering beside Mydei just enough to be taller. He really did try to smile apologetically but it must not have been very convincing.

Hyacine closed her eyes, pressed her hands together as though in prayer, and took a very deep breath. She held it until Little Ica sat on top of her head and then she fixed Mydei and Phainon in a stare that sent chills through their veins. Both of her eyes were wide with neon ripples, hypnotic and very disappointed.

“I know you’re excited but you both should be more aware of the damage you have caused,” she scolded. Mydei scoffed but when he unsummoned his lance in a flash of light, crossed his arms, and looked down, it was with a modicum of genuine shame.

Phainon let go of his sword and it too dissolved in light. He scratched at his cheek, embarrassed, and looked around at the ruined beach. The now naked tree line was leaning away from the ocean instead of reaching for it, sand had been blasted away into new dunes, and the stone shore was cracked and broken. The landscape had been changed at a fundamental level in that short spar.

“Is everyone okay?” he asked sheepishly.

“No one is hurt,” Leonnius reassured them, “but everyone is definitely awake now.”

Phainon wilted under those accusatory gazes.

Mydei sighed. “We will personally apologize to all those who were left awestruck by our formidable presence.”

“Maybe don’t word it like that to them when you do, Lord Mydei,” Castorice advised.

Pollux barked in agreement.

-

The Chryseus Leo departed with the receding tide, leaving behind the bones of the settlement and packed full of supplies for a long voyage. The crew had started grumpy and stayed grumpy after Mydei’s apology but after a few Entry Hours of sailing, the familiarity of hard work aboard the ship they loved put everyone back into good moods.

Mydei was captain again, Phainon was just one of the guys, Anaxa had begrudgingly given up the kitchen at mealtimes, and things were ‘normal.’ Or at least as normal as possible with five Demigods on board a ship sailing north to places untouched by man in twenty plus years.

There were subtle changes too, nothing bad, just different. Mydei could see them from his favorite spot at the railing. Fig Stew was with his new chimera best friend, showing Beagle how to work off that lavish lifestyle he had left behind. Vigethos’ belly was all but gone with hard work and Mydei’s Kremnoan discipline.

Hyacine and Perdikkas were assessing bandages in the warm sunlight and ocean breeze. Every once in a while they’d laugh, and the sound would carry to Mydei’s ears. Anaxa was discussing something with Hephaestion near the entrance to the galley. The other day Mydei had seen Castorice in the shrouds helping Leonnius. He had barely recognized her wearing pants and not her favorite lavender dress.

But mostly he watched Phainon. The man was standing at the railing port-side near the bow with Krateros, sketching their ideas for new carvings with charcoal, dressed for hard work. Mydei liked Phainon’s regal coat, armor, and cape, but he liked this version of Phainon too. The version that was simple, focused only on the task ahead of him with his whole heart, humble and pure, unchanged by the divine weight of his holy authority. This version was stripped down to just his boots, pants, and his favorite shirt that cut low down his chest and barely hid the black choker he always wore. He had insisted it was part of his “signature look” and Mydei was forced to agree when Phainon took it off for a day and it threw off the whole crew.

Ptolemy slapped him with a rolled-up scroll. “Mydeimos, are you listening at all?”

“Hm,” he grunted and leaned more of his weight on his arms on the rail.

“What did I just say?”

“You were requesting stew for dinner.”

“I was trying to show you the change in the Tide Line,” Ptolemy whined.

Mydei sighed. It had become harder to focus during peaceful days like this. Even in his human form, Mydei could feel the lion inside him getting drowsy in the warm sunlight and the peace of being surrounded by friends. Strife longed for combat, but combat with purpose meant enjoying the moments worth fighting for in the first place, especially the simple things like naps. Something to live for as Perdikkas would say.

“Show me,” he ordered, and Ptolemy unfurled the scroll again.

“We saw the Tide retreat after we saved you, but this is… Hyacine says it’s possible the library is no longer in Tide territory,” Ptolemy was saying, “the victory at Castrum Kremnos might have set the Tide back almost a hundred years, she won’t be able to see for sure until we’re a little closer… Mydeimos.”

“Hm?”

“Stop looking at your boyfriend for more than a minute please, captain.”

Mydei’s eyes snapped back to Ptolemy. “He is not my boyfriend.”

“You haven’t talked about it yet?” The bookworm looked unimpressed.

“It has not come up.”

“’No god could make a finer looking fellow than you are, but you are a fool,’” Ptolemy deadpanned, “have you at least fu-hmph!”

Mydei slapped his hand over Ptolemy’s mouth roughly. “No, and it is not any of your business should we choose to! I don’t care how much money you have put on the topic of my love life.”

Ptolemy bonked Mydei on the head again with the rolled-up scroll and then pulled away with the toss of his head. “We just want you to be happy, Mydei.”

“I am and he already knows that I love him. I am… waiting for him to say it.”

Mydei turned back to the railing to rest his elbows on the polished wood and leaned over. A hand settled roughly on his back with a light slap and then Ptolemy asked gently, “would you like me to kill him for you?”

Mydei snorted, a quick and simple laugh, “there is no need. If he takes too long, I will wring the words from him myself.”

“And how long is too long, Mydeimos?”

He didn’t respond right away. “I am sure I will know.”

-

“Have you told the young prince how you feel?” Krateros asked and Phainon’s knife hand slipped, very nearly ruining the scene he had been working on all Entry Hour. Fortunately, the curl of carved wood that fell to the deck was thin and the cut shallow.

“W-Where did that come from?” Phainon stammered.

“You have done nothing but recommend stories from Prince Mydeimos’ life for these reliefs,” the old man accused.

“That’s not true.” He pointed to where Krateros had sketched out Fig Stew and then Krateros put his finger above Phainon’s to point to the Mydei sketch holding that very same charcoal chimera.

“It is no secret that you two have grown close,” Krateros reminded him.

“…yeah,” Phainon relented. He turned around and went back to carving, digging firmly and confidently against the wood so the strokes would cut cleanly. Every swipe was slowly outlining Mydei’s Titan form.

“Is it something you have discussed with him?”

“Not really.”

Not since the night Mydei woke up again and kissed Phainon like he was life itself. Fighting on the beach had felt like a discussion… They hadn’t found the time to revisit that passion since setting sail. Between their duties and the threat of the Tide, Phainon wasn’t sure if it was still on Mydei’s mind at all and there certainly hadn’t been a ‘right time’ to confess his love for Mydei.
