The captain already knew that Phainon loved him, he didn’t need to say it out loud yet.

Krateros grumbled, disapproving. “Cowardice does not befit a son of Kremnos nor a god.”

His knife slipped again, nearly cutting off Mydei’s tail. “I am no coward! …I just want the moment to feel right.”

Phainon waited for Krateros to scold him, but it didn’t come. Worried the old man had simply left him entirely, Phainon looked up and over his shoulder to see Krateros still standing there, already back to work.

“…Aren’t you going to yell at me?”

He didn’t even look over. “I know a lost cause when I hear it.”

“You’re not going to give me advice?”

“Do I look like your parent?”

Phainon bit back the urge to call Krateros his grandparent and said instead, “I expected you to say something like ‘the battlefield is dangerous, and you never know when the last chance you have to say it has passed!’” Phainon’s old man voice was comically horrible, an unintended mockery. “Or ‘Mydeimos doesn’t care if it’s romantic or perfect he just wants to be with you so stop delaying your own happiness especially before the most important battle of our lifetimes!’”

Phainon paused to listen to his own words for a second and then he stood up and handed the carving knife to Krateros. “Thank you, Krateros.”

-

Mydei was just starting to send Ptolemy on his way when Phainon came up the stairs, white hair bouncing on every step except for where sticky sweat held it to his forehead. He smelled like hard work and wood shavings.

“Captain Mydeimos?” Phainon asked, “Do you have a minute?”

“What is it, Deliverer?”

Phainon smiled from ear to ear, his eyes flashed gold and then back to sapphire, and he said firmly and happily, “I love you.”

Mydei was so startled by the earnest and beloved declaration that he almost transformed. The coreflame and his heart were dancing and high-fiving and whatever else was causing that ridiculous overflowing feeling while he stood there with his arms crossed blinking at that beautiful smile that rivaled the brightness of the sun. His jaw dropped, ready to say it back, to say anything.

“Get fucked, Perdikkas!” Ptolemy shouted over the railing in Kremnoan, down to the main deck with a loud, celebratory whoop! “You and that string strummer owe me 20 each!”

The blood rushed to Mydei’s cheeks and colored his ears and chest. Endearing. His crew were endearing, really, but holy fuck they could not read the room sometimes.

Mydei threw Ptolemy over the rail to the deck below with a yelp and a crash, fuming for all of a second before he was turning back to Phainon to grab the front of that handsome man’s clothes, pulling him in tight to kiss him. He didn’t care that the crew’s attention was on them now, he really didn’t. The rest of the world faded away for that kiss, especially when Phainon held onto his wrists and pressed back with equal passion.

“I love you too, Phainon of the Chryseus Leo,” Mydei said when they pulled away and then he gave the man a playful shove. “Now get back to work before the ship falls apart without you.”

“Aye, captain,” Phainon teased with a salute, “permission to call you my boyfriend, captain?”

Mydei crossed his arms to hold his racing heart back. They’d have to talk about this later for sure…no, no more later, they had enough later. “Permission granted… would you like to speak more of it? Perhaps tonight over food?”

Phainon was almost wiggling he was so happy, Mydei could see it in the way his hand trembled and in his adorably awkward fidgeting when he reached up to scratch his face and then his hair like he did when he was particularly nervous or apologetic. “Would you like me to cook?” he asked.

Mydei’s smile immediately dropped. “No.”

-

Phainon spent the rest of his day in a state of eager bliss. He finished his chores, finished Hephaestion’s chores, and then he worked on the railings until the smell of good food called the crew to eat on the heels of two very happy, full-bellied chimeras. He wiped the oil from his hands and wandered towards the galley, but Mydeimos called him from the upper deck and Phainon answered without question.

Finally, alone in their room to discuss the culmination of yearning, the food was left forgotten on the table. There were so many better uses for their mouths right now. As Ptolemy and Hephaestion had once said, they were men of action, not words, though a few managed to slip out between heavy breaths and pants. Each one was a desperate prayer, a whispered name, a song on swollen lips longing for each other.

Mydei smelled like fresh bread and olive oil. The scent clung to his soft skin and Phainon could taste it when he dragged his tongue over hardened muscle. It lingered on his lips when they kissed and was all encompassing when they embraced.

He was soft skin and taut muscle, the kind of sculpture that the gods had made to tempt lesser men. Mydeimos was perfection incarnate in every heated touch, every soft gasp, and eager growl, a beauty that men longed for, that Phainon was humbled to even know, nevermind be given permission to touch with such intimacy.

They reached for each other with unbridled urgency that broke the first hammock in a matter of minutes and the second followed not long after. Neither of them could be bothered to care, the world had shrunk to only them, no other name on their lips, no other thought than the realization of desperation.

-

Mydei had spent the Action Hour remembering what it was like to live in a kitchen again. He happily did his job cooking for the crew and then he spent his time making a proper meal for himself and his boyfriend. Something with love and care that ultimately didn’t matter because when they met in their room that night, alone, to discuss this budding relationship, the food was left forgotten on the table.

Phainon smelled like carpentry, resin, and sweat, warm like a sunbeam. He tasted like salt and was rough along the edges like a man tempered by a hard work, but Mydei didn’t want him any other way. He was honest in a way that Mydei admired, humility honed into something boyishly handsome. Phainon was proof of overcoming adversity, of humble origins ascended to something angelic and selfless.

Every touch, every kiss, pulled sweet hymns from Phainon’s lips, even when their antics chased them to the rough ground it felt fitting in a way. They didn’t need a palace, though Mydei would give him the world if he could. They didn’t need any pomp and circumstance; there was nothing proper about this moment between warriors.

This was honest and true and entirely them. Even if he hadn’t expected this when he set those plates down on the table, still waiting, undoubtedly cold, now that Mydei rested with Phainon wrapped around him, he couldn’t imagine how a conversation would have even gone.

Phainon’s heart was still racing against Mydei’s chest. His own was pressed up close against his ribs to reach for its other half. He could still hear it when Phainon pulled away to lean over Mydei for another gentle, and chaste kiss.

Ever the wordsmith, Phainon said softly, “I love you.”

“I love you,” Mydei repeated, and that was all the conversation they needed.

-

With fair winds and suspiciously clear waters, the Chryseus Leo’s voyage to the Library of Garbaniphoro was almost a pleasure cruise with plenty of free time for the crew to weaponize their boredom into ridiculous schemes and competitions. Many of Phainon’s prior commitments were still ongoing but he made a point to participate in every proposal and contributed his own ideas at every opportunity.

He was still meeting with Perdikkas weekly and was surprised and relieved to see that Mydei was too, taking his own private sessions with the doctor to work through difficult memories.

Phainon still practiced his Kremnoan and was now passably able to speak to every crewmate in his heavy Okheman accent. He knew the story of the wandering hero by heart and was on his fifth readthrough, this time out loud with Mydeimos before bed. They had given up trying to repair the hammocks and concluded they simply were too heavy combined to share one and had rearranged the room to use the originally designed bed space as an actual bed and not shelving.

Phainon still sparred with Mydei in the Entry Hour and trained with Krateros in Parting Hour. He still fished with Leonnius once a week and helped Peucesta and Hephaestion polish and care for the ship. The only thing he ended up dropping from his schedule was lyre lessons from Peucesta and after he found the bard teaching Castorice and Hyacine how to play and harmonize, he didn’t feel particularly bad about that.

The other Demigods had already felt like part of the crew before they left but if there was any doubt remaining, that was gone now. Hyacine and Perdikkas now had hidden code words between them to complain politely about their patients. Peucesta and Castorice were harmonizing old Styxian folk lullabies in their sleep much to the chagrin of the rest of the crew. Anaxa and Krateros kept getting into stubborn yelling matches that they repeatedly insisted was all in good fun and held more structured debates with Ptolemy when the Kremnoan scholar wasn’t beta reading Castorice’s latest works or recording the Leo’s history.

It was the family that Phainon wanted to take on the world beside and that chance was literally on the horizon.

The Library of Garbaniphoro was a relic of ancient times, more so than Castrum Kremnos had been. From the ship it looked mostly intact perched high on the cliffs, but then the wind pushed the Leo around her side, and the collapsed wing of the library was a more accurate advertisement of her state of disrepair. Phainon did not care in the slightest. The main building was still standing strong and besides, the older and more rundown the better. He loved old things, old ruins, old artifacts, there was a history that spoke from the dust when open-minded explorers sought out those voices.

Centuries had not taken from her the elegance of ancient Kremnoan architecture, the strength to withstand, even as whole buildings crumbled around her down the cliffside, her façade still stood resolute. The cliff itself was as described in legend, as straight as though it had been cut and as steep as though that cut had come at the hand of the master. The most ancient parts of Castrum Kremnos still rested in the water, the tops and bottoms of buildings long worn into facsimiles of their former glory stuck on the shoals. Time had not been kind but tall pillars, covered in moss, barnacles, and other sea life still stood like spires protecting the knowledge of eons.

“…because you need me to navigate the shelves!” Ptolemy insisted as he followed Mydei across the deck. The captain stopped next to Phainon to study the distant library himself.

“We have Anaxagoras for that,” Mydei argued without turning around.

“Anaxagoras does not read ancient Kremnoan!”

“It’s possible that the tomes we are looking for are in another language entirely,” Anaxa mused, and Ptolemy fixed him with a glare.

“If there are writings in Styxian, I may be able to help,” Castorice offered. Hyacine raised her hand to say, “I was helping translate the runes of the Skyfolk back at the Grove. It was one of my secondary degrees.”

“Of course, you both will be of excellent service,” Anaxa invited.

“Mydei pleeeeease!” Ptolemy begged.

“Where’s the harm, Mydeimos?” Hephaestion reasoned. The first mate looked so much better. He had handed off the docking procedure to Krateros who was shouting to the rest of the crew behind them.

“Hmph.”

“Oh, come on, Mydei,” Phainon teased. He reached out and squeezed Mydei’s bicep, just under the decorative clasp there. “It ended up being worse for our collection when we didn’t let Ptolemy into the Grove.”

Mydei’s stubbornness cracked under Phainon’s gentleness, and he grumbled, “Fine, you may be on the landing party.”

Ptolemy mouthed, ‘thank you’ to Phainon and he responded with a thumbs up behind Mydei’s back.

“Hyacine,” Mydei called, “can you see any evidence of the Tide?”

She put a hand up over one eye and closed the other for a few seconds. When she spread her fingers to peer out from behind them the wild eye of Aquila darted about, seeing things beyond any of them. It was a clear day with clear seas, sunny and humid so Phainon doubted any lingering Tide would have the strength to put up a real fight if there were any left.

“I don’t see any monsters, Lord Mydei,” she reported.

“Be on guard all the same,” he ordered and Phainon nodded his agreement. They were dressed for combat in their usual armor, just in case, and each of them had a backpack with minimal supplies and plenty of space to take what they needed in reading material. Phainon and Mydei’s bags were full of food in case they had to stay the night up there, a reasonable assumption considering the size of the library and how deep they were into Action Hour already.

The landing party was chosen from volunteers and was thus notably small. The scholars of the Grove were all, of course, far too excited to be excluded and carried critical experience at ancient sites. But the Kremnoans were harder to convince aside from Mydei, Ptolemy, and Peucesta whose love of stories made this trip a sort of pilgrimage, but Phainon was surprised to find that Krateros and the entire Old Guard refused to set foot on shore. The old veteran had muttered something about holy ground meant only for Kings and attendants but refused to elaborate further and instead wished them well. It was an odd sentiment coming from someone who had attended the late King Eurypon and Queen Gorgo and had browsed the shelves here before.

Old dock gave way to even older stonework only a few strides away from where the ship was tied, worn smooth by the sea. There was no port here and only the one dock that had gone through thousands of repairs. The farther they walked along it the more Phainon could see the style change as though they were literally walking backwards through time to the small platform that connected the walkway to a steep path that wormed its way up to the jewel of the northern seas.

Phainon was losing his mind he was so happy. He was one more comment away from being kicked off the side of the cliff as punishment for the way he loudly noted the remnants of the old city along the cliff, the scarring in the stone from Nikador’s blade, even the bowed nature of the stone steps worn by centuries of footsteps.

“The Kadirans used to worship Aquila,” Ptolemy told Phainon as they walked. He pointed out some of the circular symbols carved on some of the steps. “Even after Kremnos conquered them and they became caretakers of the library, some of their traditions survived for many generations.”

Phainon traced the eye carving with his fingers as they passed, holding up the line to do so. “Have you heard of them, Hyacine?” he asked.

“No,” she admitted, “there were a great many city-states that worshipped Aquila, my primary focus of study was the Sky-folk, but it does not surprise me to see the Eye of Twilight is a surviving symbol.”

“Symbols that are believed to ward evil and poor intentions are fitting for a library,” Anaxa commented, “there is no other symbol on Amphoreus as widely recognized as the Eye of Twilight than perhaps the Dawn Device.”

Phainon had to pause while Mydei leaped across a small gap. The walkway ahead had washed out, whether from a storm or age it was impossible to know. The prince waited on the other side, hand extended to catch the others. Phainon stayed behind to help the girls with their jumps, giving them a little toss over the gap and into the safety of Mydei’s arms. He tossed Anaxa too with mumbled apologies but Ptolemy and Peucesta had no issues making the leap, nor did Phainon, but he appreciated Mydei’s firm grip on his arm when he landed.

“Ptolemy, do you know why Krateros wouldn’t want to come here?” Phainon asked as they started the last stretch of the ascent.

“I do not. What did he say?”

“Only that it was holy ground meant only for royalty and their attendants.”

“There are several tales about the library that may give superstitious men and women pause,” Peucesta said lightly. He was towards the back of the caravan. “Some believe that Nikador severed the library from Castrum Kremnos to leave behind their wisdom in pursuit of more violent glory. Others say that the library is cursed, as not even Georios wanted it when they sank half the world into the ocean. Or perhaps it is as simple as a man unwilling to see a beloved landmark in ruins.”

That was a humbling thought, but Phainon was undeterred and when they finally reached the top and stood beside the pillars that marked the once gates of the Library of Garbaniphoro, he was almost moved to tears. The statues that may have once adorned the tops of those pillars were long gone, leaving broken tops and vine covered carvings but they still dutifully marked the narrow path that opened beyond them to a modest sized courtyard. Leaves and sand filled the dry fountain, debris piled up along the edges and filled cold braziers, and a soft sort of peaceful quiet muted all but the sounds of their footsteps.

“The doors are intact,” Anaxa observed with his arms crossed.

“So is the surrounding frame,” Ptolemy mumbled.

The façade of the library was a massive thing, built for kings and gods two stories high in a manner reminiscent of the Kremnos Arena. The doorway was framed by pillars and sloping walls that reached as far as the cliff to guide guests into that gateway marked by arches. The double doors were twice as tall as they were wide and covered by an extended cornice. Scenes of Nikador were carved into the pediment above, faded into shadows of their former glory.

The bookworm was the first to approach the gilded door. The bronze fixtures that held the handles were shaped like lion heads, holding the rings in their teeth, but when Ptolemy gave it an experimental tug nothing budged. He tried to push. Nothing. Peucesta joined him and they tugged in tandem, but nothing moved.

“Is there a password?” Phainon asked.

“Magic was not a Kremnoan specialty,” Anaxa huffed, “nor was it one of Ancient Kadir.”

“I’m sure it’s just stuck,” Ptolemy grunted as he slammed his shoulder into the heavy door repeatedly. “It hasn’t been opened in a very long time.”

Phainon started stepping up to help, but Mydei held a handout to stop him. There was a puzzled look on his face as he studied the door.

“Ptolemy. Peucesta. Come away from there,” he ordered. Ptolemy pouted but he followed the bard down the pair of steps that led to the threshold and waited impatiently to the side.

“Mydei?” Phainon prodded.

Mydeimos stepped to the side and tilted his head, looking at the door from a new angle. Then he paced past Phainon, parallel to the façade to crouch and tilted his head again. It was like watching Beagle try to figure out a food puzzle. Back and forth to watch how the dusty bronze plating caught the light until he finally, finally stepped up and approached the door with reverence. He placed his hand on the door, pushing with his gauntlet only briefly before he crouched again, studying every inch of the door’s seam.

“Deliverer,” he called and Phainon and the other’s started forward. “Only Phainon,” Mydei corrected when he heard more than one set of footsteps. Phainon crept forward with excited trepidation, searching for whatever Mydei may have noticed until they were side by side beside this mighty threshold.

“Did you see something?”

Mydei nodded. “How old is the Goldweaver?”

Phainon frowned. “Old. At least a thousand years old.”

Mydei pressed his gauntlet to the door again and curled his fingers to drag the tips of his claws gently across the surface until they caught on to something nearly invisible until it was tugged: a golden thread.

Phainon blinked and reached to pluck it, but it held tight, no weak thing like those they had pulled from cargo in the past. Instead, he felt further down the seam of the door counting those subtle changes of texture when his fingertips brushed another thread. There were more than a dozen at least.

“Aglaea sealed the door?” he mumbled curiously to himself.

“Okhema has been at war with Kremnos for hundreds of years and Krateros was here no more than twenty years past… when could she have done this?” Mydei wondered.

“Would you like to share with the class?” Anaxa shouted from the courtyard.

“No!” they both shouted back at the same time.

“They must have been here for centuries,” Phainon guessed, “waiting to seal the doors in case of an emergency.”

“An emergency such as the Tide.” Mydei plucked at a thread again and it shimmered gold before it vanished again, too thin to be perceived without catching the light.

“But the Tide has receded, why are they still binding the doors?” Phainon wondered aloud.

Mydei’s eyes were narrow, deep in thought. Phainon could see the wheels turning in time with his own. What was Aglaea trying to protect here? Were these threads still attached to her? What value did this library have? How could she have known so far in advance to leave these threads here with this explicit purpose? Aglaea was clever and ageless, but she couldn’t see the future. Only one Demigod had the gift of Prophecy and that was…!

“Mydei,” Phainon mumbled, breathless, “I think I know what it’s waiting for.”

The Kremnoan looked up at him expectantly with a curious tilt of his head, but Phainon was focused on this lock. He made a fist with his left hand and held it to his chest and put his right hand, palm flat on the door. It took some effort, but Phainon closed his eyes and gently tapped the power of his coreflame, letting it feed into his fingertips so the golden thread could feel it, could recognize him.

The threads across the door glowed bright gold and the others waiting behind them gasped as they revealed themselves but even though they saw him, it wasn’t Phainon they wanted.

“Mydei,” he said, excited and trying to articulate, “I think they’re waiting for you. I think they’re keeping Nikador’s wisdom for the Inheritor of Strife to come and reclaim it.”

The recognition hit halfway through Phainon’s sentence and Mydei reached out with confidence. The power of Strife surged through him. Phainon felt it like a heat wave with the whispers of conflict in his ears, filling his heart with excited bloodlust and then it was gone, shattered with the threads.

With a heavy groan and long creak, the doors slowly opened outwards like a gaping maw finally letting go of a long-held breath. It smelled of papyrus and stone, dust and ink, of promise.

“Alright, Aglaea,” Phainon mumbled under his breath, “What were you hiding from the Tide?”

Chapter End Notes

I’m not able to write out all the shenanigans but please know that for like a week, every time someone called for the captain, Phainon responded at the same time as Mydei, and he always had the stupid expression: :3c After the 20th time, Mydei threw Phainon off the ship and Peucesta won five coins each from Ptolemy and Perdikkas.

chapters.title: Chapter 42: The Library of Garbaniphoro
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

No new tags

They're at the library! But someone got there first...

Chapter Notes

So 3.7 killed me for a few days and then Currency Wars owned my soul for the rest of the week. :') I am so sorry for the delay, I promise I'm still alive just taking care of irl things and farming jades for Mydei's rerun coming up. I feel like Phainon would forgive me for that so you guys can too.

3.7 gave us the ACTUAL name of the library and it's not the Library of Garbanphoro but I'm gonna commit so before people in the comments say something, I know and I am lazy ;w; That's future me's problem when the perfectionism kicks in and I've already finished the fic. That's when I'll fix the little things. :')

Old things smelled old and new things smelled new. It’s one of those things that is inherently recognizable and equally indescribable. Even if there are other scents involved that are easier to put a name to, the core of the scent is ‘new’ or ‘newness’. This library mostly smelled old, and it was divine. Phainon loved when history tickled his nose. He loved new scents too; the metallic bite of armor unworn, ink freshly applied to white paper, and the woody pine tar of a ship before her maiden voyage. But there was something so special about old smells.

Especially when those old scents were coming from a massive, legendary atrium fit for kings. The library opened immediately into a massive grand hall with arched ceilings held up by two rows of marble pillars. It was deeper than wide, maybe three, no, four times as long lit by filtered sunlight through dirty glass panes and marble shaved so thin that the sunlight made the ceiling glow brightly. Cold braziers hung from hooks on every pillar, a promise that study didn’t have to stop at sundown.

A massive statue of Nikador waited for them near the entry way, protected by curved desks that would have belonged to dutiful record keepers. Smaller statues, painted amphorae, carved plates, and tapestries lined the walls and filled display shelves. The space down the center of the hall was reserved for large statues, depictions of Gorgo slaying the Lion of Tretos, of former kings on dromas back, and Nikador fighting Aquila. Even from here Phainon could see their spears raised high, nearly piercing the ceiling.

“Curious that the way was blocked by golden threads,” Anaxa said as he stepped up beside Phainon and the hall caught his voice, amplifying it. The group was approaching the threshold with appropriate caution. They had all seen the glow of those fine threads and Aglaea was no stranger to traps. “You wouldn’t happen to know anything about that, would you, Phainon?”

“I have my suspicions, Professor, but nothing more than outlandish theories.”

Anaxa’s grunt was unconvinced but respectful.

He didn’t turn to acknowledge his teacher. It was taking every ounce of Phainon’s strength to not skip wildly into the atrium to inspect every article he could find. Nothing in here needed appraisal but he certainly wanted to give each piece the attention they deserved as though they did.

“Regardless of her motivations, she has protected a treasure of my people and possibly the answer we need,” Mydei announced as he took a single step into the library. The fine layer of dust curled around the metal of his greaves in tight curls when it was disturbed. “I owe her a great debt.”

Ptolemy shook his head and reached for Mydei’s arm, holding him back from walking any further. “Hold on, Mydeimos. It would be unwise to move on from this so quickly. Krateros was just here something like twenty years ago, and it was still open. When could she have left threads like that?”

“Lady Aglaea is over a thousand years old,” Castorice informed them, “she may have been here many lifetimes ago.”

“She must have left them here a long time ago in case the Black Tide came for the library,” Hyacine theorized out loud.

“I had the same idea,” Phainon admitted.

Mydei raised a hand to look at his fingers, there were still crumbling pieces of thread there, finer than hair, only visible in the glow of sunlight bouncing off the pillars to brighten the threshold. “And left them at a time when Kephale and Nikador were still allies.”

Anaxa didn’t bother theorizing with them. He was the one that finally had enough speculating and walked into the library as though it were his own back at the Grove. Confident steps kicked up dust as he immediately headed for the front desk to start digging around at the scrolls and tomes tucked onto the short shelf behind it. Ptolemy followed next, starting at the opposite end of the shelf.

Phainon eagerly started after them, but Mydei’s hesitation caught his attention and gave him pause as well. The prince was looking around with increasing confusion.

“Is something wrong, Lord Mydei?” Castorice asked as she gently reached for him, stopping just before touching his shoulder.

“Where are the books?” he asked genuinely.

“It is a failing on our part that you have not been to a proper library,” Peucesta lamented.

“It’s a fair question, Lord Peucesta,” Hyacine posited, “the library at the Grove had plenty of shelves in their atrium.”

“The Library of Garbaniphoro is a fortress or a vault as much as a place of study,” Phainon explained. He didn’t bother trying to hide his excitement as he rapidly recalled what he had read of the place in his school days. “Libraries that house rare and important tomes store them away from public areas and send librarians to fetch them on behalf of the scholar requesting access.”

“I imagine many of the wings are open for perusal,” Anaxa hypothesized from across the foyer. He found the tome he was looking for and dropped the heavy thing on the desk, unceremoniously wiping the dust from its spine and the edges of its pages. It was as thick as Anaxa’s hand was wide. “The oldest works will be sealed away for preservation.”

“What should we be looking for?” Hyacine asked aloud as she slowly meandered into the open space and towards the front desk. She leaned over the desk to look at the book upside down as Anaxa slowly pulled it open and started running his fingers over the delicate lines, pretending he could read the Kremnoan.

“For now, gather everything you can about the Titans, Coreflames, and the Black Tide,” Phainon told her.

“And anything about the northern Kingdoms,” Castorice remembered aloud.

“We are primarily here for the rest of Eurypon’s research,” Anaxa firmly reminded them. “But grab anything that may be even tangentially relevant,” he added with an air of condescension, as though it was frustrating that he felt like they needed the instruction to do so.

Ptolemy was also leaning over Anaxa now as Peucesta came up on the other side. Pinched between the two Kremnoans the professor looked particularly diminutive and annoyed, but they were flipping through the pages with better understanding and pointed purpose.

“Looks like we want collections beta, eta, iota, pi, rho,” Ptolemy noted.

Peucesta pointed at something on the opposite page. “West wing nu and chi too.”

“Mydei and I can take the west wing,” Phainon volunteered. The captain flashed him a look, but Phainon was already speed-walking into the depths of the hall, skipping ahead to admire each piece in passing as he searched for the best stuff.

While the center of the hall was dedicated to the kings and gods of the past the spaces between the pillars and the outside walls belonged to desks and tables for study. They were closely packed in the gaps between the different doors that lined each wall. Each gateway led to their own pocket of collections with labels carved into the frame above them.

Phainon had read about this library several times over his school years. It was famous for a lot of reasons, but it was affectionately described as labyrinthian by scholars of all ages and histories. The library may have started simple and small, but over time, as it expanded, construction had to embrace some creativity to find space to grow. Many of these pockets were still single rooms adhering to like topics, but Phainon was learning with every curious peek that some of them stretched into other floors. Most featured stairs that led towards dark expansions above and others reached into the depths, where they made use of the space beneath the ground.

“We may have benefitted from a map,” Mydei mused as he caught up to Phainon again. The prince was holding steady, walking slowly to take in the atmosphere but not pausing, whereas Phainon kept hurrying to stop in front of every relic. He would race past Mydei, get distracted and stop to study a piece of interest (and they were all of interest), and Mydei would slowly pass him again.

“Where’s the fun in that?” Phainon asked cheerfully. He skipped ahead to where there was no door, only a brightly lit opening that led to the west wing. Across the hallway the east wing had long since collapsed, filling the doorway with rubble, and leaving them with only the one remaining option.

“It’s here, Mydei,” Phainon called but his energy was firmly reined in when he saw Mydeimos pause for the first time in their steady journey towards the truth.

The captain had stopped beside a hanging tapestry, looking at it with a guarded expression, hiding how it made him feel, if it elicited feelings at all. Curious, Phainon joined him to study a window into Mydei’s own history. The image depicted a king standing on a cliff, holding an infant over the edge above a hungry sea. At his feet a woman was on her knees, hands raised palms up. She was dressed as a warrior, a true Kremnoan with long, wild hair, blonde with strawberry red tips and a sword at her side. Men stood at attention along the cliff behind them, watching.

“…if you could go back,” Phainon started to say.

“Stop.”

“Mydei-”

“No.” He didn’t say it harshly; there was no pain in his voice. “It is because of my past that I am here now. How can I not look back on this tragic moment as anything less than a blessing?”

Phainon blinked in surprise at the sentiment and then again when Mydei grabbed the leather armor strap across Phainon’s chest to pull him in for a quick kiss. Too quick for him to reciprocate. The shock had barely passed when Mydei let him go and walked past him towards the west wing. He disappeared around the corner, but Phainon stayed rooted for a moment more to study King Eurypon and Queen Gorgo.

It is because of my past that I am here now. How did that man do it? How did he always find the simplest and most profound ways to describe the storms in Phainon’s heart? Distant past, near past, it didn’t matter.

Phainon put a hand over his heart and bowed his head in respect to Queen Gorgo’s sacrifice and contemplated the flicker of grief that he still carried from Aedes Elysiae. They were both haunted by the weight of their past, but Mydei had never seemed heavy with it. What mattered was the now and the future, the future they were now empowered to save.

“Deliverer!” Mydei called and Phainon hurried to catch up.

The west wing was a maze, but they were finally getting into the readables. There were still shelves of relics, which made sense, Amphoreans were creative when it came to record keeping, but Mydei and Phainon were finally surrounded by seemingly endless rows of long shelves. The ceilings away from the atrium were low, supported by thinner pillars with fewer sources of natural light. The walls were still composed of marble but the thin sheets that allowed light to pass through were fewer and farther between. Phainon and Mydei found themselves lighting braziers as they went, where it was safe to do so. The efficient fuel in each little hanging basin was less than full but would last a few days at least without tending.

Phainon paused frequently to pull scrolls and steles from the shelves to check their contents. The labels on each shelf were faded and those they could read were not helpful. Each shelf had numerical codes that undoubtedly corresponded to a catalog at the front desk, a system that was useful to the keepers of these treasures but of little use to them now.

He was delighted to find that his studies in Kremnoan were coming in handy. While they were surprised to find some works in Okheman, the vast majority of what they found was predictably written in Mydei’s native tongue. Phainon found himself easily distracted with every book he picked up. Things written on paper, whether scrolls or tomes, were more recent additions or less important than those things written on steles or even thin sheets of brass. Some pieces were copied into multiple formats in the name of preservation, heavy when stored on metallic mediums but far more likely to last.

It was fascinating to Phainon to see what the library’s keepers considered worthy of long-term preservation. A few sheets of brass had meticulously been imprinted with the Kremnoan recipe for stewed lamb. Another set recorded the bloodline of the royal chimeras, keeping records of their pedigrees for hundreds of generations, beginning with the esteemed Absentee Master.

Everything about this place carried an air of permanence and for Phainon it also harbored an inherent romanticism. They had not said a word to each other in many quints but Mydei’s soft breathing, his heartbeat just one shelf over was a comforting background sound as Phainon read about ancient ship building techniques from a scroll.

He started to put it back but paused as Mydei removed a tome from the other side and their eyes met through the shelf. Phainon smiled at him warmly and was met with soft eyes and a gentle grunt.

“Anything?” Mydei asked.

“Not yet.”

“Hm.”

Phainon put the scroll back and then wandered around the end of the shelf so he could press in close behind Mydei to wrap his arms around the man’s waist and breathe him in. The library was cold. Mydei was warm. He rested his forehead on a strong shoulder and closed his eyes to just be, to exist in this moment, surrounded by the history that led to this single moment in time.

The Kremnoan mostly ignored Phainon, his focus was on the book in his hands before he sighed and put it back on the shelf to instead reach up to tug on Phainon’s hair. It was brief, light, and immediately followed by the firm press of fingertips on Phainon’s scalp.

“The Professor said that the oldest works may be sealed away,” Mydei whispered. To speak any louder when they were side by side would have felt blasphemous in this quiet place.

Phainon lifted his head and rested his chin on Mydei’s shoulder instead. “I wouldn’t know where to start looking for any sealed rooms.”

“Perhaps along the wall would be best,” Mydei teased.

Reluctantly, Phainon let his hands fall back to his sides, letting his boyfriend go, but Mydei turned and caught his hand before he could walk away to pull him into a proper kiss. This time Phainon was ready, and he reached up to cradle Mydei’s face, holding him tightly with his fingers entwined in those silken locks. His pinky rested over Mydei’s braid, and his thumbs gently cradled the hinge of his jaw. Mydei’s own hand settled over Phainon’s collarbone, slipping up as they kissed to loop a finger under Phainon’s collar just in case he considered trying to escape, a thought that made Phainon inwardly laugh.

They pulled away, breathlessly caught up in the moment, and Phainon leaned in again to steal with his lips the breath that Mydei had just found in their moment of reprieve but a gauntlet on his chest gave Phainon pause. While Phainon studied Mydei’s lips, his long lashes, the crimson tattoo beside his eye… Mydei was looking past Phainon with a puzzled expression.

“It makes sense,” Mydei mumbled and Phainon curiously followed his line of sight to the shelf behind him. “If she left them on the door, why would she not leave more for other purposes?”

Clinging to shelf behind them was a golden thread. It glimmered brightly, happy at their display of public affection and Phainon felt the blood rush to his cheeks and ears at the prospect of having been caught kissing in an abandoned, but still public, library. Mydei was far less concerned with that part. He pushed Phainon away so he could reach for the thread, giving it a tug to pull it free from the shelf and it brightened, shining into the depths of the library until it turned a corner.

“I didn’t see it before,” Mydei grumbled with a frown.

“The threads belong to the Titan of Romance,” Phainon mused aloud, “perhaps they reacted to our ki-“

“HKS!” Mydei snapped as he punched Phainon in the shoulder to stop him from talking. Perhaps Mydei was shy after all. He crossed his arms with a hmph and turned away but Phainon was already moving on.

Even if the thread was activated by something simple and somewhat silly, it was still here and that meant something important. Aglaea sealed the library to protect it from the Tide, something she must have known would happen via prophecy or an experienced hunch, it didn’t matter. In any case, something in this library had value and this thread might lead them to it.

Phainon took one end of the thread and started following it between the shelves. Mydei’s footsteps stayed close behind.

She led them into the depths of the west wing, lighting lamps as they went, past several walls before slipping into the impossible space under a door in a dark corner at the end of the longest stretch of bookcases yet.

“Sealed away,” Phainon whispered, musing mostly to himself but Mydei agreed with a staccato grunt. The captain was already feeling along the thin edges of the door, barely visible against the wall while Phainon fumbled to light the dark brazier hanging above the label. He almost dropped the flint twice as the two pieces clacked together over the fuel until a spark caught on the aged oil and a flickering flame finally decided to catch hold with a yawn.

Phainon held the brazier up by the chain, bringing the light up and over their arms to dispel the shadows around a tiny keyhole. Mydei picked at it with a claw, but it wasn’t big enough for more than just the sharp point. Phainon gently pushed Mydei aside so he could crouch down to look at it himself. This door and lock were not particularly heavy. It was not likely meant to be a vault so much as just inaccessible to the public which meant…

Mydei came to a similar conclusion and Phainon was calmly but firmly pushed away from the door before a Kremnoan shoulder barreled through the thing, snapping the thin lock and forcing those stiff hinges to bend. With a sleepy creak the heavy door came to stop moments before it could slam into the wall behind it.

The room beyond had two bookshelves that were half empty and a flight of stairs that led to a basement floor, but Phainon’s heart was still at the door. He ignored the pleas of the thread to follow its brightness into those dark depths and instead shuffled forward with a horrified expression to gently wiggle the door on its hinges to check that it was okay.

“…must you mourn a broken lock?” Mydei grumbled, “it had to be done.”

“Brutish Kremnoan,” Phainon huffed in mourning. “To assault a piece of history like this is abhorrent!”

“Would you have truly preferred to have searched for the key?” Phainon stuck out his lower lip in lieu of a response and Mydei stepped forward to pinch it lightly with his claws and take the light from him. “Come along, Deliverer, the answers will be worth the price.”

The stairs took a single turn on the way down, turning into a short, narrow hallway when they reached the bottom. There were two rooms on each side, no doors, just wide openings into matching small square rooms.

Phainon followed Mydei and the light into the first one. A small but sturdy square table centered the room, surrounded by short, thickly built shelves along all four walls to support the shining brass collection. There were no scrolls here, only thin stone steles and books with pages of thinly hammered brass, guaranteed to last for thousands of years without copying. The gold threads glowed around three books in this room, wrapped around each of them in loose coils before continuing to the other rooms.

The first tome that Phainon set on the table to check was thankfully written in Kremnoan. Though the foreword from the Scribe who penned this piece was quick to list the original source, a record from the lost Hyperborean ----. Phainon puzzled over the word for a moment, not sure he was reading this correctly.

“Mydei, is there more than one word for ‘kingdom’ in the Kremnoan language?”

“Not that I know of.” Mydei leaned over Phainon’s shoulder to look at the word himself and his brows wrinkled. “It does not say kingdom, it says empire.”

“I thought Hyperborea was a kingdom.”

“That was my understanding too.”

Phainon shook his head and turned the page, scanning the contents for a moment while Mydei read beside him. It was definitely close to what they were looking for, a record of the old northern kingdoms, but this was written like a fairytale, a romance between a tyrant and her loyal knight. Whether it held any historical truth was hard to determine, but folklore from the country they were looking into was at least a start.

A second book confirmed they had the right the section, but Aglaea’s threads stopped being useful beyond that. Every piece they wrapped around was a love story, tales of romance that attracted the wayward threads. Too far from their master, they must have simply defaulted to what they knew, seeking love where they could find it.

Phainon had started building a collection of works to bring back to the others for further investigation, choosing those that spoke about the political environment more than the emotional one, so he was surprised when he set another brass book on the table and realized Mydei was still reading the first book they had picked up.

“I don’t think a fairy tale will help very much, Mydeimos,” Phainon teased.

“Was it not a fairy tale that led us here?” Phainon opened his mouth to retort and for once, words failed him. He frowned, an expression that deepened when Mydei’s lips curled in a victorious smug smirk. “This tale is embellished but the figures were real. The scribe refers to scholarly works in the footnotes.”

Phainon tilted his head. “Which ones?”

Mydei went back a page, leaning back so the metal sheet wouldn’t smack his face as he scanned the margins and footnotes before reading aloud, “Rise and Fall of the Hyperborea Empire, Vol 3.” He turned a couple more pages. “Daughter of the Sea: A Study of Oceanic Peoples.” Another page flip. “Dukes of the Imperator.”

Phainon sorted through the books he had pulled to see if any of them matched. A few of them were here already and the others he found within the quint. Every time Mydei found a new reference, he told Phainon and as silly it seemed at first, the fairy tale was saving them a lot of time narrowing down potentially useful information. It was especially so when Mydei found the word ‘siren,’ proving that they were not just a storybook monster created to scare children.

From there Phainon found more proof of sea sirens as a people, creatures that lived in the depths of the ocean in a time all but forgotten, the most well-known of which came onto land to hide among humans.

That was when Phainon and Mydei closed their books and began packing them exactly evenly into their bags, determined to make a single trip of this treasure trove of information. While the temptation to curl up where they were to keep reading remained, Phainon also knew that the others would likely want a turn with this material. Anaxa especially would be eager to have every puzzle piece in front of him before he started assembly of the bigger picture. More than that, the longer they waited here the more these four rooms were beginning to feel like a tomb and Phainon was eager to taste fresher air.

Finding their way back took a quint and by the time Phainon and Mydei returned to the atrium the others had already claimed and pushed together two long tables and a pair of desks. Someone had cracked open one of the boxes on the tables to access the loose paper and ink inside and tossed out any inkwells that were improperly sealed and no longer usable. The tables were piled high with everyone’s discoveries including a rolled-up tapestry and set of decorative plates.

“Um,” Phainon started as he searched for a spot to set down their finds. His arms were starting to ache, and his shoulders were numb.

“Set it anywhere,” Anaxa ordered, distracted. He was pacing back and forth along the longest edge of the table, picking up books, scanning through them, setting them down, and scooping up another on the next pass. Back and forth, mumbling to himself, while the others snacked on food they brought and watched the Professor at work.

“Has he been like this the whole time?” Phainon asked. Castorice was the closest to them, sitting on the end of the bench. She looked up and nodded with a mouthful of figs and then hurried to help when she realized how many heavy things they had brought back. Every work thudded on the table when they set them down and pushed them into the pile to join the others within Anaxa’s reach.

The professor cut himself off mid-sentence when he spotted a thinner book that Mydei was setting down and snatched it before it could properly settle on the table.

Mydei frowned irritably. “It is written in Kremnoan,” he warned, but Anaxa was already pouring over the pages and pacing away again, mumbling in a manner that sounded like only half a conversation.

“Your man is actually insane,” Ptolemy told Phainon like it was a new discovery and not something Phainon learned on his first day of class. He was sitting on the other side of Hyacine between her and Peucesta. There were three books open on the table in front of him, but his primary focus was on their snacks. Peucesta too had set the lyre away to pick at one of two bunches of grapes while he read.

“Would you like some, Lord Phainon, Lord Mydei?” Hyacine offered. She held up the bag they brought with the bread and meats wrapped up nicely inside and Mydei gratefully took it from her. He squeezed between Hyacine and Ptolemy to be within better reach of the snacky fruits, leaving Phainon to find another spot for himself.

A part of him really considered squeezing in after Mydei anyway, to make room for everyone on the bench even if it was a very tight fit, but Phainon’s hunger for food was outmatched by his curiosity. He instead leaned over the table to see what else the others had found. Time had passed more quickly in the dark bowels of the library than he realized. The light from outside had faded to barely a glow and the others had efficiently made use of every minute to build a pile that towered dangerously up to Phainon’s eye level.

They had found the rest of Eurypon’s research notes, stories about the flame-chase, detailed, dry records tracking the Black Tide, collections of lyrics from bard songs, genealogical records, military records, on and on in what was probably only the surface of a very, very deep ocean of knowledge. Phainon watched Anaxa pace and then he watched the other five as their heads followed the professor back and forth as they ate in relative silence. Even away from the shelves in this more open place there was a reverence that hung heavy in the air and a numbness of tired minds.

Phainon leaned over to grab one of the hard rolls to chew on while he read about… what did he pick up? He put the bread in his mouth to hold it while he thumbed through paper pages. It was a collection of essays written in Okheman from a scholar that had moved from the Holy City, then to the Grove before they finally traveled here to study at this library maybe sixty years ago. They were researching coreflames, but the margins were full of notes, someone rambling about corruption in Kremnoan.

He put his thumb against the spine to hold the book open in the middle so he could take the roll from his mouth to ask, “how did you guys find so much in so little time?”

“We had help,” Hyacine beamed.

That sounded familiar. “Threads?” he asked.

“Nymphs,” Ptolemy corrected, “…did you find more threads?”

Anaxa stopped pacing and everyone stopped talking to look at him in alarm, but the professor mumbled to himself about distracting voices and instead grabbed an armful of books and stomped off to a farther corner of the hall to study.

“Don’t mind him, Lord Phainon,” Castorice reassured. She patted his arm from where she was sitting. “He is upset that everything he wants to read was found by a nymph.”

Phainon snorted, a half-chuckle in disguise, “then he will be particularly displeased when he learns how Mydei and I found our books.”

“A golden thread?” Peucesta asked. He was looking up from his book with gentle curiosity.

“Yeah, Mydei and I found it after we-” Phainon cut himself off when Mydei’s head whipped around to glare at him.

“After you?” Ptolemy prodded as he put an arm around the captain’s shoulder. Phainon could see the coy grin spread across Ptolemy’s face as he noted Mydei’s blush and rapidly came to horrible conclusions fueled by his favorite genre of literature.

“We kissed! Only kissed!” Phainon hurried to say before that imagination could get too far ahead to stop. Castorice and Ptolemy both looked disappointed.

“And the Titan of Romance revealed a golden thread to you?” Hyacine mused. There was a lightness to her tone like she was biting back a laugh.

“Mhm,” Phainon hummed as he took two long exaggerated steps to stand behind Mydei. “I wonder what else we could find if we-”

Today was just a day for unfinished sentences. Mydei’s arm looped around Phainon’s neck and pulled him down flailing and scrambling to get free. “Do you want to finish that thought out loud, HKS?”

“Kinda, yeah—Ah! Mydei stop!” Mydei’s grip tightened until Phainon had to drop his book to tap out and only then did the Kremnoan let go so a flustered Demigod could fix his hair and remember how to breathe again.

“Does it have to be you two specifically making out?” Ptolemy mused, mischievously looking down the bench at the two girls.

Peucesta came to their rescue. “I would be willing to try with you, Ptolemy.”

“You know I have nothing but love for you, Peucesta, but what would Perdikkas say?”

“Pay up.”

“That’s right and do we really want him to win?”

Peucesta sighed and picked up his lyre, answering with a sad tune that may have once been a love song.

“Don’t worry, Lord Ptolemy,” Hyacine said brightly, “even if we didn’t find any threads, the nymphs were more than helpful.”

“It is curious that the Goldweaver has played a role on this voyage,” Mydei thought aloud. He popped a grape into his mouth and then dug around in the bag for one of the meat wraps he had made before they left.

“Is it though?” Phainon asked and the others turned to look at him. “Aglaea has been leading the flame-chase for almost a thousand years, she’s been a Demigod for longer. Half the stuff here she could probably recount from memory.”

They sat in silence to consider that before Castorice asked, “so why didn’t she?”

“More questions,” Ptolemy sighed, “we have a long night ahead of us.” Mydei twisted in his seat to say something, but Ptolemy beat him to it. “We already sent a note to the Chryseus Leo. Little Ica took it down to them. They know we are well, safe, and staying the night.”

Mydei gave him a single pat on the back and reached for a book from the pile while Phainon recovered his from the floor.

“Let’s get started,” the captain ordered and Phainon eagerly obeyed.

Chapter End Notes
