Chapter Summary

No new tags

The pieces are on the table and the puzzle is coming together

Chapter Notes

I would have finished this yesterday but I got distracted reading other fics. Hot damn there are amazing writers out there.

This is mostly exposition. I'm hoping it's not too boring ;w;

By the time they had settled down to sleep, Phainon had gravitated back to the love story that the threads had first led them to. Even if the shimmering gold had only been attracted to the romance of it, Phainon felt like there was something here that wanted to be uncovered. This story wanted to be told, not buried in an ancient crypt.

He read by firelight and every time he got to an unfamiliar word he gently poked Mydei and the Kremnoan would sleepily translate. If it was a word that he didn’t recognize, Mydei would pass the book down the line to poke at Ptolemy who decided that if he had to be woken up every hour, so did Peucesta. The two would sleepily determine the most accurate translation and then pass the book back down the line until finally the patience snapped and Ptolemy yelled with sleepy tears that he wanted to be left alone until morning. The shouting summoned Anaxa, still very awake, enjoying the quiet time to study, to send all four of them back to sleep like unruly toddlers.

But good stories had a knack for finding good readers the strength to keep healthy choices at bay and Phainon was engrossed in this tale of the siren knight. When Anaxa walked away and Mydei’s breathing slowed with sleep, Phainon pulled the book from his pack once more to read.

In many ways he felt like he could relate to her, in others not so much, but his heart resonated with the themes of being lost and found. The story didn’t say how the sea siren lost her home, only that she swam from the depths alone and took on a human form to find companionship and purpose. She found joy in serving the woman she loved, her commander, the Imperator, and this love was returned in subtle ways. The Imperator threw feasts for her and their friends with roaring fires, good food, and fine wines at every reasonable opportunity, and they would dance together, unperceived in front of the bards.

That was the part that puzzled Phainon the most. On several occasions the story would describe a great battle, a grand celebration, and a dance between these two lovers, but ever conscientious of appearances, the Imperator would insist they dance in secret. How in Kephale’s name was it possible to secretly dance in the middle of a party?

He made a note of every page that mentioned the contradiction and resolved to ask his friends in the morning if it was a translation error on his part. Still trying to figure out what the author could have meant, he fell asleep on brass pages.

Phainon woke up a few quints into Entry Hour. Knowing how late he had stayed up, the others had let him sleep in but Perdikkas’ happy greeting and everyone hurrying to meet him brought Phainon back to life with a sleepy blink. He was barely sitting up and still trying to process that the doctor had joined them in the library at all when Mydei dropped a whole pomegranate in his lap and then sat down, cross-legged beside Phainon with his own.

“Perdikkas?” Phainon slurred and Mydei tilted his head. The confusion turned to recognition when Mydei’s eyes darted between Phainon and the doctor.

“He brought breakfast and another pair of eyes,” Mydei explained. The Kremnoan reached out to run his thumb over Phainon’s cheek with an amused twinkle in his eye. It was a funny sensation that left behind an uneven tingle until Phainon reached up to rub his cheek too and felt half a page imprinted there. “For a moment it seemed you confused me for him. Perhaps tonight you should join us in sleep sooner and rest on something softer than brass.”

Mydei let Phainon go to cut open their breakfast with a small knife. He made sure Phainon was eating first before he cracked open his own fruit and they picked at the seeds while they watched the others laugh around the table. Hyacine was excitedly talking to Perdikkas about some of the books they had found, Castorice and Peucesta were helping hand out food, and Ptolemy had distanced himself to read some more while he ate. Phainon couldn’t see Anaxa but that wasn’t any cause for alarm. It wouldn’t be a worry unless he went missing for more than an Entry Hour.

“I wish we could stay here longer,” Phainon mused. He popped a couple of the tart seeds in his mouth, savoring the juice on his tongue while he watched the light of Entry Hour filter in from above, leaving trails in the dust before settling on the big statue of the Lion of Tretos. A butterfly nymph was perched on the lion’s nose, sunning itself in the light.

“Spoken like one that has already solved the mystery of the Tide,” Mydei countered. Their knees bumped into each other as he turned to better face Phainon.

“No, I mean, a lot longer,” he tried to explain, “beyond any study of the Tide. I want to explore every wing, study every tapestry…” Phainon trailed off when he saw how Mydei was looking at him. “I know it’s stupid.”

“It’s not,” Mydei corrected quickly, “and there is no reason we cannot return once the matter of the Tide is settled. It is my library after all… and what’s mine is yours.” He looked away at that last part, glaring intently at the pomegranate rind that he was slowly tearing apart with the claws of his gauntlets.

Phainon’s heart warmed at the thought, and he reached out to put his hand on top of Mydei’s. “Does that apply to everything?” he asked, light-hearted and teasing.

“HKS, I meant what I said as I always do. Do not abuse my generosity.”

“I wouldn’t dream of it, Mydeimos.”

Mydei still refused to look at Phainon but any moment they may have had was chased away by the sound of staccato footfalls and the fluttering buzz of tiny wings. Anaxa was storming down the center of the hall on as straight of a path as possible with his hands full of a massive stack of papers. Trailing behind him were a pair of nymphs, one of the beetle varieties, pale blue in color, and the other was a bright pink butterfly. Anaxa paused twice to turn around and swat at them, but they just fluttered out of reach and then followed him again all the way back to the main table.

“Class is in session!” he announced loudly as he slammed that massive stack of papers down onto an open spot. The whole table jumped and while the books settled quickly there was a short scramble to keep the food from rolling away.

Phainon knew better than to keep the professor waiting. He grunted to himself as he got to his feet and held a hand out to help Mydei up. The two of them gathered close behind the others, standing to give the others space to sit on the bench. Castorice slid over to make room for Ptolemy, and he rejoined them with his own notes and breakfast in hand.

The professor scanned them all, did a double take when he realized there was an extra Kremnoan, and then decided he didn’t care. The bag under his eye was heavy with indifference.

“I can confidently announce that I know the source of the Black Tide,” Anaxa said firmly.

“Oh, is that all?” Ptolemy said sarcastically. He was still unhappy about the late night. Phainon was fighting a yawn himself.

Anaxa’s eyes snapped to Ptolemy. “Would you like to present to the class first?”

The bookworm frowned and said, “I didn’t realize you wanted to copy my answers, Professor.”

At the far end of the table, Peucesta excitedly leaned over to whisper something in Perdikkas’ ear, but the doctor lightly smacked his chest and shook his head.

“If you would fight, please do it outside,” Mydei sighed.

“There is no need, Captain Mydeimos,” Anaxa purred, “it would be faster for me to teach than test after all.”

Anaxa leaned over to shoo the two nymphs that had happily settled on his stack of papers and took the top inch in hand to thumb through them. He smiled to himself, building suspense and some annoyance before he announced, “the Black Tide is the song of Dux Gladiorum Hysilens, the Demigod of Ocean, a sea siren from Hyperborea.”

The silence hung in the air for a long breath as the information settled on the group. No one seemed wildly surprised, but no one hurried to agree either. They were all taking a second to chew on that conclusion while weighing it against what they had studied themselves. Phainon definitely felt like some explanation was missing, but nothing he had read contradicted that statement.

Anaxa’s eye traveled over all of them in turn before settling on Ptolemy, taunting the Kremnoan, and Ptolemy was trying very hard not to rise to the bait. Instead, he politely invited through gritted teeth, “would you please enlighten us on how you got to that conclusion, professor?”

“I would. Before I begin, I would remind the class of rule number two: do not interrupt me. Silence is golden. If you have something to add, raise your hand and wait to be called upon.” Anaxa waited to see if any of them would disobey at the start, but everyone held their peace and, satisfied, the professor continued, “I will begin by laying down foundational knowledge to support my conclusion. After consulting with the rest of Eurypon’s study into Nikador and corroborating with my personal experiments in the Grove on the Coreflame of Reason I can definitively conclude that the Black Tide is unable to corrupt coreflames.”

Ptolemy was already raising his hand and Anaxa sighed but went ahead and pointed at him. “A coreflame is the only power in this world strong enough to create the Tide and Titan’s do experience corruption. There are plenty of notes here and stories that describe the Titan’s descent into madness before Eurypon began experimenting on the divine body. Mydei and Phainon both said there was no speaking to the Titan and that’s to say nothing of the other gods.”

“The Titan is not the same as the Coreflame,” Anaxa reminded him, “every Demigod here can attest that any corruption from the Black Tide was cured by their ascensions, taking the Coreflames into their bodies.”

Phainon nodded, so did the girls, Mydei crossed his arms and bowed his head, agreeing.

“So, you’re suggesting that Nikador was what? Experiencing corruption that wasn’t from the Black Tide?” Ptolemy prodded and Anaxa grinned.

The professor started taking sheets of paper off the top of his stack, his mint-green ponytail bounced against his shoulder as he slapped them down in turn, while listing, “Georios, a Titan corrupted, driven mad they sank continent after continent into the sea. Aquila, a Titan corrupted, closed their eyes and brought about the eternal night until Seliose slew the god and claimed the coreflame. Janus, citing the end of their ‘immortal’ life willingly surrendered the coreflame to the first Demigod of the new era.” He dropped two chunks in quick succession. “Talanton and Mnestia, Titans on the verge of corruption, they surrendered their coreflames.” A much larger pinch of papers dropped onto the others. “Nikador, famously gone mad with bloodlust, lost their reason and became a Titan corrupted.”

The professor gave them a minute to consider before he spelled it out for them, saying, “the coreflame is not the source of the corruption, it amplifies the corruption of its bearer and that corruption may come in many forms.”

Phainon took a sharp breath through his teeth and bit his lip. Anaxa’s eye darted to him.

“Something to add, Phainon?” the professor invited.

“I just remembered something that Lady Trianne said to me is all.” When Anaxa waved to him, Phainon recalled aloud, “she told me that coreflames grant wishes, and it’s very important for their new bearers to be ready for them… that the new Demigod needs to have good wishes.”

“Exactly,” Anaxa crooned, “the Black Tide is the work of a coreflame’s power, amplifying the corrupted wish of a siren.”

“…well, damn,” Ptolemy breathed in the silence.

“The sea siren connection makes sense,” Peucesta finally weighed in with his usual soft-spoken demeanor, “the Tide song is alluring, intoxicating, and addictive as the songs of sirens are meant to be in myth… why the Coreflame of Ocean? Could she not have had the Coreflame of Law?”

“The Coreflame of Law was claimed at the beginning of the flame-chase journey by the leader of the dominate Empire on Amphoreus at the time,” Phainon explained, “Imperator Cerydra.”

“There are three coreflames that cannot be accounted for,” Anaxa said as he thumbed through his notes again, “Earth, which was claimed by the Demigod Terravox in the early days of the Imperator’s flame-chase and disappeared with him. Then there were Law and Ocean, which were last seen together in the hearts of their Demigods nearly one thousand years ago during the height of the Hyperborean Empire.”

“Cerydra famously started the flame-chase journey after becoming the Inheritor of Law,” Castorice recalled. She didn’t raise her hand, but Anaxa let it slide in favor of the discussion.

“Lady Tribbie brought her the prophecy, and she began hunting the coreflames soon after,” Hyacine remembered. The healer started sorting through her own books, looking for her source in case she was called upon to cite it.

“That same prophecy that motivated the Goldweaver to assume command of the flame-chase after the Imperator’s death. The same one that she keeps close, away from all except those she has roped onto the path beside her,” Anaxa mused.

The eyes in the room immediately turned towards Phainon who blinked in surprise and tried to rein in his fluster. “W-Why me? Castorice and Hyacine are Chrysos Heirs too.”

“Lady Aglaea never told me the prophecy,” Hyacine said.

Phainon frowned. “Castorice?” he asked, and she shook her head.

“She never told me either, Lord Phainon.”

That was admittedly very puzzling. Why would she only tell him? It was no secret that Aglaea had slowly been grooming Phainon to one day take her place in Okhema at the head of the flame-chase, but why keep the prophecy a secret? It was little more than a vague poem, a list of coreflames and generic one line well wishes.

“Did Aglaea tell you the prophecy that drives the flame-chase?” Anaxa prodded.

“Yeah, she made me memorize the core part of it,” he admitted, “but it’s not insight into the future, so much as a shopping list of generic instructions.”

“Instructions?”

Phainon nodded. “It’s stuff like-” he gestured to Mydei, “Fight to know the inspiration of Strife, that the world may know peace.” Phainon gestured to Castorice next. “Embrace the inevitability of Death, that the world may know life. Stuff like that.”

“A mandate from a distant prophecy to make use of the coreflames…” Anaxa mused.

“It starts: Red is the hand that seeks to assume the fire of the gods, the flame is discerning and knows their heart. Flow golden blood, flow. Reach for your missing pieces to quell the unease of corruption,” Phainon quoted slowly, frowning, “Losses are a constant on the flame-chase journey. Therein is the power to doom the world or save it.”

Next to him Mydei shifted his weight, his hands holding his elbows in a crossed position gripped a little tighter.

“In all these readings, has anyone come across an explicitly stated reason why the flame-chase journey began?” Anaxa asked.

Mydei raised his hand. When attention turned his direction he spoke, saying, “I found a short passage that was supposed to be an excerpt from the journal of the Imperator of the Hyperborean Empire. She consulted regularly with ‘one who could see the future’ and believed that the coreflames would destroy the world if they and their bearers were not carefully controlled.”

Hyacine slouched where she was sitting and Little Ica dropped into her lap to provide something comforting to squeeze. “Many of these books described the Imperator as a tyrant bent on conquest… if someone like that got a coreflame…” The Imperator’s ‘wish’ was not hard to deduce. She would have happily ruled all Amphoreus.

Phainon’s grip tightened on the plates in his hand, the story that painted Cerydra in a more positive light with her Dux Gladiorum, with Hysilens. He hefted it up to look at it a little more closely.

When Aglaea first took Phainon under her wing she had him study history with Lady Tribbie. They talked about Cerydra on several occasions, but it was all surface knowledge, the kind of thing that was written about here in a somewhat plain manner: dates and lists of conquests.

The Imperator had taken great pains not to be the primary subject matter of historical records despite her prominence at the time. Most of those books focused on specific events, victories, and the establishment of the flame-chase. Events that Tribbie and Aglaea never expanded on past what was written in his textbook.

At the time, Phainon thought nothing of it but now it seemed strange that Tribbie and Aglaea would keep the more personal parts to themselves, after all, they were there. Aglaea and Tribbie even made appearances in this book, however brief. They were comrades.

“Was this Cerydra a siren?” Mydei asked, “could it be her song?”

“No, there was a single siren in her army at the time,” Anaxa explained.

“The Dux Gladiorum, Hysilens,” Phainon mused aloud.

“What did I say about interrupting?”

“S-Sorry, Professor!”

Anaxa sighed and continued, “Imperator Cerydra’s Dux Gladiorum, her most loyal general, was a siren.” He held up another pinch of paper and slapped it down on top of the spent stack. “And the Inheritor of Ocean after the Imperator led her armies against Phagousa, the Ocean Titan.”

Perdikkas shook his head a little bit. “I’m sorry, I know I’m late to this study session, but I’m already lost. How does this tie back to the Black Tide?”

Rather than be annoyed, Anaxa was surprisingly patient when he said, “perhaps a timeline of events would help?” He didn’t wait for Perdikkas to agree and instead rifled through his notes until he found the page he wanted.

“Over a thousand years ago, sea sirens lived in the depths of the ocean, but an unknown catastrophe drove at least one of them to the surface where she shed her fins to walk among men. Around the same time the Kingdom of Hyperborea lost their royal bloodline and went in search of any lost heirs.” Anaxa waved his hand in circles and then took the top sheet of his notes off to set it down on the spent pile. “How Cerydra came to be the Imperator is of no consequence, what matters is that she rose to power, found the siren, and gave her a home serving as a general of her armies.”

Perdikkas slowly nodded, following so far.

“The Titans had already begun to pass their coreflames to the next era of Demigods around this time,” Anaxa explained. He paused when Perdikkas’ face wrinkled with confusion. “Has something puzzled you?”

“Maybe. Is this because they were becoming corrupted?” Perdikkas asked.

“Yes. A long life will eventually succumb to madness, even with divine power to prolong the inevitable. Many of the Titans surrendered their coreflames before this happened,” Anaxa explained, “the first of which was Janus, who left the next Demigod with the prophecy of the coreflames, which Phainon has so graciously enlightened us about. It is a warning as much as a mandate that the coreflames would need to find their next keepers to ensure their power was properly harnessed according to their purpose without succumbing to the corruption of their bearers.

“It was likely this prophecy that drove the Imperator to begin the flame-chase, but I have yet to find any works that confirm this hypothesis, not that it matters for our purposes. Regardless of motive, Cerydra began to march across Amphoreus, slowly expanding her Empire and waging war against the gods. There are detailed records of each earthly and divine conquest and mention of this Hysilens claiming the Coreflame of Ocean before she killed the Imperator and left the Empire in shambles.”

Mydei, Perdikkas, and Peucesta both started at the statement. Ptolemy was the only Kremnoan that seemed to have gotten that far in the reading. Phainon unfortunately knew that’s how Cerydra met her end. He knew when he was reading the love story too. It made everything a little bittersweet, despite the author’s best efforts to emphasize the romance of their relationship.

“Why would she do that?” Perdikkas asked.

“No one knows for sure,” Phainon admitted aloud, “Aglaea might but she never talked about it.”

Ptolemy rubbed his temples and then let his hand fall to slap on a stele. “Sometimes I forget that the Goldweaver was there. Why didn’t we just kidnap her too and bring her along?”

“Why didn’t Lady Aglaea tell us more?” Castorice wondered in a small, hurt voice.

It was a question that Phainon wanted to ask her. He was sure she had her reasons. Aglaea always had her reasons, but why lead them to books and tomes about all of this and not just tell them, tell him, herself?

His thumb brushed across the indents on the brass over the author’s name. It was a pen name for sure, Regaled Vow. This author that wrote so eloquently about these two women sounded familiar… Phainon took long steps around the bench to Anaxa’s side of the table so he could reach the pile of tomes without crawling over anyone in the process. He sorted through them quickly while everyone watched him like he had gone mad.

At least a dozen of the books that the nymphs had led them to were written by, or co-written by, the same person. The same author writing pieces that were hundreds of years apart? This one was about Cerydra and Hysilens, another was about the flame-chase, here was one about the nature of corruption in Titans, this was a collection of essays about the nature of prophecy. All of them written with similar prose, under the same name listed beside dozens of different translators.

“Lord Phainon?” Hyacine asked and he looked up.

Everyone was looking at him with a combination of confusion and curiosity. “…sorry, I just. I think Aglaea has been telling us. Look at the author names.”

Anaxa huffed irritably and Phainon realized he figured it out. “Of course,” the professor grumbled, “Regaled Vow is an anagram.”

“Goldweaver,” Phainon agreed, “that’s why she sealed the library and sent nymphs to guide us to these books, because these are her works, her recollection of events.”

“Okay,” Ptolemy grumbled, “let’s assume that the Goldweaver knew all of this, knew the Black Tide was the result of what, her friend, her coworker becoming corrupted? Why didn’t she stop it herself?”

“Maybe she couldn’t,” Phainon hypothesized, “maybe one coreflame isn’t strong enough.”

“Or we’re missing something,” Anaxa huffed. He slammed the rest of his notes down and turned around to drop heavily onto the bench, facing away from everyone to think.

Ptolemy rubbed his face with both hands, Mydei leaned against one of the pillars and scratched his chin, and Peucesta started playing his lyre. It was something contemplative and quiet.

“The conclusion is still sound,” Hyacine offered cheerfully and Little Ica chirped agreement. “We have no reason to believe the Professor is wrong about the source of the Black Tide and as long as we know what it is, we can find a way to stop it, right?”

Phainon agreed, “It has to be the Coreflame of Ocean enhancing the song of Hysilens. Somehow it’s turning the song into the Black Tide to grant her wish.”

“Why?” Mydei asked very suddenly and everyone except Anaxa turned in their seats to look at him. “Why would this Dux Gladiorum kill the woman she loved and make a wish that could create the Black Tide?”

Silence. Even the lyre stopped. The beetle nymph that had followed Anaxa chirped unhelpfully from the pillar.

“The ‘why’ might be the key to stopping it,” Hyacine reasoned.

“And none of us have found that,” Ptolemy grumbled.

“Yet,” Phainon added, trying to keep the room feeling positive, “we haven’t found it yet. There are still plenty of resources here. Has anyone found out anything about how a siren’s song works?”

“Oh, Lord Phainon, I found a few references to the Imperator making use of the song,” Castorice offered. She ran her fingers over bookmarks until she found the page she wanted and passed it over. “She used it somehow to spy on enemies.”

Phainon tilted his head and opened his own book, passing it to Ptolemy. “Ptolemy, there are several spots in this book where the auth- where Aglaea talks about the Imperator and the Dux Gladiorum dancing in secret before the bards. Will you check my translation?”

The Kremnoan raised an eyebrow skeptically and then his eyes scanned through the pages, slowly narrowing as he read more. He flipped to another bookmark and repeated the same back and forth dash with his eyes before he looked up again. “That is what it says.”

“A siren’s song weaves illusions,” Anaxa finally said. He was leaning back against the table now, slouching with his legs spread to keep from sliding off the bench entirely while he studied the pillar in front of them like it had all the answers. “A fantasia,” he added, “the coreflame likely enhanced the illusion, making it so the illusion becomes real instead of a temporary state of mind.”

“You came up with that quick,” Ptolemy grumbled and Anaxa threw a stele at him. Ptolemy barely caught it before it broke his nose and looked like he might throw it back, but the text caught his eye, and he sighed and set it down instead. “A description of a siren’s fantasia as written by Regaled Vow.”

“But why is that her wish?” Mydei asked again and Phainon was starting to feel the frustration in the room rising again.

“Aglaea took over the flame-chase journey when the Imperator was killed, right?” Perdikkas asked.

“Yeah… did you think of something?” Phainon asked.

“No, just trying to get my head around the timeline. I am only familiar with Kremnoan history,” the doctor admitted, “it is curious though. If the flame-chase was so important to preserve, why didn’t Aglaea take the Coreflame of Law?”

“Maybe someone else took it first?” Hyacine wondered aloud.

“Could a Demigod take two coreflames’ power?” Perdikkas asked.

“No, if someone could claim a coreflame that did not belong to them, Eurypon would have done so,” Mydei pointed out.

Phainon remembered how desperately they clung to Mydei’s coreflame when they had to leave him behind, how important it was to them to keep that part of his heart safe. He tried to imagine what it would be like if he were in Hysilens’ place, if Mydei were Cerydra. It wasn’t difficult to empathize with the love story that led to the tragedy.

She lost her home, traveled somewhere distant and new, fell in love… and lost that love. If they lost Mydei again Phainon wasn’t sure what form his grief and rage would take. The hatred that bubbled deep inside him from the loss of his childhood home would be impossible to contain if he lost this new, beloved family. He sure as hell would keep the Coreflame of Strife close, unwilling to part with it for even a second.

“I’m sure the Demigod of Ocean has it,” he said, mostly to himself, loud enough so the others could hear. Phainon looked down at the book again, sure of what he said, and then the book was snatched from his hands.

Professor Anaxa turned quickly so it couldn’t be snatched back, not that Phainon would hurry to reclaim it, he was more surprised that Anaxa was interested in a book written by the Goldweaver about the love between two ancient Demigods.

“I said I’m looking!” Anaxa snapped to the side. There was no one there, but everyone knew better than to point it out when he was clearly in a mood. He flipped through the pages quickly, lingering on the sheets that Phainon had marked.

“Professor…?” Hyacine tried and he ignored her for a few more page flips.

He slapped the book closed with a heavy clank and then turned around to hand it back to Phainon with a muttered, “one problem at a time.”

Ptolemy groaned and leaned forward with his hands pressed together and his thumbs on his eyes, rubbing them gently. Beside him Peucesta started playing again and it seemed to help because Ptolemy let his hands fall and focused again.

“No matter what, we’re not leaving this library until we have plan right?” he asked, “we don’t want a repeat of what happened at Castrum Kremnos.” The room collectively agreed in a series of nods and mumbled sentiments. “Then we don’t need all the answers, just the right ones.”

Phainon nodded firmly and set the book down on the table. “We all agree the source of the Black Tide is Hysilens. The Black Tide is a siren song but between the coreflames and the talismans we’re all immune so that doesn’t really matter.”

“It might,” Anaxa grumbled and Phainon paused to look at the professor.

The man had both his hands on the table and was leaning forward, head bowed. His hair was hiding his face and he didn’t look up when he gestured to the love story in front of Phainon. “They hid themselves from all the attendees of these celebrations. Attendees that consisted of their closest comrades and the Imperator’s advisors.” When no one else seemed to piece it together, Anaxa sighed and spelled it out. “The Imperator surrounded herself with Chrysos Heirs and Demigods.”

“So, the talismans only protect us from the Black Tide itself, not the song,” Ptolemy concluded.

“The coreflames, the golden blood, they will protect from the song that is filtered through the coreflame, this we have proven to be true, but I cannot confidently say that they will spare us from the song itself, not up close,” Anaxa concluded.

“So, we put wax in our ears,” Mydei suggested, “as the hero’s crew did.”

“Sometimes the simplest solution is the right one,” Castorice agreed.

“And if you’re wrong?” Perdikkas asked, genuine.

“Well, there must be a way,” Phainon pointed out, “Cerydra was not under the effects of the song. If she used this as a way to spy on her allies, then there must be a way for her to exempt herself from the fantasia.”

“Okay, I’ll work on that,” Ptolemy offered. He stood up to lean over the pile of books to start digging, shoving aside piles of documents and a couple of scrolls that promptly started to unroll. The tapestry that had been shoved in there rolled off the table where it too partially unwound.

“Lord Ptolemy, let me help!” Castorice insisted firmly as food was shoved dangerously close to the edge of the table. Phainon hurried to catch the scrolls and saw Mydei reach to recover the tapestry.

“Someone will need the answer to the question where, as well,” Anaxa mumbled to himself.

“I found a few old maps, Professor Anaxa,” Hyacine offered. She was also making a mess reaching for a few of the scrolls from the bottom of the pile. “They show the early spread of the Black Tide; she must be near the epicenter right?”

“It’s Anaxagoras,” the professor wheezed but his class had long since dissolved into unmanageable chaos and he was giving up.

Phainon was taking over instead. “Ptolemy, you’re looking for a way to dispel the effects of the siren song. Hyacine, you keep trying to find out where she might be hiding.”

“Lord Phainon, the rest of us should still try to find out why Lady Hysilens would wish for the Black Tide,” Castorice suggested, “maybe there is a way to convince her to stop singing without fighting.”

“Would the Imperator know?” Mydei asked suddenly.

Phainon glanced up at his boyfriend. The captain was holding the unfurled tapestry with a curious expression.

“You were the one reading her journal last night,” Ptolemy huffed, still busy picking out study material.

“Then I’ll just ask her.”

The room froze and all sound stopped except for that damn nymph. Anaxa drew his firearm on the fourth chirp and whipped around to search for it, but the nymph took the hint and fell silent too. Everyone slowly turned to look at Mydei who had a mischievous smirk barely curling the corner of his lip.

He turned the tapestry around to show everyone the depiction of a short woman with pale blue hair and a fiery crown. She was sitting on the back of a massive dromas with sharp, dark brown and orange scales, pointing ahead with a chess piece in her hand. At her side were three figures, Tribbie and Aglaea were immediately recognizable, the other, a pale woman with dark purple clothing, long black hair, adorned with pearls and shells must have been the siren. The background was faded but divided into four sections, each featuring a coreflame being claimed in a brief, contextless scene.

“Is this her?” Mydei asked, pointing to the woman in blue.

“It is,” Anaxa confirmed, and Mydei’s half smirk turned into a toothy grin.

“I know this woman,” he stated firmly.

Phainon felt his heart sink. Please don’t say it.

“I have seen her every time I have died,” Mydei explained, “waiting on the shore of the River of Souls.”

We’ll find another way, Mydei, please. Phainon’s heart dropped the rest of the way into his stomach.

“It would not be hard to find her again. I will get the answers we need.”

Chapter Summary

New tag: Assisted Suicide

Spoilers - CW details

Mydei and Phainon fight about the plan

Chapter Notes

Damn, we really are close to 1k kudos! Thank you all so much for the support! ;w;

“Absolutely not,” Phainon said quickly and firmly.

“Phainon, it’s a good idea,” Ptolemy started to say but he flinched back when Phainon shot him a glare. Everyone was leaning away from him. Everyone except Mydei.

“She has the answers we need,” Mydei said simply, like this was as simple as going to the market for eggs.

“So do these,” Phainon insisted, gesturing at the pile of books with a sharp wave of his arm.

“Deliverer-”

“No!” he snapped, “you don’t get to Deliverer me! Not about this.”

Everyone else at the table was holding perfectly still, unwilling to draw attention to themselves as Phainon shook. He could feel his Titan form trying to break free under the frustration, the worry, but he held it back as best he could.

“My lives are cheap,” Mydei insisted with his arms crossed and a tilt of his head.

“Really?” Phainon hissed, “you’re going to say that to me after what we talked about the night you woke up?”

“Um, maybe we should take a break,” Hyacine suggested. The others agreed through their actions, even Anaxa, excused themselves slowly from the table, leaving Mydei and Phainon behind to argue. They waited until they were both alone to even move again.

“We have time!” Phainon pleaded, “what we need is right here in this library.”

“And how long will that take, Phainon?” Mydei snapped back, “how long will it take to scour these shelves? How much ground will the Black Tide recover while we pour over ancient words on the chance that the Goldweaver recorded a method to defeat the Black Tide? The same Goldweaver that would not share these things with you in person! None of us know for certain that the answer is written here at all! It is possible she does not even know!”

“Better for us to try than for you to die!”

Mydei scoffed. “This is not up for debate, master wordsmith. I am the captain, and it is my decision, my life to use as I deem fit.”

“That’s not true anymore! What’s mine is yours, you said that!” Phainon stomped his foot down hard enough to feel pain in his leg. “And that includes your life too!”

Mydei was shaking now, a subtle shiver. Phainon could see the air starting to warp around him as his Titan also threatened to break free.

“You took a piece of me with you when you died, Mydei,” he reminded a little softer, just as insistent, “why do you want to do that to me again?”

“Because this is about more than us,” Mydei said firmly.

Phainon’s heart dropped again, and his hands clenched into fists at his side. He wanted to storm away to be angry somewhere else but if he walked away and came back to see Mydei on the floor… He shook his head violently to clear that thought.

“This is the answer, Deliverer,” the prince insisted. His boots clicked on the marble floor as he walked around the table to reach for Phainon’s hand, but Phainon recoiled before they could touch.

“You told me that you would take your deaths more seriously,” Phainon accused. He could feel angry tears welling up in his eyes, but they would not spill.

“I said, that if it is everything to you, then it will be to me,” Mydei agreed. When he reached for Phainon’s wrist again, it was swift, denying him any chance of escape to hold on tightly with no hope of a retreat. “I always mean what I say, so you understand how serious I am proposing this course of action.”

Phainon tried to rip his hand free, but Mydei held tightly to his wrist, pulling Phainon close to hug him. They struggled for a moment. The Kremnoan held on tight and Phainon pushed against him until Mydei stubbornly pulled Phainon’s wrist behind his own back trying to force the man to reach for that weak spot. The one that no one else knew, the only way to kill Mydei for good. Phainon stopped fighting when he realized Mydei’s intention and he tentatively reached for it, counting vertebrae down the line until he was pressing against that horrible weakness.

“This isn’t the end of me,” Mydei reassured, “it’s not the end of us. This is the best heading we can choose; the straightest path with the truest winds.”

Phainon’s grip on Mydei tightened. One hand moved to Mydei’s hair, coaxing the man’s face to his shoulder, the other pressed more firmly against his back.

He was still not okay with this. How could he possibly be okay with this? Images of Mydei’s bloody corpse came back in waves. There was the moment he had come to Mydei’s rescue, when this lion of a man had collapsed and the light had left his eyes. He remembered the ache of shouldering Mydei’s heavy weight when he personally carried his body back to the Chryseus Leo. Phainon had been too distraught to shed his godly form and had curled around him in their cabin refusing to let anyone see him. He had worn Mydei’s blood for days, had soaked his feathers in it while he cradled him, mourned him, begged him to return around broken sobs. It was Phainon’s blood beside Kephale’s in that bath that healed his wounds and cleansed the worst of the Tide’s corruption. Even with Perdikkas’ reassurances it had taken Mydei so long to breathe again, even longer until he had opened his eyes and spoken.

Mydei pulled away enough to take Phainon’s face in both hands, sliding them from his cheeks to the hinge of his jaw, to hold his head and neck with firm reassurance. “I know I am asking the world of you,” he said softly. Those amber eyes were taking Phainon in, searching for a measure of understanding that Phainon was not yet sure he was willing to give. For once, he wanted to be selfish, damn the world …but that wasn’t who he was, and Mydei knew it.

“You are my equal in everything, Phainon,” Mydei said gently, “you don’t get to be the only protector here.”

“Don’t,” Phainon hissed, “don’t use my own words against me.”

“I must, because I need you to be with me on this. I need you to be completely okay with this plan.”

Angry, Phainon let his hands fall to his side and tried to look away but Mydei held on, firm enough to keep him from retreating, gentle enough to not hurt him. He used his thumbs on Phainon’s jaw to tilt his head back to look him in the eyes. The press of those warm hands was everything, they stirred feelings of longing and hope from the depths of his bones to rival the anger he felt. How could he refuse that gentle request to see each other when he wanted to look away, to be angry?

“I can do this, Phainon, my heart,” he begged in Kremnoan, “this strength of mine comes from you after all. Have I not earned your faith? Do you really believe I would leave you so soon with no hope of coming back to you?”

“You weren’t there, Mydei,” Phainon growled in a pained whisper. His Kremnoan was awkward and poor, but the emotions were there, “when I held your body on the ship, not knowing when you would come back to me. I didn’t know if I’d ever get a chance to tell you how I felt.”

“Phainon, that piece of you that I took with me… how do you think I found my way home again?”

Phainon blinked away a tear before it could spill over and reached up to lightly grab Mydei’s wrists, grounding himself. “It feels as though you are choosing the world over me.”

“I am choosing the world because of you,” Mydei corrected, “because my Deliverer showed me how, because you are here with me, the man who looked beyond the borders of his home to fall in love with a pirate. I will return swiftly with the means to save everyone, especially you, and I will wake to your smiling face just as I did before.”

He shook but Mydei smiled so softly that Phainon’s trepidation was crushed under that quiet confidence. The angry heat in his belly tamed and he gently nodded. It was a subtle agreement, something so small he knew Mydei felt it more than saw it.

“Good, then I have a request of you, Deliverer,” Mydei said with a shaky waver to his voice, a slip of that resolute confidence. It made Phainon look up with suspicion, searching the fine lines of his face, the tremor in his warm embrace. “I want you to be the one to kill me.”

-

Mydei saw it in Phainon’s eyes the moment he made the request. Those shiny blue baubles like gemstones turned gold with barely concealed horror and he was burning under Mydei’s palms. He couldn’t blame Phainon for such a response, it was a big request, especially with how nervous Phainon was for this plan to begin with. So, when Phainon pulled away, he let him go.

“How can you ask that of me?” Phainon hissed after taking a few steps back. He had switched back to his native tongue and raised a hand, not quite reaching his mouth to cover it. “It’s not enough to convince me to hold your body you want me to kill you?!”

Phainon sounded frantic and Mydei tried to balance it with his own calmness, responding gently in Kremnoan, “Yes. I would have it no other way.”

“Why? Why the fuck do you think I would agree to that?!”

“Because we are equals in all things,” Mydei insisted, “because in this way it will not just be me alone enduring this pain but something we share beyond this life. Because I trust you implicitly. Because this would bind us so completely that it would be impossible for me to lose my way back to you. Because you need this too.”

Phainon was shaking and for a moment looked like he would throw up. He didn’t understand. The very thought of doing this was crushing the man under that heavy weight of responsibility but Mydei didn’t back down. He didn’t retract his demand. As hard as this would be for Phainon he genuinely believed it would help him in the long run.

Mydei did not take his lives lightly, not since he woke in Phainon’s arms. He had made a vow to Phainon that night and sealed it with his secret. To suggest this, to want to die at the hands of his beloved for the purpose of saving the world? Phainon needed to understand that this was a temporary state for Mydei. He needed to be a part of the entire process from death to rebirth to understand that every life held weight yes, but that Mydei would not leave him so easily. Phainon needed this to see that not even death could keep them apart for long.

And Mydei needed this too. As frivolous as his deaths had been, Mydei had never once taken his own life. It was a line he had never been able to cross, never wanted to cross. Reckless behavior, sure, throwing himself in the way of attacks meant for his men, of course, but he had never taken a weapon to his own body. Perhaps it was his way of appreciating his lives before Phainon had come along and given a name to that innate sense of self-preservation.

Phainon was still trying to grapple with the request and predictably, needed more time. The bright gold of his eyes shook as he glared at Mydei, anger and resentment trying to hide the immense pain that lurked in the depths of that raging spirit. When he finally blinked, Phainon turned and stomped away.

Mydei didn’t watch him go. He looked at the floor, listening instead as those stomps echoed in the atrium until they faded away entirely.

“Mydeimos?” Perdikkas asked as he approached, passing the storm that was Phainon on his way. “Is everything alright?”

“No. But it will be.”

“…you don’t have to do this, Mydei.”

Mydei sighed, crossed his arms, and looked sideways at his crewmate, one of his oldest friends. “When have I ever shied away from death, Perdikkas?”

“It’s different now.”

“Because I have ascended to divinity?”

“Because you have Phainon,” Perdikkas told him, “Because it’s not just about how you feel anymore. It’s about how he feels too.”

Mydei sighed and admitted, “I know, Perdikkas, and that is why it must be him. Give him time. We’ll have our answers soon enough.”

-

Phainon had stormed all the way outside the library and that’s when he let himself turn. His wings sprouted and uncurled, his body itched as it transformed and then he threw himself from the cliff and flew out over the sea. If Mydei hadn’t insisted on such a horrible condition, on requiring Phainon’s participation, he wouldn’t have left at all, but now Phainon just wanted space. He needed the moment to remember how to breathe, needed this space to just process this impossible thing that Mydei had requested of him.

Phainon circled the island on an updraft climbing higher and higher with intent to reach the sun that hung high in the sky, so high that the air felt like broken glass in his lungs, so thin that the black crept along the edges of his vision and the curve of the world made him feel small. The island was a speck below, the sea and the sky felt like one and it still didn’t feel far enough from this horrible responsibility.

Phainon slowly started to glide back down, letting himself fall rather than rise in a steady descent, safe and controlled. And as he fell, he thought.

Mydei was right, this wouldn’t be the end of them. The answers they needed were guaranteed if he went to the River of Souls to confront the long dead Imperator. The Kremnoan, unfortunately, knew that River well enough to get in and get out and Phainon would be the last face he saw before he took the dive and the first when he climbed back out.

It was a cruel thing to ask of Phainon, but he understood the request. The more he tried to imagine this morbid task from Mydei’s point of view, the more he realized he would want Mydei to do the same for him. He wouldn’t want the shaky struggle of having to take his own life while his friends watched. He would want a quick and painless death, held tight in Mydei’s arms, comforted in his mission as the black crept in. Perhaps Perdikkas could mix a poison, Hyacine could stop his heart, or Castorice could embrace him as Death itself, but would that be the same? Would it feel as anchoring any of those other ways?

If Mydei held him, smiling and muttering reassurances as he dove into the underworld on a mission that would save the world, would guarantee the freedom of their peoples and family, Phainon felt like he would have the strength to endure anything. That solemn responsibility would feel like a casual chore as easy as swabbing the deck or raising the sails.

As always, Mydei was right, perhaps Aglaea didn’t have all the answers, couldn’t record the solution they needed. This was, after all, something that only Mydei could do and he had come to Phainon with vulnerability, wanting Phainon to be a part of it so that he wouldn’t have to do this mournful thing alone. Maybe this was what the thread was waiting for all along, why it had to be the Inheritor of Strife that opened the door.

Phainon sighed as he glided down, still high enough to see the edges of distant islands, high enough to see the dark horizon where the Black Tide crept forward, trying to reclaim the ground it had lost when they took back Castrum Kremnos.

The clock was ticking. This wasn’t just the best way; it was possibly the only way.

Rather than return to the library immediately, Phainon glided down to the Chryseus Leo, to perch on the railing. The crew greeted him as they walked past, doing chores as though a god didn’t just land amongst them. He would always be Phainon first, their once interim captain second, and the Worldbearer third, as it should be.

“Phainon?” Leonnius asked as he paused. There was a coil of rope over his shoulder. “Did something happen?”

Not yet.

“No, I just needed to grab a couple things.” Despite his vocalized intentions, Phainon made no attempts to move. He just stood there, looking down at his friend and wondering if maybe he should ask for advice. If he pulled Krateros or Hephaestion aside and told them about Mydei’s plan, would they hurry to the library to stop him? Could they slap some sense into their prince? Or worse, would they agree?

“Would you like me to get them for you?” the runner asked. His head was tilted, face alight with worry. Phainon smiled, a warm and sunny thing that he hoped would put their friend at ease, but Leonnius’ worry turned to skepticism.

“That would be great. Trying to get my wings through doorways, y’know?” he joked.

Leonnius set the rope on a barrel and slapped his hands together. “What am I lookin’ for, captain?” he asked with a wink.

“There are two blankets on the bed in my room. I need them both.”

“Staying another night?”

“Not sure yet, we’re just playing it safe,” Phainon reassured.

Leonnius didn’t press, but Phainon still felt bad for keeping things from him. The runner left and Phainon slowly sat down on the railing. His wings fluttered in the wind, sails he could intimately feel. He closed his eyes to let the breeze soothe the pit of anxiety that still lingered in his heart, beating around the coreflame, nothing but the sounds of a lazy ship at rest, creaking under every footstep until a purr broke the spell.

A curious Fig Stew had trotted over to check on Phainon, balancing precariously on the railing to bump his head against his warm side. He pet the chimera absentmindedly, listening to those questioning, persistent awoos rumbling low in the animal’s chest. It eased some of his surface worries, even if he still felt distant.

The blankets, neatly folded, slapped onto the barrel with a whump. “You know something like this we could have just brought to you if you had sent the little horse with a note,” Leonnius said. He scooped Fig Stew up and set the hissing chimera down on the deck before the critter could fall off the railing. The chimera was less than pleased and batted irritably at Leonnius’ ankles, but the runner wasn’t paying him any mind.

“Oh Nikador, no, I couldn’t ask anyone to make that trip. Those stairs are horrible,” Phainon tried to chuckle as he reached for the bedding. It came out dry and humorless.

“Phainon.”

“Hm?”

Leonnius put his hand on the blankets to keep him from grabbing them right away. “Are you sure everything is alright?”

The smile didn’t falter, “it will be, I’m just… discouraged. It’s been difficult trying to find the information we need.”

“Damn… well, hold out hope, yeah? You know we’re all here for you, Worldbearer or not.” Leonnius gave Phainon a gentle pat and then retrieved his rope, getting back to work with a whistle. Simple, but comforting words.

Phainon scooped up the bedding and flew back to the library.

He still took his time flying back up the cliffs, using the gentle ascent on a warm updraft to gather himself, to set aside that rage born of fear and love to replace it instead with steady trust. When Phainon’s boots touched the courtyard once more he was returning to himself. His wings and halo vanished into embers, his hair turned white once more and everything became again as it was before he took that time for himself.

The others looked up at him as he passed them by. Everyone had separated to study, searching for answers in the hope they could provide a solution that spared Mydei and by extension, Phainon. It warmed his heart that they were trying and for him that was enough. He smiled at them as he passed, genuine, reassuring, until he was walking confidently up to Mydei.

The captain’s eyes darted between Phainon and the blankets with suspicion, but he didn’t say anything, just crossed his arms and let the silence weigh heavily.

Phainon cleared his throat and finally broke the silence himself with a quiet Kremnoan, “I’m sorry. That was not like me.”

“You needed to think,” Mydei acknowledged, as close to forgiveness as Phainon was going to get.

“I did.”

“And?”

“I trust you.” Phainon held the blankets up. “I’m not leaving your body on the floor.”

Mydei blinked a few times and then smiled, just a little bit, that subtle, gentle, genuine smile that Phainon loved so much.

“Am I too heavy to hold, Deliverer?” Mydei teased.

“With that body of yours, Mydei? Absolutely,” Phainon threw back.

He set the blankets down on the bench and his smile wavered, but Mydei stepped up to kiss him and brought it back. “Thank you, Phainon. This journey will be all the smoother because of you.”

“Can we not talk about it too much?” Phainon whined as he dropped his forehead to Mydei’s shoulder. “I might change my mind.”

“No, you won’t.”

“…no, I won’t.”

The others returned when Mydei called to them and Phainon stood apart while Anaxa, Castorice, and Mydei talked. For as wild and crazy of an idea as this was, Mydei was diligent and careful. If he was going to make use of this blessed curse of immortality, he wanted to do it right.

Anaxa reviewed with Mydei all the questions he needed to ask, the things they didn’t know and the things they needed confirmed. They talked a bit about what the Imperator might be like and discussed possible means to convince her to answer his questions. Phainon could hear them talking, could hear Ptolemy weighing in, catching the things that might have been missed.

He couldn’t hear Mydei talking with Castorice and Perdikkas. That discussion was quiet, more personal. The kind of thing that Phainon probably wouldn’t understand anyway. Their relationship with Death extended beyond what Phainon had experienced, as hard as that was to believe considering his history. Curiosity itched at him while they talked but by the time it had grown too great to bear, they were pulling apart and Mydei was reaching for him.

“The others will give us space,” Mydei told him softly, pulling Phainon in close with a hand on his waist as though they were about to dance. They deviated to get the blankets and a few other things, then Mydei was leading Phainon by the hand to a quieter corner of the hall.

“This is a good spot,” Mydei hummed. He was trying to be casual about this and Phainon wondered if it was a show or not. Perhaps for Mydei, this really was nothing.

In silence they folded one of the blankets and laid it down to soften the marble beside the big statue of the Lion of Tretos. The statue was raised on a dais, just a single step that they settled beside, using the raised lip as a shelf for their supplies. Mydei set out paper and a pen, his water, and a hunting knife, then he gently guided Phainon into sitting.

He felt out of his depth here, just responding to Mydei’s confidence as he sat on the blanket and leaned against the step. Mydei took off his pauldron and set it aside, letting his chiton and half cape fall to tie them around his waist. He took off his necklace and his earring too, leaving them beside the paper. Bare chested, he sat down with his back to Phainon and lay against his boyfriend’s chest. It was exactly how Phainon had held him the night he woke up, after they had rescued him from Castrum Kremnos.

“Mydei… how…?” Phainon started to ask. His eyes followed where Mydei was reaching to grab the knife. He held it in his open palm for Phainon to take but there was hesitation, and it sat there gleaming while Mydei patiently waited.

“Not like this,” Phainon whispered.

“You have the strength for it, Deliverer, I know it,” Mydei reassured. His tone was light.

“Castorice can-”

“Her touch may send me to the end of the river not the start.”

“Perdikkas can work up a medicine-”

“It will take my body longer to reject any poison than it will take to heal a familiar wound,” Mydei interrupted gently, “this will be quick and spare you from this accursed body’s reflexive struggles.”

Phainon shakily took the knife from him and held it to the side while Mydei got comfortable. He wrapped his left arm around Mydei’s shoulders to hold him firmly against his chest and took deep breaths. Mydei’s hair tickled his nose when he buried his face in blonde locks and tried to find the courage he had a quint ago. The doubt was rising until he felt Mydei’s hand on his arm.

“Phainon,” he whispered, twisting enough to look up at him, “all will be well. Trust me above all else.”

“…I promise you; the pain will pass in an instant.”

Phainon kissed Mydei’s temple and nodded, a subtle thing that made his bangs fall forward into his eyes. He twisted the knife in his hand to free up a finger to press against Mydei’s chest, noting the gap between his ribs and the angle he would need, but when he aimed the tip of the blade above its mark it quivered, tremoring in time with his doubts. What if he missed? What if he caused Mydei more pain than necessary?

Mydei’s hand curled around his own on the handle as he pressed the point against his skin where it needed to go. The sharp point barely poked his flesh and a stubborn bead of gold welled beneath the steel.

“I’ll be right back, Phainon, it’s okay to let me go,” Mydei whispered.

Phainon’s shaky grip steadied, and the knife pierced deep, as though Phainon were trying to reach beyond his love, to stab himself too. But the blade stopped short in Mydei’s heart with a pained grunt and a resolved sigh.

“Smile for me,” he ordered in a pained whisper and Phainon obeyed the best he could. Mydei’s tattoos shimmered red as his body shuddered and slowly, smiling softly in return, he stilled.

Phainon held his breath, fighting the tears that threatened to run over. There was no need for them, he knew that. Mydei would tease him relentlessly if he woke up and saw red eyes and tear stains but when Mydei’s hand slipped and his body relaxed, quiet and lifeless, he almost couldn’t help it.

“Phainon,” Perdikkas said gently as he knelt beside him. The doctor put a hand over Phainon’s, helping him pull the knife out to set it aside. Blood trickled from the wound, but Perdikkas hurried to cover it with gauze. “Just hold him, I’ve got this part.” His steady voice was calm and experienced.

“How many times have you done this?” Phainon whispered around a shuddered breath, “waited for him to come back?”

“Too many to count,” Perdikkas admitted, “what matters is that he does come back. Always.”

Phainon tightened his grip around Mydei’s shoulders and buried his face in that golden mane mumbling gentle words of affection that Mydei couldn’t hear, determined to bear him, his whole world, until the moment he returned.

-

Waking up on the shore of the River of Souls was never the same as waking up in the living world. It was more disconnected than that, like suddenly coming to awareness inside a dream. The moment of arrival is too hazy and unimportant to remember. All focus is entirely on the now, the suddenness of standing on black sand beside dark waters. Behind him stretched endless hills of faintly glowing blue flowers punctuated by ruins of kingdoms so old they no longer had names. Isolated pillars, crumbling walls, doors to nowhere… they stood as snapshots filtered through purple light that broke up the landscape and gave lingering souls something to cower around.

Mydei recognized them as landmarks from his many trips upriver and the sight of them filled him with the comfort of knowing that their plan had worked. His soul had washed ashore precisely where he had expected it to be. Even better the lingering exhaustion of the Netherealm felt quieter this time. There was always an alluring call to give up, to wash away in the river, to surrender all memories as payment to move on to the next life, but that voice was drowned by Mydei’s purpose and connection.

“More so this time than others,” he mumbled to himself when he looked down. Attached to his hand was a golden thread. It was tied in a delicate bow around his pinky finger on his right hand, fine as spider silk, the kind of thing that was easy to miss, easy to forget, utterly invisible until someone went looking for it.

He gently took hold of the manifestation, this glimmering thing, and knew in a heartbeat what it was: a blessing from the Titan of Romance. Despite its seeming fragility, this string was as strong as the finest steel, crafted by the love between Titans to bind them through actions and affections even beyond the veil of death. The longer end stretched upriver, too far for Mydei to see, vanishing in the blackness, but when he closed his eyes and gathered the thread in both hands, he could feel Phainon’s heartbeat, could hear his soft whispers. They were bound in spirit and Mydei would have it no other way.

The wayward captain let the thread go and it happily quivered behind him, a lifeline to guide the pirate home when he was ready. The unexpected comfort made his steps lighter as he started to wander, searching his memories for the woman he saw on the banks.

Time was impossible to measure here. Mydei wasn’t sure if it even flowed at the same pace. The thought crawled under his skin like a distant itch as he wandered past faded souls and crystalized memories. The river flowed beside him so smoothly it looked like glass, but he knew from experience there was a racing current hiding beneath that steady surface. He was considering wading into those depths, a shortcut to hurry this journey along when the shine of spun gold caught his eye once more.

For a moment Mydei thought it was his thread to Phainon, waving at him, unspooled enough to tangle but when he gathered their string of fate in hand there was very little slack, not enough to explain this loose string on the breeze. His heart twisted as he considered the possibility that Phainon had somehow joined him in the Netherealm, but he discarded the thought just as quickly. Phainon was no fool and the Worldbearer would not surrender his life so casually when he held Mydei’s trust so tightly.

Mydei reached for this extra string and found it taut, stretched enough that it sang a low and mournful note when plucked. One end reached back towards life like Mydei’s did, the other flowed downriver, binding two souls through a weave of romance that extended beyond the veil of death, a love so pure that it manifested as an eternal string.

He must have swam past this thread dozens of times, unaware that it existed until now. Mydei chuckled to himself. Now that he knew what it was like to be deeply in love; to be loved so completely in return… it was hard not to see it. He took this new thread in hand and with understanding in his heart he held it close and listened.

His eyes snapped open, but he held the thread tighter. Just as he could hear Phainon’s heartbeat in his own thread there were heartbeats here too, but underneath their gentle rhythm was a song. The same song that had clung to Mydei’s spirit like muck, that turned men into monsters and poisoned the sea. A song of conquest and destruction, of longing and grief …of devotion.

Mydei chuckled to himself and started following the thread, now confident of who was on the other end.

The story of the siren knight had always been one of love.

chapters.title: Chapter 45: The Imperator
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

New Character Tag: Cerydra, Hysilens New tag: Minor or Background Relationships, Cerydra/Hysilens

Mydei meets with the Imperator

Chapter Notes

Shout out to Bane who continues to be my beta reader catching my most egregious typos before my shame can be publicly posted.

Sorry this one took an extra couple days. I deliberately picked at it slowly because I wanted to get Cerydra right and make sure I didn't miss any information. The hazard of posting chapter by chapter means I have to be REALLY careful to avoid the dreaded retcon. Fingers crossed that I didn't miss something and have to frantically edit this later. @.@

Mydei’s walk through the Netherealm was accompanied by the soundtrack of the Black Tide song and steady heartbeats. It was a strange feeling as his footsteps crunched in the sand in time with Phainon’s steady heart, listening to the song without corruption through his gentle hold on the shimmering string. The coreflame burning in his chest kept him safe from the corrosion so it was puzzling that he could hear the song at all. But the deeper Mydei got the more he realized this was the song in its purest form, without the effects of the Tide. It was a simple longing, a song sung at someone’s grave in the hopes that they would hear it through that thin veil.

For as long as she had been here, Mydei was surprised that the Imperator was not further down river. She kept to the same familiar stretch of the shore, waiting patiently in different poses beside a broken stone tower. He saw the tower first and the diminutive woman second, exactly as he remembered her.

She was sitting on a stool, sideways to a stone table with her legs crossed at the knees. One hand rested in her lap; the other was propped up at the elbow on the table so she could lean her weight into a bored expression with her knuckles pressed against her cheek. Mydei would have thought her a pouty child, but her presence carried a regal formality that demanded nothing but the finest of royal manners in her presence.

It wasn’t a feeling Mydei expected and when he finally stopped and stood a few paces away, he found himself at a loss. All his practiced approaches with Anaxa just didn’t feel right in the moment. Despite being of royal blood himself, he felt a very powerful urge to bow, to lower himself beneath the weight of her presence.

“Don’t,” she said before he could and he blinked, tense and surprised he could understand her. Even with Castorice's reassurances that the land of dead had its own language, it was still a jarring experience. She turned her head to face him. “It’s only natural to long to prostrate yourself before me, but there is no need. Come, sit, very few spirits have the courage to even consider approaching me.” Her voice was smooth and confident with a lilt of arrogance that Mydei found mildly annoying, but it was hard to resist her allure.

Her eyes were teal and glittered with sharp edges like a diamond cut by a master craftsman. They matched the ends of her hair, the blue blended so seamlessly into the silver it was as though she had dipped the ends in a blue lagoon and let it bleed. Her bangs were uneven creating layers that framed her face like the fins of a tropical fish, elegant, and desirable with the rest of her hair pulled back into two braids. They met in a ponytail that reached just past her waist, bound by a black ribbon tied in a perfect bow at her nape.

Perfect was probably the best way to describe her appearance. The tapestry had failed to do her justice, from her tall and narrow crown that flickered with blue fire, to her belled sleeves, exposed shoulders, and short dress in blue and black. Long coat tails, hung from her waist in thick ribbons, weighted by golden accents to lay gently on the sand, swept back to avoid being stepped on by her high heeled boots.

Mydei found himself unwilling to disobey and when she gestured with a hand adorned by gold and silver rings he followed where she led until he was sitting across from her at this small stone table.

“How strange,” she murmured to herself, “I feel as though I have seen you before.”

“I am no stranger to this river, Imperator,” Mydei admitted.

“’Flamecrowned,’ ‘Tyrant,’ ‘Empress,’ ‘Supreme Commander,’ ‘Imperator’ …the world has given me countless titles. Those are names for the living. You may simply call me Cerydra.”

“Cerydra,” Mydei said with a gentle nod. He rolled the name around on his tongue. Something about the way she had said it with such weight and glory, it suddenly felt foreign on his lips, like he was somehow saying it wrong. “I am Crown Prince Mydeimos of Castrum Kremnos, Inheritor of Strife.”

“Oh?” she shifted in her seat, suddenly much more interested than before, “Nikador’s nation was the only one aside from Okhema that rivaled my own. It’s curious, I would not have expected a dynasty of war to treat with Hyperborea.”

Mydei tilted his head. “Did my people treat with yours in the past?” he asked.

She pointed to his finger where the thread shimmered and then delicately held up her own to show him where she was also tied with golden string. “A gift from Dux Goldweaver, one of my most loyal generals. She designed this raiment for me as well. If you bear her mark then you must have swayed her with proof of undying love towards another. Surely you must be allies for her to witness something worthy of her blessing?”

“Imper- Cerydra, do you know what has happened to the world since your passing?”

The young woman frowned. “Crown Prince of Castrum Kremnos,” she said firmly, as though announcing him to the table, “you are not here on your final voyage, are you?”

He shook his head. “No. I am not.”

“As time has marched on in this bitter place it has become harder for me to peer into the lives of the living.” She pondered her own words and Mydei’s answer before ordering, “Speak. Tell me of the world as it is now, what has become of my legacy.”

For a moment, Mydei considered declining. He wasn’t here to tell her stories, he was here to retrieve her own, but there was a longing buried deep underneath her authority. This was not the demand of a ruling Empress; it was the genuine curiosity of someone who needed to know.

So, he told her everything.

Time passed differently in the Netherealm. Mydei wasn’t sure how long it took him to tell her about the state of Amphoreus, even keeping it concise and clinical, it took time to tell her what became of her Empire. She had studied him with a guarded expression, impossible to read, stopping him only to ask clarifying questions when his descriptions were inadequate.

She was pleased when he told her about the continuing flame-chase journey, how it had produced heroes like Phainon and powerful figures like Aglaea, and didn’t seem to mind how little of her was remembered. While his initial impression of her had come across as egotistical, the more Mydei measured her reactions and input the more he realized she didn’t equate her legacy with herself and cared more about the advancement of her intentions in life than how she was perceived by history.

Perhaps it would have been better if she had been. When he told her about the Black Tide and their theory about Hysilens as the cause, Cerydra had not responded with horror or revulsion, she seemed… happy.

“The prophecy spoke true,” she mumbled, mostly to herself. “Not that I am surprised, with or without Dux Fatorum’s words this outcome was inevitable.”

“Will you tell me of your life?” Mydei asked.

“You want to know my secrets so you and the other Demigods may put a stop to the Black Tide.” She spoke with such confidence and knowing that Mydei almost missed the question under the statement.

“I do.”

“I have no desire to help you stop the Black Tide.”

“Someone very dear to me helped me embrace this death so that I could travel here to speak with you. I am not leaving until you answer all my questions. When I return to my loved ones it will be with the answer to save the world,” Mydei told her firmly. The threat was thinly veiled but she was not intimidated.

“Save the world,” she mused. Her youthful voice pitched a little higher as she purred those words. “And what do you think the Black Tide is trying to do?”

His blood chilled as she spoke.

“You have described to me a world still at war. Your own people have been trapped in conflict since the beginning of the Kremnoan Dynasty, a conflict that continues with Okhema to this day, as you have said. The Black Tide unifies the world when humanity cannot, is this not a desirable outcome? To unite all Amphoreus under a single banner? To create a world of peace?”

“The Black Tide is anything but peace, it is death and corruption, fire and ash. Those who fall to it are stripped of their humanity and become mindless monsters… That is not peace,” Mydei argued.

“And your approach to the world is any different, Strife? Kremnoans thrive on conflict, long for combat. Can you truly claim to strive for peace when bloodlust fills your veins with pleasure?” She smiled, a cruel thing that belonged to the tyrant Mydei had read about. Her gaze was half-lidded and her cheeks uneven where her hand smooshed the one up to crinkle one of her eyes. Cerydra was watching him expectantly, like a cat with a mouse. This was a game, and she was waiting patiently for Mydei to make his move so she could take another one of hers.

He contemplated carefully, trying to consider what he could say that might sway her. Phainon would have already had the right words. That master wordsmith would have loved a debate like this. All Mydei had was his honesty; sometimes that was enough.

“Imperator Cerydra,” he finally said, using the title despite her earlier disregard for it as a show of respect, “now that I have accepted my coreflame and ascended to divinity I better understand the meaning and purpose of Strife. What you have said sings true, my heart glories in combat. It was combat and conflict that made me who I am, and it was where I fell in love. It is because of strife that I have come to value the things in my life that I want to protect and seen those relationships grow strong.” He paused to look at the thread around his finger. “My relationship with Phainon is one example. We were enemies and our allyship was forged in fire and tested in strife. I cannot say if we would have found each other if our peoples were not at war… The world needs conflict, it is how humanity grows and comes to understanding in pursuit of a lasting peace, one worthy of defending.”

Mydei moved his hand to join the other in his lap, resting over his knees in loosely closed fists. “The Black Tide does not allow for growth or understanding. There is no reconciliation, no choice, no life worth living. I know from stories that your life’s ambition was to conquer all Amphoreus, to unite her people beneath one banner, but I also know that you value the rule of law and are fair above all else. As the Inheritor of Law, surely you see the injustice of this campaign.”

Cerydra’s smile never wavered, she never seemed to lose the upper hand. Even when Mydei felt like he had made the right move, said the right thing, she looked like she had expected it. “An injustice?” she crooned. “And what injustice is there in my legacy?”

“Hysilens,” Mydei said simply and Cerydra’s smile cracked. “The song that furthers your ambition is one of grief and loss. She is described as the dutiful knight, how is it fair that she must shrug aside her own desires to bear yours alone? Is it not a joy of being in love that one may shoulder the burdens of their lover beside them? I am Kremnoan, we weigh the scales differently than the Northern Kingdoms. If I am wrong, then please, educate me.”

The Imperator leaned back to sit straighter, her hand falling into her lap where she looked down, playing with the string that was tied around her pinky.

When she was slow to respond, Mydei gently asked, “Can you hear it?”

“Yes,” she said softly, for the first time, Mydei thought she may show a fleeting vulnerability. It passed quickly and she tilted her head back again, carrying herself with that same regality. “Very well, Crown Prince of Kremnos, I will tell you whatever you would like to know.”

“You will help us defeat the Tide?”

“I care not about the Black Tide,” Cerydra reiterated, “…but my Dux Gladiorum has served me endlessly for a thousand years and not once has she come to give me her report. I don’t like to be kept waiting.”

Mydei took a deep breath through his nose to tame his excitement as he tried to remember what he was supposed to ask about.

“The siren song,” he invited, “how does it work?”

“Simple, the fantasia is an illusion.”

“Does it work on Chrysos Heirs?”

“Of course it does.”

That tracked with what they had hypothesized. “It didn’t work on you.”

Cerydra’s smug smile was back. “It works on all Chrysos Heirs.”

“How were you able to spy on your allies without being seen? Or dance in front of the bards in secret?”

“A sea siren’s fantasia is one of temptation, but it is still only an illusion. Anyone can break free of the dream if they have the will to navigate its labyrinthian charm. A true leader always knows what they want and how to gain an advantage with the tools they have available to them. The answer will vary for everyone but simply knowing you are under the spell is the first step towards gaining an advantage.”

Cerydra talked with her hands. Mydei’s eyes kept darting down to follow them when she slowly waved on long sentences. The way she was speaking each movement felt deliberate, hypnotic, and his battle instincts had him on edge.

His eyes flitted back to hers and he tried to match her bored expression, hiding from her his every reaction. “Why did you start the flame-chase journey?”

“Because it was my duty,” she told him simply, “do you believe in the importance of bloodlines, Crown Prince?”

Mydei shook his head firmly. “I have seen great leaders, wise men, and noble spirits come from humble backgrounds. The Inheritor of Worldbearing is the son of farmers, whereas I am the son of Kings, we stand happily on equal ground, as it should be.”

“The Kingdom of Hyperborea did,” Cerydra told him, “the chaos that surrounded the death of their childless monarch led the people to hunt for any willing puppet that could play the role of a lost heir. It was the steward that plucked me from the people. My hair and golden blood matched that of the late royal family, and he saw in me a puppet through which he could retain power.” She reached up to play with a long strand of hair that fell over her shoulder, entwining it around her pointer finger. It didn’t feel like nervous tick when she did it, the way Mydei sometimes fussed with his braid when he was anxious. Everything Cerydra did was calculated and deliberate.

“The fool could not have known when he brought me to the palace that the treasure of the late King would choose me.”

“The Coreflame of Law,” Mydei filled in when she paused for dramatic effect.

“As the Demigod of Law, it was easy to see where the scales were imbalanced. Executing the steward and his family was my first decree as newly ascended divinity.”

Kremnoans came from a culture steeped in blood but something about the way she said it didn’t sit right with him. She spoke of them so casually but there was an underlying glee hidden in her voice. To her, lives were just there to be measured, to be weighed. Each victory was celebrated and pocketed, every question to her authority removed swiftly and without mercy.

“You have inherited a coreflame as well, Crown Prince,” she noted, sounding a little lighter but then her voice subtly dropped again, weighty when she added, “you know the responsibility we carry.”

He grunted and crossed his arms across his chest, maintaining eye contact the whole time. It was his subtle attempt to stay on equal ground with her, to meet her as a fellow monarch, but Mydei knew they were not the same. He was a runaway king, contemplating the elimination of his Dynasty and she was an Empress, the greatest conqueror in recorded history.

“When I became the Demigod of Law and began my campaign to unite the Northen Kingdoms the Demigod of Janus came to me bearing the weight of prophecy.
