My new Dux Fatorum, bearing that divine edict told me exactly what needed to be done. As the prophecy says, rewrite the fabric of Law, that the world may know order. As the only one that could accomplish such a feat, duty compelled me and as I contemplated those words I realized, corruption of the Titans was inevitable. Every catastrophe that has befallen the world has come from a Titan surrendering to their inner desires over the mandate given them by their coreflame. It is only a matter of time before they lose themselves and must be stopped. The prophecy warns as much, the power of the coreflames is to doom the world or save it. Only united and safely controlled under one rule could such power be used responsibly for the greater good.”

Mydei’s brows crinkled, enough that even this stranger noticed. Cerydra tilted her head at his reaction.

“Do you disagree?” she prodded, genuinely curious.

“I do not, you are proof of your own words, Imperator Cerydra,” Mydei pointed out, “the catastrophe of the flame-chase journey came about because you surrendered to your inner desires.”

Cerydra’s smile remained but her gaze hardened.

“As I have already said, the flame-chase has changed in these one thousand years,” Mydei told her, “The Lady Goldweaver still seeks the coreflames, hiding them away until their bearers are ready. Many consider her a hoarder of power but this voyage with Phainon has taught me much about the nature of divinity.”

He paused to study Cerydra, wondering if this was all he’d be allowed for his turn, but she did not respond and he continued.

“’Coreflames grant wishes,’” Mydei quoted, “Phainon told us these were the words of the Lady Trianne, one of the Holy Maidens of Janus, who further emphasized that while coreflames choose their bearers, those bearers must be ready before they ascend. Now that I have spoken with you, I see why the Goldweaver and Holy Maiden keep those gathered coreflames from their Demigods until they are pure-hearted and good.”

“Pure-hearted and good,” Cerydra repeated, mildly surprised. She was mulling over his implications, that she had not been ready to ascend and had come to the Coreflame of Law already corrupted. Perhaps it was more subtle than the rolling Black Tide, perhaps some good still came of her conquests. In a time of turmoil, Cerydra had been what her people needed, but it didn’t change that weighted truth.

“Imperator… Cerydra,” Mydei continued with a firm voice, “do you love her?”

The question came as a shock and a flicker of annoyance passed across her gaze like a shadow before she huffed. “A foolish question, as Imperator I love all my loyal subjects.” The thread around her finger glimmered, giving her away but Mydei didn’t call her on her deflection.

“Then surely it grieves you that Hysilens has spent the last thousand years alone in mourning.”

Cerydra raised her hand to look at the thread. Mydei couldn’t hear the song from where he was sitting but he knew she could. He pressed his advantage.

“How did you die?” he asked. “History says that it was your Dux Gladiorum that killed you.”

“History speaks true,” Cerydra confirmed, somewhat distracted. Her voice was softer around the edges, but the confidence remained. “It was my final order to her.”

Mydei’s heart started to race. “Why?”

Cerydra stood up with the soft sound of crunching sand and Mydei blinked away his surprise. She wasn’t much taller standing as she had been sitting. With both hands on the stone table and her spine as straight as a mast, Cerydra was still shorter than Mydei while he was sitting.

His grip on his elbows loosened, Mydei’s body coiled like a spring, ready to strike if she went on the attack but the feeling passed when this young woman turned away entirely. She stepped away from the table to face the river, searching for something there that Mydei realized she had been looking for all along. The water lapped near her shoes, but she stood just out of reach.

“Because I genuinely believed once that it was the right thing to do,” she admitted, and this no longer felt like a match between royals.

Cerydra bowed her head, an action that felt unnatural to Mydei as an observer. For the first time since their meeting, Cerydra seemed genuinely vulnerable. He considered moving to her side to comfort her, but Mydei didn’t want to insult her pride. So instead, he waited patiently for the moment to pass, letting her return to this moment in her own time, determined instead to simply listen.

“My court held five Demigods,” she told him when she straightened, “myself, Dux Fatorum, Dux Goldweaver, the great dromas king, Terravox, and Dux Gladiorum. I turned my armies towards Oronyx, the Titan of Time and led the march myself to demand the coreflame. They refused and instead offered council in the form of a prophecy that shook me to my very bones. We returned to Hyperborea without the Coreflame of Time, only the weight of those words.”

Cerydra turned in place to face him from the beach. There was a shine to her eyes that he didn’t expect, that felt unnatural and misplaced.

“The world may bow to a single banner, but you cannot live to see it,” she quoted and Mydei thought that end of it until she added the second path presented to the monarch by Oronyx, “abandon this conquest and know a life of love.”

“You chose the former,” he realized aloud.

“Of course,” Cerydra said, casual, “it was my duty and lifelong ambition. The life of a single Demigod weighed against the peace of all the world; what worthy ruler would not make that same decision? To sacrifice themselves for the ones they love?”

Mydei understood without hesitation. After all, he had done the same.

“I confided in my most trusted knight, the woman I loved, Helektra, my intentions. She pleaded with me to find another way, but the prophecy left no room for debate. If the flame-chase journey was to continue, if Amphoreus was to be united at last, then the scales needed to be balanced. I entrusted my duty to her and ordered her to carve the Coreflame of Law from my chest. She held me while I died, her blade in my heart.”

The stone seat beneath him felt a little too cold but Mydei dared not move. He could feel between them eerie parallels, with notable differences. Had he not just died in Phainon’s arms with a blade in his chest? But they were in this together, Cerydra and her love were not. Cerydra had the choice to live with her love and decided against it. True to both prophecies, the world would be doomed, united under one banner.

“That was her name,” Cerydra continued, rambling with her same confident enunciation as though addressing a mass of people, but that soft remained along the edges of her tone. “Hysilens was the moniker given to her when she walked from the sea but as a siren, among her own people, her name was Helektra. She was the perfect choice for the Coreflame of Ocean. Phagousa was the Titan of banquets, feasts, and celebrations, the creator of honey brew. Helektra understood and loved the Law, perhaps in a more brutal and instinctual way than I ever could, even as its bearer, but she also loved fire and music, good wine and good company.”

“The Coreflame of Ocean is no longer about celebration,” Mydei told her harshly, “how can it be? She has assumed your duty, as you requested, and her love for you has turned into a vicious wave that denies humanity any chance of a joyous tomorrow.”

“Command the tides of the Ocean, that the world may revel in song,” Cerydra quoted, “she is living the mandate of the prophecy… but it is not the song she wants to sing.”

“Her corruption will destroy the world,” Mydei agreed, “and herself.”

“It already has,” Cerydra admitted, “the moment I gave her the burden of my duty.”

“Imperator, your legacy lives on in other ways. The Goldweaver’s flame-chase has already begun uniting the world, not by erasure of identity, but by bonds much stronger than any mandate.”

Mydei stood and walked to her, holding his hand low to offer her the string that tied him to Phainon. She crossed her arms at first, refusing to budge as he approached and declining to take him up on his offer. The commanding aura was back, her feelings tucked neatly away once more as he waited patiently for her to reach out to pinch the golden thread between her pointer and middle fingers.

“The heart that beats in this thread is from a little town that was destroyed by the Black Tide. Phainon of Aedes Elysiae was taken in by the Goldweaver and became the Deliverer of Okhema, their golden son, destined to be the Worldbearer. He should be the natural enemy of Castrum Kremnos and for a time we were, but now we are bound even beyond the veil of death. It was your legacy that brought us together, your flame-chase journey, helmed by the woman who picked up your greater legacy. The rest of our people deserve the chance to learn what we have found between the two of us, to celebrate our differences as allies with song, dance, good wine, and good company.”

Cerydra closed her eyes to listen to that heartbeat while he talked, and they sparkled when she opened them again. “I suppose the continuance of the flame-chase is legacy enough.”

“When I return, I will sing your praises myself,” Mydei promised.

She scoffed and let go to cross her arms again. “I would rather be forgotten than defined... For better or worse, my legacy has already borne fruit. My flame-chase journey is working as intended, uniting the world. There is no need to assign credit.”

Cerydra let go of the string and crossed her arms again. “You have found a way to counter the effects of the Black Tide itself, have you not? Because it is the result of a coreflame’s power I assume you have used golden blood or fight exclusively alongside Chrysos Heirs to spare your men from the corruption? You said it transforms?”

Mydei blinked. Perhaps he shouldn’t have been so surprised that she put the pieces together so quickly. This was the woman that started the war against the gods, and the woman most familiar with the siren song.

“Yes, Professor Anaxagoras, the Inheritor of Reason, believes that the Coreflame of Ocean is turning the fantasia into reality.”

“This is why you asked me about the song,” she pieced together.

“Yes.”

“Then the answer is simple, is it not?” Her hand moved from her chin into a dismissive wave. “She is as any other corrupted Titan, take her coreflame and the Black Tide will cease to be.”

“You make it seem so simple,” Mydei deadpanned.

Cerydra’s smug smirk was back, “as a fellow monarch and leader of armies, you understand as well as I that sometimes the answer is that simple.”

“A simple answer does not mean a simple resolution.”

“No, and my Dux Gladiorum is an army unto herself, loyal to her final breath. She will defend my will with the force of the ocean she commands,” Cerydra cautioned, “but you are many Demigods, surely this fight will be a challenge, but it is not impossible to secure victory.”

Mydei recalled the fight with the kraken, that extension of the Tide that kept him isolated and engaged for nearly a month. Phainon and Hyacine had startled it into a retreat but how much more powerful was this Demigod up close?

“What if we had no need to fight?” Mydei wondered aloud. Cerydra studied him, visibly bored but he could feel the hum of anticipation around her as close as they were. “Could she be convinced to surrender her coreflame?”

“Dux Gladiorum answers to no one but herself.”

“She would answer her Imperator,” Mydei countered.

“Her Imperator is dead.”

“Then tell me what to say.”

Cerydra paused then, mulling that over in her head. He could see it in the subtle twitch of her finger, the way her eyes would flick from side to side as she took the idea and ran it through calculations in her head.

“If she is herself,” Cerydra reasoned, “then that may work.”

The possibility that Hysilens had lost her sanity, her ability to hear reason, lingered in the air between them.

“For a time after my death, I could see the world through our bond, but that connection has faded over time,” the Imperator admitted, “I have long wondered if it is because our love had dwindled, or if something else had happened to her. Sirens live long lives and Helektra was a Demigod, the Inheritor of Ocean on top of her increased lifespan. To sing for so long…”

“You’re worried about her,” Mydei observed.

Cerydra paused to consider her words carefully before saying, “she has been alone for a very long time.”

“So have you, but the thread still binds you.” He pointed to the thread, and she twisted her hand in the air, back and forth in a slow arc to see the thread glimmer. It was just as bright as the one around his own pinky. “I have heard her song. It is meant for you.”

Cerydra hummed. “Tell her that this song bores me. I would much prefer something lighter, befitting a joyous reunion over a drink of Divine Dew.”

“Divine Dew?” Mydei asked, worried that her message might not be specific enough.

“As a King, I must bear the weight of every move on the board. Indulging myself in honey brew would only lead to a total defeat. As such, I couldn’t drink with her in celebration after each conquest. After we retrieved the Coreflame of Ocean, I offered her a single wish, anything that was within my power to grant. She wished to share with me a drink of Divine Dew, a once-in-a-millennium vintage when we had laid aside our conquest and could finally rest in the new age that we created.”

Mydei considered that thoughtfully and then nodded with a soft smile. “I will tell her when we find her and let her know that you are waiting for her.”

“Have you found her?” Cerydra asked very suddenly and Mydei’s smile dropped, answering her question. “You have not…”

“It is only recently that we have even determined the source of the Tide is a Demigod and the Black Tide makes it difficult to search for her.”

Cerydra tapped her fingers and then announced, “then you must go to the heart of my fallen Kingdom. When our connection was stronger, I could feel the cold of the ocean as if it were ice. She will have retreated to those depths where her song is strongest.”

“Will she not have gone home? To where her kin may be?” Mydei asked.

“Home is not always where one was born. From your tale, you must know this better than I, Monarch of Kremnos,” she scolded, “can you not say with absolute certainty that your home is not beside your beloved? She will be near the place that meant the most to us, the beach where we first met on the shores of Hyperborea.”

That was a long voyage, one full of complications, but it was a start.

“Thank you,” Mydei said genuinely, “this victory will belong to you as much as it will to us.”

“Of course it will,” she huffed, letting her arms fall so she could put a hand on her hip. “I have never known loss, even in death I am not about to start.”

“Respectfully, I don’t think that’s true, Cerydra,” Mydei said gently, with a bow of his head, “to love is to lose and you wear proof of your love eternally on your hand.”

However, she felt about that, Cerydra wouldn’t say. She turned away with a huff. “Do you not have a task to complete, Crown Prince? Once one has spoken their peace, one should leave decisively.”

“You will not be alone much longer, Cerydra, I promise.”

“A leader is always alone; there is no room for anyone else at the top.”

Cerydra spoke with such finality that Mydei didn’t have the heart to respond. He left without further words but in his heart he disagreed. With a little bit of work and a little bit of love, Mydei was sure there was room enough for two.

-

His boots crunched in the sand as Mydei walked upriver, away from the waiting monarch, content to hurry back to Phainon while he mulled over what he had learned. His boyfriend’s heartbeat was slow and steady, relaxed through the thread, sending him strength and stability with every step.

“Awoo!”

Mydei’s head shot up, puzzled when he heard the little howl, eyes scanning the horizon. Perhaps he had imagined it. Not once had he seen a chimera in the land of the dead. Castorice had spoken of them as messengers, he assumed that such special creatures were kept apart from humanity to serve a greater calling.

So, when Mydei heard a happy and familiar chirp once more, he stopped and turned to look again. Orange and white fur bounded through the antila flowers that lined the sandy beach, disturbing them to race towards Mydei. He paused briefly, easily distracted, to sniff at a rock with his ears pert and his tail wiggling, before he remembered his master. Bright red eyes blinked at Mydei eagerly as he trotted through the black sand to plant himself happily at the captain’s feet.

“Fig?”

“Awoo!”

Chapter End Notes

“Is that a cat? …Is that MY cat???” - Bane

chapters.title: Chapter 46: The Son of Gorgo
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

No new tags

Mydei meets a familiar face in the Netherealm

Chapter Notes

I completely forgot, we hit 1k kudos before the last chapter! As a thanks for all the support I am willing to take post-fic requests for additional content!

A few rules:

When Fig Stew planted his little butt in the sand and looked up at Mydei expectantly, the Kremnoan wasn’t immediately sure how to react. Several feelings tumbled through him on a loop, none of them sticking and none of them showing on his face as he studied the chimera.

His scaled tail was wagging, eyes bright, ears forward, no signs of distress. Mydei could feel Phainon’s heartbeat through the thread and it was still calm, too fast to be sleeping but still at rest. Of course, Fig Stew was on the ship last he checked and Phainon was at the library. Did the Chryseus Leo come under attack?

“Are you dead?” he asked very pointedly.

Fig Stew shook his head.

Well, that was a relief. Chimeras in general were very intelligent creatures, and Fig was one of the smartest. Mydei had no reason to assume the creature didn’t understand the question and he had every reason to believe the response. It quieted a little bit of the inner turbulence that was nibbling on his insides.

“Is everyone okay?” Mydei asked next.

Fig Stew nodded.

That was good but it also explained absolutely nothing. The chimera couldn’t speak in a language that Mydei would understand so his inquiries would be limited. Asking why Fig was there wasn’t going to do any good but standing around asking dozens of questions was wasting time. Then again, the Netherealm was supposed to equalize all languages... did that include chimera speak?

“Why did you come here?”

Fig Stew stood up with a purr. He gave himself a full body shake to free himself of sand and started trotting up the hill into the sea of flowers. Mydei followed without further questioning.

Antila flowers softened every one of Mydei’s footsteps, turning the volume down on the already muted sounds of the Netherealm. It made Mydei feel exposed. Swimming upriver after every death came with an inherent turmoil. With the flow of disturbed water racing against his skin and ears, the fight back to life had always felt loud with the pound of blood and urgency. Standing on the shore was peaceful, a stillness that could only be described as quiet but not silent.

The flowers demanded silence. The babble of a River, however still, was sound that these blooms devoured. Mydei’s creaking armor and Fig Stew’s purrs, felt like unwelcome disturbances and his battle instincts loathed the implication. Souls took notice, turning to watch them pass by in various states of decay. Some were no more than shadows, others, like Cerydra had been, were still holding to their stagnation tightly enough to still look solid and whole.

Fig Stew was either oblivious to the way they turned to watch or didn’t care. He trudged along with his tail held high, the tip of it bouncing above the flowers just like his fluffy ears. The chimera didn’t detour at all on this sacred task but even traveling in a straight line it felt like they were taking time to reach wherever this creature longed to go.

If Mydei stayed down here too long, would his death be made permanent? The thread around his finger thrummed, reassuring, but Mydei still wondered if there was a timer on his immortality, one that he could not see. The realization that he could make that choice revolted him, there were people who needed him, people he needed, but from a practical curiosity about his cursed body… Was his weak spot, truly the only way to kill Mydeimos the Undying? Or could he be undone by exhaustion, a failing of stubbornness, or grief?

The thought dashed against the shore of his love and splintered into nothing at the same time Fig Stew mewled. He glanced down at those wide, slow-blinking eyes and then followed them up to another ruin of a bygone age.

It may have been the base of a watchtower at one point, Mydei recognized the structure of early Kremnoan architecture, but the bulk of the walls had long since collapsed and failed to make the journey. All that remained of them was a partial curve, too crumbled to rise to any noble height, but enough to allow for some privacy within the circle of stone floor and scraps of furniture.

There were two people there, sitting on giant stone bricks that had fallen from the wall in an age long past. One was a man that Mydei had never seen before with very short dark brown hair and stubble along his jawline and chin. He had dark eyes that softened when Mydei approached above a gentle, albeit very tired smile. Light armor adorned his lean frame, the standard tunic and bronze of the Okheman Navy, but he wore the gold cuffs and rich blue and gold chlamys of an officer.

Fig Stew bounded in leaps to the second person, throwing himself into her arms so hard that she almost fell over with a booming laugh that cut through Mydei with nostalgia sharp enough to leave his eyes wet with budding tears. He knew that laugh, that bright smile, and especially those amber, leonine eyes.

Mother? He was afraid to say it aloud lest she vanish like a mirage on water. His feet very suddenly felt heavy, rooted among the antilas, afraid to take that final step up onto the stonework.

Gorgo was ethereal and beautiful, a true Queen of Kremnos and daughter of Strife. Strength coiled in her arms and legs, muscles lean but defined. It radiated from her in the way she carried herself, head high, back straight, armor gleaming bronze under red and black fabric. And her face… the way her hair framed her face, wild and chopped, uneven and somehow so natural was a mane that settled on her shoulders. Some of it had been braided over her right shoulder, careful, even, and locked in place by a bronze aglet. It was a look that Mydei saw every time he saw his reflection in a mirror, in the water, and now here. The same chin, narrow, leonine eyes, long lashes, curved nose, and her voice rumbled with a deep purr straight from his memories.

“What keeps you, Mydeimos?” she teased. Her voice was confident, deep compared to the other women in his life, like a war drum, stirring the blood to action with every syllable. “Have you no words for your mother?”

Still stunned, Mydei slowly closed his mouth. He hadn’t realized his lips had parted in the first place and when he opened them again, no sound came out. His whole body was trying to process the surge of emotions that had piled up behind the dam.

She held Fig Stew up above her head with both hands under his little arms and he purred so loudly the flowers could not hope to dampen the reverberation. His paws reached for her, making biscuits in the air while his tail wagged like one of Peucesta’s metronomes.

“I should be proud,” she told Fig Stew, “that my son, like all great warriors, has outgrown me!”

“Awoo!”

“Mother, I-”

“BUT ALAS, MY HEART ACHES FOR MY SON. IT IS THE CURSE OF ALL MOTHERS TO LONG FOR THEIR WAYWARD CHILDREN,” she said loudly over him.

“Awoo!” Fig agreed and she laughed and bounced the chimera once before cradling him like a baby on his back to rub his tummy while he purred and made biscuits in the air.

Mydei could feel the dam inside him crack and when he finally took a step, it broke. The weight that had chained him to the ground snapped and he rushed to her. She barely had time to set aside Fig Stew and stand before Mydei’s arms were tight around her shoulders and he was racked with tearless sobs. Her arms wrapped around his torso, tight around him, grounding while he pressed his cheek to the side of her head, surprised to find such warmth from her spirit.

It was Gorgo who pulled away first and Mydei had to force himself with great difficulty to let go.

“You have grown,” she observed with pride. She put her hand on his cheek, her eyes darting back and forth as she took him in. Gorgo was not a small woman, but she still had to tilt her head to meet his eye.

A soft sound cut through the moment, the man had cleared his throat and was watching them with a sympathetic, albeit somewhat awkward smile. The sort of expression one saves for reluctant gestures.

Mydei shot this stranger a glare, but Gorgo was unbothered. She let her hand slip from Mydei’s cheek to his shoulder, then to his bicep to give him a reassuring squeeze. “I have not forgotten about you, Marcus,” she told the man without looking at him.

Gorgo pulled away from Mydei and took his hand, pulling him towards the Okheman even as her eyes drank him in with the discerning eye of a parent checking that their adult child was eating well. “As overjoyed as I am to see you, my son, I did not send for you just so you could wile away precious time with your mother.”

Fig Stew had jumped onto Gorgo’s seat, waiting patiently in a sit to be acknowledged by the Queen. Mydei noted the chimera as he was led. “Then Fig Stew led me here to-”

“Mydeimos,” she said. It was a command from a matriarch and Mydei’s eyes snapped to her before he could think any further along that line of thought. “This is Marcus and he must speak to you.”

The Okheman had a hand extended in greeting, waiting patiently while Mydei considered it. He was still so overwhelmed it took him a moment to reciprocate, clasping the man’s arm in a mutual shake.

“It is an honor, Marcus,” Mydei hummed politely, perhaps a little shallow.

“The honor is mine, Prince Mydeimos,” the man said lightly. He had a friendly air about him that reminded Mydei of Phainon. The kind of friendly that held onto a handshake for far longer than one should. “For a long time, I lamented that I would not be able to thank you.”

“Thank me?” The confusion was impossible to hide.

“For killing me.”

Mydei recoiled as though burned, taking a shuffled step backwards and letting go of Marcus with suspicion in every movement. It was the sincerity with which he said it that made the shock so much worse. Marcus was smiling as he said it and now Mydei was searching his brain for this man he simply did not remember.

Gorgo’s eyes glittered and she patted Mydei’s shoulder. “I will leave you two to talk. Peace, my son, I will not go far.”

Mydei relaxed with her reassurances but the spring in his gut was still wound tight and when she stepped away that coiled tension spread to his arms and legs, leaving him standing stiff and wary. “I’m sorry,” he told Marcus, “I don’t remember you.”

The man laughed, a short awkward thing, “Haha, that’s fine, Prince, I didn’t expect you to. When we fought I was newly changed.”

The coil turned to dread as it wrapped Mydei’s heart in chilling ice. “Changed?”

“By the Black Tide.” Perhaps it was in response to the look on Mydei’s face, but Marcus pressed a hand to his chest, the same way Phainon did when he was nervous, and tucked his head. “Ah, I’m sorry, I know this is a lot and not at all why you came here. Queen Gorgo said that you may not have been able to come at all so to stand before you with this opportunity… it’s easy to forget that you do not know me as well as I know you.”

“You know me?”

“From the stories your mother has told. Her connection to the world of the living is much stronger than mine you see. She has been comforting me with tales,” he explained. “Um, please sit, and I will do my best to better explain why it was so important that I thank you.”

It took Mydei a second to take a seat, settling where his mother had been before. She was in the flowers now, chasing Fig Stew with a child-like demeanor. Frolicking in the flowers with a chimera was not something he expected from his mother, but she somehow managed it without compromising her disciplined and regal demeanor. It set Mydei at ease to see her smile.

“She is a remarkable woman,” Marcus said gently and Mydei realized he had been staring.

“She is,” he agreed, pleasantly warm with the realization that Marcus said is and not was. He turned to Marcus then to give the Okheman his full attention and the man smiled, taking the body language as the invitation that it was.

“I was the First Mate of the Speeding Sol,” Marcus explained, “serving under Captain Phainon.”

Mydei’s eyes widened a hair and again that tightness in his chest returned. “You were on the ship the night we rescued Phainon from the water.”

A subtle nod. “I followed my Captain onto the corrupted ship and succumbed to the Black Tide.” Marcus’s hands were on his knees, slowly closing into tight fists. “It happened so fast. It’s hard to remember images but the feelings are branded onto my soul. The determination that I had to follow my captain into combat meant nothing in the face of the Tide’s overwhelming grief and despair. There was a moment before the change when the song burrowed deep, permeating my bones with absolute loss and grief so painful that my legs trembled until I fell. It was a longing that I have not felt since the day I kissed my wife and son goodbye to embark on the voyage that led to my death. You have heard the song too, right?”

Mydei nodded but said nothing, letting the man continue.

“I wept when I heard it and then screamed when it took over my body. The song is loud and all-encompassing, so I hope it makes sense when I tell you I felt the sound of my bones breaking and my head bursting, more than I heard it.” Marcus shook his head. “I am sure you have seen the change before… what I need you to know, most of all, is that the transformation is not death. What is left behind is not mindless. We become ghosts trapped in a shell that is no longer our own, but the person is still there, buried under the agony.”

Mydei resisted the urge to shudder, steeling himself to listen.

“We are driven to madness by the song that preys on our grief, filling us with a desperate loneliness that drives every movement with a frantic need to spread so we will not be alone any longer,” he paused and shame crept into the tremor of his voice. “When I turned, I saw my Captain disappear below deck and after thrashing through the transformation I set out in pursuit of him, with every intention of killing the Deliverer, because the song told me that was the only way I could obey my oath to him. A part of me knew that was wrong, screamed from behind the bars of this new prison that I did not want to do that, but my body moved without me. It was your claws in my throat, breaking through the deck of that burning ship, that freed my spirit from those chains.”

Mydei vaguely remembered that. There had been an elite Black Tide monster on the deck of that merchant vessel when the Chryseus Leo turned around and rammed Phainon’s ship. The corruption had spread so quickly… It had been unprecedented even in the detachment’s experience. He remembered the urgency with which they moved cargo from the merchant ship as the Black Tide swelled in the water below. And how surprised they all were to find a survivor in the wreckage.

“It is because of this experience that my thanks comes with a hopeful request,” Marcus pleaded. “The other Black Tide monsters… they are in pain. Even if there was a way to return them to humanity, their madness would surely persist. All that is left for them is a half-life of agony. Please, Inheritor of Strife, save them from this horror they are forced to endure.”

Marcus’ request was accompanied by a bowed head and hands pressed together as though praying. He was a devout pilgrim, sitting beside the divine, humble and with nothing to offer in sacrifice aside from his hope and faith.

“I am not your god, Okheman,” Mydei said, he tried to sound fierce and commanding, but it came out with too much awe and worry.

“No, you are not,” Marcus admitted, “but I place my faith in Strife all the same… Strife and the Deliverer.”

This wasn’t the kind of request that Mydei was comfortable accepting implicitly, not when there were already so many unknowns. They still had to stop the Black Tide from spreading before they could consider the clean-up, but perhaps there was some comfort in thinking ahead. Only hopeful people looked past the trials of tomorrow, planning beyond the frightful horizon to something brighter.

“If not I,” Mydei promised with a hand over his chest, “then the other Demigods. I will tell them what you have told me.”

“Thank you,” Marcus looked back up at Mydei with a grateful smile and then opened his mouth to speak again, but he hesitated.

“Have you more to say?” Mydei invited.

“It’s my captain,” Marcus explained.

“Phainon?”

“Yes. I have admired him for some time, and I worry that he may be harboring some guilt for what happened to the Sol and her crew,” he explained. “Will you tell him that we forgive him?”

Mydei’s heart twisted again at the thought of Phainon. “…that does sound like him,” he agreed.

“And will you ask him to…” More hesitation as Marcus swallowed, “ask him to forgive Xenia.”

“Xenia?” Mydei asked with a tilt of his head.

“She is my wife,” he explained. “And she has treated him terribly since my passing.”

This was news to Mydei, but it wasn’t a surprise. Phainon had gone off on his own the night they went to Okhema, and Mydei couldn’t possibly know every detail of when they had returned to the Holy City without him. The Deliverer was the kind of person that would seek to comfort the families of his fallen crew, to take responsibility no matter the circumstances.

Mydei nodded and then asked, “Would you like me to take a message to your wife?”

Marcus shook his head. “I love her and have been keeping my eye on her as best I can but… any message I send with you she will either reject or cling to with such fervor that she will never heal. For the sake of our son, she needs to let me go.”

“You are afraid that if you give her sign, she will never stop searching for them,” Mydei concluded.

“Yes,” Marcus whispered.

“I understand.”

“Thank you for hearing me, Prince Mydeimos. I will not keep you any longer.” He stood and offered his hand again, clasping Mydei’s arm with firm recognition when Mydei got to his feet and met the gesture. “She shrugs you away and speaks of wiling away the time, but I know she wants to speak to you too.” Marcus’ smile was warm when he gestured with a nod towards Queen Gorgo sitting among the flowers while Fig Stew headbutted under her chin to cuddle. She leaned in and whispered something into the chimera’s ear and they laughed together at whatever secret they shared.

“It was an honor, Marcus,” Mydei said genuinely.

Another nod and Marcus let go. “I will give you some privacy,” he half-mumbled. Before Mydei could say anything further, he turned and walked away, already fading. Perhaps he would linger for a time like these other spirits, Mydei couldn’t say for sure, but it was not his place to judge so he respectfully turned away.

It was then that Gorgo turned her eyes to him again, smiling a toothy grin. She sat among the flowers as Mydei walked to her, trying not to shake as he relished this moment. Every little tilt of her head, the way her fingers brushed over Fig Stew’s sides, the sound of her hum as he very slowly walked to her… Mydei wanted to sear it into his memory.

“He is a good man,” she said, nodding to where Marcus had been. “I am glad you spoke with him.”

Mydei gently lowered himself to his knees beside her and she reached out to yank him down to sit so that their shoulders were touching. It startled him into silence and she laughed.

“If I did not know better I would worry at your timidness! Is this really my son?”

“Forgive me mother, I did not expect to see you again,” he admitted.

“Mydeimos,” Gorgo tsked. She took his hand to hold in both of hers. “I have never left you.”

Fig Stew barked once and then wiggled into the space between them.

“Castorice said that someone was watching over me, that those who have died who harbor strong wills may use mediums to reach out. All this time, Fig Stew was-”

“My messenger, yes,” she told him cheerfully, “through him, I have had the honor of watching you grow into a man that I am proud to call my son.”

Mydei chuckled and scratched between Fig’s ears. “Krateros has been trusting him as though he were you. How right the old man was.”

“Krateros is a good man,” she agreed.

“Mother,” Mydei swallowed, the weight of his curiosity made his chest tight, “how are you here?”

“I have always been here Mydeimos. Do you not remember? I suppose those memories must feel as dreams to you now. You were so very young.”

He shook his head. “I remember my youth and I am grateful to have had you to raise me while I grew in the Sea of Souls along this river, but Nikador’s blade…?”

“Eurypon’s treachery,” she said darkly, “neither of us were worthy upon our deaths to fight by Nikador’s side.”

“Have you not considered moving on?” Mydei asked, mildly afraid of the answer.

“I have, but I wanted to see what became of my son. You were a little thing when you were born, Mydeimos. Your cry was so fragile and ethereal. Eurypon and I could never have imagined that such a feeble cry would come from our child. But Nikador’s own battle cry resonated with yours, and suddenly your newborn mewlings were as crystal-clear resonant as the roar off the Tretos lion. There was no denying it: you are of pure Kremnoan blood, the son of Gorgo born to take the crown!”

Mydei felt bile in his throat, the guilt of his own considerations as of late, eating through his belly. Nervous, with a voice that wavered, he asked, “Mother, I… would you love me less if I cast that crown away?”

Her hand came up to his cheek, catching his face as he tried to turn away. “Mydeimos… what needless worry hides in your heart? Even if my dreams for you were lofty the day you were born, at the core of everything you are simply my son, the ordinary child of a Kremnoan mother. You have developed yourself with determination and I am pleased here in the afterlife.

“My love for you never needed a crown. If you have doubts about this so-called glory, this inheritance of regicide, then live as you please! Gorgo, the founder of Kremnos, per their will and their yearning, summoned Nikador and earned the glory of Strife. And you, my child, can also return home with true glory under the radiance of the Lance of Fury, not as its ruler, but simply as yourself.”

Her thumb brushed across his cheek and when she pulled her hand away there was wetness there. Mydei had not even realized he was crying.

“You are the rightful heir, Mydeimos, not just of Kremnos, but of Strife itself. In you is the power to command change for our people, to become something more than what your father left behind.”

“Should I crush our legacy underfoot? This legacy of Strife that betrayed you?” he half-whispered, “is that what you would do in my place?”

“I am not you,” she scolded, “and I cannot make that decision for you. Once I believed in the spirit of Kremnos without question, and then your father threw you into the Sea of Souls. It was at that moment I realized how everything I believed in was utterly hollow. Perhaps the spirit of Kremnos had once existed, but as greed bloomed in the hearts of humanity over the years, such spirit has long faded alongside our glory. I no longer put my faith in any oath or doctrine. Now I have just one role… That of your mother, Mydeimos. Your guardian.”

You don’t get to be the only protector here.

His own words, no, Phainon’s words echoed as he studied his mother’s radiant smile. She would have loved him.

“So, Mydeimos, have you found something deserving of your protection?”

He held up his hand to her, the one with the golden thread, to reverently show her the strength of his bond. “I have, mother.”

And then he held nothing back. Mydei told her everything about his family, about Krateros as a mentor, about his closest friends in the Detachment. He told her about the moment he achieved vengeance in her name, putting an end to Eurypon for good. He described for her the Chryseus Leo and his favorite parts of sailing. But he spoke the most about Phainon. This beautiful, ethereal, perfect man, who had swooped in and stolen his very spirit with his strength and heart.

Mydei let her hold the string while he talked and Gorgo’s eyes glittered with gentle knowing as they listened to Phainon’s heartbeat and unintelligible murmurs. They were rhythmic now, consistent. He was talking. That perfect wonderful man was reading to his body, taking care of him with diligent love.

“I am sorry,” Mydei said sheepishly when his throat started to feel dry.

“For what, Mydeimos?”

“For recalling what you must already know. Fig Stew has been with me for every step of this long voyage.”

“Yes, but I like hearing it from you, while I can.”

“I can visit you again,” he said swiftly.

With equal swiftness she slapped him across the back of the head. It was so surprising and so Kremnoan that Mydei leaned away and pouted at his mother like a child.

“No, for the sake of that wonderful and patient man, no.”

“We sail to dangerous waters soon,” Mydei reasoned, “I may fall in battle.”

“No,” she said simply and with resolute firmness.

Her reaction left him flabbergasted, mouth agape, eyes wide, fumbling for what felt like an obvious explanation but she silenced him with a finger to his lips.

“You are going to treasure each life the way he does, Mydeimos,” she instructed firmly, “I saw him you know. When you stayed to fight the Black Tide, he broke beneath the Lance of Fury. It was this one’s courage and his promise to you that saved our people.” Fig Stew purred when she rubbed under his chin.

A knot was forming in Mydei’s throat at that thought, the image of a bleeding, broken Phainon pleading with a crystal wall.

“And when they retrieved your body, he did not sleep. Fig Stew and I tried to coax him to rest, but he was fire and fury turned inwards, Mydeimos. I have never seen such hatred in my life.”

“…hatred?”

“Hatred for himself,” she explained, “for not getting to you faster. He could not hold his human form his grief was so great. Not I, nor Fig, nor even Perdikkas could get to your body the way he held you. Until you started to breathe again, he was as dead to the world as you were.” Gorgo sighed and looped the golden thread around Mydei’s hand a few times and then she placed both of her hands over his. “I know, my son, that sacrifice is a tenant of Strife, and you must do everything to protect him, so I will not accept an impossible vow from a Kremnoan warrior, promise me instead that you will try.”

“I will, mother.”

“I like him, Mydeimos,” she said with a toothy grin, “it took Fig Stew some time to be sure, but I have loved him from the start. His men love him too. That Marcus had nothing but good words to say about the Deliverer of Amphoreus.”

Fig Stew made a low chirping grumble deep in his belly.

“Oh shush, Fig,” she scolded, “you could not have known that Eurypon would change so.”

“Not making that mistake twice,” the chimera grumbled.

Mydei’s eyes darted in shock to Fig Stew, accusatory, and the chimera’s face slowly turned into a half-lidded smug smile. So, he could be understood down here. Before Mydei could scold the beloved pet, Gorgo patted his thigh.

“You will need to return to him soon,” she said, still cheerful but softer now.

A part of Mydei’s heart leaped into the back of his throat as he remembered he could not stay here forever. There was a deep and painful longing coating his throat with fluff, stealing his breath to keep him from speaking, to prevent this inevitable goodbye.

“Mydeimos,” she whispered when she saw him struggling. Her palm pressed against his cheek, and he raised a hand to cover hers, to keep her there, afraid to close his eyes. “You do not need to speak to me again to know that I am beside you, but if it helps, I have a gift for you. You left behind Eurypon’s ring when you killed him, but won’t you take mine?”

He blinked and reluctantly let her go when she took her hand back to take the ring from her finger. It was a signet ring bearing the crest of Strife and cast in bronze. Where Eurypon’s ring had been encrusted with jewels, this one was simple, humble, a reminder that Strife did not bask in riches, it was practical and purposeful.

Queen Gorgo placed it in his palm and guided his fingers to close around it. “Hold it tightly, Mydeimos, and it will surely go with you.”

“I will treasure it, mother,” he promised.

She let go and rose to her feet, offering a strong hand to pull Mydei up beside her for a firm embrace that made his ribs creak. “See that you do, my son, not because I gave it to you, but for whom you will give it.”

“You are giving this to me so that I will give it away?” Mydei whined into her shoulder.

“Allow a mother to give her son this final test. I will know that you have finally broken free of our blood-soaked past, when you surrender this ring to your future.”

His arms tightened around her. “I love you, mother.”

“And I you, Mydeimos, my beloved son. I am, and always will be, proud of you.”

-

Mydei and Fig Stew walked the river together, heading upstream in bittersweet silence until the quiet darkness turned into the soft ache of a body lying still on a folded blanket. The chill of the marble floor still crept through the layers to nip at his legs but a warm chimera body, laying by his side and the rise and fall of a strong heartbeat at his back promised warmth.

Phainon’s voice cut through the stillness, getting louder as Mydei came to himself. This perfect, wonderful man was reading from their favorite book, and as promised, when he looked down into Mydei’s blinking eyes, it was with a gentle and loving smile.

“Welcome home, Mydei,” Phainon whispered.

“I told you I wouldn’t be gone long,” Mydei teased light-heartedly.

Phainon’s gentle touch rubbed along his cheeks, warm and gentle, bringing Mydei back to life with the realization that there were tears spilling from his eyes and a small, but very important weight in his palm.

chapters.title: Chapter 47: Nothing Left Unsaid
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Mydei and Phainon talk

Chapter Notes

I THINK I CAN STILL DO THIS IN FIFTY CHAPTERS. Everyone pray that I don't have to move the chapter goal posts again.

Mydei was exhausted. The revival process always hurt. He had described it to Perdikkas once, fumbling to find the right words for something he didn’t fully understand. The sensation was like realigning a broken bone in the middle of combat, when fear and pain have forced the muscles to contract. The nerves and bloody break scrape and grind, nerves roaring as they’re forced together and bound.

The realignment of the soul and body was just a shade worse. The wound had closed, the flesh mended. There was no knife in his chest, but his soul remembered the blade in his heart, and it still needed time to heal. That persistent ache, like a migraine stabbing low at the nape, couldn’t be described as bone deep. It was stitched on his soul, fraying on the edges until it could be mended, preferably by napping somewhere warm and soft.

But as the Kremnoan saying goes, there would be time to rest when he was dead.

Mydei tucked aside all the pain when he woke in Phainon’s arms. No more tears, no more attention given to those pins and needles in every joint, no time or energy to process the emotional weight of his journey that wrapped like a wire around his intestines and lungs.

The moment Anaxa realized Mydei was awake, the Professor was on his knees by the captain’s side to record his testimony of events. Everything Mydei learned from Cerydra poured from his lips like honey brew, free-flowing and slurred, while the others listened carefully. Fig Stew purred in his lap, Phainon offered him water, and the others did their best to not crowd while also satisfying their curiosity.

He described the Imperator in detail, everything that stood out about her and everything she had said about Helektra, the sea siren that hid in the ocean beside Hyperborea. Missing history was penned in the gaps, and her knowledge of the siren song was rapidly transcribed alongside the previously forgotten prophecy that had led to her eager death on the siren’s blade.

Mydei could feel the slump of his shoulders and the tremor in his hands as his body creaked. But it wasn’t the ache that held his tongue when he finished recounting his time with Cerydra. He needed to tell them about Marcus, what he had said about the Black Tide monsters and their cruel state of purgatory, but when Mydei turned enough to look at Phainon, at the bags under his eyes, the soft smile that barely hid his worry and hurt, he just couldn’t do it. Not yet. His fist stayed closed around the ring, still hidden, a secret between himself and the sleepy Fig Stew.

The pause had saved him from his monologue. Anaxa had already moved on with these new findings and taken command in Mydei’s moment of weakness. They packed books and notes while Mydei held still beside Phainon and the chimera, waiting for the foggy mush behind his eyes to clear.

Mydei moved through the motions like a ghost as they returned to the ship and disembarked from the great library, pointing north towards the fallen kingdoms. The decision was made carefully after pouring over maps, taking stock of their supplies, and consulting with Krateros and Hephaestion. He fell back into the rhythm of being the captain, of barking out orders, cooking their meals, and running his war council, but at the back of his mind he was looking for a chance to talk to Phainon about Marcus.

He knew the stress was getting to him when he woke one morning to Phainon’s frantic tapping. Mydei was partially transformed on the bed. His lion back half was on the floor, drooped like a towel over the back of a chair and his front paws were wrapped so tightly around Phainon that the man was suffocating in plush fur.

“It’s not a bad way to go, really!” Phainon had insisted with a reassuring smile and when Mydei couldn’t transform back due to stress, Phainon had stayed up with him, running a brush through his fur and humming soft lullabies.

That should have been the moment. What better time did he have to talk to this patient man who deserved to know how his crew felt in the afterlife? Phainon who was so good, so perfect, and so very haunted. Phainon who had horrible nightmares that woke Mydei from time to time, that took restraining hands and a chimera’s soft tongue to coax back into a restful sleep.

But Mydei couldn’t do it, because he wasn’t ready to admit that he saw more than Cerydra down there. Because he knew that Phainon would listen to everything, even the parts that Mydei wanted to keep to himself, and he wasn’t sure he’d be able to hold back, once those emotions were free.

As Phainon massaged his paws and crept up his Titan body to comb and braid Mydei’s hair, he thought about the ring, tucked away in a locked drawer while he slept. When Phainon’s hand gently rubbed the fading scar over Mydei’s heart, easing another ache until his eyelids fluttered with encroaching sleep, he realized he wanted to share every emotion with him, as soon as he found the words. No more beating around the bush, he wanted to be straight-forward with blunt and brutal honesty, good and bad, as Mydei had been his whole life!

So why was this so hard?

Mydei stood at the bow beside the silent head of the great lion a few Entry Hours later, eating his breakfast and watching the sea ahead. The horizon in every direction was black, it had been since Descent Hour the prior day but the roiling clouds above them split like a wound, letting in the light and guiding them north through the oily ocean. The Eye of Twilight’s power was an unprecedented advantage in this endeavor.

One of his fuzzy ears flicked at the sound of soft footsteps. Despite Mydei’s best efforts to hold his human form, his ears were slow to receive the message. Vibrant red and horribly obvious to anyone who knew that Mydei wasn’t doing it on purpose. Like this even his clothes felt itchy, and he had settled for simpler attire. His armor was left behind in the room, pending a good polish, leaving him in a short tunic, chlamys, loose pants, and knee-high boots, enough to stay warm.

He didn’t turn when Phainon stepped up beside him to lean both of his forearms on the railing. But his eyes did flick down when his boyfriend leaned forward enough for that white mop to be visible, sticking out as far as he could safely lean to look at the ocean breaking against the rostrum. It was laundry day for Phainon and a few others. He was wearing that old exomis, the one they had provided him with when he was still a prisoner. It left most of his back and chest exposed but Phainon didn’t seem to mind.

They stayed that way for a while, enjoying the breeze, however cold, in comfortable silence. Well, mostly comfortable silence. Mydei traced every scar on Phainon’s back with his eyes thrice, resisting the urge to run the length of them with his fingers. He could feel the ring in his pocket searing his skin through the fabric of his pants and his courage swayed back and forth on a pendulum. He took a breath when he felt it swing around again and opened his mouth to speak but Phainon beat him to it.

“What do you think of kids?” Phainon asked without turning and the question caught Mydei so off guard that all his bunched-up emotions unraveled into a garden-variety pile of confusion.

“…what?”

“Kids,” Phainon repeated, “do you like them?” The Deliverer shifted his weight, twisting in place to look up at Mydei from where he was leaning over the railing.

“…were you planning on having them?” Mydei asked, cautiously.

“Unless your Titan form came with more changes, no. At least not of my own.” He sounded cheerful, relaxed, but there was tiredness in his eyes, a dull to the blue.

“I like them well enough,” the captain answered after taking a moment to consider it, “why?”

“Because there are some things I didn’t tell you about… stuff that happened when you were gone,” Phainon said as he heavily rolled back onto both forearms to face the ocean again, hiding his eyes from Mydei’s slowly souring expression. There wasn’t enough guilt on Phainon’s shoulders for him to have done something egregious, but Mydei still felt like he was holding his breath.

“When we evacuated the settlement, I found a little girl hiding in the ruins of her home,” Phainon explained and then he told Mydei everything about the five-year-old orphaned daughter of Militiades, Chironome. He spoke highly of this little girl that took a swing at a Black Tide Gryphon with a toy sword, who squealed with joy at Fig Stew, and fed Phainon food to keep his strength up. Phainon’s voice was tender as he recalled the way she took her tasks seriously, protecting “Fine” all the way to the infirmary, the way she curled up against his chest to sleep, and how crushed and angry she was when Phainon left her in the care of a temporary guardian.

“I didn’t tell you before because it didn’t feel important at the time,” Phainon explained, “but I’ve been thinking about her more lately, and this world we’re trying to save so that she can grow up. This fight we’re sailing to… it didn’t feel serious enough until I considered her and now I can’t stop feeling like this isn’t just another fight. This voyage is so much bigger than all of us and I think I’m afraid.” The vulnerability in his voice was raw and gritty, and very much only for Mydei. This was not the Worldbearer wearing his reassuring smile to please the masses, this was Phainon, the farmers’ son who lost everything and never wanted to lose again. “I trust you, Mydei, I wanted you to know what’s on my mind.”

A little bud of guilt started to nibble at Mydei’s gut as he thought about the secrets he was holding onto himself.

Phainon stood up straight, pushing away from the railing and turned to face Mydei with a reassuring squeeze above the elbow. “You don’t need to tell me what secret you’re keeping, just promise me, when you’re ready, you will?”

Mydei followed that firm grip up those strong arms to Phainon’s face. His lips were lightly curled at the corners, but his smile wavered below tired but trusting eyes.

“How did you know?” Mydei sighed around his own shame. He looked down at Phainon’s chest, avoiding his gaze by studying the knotted scar in his shoulder, the one left behind by Nikador.

“Because I know you now. I remember what you were like when you were trying to find the words to tell me about my status on the ship,” Phainon remembered aloud. “I thought you hated me the way you wouldn’t look at me.” Mydei’s eyes darted up to Phainon’s in defiance of the observation. “And later when you found the warrant from Aglaea, I remember how quiet you were.” Phainon let go of Mydei’s arm to instead gently take his cheek in hand, pressing his warm and calloused palm against the wind-bitten cold that lingered there. “Whatever is haunting you, it involves me, doesn’t it?”

Mydei carefully reached up to wrap his fingers loosely around Phainon’s wrist. “It does,” he whispered, “and it is not my place to keep it from you.”

“If you’re not ready-” “No. There is no room for sulking on my ship,” Mydei said, just as he had the day they met, “nor cowardice.” Just knowing that Phainon would wait if asked, it was a comfort that Mydei hadn’t realized he needed.

“You just needed to know how you felt first, right?” Phainon asked and Mydei remembered holding Aglaea’s written words, the ones that condemned Phainon and set them on this impossible and wonderful path. That was his reasoning then. It held true now.

“And where to start,” Mydei confirmed, “I too, have had a lot on my mind.”

“…how much did you hold back when you told Professor Anaxa about the Netherealm?” Phainon asked carefully, giving him a starting point.

“Nothing that did not apply to his studies, but enough.” Mydei pulled Phainon’s hand away from his face so he could turn back to the railing, to set his hands on the new wood. Phainon and Krateros had already carved the moment Mydei had stayed to fight Nikador there by the bow. Only the most noble of stories were worthy of framing the great lion of Tretos they had said, both cheerfully ignoring his embarrassment. The raised edges felt smooth under Mydei’s bare hands.

“Meeting Cerydra was like seeing my reflection in disturbed water,” Mydei admitted, “we are not the same, but… there were similarities.”

“You are no tyrant, Mydei.”

“No, but I have asked horrible things of you,” he took a breath to say, “I am sorry I asked you to kill me.”

Phainon shook his head and went back to resting on his forearms, close enough to lean his shoulder against Mydei’s arm. “I’m sorry I ran away at first, instead of trusting you.”

“Did you not hear me, HKS? I am saying I should not have asked.”

“You’re comparing what I did to you, with what Cerydra asked of Hysilens, aren’t you?” Phainon accused and Mydei’s mouth shut. “It’s different, Mydei. It’s different, and yeah, it was hard, and yeah, it hurt to hold your body, but you were right too. Being a part of that process, beginning to end, it didn’t fix everything, but it helped. I had a lot of time while you were dead to think about it, and I realized how much I valued your trust in me.”

Mydei grunted, neutral, non-committal.

“How about I forgive you for asking and we agree to not do it again?” Phainon offered with a playful lilt in his voice.

“This is acceptable.”

“…Cerydra loved Hysilens when she asked too,” Phainon remembered aloud, “but she put her dreams of saving the world first.”

“I did the same.”

“But I get to see you again and you were thinking of me when you asked, that’s the difference.”

Mydei drummed his fingers on the railing and then turned his hand over to look at his palm. “When I was dead,” he recalled, “I was bound to you by a golden thread.”

Phainon seemed genuinely surprised by that. “Like one of Aglaea’s threads?”

“Yes, the Imperator was similarly bound to Hysilens. She mentioned that Romance must have seen a reason to bless us to bind our souls so completely.”

“I like that.” Phainon’s voice was soft and gentle. He turned enough to smile sideways at Mydei. “A monarch who fell in love with an outcast.”

“Two Demigods that believed they were saving the world.”

“We are saving the world.”

“They thought so too,” Mydei reminded him.

Phainon ran a hand through his hair. “For all we have in common, there are differences too. We aren’t clinging to prophecy.”

“I have rejected my crown,” he added.

“Their story is beautiful,” Phainon said after a moment, “tragic, but beautiful. Hysilens’ loyalty to her love is worthy of immortalization by song. Still…” His voice dropped to nearly a whisper. “She must be terribly, terribly lonely.”

“Would you do as she has?” Mydei asked, “if I perished and with my dying breath insisted you go on, to accomplish my dreams in my stead?”

Phainon thought about that, hard enough that the ends of his hair started to turn blonde, leaving them tipped in honey. A manifestation of the duress such a query stirred inside him. “I don’t know,” he confessed, “I’m not sure I want to think about it.”

The air felt heavy when Mydei took a breath. Not all conversation topics were appropriate for breakfast, depending on the morning, no conversation at all was the universal preference.

“I suppose I would,” Phainon decided after another moment, “because they would be our dreams, no?”

Mydei’s heart jumped when he heard that.

I like him, Mydeimos… I have loved him from the start.

Longing bubbled up in his belly, disagreeing with the bread and olives he had finished earlier as his insides started throwing a party, doing celebratory squats. His heart was full to bursting, singing Phainon’s name and forgetting his own.

When Mydei looked down at Phainon again, the man was smiling up at him, his cheek smooshed against his knuckles. “When did you know you were in love with me?” Phainon asked.

Mydei crossed his arms and tucked his head to think. His ears flattened as he searched through their time together. “It did not happen in a single moment,” he realized, “there was no grand gesture, no moment of revelation, I simply realized that I had been, as though there were never a time that I was not.”

He opened his eyes again to Phainon’s boyish adoration. The expression of a man so deeply in love that just a glance made Mydei feel warm and safe.

Mydei cleared his throat. “And what of you?”

“When did I know I was in love with you?”

“Yes.”

Phainon’s smile faltered. He couldn’t beam as widely when his eyebrows pinched in deep concentration. It was so cute. Mydei loved that expression.

“I wish I could say it was before Castrum Kremnos,” Phainon finally said, “and maybe I was, but I knew without any shadow of a doubt when I was on Trial in Okhema, when I told the whole city that I loved you.”

Mydei tilted his head. “You told Okhema that you loved me?”

“Mhm,” Phainon’s relaxed adoration was back, “even without Aglaea’s threads holding me accountable, the moment the words were out, I knew I meant them.”

Mydei shook his head and frowned. “You told the whole of the Holy City, but you could not tell me the moment I rose from the dead in your arms?”

Phainon scoffed and let his hand fall away from his face to slap against the railing, still leaning his weight onto his elbow. “You hadn’t been dead for a week.”

“I had yet to wake, it counts.”

“You were breathing! You had a heartbeat!”

“Do not argue semantics to avoid the accusation, silver-tongued hyena,” huffed Mydei.

Phainon groaned and bent his knees, hiding below the railing with only his fingers holding on to keep him upright. He looked like he was going to be sick if Mydei didn’t know any better. This HKS had long found his sea legs during their spars.

“Yes!” Phainon relented, “yes, I told Okhema and then hesitated to tell you. I just…I wanted it to be special. It took me awhile to realize the circumstances of a confession like that aren’t what makes it special, it’s the person I’m confessing to.”

Mydei’s cheeks and ears felt warm, his insides fuzzy and happy. With an exaggerated huff, he held his crossed arms a little tighter and turned his nose up, eyes closed. “What have I said about sentimentality on this ship, Deliverer?”

“That you love it and want more of it in your life?”

Mydei cracked one eye to peek at Phainon’s silly grin as the man stood back up and leaned in close.

“HKS,” Mydei huffed.

“Krateros said that Kremnoan sentimentality is allowed, and as I recall, you introduced us to Nikador as sons of Kremnos.” Phainon’s voice was too cheerful, too sing-song. He was stepping in closer and Mydei refused to budge, even when the man was completely inside Mydei’s personal space.

“As the Inheritor of Strife, I disown you,” Mydei announced, deadpan.

“Mm, I’ll just have to earn my way back into your good graces, captain,” Phainon hummed. He kissed Mydei’s cheek, barely grazing the heated flesh with his lips.

A part of Mydei wanted to indulge, the part of him that caved and smiled at the playful advances, but he still had more to say.

“Cerydra was not the only person I spoke to in the Netherealm,” Mydei admitted, “my mother was waiting to speak to me.”

Phainon paused and then leaned back to beam at Mydei with a shaky smile as he tried to restrain his excitement. Mydei could see the shimmer of gold flash in his eyes like it did when he was trying to keep his emotions in check. His hands came up to take Mydei by the arms, holding him lightly above the elbows.

“Mydei, that’s wonderful! …unless, it’s not?”

“It was… bittersweet.”

“Do you want to talk about it?”

No, Mydei thought.

“She likes you,” he said.

“You get the chance to talk to your mother, and you talk about me?” Phainon laughed, perhaps a little too proud of himself. Mydei punched him in the shoulder, firm enough to make a point, to shove him back, and Phainon chuckled a little harder.

“She has been watching the crew through Fig Stew,” he revealed.

“All this time Krateros was right?”

“Yes.”

“Damn… but that means she’s been with you,” Phainon said happily. He rested his hand on the rail again and stepped in close to stand beside him, ready to support Mydei as needed.

That attentiveness, that thoughtfulness and selflessness were so damn cute, it made Mydei’s heart stand at attention and filled him with the courage to share.

“Even earlier than I realized,” Mydei confessed, “she raised me in the Sea of Souls as well. I thought they were old dreams from my youth, but I know now they were memories.”

Phainon lightly punched Mydei’s arm, flirting, “Mydei, that’s amazing!”

It did warm his heart thinking about his mother’s laugh, her face, and her council, enough to make him smile and lean into Phainon. His mind drifted back to the ring in his pocket.

I will know that you have finally broken free of our blood-soaked past, when you surrender this ring to your future.

More than ever, Mydei wanted Phainon to be that future, or at the very least a greater part of it. He genuinely could not picture a life that did not include Phainon. It was hard to even remember a time without him there by his side at all. How had this crew managed before? How had they lived without this smile, this energy, this loving, selfless soul? A soul that needed them too.

I have never seen such hatred in my life. Hatred for himself.

Mydei gently reached for Phainon’s hand, giving it a firm and reassuring squeeze. This fight they were sailing to could very well be the end of them. Waiting at the end of this voyage to the edge of the map was a thousand-year-old Demigod driven by grief and love warped into madness. The only thing Hysilens had left was the duty entrusted to her by the woman she treasured, and it had become a monster that ate, ate, ate. Phainon’s parents, his childhood home… Deep in those cerulean eyes flecked with gold was a buried rage and hate, an eagerness for revenge born in the trauma and fear of an eldritch horror. Did Phainon even know how deep that well within him was?

It was time. Phainon needed to hear this.

“Mother spoke with me but she initially sought me out so I would speak with a new friend she made in the last few months, an Okheman sailor named Marcus.”

Phainon stilled. That hand on the railing tightened, clinging for support, and Mydei could see the mask going up, the careful gathering of his emotions to tuck them in a box. He hated it, he hated feeling like Phainon was trying to hide from him.

“Phainon, it’s not bad,” Mydei reassured. He reached out to grab Phainon’s shoulder, to keep him close while he told Phainon everything he remembered about the conversation with Marcus, beginning with the revelation about the Black Tide. Phainon’s trembling worsened with every word, a combination of distress and the effort of trying to hide it. Even now, Phainon was trying to hold himself together, falling back on years of impossible expectations.

“Mydei,” Phainon mumbled with a shake of his head, “why didn’t you bring this up at the library? This is about the nature of the Black Tide…”

“It changes nothing about what we must do. This task matters not if we cannot stop the siren and nothing about this knowledge helps the crew.”

Mydei reached out to brush the bangs from Phainon’s eyes, a losing battle against the breeze that gathered those silver locks again and put them right back.

“He left other messages with me, Deliverer, for you specifically. He wanted you to forgive Xenia, his wife. It would seem she has been cruel to you…?”

Phainon nodded and pain filled his expression, too great to bury. His shoulders drooped and his knees shook. “I have already forgiven her,” he admitted, “love and loss… I can’t blame her for hating me.”

You hate yourself too, don’t you? For failing them, for losing them the same way you lost your family. How long have you been holding onto this? How long have you been fighting yourself, alone?

Mydei studied him, torn between punching the self-hatred out of his boyfriend or hugging it out of him. “He also wanted you to know, on behalf of your crew, that they forgive you.”

Phainon’s head bowed and he turned away to leave, hiding again, but Mydei didn’t let him escape. His fingers wrapped around Phainon’s wrist, tight enough to hold, light enough to put him at ease. Phainon could have easily broken free if he tried but he didn’t, instead stepping away until their arms were fully extended, straining, as though Mydei were the only anchor keeping him from blowing away entirely in a raging whirlwind.

They waited like that until Phainon relaxed and the tightness of the hold loosened. His head was still bowed, hiding behind the curtain of his hair but Mydei stepped in front of him and reached out to again brush those bangs aside, this time holding them back with his hand over Phainon’s temple. Tears like diamonds peppered those long lashes, fighting the urge to fall.

“Look at me,” Mydei ordered in a soft voice and Phainon shook his head, half-heartedly trying to pull away, “Phainon of the Chryseus Leo, look at me.”

He looked so fragile like this, ethereal, divine, when he finally obeyed.

“It is time to forgive yourself,” Mydei whispered and Phainon couldn’t hold the emotions back anymore. They spilled from him in waves with broken sobs and Mydei wrapped his arms around this man’s shoulders, pulling him in and holding him tightly, letting those emotions run their course.

Phainon’s forehead slowly fell onto Mydei’s chest. He held tightly to Mydei’s chlamys as he mumbled, soft and vulnerable, “Mydei, I don’t know how.”

Mydei’s hug tightened around Phainon’s shoulders, and he rocked them in a subtle sway. “Then I will start, and you may trust my words until such time as you can trust your own.” He pressed a kiss to Phainon’s hair and leaned his cheek against his temple, whispering gently, “I forgive you, Phainon.”

The wind rushed around them as Phainon’s wings appeared, unable to hold them back as the emotions surged through him. The blue and gold pinions fluttered, indecisively moving to cocoon them both and then back to furling behind his shoulders. His whole body was shaking as he sobbed, fighting the need to do so despite Mydei’s gentle, encouraging touch.

Mydei ran his fingers through Phainon’s hair, rubbing his scalp, his neck, his shoulders, and down his back with one hand while the other held him close, keeping him anchored, safe in this sheltered harbor of his companionship. These were old tears, Mydei could tell. The kind that were pushed down every time they threatened to fall, the kind that needed to spill and were denied by a string of excuses. The kind that may have come with shame in another time, another place, if they were shed alone.

Mydei pulled back enough to take Phainon’s face in both hands, to hold Phainon still while he kissed every tear. His lips gently claimed every single one from his chin, his cheeks, and finally he kissed both eyes in turn, stealing away that sorrow until all he saw in those sunny eyes was relief.

“Here I am,” Mydei mused, trying to sound playful, “once again asking so much of you, but if anyone can accomplish this mountainous task, it is the Deliverer of Amphoreus.”

Phainon’s scoff came out awkward, trying for a chuckle, but ending up as a broken whine. His wings drooped to lay flat across the deck, too heavy, too burdened to hold. “Mydei, I told you not to call me that…”

“And I remember pinning you to a rocky beach and accepting your surrender. I told you then, you do not get to choose what we call you, Deliverer.”

“I should fight you again,” Phainon huffed, “to take that right back.”

“You would lose, but even if the heavens fell and you secured a pretty victory against me, I would never obey your winning demand,” he confessed, “because it is the truth.” Mydei’s thumb brushed under Phainon’s eye, gently rubbing a small circle there. “Not for Okhema, but for this ship, for me. You delivered us to a life we could have never known without you, and now we sail to stop the Black Tide, to save all people. Is that not the calling of a Deliverer?”

“You make it sound as though I alone am the hero here…” Phainon mumbled, still doubting.

“Every good hero in every epic has his companions, Phainon of the Chryseus Leo. It does not make him any less of a hero himself.”

Those pretty lips parted to argue some more and Mydei silenced him with his own. They pressed together, gently, sweetly and without demand, only a gentle invitation to share their burdens, and Phainon accepted it without hesitation.

They were lost in that moment, coming down from the height of emotional acceptance when the cacophony came over the forecastle deck. Phainon’s wings closed tightly behind him and Mydei’s ears flattened. He turned to glare at the offenders, but the new arrivals were completely unbothered.

“I don’t care if we’ve had favorable winds the entire way,” Hephaestion was arguing, “it is not physically possible.” The first mate was leading the small group, head on a swivel until he spotted the captain and then he was picking up the pace, walking straighter than he ever had in his life.

“You asked me to chart the stars as we sailed, Lord Hephaestion!” Hyacine argued. She was using her doctor’s voice, the one that said, ‘you will listen to me and that’s final’ while her eye of twilight darted about in its socket. “I have been watching them every waking moment and I am telling you, we are already here.”

“Hyacinthia,” Anaxa started to say but was promptly interrupted when she spun on him.

“I am the sky, Professor! I assure you; I am not reading the stars improperly!”

Neither the professor nor Krateros behind him knew how to react to her brazen behavior. Frankly, Mydei didn’t either. He had never seen the young healer raise her voice. Something about it felt wrong somehow and it left a heavy pit in his stomach. Her agitation was flooding them all with urgency.

“Mydeimos!” Hephaestion called, “will you please speak sense to her?”

Mydei crossed his arms. “Lady Hyacine?”

“I am not crazy, Lord Mydei,” she insisted. That eye of hers was extremely distracting. He was trying so hard not to stare at it. “I studied the star charts above Hyperborea, even taking into account how they may have changed over the course of one thousand years! We should already be there!”

Hephaestion sighed and slapped her on the head with the rolled-up map in his hand, a Kremnoan gesture that she did not appreciate. She swatted at it, but he pulled it out of reach and unrolled it to show Mydei, pointing at the Northern Continent and the stretch of ocean between the library and the landmass.

“Perfect seas, perfect winds, and not a single sign of land. Hyperborea was built on the shore between the ocean and a steep mountain range that protected it from the North winds. Mountains like that can be seen from a ship leagues away,” Hephaestion pointed out, “we must have at least seven more Entry Hours.”

Mydei consulted the map and then looked over the top at where Hyacine was fuming. She had no reason to lie… but there had been no sign of land, and this journey was expected to take quite a long time.

“Krateros, is it possible that we have traveled at a speed that would put us at our destination ahead of schedule?” Mydei asked.

Krateros shuffled uncomfortably. “The winds have been more than favorable, captain,” he admitted, “truthfully, I had expected to see signs of land by now, the outer isles, if not the Northern Continent itself. The chill in the wind alone is proof that we have crossed into colder waters.”

Phainon walked past Mydei and climbed up onto the railing, standing at the bowsprit and holding onto a line for balance as though he would be able to see something that no one else had caught. His fluttering wings showered them with downy feathers as they adjusted for the breeze.

“Lady Tribbie surely has given us the Blessing of Passages,” Hyacine insisted, “she has hastened our journey.”

“Be that as it may,” Anaxa snapped, still irritated at having been interrupted before, “we would have seen more than just a rock.”

Mydei’s eyes snapped up. “A rock?”

“It was nothing, Mydeimos,” Hephaestion insisted, “It looked like an isolated boulder, a few white caps where the waves were breaking, a sandbar at best. We gave it a wide berth at the start of the Entry Hour while you were making breakfast.”

Phainon dropped back down and leaned over Mydei’s shoulder to look at the map again. “We need to turn around.”

“Phainon, there is nothing there!” Hephaestion insisted.

He pointed on the map to the southern edge of the Northern Continent where the mountain range had been marked. Just as Hephaestion said, there was the city, nestled in the shadow of the tallest peak.

“The Imperator said Hysilens would go home, right? To the place that she shared with the woman she loved,” Phainon reminded them.

“To Hyperborea,” Mydei confirmed.

“The ocean around Hyperborea,” Anaxa corrected. He had poured over Mydei’s notes, he surely had them printed on the back of his eyelids by now.

“Why not both?” Phainon asked.
