Hephaestion shook his head. “Phainon that’s-”

“Turn the ship around,” Mydei ordered, “your rock, Hephaestion, isn’t guarding a sandbar.”

Phainon patted the first mate on the shoulder and said, “It’s the top of a mountain.”

chapters.title: Chapter 48: Altered Horizons
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

Hyacine has a plan, but Mydei worries they may have rushed into this a little too fast

Chapter Notes

With the holidays breathing down my neck and the new FFXIV patch coming out soon these chapters are gonna slow down a bit. I really, really want to finish this by Christmas but unfortunately a fic for fun is a little low on the priority list. I hope you guys can forgive me ;w;

Phainon wanted to believe that the moment of revelation would be enough to force the lid back down on the void that held all his emotions, but even as Krateros and Hephaestion turned and hurried to bark orders to the crew, to mobilize, feathers still fluttered in the cold wind. His wings still hung from his shoulders and when Mydei stopped on the stairs and looked back at where Phainon had been left alone, it was written on his face. Phainon could see in those amber eyes the worry of someone who could peer right through him.

He needed to move, needed to get to his gear. Hysilens would surely know that they were there, and it would take little more than a firm slap from a kraken arm to send the crew to a watery grave.

An emotional exhaustion was settling on his insides, leaving him feeling scrubbed, raw, and exposed. The relief that Mydei had given him had helped but with no time to let those feelings rest… it was just a lot, and he could feel his body wanting to shut down to escape it.

“Deliverer?” Mydei called and Phainon gave him a reassuring wave.

“I’m fine, Mydeimos. I’ll be along.”

It still took Mydei a long minute to move. The captain kept looking between Phainon and up the stairs towards where the others were scrambling in an organized chaos. When he finally went on ahead it was with a trusting look, not soft, not pitying, but with a hardness in the way his brow was set, as though ready to hurl a challenge.

Don’t keep me waiting for long, it said.

Phainon took a breath when he was alone and stepped back to lean against the great lion. His wings were pressed against that stone mane, and he leaned on the noble muzzle for support.

It wasn’t a lie when he told Mydei that he was afraid. He wished he could say that this was the fear of the fight, something easy like a child afraid of monsters, the kind of fear that could be overcome with a parent’s reassurances and a toy sword. No, this was the fear that had haunted him forever, the fear that had defined Phainon into what he was now. The fear that he hated so completely that he had come to hate himself.

He was afraid of failing, of disappointing the people he loved, of not being enough.

It was the same fear that crushed him when he read the warrant for his arrest. The same fear that drove him to rage against the inside of a Dawncloud cell. The same fear that was born when a young man buried his village in ash with a broken shovel. That terror that warped and twisted and ate at itself with violence until it could no longer be accepted, only buried under something stronger.

Hatred and vengeance burned hotter than fear.

I forgive you, Phainon.

He tried to say the words in his head with his own voice, but it was Mydei’s pleasant growl that he heard instead.

I forgive you, he tried to say out loud, but the words were stuck in his chest.

He angrily slammed his fist against the lion’s muzzle, realized what he did, and then hurried to soothe the silent stone.

“I’m sorry,” he mumbled, “I just didn’t think this would be so hard.”

Phainon sighed and leaned forward to rest his forehead on the statue, listening to the way the breeze whistled and breathed around the lion’s carved ears and open maw. Mydei gave him the first step, ending the Black Tide would be the second. His forgiveness would just have to hinge on their success, on his vengeance fulfilled.

The bubble of hate overtook the lingering fear and Phainon steeled himself again. His feathers melted away, and he found that easy smile once more. This was the fight he had been waiting for after all! There was no time to waste on trivial things.

Phainon admired his Kremnoan crewmates for a lot of reasons, not the least of which was their ability to mobilize immediately on command. Even when the crew were relaxing, making food, even sleeping, a part of them were always on alert and ready to spring into battle ready positions.

The crew’s scrambles were chaos to an untrained eye and precise execution to anyone else. In just the time that Phainon had paused to gather himself, the crew had turned the ship around, furled half the sails, were donning their gear, and the armory was opened. They had been in enemy territory since the first Descent Hour after they left the library, but it was very different realizing they had sailed over the enemy’s stronghold entirely.

Phainon passed Mydei in their room. The captain was dressing comfortably, wearing his regal and familiar red and black. He pulled the strap tight on his gauntlets with his teeth and then beckoned for Phainon with the bend of a golden claw.

“Are you well?” Mydei asked when Phainon stepped close enough to grab. Mydei’s grip was light above his elbow.

“I will be,” Phainon promised.

“Good, I need you to watch my back.” Mydei leaned forward to kiss Phainon’s cheek, holding him still with a hand against the side of his neck. His hair tickled Phainon’s nose, making him squirm, but Mydei held tight until he was satisfied.

“The war council will be on the top deck, when you are dressed.”

“Aye, captain.”

Mydei gave him one more longing look and then let him go to leave.

Phainon’s gear was technically dry. It was a good thing he had gotten up early to do his laundry. There were creases that felt cold but not wet, teetering on the edge of dry and damp, enough to eat up precious time while Phainon debated uselessly if he should wear something else. As though he had something else to wear to the battle of the millennium.

By the time Phainon had changed and left his room, the crew had prepared enough to let the initial confusion bubble back up over the urgency of following orders. They wanted to know why they were mobilizing.

Phainon saw Leonnius waiting by the rail. He caught Phainon’s gaze and fell into step beside him.

“What’s going on?” the runner asked urgently.

“Did Hephaestion not tell you?”

“Only that the enemy may be upon us soon.”

“We still don’t know how,” Phainon told him, “but we’re already at Hyperborea.” Leonnius tilted his head, puzzled.

“It’s underwater.”

“Nikador’s taint,” Leonnius mumbled in Kremnoan before swapping back to Okheman, “how are we supposed to get there?”

Phainon stopped at the bottom of the stairs to the top deck. “That’s something we’re going to have to figure out,” he grumbled, “once we have a plan I’ll let you know.”

“Of course.” Leonnius still looked worried, but he stepped back and let Phainon go to meet with the others.

Mydei had pulled together anyone that might be able to help solve their current, unexpected dilemma, so the usual suspects were there. Hephaestion, Ptolemy, and the Demigods were all discussing the situation around the navigation table. A couple of very old maps were carefully stretched open by heavy, rectangular brass rods at the curling edges.

“The mountain is the only place where anchoring would be possible,” Hephaestion was explaining.

“Are we sure it’s wise to anchor?” Ptolemy asked, “we may need to strategically retreat… Does no one else think it strange that the Black Tide has not tried to attack us?”

“Give praise to Nikador that it has not,” the first mate grumbled.

“There are no records of the Black Tide attacking with aquatic or amphibious monsters,” Professor Anaxa reasoned, “though lack of recent records does not definitively prove that they do not exist at all. She could be alone and simply have chosen not to reveal herself.”

“She doesn’t have to, so long as she is underwater, none of us can get to her,” Mydei grumbled.

“Are the talismans waterproof?” Hephaestion asked.

“You think we’re going to swim there?” Ptolemy huffed.

The first mate was already at the end of his patience, a rarity for Hephaestion. “In case someone is knocked overboard,” he all but hissed.

“My charms are waterproof, but swimming was never an option. The weight of the ocean would crush anyone who ventured too deep,” Anaxa reminded them, completely glossing over the breathing problem. His arms were half crossed, one hand cradling the opposite elbow while the other rolled a pair of crystal shards around in his palm. The sound was mildly annoying, but Phainon recognized his old teacher’s fidgeting quirks from his university days. If it helped the genius think, then he wasn’t going to complain.

“Professor, everyone, I may have a solution,” Hyacine offered, “I cannot raise Hyperborea from the depths, but I believe I can lower the sky.”

The table was quiet as everyone looked at her. Phainon hadn’t even considered that as a possibility but as the Eye of Twilight…

“If I lower the horizon,” she continued when no one answered her, “it will be as though the continent never sank. I can do it in a pocket, here.” Hyacine leaned forward and drew a circle on the map with the pencil, big enough to uncover the entire city, the mountain behind it, and a sizeable part of the bay.

“Hyacine, that’s amazing.” Phainon finally broke the frozen shock around the table. The realization that their options were not as limited as they had been in prior campaigns opened whole new doors.

“Amazing and potentially very reckless,” Professor Anaxa huffed. He had his head tilted to the side, eye closed, holding still like he was listening very intently to his own thought processes.

“Wouldn’t that displace a massive amount of water?” Ptolemy asked.

“’A massive amount of water’ is relative,” Anaxa explained, “if we were filling a fish tank, then yes, but compared to the ocean as a whole, no. The force of the displacement is more dangerous than the change in water level.” He tightened his fist and the little stones in his hand ground together and then stilled. “Hyacinthia, I will work together with you to ensure the execution of your plan doesn’t create any unexpected natural disasters.”

“I would appreciate that, Professor,” she accepted with a smile, “the change will not be permanent. I will need to hold the pocket to keep the ocean from rushing back in.”

“How long can you give us?” Mydei asked.

“I don’t know, I haven’t tried this before,” she admitted, “several hours?”

If Hyacine got them down there before Action Hour… that would give them until sundown. Phainon rested his hand on the table and leaned over the map, trying to judge how much ground they had to cover. Too much.

“If something happens to her while she’s holding the air-” Hephaestion started.

“I will protect Lady Hyacine,” Castorice offered. She raised her hand politely and then stepped in close to wrap her arm around Hyacine’s. The two of them locked together at the elbows smiling broadly at each other. “Pollux and I will keep her safe while she holds the sky.”

“There’s too much of the city to search,” Phainon observed, “and with the song…”

Mydei uncrossed his arms and leaned over the map. “Only the Deliverer and I will go looking for the siren.”

“Are you sure?” Hephaestion asked.

“We will be able to cover more ground in our titan forms.”

“And you won’t have to be as cautious with your powers,” Ptolemy pointed out, “’For a god is not easily caught – not by a mortal man.’ We will only be in your way.”

“And I need the men here,” Mydei instructed, pointing at the docks. “We have not seen aquatic Tide monsters because we have never fought beneath the ocean, but we would be fools to not consider the possibility that there is an army waiting between us and the Demigod.”

Even if there wasn’t, another line of defense between Hyacine and Hysilens would go a long way. Hyacine was creating the best opportunity for them but would also become their greatest weak spot.

“Give us a quint to make calculations,” Anaxa requested.

“That gives us time to brief the crew,” Hephaestion agreed.

“Gather the unit leaders,” Mydei ordered. He leaned over the map and marked a spot with the pencil. “This is where we need the ship to be. We will need men on the oars, treading water until we are able to drop anchor.”

“I’ll take care of that positioning, captain,” the first mate confirmed, “professor, will you check my math when I have it.”

“Of course.”

“There will be no time for goodbyes,” Mydei said firmly, “the siren may rise from the depths at any moment.”

The group scattered to do their tasks without waiting for a formal dismissal. Mydei was right, they didn’t have the time to waste.

-

Mydei had lived his whole life preparing for combat, moving from one fight to the next. Sometimes that fight was a playful bout with Hephaestion, training with Krateros, or tug of war with Fig Stew. They included exchanges with the Okheman Navy, surprise attacks from the Black Tide, and scripted piracy when raiding for supplies.

This was different. Everything about this felt different.

Standing at the bow of the Chryseus Leo beside Phainon, watching Hyacine raise her hands was not something Mydei could have ever prepared for. It took a single gesture to instantly rip open the clouds to flood the world with golden sunlight and infinite, clear sky. They shared golden blood but watching this tiny woman with wild eyes command such power made him feel entirely outclassed.

One quint. It had taken one quint for Anaxa and Hyacine to determine the best way to perform a miracle. One quint to reshape the surface of Amphoreus. One quint to gather his best friends, tell them the plan, hand out the improved talismans, and get the men in position. The water splashed against the hull as the crew rowed, twisting the Chryseus Leo in a slow circle to keep her from drifting too far on the ocean waves. This felt like too big of a fight, too high of stakes, to leave to the chaos of unknown variables, of a half-formed plan, crutching on their divinities as the easy answer to all things. As though they weren’t about to fight another Demigod, a creature of power and age and wisdom, who had a thousand years to perfect her lethality.

How long did they really have for this operation? Was the city even still intact? Could they be wrong and Hysilens was not here at all, leaving behind instead an army to intercept any trespassers?

What the hell were they thinking?

A hand grabbed his and Mydei blinked away his unease to turn his head to Phainon. He was smiling like this was just another day, as though they hadn’t spilled their hearts to each other within the Hour… as though his shining eyes weren’t still rimmed pink at the corners with old tears.

A gentle squeeze, reassuring, loving, and Mydei felt the courage inside him surge. He felt invincible. This was possible! They could save the world!

And then the weight slammed down on them, and they were ripped apart.

It punched the air from Mydei’s lungs and drove Phainon to his knees. Mydei followed a second after as his knees buckled, nearly breaking as they fought to keep upright before the deck rose to meet him. He could see Phainon struggling to breathe, his cheek pressed against the wood, just as his was. The world around them warped and tore. Beneath them the ship creaked and cracked, groaning with strain. The lines were popping, beginning to tear under the pressure.

Instinct told him to fight but Phainon’s hand found him again, looping his pinky around Mydei’s forefinger. He was still smiling, a little wobbly now, unsure, but trusting and comforting all the same.

Against the will of Strife in his heart, Mydei forced himself to relax as the weight of the Sky settled on the ship, on their shoulders. Every breath felt like choking, every tiny movement was pushing a mountain, he couldn’t hear anything now except the roar of the ocean as it rose in the corner of his eye.

A wall of water was slowly rising in the near distance. He could see the edge of it above the railing, too far away to feel the ocean spray that misted from the falling water, but close enough to filter the sunlight to create swaying patterns across their faces. They sank deeper and the weight of the world remained, until there was no longer a blue and cloudless sky, but a dark and imposing ocean, full of ink and song.

Phainon’s one-fingered grip loosened. The man’s eyes were rolling back as he struggled to breathe. Mydei tried to call to him, but his voice was buried in the roar, and it left him in a similar state of suffocation.

The black was creeping into his vision, and he thought perhaps they would perish before the battle began, but then salty, cool air flooded his lungs, the pressure abated, and the churn of the sea settled into the distant roar of waterfalls with a sudden lurch. The natural sway of the ship stopped, leaving behind an eerie stillness.

Mydei took a couple of test breaths. It was cold down here at the bottom of the ocean but as he slowly put his palms flat on the deck to push himself up, the air started to feel… normal.

Beside him Phainon did the same, pushing himself up on steady arms while he took deep full breaths through his nose and mouth. They looked at each other and slowly smiled with shared relief.

The moment was short-lived, coming to an end when Hyacine shrieked and dropped to the deck. She was covering her eyes with both hands, shoulders shaking.

“Hyacine!” Phainon called and he was up in a flash, hurrying towards her.

Castorice cut him off, wobbling on her own two feet. “Please, Lord Phainon, you haven’t the time for sympathy.”

She was right. Mydei could see from where he was stumbling to stand that their time may be shorter than anticipated. Gold blood was trickling over Hyacine’s fingers where they covered her face. Holding back the weight of the water like this was far more taxing than they anticipated and his worry for her grew to include the rest of the crew.

“We will care for her,” Anaxa insisted. He was physically pushing them away while Castorice gently placed a lavender cloak over the Sky Demigod’s shoulders.

“Deliverer,” Mydei snapped as he turned, and Phainon reluctantly and stiffly followed.

The ship had caught on the ocean floor, as they fell to meet it. Hyacine had pushed the sky lower than intended and the Leo’s belly was resting gently in the silt that settled below the harbor. A quick look over the side confirmed it.

The water they rested in was as black as the heart of an evil man, but Mydei could tell from where it rose against the hull that they were resting in no more than a puddle, less than knee deep. The beach beyond looked like low tide during a drought, exposed, while the waiting docks of the marina reached into the open air, too far away to be of use.

“Damn,” Phainon whispered beside him. The rest of the crew had abandoned oars to hurry to the deck to join them with weapons ready. Mydei caught Leonnius and Peucesta out of the corner of his eye slamming into the rail at his side to stare at the marvel before them.

Hyperborea would have been an incredible sight without the wall of water. Hyacine had carved for them a miracle: a cylindrical air bubble exactly as she had said, leaving the ocean to frame the bay, the city, and the mountain. Seawater trickled down the sheer peak face in streams and the ocean churned against the invisible walls that Hyacine had erected. Loose spray fell from them as escaped mist, scattering the sunlight above into cascades of color.

The ruins of the capital city were a whalefall, white and gleaming where the reef had yet to claim it. Silver moss and dead coral clung tightly to the stone but there were no fish, no crabs, nor creeping things. It was a tomb. A tomb that did not take kindly to the air that sapped away the comforting weight of a crushing ocean.

In the depths of the city a familiar mass churned and boiled, slimy and amorphic. Black as a night that swallowed the moon and stars, and resonating with the distant sounds of a mournful song. It bubbled taller than the palace spires and slowly started to spread. Long tentacles reached from its core as it pulled itself over the buildings and towards the shore.

“Looks like you’ll need us after all,” Leonnius huffed to Mydei. The runner pointed with his chin, a sharp nod at the beach where monsters gathered. They were different than the Black Tide monsters they had seen before. “The books never said what happened to the other sirens,” Phainon mumbled at Mydei’s side.

These creatures were fish on better days, but little was left of them but a rotting core and long, flowing fins. They were gray and sickly colored, pale at the joints and dark around reddened faceless flesh. Many of them had tears in their fins and all of them featured shimmering sharp horns.

They hovered over the sand, agitated but not hindered by the air. Like a nocturnal animal forced to scavenge in the daylight for food, they were irritable but not helpless.

For a moment both sides studied each other, trying to decide what to make of the other, trying to determine what the heck happened to create this impossible staging ground. And then the creatures shrieked and even Mydei hurried to cover his ears from that horrible sound. The war cry rallied the monsters, and they flowed towards the ship like serpents, fast and fluid, spilling over each other in a frenzy.

Krateros moved first. He was already shouting orders, calling Peucesta who relayed the commands by horn as the old vet moved down the line, tapping the helmet of each crewmate in turn before they jumped over the railing to land in the soft silt. Their talismans glowed faintly as the Tide called to them from the water, but they held and the corruption was stayed.

Rope ladders clattered down the side of the ship. Weapons splashed as spears and shields were thrown to the men that were forming the first line. They moved with deliberate, practiced haste.

Mydei counted them as they leaped, searching for the friends he didn’t have time to say goodbye to, but two of them were already missing and the battle had barely begun.

“Mydeimos,” Krateros called when he got to the prince. The old man grabbed Mydei by the forearm and Mydei returned it, holding tightly and leaning in to better hear. “These creatures are beneath you, leave them.”

“Hephaestion and Perdikkas?” Mydei questioned with a tilt of his head.

“Will complain over the victory feast that they were late to this most legendary battle,” Krateros said, “May victory be yours, Mydeimos.”

He let go and gave Mydei a firm shove before moving on to Phainon. The old man opened his mouth to speak, shook his head, and instead pulled Phainon forward by the coat to slam their foreheads together. He held it for a second and then shoved the Deliverer away before moving on to the next man.

Mydei smiled and snorted at Phainon’s bewilderment. Even a hasty and awkward Kremnoan farewell counted for something.

A roar brought them back to the present. The air vibrated with it, a melodic sound that should not have come from such an ugly mass. It shook the mountain, the city, and made waves at their feet, nearly breaking the Kremnoan line as the first of the fish monsters threw themselves with reckless abandon on the line of shields and spears where they burst into pointed shrapnel.

The distant kraken wrapped an arm around a building and wrenched it free with a thunderous crack. It crumbled as it was thrown, a launched barrage of scattered, inconsistent projectiles.

Mydei and Phainon moved in sync, leaping from the ship to take flight. The crack of the Lance of Fury shattered the largest fragments into gravel rain and a swipe of Phainon’s sword burst the rest into harmless dust. They were radiance and fury, power and pride incarnate hovering over the ship and their family at war.

The Black Tide was unimpressed.

The kraken reached for another monument to weaponize, but Mydei and Phainon had already had enough of that game. Phainon dashed ahead, blazing like the Ascent Hour sun, sword swept back beside the tail of his robes and his wings spread wide.

Mydei looked down where the Kremnoans were surging forward against a swarm, drastically outnumbered, knee deep in sludge, fighting their way up the shore. He remembered then what Marcus had said, about men and women trapped in bodies with hijacked wills. It would be so easy to trample these tiny things under foot, to save them and his crew.

The lance in his hand was heavy, the claws on his paws long and flashing with every flex, but then he saw the flash of Krateros’ sword, heard Hyacine’s pained shout, and remembered what it meant to trust, to never have to fight alone again.

Light flashed deep in the city. Phainon was dashing around the kraken, leaving long and oozing cuts. A tentacle chased him, another swiped. Gold wings flashed and one of the tentacles was severed. The beast screamed and the limb slowly melted into a runny goo.

It was bigger than last time. Even from this far away Mydei could tell that this was not the same kraken that had tormented him at Castrum Kremnos. That beast had been a shadow of this one, a puppet on a string far from home with waning power.

Mydei’s tail swished as he hefted the lance over his shoulder and extended his arm, aiming the massive bolt. He fought this thing for a month, this beast that did the siren’s bidding, a monster of the deep that she had created with her longing. And it had made a mockery of him.

Never again.

The Lance of Fury was lightning and when it pierced between the kraken’s tiny eyes with a flash of crackling red light, thunder echoed off the mountain and bounced off the walls.

Crystal erupted from its body, ripping it nearly in half. It writhed and melted as though dying but as Mydei flew to Phainon’s side it was already bubbling again, reforming.

“How amusing,” Mydei huffed, “is this to be a battle of immortals then?”

“Mydeimos, are you asking me to leave this to you?” Phainon asked, deep and annoyed. There was a wild flash in his eyes akin to offense and Mydei was almost angry that those words even crossed the man’s mind.

“How do you expect me to put an end to this creature without my other half by my side?” Crystal shards formed slowly from red glitter in the air, reforming another lance. Mydei snatched it as it finished and held it at his side with the point angled down and the shaft resting along his forearm.

“Your other half?” Phainon teased with a soft chuckle. The light lilt in his voice was back. Whatever had made Phainon quick to anger had hopefully passed. “Is this really the best time for romance?”

“HKS, perhaps I do not need you after all!”

“No, no, Mydei, I would be honored to share this victory with you.”

“Yes, you will be,” he agreed with a happy growl. Mydei’s tattoos rippled with light as crystalline dust swirled around him again. Phainon’s halo and wings shimmered, a faint glow matching the bright yellow of his eyes. Their red and gold was taunting, baiting, and those beady eyes shook with rage.

The kraken screeched as it reformed and wriggled after them, reaching as they darted through the air in opposite directions. Agile dashes brought them close to swipe at oily flesh, but every wound was repaired and Mydei felt the futility in their actions. It reminded him too much of a month of listening to the Tide song, of dying to this creature again and again.

The fear of failure bloomed in his belly like a wound that would not heal. He could hear matching frustration in every one of Phainon’s shouts as they collected severed limbs to no avail. The burning of his Coreflame’s power filled him with exhilaration and adrenaline and the joy of combat but it was sour in his mouth when he thought of his friends and family fighting on the beach. Every sound of Peucesta’s distant horn was a reminder that they were the only thing between this beast and the end of their world.

Phainon brushed past him, flying under Mydei’s paws as he was pursued by a reaching tentacle. Mydei dodged to the side and swiped his lance along its side, intercepting it moments before the ink could envelop Phainon. The rubbery flesh burst in a spray of black that peppered across them. Droplets landed on Mydei’s lips, and he raised a hand to wipe them away, tasting the bitter salt of seawater as he did.

The Worldbearer was beyond words now. Mydei could hear it in Phainon’s guttural growl, in the reckless way he swung his sword. It was on his face as he bore his teeth in a twisted grin speckled in the same black that dripped down his cheeks. Phainon had stopped caring about dodging and Mydei was spending more time watching his boyfriend’s back and staying out of the way than fighting the monster.

Their synergy was waning. He was dancing a waltz with a man that was trying to step on his toes. The flow that he had come to love standing side by side with Phainon was stilted, jarring, and awkward, until the fight stopped feeling like dance and warped instead into disjointed snapshots.

Maybe Phainon should have left this fight to Mydei… or maybe he shouldn’t have come at all. The longer they fought the more Mydei could see and feel it: the sour and corrupting rage of revenge. But who was Mydei to deny a man his chance at vengeance, when Mydei had personally exacted his own revenge on the man that killed his mother.

Oh. He left the ring in his pocket…

A tentacle came flying out of Mydei’s blind spot and he was thrown down into the city, barreling through walls as his wings spun to protect him from the worst of the impact. His body skipped across a city square before sliding across sharp coral to stop against a crumbling wall. Debris rained on him, leaving him feeling more annoyed than pained.

Gold spread across his fur and ran over his armor in rivulets, Mydei’s vision was blurry, but he could see the shine of it when he tried to move. He hit his head when he fell and there was a worrisome warmth spilling over his cheek. Paws kicked aimlessly, stretching, testing his limbs and finding them sore. Nothing felt broken, but when Mydei tried to stand again, his knees buckled and the world spun. He leaned heavily on his lance and took a couple deep breaths.

He could hear Phainon fighting still and wondered if the man had even noticed Mydei go down with his tunnel-vision as narrow as it seemed to be. That fear of failure that had made a home in Mydei’s belly started to grow, wrapping around his throat like vines.

This fight was different.

He knew the moment they committed to the plan and the truth of it pumped through his veins even now. This was the battle that would determine the fate of the world, but more than that, it was the monster under the bed. This was the creature that killed Phainon’s parents, the one that corrupted Eurypon, the one that took their homes from them.

…and the one that was taking Mydei’s partner from him before his very eyes.

Mydei forced himself to take a step forward, shook his head to clear the blood from his brow, and then the weight of a tidal wave slammed down on him again. He clawed and fought at the tentacle that wrapped around him, dragging him back across the cracked and broken ground. The Lance was pinned to his side, crystal erupted from his body, but the kraken would not let him go.

Gold flashed in the corner of his eye where Phainon was still fighting, oblivious.

That wild, crazed, gleeful look on Phainon’s face faltered when he finally noticed Mydei in the monster’s clutches. Realization spread across his features and then the beak slammed closed, and Mydei was surrounded by darkness.

Perhaps he should have been more concerned about having been consumed by a monster of the deep. A dark part of him chuckled that finally, after all these years, something in the water finally got him. But as water filled his lungs, and blackness stole his vision, the thing Mydei noticed the most was the quiet.

chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

No new CW, please note the ones that are already there. There's some graphic imagery in this chapter.

Phainon and Mydei fight the Black Tide Kraken.

Chapter Notes

I am deeply, deeply sorry this chapter was so delayed. The Ao3 curse came for me in a good way and I found out last December that I am pregnant! It's something I've wanted for a long time so I'm very excited but, unfortunately, that came at the cost of my physical ability to write the way I'm used to. I've spent the last few months resting and sort of retraining myself to write differently but just as effectively while also honing my craft, learning new punctuation, and just growing as a writer overall with the help of the Fanfic Writer's Group on Discord. I'm even hoping to clean this fic up and improve on earlier chapters as well! Some chapters have already been edited for grammar and I'm working on expanding some earlier scenes to make the story that much more seamless!

If you are also a hobby writer and seeking ways to improve, get feedback, offer feedback, and grow in a critical but friendly environment, I can't recommend this group enough: Link It is because of them and their support that this story can continue at a quality worthy of my wonderful readers! (Please be advised this is a multi-fandom, multi-ship, 18+ only environment for collaborative writers looking to workshop. If you are particularly sensitive to some themes/ships/etc, please take into account your own comfort before joining!)

I'm genuinely so excited to share the rest of this story with you all, even if it's just going to take a little longer between updates while I go through this relearning process!

Every time the kraken screamed, Phainon let the shiver of satisfaction gild the raw hatred that burned in his soul. It was the only other thing he let himself feel as he tore at the gelatinous mass with his sword and wings. Every haunting memory, every buried emotion from before this singular moment was an afterthought, waiting for the wildfire to run its course to be heard once more.

He didn’t want to feel those things. Phainon didn’t want the weight of grief, he didn’t want that fear, that desperation, that loss… hatred burned brighter than all of it.

Laid upon the pyre one by one, those feelings cracked and melted until his blood was boiling and his bones were smelting into steel. The biting cold of the ocean floor was little more than morning frost cowering in the sunlight of his ardor. And he eagerly fed the flame with wild glee.

Phainon was a predator turned loose upon his captor, a monster unleashed and adorned with broken chains – wholly divine. The coreflame in his chest burned with such immense radiance it filled Phainon to the brim with invincible confidence. So, when the kraken screamed and its limbs burst to pelt its inky blood across his face, Phainon bathed in it as an offering from a lesser being.

How dare this creature look upon his glory? How dare it consider itself on equal footing with his godhood? His was the power to command the heavens! To cradle the world with the sole responsibility of seeing it thrive, or should he decide, to see it ended with little more than a whimsical thought.

Such was Phainon’s elation as he laughed and basked in combat with this creature of the deep; as he teased and tortured the monster of his nightmares. He ripped off its limbs and left lacerations in its sides for every time the Tide had made him feel weak. When it howled in pain and rage he danced in place and drank in the sounds as sweet music; a symphony of agony that was finally giving voice to the void that had hidden inside his heart to rot since the fall of Aedes Elysiae.

That joy danced with his hatred, intrinsically intertwined with perfect rhythm, in perfect time with every cry, screech, and laugh. Until a flash of red at the corner of Phainon’s eye gave him pause and left those twirling emotions knotted in a mess of misplaced steps and broken toes.

A recent, already frayed memory of thunder at the edge of his awareness, pleaded with Phainon to remember that his cacophonous solo of eager destruction was supposed to be a duet. There was a voice in the wind, drowned out by the crack of boiling marrow in burning bones. A wild and worried face at Phainon’s back was barely clinging to his recent recollection, all but obscured by smoke.

The harmony dutifully trying to be heard under Phainon’s roaring, suffocating melody was tossed aside in a spray of ocean crashing upon a rocky shore and flash of red and gold.

Phainon spun in the air as the kraken ceased its pursuit of him, turning instead to the one who was left behind in this deadly refrain. It splashed and crashed its way to where Strife struggled to free himself from the dust and rubble.

And when Phainon could finally see beyond himself again, the Inheritor of Strife was already trapped and thrashing in the tight seal of the monster’s grip. The length of the limb was wrapped so tightly around the divine body that he could not get free, even with all the strength of a god.

And before Phainon’s eyes, that noble creature, his only companion in this struggle at the end of the world, was gone. The kraken’s beak slammed closed and the warmth of Strife’s presence vanished with a crunch, dragging with it what remained of Phainon’s restraint.

The terror and loss that he had laid upon the fire stirred in the coals. Phainon’s breaths were labored, choking gasps. His lungs were struggling to keep up and tears flowed freely, already falling in anticipation of his realization.

All this power was not enough.

He was alone again.

And it was all his fault.

“Why did you…?” he breathed, the words ripping from his throat in a rasp. Not again.

The kraken beneath him was squirming, rippling happily, celebrating.

Why did you take them all away from me? The thought played In Phainon’s head on a loop, screaming from the ashes of his burning heart with accusation in every syllable.

He was trembling in the sky, barely aloft as though on thin strings.

Hatred burned hotter than guilt.

The strings snapped.

The air around Phainon warped with the heat. His tears evaporated, leaving behind dried tracks that stretched and cracked when he curled his lip back and shook with unbridled rage. The destructive power of the sun burned inside him with reckless abandon.

The ocean that still dribbled down the mountainside in happy rivulets turned to steam to hang in the air leaving it heavy with a midsummer’s humidity. Faceless statues perched on towers cracked and burst as the permeating cold was snatched away from them with brutality. Coral crumbled in the heatwave, seaweed turned as autumn leaves before simmering away into nothing, and grains of sand clung to each other until they could no longer be parted – turned to shining glass.

“Fine then,” he growled, uncaring if the kraken could hear or understand him.

It shied away from his heat, from the fire that once burned within now burning without. One limb hurried to shield its eyes, two others pawed at its own flesh, pressing with purpose at its being. The rest reached desperately for the ruins, clinging to a past long lost to the ocean, and the secrets she kept. The kraken fought for distance even as it struggled against a swelling in its body.

At last, it understands what vengeance it has wrought, Phainon considered, however briefly, before the fire became too great. His own flesh was burning, a sickly smell of ash and rot.

The edges of his feathers were alight with the creeping red of a steady flame. They glowed with the orange of a sunset when he surged in pursuit of this embodiment of corruption. Every attempt to stave off his dive met searing winds and burning swipes of his blade, cleaving through every limb until the tip of his sword plunged deep between the kraken’s eyes.

The flesh beneath his feet boiled as he clung to the blade, pressing it deeper between angry snarls until only the hilt remained unburied; until Phainon wondered if he might go deaf from the screeching cries; until Phainon was certain he could not be removed no matter how hard the beast threw itself against crumbling buildings.

Salty steam burned away his feathers and seared his skin but still Phainon held tightly.

This is the end. This was always going to be the end for you and me.

“Come then, monster of the deep,” he crooned, low and angry. “Let us burn together.”

----

The inside of the kraken greeted Mydei with violent turmoil and a cold shock that sent needles rippling down his body. An ache that stuck to his soul as the beak locked shut with a tooth-aching grind and the undertow dragged him deep into the monster’s abyssal belly, thrashing and fighting the whole way.

Is this really happening?

He felt so small; tossed about like a doll in a hurricane. How long had it been since he last drowned?

What do I do? Mydei’s own voice inside his head sounded so young.

The panic tightened around his heart as past memories collided with present panic.

I need to get out!

He desperately fought to reach above his head, searching for the surface as he was dragged through the dark and away from all sense of direction. Mydei’s chest tightened around that final breath. Tears joined the salt of the sea. He closed his eyes tight to hide from the familiarity that sobbed in a toddler’s voice.

Not again… please not again...

The maelstrom stilled then, leaving him adrift in nothingness, at the mercy of the frigidity of the Northern seas and his own instinctual panic. Freed from the undertow, he curled up tight and covered his mouth and nose with both hands. He was afraid to open his eyes. He was afraid of losing his breath even more.

I spent my childhood drowning.

The weight of the ocean was bearing down on him from all sides. His paws – spread wide in the water – scooped helplessly in the black, searching for an equilibrium that no longer seemed to exist. Mydei was keenly aware of the seizing in his muscles as crippling cold seeped deep, reaching for the marrow in his bones.

The nightmares still linger and there are times when I feel fear looking into the heart of the black ocean.

Every joint stiffened; there was burning in his lungs, bitterness on his tongue, and new wounds stung as they tore further at the seams. Every movement exaggerated, every desperate pull in slow motion as these precious few seconds stretched into a painful perception of infinity replete with remembered words and sorrows.

None of it compared to the terror consuming his insides.

I have embraced that part of me and learned how to let it go.

Was that another lie he had told Phainon? Images of him flashed behind Mydei’s eyes at the thought.

Not this Worldbearer that Phainon had embraced, living only to rejoice in violence against the Tide. The creature that was now face to face with his demons had become a living sun, wrathfully burning and infinitely distant.

He considered instead the man from this morning: the Phainon that held such faith and love for him, who was patient, kind, and so very strong. Mydei remembered his Deliverer’s lips on his own, of strong hands on his waist, his back, and his chest. For a moment he could imagine their warmth chasing away the biting cold.

It wasn’t a lie when Mydei called Phainon his strength, his equal in everything.

He was fire and fury turned inwards, Mydeimos.

Phainon needed him. This could not be the end.

Mydei’s final breath held tight. His lungs were remembering what it was like to make the most of every second, to recover quickly in the water, to maybe reach the surface this time. The moment trapped in eternity passed and less than a minute since Mydei was swallowed, he had been lost and found himself again.

With newfound resolve he slowly opened his eyes, squinting around the salty, icy bite. Every blink brought about more clarity in the dark as he searched for the absent horizon.

He had expected a proper belly and discovered only ocean, as open and seemingly endless as the sky. And perhaps no less beautiful. The dark that had been all-consuming when first he chanced a look was not so complete on a second inspection. There were stars in the water: glimmers that caught a dim and distant light and scattered it into every color.

The glow of his tattoos flashed as he reached for crystal and the stars reflected red, lighting the water enough to see the gold of his blood swirl and dilute around him before gently drifting by on a gentle current. The brightness in the gloomy tomb overpowered what light already lived here, and it took another few blinks in the dark to see it again after his own brilliance faded. It was gentle and warm, reaching across the distance like sunbeams through layered silk.

A burn was nibbling at the edges of Mydei’s lungs in solemn reminder of his looming demise, but the memory of a twice-made promise steeled his nerves. Even with his experience, there was no more time to waste on despair and even less to spend on further hesitation.

His paws scooped at the water as he swam, wings pressed tightly against his back to minimize the drag. The hint of warmth that drifted through the silence clung to the current to beckon Mydei upstream into warmer waters.

Aside from the occasional sway in the sea and the steadily increasing burn in his lungs, Mydei’s swim was shockingly peaceful. The cold fled with every stroke, the bright flecks in the black still twinkled invitingly, and it was quiet.

The storybook spoke of voices projected over the water to reach beyond the reefs and shoals that surrounded rocky lairs. Mydei had thought for sure that this close to Hysilens the siren’s song would have carried unfiltered from her own lips. But here in the black of the belly, he couldn’t hear any melody at all. Not the alluring dirge of a grieving Demigod nor the screams and raucous percussion of war song.

The edges of his vision were starting to blur alongside the warning churn of that held breath as Mydei finally pushed closer to the light. These waters more akin to a tropical clime – warm like the comforting kindle of a heartbeat. That glow in the darkness was a horizon at sunset, the coals of a well-loved oven, filling the water with a pleasant tingle that reminded Mydei of a passionate, desperate kiss.

Filtered through a protective mesh of Tide fog was the source of the light: the heart of the monster. Gold as blood, the light seeped through gaps in the ink that swirled around the silhouette of a woman. She was curled like a troubled infant around the brightness of a coreflame, selfishly close, knees and elbows pulled in tight to her chest to keep out the world.

Mydei called to hand the Lance of Fury and with it tore at the inky membrane that kept her apart. The Tide retreated. The water stirred. Her hair, as long as she was tall, swirled around her as she tilted her chin to glare beyond him with narrow, pale eyes. They were darting back and forth in rapid twitches, focused on something outside his own senses. Her delicate fingers tipped with sharp claws clasped the Coreflame tightly, the sigil of Law bright and taunting at its core.

He treaded closer and when she still failed to notice him he reached for it.

Bubbles escaped Mydei’s lips as his lungs seized, out of time, begging for breath, and urgency turned his surgical maneuver into a frantic scramble. The Coreflame flared brighter when his fingertips brushed its surface and then the siren came back to herself.

Claws dragged through the flesh of his arm and blood clouded the water between them. It tasted of iron and salt when he gasped, losing what was left of his air as water surged through his throat and chest. The ache of it spurred Mydei to reckless action, an instinct screaming at him to find another breath, and if he could not, to die quickly and spare himself further agony.

She had the advantage in the water, but the reach of Mydei’s lance still cleaved through her flesh when he swiped in a broad arc. Her golden blood joined his to stream in elegant, glittering ribbons from their bodies that danced in the Coreflame’s light.

Imperator Cerydra’s heart, knocked free, waited between them. It didn’t try to float away. It didn’t sink. It simply waited to be reclaimed by whomever was bold enough, strong enough to reach out and take it.

For a moment they looked at each other – a furious, lonely siren, and a drowning lion, two gods recognizing each other’s power in the dark. And then she screamed and the sound ripped through the water with such violence that Mydei scrambled to cover his ears. He felt the vibrations through the choking in his chest, in every nerve and reflex. It was paralyzing and exhilarating all at once and he thought, yes, this was a worthy first death, one that he would repay in kind soon, when he revived.

But before his soul could slip away, still begging for a breath, the ocean boiled.

Mydei wished he had perished sooner.

He thrashed in the sudden violence of the bubbling water. Every nerve was alight and all was white-hot pain. The wounds on Mydei’s arm, his lungs full to bursting, nothing else mattered in the moment than this all-consuming torture. In his blurring vision he watched the skin on his hand and arm starting to scald before blinding sunlight and a surging torrent ripped him away from any remaining sense of reality. He was a leaf in a storm, a grain of sand in a whirlpool, utterly at the mercy of divine intervention that exceeded his own.

Mydei wrapped himself in crystal, fighting the pain of his bubbling skin and melting wings as the kraken evaporated at the feet of an immense and horrible power. Hot and dry air coursed over him and dimly he considered the good fortune of having found a chance to breathe. But that thought was shattered against the reef alongside his body as he fell unceremoniously into the broken city.

----

The eruption of the kraken was loud, brutal, and short. Its body ruptured with an explosive sound that rippled through the city’s bones and could be seen racing up the surrounding ocean walls like a wave. For a moment the air shook and the tumultuous ocean around them quivered like it may collapse but Phainon found he didn’t care. He could barely remember how he got to the ocean floor in the first place.

The steam seared his skin and wings. Pieces of him were crumbling into dust as the kraken’s body ceased to be, leaving behind two bodies to crash into the earth below. Covered in pale white steam it was impossible to tell which one was the siren and as Phainon considered his gentle descent the bright light of a Coreflame made the decision for him.

It glittered brightly. A bright coal in the ash of a once roaring flame, it bounced into the middle of the massive square and came to rest in the basin of a now dry fountain.

Phainon’s divinity was spent for the time being when he touched lightly on the ground, fatigued for the first time since the fight began. Sweat dripped off his nose, and he had to lean on his sword like a cane for support while shaky legs found their footing and lungs found oxygen in the humidity. His wings were gone. They crumbled away as ash after delivering him to safety on uneven ground. The Coreflame still beat in his chest, but it was quieter, resting in a gentle smolder after returning him to humanity, healed and whole.

Once glorious tile crunched underfoot. He didn’t care. The coreflame was a star in the dark and as surely as it reached for him, it would undoubtedly reach for that damned siren.

On either side, at opposing ends of the square, the dust was starting to settle where the core of the kraken had fallen. One of the falling bodies had ripped through a building, tearing off the façade in the process. The other had punched a hole in a thick curtain wall lining one side of the plaza.

Phainon’s eyes darted between each smoking impact as he started stalking towards the coreflame. He let Dawnmaker drag across the ground at his side with a sparking, screeching grind. One of those shadows would surely lunge for his throat once she recovered.

Let her come.

But the moment that stole his breath wasn’t the image of a raging siren come to reclaim a heart, it was part of his own, laying still on the stone in a mangled mess. Ice poured over Phainon in that moment. All else forgotten before he could reach his original destination.

The dust had settled, the steam dissipated, and all that was left behind was a very human Mydeimos, crumpled over a pile of shattered bricks to rest in part in a puddle of his own muddy blood. If not for his hair and clothes he may not have been recognizable at all as brutalized and twisted as his body was.

“Mydei?” Phainon mumbled in a pained whisper, rife with denial.

Mydei was going to get up.

He had to get up…

Why wasn’t he moving? They promised each other he’d take his lives more seriously!

The other body stirred in the corner of Phainon’s eye, struggling weakly behind a curtain of lingering haze to get to its feet but Phainon couldn’t look away from Mydei.

He almost tripped in the first few stumbling steps in Mydei’s direction over broken stone. The body was shiny and glittering. Blood was dripping from Mydei’s fingertips. His legs were twisted and elevated against the crumpled wall he had landed on.

A little closer, still no movement. “Mydeimos? This isn’t funny anymore!”

Mydei was facing the sky, his shoulders and head on flat ground, and one arm trapped in debris and twisted unnaturally to reach for something beyond himself. The other lay across the same ground beneath Phainon’s feet. An earring gleamed in the gore.

A little more recognition and understanding. And so much more panic.

“Mydei!” The call echoed through the plaza, playing back the urgency – the fear – in a voice that Phainon didn’t recognize immediately as his own. It was a horrible rasp, a broken cry for a broken place. “No no nononono…”

Tears pricked the corner of his wide eyes as Phainon dropped Dawnmaker with a clatter that could wake the dead. The echo covered the sound of Phainon’s heavy footsteps as he hurried to Mydei’s side.

Exhaustion pleaded with Phainon to stop. The adrenaline was wearing away without that inner fire to fuel it, but he still reached for Mydei’s shoulders and took him under the arms to drag him from the rocks.

Mydei’s corpse was little more than a finely dressed amalgamation of lacerations and burns. The smell of cooked flesh made Phainon’s stomach turn and when he pulled his hands away from Mydei’s body and found sticky skin clinging to his trembling palms he had to turn away to collapse, sob, and retch over the crumbled debris.

Blood turned bronze by dust and sand spattered his sleeves and pants when Phainon wiped the sick from his mouth. Bitterness still stuck to his tongue when he crawled on hands and knees back to Mydei’s side to shakily reach for his love’s face. There was no life in those amber eyes. He wasn’t breathing. Neither of them were now.

This was so much worse than finding Mydei bruised and broken at Castrum Kremnos, and Phainon’s seizing heart tightened at the memory. Salt burned his cheeks as tears flowed freely to drip from his chin to fall on Mydei’s neck and chest. Already the body was repairing itself. New, clean skin was visibly spreading, hastened by the Coreflame of Strife. But Phainon had already seared this horror to memory.

“Come back to me,” he whispered in a raw voice while tracing the lines of Mydei’s cheek and jaw.

With reverent caution, Phainon reached for Mydei again to pull the body into his lap, to cradle Mydei’s head on his arm like a babe while the flesh knit back together. His bones crunched as they realigned and Phainon winced at the sound and held him tighter.

He wanted to mumble words of encouragement, to ease Mydei’s return, but Phainon was still quivering. There was a knot in his throat and an emotional exhaustion caught between mournful grief and that smoldering, still burning hatred. They stole his words and left him with nothing else but hot tears, raspy sobs, and shallow breaths.

These were burns. Mydei had burned to death. His broken bones from the fall were healing faster than the regrowth of new skin, the damage was so severe. Strife’s immortality had to consider the new map of Mydei’s body carefully, stretching over exposed, red and gold musculature.

These were burns.

Phainon felt an anxious realization bubble low in his chest – a half-formed worry. Did he…?

The thought evaporated when Mydei gasped and coughed, spewing seawater across the stonework as he came back to life. For a second Mydei struggled against Phainon’s hold but a moment of recognition turned resistance into relief and both of those strong arms wrapped tightly around whatever of Phainon they could reach. They held him close with tentative strength while he buried his face in Phainon’s belly.

“Titans,” Mydei wheezed, “you’re alright.”

He smiled and hiccupped in response.

Phainon’s hands pulled at renewed flesh, grasped at Mydei’s clothes, changing every other second. It wasn’t enough. Phainon needed to hold all of him at once!

Mydei’s hand on his chest put an end to that thought. Even shaky and weakened, he pushed Phainon back and reclaimed his autonomy to sit up with some help. Unwilling to let him go entirely just yet, Phainon kept a hand on his back, possessively covering Mydei’s weak spot with his palm.

Mydei looked so tired still. Red patches on his body were still healing; the smell of burning flesh still lingered in the air beside the tart metallic bite of blood. He shook under Phainon’s hand, a not-so-subtle quiver that betrayed his exhaustion. Not that Phainon couldn’t see it in his eyes as Mydei studied his own hand for a few seconds before rubbing his face.

It was a relief to see, to remember Mydei’s immortality, but still… Phainon didn’t want to forget what Mydei looked like with saltwater trickling from his lips, skin melted down to bone, flesh bubbled and red. The longer Phainon studied the healing horrors still marring Mydei’s body the more the tug in his chest pushed and pulled between a guilt he didn’t quite understand and a vengeance he knew more intimately.

Hatred burned hotter than guilt.

Rage that had been sated was already rising again and the shadow of fearful grief was waning under the rekindled hatred in Phainon’s heart. It beat along his veins, eager to consume, to be bestial, as Mydei had once invited him to be.

Give in to that primal desire, the purest form of Strife and fight with intent to kill.

Phainon pulled his hand away from Mydei to dig his fingers into his own thigh instead and shot a glance across the square.

She was hurt, even from a distance, that much was obvious. The way she half-limped, half-dragged herself. The way she reached across her body to hold tightly to her arm. The way she slouched and stumbled and sparkled gold in the dimming light. All of it spoke to her state of being.

Phainon’s insides were coiling tight as he watched her scramble for the fountain and throw herself at the basin wall. She lingered there, slouched against the stonework, and slowly lifted her eyes to look at them with thinly veiled fury. How misleadingly frail she looked – this monster from under the bed – slumped with a long, bloody line carved down the length of her chest.

Here was the source of the creeping evil in this world. It was her song that stole from him a homeland, a family, and a future. Her will that destroyed the Grove and countless other city-states. This creature’s borrowed ambition that destroyed the Sol and his comrades, that corrupted Eurypon and sent an infant Mydei to the Sea of Souls. The destruction of the Kremnoan people, the orphaning of Chironome, countless losses that haunted Phainon…

It was her fault that Mydei had died again with such abhorrent brutality.

“Deliverer?” Mydei called but that voice was so distant already.

The breath that Phainon sucked through his teeth tasted of salt and blood. He held it tightly for a long moment before letting it go. His heart still pounded in his ears and red was creeping into the corners of his vision.

“She did this to you,” Phainon whispered low, dripping with vitriol and hate. Phainon’s heart hardened and a growl caught in his throat.

Finally, he could see the true face of his demons.

Finally, he could end it.

He could be free.

Mydei grabbed his coat as Phainon got to his feet. He could feel the tug holding him back but his eyes were locked on the siren.

“Phainon!”

Phainon wasn’t listening. All he could see was this perfectly presented opportunity.

Hysilens was beautiful and surreal. When she pulled herself over the fountain’s edge it was with a sort of primordial grace that belonged only to ancient seas. Black hair as long as she was tall fell around her face and shoulders, contrasting with the paleness of her skin and the indigo of her scales. Her tattered dress with bits of shell and coral strung through the fabric flowed around her like fins when she rose again from the basin with the Coreflame of Law wrapped in her arms.

“Phainon, come back to me!” Mydei shouted. But before the echo of his call could fade away, Hysilens darted, and like a starving predator, Phainon launched himself after her.

The tearing of his coat slowed Phainon down when Mydei tried and failed to leash him. Off balance, Phainon stumbled and Hysilens took her lead, but he was quick to recover and the ache in his legs became a minor, ignorable inconvenience.

Even burdened by injury and the Coreflame held tightly to her chest, Hysilens moved with ethereal elegance more akin to swimming rather than running. She glided across the square with barely a pause, driven by the same inhuman endurance that pushed Phainon to ignore his own limitations.

He darted for his sword first and barely slowed down to retrieve it. The weight of the blade in his hand was a comfort in the same way Phainon imagined a wolf valued its teeth. And what better way to imagine himself as he hunted weakened prey with single-minded ferocity.

“Phainon, stop!”

How dare you ask that of me! Phainon thought in a snarl. After everything she’s done to you!

But he didn’t have the breath to waste on words. Mydei’s voice was already becoming an afterthought, an echo among the dead, no more than a ghost to shrug aside.

The tails of her dress were beaded, Phainon realized as he gained on her. The ornaments looked like bones crawling all the way up to where her dress stopped at her lower back. He could see the pale of sodden flesh when her hair swayed with a stumble on a fractured staircase at the far side of the square. She was hurrying into the city. Perhaps to hide. It wouldn’t matter. Blood still dripped from her body to spatter on the stones.

By the time Phainon had surged up the stairs himself, she had vanished from his sight. It bought her precious seconds as he paused to follow her bloody footprints with his eyes.

“Not like this!” Mydei snarled behind him, much closer now, and Phainon was suddenly very aware of the warrior at his back, keeping pace.

This voyage is so much bigger than all of us and I think I’m afra-

Phainon snarled away his own words in his head.

Hatred burned hotter than fear.

He surged forward, tracking the siren with urgent desperation. He needed this. They all needed this!

Mydei’s calls stayed on his tail, but they were easy to ignore as he raced between buildings and up a mountain path until he finally caught sight of her again on the mountainside. Hysilens stumbled on the paved road ahead. And then she disappeared through one of several archways into a dark, gaping maw in the cliffside.

Soon.

It was just below the turn in the path that Phainon, single-minded and itching to seize this victory, was brought low. A weight hurtled into his back and dragged him down the slope a ways by a tight grip around his waist. He spun with Dawnmaker, but Mydei caught the blade with his gauntlet and held tightly.

Neither of them moved while they caught their breath, still bound in a tense clash while Phainon came back to himself. It took so much effort to will the tension in his arms to relax, to ease the pressure he was forcing through Dawnmaker’s grip, and only then did Mydei let go to grab for him instead. The claws of shining gauntlets curled around the strap that crossed Phainon’s chest, holding him still in conjunction with his wary gaze.

“Breathe,” Mydei ordered and Phainon thought that was a ridiculous order at first. But then he shuddered and trembled through a breath too long held and every muscle in his body made itself known. Phainon was coiled so tightly he was visibly shaking. His jaw was clenched so tight his teeth hurt and the breath that stuck in his throat burned with salt and ash.

Mydei was struggling too. He panted softly with a subtle wheeze on every inhale. There were still patches of skin on his chest and arms that were red and raw. The image of Mydei broken and melting flashed fresh in Phainon’s memory.

“She has to die,” Phainon hissed and he did not recognize his own voice.

Mydei’s brows were pinched with concern and Phainon felt like a bug pinned under glass, studied, analyzed, judged… but Mydei let go anyway. “For the right reasons, Phainon.”

He laughed through a scoff, a single bark, and then turned his rage towards Mydei to snap, “I have every reason.”

Phainon didn’t wait for Mydei to respond; he stomped up the path, relieved that the pleas had stopped. And equally relieved that Mydei’s footsteps still crunched behind him.

He’d understand later. Mydei would understand when this was all over, when Phainon was free of this darkness that chewed on his insides, had suffocated the fire that had been burning him from within. They could go back to being happy – a real happiness – when he was free.

When he could finally say those impossible words to himself.

Phainon stepped through the archway with more caution and control than before, sword at the ready, Mydei at his back. He blinked in the darkness until his eyes adjusted and the faint trickles of light that filtered from above and from the entry filled the shadows with definition.

The cave was not very deep, but it was surprisingly clean and well-kept. Circular in shape it was simple and refined with a tall ceiling and few features. Perhaps once an artist dreamed of filling the room with statues and accolades but the arches and pillars that lined the walls framed nothing at all. The only defining anything of note was a stone sarcophagus, plain, simple, and standing in the middle of the room with its lid askew.

Hysilens was there, surrounded by a neat pile of clean bones, immaculately arranged. She knelt among them with her back to the entryway and the glow of the coreflame held tightly to her chest. The light of it was a warm wash in a cold place, leaving streaks of gold on polished columns and catching on the blood soaked into the siren’s dress.

Their shadows fell upon her, and she twisted in place enough to glare at them while tears streamed freely down her cheeks from pale blue and lavender eyes. Her claws tightened around the edges of the Coreflame of Law, held high enough to tuck under her chin; held tight enough to smear her blood across its holy surface.

Phainon’s blood boiled at the display of desecration and his grip on Dawnmaker tightened until it hurt. He leaned forward to take a step but Mydei’s hand on his shoulder stopped him. The light squeeze was grounding enough to clear some of the fog, enough to really see this woman waiting for them in a tomb.

Mydei stepped up beside him and Phainon heard him take a breath to speak but Hysilens’ mouth curled in a knowing smile before the words could form. A golden glow was burning in her chest; rays of light filtered through translucent skin backlighting her ribs like a creature of the deep. The Coreflame of Ocean burned bright and Phainon’s instincts howled.

He lunged past Mydei, raising Dawnmaker, but before he could finish his swing, the siren opened her mouth and began to sing.
